units.la: Postquam de scripto à Domino Ludovico Wolzogio, Ecclesiæ Walonicæ apud Ultrajectinos Pastore, & Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ in Academia Professore, adversus Paradoxum Exercitatorem edendo, rumor ad nos delatus erat, maximum ejus me tenebat desiderium. Sperabam enim fore, ut communem causam rite defenderet, labemque, in Seniore Velthusio, Ecclesiæ Walonicæ adspersam, Pastor omnem abstergeret. Etenim & in ea me opinione diu fuisse fateor, scriptum illud Paradoxum Velthusio deberi, extabant etiam, præter communem famam, quæ probabilem hanc conjecturam reddebant, alia ejusdem viri, non multò melioris notæ, non pauca monumenta: deceptus tamen in eo fui, juxta cum plurimis. Non modo non Auctorem se, seu libri, seu editionis ejus, sed ne dicto quidem ullo, factove Adjutorem extitisse, quippe sanctè religioso jurejurando ipse affirmavit. Quod utinam de multis aliis libellis dicere eidem liceret! Nihil etiam erat hactenus, quod me admodum male, de Wolzogii erga orthodoxiam studio, sentire jusserat. Imo meliora de ipso subinde testantes diversæ sortis homines audiveram. Ut præjudiciis occupatus adversus ipsius labores non fuerim, verum de eruditione potius, & elo-quentia Wolzogiana optima quæque mihi fuerim pollicitus, præsertim cum discipulus audiret Viri celeberrimi, qui tot tantaque, orthodoxias suæ, in hisce controversiis, dedit specimina. Legi itaque, & avidissimè legi scriptum hocce Wolzogianum, at, quod dissimulare non possum, statim multa, quæ offendiculo bonis fore videbantur, offendebam. Primum erat magnus nimis & fervidus pro Velthusio ejusque nomine & honore zelus: qui eò ipsum abegit, ut virum istum, publico orthodoxias & innocentiæ Testimonio decorare non erubuerit, quin magis serio Velthusii, quam cunctorum simul Reformatorum causam egerit, ac defenderit; non sine acri, sed à Remonstrantibus & Libertinis jam usu contrito, dicterio, in illos, quos novit Velthusio & omnibus mundanis, jugum Christi & disciplinam non ferentibus, ob falso impactam animi superstitionem & animarum tyrannidem, exosos esse. At multorum errorum jam dudum Professorem esse Velthusium, ac proinde ejusdem cum ipso heterodoxias suspicionem, apud omnes, sese incursurum, novisse debuerat vir alias satis perspicax. Neque enim non novisse poterat, aut debebat, quæ tot in locis scripserat vir intimæ cum ipso consuetudinis. Ego saltem, statim ac istam Velthusii innocentiam & orthodoxias tenacem animum, a Wolzogio tantopere prædicatum vidi, de nimio inter ipsos in errore consensu, cogitandum esse, necesse judicavi. Nec me fefellit ista cogitatio, sæpissime enim utriusque collationem utilissimam deprehen-di: di: dum quæ minus aperté dixerat Wolzogius, ea magis explicatè à Velthusio dicta reperiebam. Quem agendi modum minus justum dicere non poterit Wolzogius, qui tanto orthodoxiæ Velthusianæ elogio, probasse censeri debet & sua fecisse, quæ scripserat Velthusius, quorum si ignarus fuerit, maximæ levitatis reus est. Scriptis demonstratæ ac publicè notæ heterodoxiæ crimen, Velthusio communis fama impegerat, ab ea, apud Clarissimum Arnoldum, eum purgat Wolzogius, & sic, scripta respiciens, veri-tatis orthodoxæ tenacem ipsi adscribit animum & in omni genere doctrinæ singularem eruditionem. Res ipsa etiam, quam uterque, libellis ad-versus Paradoxum conscriptis, tractat, idem non patitur solum, sed sua quadam indole nexuque poscit & requirit. Ex. gr. Lumen infusum negat Wolzogius, ut suo loco notatum est, refutat multis Velthusius. Quid ve-tat ex Velthusio, tantopere ipsi laudato, judicare de sensu Wolzogii, quem exprimit quidem, verum non ita fusè pertractat, quam factum à Velthusio. Idem in negotio de Scripturæ objectiva seu absoluta perspicuitate à me lectori videre dabitur Lib. II. pag. 110.
units.tr: After word reached us of the writing that Lodewijk Wolzogen, minister of the Walloon Church among the people of Utrecht and professor of ecclesiastical history in the Academy, was publishing against the Paradoxical Exerciser, my desire for it was very great. I hoped he would properly defend the common cause, and that the minister would wipe away the stain cast upon the Walloon Church by the elder Velthuysen. Indeed, I confess I had long been of the opinion that the Paradoxical writing was owed to Velthuysen. Besides common report, which made this a probable conjecture, there were also not a few records of the same man, not of much better repute, that lent weight to it. I was deceived in this, however, along with very many others. He not only did not show himself the author of the book or of its edition, nor an assistant in any word or deed, but he affirmed this under a solemn, religious oath, he himself affirmed. Would that he could say the same of many other little books! Until now nothing had led me to think very badly of Wolzogen's zeal for orthodoxy. Indeed, people of various sorts had from time to time borne better witness of him to me. I was not prejudiced against his labours; rather, I had promised myself the best from Wolzogen's learning and eloquence, especially since I heard he was a disciple of a most celebrated man, who had given so many and such great proofs of his orthodoxy in these controversies. So I read, and read most eagerly, this Wolzogian writing; but, as I cannot conceal, I at once stumbled over many things that seemed likely to give offence to good men. The first was a zeal too great and too fervent for Velthuysen and for his name and honour. It led him so far that he did not blush to adorn that man with a public testimony of orthodoxy and innocence. He pleaded and defended the cause of Velthuysen more earnestly than that of all the Reformed together, and not without a sharp taunt, though one already worn thin by use among the Remonstrants and Libertines, against those whom he knows Velthuysen and all worldly men, who do not bear Christ's yoke and discipline, hate because of the superstition of mind and tyranny over souls falsely charged against them. But a man otherwise quite perceptive ought to have known that Velthuysen had long been a professor of many errors, and that he would therefore bring upon himself, in everyone's eyes, the suspicion of heterodoxy together with him. For he could not have failed to know, or ought not to have failed to know, what Velthuysen had written in so many places, being a man of most intimate acquaintance with him. I, at least, as soon as I saw that Velthuysen's innocence and a mind tenacious of orthodoxy had been so loudly proclaimed by Wolzogen, judged it necessary to reflect on the excessive agreement between the two in error. Nor did that reflection deceive me, for very often I found a most useful comparison between them: where Wolzogen had said less openly, I found the same things stated more explicitly by Velthuysen. Wolzogen cannot call this way of proceeding unjust. By such praise of Velthuysen's orthodoxy he ought to be considered to have approved and made his own what Velthuysen wrote; if he was ignorant of it, he is guilty of the greatest carelessness. The charge of heterodoxy, shown by writings and publicly known, common report had fastened upon Velthuysen. Wolzogen clears him of it by an appeal to the most illustrious Arnold, and so, looking to his writings, ascribes to him a mind tenacious of orthodox truth and a singular learning in every kind of doctrine. The very subject which each treats in the books written against the Paradoxical not only permits this comparison but by its own nature and connection demands and requires it. For example, Wolzogen denies infused light, as noted in its place, and Velthuysen refutes it at length. What prevents us from judging Wolzogen's sense from Velthuysen, so greatly praised by him? Wolzogen indeed expresses it, but does not treat it as fully as Velthuysen did. The same matter, the objective or absolute perspicuity of Scripture, the reader will be able to see from me in Book II, p. 110.

units.la: E re ipsi erat, non ita palam, non ita liberè, subinde reserare & revelare quæ sentiebat, cum magis impunè à Velthusio idem perficeretur. Serò quidem nimis editus forsan dici posset, de usu rationis in Theologia, à Velt-husio tractatus, quam ut inde de ejus sensu certus esse potuerit noster, sed, præterquam quod ex intima inter illos consuetudine jam dudum illa didicisse credi potest, variis in locis alibi similia dixerat Velthusius, ut obscurum esse non potuerit, hanc ipsi sententiam esse, quam nunc ab ipso palam & prolixè propositam videmus. Quod si autem hanc sequelam evitare voluisset Wolzogius, idem encomium iterata sui tractatus editione iterum ponere, quin, aliis in locis, auctius circumferre non debuisset. Atque sic causam videt lector, quare hosce duum viros subinde conjunxerim & unum ex altero explicuerim. Equidem affectui erga Velthusium Wolzogiano ista elogia imputari possunt, verum etiam de unius sententia, aliquatenus saltem, ex alterius scripta recte judicari, sententiarum jubet convenientia. Secundum, quod itidem omnibus, quibus decessorum veneratio non plane excidit, non displicere non potest, vanitas illa est, qua omnes solus ut superasse videri posset, summorum virorum labores magno probro afficit & vituperio. Non nego profectum dari posse, quin in id omni studio incumbendum puto, ut aliorum inventis bene perceptis aliquid addatur, atque ita in veritatis investigatione semper eatur ulterius, hoc enim modo prioribus suus non eripitur, sed constat honos, qui apprimè curandus est successoribus. Sic autem corrupta nunc ferunt tempora, sic mores corruptissimi, ut nihil laude habeatur dignum, nisi quod sua se novitate commendet. Hinc contemtos videas spretosque immensi pretii labores & operas, librosque fere omnes studiosorum manibus ereptos, ut novum videatur, & à nostri seculi hominibus inventum, quicquid accuratiorem sapit rerum cognitionem, scilicet minutis ingeniis, ex nostri Velthusii judicio, studia concredita fuerunt hactenus humaniora. Quod supersuperbiæ cacoëthes utinam & nostersibi non contraxissel! De Interprete Scripturarum controversiam, juxta cum aliis Theologiæ capitibus, ulterius excutere, liberum erat Wolzogio; sed argumenta ad unum omnia rejicere, spernere phrases, decessoribus rectè usurpatas, non item. Imo ab intoleranda non longe abest superbia, quod dicat NB.nequaquam fuisse hactenus enucleatè satis expositam hanc quæstionem. Scriptorem Paradoxum ulterius inquirendi, & meditandi, occasionem dedisse, si dixisset, excusari fortasse posset; quanquam meo judicio vix quicquam insulsum illud caput protruserit, quod non à Socinianis antea dictum sit, & à nostris refutatum abundè: at hactenus, non argumenta quædam, non Phrases aliquas, sed ipsam quæ-stionem non satis, imo nequaquam satis enucleate expositam dicere, næ illud omnes modestiæ limites transgreditur, & debitam erga decessores venerationem excutit. Profectum enim quæri unicè, præ se non ferunt ista verba, quicquid postliminio dicat eorum author, sed contemtum, sed vituperium eorum, qui ante nos pro veritate felicissimè dimicaverunt. Non putem ex formula humana anxiè nimis loquendum esse; phrases tamen & loquendi modos usu jam receptos temere rejicere, egregiæ superbiæ semper à modestioribus ingeniis & ἀνθαδείας [?] signum judicatum est. Quod tamen an hodie plus quam par est non fiat ab iis, qui aliàs præ reliquis modestiam crepant & moderationem, judicent qui partium studio non aguntur. Hæc autem, de quibus hactenus, homines spectant, eorumque laudes & merita: verum quod tertio loco recensendum puto, Deum propius concernit, Scripturæ dicta quod vix ullibi reperiantur vel citentur. De Scriptura tractatum scribi, Scripturæ locis omnino vacuum, quis ferat? De Arminio, sic olim Tuissus, cum analysin noni Capitis ad Romanos institueret, per universum tractatum vix duo loca Scripturæ quibus niteretur, observante hoc Lareno, ab Arminio producuntur. Nimirum vulgare nimium est & in medio positum, Scripturas juxta Scripturas exponere: maluit Arminius tanquam Pontifex aliquis ἀνυπεύθυνον[?], non Romanus sed Batavus, juxta ingenium suum & reconditam ejus subtilitatem verbi divini interpretationem expedire. Quod quam bene quadret in Wolzogium, penes lectorem esto judicium. Neque excusari aut palliari ista socordia potest, eo, quod ad hominem sic agier oportebat. Paradoxus enim ipse Scripturæ loca citat tractatque, & ex ipsa Scripturæ consideratione, facili negotio, de ejus intelligibilitate & non universali ambiguitate convinci poterat, ut Scripturam omnem seponere non fuerit necesse. Si autem ipse Wolzogius id excipiat, regeram, non bona fide ab ipso dici posse, quod in gratiam Paradoxi, & ad hominem, ut dicimus, sic egerit, nam pag. 247. ubi Caput Paradoxi XII. examinat, sic ex suo sensu, ob usurpatam scripturam Paradoxum reprehendit, Loca Scripturæ nos putamus, (non dicit Paradoxo, tu putas, sed suam depromens sententiam) nos putamus nec proferri debere, (atque ita Reformatos carpit, qui loca, quæ explicare hic aggrediebatur Paradoxus, produxerant) nec prolata refutari, (voluit dicere explicari) ab iis, qui non-dum dum de Interprete convenerunt: sicque Parado-xum, loca à nostris prolata, suo modo expli-cantem reprehendit, ut dubium non sit, quin Wolzogius, Reformatos ob prolatam, Pa-radoxum ob explicatam Scripturam, refutans, non ad hominem, sed ex proprio sensu & se-rió statuerit, non esse huc adducendam Scri-pturam: exertè nimis hoc significat pag. 217. quam ut disputari de eo possit: Verum, in-quit, non ad hominem, sed ex suo sensu loquens, ubi de Interprete Scripturæ quæstio agitatur, velle proferre Scripturam, id mihi vi-detur, si quicquam præposterè fieri. Subterfugia igitur quærit palàm, & sibi contradicit, quoties, Scripturam huc adferendam non esse, ad hominem solum a se dictum esse prætendit Wolzogius. Mirum autem non est, eum, qui Scripturæ obliviscitur, non multum de precibus loqui, nam nec frequenter nec libenter Deum in precibus alloquitur, qui non frequenter, non libenter audit Dei alloquia, in verbo prolata; atque hoc quartum erat, quod tractatum istum minus gratum reddere videbatur pio lectori & utilem: preces quippe, tantopere in hoc negotio commendandas, vix ullibi memorat. Ut autem preces minus piè excipit, sic, quod quinto dicendum erat, Spiritum Sanctum, qui ut Spiritus precum, sic & sapientiæ & revelationis in omni cognitione est, ejusque operationes, nimis perfunctorie tractat. Neque Spiritus S. auxilium satis magnum ac necessarium ab ipso concipi poterat, mentis nostræ corruptionem non rite considerante; quare & nusquam de captivando intellectu, officio hac in re præ-fertim observando, differentem reperias nos-trum. trum. Cartesianismi è contra laudes satis am-plas & prolixas inveniri vix posse putavit, fallit tamen lectorem, dum Apologiæ suæ Parte iv. Pagina 46. Cartesii encomium me unicè in ipsum concitasse, fabulatur; non enim ita cæcus sum aut perversus, ut, præ nimio adversus Cartesianismum odio, vel ipsam veritatem non feram in homine Carte-siano: ego nec Aristotelicam profiteor Phi-losophiam, nec Cartesianam, liberam colo & veneror veramque: quæ mens Wolzo-gio si fuisset, in immodicas istas Cartesianæ Philosophiæ laudes intempestivè non erupis-set, Theologus in tractatu Theologico; sed sciri voluit, utri parti se addixerit, ego autem partes nec faciendas puto, nec sequendas. Ut displiceant, qui omne quod Aristoteles aut alii Philosophi scriptis reliquerunt vitupe-rant, dum quicquid Cartesio in mentem ve-nit, palliandum, defendendum, quin pro o-raculo habendum censent. Nempe ignobili Peripateticorum jugo abdicato, Cartesii assum-serunt, illudque haud minus propudiosum sibi fe-rendum æquum arbitrati sunt; atque ita è fossa, quod ajunt, in foveam inciderunt. Ne ergo cæ-corum instar naso nos duci patieremur, aut unius jugo excusso alterius implicemur imprudentes, &c. Sunt verba Schuleri in Præfat. ad Exam. Phi-losoph. Cartes. specim. Et revera, quod, non sine omni ratione, Baco Verulamius alicubi scri-bit de Aristotele, idem hodie de Cartesio dici possset & Cartesianis. Referam verba summi viri. Omnino, inquit, avemus (quatenus sine veritatis ac scientiarum dispendio fieri possit) vel minimum ab antiquorum aut opinionibus aut lo-quendi more deflectere. Qua in re Aristotelis,
units.tr: It was in his interest not to speak so openly and so freely, but now and then to unveil and reveal what he really thought, since Velthusius could do the same thing with less risk. It might be said that Velthusius published his treatise on the use of reason in theology too late for our author to be certain of his meaning. But apart from the fact that, given their close acquaintance, he may be believed to have known those views for a long time, Velthusius had said similar things in various places elsewhere, so it could not be unclear that this was his opinion, which we now see him setting out openly and at length. But if Wolzogius had wished to avoid this inference, he should not have repeated that same praise in the second edition of his treatise, and still less should he have circulated it more widely in other places. In this way the reader sees why I have often joined these two men and explained the one by the other. Admittedly, those praises of Velthusius may be put down to Wolzogius's affection for him, but the agreement of their opinions requires that one man's view can be rightly judged, at least in some measure, from the other's writings. Second, there is that vanity, which cannot fail to displease all who have not wholly lost their reverence for their predecessors, by which he seems to have surpassed everyone and so brings great shame and reproach upon the labours of the greatest men. I do not deny that progress can be made, and I think every effort should be devoted to adding something to the well-established discoveries of others, so that the pursuit of truth always advances further; in this way the honour of the earlier writers is not taken from them, and that honour, which must be carefully preserved, remains for their successors. But our times are so corrupt, and our morals so depraved, that nothing is thought worthy of praise unless it recommends itself by novelty alone. Hence you may see the labours and efforts of immense value despised and scorned, and nearly all the books torn from the hands of students, so that whatever has a more accurate knowledge of things seems new and invented by men of our century; namely, according to our Velthusius's judgment, the humane studies have hitherto been entrusted to minute minds. I wish that our author had not contracted this disease of excessive arrogance! It was open to Wolzogius to examine further the controversy over the interpreter of Scripture, together with the other heads of theology; but to reject all the arguments in a body, to scorn the phrases rightly used by his predecessors, is not open to him. Indeed, he comes not far from intolerable arrogance when he says NB. that this question has never hitherto been sufficiently explained. If he had said that the writer of the Paradoxes had given occasion for further inquiry and meditation, that might perhaps be excused; although in my judgment that absurd chapter has hardly put forward anything that was not said earlier by the Socinians and thoroughly refuted by our people. But to say hitherto, not of certain arguments, not of some phrases, but that the question itself has not been sufficiently, nay, never sufficiently clearly explained, this surely goes beyond all the limits of modesty and shakes off the due reverence owed to predecessors. For these words do not show, whatever their author may say afterwards, a desire for progress, but contempt and disparagement of those who before us fought most successfully for the truth. I do not think we must speak anxiously in human formulas; yet to reject lightly phrases and modes of speaking already in common use has always been judged a sign of great arrogance [ἀνθαδείας] by the more modest minds. Whether this is done today more than is fitting by those who otherwise boast of modesty and moderation above others, let those judge who are not driven by partisan zeal. These matters so far concern men, and their praises and merits; but what I think should be mentioned in the third place concerns God more closely: that the words of Scripture can hardly be found or cited anywhere. Who could bear a treatise on Scripture that is wholly empty of Scripture passages? As for Arminius, of whom Tuissus once wrote: when he undertook the analysis of the ninth chapter of Romans, scarcely two passages of Scripture on which he might rest were produced by Arminius in the whole treatise, as Lärnus observed. Of course it is too common and commonplace to expound Scriptures by Scriptures; Arminius preferred, like some unaccountable pontiff [ἀνυπεύθυνον], not a Roman but a Dutchman, to work out his interpretation of the divine Word according to his own disposition and his hidden subtlety. How well this fits Wolzogius, let the reader judge. Nor can this negligence be excused or covered over by the fact that he had to deal with a man in this way. For the Paradoxer himself cites and treats Scripture passages, and from the consideration of Scripture itself he could easily have been convinced, concerning its intelligibility and not universal ambiguity, so that there was no need to set aside all of Scripture. But if Wolzogius himself takes exception to this, I will reply that it cannot be said in good faith by him that he acted in this way for the sake of the Paradoxer and ad hominem, as we say. For on page 247, where he examines chapter XII of the Paradoxes, he rebukes the Paradoxer from his own sense, because he had used Scripture: We think (he does not say to the Paradoxer, you think, but expressing his own opinion) we think that the passages of Scripture ought not to be brought forward (and so he carps at our people who had produced the passages which the Paradoxer here set about explaining) nor, when brought forward, refuted (he meant to say explained) by those who have not yet agreed about the interpreter. Thus he rebukes the Paradoxer for explaining in his own way the passages put forward by our people, so there is no doubt that Wolzogius, refuting our people for putting forward Scripture and the Paradoxer for explaining it, did not argue ad hominem but from his own sense and in earnest, deciding that Scripture ought not to be brought in here. He states this too plainly on page 217 for it to be disputed: But, he says, speaking not ad hominem but from his own sense, when the question concerns the interpreter of Scripture, to wish to bring forward Scripture seems to me, if anything is done out of order. So he openly seeks escape routes and contradicts himself whenever he claims that he said only ad hominem that Scripture should not be brought forward here. It is not surprising, however, that one who forgets Scripture does not say much about prayers, for he who does not often or willingly hear the words of God spoken in the Word does not often or willingly address God in prayer. And this was the fourth thing which seemed to make that treatise less pleasing and less useful to the pious reader: indeed he hardly mentions prayers, which ought to be so strongly commended in this matter. But as he receives prayers less piously, so, what should be said fifthly, he treats the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of prayers, and of wisdom and revelation in all knowledge, and his operations, too superficially. Nor could the great and necessary help of the Holy Spirit be conceived by him sufficiently, since he did not properly consider the corruption of our mind; hence you will nowhere find our author discussing the captivity of the intellect and the duty to be observed in this matter especially. On the other hand, he thought that ample and lengthy praises of Cartesianism could hardly be found, yet he deceives the reader when, on page 46 of Part IV of his Apology, he fabricates that my praise of Descartes was aimed solely at him; for I am not so blind or perverse as, out of excessive hatred of Cartesianism, to refuse even the truth in a Cartesian man. I profess neither Aristotelian nor Cartesian philosophy; I cultivate and revere freedom and truth. If Wolzogius had had this mind, he would not have burst out inopportunely into those immoderate praises of Cartesian philosophy, a theologian in a theological treatise; but he wished it to be known to which party he had devoted himself, whereas I think that parties should be neither made nor followed. They are displeased who disparage everything that Aristotle or other philosophers have left in their writings, while they think whatever comes into Descartes's head must be excused, defended, and even held as an oracle. Indeed, having cast off the ignoble yoke of the Peripatetics, they have taken up Descartes's, and have considered it no less shameful to bear; and so, as they say, out of the frying pan they have fallen into the fire. Lest, then, we allow ourselves to be led by the nose like the blind, or, having shaken off one yoke, unwittingly become entangled in another, etc. These are the words of Schuler in the preface to his Specimen of an Examination of Cartesian Philosophy. And indeed, what Bacon of Verulam wrote somewhere, not without reason, about Aristotle could be said today about Descartes and the Cartesians. I will quote the words of that great man: Certainly, he says, we desire (so far as it can be done without loss to truth and the sciences) to deviate in the smallest degree from the opinions or the manner of speaking of the ancients. units.la: (addi posset Cartesii, Cartesianorumque plu-rimorum) confidentiam proinde subit mirari; qui impetu quodam percitus contradictionis, bel-lum universæ Antiquitati indicens, non solum nova artium vocabula pro libitu cudendi licen-tiam usurpavit; sed etiam priscam omnem sapien-tiam extinguere & delere annisus est. Adeo ut neque nominet uspiam authores antiquos, neque dogmatum eorum mentionem ullam faciat, nisi quo aut homines perstringeret, aut placita re-dargueret. Legatur Aristoteles, legatur Plato, legatur Cartesius, sarta modo tectaque ma-neat divina fidei nostræ veritas. Hanc si in-tactam reliquisset & immaculatam, ejus Pro-fessores contemtim nimis si non excepisset, adversariisque deridendos modo non propi-nasset, Cartesianizando, ut ita loquar, me obloquutorem sibi nunquam nactus fuisset Wolzogius. Sanctè id, si necesse foret, testa-ri possem testorque. Vorticibus suis gyrif-que circumagantur, imo absorbeantur, quam-diu velint, quos ita lubet Philosophari, non habebunt me adversarium; sed vana confiden-tia, ex gurgite isto emergens, Theologiam, receptamque in Ecclesiis doctrinam sugillare, Reformatorum sensa carpere, argumenta re-jicere, quisquis præsumet, illius, eatenus, ad-versarium me, pro viribus à Deo gratiose in-dultis, posthac fore polliceor. Atque illud de-mum est, & quidem unicè, quod me unquam de congrediendo cum Wolzogio vel somniare fecit. Varii errores, quos deprehendere in Wolzogiano scripto putabam, novaturiendi illud & in Theologia luxuriandi cacoëthes me adversus illud concitarunt. Non homines alii, non partis hujus aut illius favor, necdum enim de denunciatione Medioburgensi, aut protestatione Roterodamensi, aliorumve, ex Wolzogii sensu, sequioribus[?] super isto libello judiciis, vel fando quicquam audiveram, cum notas quasdam chartæ injicere, & periculosissimas phrases, Venerandæ classi nostræ, significare consultum judicabam, testis mihi conscientia, testes inter homines plures sunt, omni exceptione majores, imo & plures forsan, ex iis, qui postea approbationis in Synodo Walonica conscii fuerunt & consortes. Hac de re paucis. Tanti res ista Classi nostræ momenti visa est; ut, auditis & lectis quibusdam ex Wolzogiano libello thesibus, Gravamen aliquod super eo mittere ad Synodum statuerit; attamen ne quicquam temere aut inconsiderate ageretur, quatuor Pastoribus, (libelli seriem penitius examinaturis, ut & gravamen aliquod super eo concepturis, Classique sequenti illud communicaturis) hoc negotium demandavit, qui fideliter officio functi, pauca Classi exhibuerunt, quæ unanimiter gravamen Synodo mittendum iterum decrevit, hisce verbis conceptum. An non periculosum sit & falsum, imo receptæ doctrinæ repugnans. 1. Dicere, Ecclesiæ Reformatæ Theologos hactenus, aut obscurè, aut non satis dilucidè scripsisse de Interprete Scripturæ? (quoniam ab ea controversia inter nos & Pontificios ac Socinianos omnia dependent) prout in quodam libello, cui Titulus, Ludovici Wolzogii de Script. Interprete &c. pag. 5. 222. 251. factum est? 2. Dicere, eos qui Scripturam audiunt Scripturæ Interpretem, Deum non audire Interpretem pag. 203. Quando de Interprete Script. agitur, non esse huc illud adducendum, quisque suorum verborum optimus Interpres. p. 207. Etiam «sequentia: Verum ubi de Interpr. Script. quæstio agitatur, velle proferre Scripturam, id mihi vi-detur, si quicquam præposteré fieri p. 217. Deum esse Interpr. Script. non video quo fundamento nitatur. pag. 250. 3. An non sit horrendus aut ad minimum durus & imprudens loquendi modus, dicere, cum de veracitate Dei, & Verbi divini, sermo est: sufficit Deum dixisse ut sciamus eum fallere nolle, dico nolle eum falle-re, ut ne credatis non posse si velit. p. 24. Et plura ejusdem generis? Quod omne si sic: ni-mirum, ea sic scripta esse. 4. An non conduce-ret (quoniam primorum Reformatorum labor hisce spernitur & Ecclesia nostra dedecore assi-citur; Papistis vero gloriandi ansa datur, ac si in negotio tanti momenti aut hactenus er-rassemus aut saltem de eo hactenus inter nos consensus non detur) hac occasione urgere Art. 50. & 52. Ordinis Ecclesiastici de an-no 1619. Ac consequenter, per Correspon-dentes reliquis Correspondentibus Synodis, & per literas, quoniam author istius libelli hu-jus membrum est, Walonicæ, Christianæ Fri-siacæ Synodi offensam significare, addita debi-tæ & maturæ correctionis seu remedii (ordre) petitione. Qua in re neque præter ordinem le-gitimum, ac decentem quicquam egit Classis, neque imprudenter. Causa communis erat, & ad omnes Ecclesias ex æquo spectans, pro-spicere, ne recepta fidei veritas labasceret aut quicquam caperet detrimenti. Neque in alte-rius messem falcem misit suam, nondum enim, aut Classis, aut Synodus aliqua, quic-quam, quod istud negotium spectabat, hacte-nus occœperat: & si vel aliquid egisset, non minus tamen & nostræ, suum pro 'ortho-doxia zelum probare, licitum erat & decorum. Eo etiam collimabat, ut illi, quibus id præcipue incumbebat, aliorum cura excitati, serio magis & sedulo rem istam agerent. Nec primi fuerunt Frisii qui aliis Classibus aut Synodis, etiam Walonicæ, quicquam quod curam aut attentionem requirebat, indicarunt. Si quis Extracta Synodorum pervolvat, semper istam mutuam communionem consiliorum & mutuam incitationem obtinuisse statim reperiet. Remonstrantium turbas memorare, ac tum temporis quid factum fuerit narrare, non est necesse. Cum D. Vedelius in Frisia Theol. Professor, edidisset suum Constantinum, Synodus Zuid-Hollandica de eo egit non solùm, sed ipsi Vedelio serio scripsit & laborem illum sibi displicere significavit, quin Synodi Frisicæ Deputatis, aliisque Correspondentibus Synodis,eadem facienda commendavit. Vid. Act. Syn. Z.Hol. Anno1642. §.51. Sic Anno 1651. Synodus Noort-Holl. Harlem. §.47. & Ultraj. §. 32. judicavit à Pastoribus quibusdam Gallo-Belgicis editos quosdam tractatus, periculosas continere aliquas positiones & una cum Synodo Zuid-Holl. adversus istum agendi modum remedia adhibenda esse statuit. Ut novi quid à Classe nostra actum esse dici non possit, nisi à rerum Ecclesiasticarum imperitis. Deinde, quemadmodum ordinem & decorum rite servavit, sic & satis circumspectè egit idem venerandus cœtus; antequam enim ad Synodum gravamen, ut vocant, transmisit, res rite examinata, iterumque in ipsa Classe excussa est, non segniter, ut majorem quam fere adhiberi ab aliis consuevit huic negotio laborem impenderit & circumspectam prudentiam. Unde autem hoc habeat, quod falso narrat Wolzogius, Classem nimirum vix à censura, eâque publica mihi infligenda, sese continuisse, idque eam ob causam, quod deceptam se, in isto Wolzogiano negotio, per me videret, haud scio. Pudeat Wolzogium, vel potius eum, qui ita impudenter ipsi supplantavit, istius mendacii, ego saltem de ista censura ne fando quidem ante editam Apologiæ illius Wolzogianæ quartam partem quicquam audivi. Hoc scio, fuisse quendam, qui, edito libello, notatos in suo gravamine à Classe Cartesii errores incrustare & palliare sustinuit, eaque occasione aliquid, à Classis Leovardianæ ad istud negotium juxta cum me Deputatis, D. Johanne Wemero, D. Davide Acronio jam fatis functo, D. Johanne Laftdrager Collega meo in Classis Leovardiensis justam defensionem dictum esse; at & hoc scio, tantum abesse, ut ob gravaminis aut scriptionem, aut defensionem, aut quicquam eo spectans, ullus hominum censura notatus fuerit, aut ejus periculum vix evaserit, ut è contra exertè gratias egerit veneranda Classis, iis fratribus, qui ad istud negotium Deputati, Classis causam coram Synodo egerant & defenderant. Falsitatis Wolzogium accusarem, quod me, tecto licet nomine, in ista sua Apologia, tanquam convictum deceptorem traduxerit, nisi ab alio forsan ipsi impositum esse suspicarer; hoc sciat lector, ea, quæ inibi. pag. 46. &c. narrantur, nihil præter puram putam falsitatem continere, ut ex publicis tabulis docere paratus sum, & certè, si non firmiori tibicine, reliqua, quæ mamagno numero in istis Apologiæ quatuor partibus de aliis narrantur, suffulta sint, videat lector quam sublestæ & suspectæ fidei haberi debeant. Sic tamen fama crescit eundo, & mendacium fide dignum tandem judicatur, modo sit qui audacter effutire audeat. Nihilominus fidelissime se acturum promiserat p. 45. Wolzogius, testimonio nixus satis veraci. Paucis ista, quoniam me concernunt, quæ inibi sequuntur, excutiam. Quantam fidem mereatur calumniator ille, quisquis fit, qui ista Wolzogio retulit, vel ex ipso narrationis capite elucescit: il faut scavoir que le Synode de Frise est partagé en cinque Classes, id est, scien-dum est, Synodum Frisiæ in quinque Classes partitam esse: falsa computatio, cum vel pueri norint, sex esse in hac Provincia Classes, quarum deputati Frisiæ Synodum constituant. Hinc judicet lector, quali testimonio hic loci nitatur iste Apologista, hominis certe, qui rerum nostrarum omnimodam ignorantiam, aut in narrando inconsiderantiam incomparabilem ultro prodens, apud attentum prudentemque hujusce egregii testimonii æstimatorem, ulteriorem fidem non merebitur. Hic error autem, circumstantiam quippe respiciens, excusare si quis velit, ex supina tamen & turpi rerum nostrarum, quin omnis, in omnibus Synodis Belgii, ordinis, ignorantia ortus apparebit, si conferantur ea, quæ pag. 52. nugatur Apologista, ubi rem ipsam & essentialia hujusce rei describit. De Gravaminibus loquitur, ce ne sont, inquit, que de Reflexions & de Considerations, de points que l'on propose pour en deliberer au Synode, & la Classe même qui fait ses propositions, ne les examine pas avec la der-
units.tr: (this could be said of Descartes and of very many Cartesians) one is therefore moved to wonder at their confidence, who, driven by a certain impulse of contradiction and declaring war on all antiquity, have not only claimed the licence to coin new technical terms at will, but have also striven to extinguish and destroy all ancient wisdom. So much so that they nowhere name the ancient authors, nor make any mention of their doctrines, except where they either disparage men or refute their opinions. Let Aristotle be read, let Plato be read, let Descartes be read, provided only that the divine truth of our faith remains whole and covered. If Descartes had left this truth untouched and unstained, and had not too contemptuously received its professors, nor exposed them to be mocked by their adversaries, then Wolzogius would never have found me as an opponent who, so to speak, argues against Cartesianism. I could solemnly testify to this, if need be, and I do testify it. Let them be whirled round and round in their own vortices, or rather swallowed up, for as long as they like, those whom it pleases to philosophize in this way; they will not have me as an adversary. But whoever presumes, emerging from that whirlpool with vain confidence, to malign the theology and the doctrine received in the Churches, to carp at the sentiments of the Reformers, and to reject their arguments, I promise that from now on I shall be his adversary, so far as, by God's gracious gift, my powers allow. And indeed this, and this alone, is what ever made me dream of engaging with Wolzogius. Various errors, which I thought I detected in Wolzogius' writing, roused me against it, with that itch for innovation and for indulging in novelties in theology. It was not other men, not the favour of this or that party, for as yet I had heard nothing, either by report, of the denunciation at Middelburg, or the protest at Rotterdam, or of other judgments, less favourable, on that little book from Wolzogius' point of view. When I judged it advisable to note in writing certain phrases and very dangerous expressions, and to signify them to our venerable classis, my conscience is my witness; there are several witnesses among men, beyond all exception, indeed perhaps even more of those who afterwards were aware of and took part in the approval at the Walloon Synod. On this matter, briefly. The thing seemed of such importance to our classis that, after hearing and reading certain theses from Wolzogius' little book, it resolved to send some complaint about it to the Synod. Yet, so that nothing should be done rashly or inconsiderately, it committed this business to four ministers, who were to examine the series of the little book more thoroughly, and to draft some complaint about it, and to communicate it to the following classis. They faithfully discharged their duty and presented a few points to the classis, which it unanimously decided again to send to the Synod as a complaint, conceived in these words: Is it not dangerous and false, indeed contrary to received doctrine: 1. To say that the theologians of the Reformed Church have hitherto written either obscurely, or not clearly enough, about the interpreter of Scripture (since all the controversy between us and the Papists and Socinians depends on this), as has been done in a certain little book entitled Ludovici Wolzogii de Script. Interprete, etc., pp. 5, 222, 251? 2. To say that those who hear Scripture do not hear the interpreter of Scripture, that God does not hear the interpreter, p. 203. When the question concerns the interpreter of Scripture, that this is not to be brought in, each one is the best interpreter of his own words, p. 207. Also the following: But where the question of the interpreter of Scripture is at issue, to wish to bring forward Scripture, this seems to me to be done somewhat perversely, p. 217; I do not see on what foundation it rests that God is the interpreter of Scripture, p. 250. 3. Is it not a horrible, or at least a harsh and imprudent way of speaking, when the truthfulness of God and of the divine Word is under discussion, to say: it is enough that God has said it, so that we know he is unwilling to deceive; I say he is unwilling to deceive you, lest you believe he could not, if he willed it, p. 24? And many more of the same kind? If all this is so, then these things have indeed been written thus. 4. Would it not be expedient (since the labour of the first Reformers is thereby despised and our Church is marked with disgrace, while an occasion for boasting is given to the Papists, as if in a matter of such importance we had either erred until now, or at least there were no agreement among us on it until now) to press, on this occasion, Articles 50 and 52 of the Ecclesiastical Order of the year 1619; and consequently, through the corresponding classes to the remaining corresponding synods, and by letter, since the author of that little book is a member of the Walloon classis, to signify to the Christian Frisian Synod our displeasure, with the addition of a request for due and timely correction or remedy (ordre). In this matter the classis has done nothing beyond the lawful and proper order, nor has it acted imprudently. The cause was common, and concerned all the Churches equally: to provide that the received truth of the faith should not totter or suffer any harm. Nor did it thrust its sickle into another's harvest, for as yet neither the classis nor any synod had begun anything concerning this business; and even if it had done something, it was no less lawful and fitting for our classis to show its zeal for orthodoxy. It also aimed at this, that those to whom this chiefly belonged, roused by the care of others, might handle the matter more seriously and diligently. Nor were the Frisians the first to point out to other classes or synods, including the Walloon one, anything that required care or attention. If anyone should turn over the extracts of the synods, he will at once find that this mutual communion of counsels and mutual stimulation has always prevailed. It is not necessary to recall the disturbances of the Remonstrants and to relate what was done at that time. When Dr. Vedelius, professor of theology in Friesland, had published his Constantinus, the Synod of South Holland dealt with it not only, but also wrote seriously to Vedelius himself and signified that it was displeasing to them, and furthermore commended the same to be done by the deputies of the Frisian Synod and to the other corresponding synods. See the Acts of the Synod of South Holland, year 1642, §51. So in the year 1651 the Synod of North Holland at Haarlem, §47, and at Utrecht, §32, judged that certain treatises published by some Gallo-Belgic ministers contained some dangerous positions, and, together with the Synod of South Holland, resolved that remedies must be applied against this manner of proceeding. So it cannot be said that anything new was done by our classis, except by those inexperienced in ecclesiastical affairs. Then, just as this venerable assembly observed order and propriety duly, so also it acted with sufficient circumspection; for before it sent the complaint, as they call it, to the Synod, the matter was duly examined and again discussed in the classis itself, and it applied not a sluggish but a greater labour and circumspect prudence to this business than is usually applied by others. But whence Wolzogius has the false statement that the classis, I suppose, scarcely restrained itself from censure, and that public censure to be inflicted on me, and that it did so for the reason that it saw itself deceived through me in that Wolzogian business, I do not know. Wolzogius should be ashamed, or rather he who so impudently supplanted him with this lie. As for me, at least, I heard nothing even by report of such censure before that Wolzogian Apology was published, not even a quarter of it. This I know: there was a certain man who, after the little book was published, undertook to cover up and palliate the errors of Descartes noted in his complaint by the classis; and on that occasion something was said about the just defence of this business, by the classis of Leeuwarden, together with me, the deputies Dr. Johannes Wemerus, Dr. David Acronius, now deceased, and Dr. Johannes Laftdrager, my colleague in the classis of Leeuwarden. But this too I know: so far was any man censured, because of the writing or the defence of the complaint, or anything relating to it, that he barely escaped the danger of censure; on the contrary, the venerable classis openly thanked those brethren who had been deputed to this business and had pleaded and defended the classis's cause before the Synod. I would accuse Wolzogius of falsehood, because in that Apology of his, though under a veiled name, he has presented me as a convicted deceiver, were I not suspecting that this had been imposed on him by another. Let the reader know that what is related there, p. 46 and following, contains nothing but pure and simple falsehood, as I am ready to show from public records; and certainly, if the rest of what is told in those four parts of the Apology about others, in great numbers, is not supported by a firmer prop, let the reader see how flimsy and suspect a reliability they ought to be held to have. Yet rumour grows as it goes, and a lie is at last judged worthy of belief, provided there is someone who dares to blurt it out boldly. Nevertheless Wolzogius had promised on p. 45 that he would act most faithfully, relying on a testimony that was sufficiently truthful. I shall briefly examine what follows there, since it concerns me. How much credit that slanderer deserves, whoever he is, who reported these things to Wolzogius, is clear even from the very beginning of his narrative: il faut scavoir que le Synode de Frise est partagé en cinque Classes, id est, sciendum est, the Synod of Friesland is divided into five classes: a false count, since even boys know that there are six classes in this province, whose deputies make up the Synod of Friesland. Let the reader judge hence on what kind of testimony this Apologist here relies, a man who, by openly displaying his utter ignorance of our affairs, or his incomparable carelessness in narrating, will not earn further credit with an attentive and prudent judge of such an excellent testimony. This error, indeed, concerning a circumstance, might be excused if anyone wished; but it will appear to arise from a supine and shameful ignorance of our affairs, indeed of the whole order of all the Synods of Belgium, if one compares what the Apologist babbles on p. 52, where he describes the matter itself and its essentials. He speaks of the complaints, they are, he says, only reflections and considerations, points proposed for deliberation at the Synod, and the classis itself, which makes its proposals, does not examine them with the der-

units.la: derniere exactitude dans son assemblée, parce qu'elle en doit encore juger dans le Synode même. Non sunt nisi reflexiones & considerationes, eorum, quæ proponuntur, ut de iis consilium agitetur in Synodo, quin ipsa Classis, cujus sunt istæ propositiones, eas non examinat in suo consessu exactissime, quia de iis judicandum ipsi est in ipsa Synodo. Nihil quod vero simile sit hæc continent, nec verum esse potest: fratres enim, qui ad Synodum mittuntur, dum in rebus particularibus agere ipsis licet, prout rectum justumque, in ipso Synodi consessu, visum fuerit; in ea, quæ super Gravaminibus deliberatio instituitur, nihil possunt, instructi veniunt, imo de verbo ad verbum Classis suæ, super iis decreta dictare tenentur; ut non in ipsa Synodo, sed in Classibus exactissimè ista excuti debeant, quod tamen hic negat, imo cujus contrarium audacter ponit, iste Apologista: Classis autem, de cujus Gravamine in Synodo agitur, omni adhibita exactitudine, rem eo contentam, examinasse creditur. Hinc semper ejus votum, in colligendis votis, juxta cum aliis numeratur, inter ea, quæ pro Gravamine concludunt, nisi quod subinde Classis illius Deputati paulo clarius committentium suorum sensa, super eo & rationes explicare (quod vocant hypothesin aperire nostri) teneantur; adeo debent à Classe sua rite instructi ad Synodum mitti Classium Deputati, hinc, non per Capita, sed per Classes (ut dicunt) de Gravaminibus suffragia numerantur. Classis igitur in Synodo proprie non judicat, sed, quæ in Classe decreta sunt, in Synodo referuntur, & cum reliquarum Classium decretis conferuntur, quâ collatione facta, plurium Clas-siurn[?] sium suffragia decretum evadunt Synodales. Quin, quod malam fidem redolet, ipse hoc innuit pag.48. Ubi, quid Classis Franeque-rana, super isto Gravamine, in suo conventu decreverit, refert, ut ignorare non potuerit, in Classibus ea, quæ Gravamina concernunt, agitari, ac de iis singulas Classes Deputatos suos Classicali decreto instruere. Hic tamen contrarium magis è re sua esse autumavit, ne sc: decretum in isto negotio à Classe quicquam esse, lectori falsò persuaderet. Exertè vero le-gibus nostris contradicit, quod profert p. 53. Le moindre soupçon, pourveu qu'il ait quelque apparence de verité, oblige une Classe a porter les affaires à un Synode. Minima suspicio, modo ali-quam habeat verisimilitudinem, Classem, rem istam ad Synodum mittere, obligat. Certè Gra-vamina non nisi de rebus momentosis, per-spicuis, & certis, ad Synodum transmittere legibus cautum est, & res ipsa postulat; tot enim Gravamina, si ex verisimilibus, & iis quæ minimæ suspicionis causa sunt ea cudere Classes tenerentur, Synodis suborirentur, ut continua ejus requireretur congregatio. Tam absurda, tam omni praxi & legibus contraria, hic narrat Apologista; ut deridendum sese cun-ctis, rerum istarum non plane ignaris, pro-pinaverit. Ex ignorantia autem, aut alterius illusione ista si retulit, miserrimum in modum prostitui sese est passus. Malitia vero & fallen-di animus si subsit, videant ad quos ista spe-ctant, quid talis meritus sit Apologista. Hu-jus farinæ & paris levitatis plura sequentur. De nimia Cartesii & quorundam novaturientium ac in Theologiam involantium in Philofo-phando licentia, Pastorem quendam Leovardiensem coram Classe questum esse, negari non potest, neque ejus ulla pœnitentia tangi-ur, ille, quem designat Apologista. Ut id [?]rustra tam salsè illi exprobretur p. 46. quod ibi dedecori apud bonos non fore certissimè novit. Quatuor ad istud negotium à Classe missos, verum est. Quæ enim narrat pag. 46. tam procul absunt à vero, quam supradicta computatio, & de Gravaminibus eorumque natura instituta futilis nugatio potiùs, quam narratio: non enim, quod innuere vult no-ter, penes quatuor illos erat, pro sua autho-ritate, voir si l'affaire meritoit qu'on la portát u Synode. Hoc est, videre an tanti momenti hoc negotium esset, ut ad Synodum transmitti mere-tur. Etenim jam de mittendo super isto ne-gotio Gravamine decretum erat, neque etiam aut rei indoles, aut ordo ullus, hoc patitur, ut de Gravamine mittendo, aut non mittendo penes paucos arbitrium sit, quod nisi omnis ordinis nostri ignarus fuisset narrator, ne so-mniare quidem potuisset. Gravamen mitten-dum jam decretum erat, sed varia quoniam examinanda in isto Gravamine Classi vide-bantur, tum ut prudenter conciperetur, tum ut aliarum Ecclesiarum super eodem negotio leges conferrentur; aliquibus id negotii de-mandare consultum duxit; idque, non, ut illi pro lubitu quidvis statuerent, sed sua toti Classi communicarent, quod &, antequam per Classes Gravamen istud mittebatur, fa-ctum fuit. Præleegerunt igitur, toti veneran-do consessui, quatuor jam supra nominati fra-tres, sua de ista re cogitata, & quæstionibus ac mediis, ad unum omnibus, rite expensis, ac examinatis, fratres Gravamen illud ita
units.tr: They are only reflections and considerations on the matters proposed, so that counsel may be taken on them in the Synod. The Classis itself, whose these proposals are, does not examine them with the utmost exactness in its own assembly, because it must itself judge of them in the Synod. These statements contain nothing that is likely, and they cannot be true. The brothers who are sent to the Synod are free to act in particular matters as they judge right and just in the Synod's own assembly, but in the deliberation carried on concerning the Gravamina they can do nothing. They come instructed, and indeed they are bound to report word for word the decisions of their Classis on those matters. So these matters must be sifted most exactly not in the Synod itself but in the Classes. Yet this Apologist denies it, or rather boldly asserts the opposite. A Classis, on whose Gravamen the Synod is debating, is believed to have examined the matter with every exactness. Hence its vote is always counted along with the others among those that conclude in favour of the Gravamen. The only exception is that the deputies of that Classis are sometimes obliged to explain their constituents' views and reasons a little more clearly (what our people call opening the hypothesis). So the deputies sent to the Synod must be duly instructed by their Classis, and for this reason the votes on Gravamina are counted not by head but, as they say, by Classes. The Classis therefore does not properly judge in the Synod. What has been decreed in the Classis is reported in the Synod and compared with the decrees of the other Classes, and once this comparison is made, the votes of several Classes become the decision of the Synod. Moreover, he himself hints at something that smells of bad faith on p. 48, where he reports what the Classis of Franeker decided on this Gravamen in its own meeting. He cannot have been ignorant that matters concerning Gravamina are discussed in the Classes, and that each Classis instructs its deputies on them by a Classical decree. Here, however, he thought it more to his advantage to say the opposite, namely that the Classis had made no decision in this business, so as to persuade the reader falsely. But he openly contradicts our laws in what he gives on p. 53: The slightest suspicion, provided it has some appearance of truth, obliges a Classis to bring the matter to a Synod. Certainly the laws, and the nature of the thing itself, provide that Gravamina are to be sent to the Synod only concerning matters that are weighty, plain and certain. For if Classes were bound to forge Gravamina from whatever is probable or has the slightest cause for suspicion, the Synods would be overwhelmed, and their almost continual gathering would be required. This Apologist relates things so absurd and so contrary to all practice and the laws that he has exposed himself to ridicule before everyone who is not wholly ignorant of these matters. If he reported them out of ignorance, or through someone else's deception, he has allowed himself to be made a most wretched fool. But if there was malice and a desire to deceive, let those concerned see what such a man deserves. More of this same lightness of character will follow. That the Classis of Leeuwarden complained in front of the Classis about the excessive licence of Descartes and of certain innovators who fly into theology while philosophising, cannot be denied. Nor is that pastor, whom the Apologist points out, moved by any repentance. Let him vainly reproach him so sharply on p. 46, since he knows very well that it will not bring him disgrace among good men. It is true that four men were sent by the Classis to this business. But what he relates on p. 46 is as far from the truth as the above calculation, and his account of the Gravamina and their nature is a trifling babble rather than a narrative. For it was not, as he wishes to suggest to the reader, in the power of those four to decide, on their own authority, to see whether the matter deserved to be carried to the Synod. That is, to see whether this business was of such importance that it deserved to be sent to the Synod. For a decision to send this Gravamen to the Synod had already been made. Neither the nature of the business nor any order permits the choice to send or not to send the Gravamen to rest with a few people. Had the narrator not been wholly ignorant of our order, he could not even have dreamed it. The Gravamen was already decided to be sent, but since the Classis judged that many things in it needed examination, both so that it might be prudently framed and so that the laws of other Churches on the same matter might be compared, it thought fit to entrust the task to some men. This was not so that they might decide whatever they pleased, but so that they might communicate their thoughts to the whole Classis, which was done before the Gravamen was sent on through the Classes. So the four brothers already named presented to the whole venerable assembly their thoughts on the matter. Once the questions and means had been duly weighed and examined, all the brothers together decided to send the Gravamen, just as it was in fact sent. So far was the sending or not sending of this Gravamen from depending on the judgment of those four. They judged that yes, that is, that the Gravamen should be sent. But the decision had already been made by the whole assembly, which those brothers judged advisable, and after repeated deliberations, with everything duly considered, the Classis of Leeuwarden afterwards decided the same in the full assembly. And they brought complaints, he says, perhaps bloody ones, to the Synod. They brought very bloody complaints to the Synod. Indeed it was not the decision of those brothers but of the whole Classis, and the Apologist brands it with the label of very bloody complaints. Bloody brothers! Oh, the imprudent Classis of Leeuwarden, which has suffered bloody counsels to be attributed to it! It might seem a device to charge four men with cruelty that he did not dare to fasten on the Classis. Our author thought it a bold deed to accuse it of such great imprudence.

units.la: Doubtful: the first letter of "diensem" and of "rustra" is cut by the edge; read as d and f. "leges" begins with a faint long s, read as l. transmittere decreverunt, prout transmissum reipsa fuit. Tantum abest, ut ex istorum qua-tuor arbitrio, istius Gravaminis missio, aut non missio pependerit. Ils jugerent qu'oui. Illi judicarunt quod sic, sc: mittendum Gravamen esse, at in toto consensu jam id decretum erat, quod consultum judicabant isti fratres, & iteratis consiliis, rite omnibus perspectis, dein-ceps in toto consessu idem statuit Classis Leovardiensis. Et porterent de pleintes, inquit, forsan fanglantes au Synode. Et cruentas valde querelas ad Synodum detulerunt. Nimirum isti fratres, sed fallit Apologista & fallitur, non enim istorum fratrum, sed totius Classis decretum fuit, quod valde cruentarum querelarum no-mine seu stigmate insignit Apologista. Fratres isti cruenti, at ô imprudentem Leovardiensem Classem cruenta sibi supponi consilia passam! Artificium videri posset, quatuor viris impu-tasse crudelitatem, quam Classi impingere non audebat, insignis eam imprudentiæ accusari quippe satis audax facinus judicavit noster.
units.tr: To call everything that is proposed for suppressing heresies and errors bloody is the habit of another Apologist, to whom this author of ours is not at all similar in other respects, as can be seen in the treatise itself. Here consider the modesty and moderation of the man, reader. If the matter were to be handled by the law of retaliation, one could inquire whether bloody counsels against the brothers had not been put forward by others. But blood and cruelty in the Gravamen of our Classis will be seen only by someone in whose dreams blood, because of an inborn cruelty, perhaps keeps appearing.

units.la: Quicquid ad hæreses, ad errores compescen-dos proponitur, cruentum dicere, alterius cu-jusdam Apologistæ mores refert, cui in aliis ant[?] non æque similis sit hic noster, in ipso tra-ctatu videre est. Atque hic modestiam homi-nis & moderationem vide lector.Si ex Talionis lege agendum foret, cruenta adversus fratres consilia, an ab aliis agitata non fuerint, disqui-ri posset. Cruorem vero & crudelitatem, in istoClassis nostræ Gravamine,non videbit,nisi cui cruor præ insita crudelitate forsan in somniis obversetur.
units.tr: The cruel and shameless censor did not consider that in this case the several Classes and Synods of the Churches, the curators of the universities, and even the most illustrious orders of Holland and West Friesland are being accused. For everything the Classis of Leeuwarden had proposed to the Synod for suppressing novelties, it had learned from others.

units.la: Non cogitavit crudelis, venerandi cœtus, & impudens censor, plures Ecclesiarum Classes & Synodos, Academiarum Curatores, imo vel ipsos Hollandiæ & Westfrisiæ Illustrissimos Ordines, hic reos agi. Omnia enim, quæ ad novitates compescendas, Synodo media propositi, Classis Leovardiensis, ab aliis didicerat. Pestem in Theo-logia Philosophiam Cartesianam jam dudum di-xerat Hardervicena Academia. De ea compescenda deliberavit antehac Synodus Z. Hol-landiæ, anno MDCLVI. Uti & Synodus Generalis Ecclesiarum Juliacensium, Montanarum &c. Anno MDCXLIII. 13. Augusti. Idem præstitit Synodus Gelrica. Quarum ultima ab Academiæ Curatoribus & prima ab Hollandiæ Ordinibus, seria decreta impetrarunt. Sic Gelrici Curatores exerté prohibent. I. Ne ullus Professor ordinarius aut extraordinarius, directe aut indirecte, in Academia aut privatis collegiis, Cartesii aut similium Sectariorum & adhærentium dogmata doceat aut proponat, nisi forsan ad ea refutanda. II. Neve consequenter aut theses, aut Corollaria, aut quæstiones, aut problemata de iis ad disputandum proferat, cui si contrarium quis egerit, à professione sua removetor. Plura addiderunt Illustrissimi & Potentissimi Hollandiæ & Westfrisiæ Ordines. Eat nunc Apologista & cruenta clamet seu sanguinolenta consilia, Classi Leovardiensi, ex Hollandiæ Ordinum, & Gelricæ Academiæ Curatorum prudentissimo decreto, mutuo data. Quid, cum nec eousque extendatur à Classe Leovardiensi quæ proponitur cautela, magis certe cruenti Wolzogio habendi sunt laudatissimi proceres, duriora quippe decernentes, quam à Classe propositæ sunt novaturiendi remedia. Pergit in hunc modum, & pourtant le Synode ne les jugea gueres bien fondées. Synodus tamen eas judicabat parum bene fundatas. Non ita in Synodo decretum esse, prout à Classe nostra erat propositum, & ab alia quadam Classe probatum, fateor, nec tamen parum bene fundatas querelas judicabat, quæ tantum effecerunt, ut Deputatis Synodi, adversus licentiam Philosophicam, tam apud Illustrissimos D. D. Ordines, quam Nobilissimos D.D. Academiæ Curatores, ejusque Clarissimos Professores, officia sua interponerent, in mandatis datum sit. Ut falsa sint quæ sequuntur, qu'on laissa l'affaire dans l'Estat où elle avoit été auparavant, rem istam in pristino statu relictam esse. Decretum enim est, id, quod jam retuli, & in Extractis nostris Synodalibus ab isto tempore novum Titulum reperire licet, de licentia Philosophandi, hactenus in Frisiæ Synodi actis eorumve repertorio, ut dicunt, non nisi occasione istius Gravaminis, visum vel auditum. Hoccine est negotium in pristino statu reliquisse, hoccine Gravamen nostræ Classis minus bene fundatum judicasse est? Non certe talis est nostra Classis, ut cruenta quin valde cruenta cudat consilia, non ea Frisiæ Synodus, quæ crudelitatem deprehendens, eam non solum impunitam dimittat, sed & partim suam faciat; in genere enim decrevit id, quod solummodo paulo specialius & magis explicitè decretum optarat Classis Leovardiensis, eaque in Synodo non sola. Ejusdem commatis sunt, ea, quæ de suo libello refert, sic pergit, Les Messieurs les Examinateurs entreprirent aussi mon livre, & celuy qui s'étoit attacqué à Descartes, en voulant aussi à moy, parce que je loue Descartes dans mon livre, fit voir à ses Compagnons les passages de mon livre qui se troutrouvent couchés dans ce Gravamen. Domini Examinatores etiam præ manibus sumserunt meum librum, idemque, qui Cartesium aggressus erat, me itidem petens, propterea quod in libro meo laudem Cartesium, ostendit sociis suis loca libri mei, quæ in isto Gravamine prolata reperiuntur. Qui vanas Historias conscribunt vel fabulas potius, quas Romans vocant Galli, non tam veritati quam nitori & narrationis amœnitati intenti sunt, ab iis hunc narrandi modum didicisse videtur noster Walonicus Apologista. Artificium est, modo ne impo-stura dici mereatur, quod talem in modum ista referat, ac si, post habitam Classem, modo dicti quatuor fratres Gravamen illud, quod de libello Wolzogiano ad Synodum missum est, sua authoritate reliquis addidissent, quo nihil dici potest ab omni veritate remotius. Præ-lecta jam erant, ex ipso libello, coram Classe, loca; & in ipso consessu, de mittendo, super eo Gravamine non ab istis fratribus, sed ab ipsa Classe decretum. Sessione vero post ali-quot dies subsequente, ipsum Gravamen, prout scriptum erat, (est autem moris apud nos, ut, qui de mittendo quodam Gravami-ne quicquam proponit, is scripto consignatum id Classi, probandum, rejiciendum, aut mu-tandum tradat) iterum præletum, & ro-gatis super eo omnium fratrum suffragiis, sic tandem ex decreto ad Synodum missum est.
units.tr: The cruel and shameless censor, reverend assembly, did not consider that several Classes and Synods of the Churches, the Curators of the Academies, and even the most illustrious Orders of Holland and West Friesland themselves are being put on trial here. For everything the Classis of Leeuwarden proposed to the Synod in order to check novelties, it had learned from others. The Cartesian philosophy is a plague in theology, as the Academy of Harderwijk had said long before. The Synod of South Holland deliberated on suppressing it in 1656, as did the General Synod of the Churches of Jülich, Berg and so on, on 13 August 1643. The Synod of Gelderland did the same. Of these, the last obtained serious decrees from the Curators of the Academy, and the first from the Orders of Holland. Thus the Curators of Gelderland expressly forbid: (1) that no professor, ordinary or extraordinary, directly or indirectly, in the Academy or in private lectures, teach or propose the doctrines of Descartes or of similar sectaries and adherents, unless perhaps in order to refute them; (2) nor consequently bring forward for disputation theses, corollaries, questions or problems on them, and if anyone does otherwise he is to be removed from his professorship. The most illustrious and powerful Orders of Holland and West Friesland added more. Let the Apologist now go and cry out that the counsels of the Classis of Leeuwarden are bloody, or bloodthirsty, when they were borrowed from the very prudent decree of the Orders of Holland and of the Curators of the Academy of Gelderland. What? Since the caution proposed by the Classis of Leeuwarden does not reach that far, the most praiseworthy nobles should surely be regarded as more bloodthirsty by Wolzogen's standard, since they decree harsher measures than the remedies against novelties that the Classis proposed. He goes on in this manner: and yet the Synod did not judge them very well founded. The Synod, however, judged the complaints to be poorly founded. I admit that the decision of the Synod was not as our Classis proposed it and another Classis approved; nevertheless it did not judge the complaints, which had great effect in that the Deputies of the Synod were instructed to do their duty against Philosophical licence, both before the most illustrious Lords Orders and before the most noble Lords Curators of the Academy and its most distinguished Professors, to be poorly founded. So what follows is false: that the affair was left in the state in which it had been before. For it has been decreed, and under a new heading in our Synodal Extracts from that time one can find what I have just reported, concerning the licence to philosophise, which until now, as they say, was seen or heard in the acts of the Frisian Synod or its index only on the occasion of this Grievance. Is this what it means to have left the business in its former state, is this to have judged the Grievance of our Classis poorly founded? Our Classis is certainly not such as to devise bloody, or rather very bloody, counsels; nor is the Synod of Friesland such that, detecting cruelty, it would let it go unpunished and partly make it its own. For in general it decreed what the Classis of Leeuwarden had desired to be decreed only a little more specifically and explicitly, and that in a Synod that was not the only one. Of the same kind are the things he reports about his own little book. He goes on thus: The Gentlemen Examiners undertook my book too, and he who had attacked Descartes, wanting to attack me too because I praise Descartes in my book, showed his companions the passages of my book which are set down in this Grievance. The Examiners also took up my book in hand, and the same man who had attacked Descartes, coming at me too because I praise Descartes in my book, showed his fellows the places in my book which are found set out in this Grievance. Those who write vain histories, or rather the fables which the French call romances, are intent less on truth than on polish and the charm of narration; our Walloon Apologist seems to have learned this manner of narrating from them. It is a trick, though it does not deserve to be called an imposture, to relate it in such a way as if, after the Classis had been held, the four brothers mentioned had, on their own authority, added that Grievance, which was sent to the Synod concerning Wolzogen's book, to the rest, than which nothing can be said to be further from all truth. The passages had already been read out from the book itself before the Classis; and in that very assembly it was decreed, by the Classis itself and not by those brothers, that a Grievance on the matter should be sent. But at a session some days later, the Grievance itself, as it had been written (it is our custom that whoever proposes sending some grievance hands it in writing to the Classis, to be approved, rejected or changed), was read out again, and after the votes of all the brothers had been asked, it was at last sent to the Synod in this way by decree.

units.la: Minus odiosum fore putavit Apologista, si, quod à tota Classe & quidem iterato decretum est, ex quatuor istorum fratrum jussu factum esse, lectori falsò persuaderet. Omitti autem & alterum artificium non debet: scilicet, ut sic in partes suas omnes Cartesianos pertraheret, omne quod adversus ipsum Classis egit, Cartesianismi odio imputandum esse lectori persuasum voluisse. Nimirum qui Cartesium aggressus erat, ob laudatum ab ipso Cartesium, Wolzogium una voluit adoriri. Laudat fateor immodicè satis Cartesium & inconsideratè Apologista, quemadmodum Libr. I. pag. 80. notavi; illa autem adulatio tantopere non displicebat illi, quem designat, ut propterea Reformatum Pastorem oblitæ Orthodoxias argueret, quanquam justæ indignationis causam eo suppeditaverit, quod omnes Reformatorum Theologos contemtim excipere non fuerit veritus, dum, præ nimio affectu, Cartesium ad cælum usque laudibus evehit; non tamen ita affectibus agitur Leovardiensis Pastor, aut naso, quod dicitur, circumduci se patitur Leovardiensis Classis, ut propterea neglectæ Orthodoxias cuipiam dicam scribat tam solenniter. Videbit jam Lector alia fuisse & maximi momenti quæ merito à Classe reprehendi potuissent, quæque receptæ fidei non parum adversentur. Nec sola Classis Leovardiensis, sed Professores & Pastores alii, magno numero, post eam, idem de libello Wolzogiano judicarunt. Malæ fidei me suspectum lubens redderet in sequentibus, quasi, sans examiner la suitte de son discours, ny les raisons qu'il pouvoit alléguer j'aurois proposé ses passages toutes crües à la Classe, absque sequentium examine, aut rationum, quas allegare potuisset, plane crudas propositiones Classi proposuerim. An autem sequentia & rationes Wolzogianas rite ponderaverim, nec ne, hic tractatus docere poterit: deinde hic ipse coram Classe lecta fuisse, ac proinde non exarbitrio istoistorum quatuor Deputatorum posita, in Gra-vamine, ista libelli sui loca asserit, cujus con-trarium verbis paulo superioribus innuere vi-debatur. At quomodo adversus omnis gene-ris libros erroneos agier in Classibus solet & Synodis? extracta quaedam nonne proponun-tur & examinantur? sic Remonstrantes, sic Vorstius, adversus ipsam Synodum Dordra-cenam, ejusque, de ipsorum erroribus, sen-tentiam, excipiebant, ex abruptis sententiis & seorsim consideratis periodis judicasse Pa-tres. Distinguendæ sunt singulares sententiæ, quæ completum sensum referunt, ab iis, quæ, ut rite intelligantur, antecedentium requirunt & subsequentium considerationem. Posterio-ris naturæ, si fuissent illæ Wolzogianæ pe-riodi, haberet de quo conqueri jure posset, at prioris generis si sint, tergiversatur strenuè, quæritque subterfugia, quoties abruptas cla-mat sententias & periodos. An autem tales non sint, quas habet Leovardiensis Classis, dubitari non potest, ab eo, qui mente captus non fuerit. Sic sonant verba pag. 5. quæ pri-mo respicit Classis. Est quidem ista cum per se nobilis, si qua alia, de Scripturarum Interprete, quæstio, tum vel imprimis necessaria. Nam & omnem habet in se religionem Christianam, quæ nulla sit profecto, si non continenti alveo ab ipso fonte Scripturarum deducta fluat; & NB. ne-quaquam satis fuit enucleatè hactenus exposita. Quæ hic antecedentia, quæ consequentia re-quirantur, ut intelligam, eum hoc velle, ne-quaquam satis fuisse enucleate hactenus exposi-tam hanc quæstionem, ego equidem non video. Idem in reliquis primo intuitu patebit. Ut mera tergiversatio sit, quæ hic de abruptis clamat sententiis Apologista. Ego, ut errores bene detegantur, singularium sententiarum, sparsim latens venenum subinde prodentium, collationem, apprime utilem semper existi-mavi, imo necessariam. Non facile uno in loco deprehendes, quos sub veritatis umbra errantes delitescere velle, justa suspicio est. Exemplis id probare odiosum magis foret, quam difficile. Quæ deinceps pag. 47. se-quuntur non mihi, sed Apologistæ nocent, de Classe dixerat, où il n'y avoit qu'une ou deux personnes, inquit, qui me connussent, & personne qui eut lû mon livre. Cui vix unus aut alter intererat qui me cognosceret; ex livore igitur aut alio malevolo affectu nihil actum esse, eo ma-gis credendum est, ignoti quidem nulla cupi-do, nullus amor, sed nec odium est. Causa igitur ac res ipsa, non persona, libellus ipse, non Wolzogius Classi, quod & æquum erat, obversabatur. Quis etiam sapiens adversus ignotum se incitari unquam passus est, nisi ex errore quopiam innotescens, justam quid mali de se suspicandi ansam dederit, is, qui antea plane erat ignotus? Neminem vero librum suum tum temporis adhucdum legisse, pro-bare non poterit. Nollet tamen (certissime scio) Wolzogius, librum pro non probato haberi, qui à multis, à quibus nondum lectus erat, forsan probatus est. Quid ni ex ungue Leonem noscas? Malum ex quolibet defectu, ajunt Scholastici, bonum ex integra causa. Error, ex una pagina subinde detegi potest, cum de libri Orthodoxia, ut quis certus eva-dat, totum perlegi necesse sit, præsertim si de ea iis mota fuerit. Neantmoins, sic pergit, Nihilominus, ac si rationes dedisset, contrarium quæ Classi suadere debuissent, ce Ministre de Leeuwarde ayant lû les passages de mon livre, locis ex libro meo à Ministro Leovardiensi lectis; sed legerant & alii fratres, quibus in Classe li- bellus ipse tradebatur, legerunt & postea qua- tuor Deputati, iterumque ea loca in Classe lecta sunt postea: quid porro? La Classe crût d'abord, Classis credidit primo intuitu; quam falsum hoc sit, jam sæpius notatum est: primo quidem intuitu satis momentosum negotium illud, de quo in Synodo judicaretur, visum est; sed ad Synodum idem non tulit Classis nisi re rite & abunde expensa, prout aliquoties jam inculcatum est: &, licet primo intuitu tales propositiones falsas judicasset receptæque doctrinæ adversas veneranda Classis, nullius tamen præcipitantiæ rea foret, tantæ enim illæ, multorum judicio, & tam manifestæ sunt perspicuitatis, ut ulterius examen non requi- rant, præsertim cum absolutæ & plenum per se sensum referentes antecedentium & conse- quentium examine non egeant. At quid cre- didit Classis? qu'ils meritoyent qu'on en parlat dans le Synode, dignas esse, nimirum proposi- tiones illas, quarum mentio fieret in Synodo, qu'on en parlat, ac si nihil ultra intendisset Clas- sis, quam de iis ut loquerentur fratres in Sy- nodo; sequentia vero majorem habent em- phasin, & consentit qu'l'on en fit un grief, & Gravamen super iis fieri passa est; vox illa con- sentir, si pro Etymologia sua Latina sumatur, rem prout gesta est exprimit, revera enim de omnium consensu Gravamen illud mittere de- cretum est, hoc autem vult Wolzogius, qua- si rogatam, id permisisse Classem, ut fieret & passam esse, sed fallitur, cordi enim erat fratribus res tanti momenti. Deinde de excellen-te Theologiæ Doctore Franequerano loqui-tur & dicit, illum plus quam uno in loco plura in libri Wolzogiani ut & authoris defensionem posfuisse. Wolzogius ipsi est Nob. D. ejus libel-lus, eximium scriptum, hinc ad minimum ex-cellens homo vocandus iste Doctor erat Wol-zogio. At excusabit me Wolzogius, si tan-tum uno in loco aliquid de ipso, eoque non plura, quæ liber continet, defensa, sed autho-rem solummodo laudibus elatum reperisse me dixerim: nisi ita laudibus delectetur, ut eæ, uno in loco positæ, pro rerum, pluribus in locis, posita defensione, ipsi sumantur. Classes va-rias, non lectum sibi Wolzogii librum testa-tas esse, quamvis concederem, nil tamen hoc faceret pro Wolzogio, cum meram, ista de-claratio, negationem contineat. Franequera-ni autem fratres testati sunt, que la Classe de Franequer avoit trouvé que toutes choses étoyent alleguées à faux, Classem Franequeranam om-nia falso allegata esse deprehendisse. Non de-bebant tam publicè exponi quæ in cœtu fra-trum gesta putantur, alia addi possent, sed con-fessus veneratio me tenet. Ad ea quæ Apolo-gista propalavit respondebo paucis. Fratres Franequerani si hoc dixerint, procul dubio non ex Classis decreto, sed suo sensu locuti fuerunt. Classis enim, ipso narrante Wolzo-gio, non dixerat omnia falso allegata esse, se deprehendisse, sed solummodo ea sibi non con-stitisse, novimus autem quid phrasis illa ve-lit, hoc mihi non constat, pro pura enim nega-tiva sumi potest; Franequerani igitur fratres, nisi infidelitatis eos accusare velit Wolzogius, quod absit, si quid præterea dixerint, ex suo, eoque privato sensu id dixisse censendi sunt. Aderant autem auditores inter, quatuor isti Deputati fratres, de quibus supra. Hi, impe-trata venia, per maximum inter ipsos natu, virum Reverendum, testati sunt, se paratos esse, adversus quemlibet, coram facie Syno-di, optimam, in ponendis Gravaminibus, etiam citando Wolzogii libello, Classis Leo-vardiensis fidem ad oculum demonstrare, & ab omni cujuscunque exceptione statim libe-rare, addita de laeso Classis Leovardiensis, per istum Doctoris tractatum, honore querela & obtestatione: neque erant qui deinceps col-lationis cum istis Deputatis periculum subire gestiebant, libellus interim istius Doctoris, jam inter Synodi membra distributus & a quo-vis sigillatim acceptus, communi consensu & decreto authori suo reddebatur. Lubens ista praetermisissem, nisi justa, contrarium jube-ret, honoris & nominis tam impudenter ab Apologista laesi, defensio. Haec postea Classi Leovardiensi a quatuor istis Fratribus relata sunt, quae non solum verbis, sed & scripto eum in finem decreto ac concepto iis exerte, pro bene vindicato Classis honore, gratias ha-buit. Quae si negare quispiam audeat, ex Classis nostrae tabulis abunde docebo. Tan-dem, si, prout tu fabulatus es, res tota gesta fuerit, qua in re quaeso tam acrem, imo pu-blicam Censuram, quo scelere tantam indi-gnationem meritus erat Pastor ille Leovar-diensis? Classis enim consentit seulement qu'on en fit un Gravamen, qu'on en parlat dans le Synode. Loqui de istis propositionibus & Gra-vamen super iis fieri passa est, aut consentit con-sensit: absque ulla de iis facta determinatione, sic enim nugaris pag. 52. Ce Gravamina sc: ne sont, que de Reflexions & de considera-tions, des points que l'on propose pour en delibe-rer au Synode: ea non sunt nisi reflexiones & considerationes & Synodo & Classi ipsi ad delibe-randum solum propositæ, imo quæ minima su-spicionis ansa aut verisimilitudo, le moindre soupçon & quelque apparence de verité ad Sy-nodum deferre jubet. Qua in re Classis ita ab isto Pastore decepta fuit, ut publica cen-sura dignus ab ea haberi potuerit? An quod librum tuum ejusque propositiones aliquas expendendas Classi dederit? an vero quod Gravamen super iis Classis fieri decreverit? at Reflexionem, at considerationem solum ali-quam, Gravamen tale ex tua fictione conti-net.
