Minima suspicionis ansa, rem aliquam, ad Synodum ferri jubet, an ne minimam igi-tur, sequioris cogitationis, ansam, vel aliqua verisimilitudine, præbent; ea, quæ ex te ci-tata, Gravamen continet? Nihil si decretum à Classe fuit, in Synodo demum si decernen-dum erat, imo exactum examen in Classe in-stitui si non erat necesse, minima suspicionis causa si ad Synodum Classem propellat, ut tu fabulatus es: quid à Classe peccatum? qua in re Classis decepta? quin ita decepta, ut decep-tionis author Censuram eamque publicam meritus fuerit, imo vix evitaverit? deliria vi-dentur hominis, præ nimia vanitate & gloriæ cupiditate, sui vix compotis. Optassem sanè Wolzogi, ut melius tibi & Apologiæ tuæ quadripartitæ, ejusque verisimilitudini, con-suluisses: nec me ad partes ita imprudenter vocasses; antea verbis non pauca, vel in ipso Walonicæ Synodi Naerdenæ consessu, occafione istius Gravaminis in me contumeliosè satis effutieras, quæ generosè, ut in aerem sparsa, & indignatione justa minus digna, sprevissem: nunc autem, postquam publicè me lacessere; quid lacessere? ut deprehensum deceptorem & censuram publicam vix effu-gientem, salsissimè traducere voluisti, non potui vanissimas & futilissimas fabulationes & jactationes tuas non dissipare. Condonet tibi Deus, quæ adversus fratrem ita impru-denter, sic mollissimè loquar, perpetrasti.
units.tr: The Apologist thought it would be less offensive if he falsely persuaded the reader that what the whole Classis decided, and that on a second vote, was done by order of these four brethren. Nor should I pass over another trick of his: namely, that by drawing all the Cartesians to his side, he wanted to persuade the reader that everything the Classis did against him was to be imputed to hatred of Cartesianism. Indeed, he who had attacked Descartes wanted to attack Wolzogen along with him, because of the praise Descartes had received from him. I admit the Apologist praises Descartes excessively and thoughtlessly, as I noted in Book I, p. 80; but that flattery did not displease the man he is aiming at so much that he should, for that reason, accuse a Reformed minister of neglecting Orthodoxy. Yet he gave him a just cause for indignation, in that he did not shrink from scornfully taking up all the Reformed theologians, while, from excessive fondness, he raises Descartes to the heavens with praises. The Leeuwarden minister, however, is not so swayed by his feelings, nor does the Leeuwarden Classis allow itself to be led by the nose, as they say, so that it would solemnly write that someone had neglected Orthodoxy for that reason. The reader will now see that there were other and very important matters which the Classis could justly have censured, and which are not a little opposed to the accepted faith. Nor was the Leeuwarden Classis alone, but many other professors and ministers afterwards judged the same about Wolzogen's little book. He would gladly make me suspected of bad faith in what follows, as if, "without examining the course of his discourse, or the reasons he might have alleged, I had put his passages quite raw before the Classis", that is, I had proposed to the Classis plainly raw propositions without examining what follows or the reasons Wolzogen could have alleged. Whether I have weighed the following passages and Wolzogen's reasons properly or not, this treatise will be able to show. Next, he asserts in the Gravamen that these passages of his little book were read in the Classis itself, and so were not selected at the discretion of these four deputies; this seemed to hint at the contrary in words a little earlier. But how is one usually to proceed against every kind of erroneous book in Classes and Synods? Are not certain extracts put forward and examined? So the Remonstrants and Vorstius, when the Synod of Dort and its judgment on their errors were objected to, complained that the Fathers had judged from abrupt sentences and periods considered in isolation. Single statements which convey a complete sense must be distinguished from those which, to be properly understood, require what precedes and what follows. If Wolzogen's passages were of the former kind, he would have had good reason to complain; but if they are of the first kind, he struggles strenuously and seeks subterfuges whenever he cries out about abrupt sentences and periods. That the passages the Leeuwarden Classis has are not of this kind can hardly be doubted by anyone who is not out of his mind. The words on page 5, which the Classis first addresses, sound thus: "This question about the interpreter of Scripture is indeed noble in itself, as is any other, and above all most necessary. For it contains in itself the whole Christian religion, which would certainly be no religion if it did not flow from the very fountain of Scripture in its proper channel; and NB. it has by no means been sufficiently explained so far." What precedes and what follows I would need to understand that he means "this question has by no means been sufficiently explained so far", I for my part do not see. The same will be plain at first glance in the rest. So what the Apologist cries about abrupt sentences is pure evasion. For my part, to bring errors well to light, I have always thought a comparison of individual statements, which hide their poison scattered here and there and betray it from time to time, to be most useful, indeed necessary. One cannot easily detect in one place those who, wandering under the shadow of truth, are lurking, as is a just suspicion. To prove this by examples would be more offensive than difficult. What follows on page 47 does not harm me but the Apologist himself. He had said of the Classis, "où il n'y avoit qu'une ou deux personnes", he says, "qui me connussent", and "personne qui eut lû mon livre": that is, "scarcely one or two were present who knew me", and "no one who had read my book". So much the more must it be believed that nothing was done out of envy or some other ill-will, since there is no desire for an unknown person, no love, nor is there hatred either. Thus the cause and the matter itself, not the person, the little book itself and not Wolzogen, was before the Classis, as was also right. Moreover, what wise man has ever allowed himself to be stirred against an unknown person, unless someone who was previously quite unknown, having become known through some error, has given grounds for suspecting some harm about himself? But he will not be able to prove that no one had yet read his book at that time. Yet Wolzogen (I know for certain) would not want his book to be regarded as unapproved, when it has perhaps been approved by many who had not yet read it. Why should you not know the lion from his claw? The Scholastics say: evil comes from any single defect, good from a complete cause. An error can sometimes be detected from one page, whereas to be certain of the Orthodoxy of a book, one must read the whole of it, especially if a question has been raised about it. "Nevertheless", he goes on, "nonetheless", as if he had given reasons contrary to what should have persuaded the Classis: "the minister of Leeuwarden, having read the passages of my book", that is, passages from my book read by the Leeuwarden minister; but other brethren, to whom the little book itself was handed in the Classis, also read it, and afterwards the four deputies read it, and those passages were read again in the Classis afterwards. What then? "La Classe crût d'abord", "the Classis believed at first sight"; how false this is has already been noted several times. At first sight, indeed, that matter, which was to be judged in the Synod, seemed of considerable moment; but the Classis did not send it on to the Synod unless the matter had been properly and fully weighed, as has been urged several times already. And even if the venerable Classis had at first sight judged such propositions to be false and opposed to accepted doctrine, it would not be guilty of any rashness; for in the judgment of many they are so great and so manifest in their clarity that they do not require further examination, especially since, being complete and conveying a full sense in themselves, they do not need an examination of what precedes and what follows. But what did the Classis believe? "qu'ils meritoyent qu'on en parlat dans le Synode", namely, that those propositions were "worthy" that "one should speak of them in the Synod", as if the Classis had intended nothing further than that the brethren should speak about them in the Synod; but what follows has greater emphasis: "& consentit qu'l'on en fit un grief, & Gravamen super iis fieri passa est", "and consented that a grievance be made of them", and allowed a Gravamen to be made concerning them. The word "consentir", if taken according to its Latin etymology, expresses the matter as it was done; for indeed it was decreed to send that Gravamen with the consent of all. Wolzogen, however, wants it to be understood as if the Classis had permitted it when asked, and had suffered it to be done; but he is mistaken, for the brethren had the matter of such great moment at heart. Then he speaks of the excellent Doctor of Theology of Franeker and says that "he had, in more than one place, been able to defend several things in the book of Wolzogen, and also the author". Wolzogen's book is by him, the Most Noble Lord's little book, an excellent writing; hence this doctor must at least be called an excellent man by Wolzogen. But Wolzogen will excuse me if I say that I have found the author merely extolled with praises, and that something about him was defended in one place only, and not the many things the book contains; unless he so delights in praises that those praises, placed in one place, are taken by him as if the defence had been placed in many places. That the various Classes testified that they had not read Wolzogen's book, I would concede, yet this would do nothing for Wolzogen, since that statement contains a mere negation. But the Franeker brethren testified that "la Classe de Franequer avoit trouvé que toutes choses étoyent alleguées à faux", that the Franeker Classis had found that all things were alleged falsely. Things done in a gathering of brethren ought not to be set out so publicly; other things could be added, but reverence for the confessor holds me back. I will answer briefly what the Apologist has made public. If the Franeker brethren said this, they undoubtedly spoke not by the decree of the Classis but in their own sense. For the Classis, by Wolzogen's own account, had not said that it had found all things falsely alleged, but only that "they did not agree with it" for itself; and we know what that phrase means, "hoc mihi non constat", "this is not clear to me", for it can be taken as a pure negative. So the Franeker brethren, unless Wolzogen wishes to accuse them of infidelity, which God forbid, are to be considered to have spoken, if they said anything further, in their own private sense. Among the hearers, however, were those four deputy brethren mentioned above. These, having obtained leave, through the eldest of them, the Reverend man, testified that they were ready, against anyone whatever, before the face of the Synod, to demonstrate clearly to the eye the good faith of the Leeuwarden Classis in setting out the Gravamina, even by citing Wolzogen's little book, and to free it at once from every exception, adding a complaint and protest about the injury done to the honour of the Leeuwarden Classis by that doctor's treatise. Nor were there those who afterwards eagerly undertook the risk of a comparison with these deputies; meanwhile the little book of that doctor, already distributed among the members of the Synod and received singly by each, was by common consent and decree returned to its author. I would gladly have omitted these things, were it not that the defence of the honour and name so shamelessly injured by the Apologist required it. These things were afterwards reported to the Leeuwarden Classis by those four brethren, and it gave thanks to them not only in words but also in writing, drawn up and decreed for that purpose, for the honour of the Classis well vindicated. If anyone dares to deny this, I will show it abundantly from the records of our Classis. Finally, if the whole affair went as you have fabricated it, what crime, I ask, deserved such a sharp, indeed public, censure, or such great indignation, against that Leeuwarden minister? For the Classis merely "consentit", consented, "qu'on en fit un Gravamen, qu'on en parlat dans le Synode", that a Gravamen be made of them and that they be spoken of in the Synod. To speak of those propositions and to allow a Gravamen to be made concerning them; or "consentit" in the sense of "consensit", agreed, without any determination made about them; for thus you trifle on page 52: "Ce Gravamina sc: ne sont, que de Reflexions & de considerations, des points que l'on propose pour en delibérer au Synode", that is, these Gravamina are nothing but reflections and considerations, points proposed for deliberation in the Synod, and proposed to the Synod and to the Classis itself only for deliberation; indeed, the Classis bids the Synod to refer whatever has the least ground of suspicion or some appearance of truth, "le moindre soupçon & quelque apparence de verité". In this matter the Classis was so deceived by that minister that it could be thought worthy of public censure by him? Or because it allowed some of your book and some of its propositions to be weighed by the Classis? Or because the Classis decreed that a Gravamen be made concerning them? But you say "reflexion" and "consideration" only, while a "Gravamen" of that kind, in your fiction, contains... If the Classis decided nothing, and if the matter had to be decided in the Synod, indeed if no exact examination in the Classis was necessary, and if the Classis drives the matter to the Synod on the least ground of suspicion, as you fabricated: what did the Classis sin in? In what matter was the Classis deceived? Or so deceived that the author of the deception deserved, or hardly escaped, public censure? The ravings of the man seem to be those of one scarcely in his right mind, through excessive vanity and lust for glory. I would indeed have wished, Wolzogen, that you had better consulted yourself, your quadripartite Apology, and its probability; and that you had not so imprudently drawn me into the quarrel. Earlier you had blurted out, in words not a few, and quite insultingly, even in the very assembly of the Walloon Synod at Naarden, on the occasion of that Gravamen, things which I would have nobly disregarded as scattered to the wind and less worthy of just indignation. But now, since you have publicly challenged me, what challenge? since you wished to slander me most wittily as a detected deceiver hardly escaping public censure, I could not fail to dispel your most empty and futile fabrications and boasts. May God forgive you for what you have so imprudently perpetrated against a brother, and in such a soft manner I speak.

units.la: Posthac, si lubet, dicamus de erroribus, de quibus disputare decet Theologiæ operam dantes, &c. Ecclesiæ Pastores: rixis & mu-tuis dicteriis ne lædamus alii alios. Eat nunc Apologista nimium credulus, & me deceptio-nis coram Classe convictum fingat: quinimo, quoniam sic lubet, Venerandæ Classi nostræ putidissima in faciem mendacia conjiciat, la Classe de Leeuwarde a formé le Gravamen, mais elle s'en est retractée au Synode. Classis Leov. Gravamen fecit, sed in Synodo ipsa retractavit. Quot verba, tot errores; prior hujus, ut bre-vis fit, periodi pars, auctorem suum refutat, altera veritati è diametro adversa est. Priori parte Gravamen à Classe formatum dicitur, quod antea pag. 46. Lin. 14. & seqq. Les Mes-sieurs Examinateurs, Domini Examinatores fe-cisse dicebantur, qui id crude & nude solum-modo Classi exhibuerant pag.47. Lin. 1. Parte autem posteriore, certe doleo tam turpiter de-cepti Apologistæ Walonici vices, splendidis-simum refertur mendacium, quod, affirman-ti licet injungi posset probatio, ex superabun-danti inde patet, quod fratres, qui Gravami-nis in Synodo defensionem susceperant, gratias proinde à Classe retulerint, tam longe &[?] revocato Gravamine abest: novum argumen-tum, ex hujus anni Gravamine, de non in-sertis, in acta Synodalia, Gravaminibus, pro-ferre possem, ni unicum ita demonstrativum hactenus sufficere putarem. Enigitur, Wol-zogi, quantum abfuerit, à censura eaque pu-blica, quam vix evitaverit Minister ille Leo-vardiensis. Gratias cum suis Condeputatis re-tulit, pro eo, quo tu vix evitatam publicam censuram salsissimè dixisti, tam leviter, tam audacter hominis famam arrodere te pudeat Wolzogi: jam disce posthac cautius mercari. Et ista tu lingua exotica, Gallica, effutiisti. Si ex uno Apologiæ tuæ quadripartitæ argu-mento omnia nosse detur, non multum certè redhostimenti Apologistæ suo debebit Walo-nica Synodus. Atque hic tandem moderatum ac candidum agendi modum Antagonistis suis præfigere audebit, qui vel minimam fra-trem calumniandi occasionem prætermittere, imo salsissimos rumores non spargere, quin non scribere, non potuit. Quid ista ad rhum-bum, postquam superior in sua Synodo eva-serat, quid attinebat me personali litigio im-miscuisse; quid ni in melius omnia interpre-tabatur & ex amore veritatis, quæ egeram, orta esse credebat? nondum enim de denun-ciatione Medioburgensi, quin de ulla hujus libri improbatione, vel fando quicquam au-diveram, non studio partium, non Cartesia-nismi odio hæc egeram. Testari possum, me, simulac aliquas solum paginas libelli perlegis-sem, antequam laudes istas Cartesii in eo ad-vertissem, plura reperisse, quæ non impro-bare, imo, quorum quædam, non detestari, non poteram. Putabam seculi typhum, ver-ba assentatoria, aliorum contemtum in eo me statim in ipso limine offendisse, pios di-sterio punctos, hominem è contra erroribus scatentem pro innocentissimo habitum, vi-debam; & fateor ex tali vestibulo non mul-tum de sacrario sperabam, verebar ne plus adhuc esset in recessu, quam in fronte. Dixe-ram de eo quod vitium putabam, nihil de per-sona; quid igitur personae parcere Wolzogio prohibuit? Satis de istis. Si velit posthac candide agere, & rem cum re, causam cum causa placide conferre, bene: nihil mihi gra-tius accidere poterit. Nunquam quod sciam vidi Wolzogium, mali quid ipsi nunquam precatus sum, dona in ipsum à Deo collata colere, honores aut munera ipsi seu data seu connata venerari, & suspicere nunquam de-trectabo. Neque ex talibus ortum duco, qui & ob mores cives dici non mereantur; aut tam peregrinus in Christi schola sum, ut fra-trem amare & honore prosequi non didice-rim.
units.tr: Hereafter, if it pleases, let us speak of the errors about which those who devote themselves to theology ought to dispute, etc. Ministers of the Church should not wound one another with quarrels and mutual taunts. Let the overly credulous Apologist go on and pretend that I have been convicted of deception before the Classis. Indeed, since he likes it, let him fling the most rotten lies in the face of our Venerable Classis: la Classe de Leeuwarde a formé le Gravamen, mais elle s'en est retractée au Synode. The Classis of Leeuwarden drew up the grievance, but it retracted it at the Synod. Every word is an error. The first part of this sentence, however short it may be, refutes its own author, and the second part is diametrically opposed to the truth. In the first part, the grievance is said to have been drawn up by the Classis, although a few pages earlier (p. 46, line 14 and following) it was said to have been drawn up by les Messieurs Examinateurs, the Examining Brethren (Domini Examinatores), who had presented it to the Classis crudely and bare, only that (p. 47, line 1). In the second part, I grieve that the Walloon Apologist has been so shamefully deceived, and a most splendid lie is reported. Proof could be demanded of him who asserts it, but it is plain from the surplus of evidence that the brethren who had undertaken the defence of the grievance in the Synod thereupon returned thanks to the Classis, which is a long way from retracting the grievance. I could bring forward a new argument from this year's grievance, concerning grievances not inserted in the Synodal acts, but I have hitherto thought that the one so demonstrative example is enough. So, Wolzogen, see how far the minister of Leeuwarden was from that censure, and that public censure, which he barely escaped. He returned thanks with his fellow deputies for what you called, most saltily, his barely escaped public censure. Are you not ashamed to gnaw so lightly and so boldly at a man's reputation? Now learn to trade more cautiously in future. And you uttered these things in a foreign tongue, French. If it were possible to know everything from the single argument of your fourfold Apology, the Walloon Synod would not owe its Apologist much thanks. Here at last he will dare to set before his Antagonists a moderate and candid manner of acting, he who could not let pass the slightest occasion of slandering a brother, nay, could not refrain from spreading the most salty rumours, nor from writing them. Why did he meddle in a personal quarrel, what was the point of this, once the superior had got through in his own Synod? Why would he not interpret everything for the better, and believe that what I had done arose from love of the truth? For I had not yet heard anything, even by rumour, of the Middelburg denunciation, much less of any condemnation of this book. I had done these things not from partisan zeal, nor from hatred of Cartesianism. I can testify that, as soon as I had read through only a few pages of the little book, before I noticed the praises of Descartes in it, I had found many things that I could not disapprove and, indeed, some of which I could not detest. I saw that on the very threshold he had offended me at once with the pride of the age, with flattering words and contempt for others; I saw that he treated pious men with bitter taunts and regarded as most innocent a man who was overflowing with errors. And I confess that from such a vestibule I did not hope much for the sanctuary; I feared that there was still more in the recesses than on the front. I had spoken of what I considered a fault, and nothing about the person; why then did it prevent me from sparing Wolzogen personally? Enough about these things. If he wishes in future to act candidly, and to compare thing with thing and cause with cause calmly, well; nothing could happen to me more welcome. As far as I know I have never seen Wolzogen, and I have never wished him any evil; I have always cultivated the gifts God bestowed on him, and I have never refused to honour and esteem the honours and offices given or innate in him. Nor do I derive my origin from men of such a sort who do not deserve even to be called citizens because of their morals; nor am I so much a stranger in the school of Christ that I have not learned to love and show honour to a brother.

units.la: Referebam ea quæ mihi in isto Wolzogii Tractatu offendiculo statim fuisse testari pos-sum, Cartesianismi immodicas laudes ultimo recensebam, quoniam vero Wolzogio lectori suo imponere libuit, & quantum potè per-suadere, me Cartesianismi odio unicè, sal-tem præcipuè, adversus ipsum instigatum esse, removendam istam accusationem censui, ea-que occasione, & Classem nostram, & nomen meum, ab atroce calumnia vindicavi. Illi enim gravaminis imprudenter positi, ac de-inceps retractati, mihi vero, vix evitatæ cen-suræ publicæ & manifestæ deceptionis cri-men, men, impactum voluit. Plura nunc adde-rem, at nimium excrescit praefationis moles: cui finem faciam, postquam, quae scripti hu-jus occasione objici possent, breviter remo-vero.
units.tr: I was recounting what I could testify had struck me at once as an obstacle in that Tractate of Wolzogen: I recorded last the immoderate praises of Cartesianism. But since Wolzogen chose to impose on his reader, and to persuade him as far as he could that I had been stirred up against him solely, or at least chiefly, from hatred of Cartesianism, I judged that this accusation must be removed, and on that occasion I vindicated both our Classis and my own name from an atrocious calumny. For he wished to fasten on me the charge of a public censure barely escaped and of manifest deception, while the grievance was imprudently put forward and afterwards retracted. I could add more now, but the bulk of this preface grows too large. I shall make an end of it, after I have briefly removed the objections that might be raised on account of this writing.

units.la: Multa sanè sunt, quae obicem ponere huic operi debuisse videri queant, meque à scriben-do eo absterruisse. Quae quidem sex numero nunc occurrunt. Quorum primum & fere praecipuum puto, satis nunc superque disputatum & litigatum in Ecclesia esse, de praxi tandem aliquando & morum cum veritate conjunctione cogitandum: & revera, si mores, si pietatis praxin, vitamque Euangelio dignam respiciamus, tantum eorum defectum undequaque deprehendemus, ut cum Propheta plorabundi exclamare debeamus: Da salutem Jehova, nam desit beneficus: nam defecerunt veraces ex filiis hominum. Vanum loquuntur alter cum altero; labio blanditiarum artifice.
units.tr: There are indeed many things which may seem to have ought to stand as an obstacle to this work and to have deterred me from writing it. Six of these now come to mind. The first, and I think almost the chief, is that enough and more than enough has been disputed and litigated in the Church; it is time at last to think about practice and about the joining of morals with truth. And indeed, if we look at morals, at the practice of piety and at a life worthy of the Gospel, we shall find on every side so great a lack of them that we must cry out with the weeping Prophet: Help, O LORD, for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men. They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak.

units.la: Quoscunque hominum ordines exami-nes, semper ingeminare cogetur mens pietatis avida: Periit benignus è terra hac, & rectus in hominibus his nullus est. Adeo ut negari nequeat, quin omni conamine in id sit incumbendum, ut pietas, ut morum reformatio, ut vitae sanctitas, rite proponantur & urgeantur à Pastoribus, exprimantur & demonstrentur ab omnibus qui nomen Christi invocant, quorum est desistere ab injustitia. At veritas Doctrinae cum verae praxeos sit basis, & quasi fundamentum, non minori cum sedulitate, unius quam alterius curam gerere decet, cui propositum est Domino suo fidelem esse. Solet etiam pietatis verae praxis, non parum, ex doctrinae corruptelis, detrimenti capere. Eos autem nunc dies vivimus quibus ab omni parte quibuslibet novitatibus puritas receptæ confessionis infestatur, idque eò magis impunè, quo contranitentium numerus minor apparet, & sub Prophetandi quadam libertate, vel pacis ac moderationis prætextu, tutiores delitescunt qui novaturiunt: dum nemo derelictæ fidei reum haberi se patitur, imo unusquisque de invariata fide Reformata magnificè gloriatur. Longo tempore ipsi Remonstrantes, de consensu cum Ecclesia, ejusque formulis, protestabantur, ut sæpissimè ejus generis protestationibus non sit fidendum. Obviam eundum iis, qui vel tantillum à recto tramite discedunt. In lucem protrahendi, de quorum palliatis tectisque erroribus justa suspicio est. De Wolzogii vero in fide immaculata puritate, quod certi esse non possimus, duo sunt quæ faciant, primum est, quod in isto libello suo, Reformatorum phrases, argumenta, imo sententiam & causam reliquerit, alterum, quod hominem, erroribus Pelagianis refertissimum, Orthodoxum prædicaverit & adhuc tam factis, quam verbis, prædicet. Neque ab hisce multum diversa fuerunt ea argumenta, quibus Ecclesiæ nostræ Doctores Socinianismi virus à Remonstrantibus foveri, suoque tempore expectandum esse, ut crederent, inducti fuerunt. Quo jure autem superiora dixerim, aut qua injuria, ex ipso Tractatu meo haberi poterit.
units.tr: Whatever ranks of men you examine, a mind eager for piety will be forced to repeat again and again: The good man is perished out of the earth, and there is none upright among men. So that it cannot be denied that every effort must be devoted to this, that piety, the reformation of morals, and the holiness of life be properly set forth and urged by the Ministers, and be expressed and displayed by all who call on the name of Christ, whose duty it is to depart from injustice. But since the truth of doctrine is the basis, and as it were the foundation, of true practice, one ought to take care of it with no less diligence than of the other, for whoever has purposed to be faithful to his Lord. Moreover, the practice of true piety is wont to suffer not a little harm from corruptions of doctrine. Now we live in days when, on every side, the purity of the received confession is assailed by all kinds of novelties, and this all the more with impunity, the fewer the opponents appear to be, and under a certain liberty of prophesying, or under the pretext of peace and moderation, those who introduce novelties hide themselves more safely; while no one allows himself to be held guilty of abandoning the faith, indeed each one boasts magnificently of the unchanged Reformed faith. For a long time the Remonstrants themselves protested that they agreed with the Church and its formularies, so that one should very often not trust protestations of this kind. Those who depart even a little from the straight path must be confronted. Those whose erroneous opinions are covered and concealed by pretences must be brought into the light, where there is just suspicion. As for Wolzogen's immaculate purity of faith, which we cannot be sure of, there are two things that cause doubt. The first is that in this little book of his he has abandoned the phrases, arguments, and indeed the opinion and cause of the Reformed; the second is that he has proclaimed, and still proclaims by his deeds as well as his words, as orthodox a man most full of Pelagian errors. Nor were the arguments by which our Church's teachers were induced to believe that the poison of Socinianism was being fostered by the Remonstrants, and that it was to be expected in its time, much different from these. But on what right I may have said these things above, or with what injustice, can be judged from my own Tractate itself.

units.la: Veruntamen non levi de causa fratres in fratres stylum vertere fas est, quæ ratio secunda est, ex iis, quas aliis objicere posse non nego. Ejusdem, fateor, professionis homines fumus, ejusdem Ecclesiæ Pastores, nihil enim vetat easdem vocare quarum tam arcta est unio & communio. Semper lites illas, inter Orthodoxos, de rebus Problematicis fui detestatus, fraternæ tolerantiæ & moderationi in hisce multum deberi judicans ; pacis summus & charitatis filii, quâ salvâ, in multis dissentire possunt, vel ipsi fratres: at tales hodie glíscunt & serpunt novitates, quas inter Problematicas quæstiones si quis recenseat, næ ille Orthodoxiæ parum fidus æstimator est. Quas & proinde non in lucem protrahere, non detegere & refutare non possunt, quibus cordi veritas. At tales vereor ne sint varii quos Velthusius, quosque Wolzogius protulit, hoc ipso, de quo dicimus, tractatu. Sunt quædam, quæ meliorem patiuntur interpretationem,quam aliis nulla ratione inferri posse videbam. Et diffiteri non possum esse quædam, quæ tantam subinde suspicionem mihi non injecissent, nisi ex collatione eorundem conceptuum cum Velthusianis, in eadem materia, in pejus sumenda esse videbantur. Quicquid sit, neminem in excusando eo, quod ex tenerrimo veritatis amore, seu quadam paulo suspiciosiore zelotypia, ortum ducit, magis difficilem esse oportet, quam in eorum, quæ errorem præ se ferre primo obtutu videntur, palliatione sese demonstrat facilem. Hoc opusculum, quod inter multiplices, laboriosissimi ministerii, occupationes natum est, non ex alio fonte, quam ex tenerrimo, erga receptam in Ecclesia Reformata doctrinam, affectu, promanasse sancte testor. Quare & in melius id sumere bonorum erit, malos ne tanti quidem facio. Putavi & adhuc puto, multa continere Wolzogianum istud scri-ptum, quæ excitandæ sanctæ isti Zelotypiæ, apta nata sint. Quæ si rotunda, candidaque ac aperta veritatis professione, corrigere un-quam voluerit, habebit me ingenuum Or-thodoxiæ suæ præconem & amatorem. Nunc vero ipsius sensa penitius investigare licuit, neque cordati id vitio mihi vertere poterunt, postquam utriusque causam, absque ullo præ-judicio, contulerint. At quæso te, benigne & candide Lector, cum omnes Reformatos non dilucidæ tractationis, non accuratæ dictio-nis, non solidæ argumentationis, palam & ex professo Wolzogius accusaverit; An mihi in ipsius sensa, & ex quo fonte ista proma-nent, inquirere nefas erit? Quis majorem mihi erga Wolzogium, quam ipsi erga omnes Reformatorum Theologos venerationem, absque injuria, injungat? Loquentur Calvi-nus, Withakerus, Zanchius, Chamierus, Polanus, Walæus & ille dicet, quæ illis op-ponuntur, me non tangunt magnopere, illorum argumenta non stringunt, ipsis non satis ex-plorate percepta quæstio est, & quæ sunt alia contumeliæ signa; mihi vero causas i-stius dissensus perscrutanti, crimen propte-rea impingetur? A litibus cum istis heroi-bus sese si temperasset Wolzogius, Refor-matorum phrases, argumenta, sententiam, intacta si reliquisset, nunquam me adver-sarium nactus fuisset. Dissensum in mi-nutioribus ferre non posse, rixosi, imo malevoli & superbi ingenii signum est, at eundem in majoribus negligere, desi-diosi & tempori litantis. Sive frater sit, si-ve non sit, errores, periculum creare Ecclesiæ qui possent, ferendi non sunt: at tales mihi ab initio videbantur Velthusio-Wolzogiani. Sicque ad scribendum me induci non ab homine ullo, sed ipsa causa passus sum. Et per me non stabit, quin causa cum causa unicè conferatur: quo facto evitari possunt mala, quæ, aliàs fratrum disputationes comitantia, eas noxias reddunt & Ecclesiæ probrosas. Imo in Ecclesiæ communione viventes, quoties ad errores deflectunt, majus multo malum Ecclesiis imminet, iidem quam si à peregrinis & exteris docerentur. Scimus quam exiguis ab initiis ortum trahat turpissimus ille Remonstrantium Pelagianismus. Neque ullibi veritas minus tuto in dubium revocari potest, quam qua viribus humanis opposita est, & gratiam Dei, & Spiritus Sancti illuminationem, aliasque operationes profitetur. Pelagianismus altas, in homine corrupto, ex ipsa natura, radices fixit, ideoque minori opera hosce errores adoptat & recipit. Et hujus generis sunt quæ in Wolzogio, ejusque Seniore Velthusio, ferenda non erant & intacta omittenda. Ut levi de causa adversus fratrem non insurrexerim. Sanari etiam hoc vulnus commodissimè poterit, veritatem receptam aperte modo & candide profiteatur Wolzogius, quod si agere detrectet, sciat se incrustando & palliando, apud eos, qui partium non aguntur studiis, nihil effecturum; quin magis suspectam Orthodoxiam suam redditurum imposterum.
units.tr: Yet it is not without a weighty reason that I take up the pen against a brother, and this is the second reason, among those which I do not deny may be thrown at others. We are, I confess, men of the same profession and ministers of the same Church, for nothing forbids us to call those brethren whose union and communion are so close. I have always detested those disputes among the Orthodox over problematic matters, judging that much is owed to brotherly tolerance and moderation in these things; the sons of peace and charity, provided that charity is preserved, may even brethren disagree on many points. But nowadays such novelties spring up and creep about, and whoever counts them among the problematic questions is a poor judge of Orthodoxy. Those whose hearts are set on the truth cannot, therefore, fail to bring these things into the light, uncover them and refute them. But I fear that the various [opinions] which Velthuysen and Wolzogen have put forth, in this very treatise of which we speak, are of this kind. There are some points which suffer a better interpretation, which I saw could in no way be inferred otherwise. And I cannot deny that there are some points which would not have stirred such suspicion in me, unless, when compared with the Velthuysian conceptions on the same matter, they seemed to be taken in a worse sense. Whatever the case, no one should find it harder to excuse what arises from a most tender love of truth, or from a somewhat more suspicious zeal, than to show himself easy in palliating those things which at first glance seem to display error. I solemnly testify that this little work, which was born amid the manifold occupations of a most laborious ministry, flowed from no other source than a most tender affection toward the doctrine received in the Reformed Church. Therefore it will be good to take it in the better sense; I do not hold the wicked in such esteem. I thought, and still think, that this Wolzogian writing contains much which is fit to stir up that holy zeal. If he should ever wish to correct it with a frank, sincere and open profession of the truth, he will find me a free herald and lover of his Orthodoxy. But now it has been permitted me to investigate his opinions more deeply, and thoughtful men will not be able to hold this against me once they have compared the cause of each side without any prejudice. But I ask you, kind and candid reader: since Wolzogen has openly and expressly accused all the Reformed of an unclear treatment, an inaccurate diction and an unsound argumentation, will it be wrong for me to inquire into his opinions, and from what source they flow? Who, without injustice, would enjoin on me a greater reverence toward Wolzogen than he himself shows toward all the Reformed theologians? Calvin, Whitaker, Zanchius, Chamier, Polanus, Walaeus will speak, and he will say: what is opposed to them does not greatly touch me, their arguments do not bind me, the question is not sufficiently explored by them, and other signs of contempt. Yet am I, who examine the causes of this dissent, to be charged with a crime for that? If Wolzogen had refrained from quarrels with those heroes, and had left the phrases, arguments and opinions of the Reformed untouched, he would never have found me as an opponent. To be unable to bear dissent in minor matters is the sign of a quarrelsome, even malicious and proud mind; but to neglect it in major matters is the sign of a lazy man who sacrifices to the times. Whether a brother or not, errors which could create danger for the Church must not be tolerated; but from the beginning such errors seemed to me to be those of Velthuysen and Wolzogen. Thus I was moved to write not by any man, but by the cause itself. And it will not be my fault if the cause is compared with the cause alone; by this means the evils can be avoided which accompany otherwise the disputations of brethren, and make them harmful and a disgrace to the Church. Indeed, when those who live in the communion of the Church deviate into errors, a much greater evil threatens the Churches than if they were taught by strangers and outsiders. We know how from small beginnings that most shameful Pelagianism of the Remonstrants took its rise. Nor is truth anywhere more safely called into doubt than where it is opposed to human powers and professes the grace of God, the illumination of the Holy Spirit and his other operations. Pelagianism has fixed deep roots in corrupt man, arising from nature itself, and therefore adopts and receives these errors with less effort. Of this kind are the things in Wolzogen, and in his senior Velthuysen, which could not be tolerated and had to be passed over untouched. Thus I did not rise against a brother on a slight pretext. This wound too can most conveniently be healed, if Wolzogen openly and candidly professes the received truth; but if he refuses to do so, let him know that by glossing over and palliating he will accomplish nothing among those who are not driven by party spirit, and will only make his Orthodoxy more suspect in future.

units.la: Adversariis, Paradoxo imprimis, hoc scripto, gloriandi ansam datum iri, quod tertiò obtendi posset, non video; quin potius eam pænitus præscindendam autumo. Wolzogius in rei summa Reformatorum vestigia relin-quens, Socinianis aliisque veritatis hostibus de communi causâ aliquando triumphandi fortasse spem fecit, quam alio modo vix de-collandam putavi, quam si, ex Reformato-rum scriptis, Wolzogii singularitas, & inva-riata Ecclesiæ demonstraretur Professio. Ha-bet procul dubio Paradoxus de quo sibi læta-bundus gratuletur, Wolzogium si respiciat, quippe tam aperte in plurimis, quin in ipsa rei summa Reformatos deserentem, eorum-que causam tradentem: quam viam huic ho-mini totique Socinianorum impiæ gregi præ-cludi necesse fuit, quod absque Wolzogii re-futatione satis commodè fieri potuisse non vi-detur. Wolzogium culpet, non me, non alios, cui causa communis cordi est, non partis ali-cujus studium vel hominis favor. Me pro-pius ad Socinianos aut Paradoxum accedere, aut accedentes Reformatorum Theologos fingere, ne quidem ipse dixerit Paradoxus, aut ullus Socinianorum, quin nec ipse, cre-do, Wolzogius. Habebunt, fateor, dissen-sum nobis exprobrandi causam, dicti homi-nes; at quis non potius dissensus mutui quam relictæ causæ ferat opprobrium? sic non o-mnes, sed hunc vel illum, istius criminis reos esse videant, dum reliqui se Patrum suorum semitas calcare, imo ne latum quidem un-guem à pristina deflexisse fide publicè testan-tur. Receptas phrases, easque accuratas, ar-gumenta solida, verissimam sententiam, te-naciter si retinuisset ac defendisset Wolzo-gius: quid haberent de dissensu quod objice-rent adversarii. Sententiam, cum ea, quæ Socinianorum est, revera eandem tenet Pa-radoradoxus, parum interpolatam ; ut aliis plane armis adversus eum pugnare coactus non fuerit noster. Et, quid si aliis uti voluisset, quorsum solita, quæ & solida, rejiciuntur, vituperantur? Quorsum ipsam causam reliquit & in rei summa aliter sentire fecit Reformatos, quam revera senserunt & sentiunt hactenus? pedetentim in omnibus veritas amitteretur, si, ad evitandum dissensus opprobrium, dum alii paulatim ab ea deflectunt, silendum sit iis, qui novitates fastidiunt, & rerum mutatam faciem, ut ut à longinquo, non tamen obscure, prospiciunt. Et solent Ecclesiæ pacem, pacisque nomen prætexere, qui pacis vinculum, veritatem, paulatim subinde dissolvunt. Novaturientibus nihil, disseminandis suis conceptibus, magis inservit; quam, sub pacis prætextu, tutos ab omni, qua detegantur, pugna degere. Non hodie inventum illud stratagema est, quod omni seculo, illi hominum generi, in usu fuit.
units.tr: That I should give the adversaries, Paradoxus above all, an occasion for boasting by this writing, which could be urged thirdly, I do not see; rather I think that this must be entirely cut off. Wolzogen, while in the main substance leaving the footsteps of the Reformed, perhaps gave the Socinians and other enemies of the truth some hope of triumphing at some time over the common cause; I thought this could hardly be cut down except by showing, from the writings of the Reformers, the singularity of Wolzogen and the unchanged profession of the Church. Paradoxus doubtless has something over which he may rejoice gladly, if he looks to Wolzogen, who so openly deserts the Reformed in very many points, indeed in the main substance itself, and hands over their cause; this path had to be closed to this man and to the whole impious flock of the Socinians, which does not seem able to be done conveniently without refuting Wolzogen. Let him blame Wolzogen, not me, nor others to whom the common cause is dear, nor the zeal of any party or favour toward a man. That I approach nearer to the Socinians or to Paradoxus, or feign the Reformed theologians to be such, not even Paradoxus himself has said, nor any of the Socinians, nor, I believe, Wolzogen himself. They will have, I confess, a cause for reproaching us with dissent, those men mentioned; but who would not rather bear the reproach of mutual dissent than of an abandoned cause? Thus not all, but this or that man, may be seen as guilty of that charge, while the rest openly testify that they tread the paths of their Fathers and do not swerve from the old faith even by a hair's breadth. If Wolzogen had firmly retained and defended the received phrases, and those accurate, the solid arguments, the most true opinion, what could the adversaries have objected concerning dissent? Paradoxus holds, with that which belongs to the Socinians, scarcely altered, the same opinion as they; so that our man was not compelled to fight against him with entirely different weapons. And what if he had wished to use other weapons? Why are the customary things, which are also solid, rejected and disparaged? Why did he abandon the cause itself and make the Reformed think otherwise in the main substance than they truly thought and think hitherto? Little by little truth would be lost in everything, if, in order to avoid the reproach of dissent, one had to keep silent while others gradually turn aside from it, and while those who despise novelties perceive the changed face of things, though from afar, yet not obscurely. And those who gradually dissolve the bond of peace, truth, are wont to pretend the Church's peace and the name of peace. Nothing serves novelty-mongers better for spreading their conceptions than to live safe from every struggle in which they might be exposed, under the pretext of peace. This stratagem is not an invention of today; it has been in use in every age by that kind of men.

units.la: Hæc autem, quæ hactenus dicta sunt, majorem fidem mererentur, nisi probatus Wolzogii libellus esset etiam ab iis, de quorum Orthodoxia dubitare nefas videatur. Atque hoc quarto loco removendum est. Ego saltem improbatum à viris Orthodoxis vidi & audivi, antequam de ullius approbatione, vel tantillum mihi constaret. Scimus etiam per Antiperistasin quædam subinde, quin ex affectu fieri; sapienti dictum satis est, non enim quenquam lacessere est animus, quare nec explicatius hic quicquam profero. Possunt quoque relativè quædam & negativè non Heterodoxa dici, quæ in omnibus tamen eo ipso, Orthodoxa non declarantur. Sic memini à quibus[?]dam explicatas Wolzogiani libelli approba-tiones esse. Et quid si ab hoc aut illo, ob pe-culiares quasdam rationes, quicquam non probatum aliàs, jam probaretur, an hoc in præjudicium cederet omnibus? Possunt quæ-dam, ob rationes minus cognitas, in melius subinde fuisse interpretata. Casum refert Augustinus ad Bonifac. lib. 2. Cap. quem hic, sed absque ullius præjudicio, lubet adscribere. Sic Augustinus apud Latium in Hist. de Pelag.
units.tr: These things said so far would deserve greater credence, were it not that Wolzogen's booklet was also approved by men whose orthodoxy it seems wicked to doubt. And this must be set aside in the fourth place. I, at least, saw and heard it disapproved by orthodox men before I had the slightest assurance of anyone's approval. We also know that certain things sometimes happen by antiperistasis, and not without feeling; a word to the wise is enough, for I have no wish to provoke anyone, so I say nothing more explicit here. Some things may also be called non-heterodox in a relative and negative sense, yet by that very fact they are not declared Orthodox in every respect. Thus I remember that some explained away the approvals of Wolzogen's booklet. And what if something not previously approved were now approved by this or that man, for certain peculiar reasons? Would that turn to the prejudice of everyone? Some things, for reasons less well known, have at times been interpreted for the better. Augustine relates such a case in his letter to Boniface, book 2, which I am pleased to cite here, but without prejudice to anyone. Thus Augustine, as cited by Latius in his History of Pelagius.

units.la: Quinetiam Romanos Clericos arguunt, scriben-tes, eos jussionis terrore perculsos, non erubuisse prævaricationis crimen admittere, ut contra priorem sententiam suam, qua gestis Catholico dogmati adfuerant, postea pronunciarent malam esse hominum naturam; Imo vero Pelagiani falsa spe putaverant novum & execrabile Dogma Pelagianum vel Cælestianum persuaderi quorundam Romanorum Catholicus mentibus posse, quando illa ingenia, quamvis nefando errore perversa, non tamen contemptibilia, cum studiose corrigenda potius, quam facile damnanda viderentur, aliquanto lenius, quam severior postulabat Ecclesiæ disciplina, tractata sunt. Tot enim ac tantis inter Apostolicam sedem & Aphros Episcopos currentibus & recurrentibus scriptis Ecclesiasticis, etiam gestis de hac causa apud illam sedem Cælestio præsente & respondente confectis, quænam tandem Epistola venerandæ memoriæ Papæ Zosimi? quæ interlocutio reperitur? ubi præceperit credi oportere sine ullo vitio peccati Originalis hominem nasci? nusquam prorsus hoc dixit, nusquam omnino conscripsit.
units.tr: Moreover, they charge the Roman clergy with writing that, struck with terror of the order, they were not ashamed to admit the crime of prevarication, so that, contrary to their earlier opinion, by which they had been present at the proceedings in favour of the Catholic dogma, they afterwards pronounced human nature to be evil. Indeed, the Pelagians had vainly hoped that their new and execrable Pelagian or Caelestian dogma could be persuaded into the Catholic minds of certain Romans, since those minds, though perverted by a dreadful error, were not contemptible, and seemed rather to be corrected with care than easily condemned; so they were dealt with somewhat more leniently than the stricter discipline of the Church demanded. For with so many and such great writings of the Church running back and forth between the Apostolic See and the African bishops, and with the records of this cause drawn up at that see in the presence and reply of Caelestius, what letter of Pope Zosimus of venerable memory, what statement is to be found, in which he commanded that a man must be believed to be born without any fault of original sin? Nowhere did he say this; nowhere at all did he write it.

units.la: Sed cum hoc Cælestius in libello suo posuisset, inter illa duntaxat, de quibus sese adhuc dubitare & instrui velle confessus est, in homine acerrimi ingeingenii, qui profecto si corrigeretur, plurimis profuisset, voluntas emendationis, non sal-sitas dogmatis approbata est; Et propterea libellus ejus Catholicus dictus est; si quaforte aliter sapit quam veritas exigit, non ea certif-sime definire, sed detecta ac demonstrata re-spuere. Postquam vero literis ex Aphricanis partibus Romam missis, de Cælestii callidi-tate certiores facti erant Romani: non suf-ficere hominibus tardioribus & sollicitioribus, quod se generaliter Innocentii Episcopi literis consentire fatebatur, sed aperte eum debere Anathematizare, quæ in suo libello prava po-suerat, ne si id non fecisset, multi parum intel-ligentes, magis in libello ejus illa fidei venena à Sede Apostolica crederent approbata, propterea quod ab illa dictum erat, eum libellum esse Ca-tholicum, quam emendata, propter illud quod se Papæ Innocentii literis consentire ipse respondera-rat. Sed si, quod absit, ita fuisset de Cælestio vel Pelagio in Romana Ecclesia judicatum, ut illa eorum dogmata, quæ in ipsis & cum ipsis Papa Innocentius damnaverat, approbanda & tenen-da pronunciarentur, ex hoc esset potius præva-ricationis nota Romanis inurenda. Hactenus Augustinus. Fieri etiam potest, ut alia quæ-dam, circa idem opus, hic aut ille consideret, quæ alii, aut negligunt, aut consideranda non putant. Ego postquam Velthuisium, Wol-zogio tam serio tam sæpe laudatum, quin Or-thodoxum declaratum, animadverti, duum-virum istorum sententias, mutuæ elucidatio-nis causa, in eodem saltem doctrinæ capite, conferendas & comparandas sibi invicem esse, æquum & utile judicavi: quo facto non pa-rum aucta est mihi, de Wolzogiana minus pura doctrina, suspicio. Quicquid sit, à Classe nostra variæ ejusdem libelli theses rejectæ sunt, quas propterea à me itidem rejici nihil vetat ; præsertim cum Classis nostræ judi-cium, juxta cum aliis aliorum improbationi-bus, omnes subsecutas approbationes ante-vertat & fortassis avertere potuisset. Liceat mihi, & Classis nostræ, & tot summorum virorum judiciis impune subscribere. Primus qui mihi quicquam de hoc libello scripsit, vir doctus idem sentire cum Paradoxo Wolzogio judicat, dicitque libellum esse scandalosum ac prophanum & de Spiritu S. loqui ac si in medio Barbarorum aut Scytharum educatus esset ejus author. Nec tamen tum temporis de Me-dioburgensi Censura quicquam ille juxta me-cum audiverat.
units.tr: But when Caelestius had put this in his booklet, among those points about which he confessed that he still doubted and wished to be instructed, in a man of the keenest wit, who indeed, if he had been corrected, would have profited very many, the willingness to amend was approved, not the falsity of the doctrine; and for that reason his booklet was called Catholic. If perhaps he thinks otherwise than truth requires, the Church should not define these things with certainty, but reject them once they have been detected and demonstrated. But after the Romans were made more certain, by letters sent to Rome from the African regions, of the cunning of Caelestius, it was not enough for the slower and more anxious men that he confessed he agreed in general with the letters of Bishop Innocent; he ought plainly to anathematize what he had set down as perverse in his booklet, lest, if he did not do so, many less perceptive men should believe that those poisons of faith were approved by the Apostolic See in his booklet, because it had been said by that see that the booklet was Catholic, rather than corrected, on account of his reply that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent. But if, which God forbid, it had been so judged in the Roman Church concerning Caelestius or Pelagius, that those doctrines of theirs which Pope Innocent had condemned in them and along with them were pronounced to be approved and to be held, the mark of prevarication would rather have been branded upon the Romans. Thus far Augustine. It may also happen that one man, or another, considers certain other points concerning the same work, which others either neglect or do not think should be considered. After I observed that Velthuysen, so seriously and so often praised by Wolzogen, had been declared orthodox, I judged it fair and useful, for the sake of mutual clarification, that the opinions of these two men be compared and set side by side at least in the same chapter of doctrine; and by doing so my suspicion of Wolzogen's less pure doctrine was not a little increased. Whatever the case, various theses of the same booklet were rejected by our Classis, which therefore I am likewise not forbidden to reject; especially since the judgment of our Classis, together with the disapprovals of others, anticipates all the approvals that followed, and perhaps could have averted them. Let me, and our Classis, and the judgments of so many eminent men, subscribe without penalty. The first man who wrote to me anything about this booklet, a learned man, judges that he thinks the same as the paradox of Wolzogen, and says that the booklet is scandalous and profane, and speaks of the Holy Spirit as though its author had been brought up among barbarians or Scythians. Yet at that time he had not heard anything from me about the Middelburg censure.

units.la: Nec illud, quod quinto loco fortassis quis excipiet, majoris momenti est, correcta ni-mirum esse & rite explicata in Orthodoxa fi-de, morari quæ lectorem in priori libello po-tuissent : saltem illo posteriore libro intacto, priorem refutandum non fuisse. Scio equi-dem paratam ipsi Authori cunctisque ipsius fautoribus hanc exceptionem fore. At nullius plane momenti eam esse deprehendet, quisquis bene consideraverit, tam ante editam fi-dem istam Orthodoxam, quin ante visam Censuram Medioburgensem, pleraque nunc refutata, à me notata fuisse, & hunc fere in ordinem digesta. Postquam vero, de Orthodoxa fide edenda, subaudiveram, opusculum meum, longo satis tempore, donec eam per-legissem, valere jussi. Et revera mihi ab omni adversus Wolzogium scriptione temperare, si correctos errores & integram salvamque Orthodoxiam viderem, decretum erat, quod præter conscientiam meam, testari possent aliquot amici, quin testati sunt conjunctissimi Collegæ in Epistola ad quosdam Zelandos fratres, super libello Wolzogiano, data. Ut in prima hujus opusculi delineatione Fidem Orthodoxam respicere non potuerim. Quo-minus autem, ea edita, non mutaverim pro-positum, hæc erat ratio, tum quod & longe, imo plerumque alia me respexisse, quam Fra-tres Medioburgenses, diversaque plane me-thodo rem totam complexum esse, deprehen-debam, adeo ut novum laborem mea poscere judicarem, quod ex collatione patebit ad ocu-lum; tum etiam quod in iis quæ cum Medio-burgensibus eadem subinde dixi, difficulta-tem omnem non tulerit, sed auctiorem, novo scripto, reddiderit, & suspicionem magis fir-matam ac fundatam. Aliquoties contraria do-centem, subinde subterfugientem, nunc Ar-minianorum exceptionibus sua expedientem offendi: quarum unam, ante visam Ortho-doxam fidem, mihi ipsi objectam, Libr. II. p. 124. & 126. & postea in Orthodoxa fide re-pertam, speciminis gratia Lectori exhibeo. Urgetur Wolzogius, quod in Interpretatione & intellectione Scripturæ non satis multa tri-buat Spiritui, & ecce idem plane, quod Re-monstrantibus hisce regerere est solitum, ha-bet noster in Orthodoxa fide sæpius, pag. 7. 116. 166. 266. sic pag. 280. §. 11. Hic rursus de fide & conversione agit. Non est ea res La-badie, inter te & me controversiosa. & III. Hic rursus agit de conversione & gratia regene-rante, &c. Ac si ad eliciendum actum spiri-tualis intellectionis circa sacram Scripturam minus gratiæ requireretur, quam ad actum aliquem fidei aut conversionis : vel homo minus ad spiritualem intelligentiam, quam ad fidem & conversionem ineptus esset. Ex Epi-scopio ducta est, & Pelagianismi semina prodidit ista evasio, prout in ipso Tractatu demonstravi. At ne viderer me aliorum rixis immiscere, hanc Orthodoxam fidem facili alias negotio detegendam & refutandam, Authori suo relinquere consultum duxi. Nolui studio partium vel tantillum dare, vel dedisse videri. Censuram vero Ecclesiæ Mediobur-gensis si defendissem, aut Orthodoxam Fidem si refutassem, scio quantas de curata per me re aliena & me non spectante, querelas excitaturus fuissem. Maxima cum cura & zelo, ne quis sese iis immisceat, prospectum est. Hoc in genere dico, plurima non correcta sed magis corrupta prodiisse. In plurimis mea non tangi, tam sunt a meis, quæ Mediobur-genses notarunt, diversa. Hinc ad Stricturas meas ad Libr. Wolz. I. p. 8,9. 12. 15, 16, 17. 19, 20. ut & ad omnes quas in Libr. II. scripsi, plane nihil in Orthodoxa fide reperiet Lector. Ad reliquas quæ dixit, ea scopo Me-dioburgensium adaptanda erant, qui cum a meo in iisdem sæpissimè sit diversus; hinc, ut ut ad eadem, quæ ego perstrinxi, verba, vindicanda quicquam dixerit, non tamen a me motas difficultates solvit, quin nec solvere potuit nondum motas. In summa quoque rei, idem adhuc sustinet rationis arbitrium & usum normalem, qui error alia plane methodo a me refutatus, hactenus Wolzogio corrigendus restat. Attamen si audiverim id velle nostrum, aut ejus fautores, facili negotio tectos & palliatos in Orthodoxa fide illa erro-res, in lucem protraham: modo me in alieno ulcere tunc unguem esse non prætexant alii.
units.tr: Nor is that objection, which perhaps someone will raise as the fifth point, of greater weight: namely, that the errors in the earlier book could have been corrected and properly explained in the Orthodox Faith, so that the earlier book need not have been refuted, at least while the later book is left untouched. I know indeed that this objection will be ready for the author himself and for all his supporters. But anyone who has considered the matter well will find it to be of no importance at all: for many of the points now refuted, which I had noted, and had arranged in roughly this order, existed before that Orthodox Faith was published, and even before the Middelburg censure was seen. Indeed, when I had heard that the Orthodox Faith was to be published, I set aside my little work for a fairly long time, until I had read it through. And in truth I had resolved to refrain from all writing against Wolzogen, if I saw the errors corrected and the whole Orthodoxy safe; my conscience is witness, and several friends could testify to this, as indeed my most intimate colleagues did in their letter to some Zeeland brethren concerning Wolzogen's booklet. Yet in the first outline of this little work I could not have had regard for the Orthodox Faith. As to why I did not change my purpose once it was published, the reason was this: first, because I found that I had in view, and at length mostly other things, than the Middelburg brethren, and had embraced the whole matter by a plainly different method, so that I judged my labour to require a new work, as will be clear to the eye from a comparison; and second, because in those things which I had said at times in the same way as the Middelburg brethren, he had not borne the whole difficulty, but by his new writing had made it greater, and my suspicion more firm and well founded. At times I found him teaching contrary things, at times slipping away, now extricating himself with the objections of the Arminians; one of these, put to me before the Orthodox Faith was seen, is in Book II, pp. 124 and 126, and later found in the Orthodox Faith, I set before the reader as a sample. Wolzogen is pressed because he does not ascribe enough to the Spirit in the interpretation and understanding of Scripture; and lo, our author in the Orthodox Faith repeats the very same thing, which is customary to hurl at the Remonstrants, and very often at pp. 7, 116, 166, 266; likewise at p. 280, §11: Here again he treats of faith and conversion. This is not a matter of controversy between Labadie and me. And III. Here again he treats of conversion and regenerating grace, etc. As if less grace were required to elicit an act of spiritual understanding of Holy Scripture than to some act of faith or conversion, or as if man were less unfit for spiritual understanding than for faith and conversion. This evasion has been drawn from the Episcopius, and it reveals the seeds of Pelagianism, as I have shown in the treatise itself. But so that I might not seem to mix myself in the quarrels of others, I thought it wise to leave this Orthodox Faith, which could be uncovered and refuted with ease on another occasion, to its own author. I was unwilling to give, or seem to have given, the least thing to party zeal. For if I had defended the censure of the Middelburg Church, or refuted the Orthodox Faith, I know what complaints I would have stirred up, because I had dealt with another's affair, and one that did not concern me. The greatest care and zeal have been taken that no one should mix himself into these matters. In general I say this: very many things have come out not corrected but rather more corrupted. In many places my own points are not touched, so different are they from those which the Middelburgers noted. Hence, as to my Strictures on Book I of Wolzogen, pp. 8, 9, 12, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, and likewise as to all that I wrote in Book II, the reader will find nothing at all in the Orthodox Faith. As to the remaining things he said, they had to be adapted to the aim of the Middelburgers, which is very often different from mine; hence, although he has said something in defence of the same words which I criticized, he has not solved the difficulties raised by me, nor could he solve those not yet raised. In sum, he still maintains the same arbitrium of reason and normal use, and that error, refuted by me in a quite different method, remains to be corrected in Wolzogen. Nevertheless, if I hear that our side, or his supporters, wish to bring into the light those errors that are hidden and disguised in the Orthodox Faith with easy effort, I will bring them out, provided that others do not then pretend that I put my finger in another's sore.

units.la: Medioburgensium Censura eadem notat quæ ego Stricť. v 1. ad L. 1. Putavi verbis inibi ex Wolzogio citatis, ni melius explicentur ac limitentur, Pelagianismi sterni fundamenta. Sic ad ista Orthodoxa Fides. In eo sum totus, ut p. 11. probem, Scripturas non esse ina-nes characteres; sed ita comparatas esse, ut ex natura sua aliquem sensum exhibeant legenti-bus. Id ea argumentatione conficio, quod, cum nullum habere alium usum ex natura sua possint, quam ut divinæ voluntatis placita significent mortalibus, frustra dederit iis suas Scri-pturas Deus, si nequaquam intelligi possint, quia, quæ intelligi non possunt, significare nil possunt. Optimè hactenus; hoc enim rerum statu, ad erudiendum lapsum peccatorem cum data sit, necesse est, ut, positis in subjecto, quæ ad ejus aptitudinem requiruntur, hominem sapientem reddere possit ad salutem. Ea jam isto simili illustrat. Quemadmodum igitur, quando nos facultate judicandi præditos experimur, eamque nos, ut & cætera omnia, accepisse à Deo probavimus, facile nobis persuademus ejus facultatis beneficio verum nos percipere posse, quia frustra illam indulserit Deus, si non possit id præstare, ad quod efficiendum ejus est unicè apta natura. Atque ista argumentandi serie rite observata, omnem Pela-gianismi suspicionem aboleri posse putat no-ster. Sed 1. Notandum est, Wolzogium certo fine & scopo hunc conceptum profudisse; tum quod præcedens probatio hoc simile plane non requirebat; tum, quod medium' probandi magis dubium adhibetur, quam erat thesis probanda; denique quod thesis probanda in confesso sit, apud omnes, qui Scripturæ divinitatem admittunt, &c, (si dubia forsan fuerit) argumento priori sufficienter evincatur. 2. Non stringit ista ratio, quæ à facultate intelligendi sumitur, hoc enim rerum statu, longe diversa est Scripturæ, & intellectus corrupti, ratio. Scriptura corrupto homini in restitutionis morale medium data, debuit in suo genere inservire huic usui posse, nisi & frustra & illusorie egisse Deum cogitemus: idem de intelligendi facultate, in statu integro, & primitus à Deo indita, dici potest, frustra eam datam esse, ni verum percipere potuerit; at post lapsum, hominis facultatibus ita corruptis, ut spiritualiter mortuus, & quod ad istam facultatem cæcus, evaserit, ita argumentum instituere Pelagianorum est, quin Pelagianismi sternit fundamenta, ut loco citato demonstravi, & ad oculum, vel exterminis, patet. Frustra eam non indulserit Deus, apta modo, primitus indita, fuerit; licet vel ineptissima, nunc, post inobedientiam hominis & tantam contumaciam, existat. Hoc ipsa Catechetica fundamenta docere poterunt Wolzogium. Ut mirum sit eum ista palliare & defendere ausum. Duo excipit 1. Nulla, sic p. 2. mihi mentio liberi arbitrii. Quæ exceptio 1. Remonstrantium & 2. futilis est. Utrumque ostendi Libr. II. pag. 124, & 126. Addit 2. Nulla rerum cælestium mentio, ad quarum perceptionem salutarem transferunt vires arbitrii Pelagiani. At 1. Hic non in objecti sed subjecti versamur consideratione, ut vanum sit & impertinens, hic objecta distinguere quæ perpercipimus, dum de facultate disputamus quæ percipit. Deducta enim ex Dei natura aut in-dole, ut ita loquar, qua nihil frustra agit, facultatis, ad percipiendum verum, aptitudi-ne, sero nimis deinceps objecta sic distin-guas. Eadem certe aptitudo, in ipsa facultate, circa spiritualia ni existat, hoc saltem respectu, frustra indulta dici posset. Verum etiam qua tale, intellectui qua tali, ut proprium suum objectum, obversatur; neque ea consequen-tia minus sequitur in naturalibus, quam spi-ritualibus. Posset utique per peccatum ad o-mne verum percipiendum, (sicuti ad omnem cujuscunque veri perceptionem spiritualem nunc inepta est) inepta facta[?] fuisse percipien-di facultas. Quod cum non factum deprehen-dimus, non tam ex necessitate quadam, quam ex liberrima ac indulgentissima longanimitate divina id factum esse credimus. 2. Astute hoc ingerit noster, Pelagianos ad cælestium percep-tionem salutarem transferre vires liberi arbi-trii, se vero facultatem naturalem proponere extra omnem usum rerum divinarum. 1. In ge-nere locutus erat & de subjecto, jam determi-nate & de objecto loquitur & ejus diversi-tate, sed frustra, non enim de objecto sed subjecto ejusque interna habitudine sermo erat. 2. Cælestia excipit, sed & aliarum, quin naturalium, datur spiritualis & salutaris per-ceptio, ex ipsius subjecti dispositione, inde-que fluente perceptionis modo, sic denomi-nanda: an igitur ad illam valet facultas natu-ralis? sin minus; sequitur objecti distinctio-nem non tollere difficultatem, quæ circa sub-jectum (ejusque, pro sua dispositione varia, varium agendi modum) movetur. Patet igi-tur itur non tolli sed incrustari id quo Pelagianismi semina sparserat Wolzogius.
units.tr: The Censure of the Middelburgers notes the same points that I made in my Strictura v, 1, on Book I. I thought that the words cited there from Wolzogius, unless they were explained and limited more carefully, would lay the foundations of Pelagianism. So also in the Orthodox Faith: I am wholly intent on proving, at p. 11, that the Scriptures are not empty characters, but are so constituted that by their nature they present some sense to their readers. I establish this by the following argument: since they can by their nature serve no other purpose than to signify to mortals the decrees of the divine will, God would have given them his Scriptures in vain if they could not be understood at all, because what cannot be understood cannot signify anything. Very well so far. For in the present state of things, since the Scripture has been given to instruct the fallen sinner, it is necessary that, once the requirements for his fitness have been supplied in the subject, it should be able to make a man wise unto salvation. He now illustrates this with the following analogy. Just as, when we experience ourselves endowed with the faculty of judgment, and have proved that we received it from God, like all our other gifts, we easily persuade ourselves that by the benefit of that faculty we can perceive the truth, because God would have granted it in vain if it could not accomplish that for which its nature is uniquely suited, so, our author thinks, if this line of argument is properly observed, every suspicion of Pelagianism can be removed. But: 1. It must be noted that Wolzogius put forward this notion with a definite aim and purpose; both because the preceding proof did not require this analogy at all; and because the means of proof used is more doubtful than the thesis to be proved; and finally because the thesis to be proved is admitted by all who acknowledge the divinity of Scripture, and (if perhaps it was doubtful) is sufficiently established by the former argument. 2. This reasoning, which is drawn from the faculty of understanding, does not hold, for in the present state of things the case of Scripture and that of the corrupt understanding are quite different. Scripture, given to fallen man as the moral means of restoration, ought to be able to serve this purpose in its own kind, unless we are to think that God has acted in vain and deceptively. The same may be said of the faculty of understanding in the state of integrity, first implanted by God: it would be given in vain if it could not perceive the truth. But after the fall, with man's faculties so corrupted that he has become spiritually dead and blind as regards that faculty, to frame the argument in this way is the method of the Pelagians, and it lays the foundations of Pelagianism, as I demonstrated in the passage cited, and it is plain at a glance, or rather at a distance. God has not given the faculty in vain if it was suitable when first implanted, even though now, after man's disobedience and such great obstinacy, it may exist in the most unfit state. The catechetical fundamentals themselves can teach Wolzogius this. It is remarkable that he has dared to cover up and defend these things. He makes two exceptions. 1. There is no mention of free will, he says at p. 2. This exception is trivial, and it is the same as that of the Remonstrants, and the second is futile too. I showed both in Book II, pp. 124 and 126. He adds 2. There is no mention of heavenly things, to whose saving perception the powers of the Pelagian will are transferred. But 1. Here we are concerned with the consideration of the subject, not the object, so it is vain and irrelevant to distinguish here the objects which we perceive, while we are discussing the faculty which perceives. For you would distinguish the objects far too late, since the faculty's fitness for perceiving the truth is deduced from the nature or, so to speak, the disposition of God, by which he does nothing in vain. Certainly the same fitness, if it did not exist in the faculty itself with regard to spiritual things, could be said to have been granted in vain, at least in that respect. But even as such, the understanding as such is directed to its own proper object; and this consequence follows no less in natural things than in spiritual. For the faculty of perceiving any truth might have been rendered unfit through sin (just as it is now unfit for any spiritual perception of any truth whatever). When we find that this has not happened, we believe that it was not done from some necessity, but from the most free and most indulgent longanimity of God. 2. Our author cleverly adds that the Pelagians transfer the powers of free will to the saving perception of heavenly things, but he himself puts forward a natural faculty apart from all use of divine things. 1. He had spoken in general terms, and of the subject; now he speaks determinately of the object and its diversity, but in vain, for the discussion was not of the object but of the subject and its internal condition. 2. He excepts heavenly things, but there is also a spiritual and saving perception of other things, not only natural ones, arising from the disposition of the subject itself and the mode of perception flowing from it, and so named accordingly. Is the natural faculty sufficient for that? If not, it follows that the distinction of object does not remove the difficulty, which arises concerning the subject (and its manner of acting, which varies according to its varying disposition). It is plain, then, that what Wolzogius has scattered as the seeds of Pelagianism is not removed but encrusted over.

units.la: Ad ea quæ perstrinxi Stricturà vii. pag. 13, hæc addo. Inventam veritatem & detectam adhibitæ diligentiæ præmium esse & mercedem. Quam tamen absolutè non debeat Deus, diligentiam licet adhiberemus omnem. Postquam vero se promissis obstrinxit, certo diligentiam illam hanc mercedem post se trahere. Absolutè tamen inanitatem adscribi Deo, ob denegatam diligentiæ istam mercedem, non posse: nisi Papismi & meritorum de condigno ut Pelagianismi ponat fundamenta. Nihil autem quod mea infringat hic author.
units.tr: To those points which I touched on in Strictura vii, p. 13, I add the following. The discovery of truth is the reward and recompense of diligence applied. Yet God owes this diligence nothing absolutely, even if we applied all diligence. But after he has bound himself by promises, it is certain that diligence draws this reward after it. Yet it cannot be ascribed absolutely to God that he is unfair in withholding this reward from diligence, unless one lays the foundations of Popery and of merit of condignity, as of Pelagianism. Nothing here, however, which weakens my position is put forward by this author.

units.la: Stricturà decima pro Dei veracitate, adversus omnem fallendi potentiam, egi pag. 19. Hic errorem incrustat, non corrigit. In Deo, huc redit malesana Philosophatio, vult illas perfectiones esse, quibus, si eas vellet, aut posset velle, fallaciæ struendæ impendere, fallere profecto posset: atque sic dicendum esse, Deum posse fallere si velit. Sed 1. Est nugacissima principii petitio, hoc enim quæritur an quicquam sit in Deo, quapropter fallere posse dicendus sit. 2. Neque sic evitat argumentorum vires: iis enim hoc conficitur, non dicendum Deum posse, quod nullo modo velle potest, quod sanctitati repugnat, imo quod contradictionem implicat. 3. Quin idem, absit blasphemia, de quibuscunque peccatis & sceleribus dici posset: quidni, cum Deus ingenio & sapientia, & infinitis aliis di-vinis facultatibus polleat, falsum cultum, idolatriam ingeniosissimam excogitare, veritatem omnem insolubilibus argutiis perplexam reddere, imo omnia, quæ subtile requirunt
units.tr: In my Strictura x, on the veracity of God, against every power of deceiving, I dealt with this at p. 19. Here he encrusts the error, he does not correct it. Here the sickly philosophy comes back to this: he wants those perfections to exist in God by which, if he wished or were able to wish it, he could certainly deceive, by devising deceptions; and so it must be said that God can deceive if he wishes. But 1. This is the most trifling begging of the question, for what is asked is whether there is anything in God on account of which he should be said to be able to deceive. 2. Nor does he thus escape the force of the arguments; for by them it is established that God should not be said to be able to do what he can in no way wish, what is repugnant to holiness, indeed what implies a contradiction. 3. Indeed, without blasphemy be it said, the same could be said of any sins and crimes whatever: why not say that, since God excels in cleverness and wisdom, and in infinite other divine faculties, he could devise a most ingenious false worship and idolatry, render all truth perplexed with insoluble subtleties, indeed commit all those crimes which require subtle and keen wit?

units.la: **** & sagax ingenium, scelera patrare posse, dici queat? Verum quidem est, quod habet Orthod. fid. pag. 39. posse aliquid Deum quod nolit: sed nihil ad rem facit, non enim quaeritur an aliquid possit, quod non velit esse-ctum dare; sed an dici debeat, Deum exequi quicquam & efficere posse, quod voluntati, quin omni perfectioni absolute repugnet, ut velle possit. Hoc probet Wolzogius. Non ita pollet ingenio, ut vano subterfugio im-ponat lectori noster Orthodoxus. 4. Rogo an hoc deceat reverentiam, quam summo debe-mus Numini. Siccine homuncioni vanissimae ratiocinationi indulgere licet? Seraphini tecta facie Trisagion semper ingeminent & summa cum veneratione adorent sanctissimam Majestatem: vermis interim tam periculosa, tam absona attribuet veraci Israelis Deo. Eant nunc Cartesiani, modestum illud Philosopho-rum genus, & Scholasticis Theologis suam, ob involuta Dei abdita sacraria, temeritatem exprobrent & audaciam: ego, vel hoc uno specimine, cunctis palmam praeripuisse contendo Wolzogium. Tricas, nodos, problemata absurda, vana, prophana, ab aliis posthac exspectet lector, praeterquam à Scholasticis,
units.tr: And now let the Cartesians go, that modest class of philosophers, and reproach the scholastic theologians for their rashness and audacity over the hidden sanctuaries of God: I, from this one specimen alone, maintain that Wolzogius has carried off the palm from all. Let the reader hereafter expect quibbles, knots, and absurd, vain and profane problems from anyone except the Scholastics. My Orthodox man, for his part, does not have such a talent for cleverness that he can impose on the reader by vain evasion. 4.
