I ask whether this befits the reverence which we owe to the supreme Deity. Is it permitted to indulge in such a most empty little argument? The seraphim with veiled faces ever repeat the Trisagion and worship the most holy Majesty with the highest reverence; meanwhile the worm assigns to the truthful God of Israel something so dangerous and so discordant. And if you will, the Cartesians may now go, and rebuke the scholastic theologians for their temerity and audacity over the hidden secrets of God. And as for me, from this one example alone, I contend that Wolzogius has snatched the palm from everyone. Let the reader expect trifles, knots, absurd, vain and profane problems henceforth from anyone else, except the Scholastics.

units.la: Strictura XI. Majorem erga Scripturam reverentiam possit. Ad quae nihil Orthodo-xus quam sibi de Scriptura sermonem istic loci nondum fuisse. Orth. Fid. pag. 42. Quae evasio concedit quod peto, sed petitioni meae & reprehensioni occasionem datam negat. Hoc lector judicet, ego sic de de sacrosancto Dei verbo, seu oratione quam Deus suam fecit, loquentes, vix ferre possum. Verbi contemptus seculo nostro familiaris est, ab eo [?]longissimè abesse velim, quos Deus verbi præcones fecit & pro virili vindices.
units.tr: Criticism XI. He could have shown greater reverence for Scripture. To this the Orthodox author has nothing to reply except that there was no discussion of Scripture in that place. Orth. Fid. p. 42. This excuse concedes what I ask, but denies that my request and rebuke gave any occasion for it. Let the reader judge. I can scarcely bear to hear the sacred Word of God, or the speech that God made his own, spoken of in this way. Contempt for the Word is familiar in our age, and I would wish to keep far away from it those whom God has made heralds of his Word and, as far as they can, its defenders.

units.la: Limitationem Strict. XIII. requisitam addidit; Orth. Fid. p. 62. sed sero satis. Theologum, præsertim cum Antitrinitario agentem, tantamque accurationem & perspicuitatem jactantem, istius Mysterii, semper decebat esse memorem. Nam licet de Trinitate exertè non loquatur, effatum tamen, illi nisi limitetur contrarium, sine ulla limitatione ponere, accuratum scriptorem non refert & dilucidum.
units.tr: The author has added the qualification required by Criticism XIII; Orth. Fid. p. 62. but rather late. A theologian, especially one who argues against the Trinitarians and boasts of his great accuracy and clarity about that mystery, should always have remembered it. For although he does not speak of the Trinity explicitly, to lay down an assertion without any qualification, when it is not qualified to the contrary, is not the mark of an accurate or clear writer.

units.la: Ad Stricturam XIV. vix quicquam quod mea concernat, nisi quod p. 67. Orthodoxæ Fidei, absurdissimè de Ratione philosophetur. Sic disserit. Secunda perfectio, nimirum quæ capta sit ad percipiendum verum, si absit, destruitur ratio, quæ intelligi non potest, si verum sit ab ejus perquisitione alienum. Et hoc sensu verum est rationem, cum sit beneficium Dei, non esse imperfectam, ita ut verum attingere non possit. Attende quæso te Lector. Imperfectionem rationis omnem ponit in eo, quod potuerit fieri, ut longe plura cognosceret ratio: sic pag. 66. Ut vel minimam rationis corruptionem subjectivam non agnoscat: nam quod imperfecta sit ratio, id in eo situm est; quod tam multa non cognoscat, quam fieri potuisset ut cognosceret. Egregiam vero imperfectionis humanæ descriptionem! Et angeli sic imperfecti sunt, & animæ beatæ, etenim fieri potuisset ut plura cognoscerent. Sive pauca sive multa, sive naturalia sive supernaturalia cognoscat homo naturalis, cæcus tamen erit & spiritualiter mortuus; & naturaliter, & ex naturali principio agens, nihil bene agit, aut rite & spiritualiter percipere aptus est. Nec destruitur ratio, quamvis ad verum percipien-dum omnino diceretur inepta, non magis, quam si oculos habere negarem, illum, qui suos videndi facultate privasset. Oculos ha-bet, sed effossos & proinde videre non valen-tes. Sic ratio, seu facultas illa animæ, seu mens ipsa, quod ad substantiam remanet, omnem licet intelligendi amisisse diceretur aptitudinem. Deus eam creavit, fateor, & ad suas operationes aptam; nunc autem ab ani-mæ consideratione, ut purum opus divini ar-tificis conceptæ, argumentari, ad præsentem ejus statum, certe aut puerile est, aut crassis-simè Pelagianum. Non equidem ab omni perceptione veri mentem humanam corru-ptam arceo, sed nec eam aliunde, quam ex quotidiana experientia & divinæ longanimi-tatis, ac beneficentiæ consideratione, ex sacra denique Scriptura deduco. Ex eo autem quod à Deo fit ratio, si quis ejus aptitudinem ullam hoc rerum statu probare velit, is aut corruptionis nostræ inscius, aut graduum & extensionis, ut ita loquar, illius probe con-scius esse debet: sed contrahenda vela sunt.
units.tr: Regarding Criticism XIV, there is little that concerns my own work, except that on p. 67 of the Orthodox Faith he philosophises most absurdly about Reason. He argues thus: The second perfection, namely that which is fitted to perceive the truth, if it is lacking, reason is destroyed, which cannot be understood if the truth is alien to its investigation. And in this sense it is true that reason, since it is a benefit of God, is not imperfect, so that it cannot attain the truth. Please pay attention, reader. He places all the imperfection of reason in this: that reason could have come to know far more. So too on p. 66, he does not acknowledge even the smallest subjective corruption of reason; for that reason is imperfect lies in this, that it does not know as many things as it could have come to know. What a remarkable description of human imperfection! So the angels are imperfect, and the blessed souls too, for they could also have known more. Whether natural man knows few things or many, natural or supernatural, he will still be blind and spiritually dead; and acting naturally and from a natural principle, he does nothing well, nor is he fit to perceive rightly and spiritually. Nor is reason destroyed, although it would be called wholly unfit for perceiving the truth; no more than if I were to deny that someone who had deprived himself of the faculty of sight has eyes. He has eyes, but they are gouged out and therefore cannot see. So reason, or that faculty of the soul, or the mind itself, as far as its substance remains, may be said to have lost every aptitude for understanding. God created it, I grant, and fitted it for its operations; but to argue from the consideration of the soul as the pure work of the divine craftsman to its present state is certainly either childish or most crassly Pelagian. I do not indeed exclude from the human mind every perception of truth, but neither do I derive it from anything other than daily experience, the consideration of divine patience and kindness, and finally holy Scripture. But from the fact that reason is made by God, if anyone wishes to prove any aptitude of it in this present state of things, he must either be ignorant of our corruption or be well aware of its degrees and extent, so to speak. But the sails must be furled.

units.la: Unicum hoc prætermitti non debet; iden-ticè planè, ac consequenter pueriliter expli-cari ac defendi à Wolzogio tritum illud: quic-quid clare & distincte percipio id verum est: sic enim pag. 68. Tunc aliquis clare distincteque rem percipit, quando eam, sicuti in se est, percipit. Hoc est, verè percipit, cum verè perci-pit. Quæstio est, unde sciam me rem prout in se est, seu verè, percipere; respondetur, quando rem clare & distincte percipis. At quando rem clarè & distinctè percipio? cum eam percipis prout in se est. En circulum, en enunciationem omnino identicam!
units.tr: One thing must not be passed over: the well-worn saying whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly, that is true is explained and defended by Wolzogius in a way that is entirely identical and, as a consequence, childish. For on p. 68 he says: Then someone perceives a thing clearly and distinctly, when he perceives it as it is in itself. That is, he truly perceives when he truly perceives. The question is how I know that I perceive a thing as it is in itself, or truly. The answer is: when you perceive the thing clearly and distinctly. But when do I perceive a thing clearly and distinctly? When you perceive it as it is in itself. Behold the circle, behold a statement wholly identical with itself!

units.la: De Immediatis Sp. Sancti operationibus & infuso lumine, in speciem meliora subinde dixit. Omnibus autem paulo penitius expen-sis, antiquum obtinet. Aliud lumen præter verbum & quod in verbo est reipsa agnoscit nullum. Postquam multa de mentis illumi-natione sparsim disseruerat, sic tandem abdita cordis prodit pag. 285. Quid vocat internum lumen? Nil potest utique aliud esse, quam mens expurgata, quæ detersò squalore peccati, jam in-star speculi splendet, & recipit in se quam distin-ctissimè rerum objectarum imagines. Imo longe aliud quid est Wolzogi, quod lumen infusum vocant nostri, ut vel ex hoc Tractatu meo doceri poteris: est habitualiter menti inhærens quoddam principium spirituale, per Spiritum Sanctum infusum ac ingenitum, ibique con-servatum & ad singulos perceptionis spiritua-lis actus, de novo, per Spiritus Sancti imme-diatum (hoc est, non verbo contrarium aut ejus moralem & instrumentalem usum remo-ventem, sed in ipsam usque mentem, vi hy-perphysica pertendentem & penetrantem) contactum excitandum ac movendum, quo homo regenitus sic ad spiritualiter percipien-dum aptus est.
units.tr: Concerning the immediate operations of the Holy Spirit and the infused light, he has from time to time said things that look better. But when everything is weighed a little more carefully, the old view prevails. In fact he acknowledges no light other than the Word and what is in the Word. After he had scattered many remarks about the illumination of the mind, at last he reveals his hidden heart, p. 285: What does he call the inner light? It can be nothing other than a purified mind, which, the filth of sin having been wiped away, now shines like a mirror and receives within itself the most distinct images of the objects of perception. But Wolzogius's view is quite different from what our people call the infused light, as you may learn even from this treatise of mine: it is a certain spiritual principle inhering habitually in the mind, infused and implanted by the Holy Spirit, and preserved there; and it is to be excited and moved anew for each act of spiritual perception through the immediate contact of the Holy Spirit (that is, not contrary to the Word, nor removing its moral and instrumental use, but penetrating even into the mind itself with a hyperphysical power). By this the regenerate man is thus made fit for spiritual perception.

units.la: Non est mens sola expurgata, sed est propriè & formaliter ac præcisè lo-quendo gratia illa Spiritus Sancti mentem purgans & infusum illud habituale principium ob cujus inesse mens dicitur illuminata. Spe-ciosa verba sunt, quæ detersum peccati squalo-rem dicunt: at quomodo detersus ille peccati squalor est, quali Sancti Sp. operatione? Non certe, ex tuo sensu, novi alicujus & inhærentis luminis infusione, cujus natura à verbo longè alia sit & omnino diversa. Verbum quippe morale illuminationis medium est, sed hyperphysicum est, reale est, inhærens est, illud principium, quod lumen iufusum vocant Theologi. Quam longe autem ab eo tu absis, sequentia verba nimis manifestè docent. Id lumen à Spiritu Sancto venire statuo. Sic & omnes facile loquentur Pelagiani. Id lumen quo squalor peccati detergatur & mens humana expurgetur. At quale illud, non infusum & à verbo differens, quin & ab actuali cognitione, ut potentia naturalis, ab habitu, diversum? nihil minus. Rotundè te explicas his verbis: Externè adveniens lumen, NB. nil potest significare (non, nil significat, sed nil potest significare) nisi rationes & argumenta quæ menti objiciuntur. Aut igitur lumen infusum negas, aut externè illud non advenit, aut nil nisi rationes & argumenta, hoc est medium aliquod morale, significat. Sic pag. 286. argumenta è Scriptura petita, sunt illud lumen, quo mentes perfundantur. Quando igitur de mente illustrata loquitur: non intelligit eam quæ iufuso illo supernaturali donata principio, sed quæ; squaloribus peccati detersis, veritates Scripturarias quæ omne & unicum ipsi lumen sint suscipere jam apta est.
units.tr: The mind is not purified alone; rather, properly and formally and strictly speaking, it is that grace of the Holy Spirit purifying the mind, and that infused habitual principle, by whose indwelling the mind is said to be illuminated. Wiped away the filth of sin are fine words; but how is that filth wiped away, and by what operation of the Holy Spirit? Certainly not, in your sense, by the infusion of some new light inhering in the mind, whose nature is quite different from and wholly unlike the Word. For the Word is indeed the moral means of illumination, but the principle which the theologians call the infused light is hyperphysical, real and inherent. How far from this you stand, your following words show all too plainly. I hold that this light comes from the Holy Spirit. So all the Pelagians will easily speak too: the light by which the filth of sin is wiped away and the human mind is cleansed. But what sort of light is it, not infused and different from the Word, and indeed different from actual knowledge as a natural power, and from habit? Nothing less. You explain yourself roundly in these words: The light coming from outside, NB, can signify nothing (not, it signifies nothing, but it cannot signify nothing) except the reasons and arguments which are put before the mind. So either you deny the infused light, or it does not come from outside, or it signifies nothing but reasons and arguments, that is, some moral means. So too on p. 286: arguments taken from Scripture are that light by which minds are suffused. When he speaks, therefore, of the illuminated mind, he does not mean the mind endowed with that infused supernatural principle, but the mind which, once the filth of sin is wiped away, is now fit to receive the scriptural truths, which are the whole and only light for it.

units.la: In reliquis quæ rationis, in Interpretando, usum spectant, eandem, hactenus profitetur sententiam: nisi quod sæpius defæcatam & expurgatam rationem à se intelligi ingerat & inculcet Lectori. Quæ cautela ne quidem ab ipsis Socinianis negligitur, & vix ullius momenti est. Rationem enim defæcatam & expurgatam in subjecto non agnoscimus, nisi ubi Spiritus Christi dedit oculos ad viden-dum, & spirituale illud infudit intelligendi principium, mentem ipsam elevans & rege-nerans: quo facto mens illa in divinis, non ex ullius rationis aut Philosophiæ, sed ex verbi divini in religionis negotio unicè pendebit di-ctamine. Philosophiam vero, sit licet maxi-me, sit quantum per naturam licet exculta, non tamen unquam normam ac judicem, multo minus principium colet. Quod sæpe ratio est, seu Philosophia, ex sensu Wolzogii. Dubium omne Lectori eximit Orthod. Fide pag. 231. Dixerat priori libro pag. 76. Ducem esse & ministram rationem, idque duobus modis: primo ut omnia, sic sonant verba, nihil enim prorsus excipio; ut omnia, cujuscunque generis sint, revocet ad examen, videatque &c. Vis autem scire quid hoc sit rationem ducem esse? Dux dicitur, sic Orthod. Fid. Loc. cit. quando prin-cipii vicem obtinet. Viden' principii igitur vi-ces obtinet, ad cujus examen omnia, nihilo excepto, Wolzogius revocanda docet. Egregiam vero Orthodoxiam! Ego Socinianam antehac vocassem & prophanam thesin. Atque ista ad quintum caput eorum, quæ animus objicienda præsagiebat, dixisse hac vice satis erit.
units.tr: In the remaining matters concerning the use of reason in interpreting, he professes the same opinion as before, except that he often thrusts upon and impresses on the reader that reason is understood by him as purified and cleansed. Even the Socinians themselves do not neglect this caution, and it is of very little weight. For we do not acknowledge a purified and cleansed reason in any subject, except where the Spirit of Christ has given eyes for seeing and has infused that spiritual principle of understanding, lifting up and regenerating the mind itself; once this is done, that mind in divine matters will depend solely on the dictate of the divine Word in the business of religion, not on any reason or philosophy. But philosophy, however great it may be, however far it has been cultivated as far as nature allows, will never be the norm and judge, much less the principle, which we shall cultivate. Yet this is often what reason, or philosophy, is in the sense of Wolzogius. The Orthodox Faith, p. 231, removes every doubt for the reader. He had said in the first book, p. 76: Reason is the guide and the handmaid, and this in two ways: first, as the words sound, that is, all things, for I except absolutely nothing; that it may bring all things, of whatever kind they are, to examination, and see &c. But do you want to know what it means for reason to be the guide? A guide is said, so the Orthodox Faith, loc. cit., when it takes the place of a principle. See: then it takes the place of a principle, to whose examination, with nothing excepted, Wolzogius teaches that all things are to be brought. What a remarkable Orthodoxy! I would previously have called this a Socinian and profane thesis. And with this it will be enough to have dealt, for the present, with the fifth of those objections which my mind foresaw would have to be raised.

units.la: Sextò objici posset, seria sæpiusque iterata de Orthodoxia sua Wolzogii protestatio. At de ejus veritate jam disputamus, ego putem protestationem facto contrariam, de jure nullam esse. Et Velthusius idem protestatur, qui tamen tam longe à consensu cum Reformatis abest, ut de eo disputari imposterum non sit necesse: inspiciat Lector Libr. I. à pag. 106. hujus Tractatus usque ad finem. Idem vel ipse VorVorstius, Arminius aliique olim præ se fere-bant, sed frustra. Etenim non quæritur, an Orthodoxum se verbis declaret; non an post-liminio, quæ scripsit, ore forsan alibi, ut sa-num sensum, post addita non pauca glosse-mata, admittere videantur, explicuerit; sed an hoc ipso Tractatu, quem culpo, ita scripse-rit, ut ex eo nulla de ipsius heterodoxia justa suspicio suboriatur, sed è contra ejus Ortho-doxia in materia quæ ipsi præ manibus est, Lectori constet pateatque.
units.tr: Sixthly, someone might object to Wolzogen's earnest and often repeated protestation of his orthodoxy. But we are already disputing whether that claim is true. My view is that a protestation contrary to the facts is invalid in law. Velthuysen likewise protests the same thing, yet he is so far from agreement with the Reformed that there is no need to dispute about him further. Let the reader look at Book I of this treatise, from page 106 to the end. Vorstius himself, Arminius, and others once professed the same, but in vain. For the question is not whether someone declares himself orthodox in words, nor whether he later explains, perhaps elsewhere and orally, that what he wrote, after adding not a few glosses, is to be taken in a sound sense. The question is whether, in this very treatise which I criticise, he wrote in such a way that no just suspicion of his heterodoxy arises from it, but on the contrary his orthodoxy on the matter before him is plain and evident to the reader.

units.la: Varia variorum judicia non moror. Quis mihi hoc opusculo scopus sit, quis finis, Deus novit, novit conscientia, credent quin vide-bunt omnes pii. Veritatis amor & novitatis in doctrina odium me tenent, quod profiteor. Perplacent mihi verba Nobilissimi Viri & Ec-clesiarum plurimarum Reformatoris celeber-rimi, Johannis Lasci, seu à Lasco, quæ ex-stant in Epist. Illustr. & Clarorum virorum à Gabbema Frisiæ nostræ Historiographo edi-tis pag.497. Sic inibi ad Melanchthonem Vir summus. Absit hoc à me, mi Philippe, ut ego novi alicujus dogmatis author esse velim, quod præsertim nunc perturbet quoquomodo Ecclesia-rum concordiam, aut NB. sola humana Philoso-phia nitatur. Agnosco meam ipse cæcitatem quod ad rationis judicium attinet. Et ineffabile illud DEI Opt. MAX. erga humanum genus bene-ficium quo se nobis Verbi sui Divini testimonio patefecit, tanti pro mea infirmitate apud me fa-cio, ut illi SOLI MODIS OMNIBUS & mihi & aliis insistendum putem. Hinc ve-stigia virorum premo pro virili, quorum no-men pretiosum, memoria in benedictione, & doctrina, Dei verbo quippe consona, piis & verè Reformatis recepta est. Perspicuitá-tem non jacto præ aliis. Styli nitorem non promitto. Jam, sunt verba Hoornbeekii Apparat. ad Controv. Socin. pag. 88. quia disputatio instituitur, scholastica methodo rem agi convenit, & missa multa rethoricatione, rebus potiùs intendere quam verbis. Quod adeo à me factum forte alicubi, ut non careat vitio, sic rem fere solam contemplari. Memor semper quod disputandum non perorandum erat. Hinc penitius nonnunquam in Philosophica me immisi, eo luben-tius quo adversarii rationibus fere unicè malunt agere, nosque, quasi ratiocinia iniquè fugeremus, vulgo traducunt: at male. Non detrectamus cum Adversariis nostris agere utrovis modo, sive ex Scripturis ubi nuda fides requiritur; sive post illas, ex Philosophia, ubi rationibus pugnatur. Sic olim vir magnus Martinus Bucerus in Præfat. ad Explanat. in Psalmos. Scio quosdam desideraturos orationem puriorem & elegantiorem: jacturosque illud Ciceronis, Mandare quenquam literis suas cogitationes, qui eas nec disponere, nec illustrare possit: nec delectatione aliqua allicere lectorem, hominis est intemperanter abutentis & otio & literis. His nihil habeo quod respondeam, quam non datum scribere elegantius, & in hoc opere majorem dictioni curam adhibere non licuisse: tum iis solum scripsisse quos speravi condonata sermonis mei rusticitate, & scabritie, satis habituros me in Psalmis (in hisce controversiis) lucem aliquam, etiam qualicunque orationis lucerna, invexisse. Non excuso meam Barbariem sancta infantia Apostolorum, quæ, ut vis Spiritus præclarius eluceret, quavis accurata eloquentia potior fuit. Sed dum qui eloquentia valent, aliis (proh do-lor) lor ) in rebus facundiam suam exercere malunt : præstare putavi, hæc vel Barbarè tractari ab aliquibus, quam prorsus à nemine. Iaculum illud Ciceronianum existimo, ne in me hæreat, sic posse repelli: nihil minus in animo mihi fuisse, quam meas hic cogitationes literis mandare: sed propositum, mentem, quoad liceret, Psalmorum (Reformatorum Theologorum juxta Scripturas in hisce controversiis præcipue sententiam) aperire. Hanc scio tanti esse piis, ut illatinæ dictionis fastidium, modo illam intueri clarius possint, haud gravatim sint toleraturi.
units.tr: I do not dwell on the varied judgments of various people. What my aim and purpose is in this little work, God knows, my conscience knows, and all the pious will believe or see. I am held by a love of truth and a hatred of novelty in doctrine, and I profess this openly. The words of the most noble man and most famous Reformer of many churches, John Lasco, or à Lasco, which are found in the letters of illustrious and famous men published by Gabbema, historian of our Friesland, p. 497, please me greatly. There that great man writes to Melanchthon: Far be it from me, my Philip, that I should wish to be the author of some new doctrine, especially one that now disturbs in any way the concord of the Churches, or NB rests on human philosophy alone. I acknowledge my own blindness as far as the judgment of reason is concerned. And that ineffable benefit of God the Best and Greatest toward the human race, by which he revealed himself to us through the testimony of his Divine Word, I value so highly, given my weakness, that I think we must cling to him ALONE IN ALL WAYS, both for myself and for others. Hence I follow in the footsteps of those men as far as I can, men whose name is precious, whose memory is in blessing, and whose doctrine, being indeed consonant with the Word of God, has been received by the pious and truly Reformed. I do not boast of clarity above others, nor do I promise elegance of style. Now, are the words of Hoornbeek in his Apparatus to the Controversies with the Socinians, p. 88: since a disputation is undertaken, it is fitting to handle the matter by the scholastic method, and, dropping much rhetorical ornament, to attend to the things rather than the words. Whether I have done this somewhere so that it is free of fault, I scarcely know, but I have considered the matter almost alone in this way, always mindful that it was a disputation and not a speech of praise. Hence I have sometimes gone more deeply into philosophical matters, all the more gladly because our adversaries prefer to argue almost exclusively by reasons, and commonly accuse us, as if we shunned reasoning unfairly. But that is wrong. We do not refuse to deal with our adversaries in either way, whether from the Scriptures, where bare faith is required, or after them, from philosophy, where the contest is by reasons. So once the great man Martin Bucer wrote in the preface to his Explanation of the Psalms: I know that some will miss a purer and more elegant style, and will quote Cicero's saying that whoever cannot arrange or illustrate his thoughts, nor attract the reader by any delight, has no business committing them to writing, since he abuses both leisure and letters without restraint. To these I have nothing to answer except that I was not given the gift of writing more elegantly, and that I was not permitted to bestow greater care on the style of this work. I wrote only for those whom I hoped would be content, with my roughness and rudeness of speech pardoned, to have brought some light into the Psalms (in these controversies), even by whatever lamp of language. I do not excuse my barbarism by the holy infancy of the Apostles, which, so that the power of the Spirit might shine more clearly, was better than any careful eloquence. But since those who are strong in eloquence prefer, alas, to exercise their fluency on other subjects, I thought it better that these matters be handled even somewhat barbarously by some, than not at all by anyone. I think that the Ciceronian dart can be turned aside from sticking in me in this way: that I had no intention at all of committing my thoughts here to writing, but of opening up, as far as I could, the mind of the Psalms, that is, the judgment of the Reformed theologians, chiefly in these controversies, in accordance with the Scriptures. I know that this is of such value to the pious that they will bear with a distaste for Latin style, provided they can see that mind more clearly.

units.la: ADDENDUM
units.tr: ADDENDUM

units.la: BEnigne Lector. Edita est Belgicè Epistola, à me juxta cum conjun-ctissimis Collegis D. Johanne Last-drager & D. Hermanno Witzio, Latinè ad Fratres quosdam Zeelan-dos scripta, Certiorem te volue-runt una mecum dicti Collegæ, eam scriptam, eo animo ut publice extaret, nullo modo fuisse; multo minus, ut in linguam vernaculam verteretur. Adeoque nobis omnino insciis editam & translatam esse. Non equidem ulla nos scriptionis illius poe-nitentia vexat: sed accuratiorem optassemus In-terpretem, & editionis ante scriptionem notitiam: quam per temporis angustiam dare forsan Fratres non potuerunt. Consultum duximus Autographon Typographo, edendum cum isto opusculo, trans-mittere.
units.tr: Kind reader. The Dutch letter that I wrote in Latin, together with my very close colleagues Mr. Johannes Lastdrager and Mr. Hermannus Witsius, to certain brethren in Zeeland has been published and translated. My colleague has informed you, as I have too, that the letter was never meant to be made public, much less translated into the vernacular. So it was published and translated without our knowledge at all. I am not troubled by any regret for having written it. We would, however, have wished for a more accurate translator and for earlier notice of the publication, which perhaps the brethren could not give us in the short time available. We have thought it advisable to send the autograph to the printer, to be published along with this little work.

units.la: Reverendi Viri Fratres in Christo Jesu, & Symmystæ Dilectissimi, Fidelissimi.
units.tr: Reverend men, brethren in Christ Jesus, and most beloved and faithful fellow-initiates.

units.la: Jam ante aliquot hebdomadas literas vestras vidimus, sed aliquandiu glacies responsum vobis dare non permisit, quod nox nisi certò & securè mittendum videbatur. Mira-
units.tr: We saw your letter some weeks ago, but for some time the ice did not allow us to reply, since it seemed that the letter should be sent only with certainty and safety. We were amazed

units.la: Miratos vos fuisse dicitis, Wolzogii, in li- bello isto, de Scripturarum Interprete tam pro- lixè detectum & luculenter demonstratum ingenium moresque, auctumque illum ani- mi vestri motum inexspectato approbatio- nis Walonicæ nuncio. Merito id omnes veri- tatis amantes concernere judicatis, præsertim dum tanta moliri Zatanam palam constet, si- gnificato posteà quod charitatis Spiritus vobis indidit, de nobis, nostroque erga veritatem, quæ secundum pietatem est, affectu, judicio; petitis, ut Libellum Wolzogii, Notasque Ec- clesiæ Walonicæ, quæ Medioburgi est, legamus, examinemus &, ad sequentes Quæstiones, no- stram scripto depromamus sententiam, quarum prior est. An nullæ positiones aut assertiones in prædicto libello occurrant ambiguæ, aut malè sonantes ( exempli gratia, Pelagianum quid, aut Socinianum, aut Remonstranticum quid, aut Papisticum, aut Libertinicum, &c.) aut periculosæ, aut scandalosæ, aut piarum au- rium offensivæ, aut falsæ, seu erroneæ, aut hæreticæ, aut blasphemæ? Secunda: An li- bellus ille Wolzogii solide refutet monstrosam illam & omnibus Reformatis detestandam opi- nionem, ejusque adductas rationes de Philoso- phia Scripturæ Interprete & norma infallibi- li, &c. Tertia An consequenter solide, accu- rate & fideliter defendat communem senten- tiam Protestantium & Reformatorum de Ju- dice, norma & Interprete, oppositam senten- tiæ Papistarum & Socinianorum ac Liberti- norum? Uti pro benevolo erga nos affectu ve- stro Viri Rever. gratias vobis debemus maxi- mas, sic Ecclesiis gratulamur ex animo, quæ vobis gaudent Pastoribus, fidissimis revera & strenuis verae religionis, hoc est, Veritatis Pie-tatisque vindicibus & propugnatoribus. Et quanquam nos tenuitatis nostrae conscii, quam parum à nobis expectari merito possit, aut pro-mitti Ecclesiae, non ignoremus, affectum tamen nostrum & animum Veritati receptae, & se-cundum illam, Pietati deditum esse, profiteri non erubescimus; quodque tales etiam apud vos habeamur gloriae ducimus in Domino, & stimulo erit, quo magis magisque incitemur. Corrupta videmus tempora moresque & dole-mus, non tamen vadimonium deserendum, sed toto nisu impetuque, novitatum æstui, con-traeundum putamus potius, ne Zatanae demus locum. Quoniam igitur è re esse, pro vestra prudentia, judicastis, & nostrum de Wolzo-giano isto opere suffragium, rogare. En brevi id exponemus, displicet nobis & detestamur. 1. Quod Theologos omnes, quotquot hactenus sedulo nec minus docte & accurate in expli-canda propugnandaque veritate, operam suam feliciter collocarunt, spernat contumeliose sa-tis: quasi rem quae omnem continet in se re-ligionem, non satis dilucide hactenus tra-ctassent. Dum interim Velthusius, qui errori-bus scatet, Orthodoxiae tenax ipsi caput est. Opprobrium Ecclesiae non tolerandum. 2. Quod pag. 24. dicat Deum posse fallere si velit: quae verba etiam à Classe nostra condemnata pro-cul dubio audivistis. 3. Quod totam de Inter-prete Controversiam rationis decisioni commit-tendam statuat. 4. Quod in rei summa idem revera, si res penitius consideretur, cum So-cinianis sentiat. 5. Quod varios & multipli-ces diversi generis errores dictet. At, quod vobis notum esse volumus, cum unus ex nobis, nimirum, cui hasce scribendi opera communi consensu à nobis injuncta est, Joh. V. W. Tractatum jam jam prælo tradendum, in parato habeat, quo totum Wolzogii Tractatum discussum videbitis, ulteriori sententiæ nostræ declarationi jam supersedebimus & ad propositas Quæstiones hoc breviter respondemus. Ad primam. Negando nullas, &c. cum certi simus multas variis, ex istis, epithetis decorandas positiones, occurrere. Ad Secundam & Tertiam dicimus, tantum nostro judicio abesse, ut alterutrum egerit, ut potius in communi causa sæpe sit prævaricatus turpiter. Reformatorum enim argumenta non solum palam & phrases deserit, sed rejicit, culpatque & propius Socinianæ, quam Orthodoxæ, quod ad summam rei, thesi accedit manifeste. Ut fusè, à jam dicto Joh. v. W. coram facie Ecclesiæ demonstrabitur. Audiveramus de Orthodoxa ipsius fide, speciali Tractatu promulganda, sperabamusque fore, ut se tanta, tam justa, erroris suspicione liberaret, & animus erat, prædicto Collegæ nostro, pro candore, si hoc præstitisset Wolzogius, prioris imprudentiæ oblitæ nihilque adversus ipsum intentandi: verum expectationem nostram fefellit & magis irretitum sparsim & perplexum in scenam prodiisse dolemus. Pergite Viri Rever. invigilare & prospicere, ne Veritas, ne Pietas, reipublicæ Christianæ bases, & fulcra, impune quatiantur, concutiantur. Nobis exemplo eritis, per Dei gratiam, quibus nihil in votis magis est, quàm pro fide semel Sanct. tradita, pro viribus nobis à Deo datis, decertare fideliter. Ut sic veritate sarta tectæ, rejectis dogmatum novitatibus Ecclesiæ quies sit novamque vi…tam , pristinæ receptæque fidei inædificatam,
units.tr: You say that you were amazed, when you read Wolzogen's little book on the Interpreter of Scripture, at the character and conduct so fully exposed and clearly demonstrated in it, and that your mind was moved by the unexpected news of the Walloon approval. You rightly judge that all lovers of truth should be concerned by this, especially since it is plain that Satan is attempting such great things. Then, with the Spirit of charity which you have been given, you ask that we should read and examine Wolzogen's book and the Notes of the Walloon Church at Middelburg, and set out our opinion in writing on the following questions, of which the first is this: whether any positions or assertions in the said book are ambiguous or ill-sounding (for example, something Pelagian, or Socinian, or Remonstrant, or Papist, or Libertine, etc.), or dangerous, or scandalous, or offensive to pious ears, or false, or erroneous, or heretical, or blasphemous. The second: whether that book of Wolzogen's soundly refutes that monstrous opinion, detestable to all the Reformed, and the reasons it adduces about philosophy as the interpreter of Scripture and an infallible rule, etc. The third: whether it consistently, soundly, accurately and faithfully defends the common opinion of the Protestants and Reformed about the judge, the rule and the interpreter, which is opposed to the opinion of the Papists, the Socinians and the Libertines. We owe you the greatest thanks, Reverend men, for your kind affection towards us, and we rejoice from our hearts for the churches that have you as ministers, most faithful and zealous indeed, defenders and champions of true religion, that is, of truth and piety. Although we are aware of our own small abilities, and how little the Church can rightly expect or be promised from us, nevertheless we are not ashamed to profess that our affection and mind are given to the truth that has been received and, according to it, to piety; and we glory in the Lord that we are held in such esteem by you as well, and it will be a spur by which we are urged more and more. We see the times and morals corrupted and we grieve, yet we think that we must not desert the post, but rather, with all our effort and force, resist the heat of novelties, lest we give place to Satan. Since, therefore, you have judged, in your prudence, that it is fitting to ask also for our opinion on this work of Wolzogen's, behold, we shall briefly set it out: we dislike it and detest it. 1. That he scornfully despises all the theologians who, as many as there have been, have diligently, no less learnedly and accurately, laboured happily in explaining and defending the truth; as if they had not hitherto treated sufficiently clearly a matter that contains all religion within itself. Meanwhile Velthuysen, who abounds in errors, is himself the chief defender of orthodoxy. A reproach to the Church that must not be tolerated. 2. That on page 24 he says that God can deceive if he wishes; you will surely have heard these words, which our Classis also condemned. 3. That he resolves to commit the whole controversy about the Interpreter to the decision of reason. 4. That in the substance of the matter, if the matter is considered more closely, he really agrees with the Socinians. 5. That he dictates various and manifold errors of different kinds. But, as we want you to know, since one of us, namely the one to whom by common consent this writing has been assigned, Johannes Vander Waeyen, already has in hand the treatise about to be handed to the press, in which you will see Wolzogen's whole treatise discussed, we shall now forgo any further declaration of our opinion and answer the proposed questions briefly here. To the first: we deny that there are none, etc., since we are certain that many positions occur that deserve to be adorned with some of those epithets. To the second and third we say that he is so far from having managed either of these that he has often shamefully prevaricated in the common cause. For he not only deserts the arguments and phrases of the Reformed, but rejects and blames them, and he clearly approaches the Socinian rather than the orthodox position on the main point of the matter. This will be demonstrated at length, before the face of the Church, by the above-mentioned Johannes Vander Waeyen. We had heard of a promised special treatise setting out his orthodox faith, and we hoped that he would free himself from so great and so just a suspicion of error; and it was our intention, for the sake of frankness with our said colleague, that if Wolzogen had done this, he would forget his earlier imprudence and we would bring nothing against him. But he has disappointed our expectation, and we grieve that he has come forward on the stage more entangled, scattered and perplexed. Go on, Reverend men, keeping watch and taking care that Truth and Piety, the foundations and supports of the Christian commonwealth, are not shaken or struck with impunity. You will be an example to us, by the grace of God, we who have nothing more at heart than to contend faithfully, with the strength God has given us, for the faith once delivered to the saints. units.la: JOHANNIS vander WAEYEN PRO VERITATE, & genuina Reformatorum sententia ADVERSUS LUD. WOLZOGIUM DISCEPTATIONIS LIBER PRIMUS, In Universum Wolzogii Tractatum Stricturas continens: Addita subinde de variis argumentis uberiore paululum Digressione.
units.tr: JOHANNES VANDER WAEYEN, IN DEFENCE OF THE TRUTH AND THE GENUINE OPINION OF THE REFORMERS, AGAINST LUDOVICUS WOLZOGIUS: THE FIRST BOOK OF THE DISPUTATION, containing strictures on the whole treatise of Wolzogius, with a somewhat fuller digression on various arguments added here and there.

units.la: Multa sanè in opusculo illo Wolzogiano reperiuntur, quæ in veritatem simul & receptam Reformatorum fidem incur-runt; sed diversi planè generis, alia Con-troversiæ de Scripturarum Interpreta-tione apicem vel non tangunt, vel ad minimum ab ejus pertractatione sejungi queunt commodissimè, alia verò ipsam rei summam concernere videntur pro-pius. Illa transiliens lubens statim rem ipsam aggres-sus fuissem, sed multorum malesanorum conceptuum pondus, veritatis studium, Ecclesiæ Reformatæ talia rejicientis honos, præcipue vero Dei gloria in causa sunt, quominus istas Syrtes intactas præternavigare potuerim. Quapropter antequam, ipsius Controver-siæ caput quæ spectant, eruam; primum strictim juxta totius libelli seriem quædam minus orthodoxe, aut prudenter, aut pie dicta notare consultum duxi; postea quæ de Scripturæ Interpretatione ipsa dictat Wolzogius, excussurus breviter & candide.
units.tr: Certainly many things are found in that little work of Wolzogius which run counter both to the truth and to the faith received by the Reformers. But they are of quite different kinds. Some do not touch the heart of the controversy about the interpretation of Scripture, or at least can be conveniently separated from its treatment. Others seem to bear more directly on the substance of the matter itself. I would gladly have passed over the first kind and gone straight to the question itself. But the weight of many ill-advised notions, my zeal for the truth, the honour of the Reformed Church, which rejects such things, and above all the glory of God, have prevented me from sailing past these shoals untouched. Therefore, before I bring out the points that concern the controversy itself, I have judged it advisable first to note briefly, following the order of the whole little book, certain things said in a less orthodox, less prudent or less pious manner. After that I will briefly and candidly examine what Wolzogius lays down about the interpretation of Scripture itself.

units.la: Totius tractatus dicendi modum consideranti, in ipso limine, offensam dare videtur author. Paradoxon quippe vocat Exercitatorem, quem Heterodoxo-taton dicere debuisset: scio equidem, decoravit sese ipse isto elogio profanus Scriptor, sed orthodoxum & veracem quid si addisset? quidilla vocabula velint, jam dudum notum est. Melius in ipsa fronte scapham vocasset scapham, ut ne forsan Heterodoxi hominis minis deterritus videretur, aut moderati & modesti nomen omni pretio redimendum ratus. Malorum vi-tuperia laudes esse & modestiam ac moderationem illam qua hujusce mundi favor acquiritur, teporem ac vitium detestandum, utinam & Wolzogius semper cogitaret! Ex socordia factum esse, quod culpo, plura sunt quae minus credendum, probent; primum, authoris ad verba & phrases attentus animus, ἀχείβεια[?] ejus enim in hisce tanta se prodit, ut in id unice incubuisse videatur, ne stylus, ne Dictio ullibi minus elegans minus Latina foret Criticis, de re ipsa, saltem sive orthodoxis placeret, sive displiceret Theologis, minus sollicitus. Ab illis etenim dissensum profiteri, in illis obscuritatem, inter illos discrepantiam clamare, nihil est; Latinitas modo ne Ciceroni displiceat, aut Classicis. Deinde alia loca in quibus in eundem impegit lapidem. p. 2. p. 4. p. 94. imo honorifice de i-pso loquitur p. 5. & hominem opera pretium fecisse judicat. Denique quod aliquando praeter phrasin in hoc tenebrione carpat nihil, ut posthac patebit: huic certe, qui omnes ad unum Theologos, obscuritatis, Clariss. Arnoldum, virum de Ecclesiis optime meritum, imprudentia accusat, quid causae sit; quod hunc ita molliter excipiat; conjiciat lector. Scilicet dantur hodie, qui satis in fratres saeviri posse vix putant, dum interim, cum Remonstrantibus & quibuscunque Heterodoxis, placide & fraterne agi volunt: sic nunc mores ferunt & tempora, ideoque sic decet quos lubet δαλύειν τῆς ἡμιεῷ[?]. Non quod putem adversæ partis homines calumniis proscindendos esse: potius argumentorum pondere & veritatis certandum ener-gia est. Maledicant qui falsa dicunt; humanitas decet veritatis filios, & charitas: agendum tamen pro rei pondere graviter & serió, atque Orthodoxos dum quis vellicat, Heterodoxos & quidem contumaces, imo ir-risores, leniter excipere, quid jubet? quicquid sit, non est quod ego, qui frater, qui Symmysta, pro veritate scribens, & quidem placidè, sic enim est animus, mihi mali quid metuam à Wolzogio. Quæ alibi, forsan largiter satis, in ignotum σωϑελον[?], & contumeliosè dixit, non repetam, liberioris forsan oris est, quæ scri-bit magis ruminans. Veritatis etiam nunc ago, non meam causam, nisi in quantum illa mea est, & ego illius filius ac pro tenuitate Doctor sum in Ecclesia.
units.tr: Considering the manner of speaking of the whole treatise, the author seems to give offence right at the threshold. He calls the Exercitator a Paradoxon, when he ought to have called him the most heterodox. I know, of course, that the profane writer has adorned himself with that title; but what if he had added "orthodox and truthful"? What these words mean has long been known. It would have been better to call a boat a boat at the very front, lest he seem frightened by the threats of a heterodox man, or thought that the name of a moderate and modest man had to be bought at any price. Would that Wolzogius always kept in mind that the censure of evils is praise, and that the moderation and restraint by which the favour of this world is won are a lukewarmness and a fault to be detested! That what I blame arose from carelessness is shown by several things that are hardly to be believed. First, the author's mind is so intent on words and phrases (his accuracy [ἀκρίβεια] in these matters is so evident) that he seems to have devoted himself solely to ensuring that his style and diction are nowhere less elegant or less Latin in the eyes of critics. As for the matter itself, whether it pleases or displeases orthodox theologians, he is less concerned. To profess dissent from them, to cry out about their obscurity and their disagreement among themselves, is nothing. Only his Latin must not displease Cicero or the classical writers. Next, there are other passages where he stumbles over the same stone: p. 2, p. 4, p. 94. Indeed he speaks of the man honourably on p. 5 and judges that he has done a service worth the effort. Finally, that he finds almost nothing to carp at in this fellow except his style, as will appear hereafter; the reason why he accuses this writer, who blames all the theologians without exception of obscurity, of imprudence (Arnoldus, a man who deserved very well of the Churches), and why he receives him so gently, let the reader guess. Clearly there are today men who hardly think they can rage enough against their brethren, while at the same time they want to deal calmly and brotherly with the Remonstrants and with any heterodox persons whatever. Such is the fashion of the present time, and so it is fitting for those who wish to [δαλύειν τῆς ἡμιεῷ] to act. Not that I think the men of the opposing party should be torn apart with calumnies. Rather, the battle must be fought with the weight of arguments and the energy of truth. Let those who say false things curse; humanity and charity befit the sons of truth. Yet one must act seriously and gravely, in proportion to the weight of the matter. And what does it command, when someone nips at the orthodox, to receive the heterodox, and indeed the obstinate and even the mockers, gently? Whatever the answer, there is no reason for me, a brother and a fellow-member of the Church, writing for the truth, and that calmly (for such is my spirit), to fear any harm from Wolzogius. What he has said elsewhere, perhaps quite abundantly, against some unknown [σωϑελον] and in insulting terms, I shall not repeat. What he writes here is perhaps of a freer mouth, written with more rumination. I am also pleading now not my own cause, except insofar as that cause is mine, and I am a son of the truth and, according to my small ability, a teacher in the Church.

units.la: Scriptionis suæ causam tradit author in Epistola nuncupatoria, in quâ, uti verè dicitur, à viris eruditis sufflamen (heterodoxam sententiam respicit) injectum esse ita ut certissime hoc ipsius scripto plane non opus fuerit, cum causæ satisfactum putet; ita qui ab hoc authore id dici queat & quo animo, is judicet qui è contra p. 5. ipsum audiverit ita differentem, & ne-quaquam fuit hactenus satis enucleatè expositä hæc quæstio. Nimis citò sibi contradicit. Deinde si verum sit, dic qui fuerint, qui hanc causam bene defenderint, non Polanus non Chamierus, non Whita-kerus non Zadeel, non Reformatorum ullus, quorum argumenta rejicis autocratorice, pleraque non feriunt scopum, duo quidem priora argumenta non. ideo[?] quid habeant soliditatis, tertium solum aliquatenus stringit, quartum audirem nisi &c. quintum, sextum & septi-mum non stringere cum Exercitatore sentio: tua verba sunt Wolzogi p. 247.249. Certare potius uter majo-rem de Reformatis victoriam reportet cum tuo paradoxo, quam illos defendere videris. Quis non eru-bescat quin irascatur, qui maximorum virorum cogitata tam contumeliose rejecta videat ab homine non vitio? ignosce lector, si non satis acriter pungam istum[?] qui heroas illos tanto vituperio afficit, sed senti[?] posthac vires istorum argumentorum. Sordet illa, qua decoratos circumgestas in prælogio, quorum in ipso opere causam tam deseris turpiter. Quid[?] putas igitur causæ satisfecisse, si istorum luminum dicta quisquiliarum instar rejicis? revoca dictum, non serio loquitur tua dedicatio; non egent tuis laudibus viri illi, supra iram, supra invidiam jam dudum elatus[?] in Ecclesia, non demereberis assentatione mortuos nec frustra etiam vellicabis & impune; monstrabitur[?] verum tibi, præter mentem, excidisse, cum causam satisfactum diceres.
units.tr: The author sets out the cause of his writing in the dedicatory epistle, where, as is truly said, the objection (he refers to the heterodox opinion) has been raised by learned men, so that certainly there was no need for this writing of his at all, since he thinks the cause has been satisfied; let him judge how such a thing can be said by this author, and with what intention, who has heard him on the other side (p. 5) speaking thus: and by no means has this question hitherto been set out clearly enough. He contradicts himself too quickly. Next, if it is true, say who they were who defended this cause well: not Polanus, not Chamier, not Whitaker, not Zadeel, not any of the Reformers, whose arguments you reject in an autocratic manner: most of them do not strike the mark; the first two arguments certainly do not; as to what solidity they have, the third alone touches it to some extent; I would hear the fourth, unless etc.; I feel with the Exercitator that the fifth, sixth and seventh do not touch it; these are your words, Wolzogius, p. 247, 249. You seem rather to be contending with your paradox over which of you will win the greater victory over the Reformed than to be defending them. Who would not blush and grow angry to see the thoughts of the greatest men rejected so insultingly by a man without fault? Forgive me, reader, if I do not sting sharply enough the man who treats those heroes with such contempt; but I will hereafter feel out the strength of their arguments. That display of decorated men which you parade in the preface is worthless, when in the work itself you so shamefully desert their cause. What, then, do you think you have satisfied the cause, if you reject the sayings of those lights as trifles? Take back the statement; your dedication is not serious. Those men do not need your praise; they have long since been raised in the Church above anger and envy. You will not win favour by flattering the dead, nor will you vellicate them in vain and with impunity. It will be shown that the truth slipped from you against your intention, when you said that the cause had been satisfied.

units.la: Verum scripti causam habe lector, causæ quidem, at-non famæ satisfactum erat; non causa veritatis igi-tur, sed fama nobis huncce librum peperit, ipso au-thore indice, nec enim causæ sed famæ isthoc opus erat, siccine fama præ veritate vobis cordi est? famosus sit qui talis est, oportet. Laudem, de qua statim, in ipso opere revocat, ut audivimus, in hoc autem effato ita constans est, ut aliis verbis idem in ipso limine repetere debuerit; quæstionis momentum evocare, inquit, sed necessaria Synedrii quædam defensio ea demum exprimere poterat hoc opus. Jam scimus, utrum pluris facias, famam tuam, an vero Dei & Veritatis causam. Siccine decet ministrum Christi? quando æquis passibus incedunt & simul infestantur, utraque defendi potest nostra fama & veritas divina, sed suo quæque ordine, ego saltem potius huic quam illi satisfactum vellem, & dum fama mea vocat, libenter à Dei causa premerer. Deinde quis mortalium vestræ Ecclesiæ tantum impegerat scelus? quis de ea vel per somnium cogitaverat? vel an Velt-huisen tua est Ecclesia, tuum Synedrium? an ipsius decus & gloria sic tibi cordi sunt, ut quicquid ille patitur, tangat vos omnes & quidem tam vehementer, ut, dum veritatis quæ Dei causa scriptionem evo-care, ipsius ad minimum eandem exprimere valeat? nonne plus satis hunc evehis? qui totus in eo esse videtur, ut ordinem nostrum deprimat & conculcet pedibus. Quando ipsius scripta cogito non tam parum Paradoxus mihi videtur, ut talem fœtum ab ipso produci non posse judicem. Scio equidem, insurrexit adversus Anonymum, sed vereor ne lector frustra dissensum quærat, quanquam animum aliquando, studio concitatiorem, exprimere voluerit: quicquid sit, quem non pudet in maxima Theologorum capita & pectora dicteriorum tela vibrare; illine mirum erit leviter & quidem tecto nomine, alicujus criminis reum agi? licebit ipsi omnia insolenter æque ac impotenter in quoscunque effutire, & dum ipsius umbra vel extremo tangitur digito, tanti ciebuntur motus? tanti, quantos ne læsa quidem ciet veritas! omnes Theologi moriantur inulti, ipsorum nomen, à Paradoxo nebulone, violetur, conculcetur, argumenta Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, imo Confessionum nostrarum vellicentur; explodantur indefensa per non solum, sed te spectatore, sed adstipulatore. Velt- husii[?] modo nomen honosque, laudesque maneant semper: per ipsum vestra Ecclesia multis si cordi sit, abunde satis ipsi proxeneticum reponditur. Non magni laboris foret, ex Velthusianis, similia proferre, si non eadem, cum iis, quæ scripsit Anonymus. Sententia quasi adversa, sub refutationis specie, optime aliquando stabiliri poterit. At tantum virum aggredi, næ istud periculosum est. Historiam molitur Medicus & omnibus, quos novit Zelotas esse quæcunque exprobrabit. Hæc tum erit ista charitas, hæc moderatio quam etiam circa alienos à fide requirit. Pa-tebit affectus, iram praecipuè & livorem illa pro-trusisse,ex proprio ore judicetur. Mutatum stylum de-prehendes quoties fratres contra insurgit. Sociniani-zantes Anabaptistas bonos ut cives defendit, dum fra-tres ut Papizantes vapulant. Historiam tuam quod at-tinet, an nescis Medice, praecedentia peccata conversis in faciem conjicere, Diabolicum esse & Satanæ opus? quid si jam istorum, quæ putas, scelerum veniam im-petraverint à supremo judice? quid, si cum Davide peccata juventutis confiteri, deprecari non erubue-rint? quid tibi à vindice supremo expectandum erit, fratres ita accusanti fratri? tu, qui ob rationes poli-ticas, nescio quæ non horrenda tolerari posse, à Magistratu doces, fratrum nuditatem ita detegere vellesvirulenter? doleo sane vices tuas, perversitatem tuam Velthuisi! at non deerunt, per Dei gratiam, qui furoris tui bruta contemnent fulmina, non dee-runt, si in piorum capita insolenter debacchari velis, qui tela tua retundent serio. Si quis in tuam, si multo-rum Collegiorum non Ecclesiasticorum vitam o-mnem curiosius inquireret & exactius, scias non de-fore, quibus detectis, plures quam tui Zelotæ, co-ram omnibus prostituerentur: si ebrietas, perfidia, quotidianus & domesticis molestus nominis divini abusus, si pejerationes, si injustitia omnis, si scor-tatio aut aliud enorme peccatum & forsan in juventu-te patratum, infamem reddat, & revelari necesse sit, alios quam Zelotas illos decoratos videre posses. Ho-sti etiam vera dicenti vix ulla fides, & quos rationi-bus convincere non potes, frustra petes calumniis, non decet id cordatos, non Magistratum gerentes & quidem in Synedriis. At ne te provocari per me pu-tes, silentium tibi conscientia & munus suadere de-bent, idem & per me fieret, si tibi essem tanti: nec et-iam multum terroris mihi incussum cogites. Sunt qui liberum solum habitant, ubi neminem inauditum condemnari videas: is mihi scopus est, ut te malitiae tuae convincam & Sycophantam agere desinas: malè promissis rescinde fidem. Interim bona conscientia quae mihi solatio est, hoc suggerat, quod laus sit ho-minis maxima displicere pravis, laudari verò à tur-pibus vera infamia. Age jam quod velis, contemne haec, vitupera, ride: veritatem tamen & pietatem quamvis petulantissimè oppugnatam, non ab omni-bus deserendam scito. Tempora mutantur saepius, & valeant tempora, venit aeternitas, vivit Deus!
units.tr: But, reader, take note of the reason for the writing: the cause indeed, but satisfaction was not made to reputation. So it is not the cause of truth but his reputation that produced this book for us, as the author himself indicates. For this work was meant for his reputation, not for the cause. Is your reputation so dear to you, then, before the truth? Let the man who is like this be infamous. Later he takes back the praise, as we have heard, in the work itself, but in this statement he is so consistent that in the very preface he ought to have repeated the same thing in other words: he says he would bring forward the importance of the question, but only to set forth some defence of the Synod could this work be produced. We now know which you value more, your reputation or the cause of God and of truth. Is this fitting for a minister of Christ? Since both advance with equal steps and are attacked together, both our reputation and divine truth can be defended, but each in its own order. I, at least, would rather have satisfaction made to the one than the other, and while my reputation calls, I would gladly be pressed from the cause of God. Next, what mortal had brought such a crime upon your Church? Who had even dreamed of it? Or is your Church, your Synod, Veltheusen's? Are its honour and glory so dear to you that whatever it suffers touches you all, and so violently that, while it is able to bring forth the writing of the truth which is the cause of God, it can at least set forth the same for itself? Do you not exalt this man enough? He seems wholly intent on pressing down our order and trampling it underfoot. When I think of his writings, he seems to me no little paradoxical, so that I could not judge such an offspring to be produced by him. I know, of course, that he rose against the Anonymous, but I fear the reader will seek a disagreement in vain, although at times he has wished to express a mind stirred up more by zeal. Whatever the case, is he not ashamed to hurl the darts of insults against the greatest heads and breasts of the theologians? Will it be any wonder if, from there, someone is lightly, and indeed under a hidden name, brought to trial for some crime? He will be allowed to pour out everything insolently and impotently against whomever he likes, and when his shadow is touched even by the tip of a finger, such great commotions are stirred up, such as not even truth, when wounded, stirs up! Let all the theologians die unavenged; let their name be violated and trampled by a paradoxical scoundrel; let the arguments of the Reformed Church, indeed of our Confessions, be plucked at; let them be explode undefended, not only in your sight, but with your agreement and support. Only let the name, honour and praises of Veltheusen remain forever. If your Church holds Ecclesia multis dear through him, enough and more is restored to him as a reward. It would be no great labour to bring forward, from the Veltheusians, similar things, if they were not the same as those which the Anonymous wrote. An opinion, as it were opposed, under the guise of refutation, can at some time be very well established. But to attack so great a man, indeed, that is dangerous. The physician undertakes a history and calls everyone whom he knows to be zealots whatever he reproaches them with. This, then, will be that charity, this moderation, which he requires even towards those who are alien to the faith. His passion will be revealed; it will be judged from his own mouth that he has thrust forward anger and especially envy. You will detect a changed style whenever he rises against the brethren. He defends the Socinianizing Anabaptists as good citizens, while the brethren are beaten as Papists. As for your history, Doctor, do you not know that to throw preceding sins into the face of the converted is diabolical and the work of Satan? What if they have now obtained pardon of those crimes, which you think they committed, from the supreme judge? What if they were not ashamed to confess and beg for the sins of their youth, as David did? What is to be expected from the supreme avenger for you, accusing a brother in this way? You, who teach that on political grounds some not dreadful things may be tolerated by the magistrate, did you wish to uncover the nakedness of the brethren so virulently? I truly grieve for your situation, and for your perversity, Veltheusen! But there will not be lacking, by the grace of God, those who will despise the brutish thunderbolts of your fury; there will not be lacking those who will seriously blunt your weapons, if you wish to rage insolently against the heads of the pious. If anyone should inquire more carefully and exactly into the whole life not of your ecclesiastical colleagues only but of many others, know that there will not be lacking those whose faults, once uncovered, would be exposed before all, more than your zealots. If drunkenness, treachery, the daily abuse of the divine name, troubling your household, perjuries, any injustice, fornication or some other enormous sin, perhaps committed in youth, were to render a man infamous and it were necessary to reveal it, you would see others than those adorned zealots. Nor is there any faith to be given to an enemy who speaks the truth, and whom you cannot convince by arguments, you will seek in vain by calumnies; this is not fitting for the prudent, least of all for those who hold office, and indeed in Synods. But lest you think you are being provoked by me, your conscience and office ought to counsel you silence; the same would also be done by me, if I were of such importance to you. Nor should you think much terror has been struck into me. There are those who inhabit a free land, where you may see no one condemned unheard; this is my aim, that I may convict you of your malice and make you stop playing the sycophant: break your faith by your evil promises. Meanwhile, a good conscience, which is my comfort, suggests this: that it is the greatest praise of a man to displease the wicked, while to be praised by the vile is true infamy. Come now, do what you will; despise these things, reproach them, laugh at them: but know that truth and piety, though most shamelessly assailed, are not to be abandoned by all. Times change often; let the times be well. Eternity comes; God lives!

units.la: Verum praeter Velthuisii famam aliud adhuc restat. Jam gaudebant, inquit, invidi heterodoxiam apud e-ruditos impingi, sicut apud plebeculam, impacta morum laxitas est, Ecclesiae sc.[?] Walonicae. Siccine quod Velt-huisio, id tuae impingitur Ecclesiae? ego sane etsi Velt-huisium Heterodoxotaton dicerem, de injuria conque-rerer, si hoc ut Ecclesiae tuae impactum haberetur: non enim Papanae parvum simulachrum fingitis, cujus Velthuisen Caput sit & Princeps. Liberè loquar, saepius miratus sum, Ecclesiae Seniorem, Walonicae Synodi membrum tot ac tanta in orthodoxiam incurrentia & pietatem scribere impunè. An ille formulis, prout Seniorem decet, subscripsit? ego eum ex formulis, multorum errorum convincere paratus sum. Speci-mina aliquot ad hujus prioris libri calcem reperiet lector. Et, si vestrum dicitis quod scribit Velthuisius merito heterodoxias accusabimini. Ille jam, publico Ecclesiae Reformatae elogio, veritatis orthodoxae te-nacem in pectore gerit animum, ut in Paradoxi libro ne umbra quidem veri Velthuisii apparere dici debeat.
units.tr: But beyond Velthuysen's reputation there remains something else. Now the envious were rejoicing, he says, that heterodoxy was being fixed upon the learned, just as, among the common folk, the laxity of morals has been fastened, on the Church, namely, of the Walloons. Is what is fastened on Velthuysen thus fastened on your Church? I, indeed, though I would call Velthuysen the most heterodox of men, would complain of an injury if this were held to be fastened upon your Church; for you are not fashioning some little Papal image whose head and prince is Velthuysen. I will speak freely: I have often wondered that an elder of the Church, a member of the Walloon Synod, should write so many and such great things that run into heterodoxy and impiety with impunity. Did he subscribe to the formulas, as an elder ought? I am ready to convict him of many errors from those formulas. The reader will find some specimens at the end of this first book. And if you say what Velthuysen writes, you will be accused of heterodoxy with justice. He already bears in his breast, by public praise of the Reformed Church, a mind tenacious of orthodox truth, so that in the book of the Paradox not even the shadow of the true Velthuysen ought to be said to appear.

units.la: Quo ruimus! hiccine sua satis innocentia tutus est, nec fortioribus armis, ubi defendendus erit, quam suus defendetur? meo judicio, is qui talia docet & scripta probat Heterodoxus uterque, sit pastor, sit Senior, sit Ecclesia, sit Synodus. Omnes Reformatos testor. Veritas autem non solum in discrimen venerat, etiam morum erat impacta laxitas; sed libertatis forsan est, non laxitatis, quod offendit plebeculam, Christianae libertatis nesciam. Gratulor autem tibi, si absis ab utraque, ut à superstitione animi & ab animarum tyrannide te abesse profiteris; sed cavendum semper ne ab uno extremo in aliud eatur. Memini Remonstrantes hanc hederam vino suo jam dudum propendisse, & erga Socinianos, aliosque haereticos fraternum animum demonstrasse, dum Reformatis olim fratribus, ea denegatur aequitas: sunt & alii quos in omnibus, praeterquam in piorum fratrum naevis obtegendis, moderatos inveneris. Queruntur de animarum, de Ecclesiarum Tyrannide, ait Junius, in Antapolog. p. 98. 99. at nunc causa leviores querimoniae: quidni & cum Remonstrantibus de pastorum & doctorum exauthoratione clamat (ibidem apud Jun.) & illos qui talia cudunt in fratres consilia aliisque suggerunt, detegit?
units.tr: Whither are we rushing! Is he so safe in his own innocence that, where he is to be defended, he will not be defended by stronger arms than his own? In my judgment, whoever teaches such things and approves such writings is a heterodox man on either side, whether he be minister, elder, Church or Synod. I call all the Reformed to witness. But the truth had not only come into danger; the laxity of morals had also been fastened upon it; yet perhaps it is of liberty, not of laxity, that what offends the common folk, ignorant of Christian liberty, is the matter. I congratulate you, however, if you profess that you are apart from both, as from the superstition of the mind and from the tyranny over souls; but one must always beware lest one pass from one extreme to the other. I remember that the Remonstrants long ago inclined this ivy to their own wine, and showed a brotherly spirit toward the Socinians and other heretics, while to the Reformed brethren of old that fairness is denied. There are also others whom you would find moderate in all things, except in covering the blemishes of the pious brethren. Junius, in the Antapologia, pp. 98–99, says: They complain of the tyranny over souls, of the tyranny over the Churches; but now the complaints are of lighter causes. Why not also, with the Remonstrants, cry out over the deposition of pastors and teachers (in the same place, quoted from Junius), and expose those who devise such counsels against the brethren and suggest them to others?

units.la: Ad ipsum tractatum me conferens, difficillima audio tempora p. 5. vere scribis Wolzogi, difficillima sunt tempora; sed non omnes eundem periculorum fontem respicimus: sunt, qui talia scribentes aut dicentes ferulam & virgas fere exspectare debeant: sed tu impune dixeris, imo scripseris, modo tibi, quod ad causas, cum quibusdam, eadem non sit sententia: meam si vis? adversus pios & pietatem Vatinianum odium, Libertinismus, religionis contemtus, vitae profanitas, disciplinae defectus, peccatorum infrunita & impunita simul licentia, Papistarum, Socinianorum; quin quorumvis, indomita audacia; Ecclesiasticorum, aliorumque factiones, tepiditas, mundanitas, ἀθεωπαρεισκεια[?], κακοζηλεια[?]; deinque omnis generis grassantium peccatorum inenarrabilis multitudo: haec sunt quae periculosa efficiunt tempora. Utinam correctioni studeremus, quantum possumus omnes! hoc tuam, hoc meam persona, nobis à Christo impositam decet. Sed quod abnegandum tibi, aliis, mihi, commendo præcipuè, mundana gloria est, & hominum favor. Non quod de honore quem uterque Magistratibus debemus, quicquam delibatum, sed nec eum assentationis embammate delibutum velim. Christi servum nil minus decet quem ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν, utinam cum Apostolo & nobis liceat gloriari, 1 Thess. ii.4, 5, 6. Loquimur non ut hominibus placentes, sed Deo exploranti corda nostra: nec enim unquam sermone assentatorio usi sumus, sicut nostis, nec avaritiæ causa quicquam prætexuimus: Deus testis est. Neque ex hominibus quærentes gloriam. Egosaltem persona non à Dominis sed à Domino Jesu per Ecclesiam mihi impositam, decere id putem: ut ille sic mihi evadat Clementissimus. Quanquam & amplissimorum Magistratuum & Clementissimarum summarum potestatum, omni, salva Conscientia, pretio, favorem & gratiam redimenda velim. Sed Synedrii Walonici læsam famam dixerat, quicquid sit, huncce virum, pro Synedrii aut Velthuisii potius gloria, tam strenuè dimicantem, quis ferat? dum omnes quotquot sunt aut fuerunt Reformatorum Theologos tanto probro, affici non patitur solum, sed & assi-cit, ut quæstionem quæ omnem habet in se religionem Christianam ut ait p.5. nequaquam satis hactenus enucleatè tractasse, ipso judice, dici mereantur. Siccine veneranda colemus Capita? mali semper omnis in Arminio habebatur, quod tam parvi pretii Calvinum, Bezam & alia Reformatæ Ecclesiæ decora judicabat. Sic tandem patebit quinam prædecessorum premant vestigia, qui nova crepent: non possum quin erumpam in verba Magni Buceri, quæ habet in Ex- plan. Pf. 1-6. inhumanum est, nedum indignum filiis Dei, verè pios, vereque doctrinæ Sacræ studiosos, ac non parum de Ecclesia Christi suis scriptis meritos, temerè adeo in ordinem cogere, adeoque omnem illis authoritatem derogare. Id quod plerique sibi nescio quo Spiritu turbulento hoc nostro seculo nimium quam licenter permiserunt. Compendium celebritatis multis mirum in modum placere video, ait Hoornbeeck, ex mera quod captatur novitate, quibuscunque paradoxis avidè se addicendo, ut cum iis nomen suum quoque eat in orbem, quod vel ex se, vel studio adstruendi communem veritatem & ædificationem se adipisci posse desperant, quæ ingeniorum quædam est, & damnosa multis, temulentia dicam, an arrogantia? certè vanitas maxima & certè vereor ne aliquando necesse evadat, ut Christianus Magistratus videat & dicat, quæ Imperator Honorius, quem piissimum vocat in vita Augustini Possidonius, olim. Ad conturbandam inquit Catholicæ simplicitatis lucem puro semper splendore radiantem, dolosæ artis ingenio, novam subito emicuisse versutiam, pervulgata opinione cognovimus: quæ fallacis scientiæ obumbrata mendaciis & furioso tantum debacchata luctamine, stabilem quietem cælestis conatur attrectare fidei, dum novi acuminis commendata vento, insignem notam plebeia æstimat vilitatis, sentire cum cunctis; ac prudentiæ singularis palmam fore communiter approbata destruere. Tanquam altius supraque vulgi ingenium spiraturi, si videantur communem sapientiam ut vilem negligere, quod alibi de quibusdam Barclaius. Sed pergendum est. Antequam autem pergamus, notandum videtur qualis persona Wolzogio sit imposita, si Academicam respiciat, ea saltem nihil cum hujusmodi materia habet commercii. Historias enim non Theologiam docendi Provincia, & ni fallor extra ordinem, ei demandata est, malè igitur verba interpretaturus est quisquis Theologiæ vel Doctorem vel quod majus est Professorem inde collegerit, quanquam ut verum fatear, verba sic sonent, ut vix aliter intelligi posse videantur, quapropter ne vanæ gloriolæ captator in eo habeatur, vereor. Quod ad eam quam in Ecclesia Walonica sustinet, pastor est, cui juxta mecum, conciones incumbunt, visitationes & Catechisationes, prout decreto Synodi Nationalis Dordracenæ cautum & ejus subsignatione à Wolzogio promissum est. Eam vero ipsi à Clementissimis Dominis suis impositam, quandoquidem gloriæ ducere videtur, non equidem invideo, miror magis. Me quod attinet, maximum id mihi sanctæ parrhesiæ fundamentum & diligentiæ coram Deo calcar erit, quod absque ullo ambitu ab Ecclesia Jesu Christi ejusque corpore representativo, juxta praxin & legem divinam vocatus sim Ecclesiæ Leovardiensis Pastor. Nisi & in eo cum Velthuisio, ministerio detrimentosum errorem alat, Concionatoris & Presbyteri functiones easdem esse & nullius authoritatis supra ea, quæ unusquisque fortassis proprio motu agat, donec per Magistratus fiant personæ publicæ, tum enim jus & potestatem habent à Magistratibus, sed talem quæ longe differt à ministerio verbi quod in hodiernis concionatoribus omni potestate & auctoritate destitutum est. Scilicet fallere non debuit Proverbium, omnis Monachus Apostata est osor sui ordinis. Velthuisius enim ex ministerii Candidato jam Medicus evasit, magna Eccl. jactura sc.
units.tr: Turning to the treatise itself, I hear, Wolzogen, that you write truly that the times are most difficult, as p. 5 says. But we do not all look to the same source of danger. Those who write or say such things ought to expect the rod and the cane, yet you may say, indeed write, with impunity, provided that you do not hold the same opinion as some others about the causes. If you want my view: hatred of the godly and of godliness, the Vatinian hatred, libertinism, contempt of religion, the profanity of life, the failure of discipline, an unbridled and unpunished licence for sins, the untameable audacity of the Papists and the Socinians, and of anyone else; the factions of churchmen and others, lukewarmness, worldliness, ἀθεωπαρεισκεια [?] and κακοζηλεια [?]; and finally the unspeakable multitude of sins of every kind that run riot: these are what make the times dangerous. Would that we all, as far as we can, were eager for correction! This is what your office and mine, laid on us by Christ, requires. But what I especially commend to you, and to others, and to myself, is that we must renounce worldly glory and the favour of men. I do not mean that any of the honour we both owe the magistrates is to be diminished, but I would not have it smeared with the varnish of flattery. A servant of Christ should least of all seek to please men [ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν]. May we too, with the Apostle, be permitted to glory: "We speak not as pleasing men, but God, who tests our hearts. For we never used flattering speech, as you know, nor did we put forward any pretext of greed; God is witness. Nor did we seek glory from men" (1 Thess. ii. 4, 5, 6). For my own part, I think it fitting that I was called, not by lords but by the Lord Jesus through the Church, to be minister of the Church of Leeuwarden. I would gladly win the favour and grace of the most distinguished magistrates and most gracious sovereign powers, but with a clear conscience and at no price. But you say the Walloon Synod's reputation was harmed. Whatever the case, who can bear this man fighting so vigorously for the glory of the Synod, or rather of Velthuysen, while he not only allows all the Reformed theologians, whoever they are or have been, to be stained with such disgrace, but even brings it about that the question, which, as he says on p. 5, contains in itself the whole of the Christian religion, deserves to be called, by his own judgment, not yet sufficiently unfolded? Shall we cultivate such venerable heads? Arminius was always thought to be the worst of men, because he judged Calvin, Beza and the other ornaments of the Reformed Church to be of such little worth. So at last it will be clear which of the predecessors they follow, who clamour for novelties. I cannot help breaking out into the words of the great Bucer, in his Explanation of the Psalms: It is inhuman, let alone unworthy of the sons of God, to force into line so rashly men who are truly pious, truly devoted to sacred doctrine, and who have deserved not a little of Christ's Church by their writings, and to take away all authority from them. This many have permitted themselves far too freely in this our age, by some turbulent spirit I know not what. I see that a means of popularity pleases many in a wonderful way, says Hoornbeeck, from the mere novelty they seek, by eagerly devoting themselves to any paradoxes, so that their name too may go around with them; because either by themselves or by their zeal for establishing the common truth and edification they despair of being able to attain it. This is a kind of disease of minds, and harmful to many: intoxication, I should say, or arrogance? Certainly it is the greatest vanity, and I fear lest at some time it become necessary that a Christian magistrate see and say what the Emperor Honorius, whom Possidonius in his Life of Augustine calls most pious, said long ago: "To disturb the light of Catholic simplicity, which always shines with pure splendour, a new cunning, by the ingenuity of a deceitful art, has suddenly flashed forth, as we have learned from common report. Shadowed by the lies of a fallacious learning, and raging only in a frenzied struggle, it tries to handle the stable rest of heavenly faith, while, carried on the wind of a novel cleverness, it judges it a mark of plebeian cheapness to feel with all, and to destroy what is commonly approved, as if the palm of singular prudence would belong to it. As if it were about to rise higher than the common intellect, if it seems to neglect common wisdom as worthless, as Barclay says elsewhere of certain people. But we must go on. Before we do, it seems worth noting what office Wolzogen holds, if we consider his academic post; that at least has nothing to do with this kind of subject. For he is appointed to teach history, not theology, and, unless I am mistaken, outside his regular duties; so whoever, interpreting his words badly, infers from them that he is a teacher of theology, or, what is greater, a professor, is mistaken, although, to tell the truth, his words sound so that they seem scarcely capable of being understood otherwise. For this reason I fear he may be thought a seeker of empty glory. As for the post he holds in the Walloon Church, he is a minister, whose duties, as I understand it, are the sermons, visitations and catechising, as the decree of the National Synod of Dort provided and as Wolzogen promised by his signature. I do not begrudge him that office, which was laid upon him by his most gracious lords, since he seems to count it a glory; I rather marvel at it. As for me, the greatest foundation of holy frankness and the spur of diligence before God will be this: that without any ambition I was called, according to the practice and law of God, by the Church of Jesus Christ and its representative body, to be minister of the Church of Leeuwarden.
