Unless, along with Velthuysen, he nourishes the harmful error in the ministry that the offices of preacher and elder are the same and have no authority beyond what each might perhaps do of his own accord, until they are made public persons by the magistrates; for then they have right and power from the magistrates, but a power that differs far from the ministry of the Word, which in today's preachers is destitute of all power and authority. Certainly the proverb should not have deceived him: every monk who has apostatised hates his own order. Velthuysen, indeed, from a candidate for the ministry has already become a physician, a great loss to the Church, namely...

units.la: Pagina ii. aliquid occurrit quod sicco pede transeundum non est: sic sonant verba, quæ notanda serio.
units.tr: On page ii. something occurs that must not be passed over dry-shod; the words sound thus, and they are to be noted seriously.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur, quando nos facultate judicandi præditos experimur, eamque nos ut & cætera omnia, accepisse à Deo probavimus, quia illum nihil agere nullo fine probavimus, facile nobis persuademus ejus facultatis beneficio verum nos percipere posse, quia frustra illam nobis indulserit Deus, si non possit id præstare, stare, ad quod efficiendum ejus est unicè apta natura. Eo ipso quod facultas intelligendi à Deo creata est, putat, quia Deus nihil frustra agit, eam sufficere debere ad percipiendum verum, quod proprie ejus objectum est, alias eam frustra nobis indultam fore. Rudè satis omnia, & ni melius explicentur ac limitentur, Pelagianismi hic fundamenta palam sterni, certum est. De vero loqueris, sed quodnam, cujus generis verum intelligis? cum enim æqualiter se intellectus ut facultas simpliciter, habeat, ad spirituale ac naturale verum; quidni eodem fundamento, illum frustra, si spirituale, si omne verum capere nequeat, inditum dixerim? ad id enim contemplandum præcipue mens nobis data est. Deinde ut de diverso genere, sic de gradu veri etiam dici posset, tandemque omnis generis, quodcunque, etiam abditissimum, quod verum est, debere percipi posse, (cujus contrarium docet p. 18. sunt talia in Scripturis quæ tum demum intelligentur quando esse desinet Scriptura.) alias & simili modo argumentabor, liberum frustra esse hominis arbitrium, ni bonum spirituale appetere aptum sit: frustra hominis animam ni ad communionem Dei pervenire queat; nam ad id unicè, &c. An lapsus Adamici oblitus es? facultatem ante lapsum si consideres, bene concludis, sin vero post lapsum, pessimè. Illine frustra oculi dati sunt, qui sese visu postquam orbavit, jam videre nihil potest? quidni & Christum frustra proponi peccatori, & verbum prædicari, ni illum amplecti, hoc salutariter intelligere possit; verum Deum nosse, loquentem intelligere, mens poterat integra, sed neutrum corrupta, nec tamen frustra est. Scripturam proponi omnibus hominibus ut intelligant, & proinde à quovis posse intelligi, Socinianum est & quidem πρῶτον ψεῦδος, notante Maccovio. Ineptus homo est & mortuus, ineptæ etiam & mortuæ omnes facultates ejus, illarumque quæque circa sua objecta: ita ut è contra potius dixerim, fa-cultas nostra apta si sit ad agendum id, cui apta primo nata fuit, nulla corruptio agnoscitur, originis pec-catum negatur. Nec juvat dicere lapsis jam, non inte-gris verbum scriptum esse; non enim proponitur ut omnes intelligant; sed de hisce postea ex professo. u-nicus enim hic locus non est, ubi remisse nimis, de nostra caecitate scribit, quis jam mirabitur non bene Scripturae ab ipso describi interpretem: malo enim cognito, bene mederi non poterat.
units.tr: Therefore, just as when we experience in ourselves the faculty of judging, and have proved that we received it from God, as we received all other things, because we have proved that he does nothing without a purpose, we easily persuade ourselves that by the benefit of that faculty we can perceive the truth, because God would have granted it to us in vain if it could not accomplish that for which its nature alone is fitted. From the fact that the faculty of understanding was created by God, he thinks, because God does nothing in vain, that it ought to suffice for perceiving the truth, which is its proper object; otherwise it would have been granted to us in vain. It is certain that in these matters everything is crudely laid down, and unless it is explained and limited better, the foundations of Pelagianism are openly laid here. You speak of the truth, but which truth, of what kind, do you mean? For since the intellect, as a faculty, stands equally towards spiritual and natural truth, why should I not say, on the same foundation, that it has been given in vain if it cannot grasp spiritual truth, or all truth? For the mind was given to us chiefly to contemplate that. Next, one could say the same of the kind of truth as of its degree, and finally that whatever kind of truth it is, even the most hidden, which is true, ought to be able to be perceived (the contrary of which p. 18 teaches: there are things in the Scriptures which will be understood only when Scripture ceases to exist). Otherwise I will argue in a similar way that human free will is in vain, unless it is fit to desire spiritual good; the human soul is in vain unless it can come to communion with God; for it is solely for this... Have you forgotten the fall of Adam? If you consider the faculty before the fall, you conclude rightly; but if after the fall, very badly. Were the eyes given in vain to a man who, having blinded himself to sight, can now see nothing? Why should Christ not be offered to the sinner in vain, and the Word preached in vain, unless he can embrace Him and understand this to his salvation? The mind could know God and understand one speaking while it was whole, but being corrupted in neither respect, it is not in vain. That Scripture is set forth to all men that they may understand it, and therefore can be understood by anyone, is Socinian, and indeed the first falsehood [πρῶτον ψεῦδος], as Maccovius notes. Man is unfit and dead, and all his faculties are unfit and dead, and each of them as regards its objects; so that, on the contrary, I would rather say that if our faculty is fit for doing that for which it was originally fitted, no corruption is recognised and original sin is denied. Nor does it help to say that the written word was given not to the fallen but to the whole; for it is not set forth so that all may understand; but of these things later, in their proper place. For this is not the only place where, too carelessly, he writes about our blindness; who will now be surprised that the interpreter of Scripture is not described well by himself? For, the disease being unknown, he could not heal it well.

units.la: Eandem Scholam redolet, quando de Caelestis ve- ritatis intelligibilitate sic disserit p. 12. quam si o-mnem adhibeamus diligentiam quae in ejusmodi rebus exigi ab homine jure queat, ego veritatem inveniri posse statuo, aut adscribendam inanitatem Deo esse, I Quis nisi Pelagius, multa, hoc rerum statu, jure ab ho-minibus peti posse, quae praestare non potest, neget? infantesillud docet Palatina Catechesis. II. Quid? an igitur Deo inanitas adscribi debet, ni homo, adhi-bita tanta diligentia, quanta, in eo, exigi jure po-test, caelestem veritatem percipiat? nisi subjecti mu-tationem, novi luminis habitualis infusionem ponas prius, fruastra omnis labor, naturalis industria o-mnis: vel an Philosophanti eo usque Pelagianum vi-rus surrepsit clanculum, ut jure jam peti non posse', quod praestari non potest, videatur? miror si quis hic Heterodoxiam non viderit. Sed veritatem inve-nire, forsan sensum literalem percipere, tibi est; ve-rum praeterquam, quod longius procedere videaris, cum caelestem veritatem dicas antea, nihilominus ex isto tuo fundamento inanitas Deo adscribenda erit; horreo! nam ut intelligi non solum, sed etiam salu-tariter intelligi queat, requiritur ad scopum & finem Scripturae rite acquirendum. Jure igitur sic infero nisi salutariter inveniri possit veritas ab homine, tantantam sedulitatem adhibente, quanta jure petipo-test, ergo, &c. nec est quod excipias, subjecti mutatio-nem, novi principii in intellectum infusionem, in-ter illa, quæ jure exigi queunt, numerari non posse: Reclamant enim omnes quotquot Pelagii erroribus non sunt in transversum acti: vanus certe non est aut inanis Deus ille tremendus & verax, etsi frustra homo naturalis, omnem adhibeat juxta vires suas, diligentiam; quanquam id fieri non putem, sed fiat, quid inde? nisi bonum usum naturalium, supernaturali gratia, ex congruo cum Jesuitis & Remonstran-tibus, prosequendum putes. Intelligatur modo cælestis veritas ab iis quibus intelligendi principium gratiosè indulget Deus, qui miseretur cujus vult. hæredes testamentum intelligere bene soli queant, frustra & in cassum perdant operam reliqui, testator finem obtinet intentum. Vobis, reliquis non item, datum est, nosse &c. ait Christus, & ni nimium Philosophiæ tuæ indulsisses, Christi verba expendisses melius, quæ refert Matth. Cap. xi. 25. gloriam, tibi tribuo, pater Domine Cæli & terræ, quod hæc occultaveris à sapientibus & intelligentibus: & ea retexeris infantibus. etiam Pater, quia ita placuit tibi.
units.tr: It smells of the same school when he discusses the intelligibility of heavenly truth like this (p. 12): "If we apply all the diligence that can rightly be demanded of a man in such matters, I hold that the truth can be found, or else emptiness must be ascribed to God," Who but Pelagius would deny that, in the present state of things, many things can rightly be demanded of men that they cannot perform? The Palatine Catechism teaches this even to infants. II. What then? Must emptiness be ascribed to God, unless a man, applying as much diligence as can rightly be demanded of him, grasps heavenly truth? Unless you posit first a change of the subject, an infusion of new habitual light, all labour is in vain and all natural industry is nothing. Or has the Pelagian poison crept so secretly into this philosopher that what cannot be performed seems no longer rightly to be demanded? I would be surprised if anyone did not see heterodoxy here. But you say that to find the truth, perhaps to perceive the literal sense, is up to you. Yet apart from the fact that you seem to go further, since you first call it heavenly truth, nonetheless on your own foundation emptiness will have to be ascribed to God. I shudder! For that it may be understood, not only understood but understood savingly, is required to attain rightly the aim and end of Scripture. Therefore I rightly infer: unless the truth can be found savingly by a man applying as much diligence as can rightly be demanded, therefore, etc. Nor is it an objection that a change of the subject and an infusion of a new principle into the intellect cannot be counted among those things that can rightly be demanded. For all who have not been driven headlong by the errors of Pelagius protest against this. That awesome and true God is surely not empty or vain, even if natural man, applying all the diligence he can according to his strength, accomplishes nothing; though I do not think this happens, but suppose it does, what follows? Unless you think the good use of natural things is to be pursued, with supernatural grace, in agreement with the Jesuits and the Remonstrants. Let heavenly truth be understood only by those to whom God graciously grants the principle of understanding, who has mercy on whom he wills. Heirs alone can rightly understand a testament; the rest lose their labour in vain and to no purpose, while the testator attains the end he intended. "To you it is given to know," etc., says Christ, and had you not indulged your philosophy too much, you would have weighed Christ's words better, which Matthew reports in chapter 11, verse 25: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to babes. Yes, Father, for so it was well pleasing in your sight."

units.la: Explicatione aut correctione egent & illa quæ habet p. 23. ubi mentis vitium describens, sic loquitur, quæ, mentes sc., cum sint obducta tenebris na-turalis ignorantiæ, quibus comprehendo omnia impedi-menta salutaris cognitionis. Quod homo ita dilucide agens, obductum tenebris dicat, quem visu orba-tum, cui oculos effossos, quos cæcos dicere potuis-set, magis emphaticè, magis perspicuè, transfeat; sed cum, sub tenebris naturalis ignorantiæ, omnia impedimenta salutaris cognitionis, comprehendit, im-pingere videtur, aut intricatè loqui: scimus enim mulmulta dari salutaris cognitionis impedimenta, quæ sub tenebris naturalis ignorantia comprehendi nequeant; nisi cum tempore acquisita præjudicia & infinita alia naturalem ignorantiam putet, id est, peccatum originale cum actualibus confundat. Obscure satis. Nec suspicor tibi istum sensum, cum hæc scriberes, fuisse, non sub tenebris naturalis ignorantiæ, sed sub mentium vitio reliqua impedimenta comprehen-dere[?]. Nam nec constructio hoc patitur, nec perspicuitas. perspicuus esse præ reliquis debuisses, qui ita temerè Calvinos, Zanchios, Junios, Whitakeros, Chamieros, imo omnes simul reformatos obscuritatis reos agis, & quidem in negotio quod omnem in religionem habet: sed te extricare conaris cum diversis eâdem paginâ, sunt enim sua culpa in hanc cæca-tem prolapsi, qui mente perspicaci, nullisque præconceptis opinionibus gravata, fuerant conditi. Dubito autem quid velis cum pag. seq. ita emphaticè itidem inculcas, sua solius culpa defæcatam mentem hominem adhibere non posse. Putasne 1 tum demum non posse quando reliqua cognitionis impedimenta supervenerunt? 2 vel Deum in culpa fore ni homo concipiatur posse? 3 Aut agnoscis solummodo personalem culpam ? ex peccato personali & actuali profluentem, originalem vero, utpote non ita suam, non item ? imputatur sanè & inhæret, damnat & corrumpit originis peccatum: ut autem in hoc negotio alios magis lucide scripsisse, & jam non demum lucem nobis effulsisse videat lector. Calvinum audiamus hanc cæcitatem explicantem, more suo, solide & perspicue. [?]i persuasum nobis foret, (quod extra controversiam esse debet) naturæ nostræ deesse quicquid cælestis Pater electis suis per Spiritum regenerationis confert, hic nullus esset hæsitandi materia, sic enim loquitur populus fidelis, quoniam apud te est fons vitæ & in lumine tuo videmus lumen, idem testatur Apostolus, cum ait ne-minem minem posse dicere Dominum Jesum nisi in Spiritu Sancto & Joh. Bapt. stuporem discipulorum videns exclamat, neminem posse accipere quicquam, nisi datum illi fuerit desuper. donum autem ab eo intelligi de speciali illuminatione, non communi naturae dote inde constat; quod tot verbis, quibus Christum commendaverat discipulis suis, nihil se profecisse conqueritur. Video inquit verba nihil esse ad mentes hominum de rebus divinis imbuendas, nisi Dominus per Spiritum suum intelligentiam dederit: & Textum Deut. xxix. 2. referens, sic infert: quid plus exprimeret, si nos vocaret stipites in operibus Dei considerandis? unde Dominus per Prophetam, singularis gratiae loco, pollicetur se daturum Israelitis cor, ut ab illis cognoscatur: nimirum immuens, tantum hominis mentem Spiritualiter sapere, quantum abs se illustrata fuerit. hoc quoque dilucide sua voce confirmavit Christus, cum diceret neminem venire ad se posse, nisi cui datum a Patre suo foret: quid? annon ipse est viva Patris imago, in qua totus gloriae ejus splendor nobis exprimitur? ergo non potuit melius ostendere, qualis sit nostra ad cognoscendum Deum facultas, dum ad cernendam ejus imaginem, ubi ita palam exhibetur, oculos nobis esse negat. quid? annon sua quoque legatione fideliter defunctus est? ita est sane sed nihil efficitur ejus praedicatione, nisi interior Magister Spiritus viam ad animos patefaciat: ergo non veniunt ad eum, nisi quia a Patre audierunt & edocti sunt[?]. qua ista dicendi & audiendi ratio? nempe ubi aures ad audiendum, & mentes ad intelligendum, Spiritus mira & singulari virtute format --- cui novam mentem Spiritus Sanctus sua illuminatione fecerit. ---
units.tr: Those things also which he has on p. 23 need explanation or correction. Describing the defect of the mind, he speaks thus: "which minds, since they are overspread with the darkness of natural ignorance, by which I comprehend all the impediments of saving knowledge." A man who speaks so lucidly, who says "overspread with darkness" of someone blinded in sight, whom he could have called blind with their eyes gouged out, passes over more emphatically and more clearly; but when he comprehends "under the darkness of natural ignorance, all the impediments of saving knowledge," he seems to stumble or to speak in a tangled way. For we know that many impediments to saving knowledge exist which cannot be comprehended "under the darkness of natural ignorance"; unless he thinks that prejudices acquired over time and countless other things are natural ignorance, that is, he confuses original sin with actual sins. Obscure enough. Nor do I suspect that when writing this you meant not "under the darkness of natural ignorance" but that you comprehend the remaining impediments "under the defect of minds". For neither the construction nor clarity allows it. You ought to have been clearer than others, you who so rashly accuse Calvin, Zanchius, Junius, Whitaker, Chamier, indeed all the Reformed together, of obscurity, and that in a matter which concerns all religion. But you try to extricate yourself with a different reading on the same page: "for they have fallen into this blindness through their own fault, who were created with a keen mind, not burdened by any preconceived opinions." I doubt, however, what you mean when on the following page you insist just as emphatically: "a man cannot admit a mind cleansed of itself by its own fault alone." Do you think 1. that it is impossible only once other impediments to knowledge have supervened? 2. Or that God would be at fault unless man is conceived to be able? 3. Or do you acknowledge only personal fault, flowing from personal and actual sin, but not likewise original sin, as not so much one's own? Yet original sin is certainly imputed, adheres, condemns and corrupts. But that the reader may see that others have written more lucidly on this matter, and that light has not dawned on us only just now, let us hear Calvin explaining this blindness, in his own manner, solidly and clearly. "If it were persuaded to us (which ought to be beyond controversy) that whatever the heavenly Father confers on his elect through the Spirit of regeneration is lacking in our nature, there would be no matter for doubt here. For thus the faithful people speaks: 'because with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we see light.'" The Apostle likewise testifies when he says that no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit; and John the Baptist, seeing the amazement of the disciples, exclaims that no one can receive anything unless it has been given him from above. That this gift is to be understood of a special illumination and not of the common endowment of nature is clear from this: that he complains that he has made no progress despite so many words with which he had commended Christ to his disciples. "I see," he says, "that words are nothing for imbuing human minds with divine things, unless the Lord gives understanding through his Spirit." And quoting the text of Deuteronomy 29:2 he adds: "What more could he express if he called us stocks in considering the works of God?" Hence the Lord, through the Prophet, promising as a singular grace that he will give Israel a heart by which they may know him: plainly showing that the human mind savours spiritual things only as far as it has been enlightened by him. Christ too confirmed this clearly in his own words, when he said that no one can come to him unless it has been given him by his Father. What then? Is he not the living image of the Father, in whom the whole splendour of his glory is expressed to us? Therefore he could not better show what our faculty for knowing God is, since, when his image is so plainly displayed, he denies that we have eyes to discern it. What then? Has he not also faithfully discharged his embassy? So it is indeed, but nothing is accomplished by his preaching unless the inner Teacher, the Spirit, opens the way to hearts. Therefore they do not come to him unless they have heard and been taught by the Father. What manner of speaking and hearing is this? Surely where the Spirit by a wondrous and singular power forms the ears to hear and the minds to understand... to whom the Holy Spirit by his illumination has made a new mind.

units.la: Priulus[?] --- quem vocat animalem? nempe qui naturae lumine nititur, ille, inquam, nihil in spiritualibus mysteriis Dei comprehendit: quid ita? NB. an quia per ignaviam negligit? imo etiamsi enitatur, nihil potest: quia scilicet Spiritualiter dijudicantur. quid istud significat? quia humanæ perspicaciæ penitus abscondita, per solam Spiritus revelationem patefiunt: adeo ut pro stultitia ducantur, ubi Spiritus Dei non illucet. Ante autem supra oculorum, aurium, mentium capacitatem extulerat, quæ præparavit Deus diligentibus se, quin sapientiam humanam NB, quasi velum quoddam esse testatus fuerat, quo mens à cernendo Deo impeditur. Quid volumus? pronunciat Apostolus infatuatam à Deo sapientiam hujus mundi: & nos scilicet acumen illi tribuemus, quo ad Deum & cælestis regni adyta penetrare possit? facessat à nobis tanta vecordia. --- neque hic garriat. hactenus Calvinus. Non possum non hisce adjungere quæ habet Strangius: duplex autem est cæcitas & durities. Una naturalis, quæ nobis innata est in statu corrupto, ex transgressione Adami ad nos derivata, de qua dicitur homo animalis, &c. 1 Cor. 2. 14. sic durities & cor resipiscere nesciens, de quibus loquitur Apostolus Rom. 2. v. 5. naturalia sunt cuivis homini corrupto. Alia est cæcitas & durities accersita seu acquisita, vel superveniens, quæ per voluntariam malitiam attrahitur, & nihil aliud est, quam incrementum cæcitatis & duritiei naturalis peccandi consuetudine adaucta: quando nempe insita cæcitas & durities contempta scientia ac conscientiæ usu augetur. Prior illa cæcitas est peccatum & causa peccati, posterior est & peccatum & causa peccati & pœna peccati.
units.tr: Priulus ... whom does he call animal? Surely the one who relies on the light of nature; that one, I say, comprehends nothing of the spiritual mysteries of God. Why so? Is it, perhaps, because he neglects them through laziness? Nay, even if he strives, he can do nothing, because they are spiritually discerned. What does that mean? That they are hidden entirely from human insight and are disclosed only by the revelation of the Spirit, so that they are counted as foolishness where the Spirit of God does not shine. Earlier, however, he had said that the things God has prepared for those who love him lie beyond the capacity of eyes, ears and minds; indeed he had declared human wisdom to be a kind of veil by which the mind is hindered from seeing God. What do we want? The Apostle declares the wisdom of this world to have been made foolish by God; and shall we surely ascribe to it the keenness by which it could penetrate to God and the sanctuaries of the heavenly kingdom? Let such madness be far from us. Let him not chatter here. So far Calvin. I cannot but add to these what Strangius has: "Now blindness and hardness are of two kinds. One is natural, which is innate in us in a corrupt state, derived to us from the transgression of Adam, of which it is said that the natural man, etc. (1 Cor. 2:14); likewise the hardness and the heart that does not know how to repent, of which the Apostle speaks (Rom. 2:5). These are natural to every corrupt man. The other blindness and hardness is acquired or supervening, which is drawn on by voluntary malice, and is nothing other than an increase of natural blindness and hardness, augmented by the habit of sinning: namely, when the inborn blindness and hardness is increased by despising knowledge and by the practice of conscience. The former blindness is both sin and the cause of sin; the latter is both sin and cause of sin and punishment of sin."

units.la: Ne queratur autem Wolzogen elenchum à me ignorari & omnia hæc ab ipso concedi, hoc enim saltem evincitur, tam longè abesse, ut illi, de omnium Theologorum obscuritate quicquam dicere licuerit, ut ipse potius intricatissimè & obscurissime scripsisse ex illis convincatur. Posthac prudentius agat, & heterodoxias amolietur suspicionem, si heterodoxus non sit.
units.tr: Lest anyone complain that I have ignored Wolzogen's refutation or have granted all of these points to him, this much at least is clear: he is far from entitled to say anything about the obscurity of all theologians, since he is himself convicted of having written in a most tangled and obscure way. From now on let him act more prudently, and let him remove the suspicion of heterodoxy, if he is not heterodox.

units.la: Hisce minus intentus, quæ Controversiam capi-talem propiùs aliquantulum respiciunt, clarè & di-stinctè percepit & scripsit: specimen videamus. Sic ait p. 16. Fatemur esse quædam in Scripturis quæ non valeamus assequi: non tantum vitio mentium ---- aut sublimitate rerum ---- sed ipsa Scriptura quadam con-stitutione p. 18. esse talia in Scripturis credo quatum[?] demum intelligentur ab hominibus, quando esse desinet Scriptura, p. 83. non futurum unquam ut assequa-mur omnia quæ Scripturis traduntur. Hæc autem conferantur cum sequentibus. p. 17. Nec unquam talem in Scripturis extitisse locum qui nunquam & à nemine intelligi posset. p. 19. dubium non est quin ali-quando, quin alicui, etiam qua parte nobis videtur obscurissima, vel intelligi, vel intellectum iri, si non sit aliquando intellecta, aut posse saltem intelligi, si rite legatur statuere possimus. p. 149. interesse divinæ gloriæ puto, ut ne quid memoriæ prodi jusserit, quod non intelligatur ab iis quorum gratia id fecerit. Imo ipsa p. 15. Ubi paulò ante, lin. 17. dixerat, non quod omnia pervia velim in Scriptura statuere Lin. 22. & seqq. ait, nil ita scriptum à Deo esse ut --- non aliquis inde sensus, ex mente quoque Dei, erui queat. Qua ut intelligam qui conciliari possint, opus habeo Interprete. p. 128. Extundat inde perspicuitatis tantopere jactatæ lucem qui velit. Ego præter contradictiones, ad minimum, egregias ἐναντιοφανείας, vix quicquam reperio: præterquam quod quædam, accuratiùs pensitata, ab heterodoxias crimine vix immunia apparerent. Turpe est Doctori, cum culpa redarguit ipsum. Nollem per Wolzogium, omnes Theologos, non dilucidæ tractationis infumulatos: sed mirabiliora sequentur. Unum velim, nimirum ut mihi locum vel unicum indicaret, ubi ita directè Paradoxo, quem vocat, ac quidem hic sibi ipsi contradicit. Ego saltem talem invenire non potui.
units.tr: Paying less attention to these matters, he has written clearly and distinctly about the points that touch more closely on the chief controversy. Let us look at a sample. On page 16 he says: We admit that there are some things in the Scriptures which we cannot attain, not only because of the fault of our minds or the sublimity of the matters, but because of a certain constitution of Scripture itself; on page 18: I believe there are such things in the Scriptures that they will not be understood by men until Scripture ceases to be; on page 83: It will never come about that we attain all that is delivered in the Scriptures. Now let these statements be compared with the following. On page 17: Nor has there ever been in the Scriptures a passage that could never be understood by anyone. On page 19: There is no doubt that we can establish that at some time, or by someone, even in the part that seems to us most obscure, it either is understood or will be understood, or at least can be understood if it is read rightly. On page 149: I think it is a matter of divine glory that He has commanded nothing to be handed down to memory which is not understood by those for whose sake He did it. Indeed, on page 15, where a little earlier, at line 17, he had said not that I wish to establish that all things in Scripture are open, at line 22 and following he says: nothing has been written by God in such a way that some sense cannot be drawn from it, also from the mind of God. In order that I may understand how these can be reconciled, I need an Interpreter. On page 128, let whoever wishes try to extract a light of the clarity so much boasted of from this. For my part, besides contradictions, and at least outstanding apparent contradictions [ἐναντιοφανείας], I can find hardly anything, except that certain passages, weighed more carefully, would appear scarcely free from the charge of heterodoxy. It is shameful for a teacher to be refuted by his own fault. I would not wish to be taken as saying that all theologians are overwhelmed by Wolzogen's unclear treatment; but more astonishing things follow. I would like just one thing: that he should point out to me one place where he so directly contradicts the Paradox, as he calls it, and indeed here he contradicts himself. I, at least, have not been able to find such a place.

units.la: Pagina 24. illud occurrit, quod veneranda Classis Leovardiensis, unanimiter, absurdum judicavit, in suo ad Synodum Anni 1668. missó gravamine: sic sonant verba, sufficit Deum dixisse, ut sciamus eum fallere nolle. Dico nolle eum fallere, ut ne credatis non posse, si velit, cum enim omnis qui alterum fallere aggreditur, eo censeatur in ista re quodammodo superior esse, & vel acumine quodam ingenii, vel potentia, aliave quacunque facultate praestare, sitque Dei, tum sapientia tum potentia, caeteraque omnia attributa infinita; quis non videt creaturas etiam perfectissimas, quia sunt semper finitae, eopse quod creaturae, ab infinito creatore posse in errorem induci. Pia mens qui haec non detestabunda, non gemebunda legat? tales in sinu fovet Ecclesia. Putem Averroem & alios crudum illud ἀπροληψίας [?] & θεοφυγίας [?] dogma, non magis a Christianismo absterruisse, quam istud Judaeis & cunctis infidelibus scandalo futurum sit, si innotescat. Deo fallendi potentia est? horret animus! idque perfectionem dicit? nae, illud idolum evadet, quod fallere queat: scilicet similia dixerant Cartesius & Venerandus sc: Senior Velthuysen & pauci lucis filii. Excusent, pallient, quocunque colore velint: non decet tamen ita de Summa & tremenda Majestate irreverenter & prophane loqui. Verax Deus & Vindex audit: ignoscat tibi istud enorme dictum! At vero se parum hic Theologum, qui potentiam Dei recte percipiat, ostendit Cartesius, ait Schulerus, mutetur nomen & omnia quadrabunt: nos, ait idem ad §. xxix. nec voluntatem nec potentiam fallendi in Deo esse posse constanter asserimus. Notandum fallendi potentiam magnae imperfectionis esse signum; nam, qui fallit alium, mentitur, eique pro ipsa veritate speciem duntaxat illius seu apparentiam obtrudere conatur. Qui mentitur, aliud interne sentit, & aliud externe sive voce sive signo signo enunciat, adeoque à se ipso dissentit, & quasi duplex est; cum autem duplicitas & dissensio in Deum non cadant, quia summè unus & simplex est, utique nec mentiendi aut fallendi in ipso potentiam esse posse, evidens evadit: cumque Deus sit ens absolute perfectum, utique & veracitatem, quae voluntatis perfectio est, eminentissimo modo in ipso contineri, manifestum est; & hoc sensu Veteres olim Deum αὐτοαληθείαν[?] dixere.
units.tr: On page 24 there occurs something which the venerable Classis of Leeuwarden unanimously judged absurd, in its grievance sent to the Synod of the year 1668. The words run thus: It is enough that God has said that we may know He is unwilling to deceive. I say He is unwilling to deceive, so that you do not believe He could not if He wished; for since everyone who sets out to deceive another is thought in that matter to be in some way superior, and to excel either by some keenness of wit, or by power, or by whatever other faculty, and since God's wisdom, power, and all His other attributes are infinite, who does not see that even the most perfect creatures, because they are always finite, precisely as creatures, can be led into error by the infinite Creator? What pious mind could read these things without detesting and lamenting them? Such things the Church nurses in her bosom. I think that Averroes and others were no more deterred from Christianity by that crude dogma of "lack of providence" [ἀπροληψίας] and "flight from God" [θεοφυγίας] than this will be a stumbling block to the Jews and all unbelievers if it becomes known. Is there a power in God to deceive? The mind shrinks in horror! And he calls this perfection? Indeed, that will become an idol able to deceive. Clearly Descartes and the venerable Senior Velthuysen, and a few sons of light, have said similar things. Let them excuse, gloss over, and colour it as they will: it is not fitting to speak so irreverently and profanely about the supreme and awesome Majesty. The truthful God hears, and He will avenge; may He pardon you for that monstrous saying! But Schuler says that Descartes shows here that he is a theologian who does not rightly perceive the power of God; let the name be changed and everything will fit. We, says the same author in §29, constantly assert that there can be in God neither will nor power to deceive. It should be noted that the power to deceive is a sign of great imperfection; for he who deceives another lies, and tries to thrust upon him not the truth itself but merely its appearance or semblance. He who lies thinks one thing inwardly and states another outwardly, by voice or by sign, and so is at odds with himself and is, as it were, double; but since duplicity and dissent do not fall upon God, who is supremely one and simple, it becomes evident that there can be no power of lying or deceiving in Him; and since God is a being absolutely perfect, it is clear that truthfulness, which is the perfection of the will, is contained in Him in the most eminent manner; and in this sense the ancients once called God truth itself [αὐτοαλήθειαν].

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur tenebrarum causa Sol esse nequit, quia natura sua lucidus est, ita neque erroris, mendacii aut falsitatis causa Deus esse potest, quia natura sua verax est, ut dictum. Praeterea cum mendacium procedat vel ex ignorantia, vel ex errore judicii, vel ex malitia morali, quorum nihil in Deo esse potest, cum sit omniscius, summè sapiens & infinite bonus, utique erroris, falsitatis, aut mendacii causam ipsum esse non posse colligitur. Scitè admodum & acutè Vir Doctus ita de Wolzogio. Novi similes & alios Interpretes Cartesii, prorsus insubidos, quique mali videntur in opprobrium sui praeceptoris. Ita nuper nonnemo, tanquam juxta mentem Cartesii, pronunciavit, posse Deum fallere si velit, sed non velle. Quo nihil dici potest, ut mollissime loqui, inconsideratius. Huc nimirum recidit male sana Philosophatio; Deum posse quidem a vero deficere si velit, sed non velle. Deum posse quidem fieri non Deum si velit, sed non velle. Solida argumentatio.nam revera qui potest aliqua imperfectione laborare, is potest esse non Deus, jam autem fallere ne quidem concipi potest sine falsitate & imperfectione. Purus etiam Scepticismus docetur hac methodo: si enim fieri queat, ut Deus unquam fallat, unde certus eris Deum non fallere in omnibus? dicat licet in verbo suo expressis verbis, ego non fallo, eo ipso enim quod ponatur eum posse fallere, imo verbale mendacium proferre, quod concedit Cartes & ex eo cum Pastore hocce, Senior Velthuysen, unde novero eum nunc hisce ipsis verbis hoc non agere, non fallere, etiam dum dicit, ego jam non fallo: Deinde fit enunciatio quædam singularis, unde constabit an Deus eâ fallat nec ne ; vide quò eas bone Vir. Nunc clament Pontificii, Remonstrantes aliique nos Deum peccati facere authorem, saltem ipsi peccandi potentiam adscribi. Nunc merito Papistis & Ubiquitariis vapulabimus, πολυτο-πίαν & παντοπίαν [?] impossibilem dicentes, dum interim mentiendi, saltem fallendi, potentiam Deo tribuimus. Denique mendacia officiosa loquens, Deum imitabitur: apage ineptas istas nugas dicam an horridas blasphemias. Tam brevis tibi præ nimia perspicuitate fuit memoria Wolzogi, ut verborum paulò ante, imò eadem pagina, dictorum oblivio te ceperit? à veritate falsum proficisci, à bonitate deceptio-nem, perfectissimæ naturæ repugnat. Deum falsum dicere non posse: jam vero fallere posse, non tantum non repugnat, sed perfectio videtur: quod perfectissimæ naturæ repugnare dixerat, jam Deo tribuitur, egregie sane & perspicue. Nec evadis dicendo, id ta-men eum velle negamus, at unde hoc tibi constat? qui scis, toto verbo suo, te non fallere Deum, etiam dum se non fallere dicit? dic jam ubi pedem figas. Sed audiamus, ea enim decipiendi voluntas concipi vix potest, quin aliquid habere censeatur, vel malitiæ con-junctum, vel imbecillitatis animi, quæ cum utraque magnam arguant imperfectionem, ab eo removenda, quem &c. Pudeat te! quid dicis? intelligi vix &c. tam tenuiter, tam meticulosè vera dicis: & quid si vix? tu igitur Deo tribues quicquam, quod absque mali-tiâ conjuncta & imbecillitate animi, concipi vix potest? Scriptura aliquid perspicuè si dixerit, rationi tuæ modo repugnare videatur, commodè explicandam censes: jam quod Scriptura, quod ratio clamant, dictant diserte, vix audes eloqui? Bileam te doceat, Deus fortis non est homo qui mentiatur, aut filius hominis quem poeniteat: an ipse dixerit & non faciet? aut loquutus fuerit & non præstabit illud ? Exsertius vero Apostolus Tit. 1. 2. Deus ille mentiri nescius. Imo veritas Joh. xiv. 6. Qualem tandem discemus
units.tr: Therefore, just as the Sun cannot be the cause of darkness because it is by nature bright, so God cannot be the cause of error, lying, or falsehood, because by His nature He is truthful, as has been said. Moreover, since lying proceeds either from ignorance, or from an error of judgment, or from moral malice, none of which can be in God, since He is all-knowing, most wise, and infinitely good, it follows that He cannot be the cause of error, falsehood, or lying. The learned man has spoken most skilfully and acutely of Wolzogen in this way: I know similar and other interpreters of Descartes, utterly foolish, who seem to be bad to the disgrace of their teacher. Thus recently someone, as though according to the mind of Descartes, pronounced that God can deceive if He wishes, but does not wish to. Nothing can be said that is more inconsiderate, to put it very mildly. This, of course, is where a badly sound philosophizing comes down: that God can indeed fall away from the truth if He wishes, but does not wish to; that God can indeed cease to be God if He wishes, but does not wish to. A solid argument! For indeed whoever can labour under some imperfection can be not God, and yet deceiving cannot even be conceived without falsehood and imperfection. Pure scepticism is also taught by this method: for if it can happen that God ever deceives, how will you be certain that God does not deceive in everything? Let Him say in His word, in express words, "I do not deceive"; for by the very fact that He is supposed able to deceive, indeed to utter a verbal lie, which Descartes concedes, and with him this minister, the elder Velthuysen, from which I shall know that He is not doing this now in these very words, that He is not deceiving even while He says "I do not deceive now", then there arises some singular statement by which it will be established whether God deceives by it or not. See where these things lead, good sir. Now let the Papists, Remonstrants, and others cry out that we make God the author of sin, or at least ascribe to Him the power of sinning. Now we shall rightly thrash the Papists and Ubiquitarians, who call multi-location [πολυτοπίαν] and ubiquity [παντοπίαν] impossible, while meanwhile we attribute to God the power of lying, or at least of deceiving. Finally, one who speaks dutiful lies will imitate God: away with those inept trifles, I should say horrible blasphemies! Has the memory of Wolzogen been so short for you, from excessive clarity, that you have been seized by forgetting what was said a little before, indeed on the same page? For falsehood to proceed from truth, or deception from goodness, is repugnant to the most perfect nature. That God cannot speak falsely: now indeed that He can deceive is not only not repugnant, but seems to be perfection. What he said was repugnant to the most perfect nature is now attributed to God, quite plainly and clearly. Nor do you escape by saying that "we deny that He wills it"; but how do you know this? How do you know, from the whole of His word, that God does not deceive, even while He says that He does not deceive? Now say where you plant your foot. But let us hear: for a will to deceive can hardly be conceived without being thought to have something joined to it, either malice or weakness of mind, which, since both indicate great imperfection, must be removed from Him who etc. Shame on you! What do you say? That it can hardly be understood, etc.; you speak true things so thinly, so timidly. And what if it is "hardly"? Do you then attribute to God anything that can hardly be conceived without joined malice and weakness of mind? When Scripture has clearly said something which seems to be opposed to your reason, you think it should be conveniently explained; but do you hardly dare to utter what Scripture and reason cry out and dictate plainly? Let Balaam teach you: God is not a man that He should lie, nor the son of man that He should repent; has He said, and will He not do it? Or has He spoken, and will He not fulfil it? More plainly still, the Apostle in Titus 1: God, who cannot lie. Indeed, the truth in John 14:6. What sort of theology shall we learn in the end? Will it be said that God can do something which cannot be said He wills, unless some malice or weakness of mind is attributed to Him? Bisterfeld rightly says in his Pneumatics, chapter 56: the executive power of God is the active power by which God can do all things outside Himself, by which He freely wills...

units.la: Theologiam ? dicetur Deus aliquid posse quod non potest dici velle, nisi aliqua ipsi tribuatur malitia, aut animi imbecillitas. Optime Bisterfeldius Pneu-matices Cap. LVI. Potentia Dei executiva est poten-tia activa, qua Deus omnia extra se facere potest, qua libere velle potest. Repugnat potentiæ ut agat, quod impossibile est absolute, voluntas ut velit. Imo sunt inter Scholasticos qui putent voluntatem formaliter idem esse in Deo cum potentia. Divina voluntas juxta nostrum Amesium, habet rationem potentiæ, ut est principium effectivum. Qui conceptus, quanquam minus accuratus videatur P. Voetio, nihilominus tamen certum est, ut loquitur Maresius, in sensu identico & materialiter, omnia in Deo esse Deum, & voluntatem coincidere cum potentia & vice versa. Dicat jam Doctor dilucidus, qui aliquid cum voluntate ita pugnet, ut etiam in sensu diviso illud Deum velle repugnet, quod tamen potentiæ perfectio, requirit ut possit. Optime Paradoxus alibi sic de veritatis Spi-ritu, in quem ne umbra quidem falsitatis aut fallaciæ cadere potest, quæ probat Wolz. p. 143. Fidei divinæ subesse falsum posse, cum statueret Maccovius, omnibus fere displicebat: Hoc autem quod tu ais, ulterius progreditur. Ille Dei sinceram veracitatem, aliorum judicio, minuebat, quid jam de tuo conceptu dicet Reformatus orbis ? quadrant hic verba Raimundi de Sabunde: Magis audienda sunt verba ejus, qui non potest mentiri, quam illius qui vel fallere vel falli potest. Commentum de potentia peccandi in Christo, ab Arminio, ex Scoto, Durando, &c. ad liberi arbitrii defensionem propositum, scimus quanto-pere pere bonis & orthodoxis omnibus displicuerit, testes sint, Voetius, qui horridas vocat & profanas, de hac Quæstione, Scholasticorum disceptationes. Triglan-dius,etsi Apologia non aperte audeat Arminii vestigia premere, sic loquitur, exhorrescere oportet ad hac ani-mum quemvis pium, & rite considerantem, qua & qualis sit persona ista θεάνθρωπος[?]. Quantum autem illa adhuc distent, quis non videt? nisi qui divinam naturam humanæ, creaturæ creatorem præferre, nondum didicit. Quanto enim divinitas humanitate major est, tanto pejor est Wolzogii, in hoc negotio, quam Arminii error, hic Christo & quidem secundum humanam naturam, ille Deo fallendi potentiam tribuit, uterque impie & arroganter. Cloppenbur-gius Arminianos in eo refutaturus, hoc absurdo eos premit, quod tueri non possunt, infallibilem Christi veracitatem in Doctrina. Quid autem dixisset, si hoc non solum, non absurdum esse, sed & Deum fallere, verbale mendacium proferre posse regessissent? non expectabat tam crudum ab ipsis Remonstrantibus dogma. Jam si viveret, ex Pastore Ecclesiæ Reform. idem & pejus intelligeret. Evigilet Eccl. Reform. & tantam labem maculamque abstergat solenniter & cito.
units.tr: Theology? It will be said that God can do something which cannot be said that he wills, unless some malice or weakness of spirit is ascribed to him. Bisterfeld rightly says in his Pneumatics, chapter 56: The executive power of God is an active power, by which God can do all things outside himself, by which he can will freely. It is inconsistent that the power to act should be impossible in an absolute sense while the will to act is possible. Indeed, some among the Scholastics think that in God the will is formally the same as the power. According to our Amesius, the divine will has the character of power insofar as it is an effective principle. Although this concept may seem less accurate to P. Voetius, it is nonetheless certain, as Maresius puts it, that in an identical sense and materially, everything in God is God, and that the will coincides with the power and vice versa. Let the learned doctor now say what it is that so opposes the will that, even in a divided sense, God's willing it is inconsistent, when yet the perfection of power requires that he be able to do it. Paradoxus, elsewhere, rightly speaks thus of the Spirit of truth, on whom not even a shadow of falsehood or deceit can fall, which Wolzogen cites at p. 143. When Maccovius asserted that falsehood could be present in divine faith, almost everyone was displeased. But what you say goes further still. He diminished, in the judgement of others, the sincere truthfulness of God; what will the Reformed world now say of your concept? The words of Raimund of Sabunde fit here: The words of one who cannot lie are to be heard more than those of one who can either deceive or be deceived. We know how greatly the fiction of the power of sinning in Christ, put forward by Arminius from Scotus, Durandus, and others, in defence of free will, displeased all good and orthodox men. Let Voetius be witness, who calls these horrid and profane disputations of the Scholastics on this question. Triglandius, although in his Apology he does not openly dare to tread in the footsteps of Arminius, speaks thus: every pious man who rightly considers what and what sort of person this God-man is ought to shrink back from such thoughts. How far, however, these are still apart, who does not see? Unless one has not yet learned to prefer the divine nature to the human, the Creator to the creature. For the greater the divinity is above the humanity, the worse is Wolzogen's error in this matter than Arminius's: the latter attributed the power of deceiving to Christ, and that according to his human nature, while the former attributes it to God; both do so impiously and arrogantly. Cloppenburg, when about to refute the Arminians on this point, presses them with this absurdity: that they cannot maintain the infallible truthfulness of Christ in doctrine. But what would he have said if they had replied that this was not only not absurd, but that God could also deceive and utter a verbal lie? He did not expect so crude a dogma from the Remonstrants themselves. Now if he were alive, he would understand the same thing, and worse, from a minister of the Reformed Church. Let the Reformed Church awake and wipe away so great a stain and blot solemnly and quickly.

units.la: Pagina 26, & 27. quædam minus reverenter dicta vide, de oratione Scripturæ, loquens, eas more pror-sus humano exaratas esse dicit. Scio hoc aliquo respectu dici forsan posse, sed etiam de Deo & divinis vera loqui periculosum cum sit, non absque limitatione & debita observantia id fieri necesse est: quod si cogitasset, non ita leviter de sacri majestate styli loqueretur, ac si credulitati Theologorum imputandum sit, quod ex ea, Scripturæ divinitas probari posse putetur, & in ejus explicatione non aliter esse versan-dum, quam in aliorum librorum interpretatione: Fateor hæc omnia excusari posse, nisi, saltem jactata, perspicuitas deesset, & limitata ἀκρίβεια; crudum enim dictu est, non aliter in explicatione Scripturæ versandum, quam aliorum librorum. Rem ipsam posthac dabimus per Dei gratiam. aliter Baco Verulam. alter autem Interpretandi modus, (quem pro excessu statuimus) videtur primo intuitu sobrius & castus; sed tamen & Scripturas ipsas dedecorat, & plurimo Ecclesiam afficit detrimento, is est (ut verbo dicamus) quando Scriptura divinitus inspirata, eodem quo scripta humana, explicantur modo. Hæc utinam cum lusu schacchico, ex eodem de Augment. Scient. Lib. ix. Cap. didicisset author! Argumentum à Styli Majestate, ab Episcopio, quem sæpius quam Calvinum sequitur Wolzogen, rejectum scio. Tu si rejicias, dicas dilucide, & adversarium habebis quemcunque Reformatum Theologum. Quanquam fides illa etiam generalis, judice Cloppenburgio, Triglandio multisque aliis, sine aliqua, communi saltem Spiritus Sancti illuminatione, haberi nequeat, aut Scriptura ut Dei verbum recipi, nihilominus argumenta Scripturæ insita ejus divinitatem affatim demonstrant. Methodus enim & demonstratio fidei illius, sc: qua Scriptura ut Dei Verbum recipitur, non est petenda apud infideles, ad fidem adducendos, ex interno illo Spiritus S. testimonio. Pendet ergo ea, donec intus persuadeantur, ex pondere illorum argumentorum quorum primum est Styli Majestas. Credunt igitur Theologi ex Scriptionis Majestate probari Scripturæ divinitatem, negat Episcopius. Wolzogius quid sentiat, lectori divinandum relinquit. Quod enim de impressa Scripturæ imagine Dei habet p. 54. non excusat; nondum enim constat, an Styli Majestas ad hujus imaginis lineamenta pertineat, ex ipsius sententia, nec ne.
units.tr: On pages 26 and 27 see certain things said with less reverence, where, speaking of the style of Scripture, he says that they were written entirely in a human manner. I know this may perhaps be said in some respect, but since it is dangerous to speak truly even of God and divine things, it must be done not without qualification and due reverence. If he had considered this, he would not speak so lightly of the majesty of the sacred style, as though it were to be imputed to the credulity of theologians that the divinity of Scripture is thought to be provable from it, and that in its explanation one should not proceed otherwise than in the interpretation of other books. I grant that all these things could be excused, were it not that at least the boasted clarity and a limited accuracy are lacking; for it is a crude statement that in the explanation of Scripture one should not proceed otherwise than with other books. By God's grace we will treat the matter itself hereafter. Otherwise Bacon of Verulam, the other mode of interpreting (which we set down as an excess) seems at first glance sober and chaste; yet it both dishonours the Scriptures themselves and inflicts great harm on the Church; it is (to put it in a word) when inspired Scripture is explained in the same way as written human works. I wish the author had learned this, along with the game of chess, from the same book of Bacon's On the Advancement of Learning, Book 9, chapter. I know that the argument from the majesty of style is rejected by Episcopius, whom Wolzogen follows more often than Calvin. If you reject it, say so clearly, and you will have as your adversary any Reformed theologian whatever. Although that general faith, according to Cloppenburg, Triglandius, and many others, cannot be had without some common illumination of the Holy Spirit, or Scripture be received as God's Word, nevertheless the arguments inherent in Scripture abundantly demonstrate its divinity. For the method and demonstration of that faith by which Scripture is received as the Word of God is not to be sought among unbelievers, to bring them to faith, from that inner testimony of the Holy Spirit. It depends, therefore, until they are persuaded inwardly, on the weight of those arguments, the first of which is the majesty of style. Theologians therefore believe that the divinity of Scripture is proved from the majesty of the Scriptures; Episcopius denies it. What Wolzogen thinks he leaves for the reader to guess. For what he says at p. 54 about the image of God impressed on Scripture does not excuse him; for it is not yet clear, by his own opinion, whether or not the majesty of style belongs to the features of this image.

units.la: Pagina 31. Ratio fidei lumen sæpe mutuatur, dicit author. Rursus non satis dilucide. Videri enim po-test, statuere Philosophiam illustrari à Scriptura, sed inde concludi forsan posset, Scripturam dogmatizare etiam in naturalibus, quod Lipstorpium post conver-sionem, Velthuisium, Wittichium, aliosque lucis filios, vereor ne offendat. Scriptura rationis lumini etiam aliquid debet ait author, sed audi. Fidei est rationi prae-scribere, & id facere, ut ne sit opus ratione. Sin ratio-nem requiris, & quaerendum putas, ergo non credis. Ut certe ratione sua abuti convincantur, quicunque hac in parte nimis rationales videri volunt. Quid aliud est rationis naturalis nisus, in religionis negotio, quam religiosa quaedam insania, imo verius irreligiosa stultitia, & rationale delirium. Verba sunt Heidani. Lubet adscribere quae Heereboord huic negotio inservientia, scripsit, etiam cum rationis & Philosophiae causam strenuè agebat adversus Amesium, quantum inquit differunt πιστεύειν[?] & λογίζεσθαι[?], hoc est credere & ratiocinari, tantum differunt haud dubie, πίστις & ἐπιστήμη, sive scientia, id est, habitus assentiendi propositionibus demonstratis: quare cum Theologia sit, πίστις, & Philosophiae pars, quae de Deo, reliquisque incorporeis disserit, sit ἐπιστήμη, sequitur, diversos esse mentis habitus, etiamsi habeant idem objectum. ---- in Theologia revelata longe aliter se res habet: illa enim, non rationes sequitur, sed in Dei αὐτο-πίστει fide, quae omnibus rationibus ac demonstrationibus certior est ac firmior, sine ulla inquisitione atque examine acquiescit: & sine erroris metu. Hæc clara sunt, at de hisce impostorum latius.
units.tr: On page 31 the author says: Reason often borrows its light from faith. Again, not clearly enough. For it may seem that he is asserting that philosophy is illuminated by Scripture, but from this it might perhaps be concluded that Scripture also teaches in matters of nature; I fear this would offend Lipstorp after his conversion, Velthuysen, Wittich, and other sons of light. Scripture also owes something to the light of reason, the author says; but listen: It is for faith to prescribe to reason, and to do this so that there is no need for reason. But if you ask for reason, and think it must be sought, then you do not believe. Certainly those who wish to appear too rational in this respect are convicted of abusing their reason. What else is the striving of natural reason in religious matters but a certain religious madness, or rather an irreligious folly and rational delirium? These are the words of Heidanus. I should like to add what Heereboord, who served this matter, wrote, even while vigorously defending reason and philosophy against Amesius: As far as believing [πιστεύειν] and reasoning [λογίζεσθαι], that is, to believe and to reason, differ, so undoubtedly do faith [πίστις] and knowledge [ἐπιστήμη], or science, that is, the habit of assenting to demonstrated propositions, differ. Therefore, since theology is faith, and philosophy, which treats of God and the other incorporeal things, is knowledge, it follows that they are different habits of mind, even though they have the same object. ---- In revealed theology the matter stands far otherwise: it does not follow reasons, but rests, without any inquiry or examination, in God's own faith [αὐτοπίστει], which is more certain and firmer than all reasons and demonstrations, and without any fear of error. These things are clear; but more about these impostors later.

units.la: Pagina 33. occurrunt hæc verba: qui omnes perfectiones cum alio communicat, ipsum amittere eas necesse est, quae dividi non possunt. In hisce ἀνεξ[?]έσιαν[?] desidero & perspicuitatem aut veritatem & orthodoxiam; illam, si salvam velit de S.S. Trinitate doctrinam; hanc si verba sua intellecta velit prout jacent. Nisi enim addat se de personalium, non vero ab-solutarum perfectionum, communicatione loqui, quæque fiat cum eo, qui sit alterius essentiæ, procul dubio errat gravissime. Utraque enim processio, sic felicissimus ille Socinianæ blasphemiæ debellator Bi-sterfeldius, in divinis est communicatio divinæ essentiæ & quidem immanens, simul cum omnibus perfectio-nibus. Pater autem dando filium habere vitam in se, eo vitam non amisit, communicavit tamen. Si autem dictam limitationem addat, summæ inadverten-tiæ reatum, pro tantopere jactatæ perspicuitatis encomio, fateri debebit necessario.
units.tr: On page 33 these words occur: He who communicates all perfections to another necessarily loses those which cannot be divided. In these words I miss both clarity and truth and orthodoxy: clarity, if he wishes to keep the doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity safe; truth, if he wishes his words to be taken as they lie. For unless he adds that he is speaking of the communication of personal, and not of absolute, perfections, and that this is done with one who is of another essence, he undoubtedly errs most gravely. For each procession, so says that most fortunate opponent of Socinian blasphemy, Bisterfeld, in the divine persons is a communication of the divine essence, and indeed an immanent one, together with all perfections. But the Father, in giving the Son to have life in himself, did not thereby lose life, but communicated it. If, however, he adds the said limitation, he must necessarily confess to the guilt of the greatest carelessness, instead of the praise of the clarity so much boasted of.

units.la: 14. Properamus ad examen effati quod refert p. seq. sic ibi author, rationem Dei beneficio nobis indultam dixerat, cui, inquit, quando clare distincte-que percipit, si quid esse contrarium possit, quod sit tamen verum, non video qui possit ab omni dolo sanctissimum numen absolvi. Proram scilicet videmus novæ Philosophiæ & puppim, duo autem de hoc effato disquiri possunt, toto genere diversa. Primum, an effa-tum istud verum sit, quicquid clare & distincte percipio illud est verum: Alterum, an concessa huic axiomati veritate, tuto pro veritatisnorma & regula idem recipiatur. Illud disquirendum Philosophis. Nec enim libertati Philosophicæ detrahendū quicquam est, modo ne in infrunitam degeneret licentiam. Cui si Ecclesiæ invigilandum aut attendendum non esse quis dixerit. Is nec Philosophiam, nec Theologiam, nec quid sit Censura, de qua loquitur, hactenus didicit. Philosophica fateor ad Pastorum Ecclesiæ tribunal non pertinent, sed an Philosophi in Theologiam quando involant, procul inde non arcendi & quidem à Theologis? hoc autem, utpote maximi periculi, displicuit, præcedenti anno, omnibus Classis Leovardiensis membris; ita, ut gravamini, de damnosis, quæ ingruunt, novitatibus, inter alias, etiam hanc quæstionem, Synodo examinandam tradere ipsis vi-sum fuerit. Quoniam vero Wolzogio, nulla cogente ratione, etiam hoc effatum adoptare placuit, age-dum paucis id expendamus. Sic igitur juniores Philo-sophi, Quicquid clare & distincte percipio, illud est ve-rum. Varius hujus effati potest esse sensus. 1. Vel enim significat omnia quæ percipio, modo clare & distincte, etiamsi simpliciter solum apprehendam, ea sunt vera; hoc autem sensu salsissimum istud axioma est. Etenim mens nostra, cum habeat facultatem re-præsentandi divisim, ea, quæ cognoverat conjunctim & vice versa, ita ut clare & distincte repræsentari queant conjunctim, quæ revera non existunt nisi divisim: Quid vetat montem aureum aut simile quid, non repugnanter fictum, clare & distincte mihi re-præsentare quod tamen existere nullo modo, certum est. Jam dudum docuit Scaliger in simplici, apprehen-sione, intellectione nullam esse veritatem. Et error, cum, ex mente Cartesii, voluntatis sit, judicium quippe in voluntate collocat, procul omni dubio in sim-plici apprehensione, quippe quæ actus est intellectus, voluntatisque actionem omnem antecedens, verum vel falsum esse non potest; simplex autem apprehensio cum etiam clara & distincta esse possit, sequitur necef-sario non omne esse verum quod clare & distincte percipio, hoc sensu. Illud est quod in negotio de Idea Dei notavit Ignatius Derkennis, conceptum simpli-cem & apprehensivum confundi cum discursivo & ju-dicativo. Deinde omnes res possibiles clare & distin-cte cum percipiamus, non aliter, ex mente Cartesii, quam ut existentes, quapropter ap-plicato hoc effato sequetur, omnes res possibiles exi-stere revera: nec juvat dicere, eorum tamen existen-tiam inde non sequi; ex idea enim Dei ista ratione deducis Dei existentiam, quia Deum concipere te non posse dicis, nisi conceptum ingrediatur existentia, cum autem clarum & distinctum de possibilibus con-ceptum itidem ingrediatur existentia, ut dicit Carte-sius, quidni & inde sequitur, quod dictum est, res illas omnes æque ut Deum actu existere? præsertim cum omnino à NOSSE ad ESSE valeat juxta Cartesium consequentia? Existentia quidem Dei, non ut possibilis concipitur, sed ut actualis, at id & obtinet in reliquis, essentia enim rei,ut absque actualitate,absque existen-tia, non poterat concipi, sic & necessario existentia igitur etiam ut actualis concipi debet. Diversam eo-rum rationem si dicas, quia non intelligimus necesse esse, ut actualis existentia cum aliis aliarum rerum pro-prietatibus conjuncta sit, verum quod intelligamus existentiam actualem necessario & cum reliquis Dei attributis conjunctam esse. Regero hæc optime dici secundum rei veritatem, non vero tuam Philoso-phandi methodum. Cum enim ex eo quod clare & distincte rem percipis, (quæ perceptio apprehensio tantummodo simplex, vel te teste, est, vel esse posset, quamque tu contradistinguis judicio) colligas, quid de repræsentati natura dicendum sit; in utriusque au-tem tum Dei tum aliarum rerum ideis semper tibi re-præsentetur conjunctim cum aliis attributis existen-tia, quæ an separari possit nec ne, illa cognitione non-dum cognoscis, cum id judicare fit, utique æque ex clara & distincta cognitione ideæ aliarum rerum, quam ex idea Dei, existentia sequetur, quippe in utriusque prima simplici apprehensione juxta te inclu-sa, & ad eam ut concipi possit requisita. Sed alio sensu an admitti ut veritatis norma possit hoc effatum vi-deamus, vel igitur 2. hoc vis, omne illud quod tu clare & distincte concipis existere, illud etiam revera existere. At 1. sic non docet Cartesius, quærenti enim quomodo sequatur cogito E. sum: Respondet his ver-bis, in hac prima cognitione nihil occurrit, quam clara quædam & distincta perceptio ejus quod affirmo; quæ sane[?] non sufficeret ad me certum de rei veritate redden-dum, si posset unquam contingere, ut aliquid quod ita clare & distincte perciperem falsum esset: hinc generalis illa regula, quicquid, &c. 2. necdum sequitur, posset enim a te ficta, ex te orta esse talis rei finitae saltem idea, ad minimum non constat, an ex te ipso re simili nullibi existente ista idea ortum habeat, an vera res quaedam sit, quae se tibi offerens tale sui repraesentamen tibi reliquum fecerit: sicque nihil adhuc evincis. Porro sit quaedam res & revera sit, habeas ejus ideam & quidem veram, eam intueare: cum autem aliquam huic simile tibi ipsi finxisse potuisses, unde jam constabit, te revera veri hominis e. gr. ideam intueri & non aliquam fictam, illi similem, cujus itidem habes claram & distinctam perceptionem. 3. Imo ipse Car-tesius ei non fidit: dicit enim se nulla alia Physices principia posuisse quam quae evidentissime perspecta erant, ut & nihil inde nisi per Mathematicas id est necessarias & evidentes consequentias collegisse, & omnia ista ita naturae Phænomenis ad amussim consensisse, ut injurio in Deum fore dicat, si qui causas rerum, hoc pacto ab ipso inventas, falsas suspicarentur. Quo facto clare & distincte concipit rerum naturam & ordinem se tali modo habere. Nihilominus clara hac & distincta hujus ordinis conceptione non obstante, de tota sua dissertatione ipse sic loquitur. Quinimo etiam, ad res naturales melius explicandas, earum causas altius a se repetitas, quam ipsas unquam extitisse existimet. & in margine dicit, se hic hypothe-ses nonnullas assumturum quas constat esse falsas. Ne-que etiam ei fidere potuit, concedit enim, aliis hy-pothesibus pro fundamento jactis, eadem naturae Phænomena, alia prorsus, quamvis operosiore for-san, methodo, etiam clare & perspicuè explicari, sic-que & clare & distincte concipi posse. Quinimo evi-denter ejus falsitatem profitetur, falsam enim rerum dispositionem & hypotheses dicit, quas clarè & distin-ctè conceptas narrat. Et mirum est, cum clara illa & distincta perceptio, ipso judice, mentem defæcatam & præjudiciis liberam prærequirat, hoc est Cartesii Philosophantem methodo, eum nemini authorem esse velle, ut simile quid aggrediatur. Nisi tanti non esse hanc regulam ipse judicasset. Si enim unica hæc veritatis via sit & norma, quid attinet id dissuadere, quod in quolibet ea regula rite usuro prærequiritur?
units.tr: 14. We now come to the saying that the author quotes on the following page. There he says that reason, granted to us by God's favour, "when it perceives clearly and distinctly, if anything can be contrary which is nevertheless true, I do not see how the most holy divinity can be acquitted of all deceit." Clearly we see the prow and stern of the new philosophy. Two questions can be raised about this saying, entirely different in kind. First, whether the saying is true: whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly, that is true. Second, granting the truth of this axiom, whether it may safely be adopted as the norm and rule of truth. The first question is for the philosophers. Nothing should be taken away from philosophical freedom, provided it does not degenerate into unbridled license. If anyone should say that the Church need not watch over or attend to this, he has learned neither philosophy, nor theology, nor what the censure is of which he speaks. I admit that philosophical matters do not belong to the tribunal of the Church's ministers. But when philosophers break into theology, should they not be kept away from there, and indeed by theologians? This question, as being of the greatest danger, displeased all the members of the Classis of Leeuwarden in the previous year. So much so that, in their complaint about the harmful novelties that are pressing in, they thought fit to hand over to the Synod for examination, among other things, this very question. But since it has pleased Wolzogen, without any compelling reason, to adopt this saying too, let us weigh it briefly. So the younger philosophers say: Whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly, that is true. The sense of this saying can vary. (1) It may mean that everything I perceive, provided it is clear and distinct, is true, even if I apprehend it only simply. In this sense the saying is most false. For our mind has the faculty of representing separately things it has known together, and vice versa, so that things which in reality exist only separately can be represented clearly and distinctly together. What prevents me from clearly and distinctly representing to myself a golden mountain, or something similar, not inconsistently imagined, which yet certainly does not exist anywhere? Scaliger long ago taught that in simple apprehension, in understanding there is no truth. And error, since on Descartes' view it belongs to the will (for he places judgement in the will), undoubtedly cannot lie in simple apprehension, which is an act of the intellect and precedes every act of the will; it can be neither true nor false. Since simple apprehension can also be clear and distinct, it necessarily follows that not everything I perceive clearly and distinctly is true, in this sense. This is what Ignatius Derkennis noted in the matter of the idea of God: the simple, apprehensive concept is confused with the discursive and judicative. Again, since we perceive all possible things clearly and distinctly, on Descartes' view we perceive them only as existing. Therefore, applying this saying, it will follow that all possible things really exist. Nor does it help to say that existence does not follow from them. For from the idea of God you deduce God's existence by this reasoning, because you say you cannot conceive God unless existence enters the concept. But since, as Descartes says, existence likewise enters the clear and distinct concept of possibles, why should it not also follow, as has been said, that all those things actually exist just as God does? Especially since, according to Descartes, the inference from knowing to being holds entirely? The existence of God is conceived not as possible but as actual. Yet this holds for the rest too: the essence of a thing cannot be conceived without actuality, without existence. So existence too must necessarily be conceived as actual. If you give a different reason, namely that we do not understand it to be necessary for actual existence to be joined with the other properties of things, but we understand that actual existence is necessarily joined with the remaining attributes of God, I reply that these things are rightly said according to the truth of the matter, but not according to your method of philosophizing. For from the fact that you perceive a thing clearly and distinctly (which perception is, by your own testimony, or could be, a mere simple apprehension, and which you distinguish from judgement), you infer what must be said about the nature of the thing represented. Yet in the ideas both of God and of other things, existence is always represented to you together with the other attributes. Whether it can be separated from them or not, you do not yet know from that knowledge, since judging this is a separate act. Then, certainly, from the clear and distinct knowledge of the idea of other things existence will follow just as much as from the idea of God, since in the first simple apprehension of each, by your own account, existence is included and required for the thing to be conceived. But let us see whether this saying can be admitted as a norm of truth in another sense. (2) Or else you mean this: everything you clearly and distinctly conceive to exist, that also truly exists. But (1) Descartes does not teach this. When asked how I think, therefore I am follows, he answers in these words: In this first knowledge there is nothing except a certain clear and distinct perception of what I affirm; which certainly would not suffice to make me certain of the truth of the thing, if it could ever happen that something which I perceived so clearly and distinctly were false: hence that general rule, whatever, etc. (2) Nor does it yet follow. An idea of such a finite thing may have been feigned by you and arisen from yourself. It is not established whether this idea has arisen from yourself, with a similar thing nowhere existing, or whether it is some true thing which, offering itself to you, left you such a representation of itself. So you prove nothing yet. Further, suppose there is a certain thing which really is, and you have its idea, and a true one, and you gaze at it. But since you could have feigned something similar to it for yourself, how will it now be established that you truly gaze at the idea of, say, a real man, and not some fictitious one like it, of which you likewise have a clear and distinct perception? (3) Indeed Descartes himself did not trust it. He says that he laid down no other principles of physics than those perceived most evidently, and drew nothing from them except by mathematical, that is, necessary and evident consequences. He says that all these things agree so exactly with the phenomena of nature that it would be an injustice to God if anyone suspected the causes of things, found by him in this way, to be false. By this he clearly conceives the nature of things and their order to be so disposed. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this clear and distinct conception of the order, he himself speaks thus throughout his whole dissertation: Moreover, even to explain natural things better, he has traced their causes further back than they ever existed, and in the margin he says that he will here assume some hypotheses which are known to be false. Nor could he trust it, for he concedes that, with other hypotheses laid as foundation, the same phenomena of nature can be explained clearly and perspicuously by an entirely different method, perhaps more laborious, and so can be clearly and distinctly conceived. Indeed he openly professes its falsity, for he calls the arrangement of things and the hypotheses which he describes as clearly and distinctly conceived false. And it is remarkable that, since that clear and distinct perception, by the judgement of the author himself, requires a mind purified and free from prejudices, that is, the method of Descartes' philosophizing, he does not wish to be the author to anyone for undertaking something similar. Unless he judged this rule to be of no great worth. For if this is the only way and norm of truth, why does it matter to dissuade what is required of anyone who will use this rule rightly?

units.la: Exponam brevibus quid de re tota sentiam. Rei perceptio & receptio in mente est nostra intellectio, sit verbo venia, prout autem magis vel minus distinctè & clarè ejus rei quasi imaginem, ne autem de corporibus solum loqui videar, repræsentamen dicam, conceptum, ideam, habemus, eo magis eam rem cognoscimus: plane ut varias inter hominis pictu-ras, una magis, altera minus, exemplari similis est. Hæc autem proprie rerum spectant naturam & attributa essentialia, existentia enim rei aliquando magis certa esse potest, illi qui minorem in se habet rei similitudinem, quam illi qui majorem, quod in rebus fidei abunde patet. Quoniam vero, verum esse quid potest, quod nec clarè nec distinctè à me cognoscitur. Et fictum, quod clare & distincte percipio. Imo aliquid cognosci quod ad τὸ ὅτι, cujus interim naturam & non clare & distincte cognosco, sequi videtur regulam vix ullius esse momenti. Manet enim semper id unicè inquirendum, non, an clara sit & distincta mea perceptio, sed an objecto conveniat nec ne, & in quantum, an detur conceptus cum re adæquatio, quæ vox, cum absque periculo, de conceptu infiniti usurpari non possit, potius dicam, convenientia & in quantum detur, quod cum ope legitimæ ratiocinationis sciri debeat, tandem redibimus ad pristinas Philosophandi leges & nihil tanta gloriatione digni, in ista regula reperiri posse, certi evademus. Non etenim mea perceptio, non mea perce-ptionis claritas & perspicuitas, veritatis norma est, sed illud potius pro norma habendum, ex quo de con-ceptus mei, cum re ipsa convenientia, aut discrepan-tia, certior evadere possum: quod claritas & perspi-cuitas illa, esse semper non potest, ut ex supra dictis constat. Non enim statim in se clarum est, evidens, necessarium & certum quod tale videtur homini, etiam conscio sua perceptionis: ---- unde liquet NB. quamli- bet conscientiam nostra perceptionis, nisi irradietur lu- mine fidei, eam errori non subducere. Si dicas te per claram & distinctam perceptionem nihil aliud intelli-gere, quam rei ipsius, menti, quod ad omnia, ut ita loquar, lineamenta, a corporeis enim voces de-sumi necesse est, repraesentationem prout est extra mentem: teque dicere illam cognitionem esse veram cognitionem. Non quidem inficior, sed dico 1. te-tum solum eam cognitionem vocare veram, quae comprehensiva est, qua res tota, & ejus omne, ut ita loquar, cognoscitur. 2. te identicam tum proferre enunciationem, aut ad summum, definitionem, veri conceptus comprehensivi, non autem omnis concep-tionis& cognitionis firmam regulam. Idem enim est ac si diceres quicquid vere percipio, id vere percipio, nam clare & distincte concipere hoc sensu, est rem concipere prout est, id est vere percipere, in iis quae comprehenduntur. Multis hoc effatum commendat Velthuysen, eaque quinque argumentis complecti-tur, quae ita authori placuere, ut in diversis tractati-bus, iisdem paene verbis eadem reponat. 1. Primum est, Quod clare & distincte percepta nobis tantum so- leant persuadere. idem Wolzogius alibi, si sit vera inquit persuasio a veritatis orta cognitione fuerit. Sed 1. principium petit turpiter, illud enim in quaestione est. 2. directe contrarium docet Velthuysen, & asse-ctibus abreptus, dum Enthusiastas insectatur, axio-matis matis sui oblivione captus videtur, fatetur enim & conqueritur alibi, homines dari qui tantopere à suis imaginationibus afficiantur, ut facile sibi persuadeant, falsa esse non posse, quæ ita sese menti insinuarunt: falsa licet sint, de talibus enim loquitur. Multis enim, vel Cartesio teste, possumus assentiri, quæ non nisi perobscure & confuse cognoscimus. En igitur persua-sionem absque clara &c. en persuasionem non à veritatis cognitione ortam ! 3. Reclamat omnis experientia, quotus enim quisque est, qui non sæpe à falsis, à fictis persuadeatur? nonne Protoplastis in ipso innocentiæ statu Diabolus salsissimis rationibus falsa persuasit? Si autem dicas, præcipitantiam aut præjudi-cium id fore, non persuasionem, de nomine te litigare, principium petere te constat. Ciceroni persuasus dicitur etiam qui opinione imbutus: hic autem persua-sionem voco, qua aliquis ad aliquid credendum aut faciendum animo permotus est: illud autem non veritate solum, sed & falsitate, sub veri specie, fieri posse, imo fieri sæpe, nemo sanus negaverit: sic Achab à Spiritu malo persuasus dicitur, sic quotidie errantibus peccatoribus, persuadentur falsa malaque. Imo si nihil nisi veritas persuasionem efficiat, à peccato omni, ab omni errore, immunes erimus omnes, quippe peccatum & error persuadere non possunt, saltem non solent. Impetrare à nobis non possumus, inquit, ut obscure & confuse cognitis, quamdiu talia nobis apparent, assensum præbeamus. At 1. multa procul omni dubio, quæ verissima licet sint & necessaria, sic à te non admittentur, præcipue autem, fidei Mysteria, quorum incomprehensam abyssum, cerebellum nostrum distincte non recipit, quamvis clare, utraque voce ex mente Cartesii explicata. 2. Quid? si quis putet se clare quid & distincte percipere, falso licet id putet, dubitandum tamen non est, quin ista perceptio imaginaria permotura sit & persuasura: Quod in peccatis, in falsis dogmatibus, in correctis propriis erroribus, luculenter videre est. 11. Quod objicit Medicus secundo, sic sonat.
