Cum clara & di-stincta perceptio sit aliquid; Concedo: sed quid jam porro? & omnes actus peccaminosi, omnes actus intellectus erronei, voluntatis perversi, sunt aliquid: quid tum? cumque constet nos istius rei auctores non esse: nisi scirem quam concitatè adversus Enthusiastas egeris, certè de tuo Enthusiasmo mihi suspicio subori-retur, nullius ingenium hæc assertio magis sapit, quam stolidi Weigelii, Schwenkfeldii aut similium, qui itidem non nos sed Deum agere in nobis fingunt, ita ut nos nostrarum actionum causa non simus, sed Deus: Si velis autem orthodoxe ista explicata, id dixisse credendus es, nos quidem proximè, ut omnium nostrarum actionum, sic præsertim perceptionis & cognitionis nostræ, causas esse; non independenter, sed solum in genere causæ secundæ. Id quidem non infitior, novi enim, omne quod in universo ullibi realitatem habet & entitatem, idem in tantum à Deo esse in genere causæ primæ: sicque fateor, omnem entitatem, omnem realitatem claræ istius perceptionis à Deo esse, in genere causæ primæ: sed an inde sequitur eandem à nobis non esse in genere causæ secundæ? sic argumentantur ab una parte Enthusiastæ, ab altera Pelagiani, illi ut omnia Deo transcribant, hi ut, gratiam & providentiam Dei spernentes, hominem, ejusque vires in cælum usque evehant: Quidni porro idem, de omni perceptione, etiam non clara, etiam non distincta, imo falsa, quidni de omni actu peccaminoso dici posset? Deum enim omnia, in tantum authorem habent, sed in genere causæ primæ, in quantum entia, in quantum realia sunt, licet & à creaturis in genere causæ secundæ proveniant. Pergit Velthuysen & urget hanc perceptionem à Deo esse eo magis statuendum, quod inter claram & distinctam cognitionem & inter assensum, quem voluntas tali di-stincta & clara cognitioni praebet, talis sit nexus, qui ne-cessario Deum auctorem habet. At unde ille nexus in genere nisi ex eo, quod taliter hominem creaverit Deus, ut intellectus perceptionem soleat sequi voluntas, (modo objectum activitatis ejus sphæram ne excedat, modo ne aliqua impotentia obicem ponat, quod addo ne illuminatam mentem ad regeneratio-nem perficiendam, quis putet sufficere, qui error, ex Velthuisii verbis, forsan extundi posset.) Quando autem signatus aliquis, in individuo, actus, vi illius nexus proveniens, consideratur, quid in eo singulare est, præter id, quod veritas concursus, tam provi-dentiæ, quam gratiæ, docet de singulis & universis creaturæ rationalis actibus? nexus ille Deum auctorem habet, ut dictum est, fateor: at nihil hinc pro tuo effato, ut patet itidem ex dictis. Deinde certum est omnem & universum illum, inter istarum facultatum operationes, nexum naturalem, à Deo esse: nemo autem inde omne, in quo exeritur iste nexus aut pa-tet, Deo sic tribuet, quin Deum omnis erroris, omnis peccati, fecerit causam: à quo tam longe hi Doctores absunt, ut potius adversarios in hoc negotio ejus criminis reos agant. Sic enim Wolzogen, Non video qui ab omni dolo sanctissimum Numen possit ab-solvi. Paulo modestiori dictione, quam Cartesius, sic enim ille, merito deceptor esset dicendus Deus; Longe aliter Celeberr. Maref. Nec si erremus in iis quæ putamus nos clare & distincte percepisse, id adscribendum esset ipsi Deo, Creatori mentis humanæ, sed nostræ ex peccato corruptioni, ex qua factum est, ut oculus rationis se habeat ad veritatem, quemadmodum oculus noctuæ ad lucem, ut Aristoteles loquitur. Hor-renda mihi hæc sunt, inquit Schulerus. Ecquis enim Deum, absolutum omnium Dominum, constringat, ut perfectam mentem, aut intellectum falli nescium, nobis concedat? Nonne enim Deus est, qui mutum creavit, aut surdum, aut sensibus valentem, aut cæ- cum? Nonne fatendum nobis, mentem nostram ad errandum perquam esse proclivem, nosque animam possidere ab origine occæcatam, & tenebris plus quam Cimmeriis natura involutam? Et, nunquid propterea Deum deceptorem faciemus nos, quem veracissimum esse, omnisque veritatis fontem jam ante demonstratum fuit? Viderint jam Cartesiani, quomodo non deceptorem faciant Deum, cum animam ab origine imperfectam, obtenebratam & cæcam quasi inditam nobis esse, tum ex Theologia, tum ex vera Philosophia, certum sit. Fateor quidem ista, quæ veritati repugnant, nequaquam evidentia, nedum vera fuisse, talia tamen visa ipsis fuisse existimo. Quin & ipsi rogati de iis nullo modo dubitasse se strenuè affirmabunt. Hoc tamen evidens non videri solum, sed esse censeo, Deum nequaquam ipsius fallacia aut erroris causam esse, eam proinde in nobis seu in mentis nostræ imperfectione quærendam esse, ex dictis apparet. Sicut enim omnia icterico corpora evidenter flava apparent, quæ flava non sunt, propter humorem biliosum quo ipsius oculus suffusus est; perinde etiam haud mirum quod homini mente vitiosa & corrupta prædito[?] non omnia ita appareant, ut revera sunt: sive quod falsa aliquando pro veris, ab ipso apprehendantur. Si vero hoc velint; claritatem eam esse aliquid, ac proinde etiam à Deo esse: At, bene rursus in genere entis: & semper manet nodus, unde sciam me clare scire, quoniam sæpe putavi claram cognitionem esse, quam postea falsam deprehendi: sicque nihil hactenus evicisti: semper enim manet, superius mota difficultas. Tandem unde constabit Philosopho, hominem[?] peccato quodam non meritum tantam mentis corruptionem, ut in omnibus semper fallatur? Videmus maximis mentem à natura tenebris ob-essam, & quidem in spiritualibus tantis, ut simus tenebræ, nebrae, & ne vel unicum verae intelligentiae actum exerere apti. Unde jam noverit Philosophus sic & in omnibus rem non habere? Imo quoniam Dei perfectioni repugnare putat, habere mentem quae clare percipiens fallat, quidni repugnat habere talem ut unquam falli possit? Acu totam hanc rem tangit Vir Summus P. Gassendus, cujus verba lubet adscribere quippe cui, Schoockio judice, hactenus nemo ex Pa-tronis hujus argumenti, cum ratione respondere potuit. Sic ille. Verum tametsi dubitet nemo, quin Deus sit author clarae distinctaque notitiae; An non videmus esse multos, qui putent se habere claram, distinctamque no-titiam, & tamen fallantur? Dicis non habere reipsa ta-lem; alioquin enim non fallerentur; neque enim nisi ali-quid norint, cujusmodi est; id clare, & distincte no-rint, quandoquidem ne norunt quidem. At quia nihi-lominus tam illi putant se habere, cum non habeant, quam alii se putant habere, cum habeant; & utrique pro certo habeant Deum esse, authorem esse, deceptorem non esse: An non superest Methodus tradenda, qua illi agno-scant se ita habere claram distinctamque notitiam, ut non fallantur; isti ita non habere, ut fallantur.
units.tr: I will briefly set out what I think about the whole matter. The perception and reception of a thing in the mind is our understanding (illud let the word be forgiven), and the more or less distinct and clear image, as it were, of that thing that we have, which I will call a representation, concept, or idea (so that I do not seem to speak only of bodies), is what makes us know that thing the better, just as among various human portraits one is more and another less like the original. These things properly concern the nature and essential attributes of a thing, for the existence of a thing can sometimes be more certain to one who has a smaller likeness of it in himself than to one who has a greater, which is abundantly clear in matters of faith. But since something can be true which I do not know clearly and distinctly, and something false which I perceive clearly and distinctly, indeed since to know that something is (τὸ ὅτι [to hoti]), while I do not know its nature clearly and distinctly, seems to follow a rule of hardly any weight, the only thing to inquire into is not whether my perception is clear and distinct, but whether it agrees with the object or not, and to what extent there is an adequation of concept and thing. Since the word "adequation" cannot safely be used of the concept of the infinite, I would rather say "agreement," and how far it extends, which must be known by means of sound reasoning. In the end we shall return to the old laws of philosophizing and see that nothing worthy of such boasting is to be found in this rule. For it is not my perception, nor the clarity and perspicuity of my perception, that is the norm of truth; rather that should be held as the norm by which I can become more certain whether my concept agrees or disagrees with the thing itself, because that clarity and perspicuity cannot always be present, as is clear from what was said above. For what seems clear, evident, necessary and certain to a man, even one conscious of his own perception, is not on that account clear, evident, necessary and certain in itself: from which it is plain (NB) that no consciousness of our perception, unless it is illumined by the light of faith, keeps it from error. If you say that by a clear and distinct perception you mean nothing other than the representation of the thing itself in the mind, as it is outside the mind (for words must be drawn from bodily things, to speak of every outline, as it were), and that you call this cognition true cognition, I do not indeed deny it, but I say: first, that you call only that cognition true which is comprehensive, by which the whole thing and all of it, so to speak, is known; second, that you are then putting forward an identical proposition, or at most a definition of a true comprehensive concept, and not a firm rule of all conception and cognition. For it amounts to saying: whatever I perceive truly, I perceive truly. For to conceive clearly and distinctly in this sense is to conceive a thing as it is, that is, to perceive truly, in those things that are comprehended. Velthuysen commends this saying to many, and he sums it up in five arguments, which pleased the author so much that in various treatises he repeats the same things in almost the same words. 1. The first is: that things perceived clearly and distinctly are wont to persuade us only. Wolzogen says the same elsewhere: if the persuasion is true, it must have arisen from a cognition of the truth. But first, he shamefully begs the question, for that is what is in dispute. Second, Velthuysen teaches the direct opposite, and, carried away by his feelings while he attacks the Enthusiasts, he seems to have forgotten his own axiom; for he admits and complains elsewhere that there are men who are so strongly affected by their own imaginations that they easily persuade themselves that things which have insinuated themselves into the mind in this way cannot be false: though they may be false, for he is speaking of such people. For we can assent to many things, even, by Descartes' testimony, which we know only very obscurely and confusedly. Here, then, is a persuasion not without a clear perception, here is a persuasion not arising from knowledge of the truth! 3. All experience cries out against him; for how few are there who are not often persuaded of falsehoods and fictions? Did not the Devil, even in the state of innocence, persuade our first parents of the most false things by the most specious reasons? If you say that this would be rashness or prejudice and not persuasion, it is plain that you are disputing about the name and begging the question. Someone who is steeped in opinion is also said to be persuaded, as Cicero says; I, however, call persuasion that by which someone has been moved in mind to believe or do something; and no sane person will deny that this can happen not only through truth but also through falsehood, under the appearance of truth, and indeed that it often does: so Ahab is said to have been persuaded by an evil spirit, and so every day sinners in error are persuaded of false and evil things. Indeed, if nothing but truth produced persuasion, we would all be immune from every sin and every error, since sin and error cannot persuade, at least they are not wont to. We cannot bring ourselves, he says, to give assent to things known obscurely and confusedly, as long as they appear so to us. But first, many things, which are most true and necessary, will undoubtedly not be admitted by you in this way, especially the mysteries of faith, whose incomprehensible depth our little brain does not take in distinctly, although they are clear, both words being explained in Descartes' sense. 2. What then? If someone thinks he perceives something clearly and distinctly, though he is wrong to think so, there is no doubt that this imaginary perception will move and persuade him: which is plainly seen in sins, in false doctrines, and in the correction of one's own errors. 11. What the physician objects in the second place runs thus: since clear and distinct perception is something; I grant it: but what then? All sinful acts, all erring acts of the intellect, all perverse acts of the will, are something: so what? And since it is established that we are not the authors of that thing: if I did not know how vehemently you have attacked the Enthusiasts, I would certainly suspect your own enthusiasm, for no one's intellect savours of this assertion more than that of the foolish Weigel, Schwenkfeld, or their like, who likewise pretend that not we but God acts in us, so that we are not the cause of our own actions, but God is. If, however, you wish to explain these things orthodoxly, you must be believed to have said that we are indeed the proximate causes of all our actions, and especially of our perception and cognition; not independently, but only in the genus of secondary cause. I indeed do not deny this, for I know that everything that has reality and entity anywhere in the universe is, to that extent, from God in the genus of primary cause; and so I confess that all the entity and all the reality of that clear perception is from God, in the genus of primary cause. But does it follow from this that it is not also from us in the genus of secondary cause? Here the Enthusiasts argue on one side, and the Pelagians on the other: the former so as to ascribe everything to God, the latter so as to despise the grace and providence of God and exalt man and his powers to heaven. Why could the same not be said of every perception, even one that is not clear, not distinct, indeed false, why could it not be said of every sinful act? For God is the author of all things, to the extent that they are beings and real, in the genus of primary cause, although they also proceed from creatures in the genus of secondary cause. Velthuysen goes on and urges that this perception must be held to be from God all the more, because between clear and distinct cognition and the assent which the will gives to such distinct and clear cognition there is such a connection that it necessarily has God as its author. But whence that connection in general, except from the fact that God so created man that the will usually follows the perception of the intellect (provided the object does not exceed the sphere of its activity, and provided no impotence puts an obstacle in the way, to which I add: lest the enlightened mind, who would think it enough for the work of regeneration, be led into error, which might perhaps be drawn out of Velthuysen's words.) But when some particular act in an individual, arising by virtue of that connection, is considered, what is singular in it, beyond what the truth of concurrence, of providence as well as of grace, teaches concerning all the acts of the rational creature, singly and universally? That connection has God as its author, as has been said, I confess: but nothing follows from this in favour of your saying, as is likewise plain from what has been said. Further, it is certain that all that natural connection between the operations of these faculties is from God; yet no one will therefore attribute to God every case in which this connection is exercised or manifest, without making God the cause of every error and every sin: from which these teachers are so far removed that they rather charge their opponents in this matter with the guilt of that crime. For thus Wolzogen: I do not see how the most holy Deity can be absolved from all deceit. In a rather more moderate manner than Descartes, for he says: God would rightly be called a deceiver; the very celebrated Maref. speaks quite differently: Nor, if we err in those things which we think we have perceived clearly and distinctly, is that to be ascribed to God himself, the Creator of the human mind, but to the corruption of ours from sin, from which it comes about that the eye of reason stands towards truth as the eye of an owl towards light, as Aristotle says. These things are horrible to me, says Schuler. For who would constrain God, the absolute Lord of all, to grant us a mind or intellect that cannot be deceived? Is it not God who created the dumb, or the deaf, or those strong in the senses, or the blind? Must we not admit that our mind is very prone to err, and that we possess a soul blinded from its origin, and involved by nature in darkness more than Cimmerian? And shall we therefore make God a deceiver, whom it has already been demonstrated is most true and the fount of all truth? Let the Cartesians see how they do not make God a deceiver, when it is certain, both from theology and from true philosophy, that the soul has been given to us from its origin imperfect, obscured and, as it were, blind. I admit indeed that those things which contradict the truth are by no means evident, let alone true, yet I think they seemed so to those who held them. Indeed, even when questioned about them, they will vehemently affirm that they had no doubt about them at all. Yet that this is not only seen to be evident but is so, I hold: that God is by no means the cause of its falsity or error, and that therefore it must be sought in us, or in the imperfection of our mind, appears from what has been said. For just as all things appear evidently yellow to jaundiced bodies, though they are not yellow, because the eye is suffused with bilious humour, so too it is no wonder that to a man endowed with a vicious and corrupt mind not all things appear as they really are, or that false things are apprehended by him as true. But if they wish this: that that clarity is something, and therefore is also from God: well, granted again in the genus of being; yet the knot always remains, how I can know that I clearly know, since I have often thought that a cognition was clear which I afterwards found to be false: so you have proved nothing so far, for the difficulty raised above always remains. Finally, how will the philosopher establish that man, by some sin not deserved, has such a corruption of mind that he is always deceived in all things? We see the mind beset by the greatest darkness from nature, and indeed in such great spiritual matters that we are darkness, and shadows, and not fit to exercise even a single act of true understanding. How then can the philosopher know that he does not have this condition in all things? Indeed, since he thinks it repugnant to the perfection of God to have a mind which, perceiving clearly, deceives, why should it not be repugnant to have one that could ever be deceived? The very distinguished P. Gassendi touches the whole matter with a needle, and I am pleased to set down his words, since, in the judgement of Schoock, no one among the patrons of this argument has so far been able to answer him with reason. Thus he: Although no one doubts that God is the author of clear and distinct notice, do we not see that there are many who think they have a clear and distinct notice, and yet are deceived? You say they do not in fact have such a notice; otherwise they would not be deceived; for unless they know something, of what kind it is, they do not know it clearly and distinctly, since they do not even know it. But because they nevertheless think they have it when they do not, just as others think they have it when they do; and both hold for certain that God is, that he is the author, and that he is not a deceiver: is there not still a method to be set forth, by which those others may recognise that they have such a clear and distinct notice that they are not deceived, while these others do not have it in such a way that they are deceived?

units.la: III. Tertium argumentum juxta cum reliquis ad numerum augendum additum videtur: Habemus in nobis, inquit, Ideam veri & falsi, certi & incerti judicii. Sed accuratius examinantes, quare enunciemus aliquid certum & verum esse, quare falsum & incer-tum, apparet claram & distinctam cognitionem esse. Et qui profitetur se aliquid clare scire, simul sibi persua-det, se illam rem clare cognoscere. Priora verba ponunt quod in quaestione est. Posteriora vero, identica sunt: clare scire & clare cognoscere nisi multum dif-ferant. Semper remanet quaestio, an ille conceptus ipsam rem exprimat & cum re conveniat, quod non ex claritate absolute, sed cum exemplari congrua vi-dendum, sicque multo molimine es ubi eras.
units.tr: III. The third argument is added, like the others, apparently to increase the number: We have within us, he says, an idea of true and false, of certain and uncertain judgment. But when we examine more carefully why we pronounce something certain and true, and why false and uncertain, it appears to be a clear and distinct knowledge. And whoever professes that he clearly knows something at the same time persuades himself that he clearly recognises that thing. The first words assume what is in question. The last words are the same thing, since to know clearly and to recognise clearly do not differ much. The question always remains whether that concept expresses the thing itself and agrees with the thing, and this must be judged not from clarity considered in itself but by comparison with its exemplar. So with great labour you are back where you started.

units.la: I V. Quartum non probat, sed Autocratorice determinat potius & dictat. Aut hæc est regula aut nulla, hoc quæritur, nam qualemcunque demonstrationem requiras,nunquam ea nobis potest esse scientiæ fundamentum, nisi quando clare & distincte cognoscatur. Id est, nulla est ergo hæc, præterquam quando, quod probandum erat, supponis; prodis clare ex Scepticismo emergendi vix nullam tibi viam reliquam præter istam, quam insufficientem & licet sufficientem, nec tutam, nec universalem vidimus. Deinde quid si adhuc scientiæ omnis lateat fundamentum & via? non sequitur, aut hæc, aut nulla, posset enim alia adhuc ignota aliquando inveniri forsan: Saltem vera nondum inventa esse.
units.tr: IV. The fourth does not prove anything but rather dictates by fiat. Either this is the rule or there is none; this is what is asked, for whatever demonstration you require, it can never be the foundation of knowledge for us unless it is known clearly and distinctly. That is, there is no such rule except when you assume what was to be proved. You clearly show that there is scarcely any way left to you for emerging from scepticism except that one, which we have seen to be insufficient, and even if sufficient, neither safe nor universal. Furthermore, what if the foundation and way of all knowledge is still hidden? It does not follow that it is either this or nothing, for perhaps some other way, still unknown, may sometime be found. At least the truth has not yet been found.

units.la: V. Pro quinto argumento rursus idem repetit, Quacunque alia fingi possit regula, illa nunquam poterit aliquem usum præstare: vides? hoc est de quo disputamus. Quia non possumus non clare & distincte perceptis assentiri, & obscure intellectis talem assensum negare. Qui potuerunt igitur Protoplasti in errorem induci? Nimirum, sub istis montibus inquit erant & erant sub montibus istis. Non est quod ambigamus aut dubitemus, an Logicam Aristotelis aut Rami abdicaverit, ea enim talia argumenta docere non potuissent: Sic norunt isti homines, conceptibus suis irreliti, ἀσποβατῖν[?], putantes interim præter oracula se fundere nihil. Unum autem prætereundum hic non videtur, nimirum manifestissimum in hoc negotio committi circulum. Postquam enim pro regula generali receptum est, axioma jam dictum, illud nempe omne verum esse, quod clare & distincte percipis, an dubium[?] accurrit, an non potentissimus Deus facere possit, ut erres, in iis, quæ mentis oculis quam evidentissime te intueri putares, consequenter an non facere possit, ut hæc regula tua esset falsa: ut autem illud tollatur, dicis, examinare debeo an sit Deus, & si sit: si sit, an possit esse deceptor; hac enim re ignorata, non videor de ulla alia plane re certus esse unquam posse
units.tr: V. For the fifth argument you again repeat the same thing: Whatever other rule could be devised, it could never be of any use. Do you see? This is the very point we dispute. Because we cannot help assenting to things clearly and distinctly perceived, and cannot refuse such assent to things obscurely understood. How then could the first human beings have been led into error? Surely, he says, they were under those mountains, and they were under those mountains. There is no need for us to doubt or question whether he has renounced the logic of Aristotle or of Ramus, for they could not have taught such arguments. So these men, entangled in their own concepts, are dancing on wineskins [ἀσκοβατεῖν], meanwhile thinking that they pour forth nothing but oracles. One thing, however, does not seem to be passed over here: namely, that a most manifest circle is committed in this matter. For once it has been accepted as a general rule that the axiom just stated is true, namely, that whatever you perceive clearly and distinctly is true, the doubt arises whether the most powerful God can make you err in those things which you think you see with the eyes of the mind most evidently, and consequently whether he cannot make this rule of yours false. But to remove this, you say, I must examine whether there is a God, and if there is, whether he could be a deceiver. For unless this is known, I seem never able to be altogether certain of any other thing.

units.la: Sed quo medio illud evincis? nempe hoc, quod, cum idea Dei maxime clara & distincta sit & plus realitatis objectiva quam ulla alia contineat, nulla est per se magis vera, nec in qua minor falsitatis suspicio reperiatur. Deinde ex hoc uno, quod talis idea (supple clara & distincta entis independentis & habentis omnes illas perfectiones, & nullis plane defectibus obnoxii, ut paulo ante dixeras) in me sit, sive quod ego ideam illam habens existam, adeo manifeste concludo Deum etiam existere &c. ut nihil evidentius, nihil certius ab humano ingenio cognosci posse confidam. Verum quid inde? ex quibus satis patet, illum fallacem esse non posse omnem enim fraudem, & deceptionem a defectu aliquo pendere lumine naturali manifestum. Annon hic manifestissimus circulus? probas enim Deum summe perfectum esse, ex eo quod clare & distincte percipias[?] ipsum talem esse; probas vero id quod clare & distincte percipis verum esse &c. eo quod Deus sit summe perfectus, nullo vero modo fallax. Canonis veritas ex Dei perfectione, Dei perfectio ex hoc Canone.
units.tr: But by what means do you prove that? Namely by this, that since the idea of God is most clear and distinct and contains more objective reality than any other, there is none in itself more true, nor in which less suspicion of falsity is found. Then from this one thing alone, that such an idea (supply: clear and distinct, of an independent being having all those perfections and plainly subject to no defects, as you said a little earlier) is in me, or that I, having this idea, exist, I conclude so manifestly that God also exists, etc., that I am confident nothing more evident or more certain can be known by the human mind. But what follows from this? From which it is sufficiently clear that he cannot be deceitful, for it is manifest by the natural light that every fraud and deception depends on some defect. Is this not the most manifest circle? You prove that God is supremely perfect from the fact that you perceive clearly and distinctly that he is such; but you prove that what you perceive clearly and distinctly is true, etc., because God is supremely perfect and in no way deceitful. The truth of the canon rests on God's perfection, and God's perfection rests on this canon.

units.la: Vidit Cartesius sibi istam difficultatem cum mille aliis, à Gassendo, solide motam non solum, sed in instantiis strenue defensam & demonstratam. Ne autem palam coram toto mundo Gassendus de ipso triumpharet, astute praelium detrectavit, indignas Gassendi Instantias suo examine jactans, & brevi Epistola ad Cl. R. sese subducens. Tanto tamen hujus argumenti tangebatur sensu, ut dolorem premere aut dissimulare non potuerit. Sic enim dicta Epistola, Objiciunt me in probanda Dei existentia in circulum incidere &c. Nihil autem respondet praeter, Inspice ea de re Responsionem meam ad secundas Objecti. N. 3. & 4, & partem sec. Resp. ad Quartas circa finem. Ne vero, Cartesium jam dudum motam difficultatem removisse[?] movisse dicant adversarii, agedum videamus loca citata. Sic loco priori, ubi dixi nihil nos certo posse scire, nisi prius Deum existere cognoscamus, expressis verbis testatus sum, me non loqui nisi de scientia earum conclusionum, quarum memoria potest recurrere, cum non amplius attendimus ad rationes ex quibus ipsas deduximus. Principiorum enim notitia non solet à Dialecticis scientia appellari. Quid illa sibi velint, dicat. Videtur hoc velle se aliquid excepisse, dum diceret se nihil scire, nimirum quædam principia, quæ non aliarum rationum ope, sed per se patent. At ipse dicis, hæc sciri aut nescire non dicenda. Et quando nihil dicis, quis hoc non universaliter sumeret? Videamus autem annon sibi turpiter contradicat, dum se aliquid excepisse dicit. Sic loquitur Meditat. I. cogor fa- teri nihil esse ex iis, quæ olim vera putabam, de quo non liceat dubitare --- & ab iisdem non minus quam ab aperte falsis assensionem cohibendam. Quis hic exceptionem, sine contradictione, fingat? Postquam, multis circumactus, se esse, eo, quod cogitabat, evicit Medit. II. exerte ait, se hoc unum verum esse affir- mare, negare cetera. Et ad finem ejusdem Meditat. Nihildum enim aliud admitto in me esse præter mentem. Hæc jam limita, & quædam post factum excipe, certe dicta revocabis apertissime, manifestum adversus istam limitationem præbes alibi testimonium, ubi Atheum scire negas tam imperfectæ se naturæ non esse, ut fallatur etiam in iis quæ sibi quam evidentissima apparebunt, illoque dubio liberari nunquam NB. nunquam posse, nisi a vero, & fallere nescio Deo, se creatum esse prius agnoscat. Dei ergo existentia ante omnia præcedat necesse est, & hoc est quod jam negas, pallias, declinas. Imo princip. I. §. 5. signate docet, non demonstrationes solum, sed & principia, vel Mathematica, in dubium vocanda esse, etiam ea quæ hactenus putavimus esse per se nota: maxime quia audivimus esse Deum &c. & §. 7. ego cogito, & hæc veritas est omnium prima & certissima NB. prima. Deinde positto, te non omnia sic complexum esse, anne sic omne circuli committendi evitas periculum? Sed alterum locum inspicio N. 4. Idemque fere ibi innuit ad finem; hoc vult, esse quædam tam perspicua, ut de iis dubitari non possit, modo de iis cogitemus: at quam consequenter, jam vidimus. Exemplum affert, ut quod ego dum cogito existam. Oblitus autem videtur eorum, quibus mediantibus, demum ad istam veritatem, aut potius, istius veritatis certitudinem, se pervenisse dixerat Medit. 1, & 2. Imo Meditat. demum secunda, postquam in initio dixerat: In tantas se dubitationes hesterna meditatione conjectum, ut nequiverit amplius earum oblivisci, nec viderit tamen qua ratione solvenda essent, sed tanquam in profundum gurgitem ex improviso delapsum ita turbatum fuisse ut nec potuerit in imo pedem figere, nec enatare ad summum. Enitar tamen, inquit, & tentabo enatare. ---- Inter alia fingit, nullas mentes, & se non esse, oggerit autem, imo certe ego eram si quid mihi persuasi: iterum hæret, sibi objiciens: sed est deceptor &c. regerit autem, haud dubie igitur ego sum si me fallit &c. adeo ut omnibus satis superque pensitatis denique statuendum sit hoc pronunciatum, Ego sum, Ego existo, necessario esse verum. Viden' per quot ambages, quot laboriosos gyros & anfractus, post hesternam dubitationem, post omnia satis superque pensitata, denique eò perveniat? Jam vero libenter lectori imponeret, quædam ab ipso credi tam perspicua, ut nunquam possimus de iis cogitare, quin vera esse credamus. Contrarium tot ambages jam enumeratæ probant. At jam concesso hoc ante omnia tibi constitisse, nec per tertium te id evicisse: in reliquis tamen, quæ rationum ope addiscis, perpetuo oberras circulo, quod ad reliqua enim, quæ jam te novisse putas, si rogem unde ea noveris esse vera? nonne dices, quia clare & distinête percipio ea? si pergam & dicam unde scis ea quæ clare & distinête percipis esse vera? nonne dices, quia alias Deus deceptor foret & sic non perfectissimus? Urgeo autem: unde scis Deum esse? eum perfectum esse? deceptorem non esse? dices quia ea omnia ingrediuntur claram & distinctam de Deo perceptionem, non possum intueri Ideam Dei, non possum clare &distincte percipereDeum,nisi exi-stentem & perfectum ac proinde non deceptorem. Viden'? Idem per idem. Quod clare& distincte percipio verum est, quia Deus fallere non potest. Fallere autem Deus non potest, quia clare & distincte id percipio. Videre hactenus non potui qui sese ab ea turpi hallucinatione defendat. Quæ habet ad finem Part.2. Resp.iv. coincidunt cum præcedentibus, ut ipse innuit. Sed de hisce forsan Deo volente alias pluribus. Ingenue dico quæ alibi in Regium Cartes. Mirari subit hominis confidentiam, quod tam facile, tam pau-cis verbis, putet se omnia posse evertere, quæ Gassendus longa & attenta meditatione composuit, libroque integro explicuit.
units.tr: Descartes saw that this difficulty, which Gassendus had raised not only solidly but also defended and demonstrated vigorously by instances, was among the thousand others. To avoid openly triumphing over him before the whole world, Gassendus was cunningly declined the battle, boasting that the unworthy instances of Gassendus were to be examined by himself, and withdrawing in a short letter to the most distinguished R. Yet he was so touched by the sense of this argument that he could not hold back or conceal his pain. For the letter said: They object that in proving the existence of God I fall into a circle, etc. But he answers nothing except: Look into my reply on this matter to the second objections, nn. 3 and 4, and part of the second reply near the end of the fourth. But lest his opponents say that Descartes had long since removed a difficulty that had been raised, let us see the passages cited. Thus in the first passage, where I said that we cannot know anything with certainty unless we first recognise that God exists, I expressly stated that I was speaking only of knowledge of those conclusions whose memory can recur when we no longer attend to the reasons from which we deduced them. For the knowledge of principles is not usually called science by the dialecticians. Let him say what those words mean. He seems to mean that he excepted something when he said he knew nothing, namely certain principles that are evident not through the aid of other reasons but through themselves. But you yourself say that to know or not to know these things is not to be spoken of. And when you say nothing, who would not take this universally? Let us see, however, whether he does not shamefully contradict himself when he says that he excepted something. Thus he speaks in the First Meditation: I am forced to confess that there is nothing among those things which I once thought true about which it is not permissible to doubt... and assent must be withheld from them no less than from things plainly false. Who here, without contradiction, could invent an exception? After being driven about by many things, he proved in the Second Meditation that he is, from the fact that he thought; he states plainly that he affirms this one thing as true and denies the rest. And at the end of the same Meditation: For I admit nothing else in me to exist besides mind. Now limit these words, and make certain exceptions after the fact; you will certainly revoke what was said most openly. Elsewhere you offer manifest testimony against that limitation, where you deny that the atheist can know that his nature is not so imperfect that he is deceived even in those things which appear to him most evident, and that he can never, NB never, be freed from this doubt unless he first recognises from the true and non-deceiving God that he has been created. Therefore the existence of God must necessarily come before all things, and this is what you now deny, evade, and decline. Indeed, in Principles I, §5, you explicitly teach that not only demonstrations but also principles, even mathematical ones, must be called into doubt, even those which we have hitherto thought to be known through themselves, especially since we have heard that there is a God, etc.; and §7: I think, and this truth is the first and most certain of all, NB first. Furthermore, granting that you have not embraced all things in this way, do you thus avoid the danger of committing the circle? But I look at the other passage, n. 4, and near the end it hints at about the same thing: he means that some things are so evident that they cannot be doubted, provided we think about them. But how consistently this is done we have already seen. He offers an example: such as that I, while I think, exist. Yet he seems to have forgotten by what means, as he had said in Meditations I and II, he came to this truth, or rather to the certainty of this truth. Indeed, in the Second Meditation, after saying at the beginning: Having been cast by yesterday's meditation into such doubts that I could no longer forget them, nor did I see by what means they were to be resolved, but was thrown suddenly as into a deep whirlpool, so that I was so troubled that I could neither set foot on the bottom nor swim to the surface; yet I will try, he says, and I will attempt to swim. Among other things he feigns that there are no minds, and that I am not; but he objects to himself: yet surely I was, if I was persuaded of anything; again he sticks, objecting to himself: but there is a deceiver, etc. He replies: undoubtedly then I am, if he deceives me, etc., so that after all has been weighed sufficiently and more than sufficiently, this proposition must finally be laid down: I am, I exist, is necessarily true. Do you see through how many detours, how many laborious circlings and windings, after yesterday's doubt, after everything has been weighed sufficiently and more than sufficiently, he finally arrives there? Now indeed he would gladly impose on the reader that some things are believed by him to be so evident that we can never think of them without believing them to be true. The many detours just listed prove the contrary. But granting that this was first established for you, and that you did not prove it through a third thing, in the rest, which you learn by means of reasons, you wander perpetually in a circle. For if I ask about the rest, which you think you already know, how you know that they are true, will you not say: because I perceive them clearly and distinctly? If I go on and ask how you know that the things you perceive clearly and distinctly are true, will you not say: because otherwise God would be a deceiver and thus not most perfect? I press further: how do you know that God exists? That he is perfect? That he is not a deceiver? You will say: because all these things enter into a clear and distinct perception of God; I cannot behold the idea of God, I cannot clearly and distinctly perceive God, unless he exists and is perfect, and therefore not a deceiver. Do you see? The same through the same. What I perceive clearly and distinctly is true, because God cannot deceive. And God cannot deceive, because I perceive this clearly and distinctly. Hitherto I have not been able to see anyone who defends himself from this shameful hallucination. What he has at the end of Part 2, Reply IV, coincides with what precedes, as he himself hints. But perhaps, God willing, we shall discuss these matters more fully elsewhere. I frankly say what I have said elsewhere, in the King's [book] on Descartes: It comes over one with wonder at the man's confidence, that he thinks he can overturn in so few words, so easily, everything that Gassendus composed by long and careful meditation and explained in a whole book.

units.la: Non satis circumspectè, imo non pro rei veritate, agit pag. 39. ubi de consequentiis ex Scriptura deductis loquitur hisce verbis: Ratio has[?] docet, quemadmodum priora ( capita sc: doctrinaque fundamenta, ) in solam transcribuntur Scripturam. Consequentiarum igitur & veritatum ex aliis Scripturariis veritatibus dedu-ctarum analysis, in rationem est. Ut in lusu Schac-chico, juxta leges lusus agendum quidem, ita tamen ut inde sequentia nostro ingenio debeantur. Idem docet alibi, consecutiones rationis quoque NB. arbitrio disceptari. Etsi enim habeant in revelatione fontem, quicquid, non aliquid, sed quicquid indeprofluit itidem ( nimirum, non aliter quam ea, de quibus dixe-rat, quæ habent in natura constantem veritatem ) rationi acceptum ferri debet. Distinguendum probe quid in consequentiarum deductione præstet ratio; ratio est subjectum veritatis post factam debitam Scripturæ veritatisque Scripturariæ considerationem collationem, recipiens, sic conferendo veritates Scripturarias cum veritatibus Scripturariis, Textus cum Textibus, phrases cum phrasibus, & inde conclusiones eliciendo, ita ut ratio hic usum præstet instrumentalem & subjecti recipientis. Et quamvis aliquando rationis axiomata & veritates tam naturaliter insitæ, quam ex iis ut principiis deductæ, in auxilium vocentur & ministerium præstent, conclusiones tamen inde deductæ non in rationem, sed in Dei revelationem transscribuntur supernaturalem, ita ut sint, cum reliquis, certæ, perspicuæ, divinæ, æqualis authoritatis. Audiamus Reformatos ut constet quam bene Wolzogio cum ipsis conveniat. Quicquid in Scripturis expresse traditum, vel inde evidenter deductum, NB. credimus in Ecclesia propter NB. authoritatem Scripturæ. sic Paræus; & tantum abest ut rationi ea accepta ferat, ut doceat pro Scripturis habenda & credenda non ea solum, quæ expresse leguntur in Scripturis sacris; sed etiam quæ evidenter inde deducuntur. Indicem agit ratio, veritates in Scriptura non ita manifeste traditæ nobis ope rationis deteguntur, detectæ autem, non ministri, non indicis, sed ipsius scripturæ, ipsius Dei revelantis authoritate nixi, eas recipimus, rationis licet ope repertas, sed in Scriptura. Res clara est: Quicquid enim per bonam consequentiam ex Scriptura deducitur, illud ipsum est Scriptura, ait Maccovius, & quatenus ista ratiocinatio Divina revelatione potissimum nititur, atque ex ea conclusionem colligit, quæ ex principiis naturalibus solis, colligi nunquam potuisset; talis conclusio etiam de fide est, ut docet Venerandus & charissimus Præceptor meus Andreas Essenius. Ita ut non Philosophiæ dictamina, sed Christi & Apostolo-rum rum doctrinas rejicere dicantur Bisterfeldio, qui do-ctrinas etiam variis consequentiis inde deductas reji-ciunt. Magis consentire videtur Wolzogen cum iis, quos ut adversarios introducit Camero, qui de veri-tate per consequentiam quaerunt, quae sit in iis certitudi-nis conditio, fideine an rationis? Quod si jam totum hoc pendet à ratione, non autem mere à fide, sequitur omnino in controversiis; etiam iis ad quas adhibetur Scriptura, rationem principem locum obtinere. Ista con-cederet Wolzogen, imo similia docet, ut vidimus, quicquid enim per consequentiam ex Scriptura, &c. id rationi acceptum ferri debet. Longè autem aliter Camero, sic ille: Insanire quidem jam illud est, si quis putet diversum esse id, quod concluditur, ab eo, unde conclusio deducta est, id quod inde primum liquet, quod omnis conclusionis ratio ab hoc pendet principio, quod ea quae sunt uni tertio aequalia, eadem hactenus inter se aequalia sunt, quae ratio est syllogismorum quos vocant ex omnibus affirmantibus: Itaque si quod sit Verbum Dei quod doceat medium ejusmodi ut conveniat utri-que subjecto & praedicato conclusionis, necesse est id ipsum Verbum docuisse conclusionem esse veram, & post quaedam. Ergo, nisi velimus cum ratione insanire, si ex Scr. aliquid deducitur, consequentia vero necessaria sit, necesse est ut id quod ex Script. deductum est id ipsum sit quod Scriptura nos voluit docere: At vero jam quod Scr. nos voluit docere, id ipsum est Dei verbum. Denique repugnat consilio Dei & menti Sp. S. quod ajunt, Id quod ex verbo Dei colligitur non esse idem Dei verbum. Et quemadmodum ad Philosophiam pertinent omnes conclusiones, quae ex principiis Philosophiae deducuntur, habenturque, ut ita dicam, pro Philosophicis, sic plane quacunque conclusiones ex Dei Verbo deducuntur, eadem, (non rationi, ut vult Wolzogen, acceptae ferendae) pro Dei verbo habendae sunt, adeoque pro divinis: & caput illud finiens concludit, demonstratum esse, esse Dei verbum quicquid ex Dei Verbo colligi potest. Non quidem abolet rationis usum, sed definit, docens: Duo esse discendi instrumenta, sensum & rationem, quorum neutrum tamen discendi argumentum est. Argumentum fidei est id propter quod credimus, instrumentum vero fidei hoc pacto dicetur ratio, sed fide jam instructa --- nunquid ideo volent quicquid ita deducitur niti ratione, non vero fide? Quæ cum ita se habeant, facile videre est; NB. non esse tanquam perceptum ratione, sed fide tenendum quicquid ex Verbo Dei justa & legitima consequentia colligitur. Sic Spanhemius qui ex professo & more suo accurate & solide hanc controversiam tractavit aliquot Disput. Consequentia materialiter sunt Dei Verbum & quoad rem: & peccari falsa suppositione, conclusionem fore Philosophicam, id est quæ rationi tota debeatur. Ratiocinatio non est principium rei, sed cognitionis rei, imo non tam principium quam instrumentum. Fusè ista ex Patribus aliisque persequitur Rivetus. Maresius c. Valerianum M. Dallæus de Fidei ex Scripturis demonstrat. præsertim Parte I. Cap. xii cujus argumentum Wolzogianæ thesi è diametro contrarium sic habet. Fidem, quæ iis adhibetur quæ sunt ex Scripturis ratiocinando conclusa, non humana ratione, sed Scripturis divinis niti. & Cap. ix. Quicquid ex Script. dilucide ac necessario concluditur, id verum, ac divinum, ac velut aliquam ipsarum Scripturarum partem, censendum esse. Magna etiam, modo non major, credendorum & agendorum pars, ex sententia Wolzogii, rationi accepta ferenda erit, si omnia quæ rationis ope eruuntur, in rationem transscribenda, uti ipsi videtur, sint. Mira sane & nova sunt ista auribus Reformatis: Nam certe nisi in rebus fidei rationem præcedat authoritas, abrogatur Deo Magisterium, & fidei est rationi præscribere, ita ut non sit opus ratione: ait Heidanus. Hoc demum est Theologicum probationis genus, quod ex ScriScripturis petitur. Alia rationes in divinis etsi fidem ad-juvent: tamen non faciunt, nec semper cogunt. Sola igitur ea, quae vel expresse sunt scripta, vel ex scriptis evidenti & bona consequentia deducuntur, credenda sunt in Ecclesia, eaque authoritate divina nituntur. Hæc Parœus. Scripturæ enim docent, quod ex illis, quæ dicit, consequitur ait Coccejus. Quasi, inquit idem, non, quæ necessario consequuntur ex scriptis & immediate revelatis, æquipolleant revelatis, & Dei testimonium sint. Christus, quod ex Scr. consequitur, non intelligere, vocat ignorare Scripturas Mat. xxii. 29. In iis, ait Bucerus, quorum notitia certa & indubia ad salutem non requiritur necessario, exercent & eruditunt se invicem fideles. At quomodo? longe aliter ac quidem somniat noster, sed ex verbo Domini, non ex carnis ratione probabilibus. Dicet autem Wolzo-gen se lubenter concedere, imo statuere, ea, quæ consequentiarum ope eruuntur ex sacris, esse divinæ authoritatis: quia fontes ipsi semper Deo adscribuntur auctori. Non magis autem aut aliter quam illi, qui ludum latrunculorum, ac ludendi leges dedit, ludus & ludendi ratio debentur, omnia vero stratagemata & insidiæ quæ juxta leges adhibentur, ingenio arbitrioque ejus qui ludit, tribuenda sunt. Sic igitur Deo quatenus ludum instituit, sic rationi &c. vide jam quid Deo magis, in consequentiis debeatur, quæ ex Scriptura, quam in iis quæ ex principiis insitis profluunt, nihil sane, utrisque enim commune est principia & leges à Deo accepisse. Alibi aperte prodit, quod hic latet aliquantulum: hoc vult, ideo solum ea, quæ per consequentias & ope rationis scimus, ex Scr. à Deo esse, quia author rationis Deus est: sic enim loquitur, ratio hac docet, consequentias scilicet, quemadmodum priora, quæ aperta sc: & consequentiarum ope non indigentia occurrunt, in solam transcribuntur Scripturam. Sunt tamen utraque divinæ authoauthoritatis, at quare? quia fontes, ratio sc., cui consequentias ferre acceptas debemus, & scriptura semper Deo adscribuntur auctori. Apertius agit Velthuysen, nam illa cognitio, inquit, de naturali loquitur, vera ortum suum habet ex principiis a Deo menti concessis: potestque eadem illa cognitio recte divina vocari, & de ea enunciari quod sit a Patre luminum: & tam tuto illi fidimus, quam, cognitioni, quam revelatio in nobis peperit: eadem plane Paradoxus. Viden' sic divina sunt, quae ope rationis, per consequentias novimus, quia sc: a Deo ratio. Sic tandem tota Philosophia vestra, modo Cartesii regulae, quarum ope mens nostra se abstinere potest, ut nunquam erret, observentur, aeque certa erit ac Sacra Scr. illa enim fontem habet qui Deo adscribendus. Æquiparanda saltem erit iis, quae per consequentiam, ope rationis, ex Scriptura cognoscuntur, ea enim rationi tribuenda. Siccine? hoc proprie divinae authoritatis esse, putabam dici posse, quod propter authoritatem infallibilemque Majestatem Dei recipitur, quod omne in auctoritatem loquentis Dei resolvitur: non quia ratio, quia rei probabilitas id poscere videbantur, sed Deus, sed Dei Verbum revelabat. Cujus auctoritas pro omni ratione habetur. Quorum autem analysis est in rationem, quae rationi accepta ferenda, transscribenda, ut fundamenta religionis Deo, ea divinae authoritatis esse hactenus non didici. Didici enim revelatam Theologiam distinguere a naturali, & solum Dei Verbum ut infallibile & divinae authoritatis recipere: a Deo est quidem ratio, fateor: at non ideo conficitur auctorem eum esse interpretationis, addo & deductionis consecutivae, ut ita loquar, quae fit ope Philosophiae, seu rationis; nisi velimus dicere omnium rerum quae ab homine proficiscuntur auctorem esse Deum, quia auctor est anima, est auctor corporis, est utriusque facultatis auctor. Sic propria vineta caedens, directe saltem Seniorem suum refutans, alibi Wolzogius: horum autem hoc loco nondum meminerat.
units.tr: He does not act with sufficient care, indeed not in accordance with the truth of the matter, on p. 39, where he speaks of consequences drawn from Scripture in these words: Reason teaches this, just as the former (that is, the chapters and fundamental doctrines) are transcribed into Scripture alone. So the analysis of consequences and truths deduced from other scriptural truths belongs to reason. It is to be carried out as in a game of chess, indeed according to the rules of the game, but in such a way that the consequences are owed to our own ingenuity. He teaches the same elsewhere: the consequences of reason also (note this) are open to debate by human judgement. For although they have their source in revelation, whatever flows from it, not merely something but whatever flows from it, likewise (namely, not otherwise than those things of which he had said that they have a constant truth in nature) ought to be credited to reason. We must distinguish carefully what reason contributes in the drawing of consequences. Reason is the subject receiving truth after the due consideration and comparison of Scripture and scriptural truth has been made, thus comparing scriptural truths with scriptural truths, text with texts, phrase with phrases, and drawing conclusions from them, so that reason here exercises an instrumental function and that of a receiving subject. And although sometimes the axioms and truths of reason, both those innate by nature and those deduced from them as principles, are called in as aids and perform a service, the conclusions drawn from them are nevertheless not transferred to reason but to the supernatural revelation of God, so that they are, along with the rest, certain, clear, divine, and of equal authority. Let us hear the Reformed, so that it is clear how well they agree with Wolzogen. Whatever is expressly taught in the Scriptures, or evidently deduced from them, we NB. believe in the Church on account of the NB. authority of Scripture. So Paraeus; and far from this being credited to reason, he teaches that those things must be held and believed as Scripture, not only those that are expressly read in the holy Scriptures, but also those that are evidently deduced from them. Reason acts as a pointer: truths not so plainly handed down in Scripture are uncovered for us by the aid of reason; but once uncovered, they are received not on the authority of reason as minister or pointer, but on that of Scripture itself and of God revealing, although they were found with the help of reason, yet they are in Scripture. The matter is clear: For whatever is deduced from Scripture by a good consequence, that very thing is Scripture, says Maccovius; and insofar as such reasoning rests chiefly on divine revelation and draws from it a conclusion which could never have been drawn from natural principles alone, such a conclusion is also of faith, as my venerable and most beloved teacher Andreas Essenius teaches. So it is said that Bisterfeld rejects not the dictates of philosophy but the doctrines of Christ and the Apostles, since he rejects doctrines drawn from Scripture by various consequences. Wolzogen seems to agree more with those whom he introduces as opponents to Cameron, who ask concerning the truth through consequence, what is the condition of certainty in these matters, faith or reason? For if this whole matter depends now on reason, and not purely on faith, it follows that in controversies, even those in which Scripture is appealed to, reason holds the chief place. Wolzogen would concede these things; indeed, as we have seen, he teaches similar things: whatever is drawn from Scripture by consequence, etc., must be credited to reason. Cameron, however, speaks quite differently: It is indeed madness to think that what is concluded is different from that from which the conclusion is drawn, which first becomes clear from the fact that every reasoning of a conclusion depends on this principle, that things which are equal to one third thing are equal to each other, which is the basis of the so-called syllogisms of all affirmative terms. Therefore, if there is some Word of God which teaches a middle term such that it agrees with both subject and predicate of the conclusion, it is necessary that this very Word has taught that the conclusion is true, and after some words: Therefore, unless we want to be insane in reason, if something is deduced from Scripture, and the consequence is necessary, it is necessary that what is deduced from Scripture is itself what Scripture wished to teach us. But what Scripture wished to teach us is itself the Word of God. Finally, it is contrary to the counsel of God and the mind of the Holy Spirit to say that what is gathered from the Word of God is not the Word of God itself. And just as all conclusions which are deduced from the principles of philosophy pertain to philosophy and are held, so to speak, as philosophical, so plainly whatever conclusions are deduced from the Word of God are to be held as the Word of God (not to be credited to reason, as Wolzogen wishes), and therefore as divine. And at the end of that chapter he concludes that it has been demonstrated that whatever can be gathered from the Word of God is the Word of God. He does not indeed abolish the use of reason, but he defines it, teaching: There are two instruments of learning, sense and reason, neither of which, however, is the ground of learning. The ground of faith is that on account of which we believe; the instrument of faith, in this way, is called reason, but reason already instructed by faith. Will they therefore want whatever is so deduced to rest on reason and not on faith? Since these things stand thus, it is easy to see that whatever is gathered from the Word of God by just and legitimate consequence is NB. not to be held as perceived by reason, but to be held by faith. So Spanheim, who treated this controversy ex professo, accurately and solidly, in its own manner, in several disputations: Consequences are materially the Word of God, both in matter and in substance; and it is an error by a false supposition that the conclusion would be philosophical, that is, wholly owed to reason. Reasoning is not the principle of the thing, but of the knowledge of the thing, indeed not so much a principle as an instrument. Rivet pursues these matters at length from the Fathers and others. Maresius, against Valerianus; M. Dallaeus, On Faith Demonstrated from the Scriptures, especially Part I, chapter xii, whose argument is diametrically opposed to Wolzogen's thesis, states: That faith which is given to those things that are concluded from Scripture by reasoning rests not on human reason but on the divine Scriptures. And chapter ix: Whatever is clearly and necessarily concluded from Scripture is to be judged true and divine, and as some part of the Scriptures themselves. Also, according to Wolzogen's opinion, a great part, if not a greater part, of the things to be believed and done will have to be credited to reason, if everything that is brought out by the aid of reason is to be transcribed into reason, as he himself thinks. These things are indeed strange and new to Reformed ears: for surely, unless in matters of faith authority goes before reason, the teaching office of God is abrogated, and it is for faith to prescribe to reason, so that there is no need of reason, says Heidanus. This is finally the theological kind of proof, which is sought from the Scriptures. Other reasons in divine matters, although they aid faith, do not make it, nor always compel it. Therefore only those things which are either expressly written or deduced from the writings by evident and good consequence are to be believed in the Church, and they rest on divine authority. Thus Paraeus. For the Scriptures teach what follows from those things which they say, says Coccejus. As if, he says the same, those things which necessarily follow from written and immediately revealed things were not equivalent to revealed things and were not the testimony of God. Christ calls not understanding what follows from the Scriptures ignorance of the Scriptures (Matt. 22:29). In those things, says Bucer, the knowledge of which, certain and undoubted, is not necessarily required for salvation, the faithful exercise and instruct one another. But how? Far differently than our man dreams, but from the Word of the Lord, not from probabilities of the flesh's reason. Wolzogen, however, will say that he gladly concedes, indeed affirms, that those things which are brought out from the sacred books by means of consequences are of divine authority, because the sources themselves are always ascribed to God as author. But no more and in no other way than the game of draughts, and the rules of playing, are owed to him who gave the game and its rules, but all the stratagems and snares which are employed according to the rules are to be attributed to the ingenuity and judgement of the one who plays. Thus, then, to God insofar as he instituted the game, thus to reason, etc. See now what is owed more to God in the consequences drawn from Scripture than in those which flow from innate principles: nothing indeed, for both have in common that they received principles and laws from God. Elsewhere he openly betrays what here lies a little hidden: he means that only those things which we know by consequences and by the aid of reason are from God in Scripture, because the author of reason is God; for he speaks thus: this reason teaches, namely the consequences, just as the former, which are open, that is, do not need the aid of consequences, are transcribed into Scripture alone. Yet both are of divine authority, but why? because the sources, namely reason, to which we owe the consequences, and Scripture, are always ascribed to God as author. Velthuysen treats the matter more openly: for that knowledge, he says, which concerns the natural, true, has its origin from the principles conceded by God to the mind; and that same knowledge can rightly be called divine, and it may be said of it that it is from the Father of lights; and we trust it as safely as the knowledge which revelation has produced in us: exactly the same paradox. Do you see how those things are divine which we know by consequences through the aid of reason, because reason is from God? Thus, finally, your whole philosophy, provided the rules of Descartes, by whose aid the mind can abstain so as never to err, are observed, will be as certain as the holy Scripture, for it has a source which must be ascribed to God. It will be at least to be put on a par with those things which are known from Scripture by consequence, by the aid of reason, for these are to be attributed to reason. Is that so? I had thought it could be said properly to be of divine authority what is received on account of the authority and infallible majesty of God, which is all resolved into the authority of God speaking: not because reason or the apparent probability of the thing seemed to require it, but because God, because the Word of God, revealed it. Whose authority is held in place of all reason. But those whose analysis is into reason, which must be credited to reason, transcribed, so that the foundations of religion to God...: those I have not hitherto learned to be of divine authority. For I have learned to distinguish revealed theology from natural, and to receive only the Word of God as infallible and of divine authority. It is indeed from God that reason exists, I grant: but it does not thereby follow that he is the author of the interpretation, I add, and of the consequential deduction, as I may say, which is carried out by the aid of philosophy, or of reason; unless we want to say that God is the author of all things which proceed from man, because he is the author of the soul, he is the author of the body, he is the author of both faculties. Thus Wolzogen, cutting his own vines, directly refuting at least his own elder, elsewhere; but of these he had not yet made mention at this point.

units.la: Quid sibi velint hæc verba scire aveo, sic p.45. Nec aliunde, voluntate hominum verbis & characte-ribus significationes inditas dixerat, & subdit: Nec aliunde proficiscitur, quod non una sit omnium lingua. An confusionem linguarum singulari judicio Dei hominibus immissam neget, an concedat, clare & di-stincte non exprimit, verba autem prout jacent, Ba-belis confusionem negare videntur. Remitto lectorem ad Bochartum, aliosque.
units.tr: I would like to know what these words mean. On p. 45 he wrote, "Nor from elsewhere," saying that meanings were given to words and characters by the will of men, and he adds: "Nor does it arise from elsewhere that there is not one language for all." Whether he denies or concedes that God, by a singular judgment, sent the confusion of tongues upon men, he does not state clearly and distinctly. But the words, as they stand, seem to deny the confusion at Babel. I refer the reader to Bochart and others.

units.la: Pagina 50. Lib.18,19. Præ omnibus accuratus videri vult Wolzogen, & errorem se communem se-qui debere queritur: At non ita facile, non leviter, omnes una simul, literatissimi & accuratissimi Theologi, puerorum instar reprehendendi erant, non omnis abdicanda decessorum veneratio: Et quid est quod prætexas ? phrasis minus accurata est: Interpres dici-tur qui proprie Interpres non est. Sed sit ita, an ne una quidem phrasis absque nota dimittenda erat? deinde erras Wolzogi, & mentem nostrorum, aut non percipis, aut pervertis. Homo quisquis sit, qui verba cum sensu rite nectit, juxta te, Interpres est, recte nimirum pro suo judicio, quod Theologi vocant, discretivo. Nec & nostri aliter homini hoc judicium imponunt, nullum enim nunc in Ecclesia judicem visibilem &c, agnoscimus: sed rei, Scripturæ nimirum ipsi, ut po-stea videbimus fuse: quoniam vero, ut docet Mare-sius & te procul dubio etiam docuit, nullam hic realem distinctionem admittimus, ut Pontificii & Socinia-ni, inter normam & judicem supremum, nisi in quan-tum distingui potest inter Scripturam ipsam & Deum in ea loquentem. Hinc phrasis ista, quam carpis, ortum ducit. Scriptura enim ipsa cum sit interpretationis suæ norma, ita ut ipsa rationem per modum objecti ducat ut ne erret in hoc interpretationis judicio, dicta fuit merito sui interpres: Rem quæris quæ hominem, in interpretandis Scripturis, ducat, per modum objecti, hanc proprie interpretem dicendam putas, hanc autem Scripturam dicunt Orthodoxi, Philosophiam Paradoxus, ita ut ille etiam, non persona, sed rei, hanc provinciam demandandam censuerit: Quid igitur restat quod corrigas, nisi proprium carpendi cacoëthes?
units.tr: On p. 50, book 18, 19. Wolzogen wants to appear the most accurate of all, and complains that he must follow a common error. But it is not so easy, nor is it a light matter, that all the most learned and most accurate theologians together should be rebuked like schoolboys; the veneration of our predecessors is not to be wholly abandoned. And what is it you find to object to? The phrase is less accurate: "an interpreter is called one who is not properly an interpreter." Granted, but was not even one phrase to be let go without remark? Then you are mistaken, Wolzogen, and you either do not perceive or you distort the mind of our people. "Whatever man, whoever he is, who rightly joins words with sense, is by your account an interpreter": rightly so, by his own judgment, which theologians call "discretive." Nor do our people impose this judgment on a man in any other way: for we acknowledge no visible judge in the Church now, etc., but the thing itself, namely Scripture, as we shall see later at length. Since, as Maresius teaches, and doubtless you have also taught, "we admit here no real distinction, as the Papists and the Socinians do, between the norm and the supreme judge, except insofar as one can distinguish between Scripture itself and God speaking in it." Hence arises the phrase you carp at. For Scripture itself, since it is the norm of its own interpretation, so that it guides reason, by way of object, lest it err in this judgment of interpretation, has rightly been called its own interpreter. "You are seeking a thing that guides a man in interpreting Scriptures": by way of object, you think this should properly be called the interpreter. But the Orthodox say this is Scripture, and the Paradoxical say it is philosophy, so that he too has judged this office to be committed not to a person but to a thing. What then remains for you to correct, except the proper itch of carping?

units.la: Ejusdem commatis est, quod eadem pagina, cen-sorie satis à te dictum, occurrit, sic sonant verba. Tota quæstio sc: de Interpretatione Scr. probe distinguenda à duabus aliis, quæ non semper ab omnibus æque distinguuntur. Quorsum nota illa? scilicet ne semper non probaret, ab aliis hactenus non satis dilucide tractatam hanc quæstionem esse, eamque nunc demum ultimam limam Wolzogio debere: sed fallitur & modo locos communes, etiam notissimos, inspiciat, sese falsum esse deprehendet. Quid sit quod non distinguant multi, audiamus; separatim quæri potest 1. quamobrem assensum demus iis rebus, quæ Scripturis comprehenduntur. 2. quamobrem credamus has esse Scripturas 3. quamobrem hunc statuamus & non alium Scr. sensum. Ipse confuse agit, ut videt lector; sed omnes hactenus, quotquot unquam locum de Scr. pertractarunt, semper bene distinxerunt hasce quæstiones 1. quidnam illud sit, quod nobis persuadeat, Scripturam divinam esse, quod tractant quando agunt de authoritate. 2. quidnam, quod me doceat hos libros, non alios, esse, eam Scr. quod tractant, quando agunt de Canone 3. quidnam illud sit quod nos moveat hunc Textum sic sumere, non aliter, quod tractant, quando agunt de Interpretatione Scripturæ. Probarem ista nisi & Catechumenis jam dudum nota essent. Sed videtur omnem ansam alios corrigendi, notandi, captasse sedulo, ut sc: pateret, jam demum Theologiam exspectandam, quae ope novae Philosophiae, accurata sit futura.
units.tr: Of the same sort is what occurs on the same page, which you have judged sufficiently censorious. The words sound thus: "The whole question, namely concerning the interpretation of Scripture, must be carefully distinguished from two other questions, which are not always equally distinguished by all." Why that note? Surely lest he should prove that this question has hitherto not been treated clearly enough by others, and that it now at last owes its final polish to Wolzogen. But he is mistaken; if he would only look at the common topics, even the best known, he would find himself to be wrong. Let us hear what many do not distinguish. The following may be asked separately: (1) why we give assent to the things contained in the Scriptures; (2) why we believe these to be the Scriptures; (3) why we settle on this sense of Scripture and not another. He himself proceeds confusedly, as the reader sees. But all who have hitherto treated the place concerning Scripture have always distinguished these questions well: (1) what is it that persuades us that Scripture is divine, which they treat when they deal with authority; (2) what is it that teaches me that these books, and not others, are Scripture, which they treat when they deal with the Canon; (3) what is it that moves us to take this text in this way and not otherwise, which they treat when they deal with the interpretation of Scripture. I would prove these things, were they not already long known even to catechumens. But he seems to have eagerly seized every opportunity of correcting and remarking on others, so that it might appear that theology was only now to be expected, which by means of the new philosophy will be accurate.

units.la: Pagina 59. Gravissime errat Wolzogius, eodem enim modo in explicatione Veteris Testamenti versatos, simili ductu à Spiritu Sancto, in ejus explicatione, ductos esse Apostolos putat, ac reliquos fideles. Extraordinarium Spiritus ductum Apostolis concedit & ordinarium qui & nostrorum temporum est, sed quo sensu ista? Extraordinaria vis Spiritus illos egit & immediata in revelandis iis, quae dispensationi Novi T. erant singularia, quaeque nullis adhuc Scripturis continebantur. Veritates enim multas non potuerunt certas credere nisi testimonio nixi Spiritus extraordinario. Ordinaria autem, ligata & quae nostrorum temporum, adjuti sunt in iis interpretandis quae jam scripta erant. hoc enim demum modo vim suam exeruisse Spiritum in Apostolis patet, faciendo, ut, quae Moses & Prophetae habebant, oculatiores jam, quam antea, perviderent. An igitur non aliae plane authoritatis erant Apostolicae, quam nostrae interpretationes? Annon distinguendum est donum Prophetiae extraordinarium ab ordinario, cujus sensus Prophetis subjiciendi erant? donum Prophetiae hic non stricte, sed etiam pro Scripturas interpretandi dono, accipio. Putas igitur in Scripturae Veteris explicatione infallibiles non fuisse? videris hoc statuere. ignoras enim, an hac via sit usus Spiritus Sanctus, ut infallibiles essent in interpretando. Vereor ne tandem ipsorum Apostolorum Interpretationes ad incudem revocentur. Quid vetat iterato exigere ad amussim in quibus infallibiliter ducti non fuerunt? Imo, si in interpretandis iis quae Moses habet & Prophetae, infallibiles non fuerunt, etiam in scribendo infallibiles non fuisse certum est, quanquam ab eo abhorrere Wolzogius videatur. Apostolorum enim & N.T. scripta, magnam partem, Interpretationes continent Veteris. Ego autem in omnibus, quæ Apostoli qua tales, aut ore, aut scripto, suos docuerunt, infallibili Spiritus vi & assistentia adjutos ductosque credo, credit & Ecclesia Reformata, imo Christiana omnis, & turpe est hominem, blasphemum alias, in eo veritatem te melius docuisse. sic ille. Extraordi-narium divini Spiritus lumen affulsisse Prophetis, Euangelistis, atque Apostolis, reliquisque sacrorum codicum scriptoribus, in Dei verbo intelligendo atque interpretando apud omnes in confesso est: his enim, ut habet Polanus, per immediatam revelationem, absque labore & industria, verum Scripturæ sensum revelavit Sp. S. qua ratio, sunt verba Chamieri, nunc nulla ex-spectatur. Wolzogen vero nostrorum temporum Spiritus vim dicit, qua adjuti Apostoli, in interpretando versati sunt. Hæc jam orthodoxa sunt.
units.tr: On p. 59. Wolzogen errs most gravely. For he thinks that the Apostles, who were likewise engaged in the explanation of the Old Testament, were led by the Holy Spirit in its explanation in the same way as the rest of the faithful. He grants the Apostles an extraordinary guidance of the Spirit and an ordinary one, which also belongs to our times. But in what sense is this? An extraordinary power of the Spirit drove them, and it acted immediately in revealing those things which belonged to the dispensation of the New Testament, singular things which were not yet contained in any Scriptures. For they could not hold many truths as certain except by resting on the extraordinary testimony of the Spirit. But in the ordinary, bound and belonging to our times, they were helped in interpreting those things which were already written; for it is clear that the Spirit exerted its power in this way in the Apostles, by causing them to perceive, more clearly than before, what Moses and the Prophets had. Were their apostolic interpretations, then, not of entirely different authority from our interpretations? Must not the extraordinary gift of prophecy be distinguished from the ordinary, to whose sense the Prophets were to be subjected? I take the gift of prophecy here not strictly, but also for the gift of interpreting the Scriptures. Do you therefore think they were not infallible in the interpretation of the Old Scripture? You seem to hold this: "for you do not know whether the Holy Spirit has used this way, so that they would be infallible in interpreting." I fear that at last the very interpretations of the Apostles will be called back to the anvil. What forbids demanding again, to the last point, those things in which they were not led infallibly? Indeed, if they were not infallible in interpreting what Moses and the Prophets wrote, it is certain they were not infallible in writing either, though Wolzogen seems to shrink from this. For the writings of the Apostles and of the New Testament contain, for the most part, interpretations of the Old. But I believe that in all the things which the Apostles, as such, taught their people, whether by word or in writing, they were aided and led by the infallible power and assistance of the Spirit. The Reformed Church believes this, indeed all Christianity does, and it is shameful for a man, otherwise a blasphemer, to have taught the truth better in this respect. Thus he. "That the extraordinary light of the divine Spirit shone upon the Prophets, Evangelists, and Apostles, and the other writers of the sacred books, in understanding and interpreting the Word of God, is agreed by all; for to them, as Polanus has it, through immediate revelation, without labour and diligence, the Holy Spirit revealed the true sense of Scripture; a method which, in Chamier's words, is now not to be expected." But Wolzogen speaks of the power of the Spirit of our times, by which the Apostles, when engaged in interpreting, were helped. These things are now orthodox.

units.la: Pagina 73. Fatetur multa non intelligi in Scriptura propter illam ambiguitatem, quam reliquit Deus. Certe vereor ne nimis irreverenter ambiguitas in Scr. à Deo relicta dicatur, quasi contineret Oracula, partim flexiloqua & obscura, partim ambigua, & quæ ad Dialecticum referenda sint, ut alibi Cicero. Ignorantia nostra, rerum Majestas, Spiritus mensura non consummata, aliaque, cuncta quidem intelligere non sinunt; verum Scripturæ ambiguitatem tribuere multa sunt quæ prohibent. Verba subinde & sententiæ occurrunt quæ minus facilè intelliguntur, intelligerentur autem procul dubio, si, majori Sp. copia, accuratius omnia, quæ in Scripturis exstant, exigere concederetur. Pertendimus, locorum, quæ δυσ-νόητα vocat Petrus, obscuritatem, nostræ imbecillitati esse adscribendam, non ipsimet Scripturæ, ait Maresius.
units.tr: On p. 73. "He admits that many things are not understood in Scripture because of that ambiguity which God left in it." Certainly I fear it is too irreverent to say that ambiguity was left in Scripture by God, as if it contained oracles partly obscure and ambiguous and to be referred to the dialectician, as Cicero says elsewhere. Our ignorance, the majesty of the things, the measure of the Spirit not being fully given, and others, indeed prevent everything from being understood; but there are many things which forbid attributing ambiguity to Scripture. Words and sentences occur which are less easily understood, but they would doubtless be understood if it were granted, with a greater abundance of the Spirit, that everything in the Scriptures be examined more accurately. "We maintain that the obscurity of those passages which Peter calls hard to understand [δυσνόητα] is to be ascribed to our weakness, not to Scripture itself," says Maresius.

units.la: Correctione itidem egent ea, quæ sparsim de Ar-ticulis fundamentalibus docuit author, quoniam autem eadem hac pagina earum mentionem injicit, quæ alibi etiam de eadem re dixit, congerenda & examinanda necesse duxi, quo facto statim deprehendi, non recte, non orthodoxe ab ipso tradi, quæ spectant 1. Eorum paucitatem 2. Perspicuitatem 3. Certitu-dinem.
units.tr: Those things also need correcting which the author has scattered about concerning the fundamental articles. Since he mentions them on this same page, and has said about the same matter elsewhere, I thought it necessary to gather and examine them together. When this was done, I immediately found that they were not rightly or orthodoxly delivered by him, with respect to (1) their fewness, (2) their clarity, and (3) their certainty.

units.la: 1. Paucitatem quod attinet: Fateor equidem, quis pracise numerus & quantus dogmatum fundamentalium sit, quæ absolute ad salutem exiguntur, eamque formaliter, atque ad punctum quasi arguunt, forte tam exacte definiri non posse. Nihilominus tamen non adeo pauca sunt dicenda, cum Socinianis & Remonstrantibus. Sic autem Wolzogen Christiana Religio intra angustos limites conclusa circumscribitur, si fontes spectes & ipsa capita, doctrinaque fundamenta. Quæ verba, licet excusari fortasse, aliquot limitationibus adhibitis, possent, ab errore libera nullus Orthodoxorum dixerit, postquam contulerit, quæ habet Libro secundo, ubi hæc occurrunt verba, ea quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, sunt multo quam NB. vulgo credi solet pauciora. Nisi in Theologis nostris & Theologia jejunus sit valde, ignorare non potuit, quanto cum Zelo nostri hæc rejecerint, postquam à Socinianis excogitata, per Remonstrantes reponebantur.
