Quid igitur movere potuit nostrum, eadem, imo duriora scribere, vel an ne quidem tanti facit, a nostris deflexisse, & Socinianis & Remonstrantibus ὁμόψηφον[?] subinde videri? {*} sic olim Remonstrantes, Non negamus esse nonnulla creditu ad salutem necessa-ria pracise sed NB. ea pauca esse arbitramur. Plus dicit Wolzogen, pauciora quam vulgo credi solet. Sic au-tem D.D. Censores. Quid enim vetat Clarissimorum virorum verba reponere, dum eadem, imo pejora sint, quæ vidimus? {†} Sic igitur Censores.Et hic genium at-
units.tr: 1. As for the paucity: I grant that the exact number and extent of the fundamental doctrines that are absolutely required for salvation, and that formally, as it were to a point, define it, perhaps cannot be fixed so exactly. Nevertheless, not so few things are to be said, with the Socinians and Remonstrants. Thus Wolzogen: The Christian religion, shut up within narrow limits, is circumscribed, if you look to its sources and to its heads and fundamental doctrines. These words, though perhaps they could be excused with some qualifications applied, no Orthodox writer would call free from error, once he has compared what Wolzogen says in Book Two, where these words occur: those things which are necessary for salvation are much fewer than NB. is commonly believed. Unless our theologians and theology were very ignorant, he could not be unaware with what zeal our people rejected these claims, after they had been devised by the Socinians and were put forward again by the Remonstrants. What then could move our man to write the same things, or even harsher ones? Or does he not care at all that he has departed from our people and at times seems to agree (ὁμόψηφον[?]) with the Socinians and Remonstrants? {*} So once the Remonstrants: We do not deny that there are some things that must be believed for salvation, strictly speaking, but we judge these to be few. Wolzogen says more: fewer than is commonly believed. So too the most worthy Censors. For what prevents us from repeating the words of most distinguished men, when the same things, or even worse, are what we have seen? {†} So the Censors. And here we notice the genius and

units.la: * Præfat. ad Confessionem Remonstrantium. que Spiritum Socinianum advertimus. Semel enim certum esto, ait Socini defensor Theoph. Nicolaides ad sa-lutem necessaria paucissima esse. Tria, inquit glorio-sus Socinianae haeresios Triumphator Hoornbeekius, Vir, cujus memoria, piis in benedictione est, ad sen-tentiam adversariorum annotanda hic nobis sunt, & primum quidem, quod dicere solent dogmata ad salu-tem necessaria esse paucissima. Etiam Remonstrantes Apol. p. 11. citatque locum, a suis in eadem & sta-tione & doctrina orthodoxa praedecessoribus cita-tum, ex Theophilo Nicol. Rhetorfortis, Thesin Arminianam dicit, quae sic sonat: Dogmata ad salu-tem scitu necessaria sunt paucissima. Ut ut tam pauca sint, ait idem, ut omnia sub generalibus duobus capi-tibus, nempe de fide & obedientia, forte sub una voce Theologia comprehendantur; attamen credenda, facien-da, petenda non sunt pauca, si in particulari enumeren-tur. Hoc modo possit quis dicere pauca esse fundamenta-lia in Astronomia, nempe, scire naturam & motus corporis mobilis circa medium mundi. Totum hoc ne-gotium pertractare supersedeo, adeat Lector, dilectis-simi & Venerandi Praeceptoris mei, Gisberti Voetii, hac de re Diatribam exactissimam. Exceptiones Re-monstrantium ex Acontio, Jacobo Rege, Molinaeo, Casaubono aliisque, refutat solide Triglandius Anta-pol. pag. 11, 12. & seq. breviter ea tractat Isaacus Junius Antapol. pag. 44, 45. & fuse Rhetorf. Lib. citato.
units.tr: * Preface to the Confession of the Remonstrants. spirit of the Socinians. For let it be certain once and for all, says Theophilus Nicolaides, defender of Socinus, that very few things are necessary for salvation. There are three things, says Hoornbeek, the glorious triumphator over Socinian heresy, a man whose memory is blessed among the pious, that we must note here regarding the opinion of our opponents. And first, that they are accustomed to say that the doctrines necessary for salvation are very few. The Remonstrants too, in their Apology, p. 11, cite a passage, taken by their predecessors in the same position and orthodox doctrine, from Theophilus Nicolaides Rhetorfortis, which they call the Arminian thesis, and which runs thus: The doctrines that must be known for salvation are very few. However few they are, says the same writer, so that all are comprised under two general heads, namely faith and obedience, or perhaps under the one word theology, yet the things to be believed, done and sought are not few if they are enumerated in particular. In this way one could say that there are few fundamentals in astronomy, namely, to know the nature and motions of a moving body around the centre of the world. I refrain from treating this whole matter at length; let the reader go to the most exact treatise on it by my dearest and most venerable teacher, Gisbert Voetius. Triglandius solidly refutes the Remonstrants' objections drawn from Acontius, James I, Molinaeus, Casaubon and others, Antapologia pp. 11, 12 and following. Isaac Junius treats them briefly in Antapologia pp. 44, 45, and Rhetorfortis at length in the book cited.

units.la: 2. Perspicuitas horum Articulorum antehac à Socinianis & Remonstrantibus ita fuit depraedicata, ut & in eo Orthodoxos adversarios nacti fuerint. An autem Wolzogium superent, judicet lector, sic ille, credimus semper ea quae salus nostra exigit ut sciamus, esse obvia, & ita clara, ut ab omnibus intelligi possint. In quibus sic voluntatem Deus expressit ut non possimus de ea dubitare. Quaedam dicit tanta luce non esse circumfusa, ut non studio saltem & industria sit opus ad illa pervidenda; studium illud refert & industriam & subdit. Ego vero nego haec omnia iis convenire, quibus ad salutem opus habemus, quae cum sint clara, tanto non egent apparatu, nec igitur etiam studio & industria. Vide quo haec tendant.
units.tr: 2. The clarity of these articles was formerly so extolled by the Socinians and Remonstrants that they also found orthodox opponents in this respect. Let the reader judge whether he surpasses Wolzogen. Thus he says: We believe that those things which our salvation requires us to know are always obvious and so clear that they can be understood by all. In these things God has expressed his will in such a way that we cannot doubt it. Some things he says are not surrounded by such light that at least study and diligence are not needed to see them clearly; he mentions that study and diligence, and adds: But I deny that all these things apply to those things which we need for salvation, since, being clear, they do not need such apparatus, nor therefore study and diligence. See where these things lead.

units.la: 1. Sunt ita obvia & clara ut ab omnibus intelligi queant.
units.tr: 1. They are so obvious and clear that they can be understood by all.

units.la: 2. Ut de iis dubitari non possit.
units.tr: 2. So that they cannot be doubted.

units.la: 3. Ut studio & industria non egeant. Exscribam solummodo quaedam ex Triglandio & Profess. Lei-densibus & Judicium sit penes lectorem; dixerant Censores, fundamentalium discretionem, laborem atque opus etiam requirere, ad ea sic Episcopius: equidem tempus est palinodiam canere & cum Pontificiis in gratiam redire, ac deinceps statuere Scripturam non esse perspicuam & claram in iis quae praecise ad salutem creditu sunt necessaria, vel si id aperte profiteri non velit, de Walaeo loquitur, tempus est ut nos doceat, qua ratione claritas & perspicuitas Scripturarum, cum ingenti ista difficultate possit conciliari. Non satisfaciet, si dicat, Scripturam claram quidem esse, sed non nisi iis, omnibus dixerat Wolzogen, qui speciali efficacia gratia lumine a Sp. Dei collustrantur, ut eam possint intelligere. Eodem modo argumentatur Velthuisen: quomodo inquit, Scriptura posset dici perspicua in rebus ad salutem necessariis, si non sit intelligibilis Spiritu illo de-stitutis? Sic autem ad ista Triglandius, Pudeat arrogantem illum ac fastuosum magistrum tam crassa ac foeda ignorantia. An illa fuit de perspicuitate Script. inter Pontif. & Reform. controversia? &c.
units.tr: 3. So that they need no study and diligence. I will copy out only some things from Triglandius and the Leiden professors, and let the judgment rest with the reader. The Censors had said that discerning the fundamentals requires labour and effort too. To this Episcopius replies thus: Indeed it is time to sing a palinode and return into favour with the Papists, and thereafter to declare that Scripture is not perspicuous and clear in those things which are strictly to be believed for salvation; or if he is not willing to profess this openly, he speaks of Walaeus, it is time he taught us by what method the clarity and perspicuity of the Scriptures can be reconciled with that great difficulty. It will not satisfy if he says that Scripture is indeed clear, but only to those (Wolzogen had said to all) who are illuminated by the light of God's Spirit with a special and effective grace, so that they can understand it. Velthuysen argues in the same way: How, he says, could Scripture be called perspicuous in matters necessary for salvation, if it is not intelligible to those destitute of that Spirit? Thus Triglandius on these matters: He should be ashamed, that arrogant and haughty master, of such crass and foul ignorance. Was that the controversy about the perspicuity of Scripture between Papists and Reformed? &c.

units.la: Dicis ab omnibusintelligi posse, quae fundamentalia putas, Wolzogi, & de iis dubitari non posse, fovesne igitur istam Libertinorum haeresin, ea demum quae extra controversiam sunt, ut sufficientia sic & necessaria esse? (fallacia Socinianorum est, ait Coccejus, qui dicunt, necessaria esse in iis, quae nullam habent controversiam, dubitationem diceret Wolzogen) sin minus, ut confido, loquere explicatius & cave ne eadem dicas cum Heterodoxis, si Orthodoxus haberi velis. Sed posthac de perspicuitate ista latius.
units.tr: You say, Wolzogen, that everyone can understand what you think fundamental, and that no doubt can be cast on it. Do you therefore favour that Libertine heresy, that only those things which lie beyond controversy are both sufficient and necessary? (It is a fallacy of the Socinians, says Coccejus, who say they are necessary in those things which have no controversy; Wolzogen would say doubt.) If not, as I trust, then speak more explicitly, and beware of saying the same things as the Heterodox, if you wish to be held Orthodox. But more on this clarity later.

units.la: 3. Certitudinem firmam satis non tribuis iis, quae, praeter pauca illa fundamentalia tua, interpretationis ope & industriae, ex sacris eruuntur; ita ut fundamentalia solum certa & indubitata credas: sic enim de reliquis loqueris, in cateris, de iis quae salus exigit ut sciamus, locutus eras, in cateris autem non agnosco inquis ullum infallibilem interpretem. Quae re-ferre, refutare est: sed libro posteriore, in tractatione primariae quaestionis, haec examinanda venient, hic notanda saltem videbantur.
units.tr: 3. You do not grant sufficiently firm certainty to those things which, apart from your few fundamentals, are drawn from the sacred writings by the aid of interpretation and diligence; so that you believe only the fundamentals to be certain and indubitable. For thus you speak of the rest: concerning the rest, about those things which salvation requires us to know, you had spoken, but concerning the rest you say I recognise no infallible interpreter. To report these is to refute them; but in the second book, in the treatment of the primary question, these matters will come up for examination. Here they seemed worth noting only.

units.la: Transfilio ad pag. 81. Ubi dicit, nescivisse aliquando quid scriberent sacri amanuenses. Quae verba, quamvis aliquo respectu, in aliquibus, veritatem habeant, magis tamen reverenter se gessisset Wolzogius, si ea, aut reticuisset, aut ita limitasset, ut offensam dare apta non essent. Res ipsas, Prophetiarum eventus, visionum significationes ad tempus aliquando, vel semper forsan, aliqui ignorarunt, non tamen ea quae scriberent ignorabant, eo sensu, quem hisce verbis subesse doces pag. 126. nimirum quod alienata mente scripserint & oracula fuderint. Praeterquam enim, quod non tam scribentes, quam visionibus in-tenti, & oracula a Deo variis modis recipientes, in ex-stasi fuisse Vates subinde constet, aliter longe de ista exstasi Philosophatur Bisterfeldius, qui non tam ad mentis alienationem, quam ejus congruam, ad sacro-rum omnium, & praesertim quae ipsis obtingebant re-velationum, studium, applicationem, excessus & raptus Prophetarum referendos putat, quibus Verbo Dei perci-piendo ita fuerint intenti, ut aliis animalibus vix vaca-verint verint functionibus. Num. xxiv. 4. Ez.i. 2 Cor.xii. Apoc.i.
units.tr: Passing on to p. 81, where he says that the sacred amanuenses at some time did not know what they were writing. Although these words may hold true in some respect and in some cases, Wolzogen would have conducted himself more reverently had he either kept silent or qualified them so that they would not be apt to give offence. The things themselves, the outcomes of prophecies and the meanings of visions, some men at some time, or perhaps always, did not know. Yet they did not know what they were writing, in the sense which you indicate underlies these words on p. 126, namely that they wrote with a deranged mind and poured out oracles. For apart from the fact that the prophets, intent less on writing than on visions, and receiving oracles from God in various ways, are sometimes clearly shown to have been in ecstasy, Bisterfeld philosophises quite differently about this ecstasy. He thinks it should be referred not so much to an alienation of mind as to its fitting application and zeal for all sacred things, and especially for the revelations that came to them: the excesses and raptures of the prophets, by which they were so intent on perceiving the Word of God that they scarcely had leisure for other animal functions. Num. xxiv. 4. Ez. i. 2 Cor. xii. Apoc. i.

units.la: Pagina 83. Curiosum Scripturæ venatorem vocat, qui nisi evadat sanctus scrutator, nullos certe, labore ullo, aut opera, dignos profectus, in Scripturæ intellectione faciet. Procul omnem curiositatem arcessunt, qui reverentem sacrorum discipulum nobis pingunt pii Theologi, nec tanta, venustatis loco, luxuries surrepere ipsi debuisset, ut, quod vitium sonat, quo nullum datur, quod intellectioni Scr. majorem ponat obicem, ad virtutem in hoc negotio commendatissimam exprimendam, verbum adhiberetur. Curiosum est, teste, omni fide, digno in hisce, Cicerone, ea scire velle, quæ ad nos non pertinent. Quod vitium detestantur Zanchius, Polanus, aliique, præsertim, ubi Scripturæ scrutatorem formant. Didici ex Danæo, Augustinum, fuse Libr. de Utilitate credendi Cap. ix. explicare quid sit curiosum esse. Præterirem ista, nisi offenderet me tam parca pietas, in tali negotio, & circumspecta sæpe minus dictio.
units.tr: Page 83. He calls him a curious hunter of Scripture, who, unless he becomes a holy searcher, will certainly make no progress worth any labour or effort in understanding Scripture. Those who depict for us the reverent disciple of sacred things, the pious theologians, take great care to keep away from all curiosity. Nor should such a luxuriant ornament have crept in, so that a word which sounds like a vice, and which is no small obstacle to understanding Scripture, should be used to express a virtue most commended in this business. Curiosity, as Cicero, a witness worthy of all faith in these matters, says, is wanting to know those things which do not pertain to us. Zanchius, Polanus and others detest this vice, especially where they shape the scrutiniser of Scripture. I learned from Daneus that Augustine, in his book On the Usefulness of Believing, chapter 9, explains at length what it is to be curious. I would pass these things over, were it not that such a meagre piety, and a wording often less careful than it should be, offended me on so serious a matter.

units.la: Sequuntur Strictura ad LIBRUM SECUNDUM.
units.tr: Here follow the Strictures on the SECOND BOOK.

units.la: Miro verborum strepitu, prælium armatorum militum quasi describeret, exorditur librum posteriorem, nihil autem tanto apparatu dignum præstitit, maxime licet sibi placeat, tam multa uni distinctioni inædificando, quasi arcem ferat, quæ totum adversarii & omnem simul impetum sustineat immota? distinguit inter eum qui sibi, & eum, qui alteri Scripturam exponit, aut interpretatur: putatque, Auctorem Paradoxum conficiendum, hoc unico distinctionis telo. Non possum autem ab ejus examine omni me continere, præsertim quia jam priori libro eam posuisse & fuse explicasse non fuit satis, adeo ipsi arridebat subtile hoc inventum. Sed sciat 1. Tritissimam esse & notissimam hanc distinctionem, qua, aliud quid sit, sibi, aliud alteri interpretari quicquam, do-cetur. 2. Credendum non esse Paradoxum istum, ita omni cognitione Theologica vacuum esse, ut eam ignoret. 3. denique ut dicam quod res est, non pu-tem eam, ullius in hoc negotio momenti esse, imo nullus dubito, quin majorem ἀκριβείαν[?] demonstra-turus fuisset, si eam aut omisisset, aut tanti non fe-cisset. Alio fultus tibicine adoriri debebat adversa-rium. Disputatur proprie, quidnam illud tandem sit, quod me per modum objecti movere debeat, ut cre-dam hunc, non alium, hisce verbis subesse sensum. Illud autem idem esse debere sive mihi, sive alii sim persua-surus, tam certum est ut quod certissimum. Quare hic extra oleas vagatur, qui tanta huic distinctioni tribuenda censet. Duo erant, quibus libro priori, distinctionem sc. illam, probare conabaris. 1. pri-mum, quod alteri extorquere assensum nequeas: at ni-hil hoc ad rem, quia quæritur, quid ipsum convincere debeat nec ne, quod idem est sive persuadeat sive non persuadeat. 2. secundum, alteri te admovere non posse, qua te commovent ut credas: sed quid tandem illud est quod te per modum objecti moveat? me saltem mo-vet ipsa Scriptura. facit quidem Spiritus, ut eam recte conferre, examinare, excutere, aptus evadam, eam-que vim, fateor, eam perfectionem, aptitudinem, dispositionem, alteri dare non possum. Quæ autem me per modum objecti movere dici possunt, argu-menta sunt, rationes sunt, ex ipsa scripturæ materia, stylo, aliisque profluentia, hæc autem alteri referre quid vetat? quid in iis est, quod eloqui nescias, cum scribi possit? vereor ne increpationem Velthuisii me-rearis, qua Enthusiasmi accusat eos, qui putant se quibusdam moveri rationibus, quas ipsi soli & sui similes percipiant. Spiritum fateor, alteri dare non po-tes, sed iterum jam ad subjectum relabimur, ejusque dispodispositionem, dum de eo, quod per modum objecti moveat, revera sermo est. Quapropter magna licet differentia sit, inter eum qui sibi, & eum qui alteri, interpres est, non tamen in eo, de quo tibi cum Para-doxo praecipua lis est, ea collocari potest, eadem enim ratio, sive ex re, sive ex loquendi usu, sive ex ipsa Scriptura petita sit, quae te per modum objecti movere debet ad hunc vel illum sensum amplectendum, itidem adhibere & debet & potest, ad alios persuaden-dos. Non enim proprie quid elevet, vi interna hy-perphysica, subjectum, quaeritur; sed quid externe, moraliter, a parte objecti, illud sit, ex quo videam, discam, certus fiam, de Scripturae sensu. Id quo is, qui ratione uteretur, adduci posset ac deberet, ut de veritate alicujus interpretationis se persuaderi pateretur. Nam & qui sibi est Interpres, aliqua certa ratione movetur; & qui aliis inservit, eandem adhibere potest. sic ipse disseris pag. 92. Non est igitur, quod ita, de isto in-vento, tibi gratuleris. Non tangit enim, id quod in quaestione est, ut vidimus. At dicis pag. seq. Inter-terpres privatus sibi tantum consulit, bene; sed quid-nam illud sit, quo sibi per modum objecti consulat, id quaeritur, id, sive secum, sive cum alio ipsi res sit, idem est & erit. Quod autem adversus Paradoxum, inde, ad pacem conficiendam, Interpretis hujus in-sufficientiam, probare volueris, mirum est. posito enim, quod quisque rite sibi consuleret, rectaque norma recte uteretur, an non pax inde & tranquilla quies sperari poterit? Corporis omnia membra & sin-gula suum cum faciunt, totum optime valebit certis-sime. Nec video te candide agere cum adversario tuo, cum eum dicis, Conditiones eas ponere Interpretis, quae certam habeant & invictam persuasionem : persua-dendi vim credo, sed ut actu persuadeant semper, non credo tales statuere, aut sibi imaginari, hominem, stolidus licet satis sit alias. sic loquitur Cap. 1. §. 1. qui verum genuinumque divinarum literarum sensum indicare valet, ac demonstrare certò ac indubitate. Norma scilicet, utens, atque regula, certa, minimeque fallaci. Quam si sequatur interpres, fore putat, ut certam habeat veritatem, & modo ne, à parte sub-jecti docendi, obex ponatur, persuasionem. Nec errat in eo Paradoxus, sed, quod Philosophiam, hanc nor-mam, dicat, id demum longissime à veritatis disce-dit recto tramite. Nam quicquid tandem sit, quod me in Interpretando ducet; infallibile persuadendi-que, in suo genere, vi præditum sit oportet procul omni dubio. Quod dum suo vindicat Interpreti, perperam rogas adversarium, Quis publicus Inter-pres, hoc sibi sumat in aliorum animos imperium? sive enim publicus, sive privatus, nihil ad Paradoxum.
units.tr: With a great clatter of words, as if describing the battle of armed soldiers, he opens his second book. Yet he has achieved nothing worthy of such display, however much he pleases himself by building so much on a single distinction, as if he were raising a citadel that could withstand the whole attack of his opponent and every assault at once, unmoved. He distinguishes between the one who expounds Scripture for himself and the one who expounds or interprets it for another, and he thinks the Paradox-writer can be overthrown with this single weapon of distinction. I cannot, however, refrain entirely from examining it, especially since it was not enough to set it out and explain it at length in the first book; so much did this subtle invention please him. But let him know this: (1) this distinction, by which it is taught that to interpret something for oneself is one thing and to interpret it for another is another, is most trite and well known; (2) one should not believe that this Paradox-writer is so empty of all theological knowledge that he is ignorant of it; (3) finally, to say what the matter is, I do not think it is of any weight in this business. Indeed I doubt not that he would have displayed greater exactness [ἀκριβείαν] if he had either omitted it or not made so much of it. He ought to have attacked his opponent with another prop. The question is properly what it is that ought to move me, as an object, to believe that this sense, and not another, lies under these words. That it must be the same whether I persuade myself or another is as certain as anything most certain. Therefore he wanders beside the olive grove who thinks so much should be attributed to this distinction. There were two things by which you tried, in the first book, to prove that distinction. (1) First, that you cannot extort assent from another. But this has nothing to do with the point, because the question is whether what is to convince him ought to convince him or not, and that is the same whether it persuades or does not persuade. (2) Second, that you cannot bring another to what moves you to believe. But what, pray, is that which moves you as an object? Scripture itself moves me, at least. The Spirit indeed makes me fit to compare, examine and scrutinize it rightly, and that power, I admit, that perfection, aptitude and disposition, I cannot give to another. But the things which can be said to move me as an object are arguments and reasons, flowing from the very matter of Scripture, its style and other things. Why does anything prevent me from reporting these to another? What is there in them that you cannot express, since it can be written? I fear you will deserve the rebuke of Velthuysen, who accuses of enthusiasm those who think they are moved by certain reasons which only they themselves and those like them perceive. I grant you cannot give the Spirit to another, but again we slip back to the subject and its disposition, since the talk is really about what moves as an object. Therefore, although there is a great difference between one who is an interpreter for himself and one who is an interpreter for another, yet in that matter about which your principal quarrel with the Paradox lies, this difference cannot be placed. For the same reason, whether it is drawn from the thing itself, from the usage of speech, or from Scripture, which ought to move you as an object to embrace this or that sense, both ought and can be used likewise to persuade others. For the question is not properly what raises the subject by an inner, hyperphysical force, but what it is externally, morally, from the side of the object, by which I may see, learn and become certain about the sense of Scripture. That by which the one who used reason could be led and ought to be led, so as to allow himself to be persuaded of the truth of some interpretation. For he who is an interpreter for himself is moved by some certain reason, and he who serves others can use the same. So you argue at page 92. It is therefore no reason for you to congratulate yourself so on this discovery. For, as we have seen, it does not touch what is in question. But you say on the following page: A private interpreter consults only himself, well; but what it is by which he consults himself as an object, that is the question, and whether he has to do with himself or with another, it is and will be the same. That you wished to prove, against the Paradox, the insufficiency of this interpreter for establishing peace, is strange. For granted that each man rightly consulted himself and used a right rule, could peace and tranquil quiet not be hoped for from this? When all the members and parts of the body perform their own function, the whole will certainly be in excellent health. Nor do I see you dealing fairly with your opponent when you say that he sets up these conditions of the interpreter, which have a certain and unconquerable persuasion. I believe in the power of persuading, but I do not believe he sets up, or imagines, such conditions as always actually persuade, though he is stupid enough in other respects. So you speak in chapter 1, section 1: who can indicate the true and genuine sense of the divine letters and demonstrate it certainly and indubitably. A norm, namely, using, and rule, certain and least fallible. If the interpreter follows this, he thinks he will have certain truth, and provided that nothing stands in the way on the side of the one being taught, persuasion too. Nor is the Paradox-writer wrong in this; but in calling philosophy this norm, he departs far from the straight path of truth. For whatever it is that will lead me in interpreting, it must without doubt be endowed with an infallible power of persuading in its own kind. While you claim this for your interpreter, you wrongly ask your opponent, Who is a public interpreter, who would take to himself this rule over the minds of others? For whether public or private, it is nothing to the Paradox-writer.

units.la: Rem ille quærit quæ nos ducat, non personam. Aut si personam, hac re utentem quærit, non alium. Illum nimirum, qui, juxta illam normam, interpre-tetur. Eumque hoc agens, dicit infallibiliter & certo interpretari, modo norma recta sit, bene habet. At in animos sibi imperium sumere arrogans est, fa-teor; sed tu explicaturus, e. gr. primum caput Johannis, an non putas certa invictaque argumenta, quæque ea legentem vel audientem convincere debeant, ac persuadere, idque in suo genere possint, tibi suppetere, quibus probes æternam Christi divi-nitatem istic doceri, non secundæ sed primæ crea-tionis istic mentionem fieri & sic porro; an tamen inde merito quis collegerit, te imperium in animos, aut tibi, aut interpretandi normæ tuæ, deferre? An non putas te, certò ac indubitate, hoc tuo Tractatu, veram de Scripturæ Interprete probasse sententiam & demonstrasse? an propterea animarum imperium hac in causa te ambiisse, jure quis dixerit? Alia est objectiva, quam dicimus, convictio, subjectiva alia. Talem se invenisse putat Paradoxus Interpretem, qui priorem efficere valeat convictionem. Idem tu tibi de tuo imaginaris, ego, quæ ex Reformatorum sententia, Interpretandi norma dicitur, eam convictionem dare posse & debere, statuo. Quæ autem postea, longa serie, adversus Paradoxum disputas, nihil faciunt ad rem, ille putat, remillam, quæ in interpretatione nos movere per modum objecti debet, infallibiliter hoc posse agere debere, ego etiam de mea, idem tu item de tua, quæcunque tandem sit; in fundamentalibus eam saltem infallibilem à te agnosci, in-nuis pag. 251. imo hoc certum est, si quis bene, perfecteque uti posset ea re,de qua disputamus, procul dubio nunquam erraret, ita ut ex eo, quod omnis error evitari in interpretando non possit, non sequatur ejus rei in suo genere imperfectio ulla aut fallibilitas, non magis quam si quis veram claram & distinctam perceptionem, infallibilem regulam non esse Cartesianis objiceret, quoniam nemo ea infallibiliter utitur, imo sic adhiberi non vult Deus,quia errorum nos obnoxios fieri permittere voluit. Imo res illa, quam quæritis, debet esse infallibilis, ut patet; & hoc voluisse videtur Paradoxus,frustra proinde & immerito hoc in negotio à te lacessitus. Revera etiam exstirpare omnem hæresin in suo genere res illa apta esse debet. Nec obstat Deum voluisse ut essent hæreses, eodem enim argumento etiam Scripturarum posses evincere πρὸς ἔλεγχον insufficientiam. Cogitando te talem tibi imaginari non posse, qui ea re, quæcunque tandem sit, absque ulla hallucinatione utatur, credo, sed rem ipsam talem non esse, ut si ea rite uteremur, in omnibus, certo Scripturas nos esse intellecturos inde concludere; idem esset, ac si quis, Scripturam, ex eo, ad nos ducendos in pietate, imperfectam esse, argueret, quia nemo hactenus illius ope ad perfectam sanctitatem pervenisse recte creditur. Rem illam Interpretem vocari non debere dicit pag. 95. sed qua ratione, vidimus mus adLib.1,Strict.17. Ex dictis ergo constat immerito te exagitare tuum Paradoxum, eo quod Interpretem finxerit, qui nullibi inveniatur; dato enim quod non homini alicui, sed rei istud infallibiliter interpretandi privilegium deferat, ut vidimus, quid superest quod carpas? hic pulverem cies & p. 191. concedis omne, quod vult adversarius, de suo interprete, aut potius, de suae interpretationis norma, Philosophia, eaque, non, ut ea utuntur homines, sed in idea consiberata, sic enim ut sumantur ejus verba candor requirit. Quas sane, (de conditionibus loqueris, quas hoc loco ita exagitas) conditiones Interpretis ea lege admitto, si Interpretem illum removeat ab usu hominum, & ab eorum vitiis, & hac mente hanc sententiam proponat, ut ea res, qua nititur veritas interpretationis, talis esse natura dicatur, qua possit ac debeat hominem utentem ratione persuadere, idque tam certo, ut errare in ejusmodi judicio minime queat. Nihil ultra petit aut ponit Exercitator, quorsum igitur haec concitationis animi disputatio, nisi ut videaris dissentire? nec hic dissensum requirebat orthodoxa fides.
units.tr: He is asking what leads us, not what person does. Or if he asks about a person, he asks about one who uses this thing, not another; namely, one who interprets according to that norm. And when he does this and says that he interprets infallibly and certainly, provided the norm is right, all is well. But I grant that to take rule over the minds for oneself is arrogant. Yet you, about to explain, for instance, the first chapter of John, do you not think that you have at hand certain and unconquerable arguments, which ought to convince and persuade the one who reads or hears them, and which can do so in their own kind, by which you may prove that the eternal divinity of Christ is taught there, that the mention there is of the first creation and not the second, and so on? Yet would anyone rightly conclude from this that you claim rule over the minds, either for yourself or for your norm of interpretation? Do you not think you have proved and demonstrated in this your treatise, certainly and indubitably, the true opinion about the interpreter of Scripture? Could anyone rightly say that you have sought dominion over souls in this cause because of it? There is one conviction that we call objective, and another that is subjective. The Paradox-writer imagines he has found an interpreter who can produce the former conviction. You imagine the same about yours, and I affirm that the interpretive norm called the Reformers' opinion can and ought to give that conviction. But as for what you afterwards argue, in a long series, against the Paradox-writer, which has nothing to do with the matter, he thinks that that thing which ought to move us in interpretation as an object can do this infallibly and ought to do so. I think the same of mine, and you of yours, whatever it may be. At least you acknowledge it as infallible in fundamentals, as you hint at page 251. Indeed it is certain that if anyone could use that thing we are discussing well and perfectly, he would undoubtedly never err. Therefore, from the fact that every error cannot be avoided in interpreting, it does not follow that there is any imperfection or fallibility in that thing in its own kind, no more than if someone objected to the Cartesians that a clear and distinct perception is not an infallible rule, since no one uses it infallibly; indeed God does not want it to be used in this way, because he willed to allow us to be liable to errors. Indeed that thing which you seek must be infallible, as is plain; and this seems to be what the Paradox-writer wanted, so you are provoked in this business in vain and undeservedly. In fact that thing ought also to be fit, in its own kind, to root out every heresy. Nor does it stand in the way that God willed there should be heresies; for by the same argument you could also prove the insufficiency of the Scriptures for refutation [πρὸς ἔλεγχον]. Thinking that you cannot imagine yourself such that you use that thing, whatever it is, without any hallucination, I believe; but that thing itself is not such that, if we used it rightly, we would certainly understand the Scriptures in all things. To conclude this would be the same as if someone argued that Scripture is imperfect for leading us in piety, because no one so far is rightly believed to have reached perfect holiness by its help. That thing ought not to be called an interpreter, he says at page 95; but for what reason, we have seen at Book 1, Strictures 17. From what has been said, then, it is plain that you undeservedly harass your Paradox, because he has invented an interpreter who is found nowhere. For granted that he grants this privilege of infallibly interpreting not to some man but to a thing, as we have seen, what is left for you to carp at? Here you raise dust, and at page 191 you concede everything that the opponent wants about his interpreter, or rather about the norm of his interpretation, philosophy, and that not as men use it, but as considered in idea; for so, if candour requires, its words must be taken. I certainly admit these conditions of the interpreter (you speak of the conditions, which you here harass in this way), on this condition, if the interpreter is removed from the use of men and from their faults, and with this intention he puts forward this view, that the thing on which the truth of the interpretation rests is said to be of such a nature that it can and ought to persuade a man who uses reason, and that so certainly that he cannot err in such a judgment. The Exercitator asks for nothing more and sets down nothing more. Why, then, this agitated dispute of spirit, unless you wish to appear to dissent? Nor did orthodox faith require dissent here.

units.la: Saepe video, libenter reprehendendi Paradoxi, in minutiis ansam captasse Wolzogium: sic nimirum debebat, ne omnis pugnae species evanesceret, in re ipsa enim quam parum distent Libro II. demonstrabo. Sugillat pag. 98. obscuritatis & perspicuitatis definitiones a Paradoxo traditas, perspicuum dixerat quod primo intuitu patet, sed Wolzogius criminatur eum non exerte satis, quid sit primo intuitu patere vel latere, declarasse. At cum per se pateat, quid sit primo intuitu patere, ita ut statim clare id & distincte percipiatur, quid attinebat multis id declarare? Recte alibi Schulerus ad definitionem Cartesii, qua claram & distinctam perceptionem definierat, Meo quidem judicio hac definitione perfectionis clara eadem non clarior, sed obscurior facta est. Et profecto si sit aliquid, quod explicatione aut definitione non indigeat, est id quod clarum dicimus. Hæc optime huc quadrant. Non ex-plico, ait Cartesius, alia multa nomina, quibus jam usus sum, vel utar in sequentibus, quia per se satis nota mihi videntur: hæc optimo jure hisce regereret Paradoxus. Uti etiam illa quæ Wolzogius de veritate Logica & Ethica disserit, non feriunt Paradoxon, nisi in quantum videatur statuere in Scripturam Logicum differre sensum ab Ethico, cum revera ut notat D. Essenius hic coincidant. nec juvat quod addit Wolzo- gius, nondum de divina oratione ipsi sermonem esse, contrarium enim diceret Paradoxus, sicque ista omnia disjiceret. Quærit enim Scripturæ interpretem, exempla Scripturaria in isto discursu profert. Quapropter extra oleas vagatur noster, dum interpretem de auctoris mente nullo modo, sed verborum sensu laborare asserit. sensus enim verborum & mens authoris in scripto, de quo sermo est, non possunt non coincidere, nisi Deus, contra mentem ire posse dicatur. Sic ipse doces, mentem authoris ejus verbis hic con-gruentem esse. quæ enim de amanuensibus subdis nihil sunt, quoniam in confesso est non tam de amanuen-sium, de Petri, de Pauli, quam quidem de Dei, per ipsos Loquentis, mente sollicitum lectorem esse.
units.tr: I often see that Wolzogius has seized on trifles in order to find fault with the Paradoxus, since he evidently had to do so, lest every semblance of a fight vanish. In substance, however, I will show in Book II how little they differ. On p. 98 he taunts the definitions of obscurity and perspicuity given by the Paradoxus. The Paradoxus had said that the perspicuous is what is evident at first sight, but Wolzogius complains that he has not sufficiently explained what it is to be evident or hidden at first sight. Yet since it is self-evident what it is to be evident at first sight, so that it is clearly and distinctly perceived at once, what was the point of explaining it at length? Schuler rightly remarked on Descartes's definition of a clear and distinct perception: "In my judgment, by this definition the clear has not become clearer but more obscure." And indeed, if there is anything that needs no explanation or definition, it is what we call clear. These words fit the case perfectly. "I do not explain," says Descartes, "many other terms which I have already used or will use in what follows, because they seem to me sufficiently known in themselves." The Paradoxus could rightly reply to Wolzogius in these same words. Likewise, what Wolzogius discusses concerning logical and ethical truth does not strike the Paradoxus, except insofar as he seems to hold that the logical sense of Scripture differs from its ethical sense, whereas in fact, as Essenius notes here, they coincide. Nor does it help that Wolzogius adds, "there is not yet any question about divine speech," for the Paradoxus would say the opposite, and so all of this would collapse. For he is seeking an interpreter of Scripture and brings forward scriptural examples in this discussion. Therefore our author wanders off course when he asserts that the interpreter labours not at all over the mind of the author, but only over the sense of the words. For the sense of the words and the mind of the author in the writing under discussion cannot fail to coincide, unless God can be said to act against his own mind. Thus you yourself teach that "the mind of the author agrees with his words here." As for what you add about amanuenses, it amounts to nothing, since it is agreed that the reader ought to be concerned not with the mind of the amanuenses, of Peter or of Paul, but with the mind of God, who speaks through them.

units.la: De Idea Dei, Wolzogius loquitur p. 135. Atque sic omni occasione se Cartesianum demonstrat. Quoniam autem ea de re ante aliquot annos abunde egit, singulari Tractatu Stephanus Eszekius: & sua pro-mittit Clariss. Vogelsangh: lectores eo remitto. Ut & ad Disquisitionem Gassendi, opus sane in isto ge-nere perquam laudabile.
units.tr: Wolzogius speaks of the idea of God on p. 135, and in doing so shows himself a Cartesian on every occasion. Since Stephanus Eszekius dealt with this matter fully a few years ago in a separate treatise, and since the most distinguished Vogelsang promises his own, I refer readers to them, as also to Gassendi's Disquisitio, a work truly most praiseworthy in this kind.

units.la: Postquam multa jam disputavit; quædam enarrat, quæ adversarius cogatur suo subducere interpreti, vel saltem ab eo non expedienda fateri. Inter alia creationem memorat, quam putat ad veritates referri non posse, hoc dixerat Paradoxus, omnem locum veritatem quandam docere, eamque rationi examinandam, ut sic omnia ad veritatis naturam redacta, rationis simul imperio, traderentur, regerit Wolzogen, multa in sacris ad veritates tales referri non posse & inter alia creationem; quam bene ista aut male posteriori libro videndum erit, id solum nunc notandum, quod, nisi creatio ad res facti referatur, necessario sequi velit, nos scire non posse an sit conditus mundus a Deo, aut in quem finem. Illud igitur pro mera liberalitate largitur, si rationi examen relinquatur, fore, ut sciri non possit conditum a Deo mundum esse. Quid, an putat igitur sanam rationem eousque non pertingere, ut mundum, ut motum, ut materiam, vel quicquam praeter Deum, ab aeterno non extitisse probare valeat. Ego nihil magis certo aut clare demonstrari posse confido. Si Cartesium consulas, ille aegre feret, te temporis divisa, a se invicem nullo modo pendentia, momenta, processus in infinitum impossibilitatem, imo ipsam Ideam Dei id nondum docuisse. Quae, dum Deum tibi, ut summum bonum, repraesentat & perfectissimum, satis etiam innuit, ut ex ipso, sic ad ipsum, omnia creata esse. Sicque creationis & τὸ ὂν[?] & finis constaret etiam ratione judice primario. Alia vero plurima ab isto ultimo fine diversa, quae forsan Deus intenderit, sciri non posse, nisi per revelationem, non inficior, licet de ultimo illo, quod Prov. xvi. 4. Salomo ponit, etiam ex ratione edoceri hominem posse non dubitem, subordinatos propterea fines nisi respiciat Cartesius manifesti erroris convincetur, quando dicit: Ita denique nullas unquam rationes circa res naturales a fine, quem Deus aut natura in iis faciendis sibi proposuit, desumemus, quia non tantum nobis debemus arrogare, ut ejus consiliorum participes esse putemus. Summus enim finis necessario Deus ipse est, quod & docet ratio, reliquorum licet nonnulli sola revelatione cognoscantur.
units.tr: After he has already disputed at length, he recounts certain points which his opponent is compelled to withdraw from his own interpreter, or at least to admit cannot be resolved by him. Among other things he mentions creation, which he thinks cannot be referred to truths. The Paradoxus had said that every passage teaches some truth and must be examined by reason, so that, once all things are reduced to the nature of truth, they may be handed down under the authority of reason at the same time. Wolzogen replies that many things in Scripture cannot be referred to such "truths," and among them creation. How well or badly he does so is for the later book to examine; the only thing to note now is that, unless creation is referred to matters of fact, he must necessarily grant that "we cannot know whether the world was made by God, or to what end." He therefore concedes, out of sheer generosity, that if the matter is left to reason's examination, it will follow that it cannot be known that the world was made by God. What then? Does he think that sound reason does not reach so far as to prove that the world, motion, matter, or anything apart from God has not existed from eternity? I am confident that nothing can be demonstrated more certainly or clearly. If you consult Descartes, he will be displeased with you, for he has not yet taught that times divided into moments which in no way depend on one another, or processes extending to infinity, are impossible, nor even the idea of God itself. Yet this idea, while it presents God to you as the highest and most perfect good, sufficiently hints that all created things exist from him and likewise to him. Thus the being of creation [τὸ ὂν] and its end would also be established, with reason as the primary judge. I do not deny that very many other things, different from this ultimate end, which God may have intended, cannot be known except by revelation. But I do not doubt that man can be taught by reason about that ultimate end which Solomon states in Prov. 16:4. Therefore, unless Descartes considers subordinate ends, he will be convicted of a manifest error when he says: "Finally, then, we shall never draw any reasons concerning natural things from the end which God or nature has proposed to himself in making them, because we must not presume so much as to think ourselves sharers in his counsels." For the highest end is necessarily God himself, as reason also teaches, although some of the remaining ends are known through revelation alone.

units.la: Prophetias dicit totam sibi vindicasse fidelium sub Veteri Testamento fidem. Quod si ita in universum verum 1. non debuerat dicere, paulo ante, caeremonias sic Christum adumbrasse antiquo populo ut Christum venturum vix aliunde certius intelligerent. Nisi, quas tamen diversas refert, coincidere putet Prophetias cum caeremoniis. Si enim Prophetiae totam fidem sibi vindicant, vel sequitur nullam sibi caeremonias vindicasse, praeter quas tamen vix aliunde Christum certius intelligebant, vel caeremonias idem esse cum Prophetiis, quod tamen ipsi Wolzogio contradiceret, quippe qui separatim, ut diversa argumenta, adversus Paradoxum, caeremonias narrat & Prophetias.
units.tr: He says that he has claimed for himself the whole faith of believers under the Old Testament by means of the prophecies. But if that were true in general, he should not have said a little earlier that the ceremonies so represented Christ to the ancient people that they could hardly have understood more clearly from any other source that Christ was to come. Unless he thinks that the prophecies coincide with the ceremonies, which he nevertheless describes as different. For if the prophecies claim for themselves the whole faith, it follows either that the ceremonies claimed nothing for themselves, though by them they hardly understood Christ more clearly from any other source, or that the ceremonies are the same as the prophecies. This, however, would contradict Wolzogius himself, who, when he sets out against the Paradoxus, narrates the ceremonies and the prophecies separately, as different arguments.

units.la: 2. Praesentia bona etiam per fidem videbant multa & possidebant spiritualia, peccatorum nimirum remissionem, sanctificationem &c. quae tamen ad Prophetias non pertinebant, nisi alio absurdo promissa easque repleta ad Prophetias referat. Imo praeterita quam plurima, creatio, lapsus, & ejus generis magno numero alia, nonne sibi fidem vindicabant Patrum? ô accuratum & perspicuum Theologum!
units.tr: Second, they saw present goods also through faith, and possessed many spiritual goods, namely the remission of sins, sanctification, and so on. These, however, did not pertain to the prophecies, unless by another absurdity one refers promised and fulfilled things to the prophecies. Moreover, very many past things, creation, the fall, and a great number of other things of this kind, did not the faith of the Fathers claim these for itself? O accurate and perspicuous theologian!

units.la: Postea quid homini integro notum fuerit nec ne disserit author, putatque ne suspicari quidem potuisse, se unquam, si laberetur, conciliari posse & in gratiam redire. Nolim equidem contentiose de hisce agere, aut temere determinare quicquam, dubium tamen videtur, an non conceptus, quem de Dei omnipotentia habuit & omnisufficientia, simile quid suggerere aptus fuerit, praesertim si conciliatio hominis cum Deo causas, easque plurimas, habeat, quas in natura Dei, quam optime cognovit, fundatas dicit Wolzogius: Ratio-nes, nes, quanquam ipsa thesis non displiceret, minus so-lidas judicarem. Prima revera idem per idem probat. Ideam, sic sonat, secum natam redemtionis habere non potuit, quia cum perfectus esset conditus, & ad id, ut in ea perfectione vitam ageret, scire quidem potuisse imaginor, quanam esset natura sua perfectio, quid ad illam conservandam requirebatur, imo quid illam corrumpere posset, sed qua ad restituendum hominem lapsum faciunt, nil habent cum eodem stante commune. Ergo à natura sua nil, nil de redemtione dicere voluit, potuit erudiri. Conclusionem video, sed medius terminus nullibi comparet, cognovit quid ad integritatem, non igitur quid ad restaurationem requireba-tur, egregie, cognovit quod in confesso, ergo id, de quo disputatur, non cognovit. Vides Wolzogi quam belle ista cohæreant quam firmo talo argumentum fundes? sequelam enim nullam habet, nisi unum quod uterque concedit, cum eo quod removendum contendit non consistat: quod tantum abest ut probes ut de eo ne quidem cogitasse videaris. Et revera contrariorum cum sit, se mutuo menti ingerere clarius, præsertim comparata invicem, suspicari quis posset, ex eo quod videbat, quid ad integritatem ejusque conservationem necesse erat, adductis præcipue iis, quæ de Divina omnisufficientia noverat, eum aliquid cogitare de restauratione potuisse. Altera ratio ex eo desumta est, quod & à Deo revelatum Adamo non sit, id de quo sermo est, quoniam nec verbulo hoc innuit Scriptura, hactenus bene ut probet non constare contrarium ejus quod negat, sed & vehementer inquit pugnat, cum sapientia Dei, quod tam certo asseverare non ausim, uti etiam non probat Wolzogius, supponit quidem, ostendando remedium peccati, peccandi occasionem homini datam fore, non probat nisi, hac veritate non abuti non potuisse, hominem integrum, evincat. Quod credendum non videtur, quo[?]niam hominem lapsum & per regenerationem non-dum plene restitutum, ea non solum non abuti sæpe, sed maximum constantiæ & pietatis stimulum in ea reperire certum, & contra eos qui perseverantiæ certitudinem, plenæque, a corpore peccati, libera-tionis firmam fiduciam negant, etiam ex eo quod peccandi occasionem sic datam prætendant, pro-batum est. Quod porro de Adamo statuit pag. se-quente, examen meretur. Sed nec Trinitatis Myste-rium, inquit, ipsi fuisse notum, nisi manifestante Deo, videtur affirmandum. Scio Amyraldum alicubi sic sentire, Adamo nimirum, non innotuisse Trinitatis Mysterium & quidem variis rationibus, ut putat id evincentibus. Ego quidem temere quicquam in isto negotio determinare nolim, nihilominus tamen plura sunt, quæ non leviter aut obscure contrarium probare videntur. Essentiam eum novisse & proprie-tates Dei credit Wolzogius, verum majus errandi in eo periculum videtur, si Trinitatem, quam si, hoc aut illud attributum, minus noveris. Imo quid ni dicitur de natura & ut ita loquar essentia Dei esse, tribus ut subsistat modis? Sic enim Bisterfeldius hac de re disse-rit, quam ratiocinationem meam non facio, adoptat eam Clauberg. Tantum abest ut productio divina per-sectioni repugnet, ut potius infinita ejus eminentia eam necessario requirat. Quam thesin sic prosequitur. Et-enim cum in Deo sit infinita potentia activa seu produ-ctivitas, necessum est, ut in ipso quoque sit infinita pro-ductio, & infinitum productum; secus infinita illa po-tentia activa nunquam haberet vel actum vel termi-num adæquatum: quod prorsus est inconveniens; cum omnis potentia activa sit propter actum suum adæqua-tum: jam vero nulla vel creatura vel creaturarum collectio potest esse productum revera infinitum; siqui-dem solus Deus sit revera infinitus: ergo necesse est, ut productum illud infinitum sit Deus, & quidem idem Deus qui est producens, cum Deus ille qui est infinitus sit essentia unicus. Quibus positis sequeretur, si Adamo indita fuerit recta, de Deo, ejusque proprietatibus cognitio, necesse esse ut & Trinitatem ex summa & naturali perfectione ac eminentia, sit verbo venia, profluentem agnoverit. Seraphini etiam, perfectionem Dei summam, intime contemplantes, ejus ἀκμὴν[?] quasi in Trinitate ista collocasse videntur, Jesaiae vi. Cap. inclamantes Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dominus exercituum! Adde, quod, non solum quod sit, sed & quis sit Deus, procul omni dubio, cognoscere, Adami perfectio requirat. Nisi enim quis id noverit, semper rogare dabitur cum Pharaone, quis est ille Deus? Merito etiam, Articulum, si quenquam, fundamentalem statuunt Reformati dogma de Trinitate. Neque etiam post incarnationis demum tempus, sed & ab aeterno verum esse putem, quisquis non habet, aut non honorat Filium, is non habet non honorat Patrem. Sequeretur deinceps, fidem Adamicam, vel potius cognitionem, objecto non distingui a Gentili, Judaica, Muhammedana. Quomodo autem Christiana fides, Adami Theologia dico ego, tota essentia & forma distingui debeat ab Apostasia & perfidia Judaica, & quidem speciatim hoc dogmate de uno vero Deo, accurate & evidentissime, contra Socinianos demonstravit, Cl. Vedelius, in Tract. de Deo Synagogae. Adde quod usus Practici morales non pauci inde nobis profluant, ut fuse docet Venerandus Senex G. Voetius Loc. cit. & quidem multi eorum tales, qui integrum aeque spectant, ac restituturum hominem. Quare & legi morali, Adamo reipsa itidem datae, se talem praefixit Deus ut qui sit Jehova Elohim. Ut non referam, magnum revera Socinianis praetextum dari, si id statuas aut in dubium revoces an Adamus &c. ratio est, quia de necessitate credendi dogma de Trinitate contendentibus, oggerent, hactenus se talem, de Deo, homini notitiam adscri-bere, qualem in Adamo integro fuisse ille statuit qui Trinitatem ipsi cognitam non fuisse asserit. Quod non parum orthodoxos stringet, quippe imaginem Dei, partim in cognitione sitam fuisse, ad eamque nos, quoad cognitionem redintegrandos ex Col.iii. dum docent, respondebunt Sociniani, se largiter sa-tis nobiscum agere, modo concedant, restituti ho-minis cognitionem, quoad objectum primarium, eandem esse cum integri, id est Deum innotescere unum essentia, non personis trinum. Sicque paria faciet hactenus restitutus cum integro cujus excellentiam eo in loco praedicari judicamus. In Evangelii dispensatione & redemptionis opere, peculiares Filio & Sp. S. partes esse, sicque jam utriusque mentionem saepe in scriptis sacris, ista occasione fieri, non equidem inficior: sed notari velim haec duo, primo, quod absolutus etiam, moralis & homini integro debitus cultus, omnino requirere videatur, ut Deum agnoscat qualis est colatque triunum: relatio redemptoris quidem supervenit occasione peccati, trina au-tem subsistentia, Deo coaeterna est, &, ut ita loquar, naturalis & essentialis, ita ut Deum esse, summe perfectum esse, ponat, triunum esse tribusque modis subsistere. Deinde non minus certum est omnes personas, secundum suum quamque subsistendi operandique modum ac ordinem, in opere, etiam creationis, agnoscendas, quapropter & non minori cum emphasi, in narratione primae, quam secundae creationis exerta & copiosa Filii & Sp. Sancti mentio habetur. Praeterquam enim, quod vox Elohim, saepius repetita, in historia creationis Gen. i. id toties inculcet, summopere notandum videtur, quod homi-nem creaturus, Deus ille Elohim, consilium quasi ineat, dicente Patre, Filio & Sp. S. faciamus homi-nem &c. multis pluralitatem personarum significante. iii.
units.tr: Afterwards the author argues about what was or was not known to man in his integrity. He thinks that man could not even suspect that, if he fell, he could ever be reconciled and restored to favour. I would not wish to argue about these matters contentiously or to determine anything rashly, yet it seems doubtful whether the concept he had of God's omnipotence and all-sufficiency was not fitted to suggest something of the kind, especially if the reconciliation of man with God has causes, and very many of them, which are (as Wolzogen says) founded in the nature of God, which he knew very well. The arguments, though the thesis itself would not displease me, I would judge less solid. The first in fact proves the same thing by the same thing. He could not have had a redemption born with the idea, so it runs, because, since he was created perfect, and to live in that perfection, I imagine he could indeed know what his perfection was, what was required to preserve it, and even what could corrupt it; but the things that serve to restore fallen man have nothing in common with man standing. Therefore he could not be taught about redemption from his own nature. I see the conclusion, but the middle term appears nowhere. He knew what was required for integrity, not therefore what was required for restoration. He knew well what is granted, therefore he did not know the thing under dispute. You see, Wolzogen, how nicely these things hang together, and what a firm heel you give your argument! For there is no consequence here, except one thing both concede, which does not agree with what you are trying to remove. So far from proving your point, you seem not even to have thought of it. And indeed, since opposites set each other off more clearly when they are compared, one might suspect that from what he saw was necessary for integrity and its preservation, especially from those things he knew about God's divine all-sufficiency, he could have thought something about restoration. The second argument is drawn from the fact that the matter in question was not revealed to Adam by God, since Scripture does not hint at it even in a word. Thus far, he proves well that it is not established that the contrary of what he denies is true, but he also says that it strongly conflicts with the wisdom of God. I would not dare to assert this so confidently, and Wolzogen does not prove it either. He assumes that by showing a remedy for sin, an occasion of sinning would be given to man, and he only proves, if he proves anything, that man in his integrity could not have abused this truth. That does not seem credible, since fallen man, not yet fully restored by regeneration, not only often abuses it, but finds in it the strongest spur to constancy and piety. It has been proved also against those who deny the certainty of perseverance and the firm confidence of full deliverance from the body of sin, by their pretending that an occasion of sinning is thus given. What he lays down next about Adam, on the following page, deserves examination. But it seems, he says, that the Mystery of the Trinity was not known to him, unless God revealed it. I know that Amyraut somewhere holds this view, that the Mystery of the Trinity was not known to Adam, and indeed on various grounds, which he thinks prove it. I myself would not rashly determine anything in this matter, yet there are several considerations which seem to prove the contrary not lightly or obscurely. Wolzogen believes that Adam knew the essence and the properties of God, but there seems to be a greater danger of error in not knowing the Trinity than in knowing less of this or that attribute. Indeed, why should it not be said that the nature, and, so to speak, the essence of God, subsists in three modes? For Bisterfeld discussed this matter in this way, and Clauberg adopts his reasoning, which I do not make my own. So far is divine production from being repugnant to perfection, that rather its infinite eminence necessarily requires it. He follows this thesis thus: For since there is in God infinite active power, or productivity, it is necessary that in him there should also be infinite production and an infinite product; otherwise that infinite active power would never have a proper act or term: which is utterly inconsistent, since every active power exists for its proper act. Now no creature or collection of creatures can be a truly infinite product, since God alone is truly infinite. Therefore it is necessary that this infinite product be God, and indeed the same God who is the producer, since that God who is infinite is one in essence.* From these premises it would follow, if the right knowledge of God and of his properties was implanted in Adam, that he necessarily recognised the Trinity as flowing (so to speak) from the highest and natural perfection and eminence. The seraphim too, gazing intently upon the supreme perfection of God, seem to have placed its [akmē] in this Trinity, crying out in Isaiah 6, Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord of hosts! Add that Adam's perfection required him to know, beyond all doubt, not only that God is but who God is. For unless a man knows this, he will always be asking, like Pharaoh, Who is that God? Rightly too the Reformed hold the doctrine of the Trinity to be a fundamental article, if any is. Nor do I think it true only from the time of the incarnation, but from eternity, since whoever does not have or does not honour the Son, does not have or honour the Father. It would follow next that the Adamic faith, or rather knowledge (I mean Adam's theology), would not be distinguished in its object from Gentile, Jewish, or Muhammadan belief. How the Christian faith, I mean the whole essence and form of Adam's theology, ought to be distinguished from Jewish apostasy and perfidy, and especially on this doctrine of the one true God, has been shown accurately and most clearly against the Socinians by the learned Vedelius, in his treatise on the God of the Synagogue. Add that no few practical and moral uses flow from this for us, as the venerable old man G. Voetius teaches at length in the work cited; and many of these uses look equally to the restored man as to the man in integrity. Hence God, to whom the moral law was likewise actually given to Adam, has presented himself as one who is Jehovah Elohim. Not to mention that the Socinians would be given a great pretext, if you were to assert, or call into doubt, whether Adam etc. The reason is this: those who contend for the necessity of believing the doctrine of the Trinity will object that, so far, they ascribe to man such a knowledge of God as he who denies that the Trinity was known to him holds to have been in integrated Adam. This will press the orthodox not a little, since they teach that the image of God lay partly in knowledge, and that we are to be restored to it, as far as knowledge is concerned, from Colossians 3. The Socinians will reply that they deal quite generously with us, provided we concede that the knowledge of restored man, as regards the primary object, is the same as that of man in integrity, that is, that God is known as one in essence, not three in persons. Thus far the restored man will be on the same footing as the integrated man, whose excellence we judge to be praised in that place. I do not deny that in the dispensation of the Gospel and in the work of redemption the Son and the Holy Spirit have their particular parts, and that mention of both is often made in the sacred writings on this occasion. But I would like two things to be noted. First, that the absolute, moral worship due even to man in integrity seems wholly to require that he acknowledge God as he is and worship him as triune. The relation of Redeemer indeed came upon the occasion of sin, but the threefold subsistence is coeternal with God and, so to speak, natural and essential, so that to posit that God exists is to posit that he is most perfect, triune, and subsists in three modes. Next, it is no less certain that all the persons are to be recognised in the work, even of creation, according to the mode and order of their subsisting and working; therefore in the narrative of the first creation, no less than of the second, there is a copious and emphatic mention of the Son and the Holy Spirit. For apart from the fact that the word Elohim, repeated so often in the history of creation in Genesis 1, inculcates it so frequently, it seems most important to note that when God was about to create man, that God Elohim, as it were, took counsel, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit saying, Let us make man, etc., which signifies a plurality of persons. iii.

units.la: Sic Sp.S. aquis incubasse dicitur expresse. Johanne[?] divinitatem τῷ λόγῳ[?] peculiari ratione ex opere primæ creationis deducit, eandem Filio exserte tribuit[?] Paulus; in Filio agnoscunt, laudant Angeli. Agnovit etiam procul dubio Adamus. Sed non novit, dicit Wolzogen, nisi manifestante Deo, fit ita, indita cognitio etiam Dei manifestatio est, at aliud quid putat, nil enim cogitamus, sic argumentatur, in ima-gine Dei, quod ultra essentiam divinam, ejusque pro-prietates ascendat altius. 1. non cogitamus, ergo &c. optime! sic discimus hodie ratiocinari, non cogito non percipio, ergo non est, memini eandem metho-dum tribui Judæo cuidam apud Genebrardum, qui Trinitatem oppugnaturus sic disserit, Existentiam ejus mens concipere prorsum nequit. Eodem prorsus argumento. Sed Wolzogi, an tu ex idea, imper-secta sane, quam nunc de imagine Dei tibi formas argumentaberis dum de homine integro sermo est? Et posito quod ita sit, quod ultra essentiam, ejusque proprietates non ascenderit, cum de essentia sit Deo, uti supra diximus triunum esse, idque ex infinita fluat perfectione, quis inficiabitur, cognita rite essentia, ejusque perfectione, cognitam simul Trinitatem esse? Vel an putas, & Angelis id non innotescere, nisi præter concreatam cognitionem, qua gaudent, insuper hoc Mysterium reveletur? Et si non Angelis; quorsum homini talem revelationem necessariam fingis? Ideam Dei nobis inditam dicis, quæ Deum referat, an credendum putas, talem indi Adamo non potuisse, quæ ipsi Deum triunum repræsentaverit, si indi potuerit, quid ambigis? quid te cogit eam imperfectionem fingere, scilicet, quia nunc eam ta-lem non cogitamus: sed talem nunc cogitare non va-les forsan. Ex revelatione dicunt, qui Ideam istam propugnant, postquam innotuit S. S. Trinitas, Ideam habemus Trinitatis, & idem ipsis est negare Ideam Trinitatis, quod credere eam sine ullo ejus conceptu ad-eoque credere quod nescias. Quidni jam Adamo ea ab initio indi potuit, qualis ope revelationis in nobis de-mum evadit? praesertim cum Adami cognitio exem-plar ejus sit, quam nos per regenerationem acquiri-mus, judice Apostolo Col. iii. tu licet talem nunc non cogites. Non magis solida sunt quae sequuntur, sic ex supra positis adversus Paradoxum concludit. Quae cum cum ita sint, nimirum Adamum citra revelatio-nem illa scire non potuisse, id hinc concludo, non de-bere nos putare, veritates istas Scripturarias magis nobis esse cognitas ratione tantum utentibus posse, quam in perfecto statu collocato homini. At ubi hoc Exercita-tor? veritates istas nobis a natura & ratione esse co-gnitas. Non tam stolidus est, ut putet Christi nati-vitatem, Passionem, fidei in Christum necessitatem, &c. ratione innotescere, nec ullus Socinianorum un-quam ita deliravit. Quemadmodum enim hominum nemo consilia quae alter mente sua agitat scire potest, quamdiu ipsi non revelentur: ita multo minus Dei con-silia quamdiu in mente ejus latent, agnoscere. Re-velantur &c. sic homo Socinianus. Videmus Dei mysteria ab hominibus intelligi non posse, nisi a Deo revelentur; sed revelata posse intelligi, ait Schligh-tingius. Neque enim alia ratione Dei arcana homini fas est cognoscere, inquit Crellius. Ut frustra Wol-zogius rem istam tanto conatu probaverit, a ne-mine quippe negatam. At posito, quod & Sociniani & Paradoxus Wolzogio ultro largiuntur, istas veri-tates ratione non innotescere, quid inde? concludo inquit nullam proinde esse interpretationem quae a solis veritatibus petenda sit. Id vult Paradoxus, non a veritatibus insitis omnem fluere & pendere interpre-tationem, ita ut nulla veritas loco alicui inesse cre-denda sit, nisi quae prius in mente fuerit ex principiis naturalibus elicita, vel saltem elicienda, contrariuim enim jam vidimus; sed hoc vult, nihil in Scriptura esse praeter veritates, quas licet invenire non potuisset latentes, revelatas dijudicare tamen queat, & examinare an possibiles sint nec ne, ratio. Quae genuina Socinianorum est sententia. Quam non evertit Wolzogen, qui solum concludit, quod Sociniani conce-dunt, veritates nimirum multas, ante revelationem ut excogitari, sic dijudicari ratione non posse. Sed fusius ista videbimus postea. Quare & non stringunt quae habet pag. 177. si ex veritatibus judicandum, jam nihil interesse, legemne scripto Deus nobis tradidisset, an cordibus tantum natura insculpsisset. Regeret enim Paradoxus, de multis ne quidem somniare rationem, nondum revelatis, dum post revelationem tamen à ratione judicari & discerni queunt optime. Sicque multum revelationem superad-dere rationi, ratio licet judicandi etiam de revelatis maneat norma:
units.tr: So the Holy Spirit is said expressly to have brooded over the waters. John derives the divinity of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ] in a special way from the work of the first creation, and Paul expressly attributes the same divinity to the Son. The angels recognise and praise him in the Son. Adam without doubt recognised him too. But Wolzogen says that Adam did not know except by God's manifesting, so that the implanted knowledge is itself a manifestation of God. Yet Wolzogen thinks otherwise, and argues thus: we think nothing beyond the divine essence and its properties, in the image of God, which rises higher. (1) We do not think it, therefore etc. Excellent! This is how we learn to reason today: I do not perceive it, therefore it is not. I recall the same method being ascribed to a certain Jew in Genebrard, who, about to attack the Trinity, argued thus: the mind is utterly unable to conceive its existence. By exactly the same argument. But Wolzogen, do you argue from the idea, certainly very imperfect, which you now form for yourself of the image of God, while the talk is about man in his integrity? And granting that it is so, that it did not rise beyond the essence and its properties, since, as we said above, God is triune in his essence, and this flows from his infinite perfection, who will deny that once the essence and its perfection are rightly known, the Trinity is known at the same time? Or do you think that this is not known even to the angels, unless, beyond the co-created knowledge which they enjoy, this mystery is also revealed to them? And if not to the angels, why do you imagine such a revelation necessary for man? You say the idea of God implanted in us represents God. Do you think such an idea could not have been implanted in Adam, one that would have represented the triune God to him? If it could have been implanted, why do you hesitate? What compels you to feign that imperfection, namely that now we do not think it so? Perhaps we are not now able to think it so. Those who defend this idea say that, after the Holy Trinity became known through revelation, we have the idea of the Trinity; and for them to deny the idea of the Trinity is the same as to believe it without any conception of it, and so to believe what you do not know. Why could that idea not have been implanted in Adam from the beginning, in the form which through revelation it at last takes in us? Adam's knowledge is the pattern of what we acquire through regeneration, the Apostle Col. 3 being the judge. You, although now you do not think it so. What follows is no more solid. From the points above he concludes thus against the Paradoxus: Since these things are so, namely that Adam could not know them without revelation, I conclude from this that we ought not to think these Scriptural truths are more known to us, who use reason alone, than they were to man placed in a perfect state. But where does this Exercitator say that those truths are known to us by nature and reason? He is not so foolish as to think that the birth of Christ, his Passion, the necessity of faith in Christ, etc., are known by reason, and no Socinian has ever raved so. For just as no one among men can know the plans which another turns over in his mind, as long as they are not revealed to him, so much less can one recognise the counsels of God as long as they lie hidden in his mind. They are revealed, etc.: so says the Socinian. We see that the mysteries of God cannot be understood by men unless they are revealed by God; but that revealed things can be understood, says Schlichtingius. For by no other way is it lawful for man to know God's secrets, says Crellius. So Wolzogen has proved this with great effort, though no one has denied it. But granting, as both the Socinians and the Paradoxus freely concede to Wolzogen, that these truths are not known by reason, what follows? He concludes, that there is therefore no interpretation which is to be sought from the truths alone. The Paradoxus does not mean that all interpretation flows and depends on innate truths, so that no truth is to be believed to lie in a passage unless it first arose in the mind from natural principles, or at least could be elicited from them, for we have already seen the contrary. He means rather that nothing is in Scripture except truths which reason, though it could not have discovered them while hidden, can nevertheless, once revealed, judge and examine as to whether they are possible or not. This is the genuine opinion of the Socinians. Wolzogen does not overturn it; he only concludes what the Socinians concede, namely that many truths cannot be thought out before revelation, nor judged by reason in that way. But we shall look at these things more fully later. Therefore what he says at p. 177 does not touch the point: if judgment is to be made from the truths, then it makes no difference whether God had given us the law in writing, or had only engraved it on our hearts by nature. For the Paradoxus would reply that reason does not even dream of many things not yet revealed, whereas after revelation they can very well be judged and discerned by reason. And so, although revelation adds much to reason, reason remains the norm for judging even revealed things.

units.la: Pagina 180. dicit, omnes veritates aeternas nulli-que mutationi obnoxias esse. Haec thesis ulteriorem penitioremque requirit disquisitionem, Vel enim hoc vult verum esse in sensu, ut vocant, composito, con-sequenter ad decretum Dei, vel divisio, hoc est antecedenter ad idem Dei decretum. Si sensu priore, bene habet, statuimus enim ut res omnes sic & veritates ab aeterno ordinatas esse, ac omnia esse & fieri juxta immobilem illam aeternamque legem. Hoc sensu legem aeternam accepit Thomas 1, 2. Q. 93. a. 1. cum ait, eam nihil esse aliud, quam rationem divinae sapientiae, secundum quam dirigit omnium creaturarum motus & actiones, sic revera omne quod jam existit, quod verum est &c. veritatis erat aeternae & immutabilis. Considerari autem ea potest, vel in genere respectu omnium, vel cum peculiari relatione ad homines, & cognoscitur aliquatenus per impressionem, mediante lege naturæ: Hæc enim partialis est expressio legis æterna. quicquid enim requirit νόμῳ ἐμφύτῳ [?] lex naturæ insita, illud quoque sancivit νόμῳ ἀιωνίῳ [?] lex æterna. Nimirum tam naturalis quam libera. Si autem sensu posteriore putet omne id verum esse antecedenter ad Dei decretum, jam falsum est illud effa-tum 1. in rerum eventibus nexibusque; potuissent aliter enim omnia per decretum ordinata esse: 2. in axiomatis: quorum quædam, de rerum natura & essentia, quædam de moralibus, nobis insita, aut saltem ex insito principio elici posse, comperimus: hæc quod attinet, nullus dubito, quin inter illa quæ-dam compareant, quæ cum à jure Dei positivo & libero pendeant, æternæ veritatis & immutabilis dici[?] non possunt. In ea enim versor sententia, talia dari, quæ pro suo beneplacito Deus nobis ut injunxit, sic & indere potuit, quare & minime confundendas pu-tem, leges Deo naturales, cum iis, quæ nobis tales , sicuti enim liberum Deo fuit nos tales fingere quales vellet, sic & pro suo placito universam hominum multitudinem obligantia præcepta libere dare, imo & hominibus indere potuisse clarissimum videtur. Quod si probe notaretur, viderent procul dubio Antisab-bathici, se in cassum laborare, dum Sabbathum Deo naturale non esse, hoc est, præceptum illud ex ipsa essentiæ divinæ sanctitate, necessario non fluere, à nobis largiter concedi cum vident, se nullo negotio idem morale non esse, imo ne quidem esse posse, ilico probatum dedisse gloriantur. Hoc debebat evin-ci, nullum præceptum, Deo positivum, nobis mo-rale & insitum esse posse. En Rhodus! en saltus! id probent disputatores, huc enim ultimo recidit tota illa controversia, quod si nondum viderint, ignorantiæ, si autem viderint, quoniam id semper ponunt, nunquam probant, malitiæ reos esse, merito quis illos dixerit. Ultimus ille Burmanni hyperaspistes hoc agat, hoc examinet, habebit quo pugnos prurientes exerceat, cramben recortam apponere, eamque calumniarum, sycophantiarum, mendaciorum, detorsionumque fœtido embammate delibutam, artis non est sed impudentis & malevoli animi signum infallibile.
units.tr: Page 180 says that all eternal truths are subject to no change whatever. This thesis requires a further and deeper inquiry. For he either means this to be true in the so-called compound sense, that is, consequent upon God's decree, or in the divided sense, that is, antecedent to that same decree of God. If in the former sense, it is well: we hold that all things, and truths too, were ordained from eternity, and that everything is and comes to pass according to that immovable and eternal law. In this sense Thomas took the eternal law (1, 2, Q. 93, a. 1), when he said that it is nothing other than the reason of divine wisdom, by which it directs the motions and actions of all creatures; thus in truth everything that now exists, and everything that is true, belongs to the eternal and immutable truth. Now this law may be considered either in general with respect to all things, or with a particular relation to men, and it is known to some extent through the impression of the law of nature, for this is a partial expression of the eternal law. Whatever the innate law of nature [νόμῳ ἐμφύτῳ] requires, the eternal law [νόμῳ ἀιωνίῳ] has also ordained: the law which is at once natural and free. But if he thinks in the latter sense that everything is true antecedent to God's decree, then that saying is false: (1) in the events and connections of things, for all things could have been ordained otherwise by decree; (2) in axioms. We find that some of these, concerning the nature and essence of things, and some concerning moral matters, are implanted in us, or at least can be elicited from an implanted principle. As for these, I do not doubt that among them there appear some which, since they depend on the positive and free law of God, cannot be called eternal and immutable truth. For I hold the view that there are such things which God, by his own good pleasure, has enjoined on us as he pleased, and which he could equally have implanted.
