Hence I think that God's natural laws must by no means be confused with those which he has made to be such for us. For just as it was free for God to make us such as he wished, so also it seems most clear that by his own pleasure he could freely give precepts binding the whole multitude of men, and even implant them in men. If this were properly noted, the Antisabbatarians would undoubtedly see that they labour in vain. While they see that we largely concede that the Sabbath is not natural to God, that is, that this precept does not flow necessarily from the holiness of the divine essence, they boast that they have at once proved that it is not moral, nor even can be so, with no trouble at all. This they ought to have demonstrated: that no precept positive to God can be moral and implanted in us. Here is Rhodes, here is the leap! Let the disputants prove it; for the whole controversy comes down to this point. If they have not yet seen it, that is ignorance; if they have seen it, since they always assume it and never prove it, they are guilty of malice, and one may rightly call them so. Let Burman's last defender, the Hyperaspistes, take this in hand, examine this, and he will have something to exercise his itching fists on: to serve up a cabbage reheated, and smear it with the stinking ointment of calumnies, sycophancies, lies and distortions. This is not a sign of skill, but an infallible sign of an impudent and malicious mind.

units.la: Tritum merito axioma vocat, Philosophorum illud, frustra fieri per plura, quod potest fieri per pauciora, sed sano sensu usurpandum monet Wolzogius, & exemplo adducto illustrat, creationem refert, cui revera totos sex dies impendit sapientissimus & potentissimus artifex. hic autem an hoc axioma usu veniat disquisiturus, miram exercet crisin. creationis vox, inquit, ab ambiguitate liberanda venit. Si enim simplicem productionem rerum illam significare velimus, dubium non est, quin compendio potuerit agere Deus. Sed si per creationem intelligimus illam productionem rerum, in qua non tantum potentiam sed & sapientiam suam voluit elucere Deus, quæ nobis esset ordinis exemplum, quæ laboris & quietis similitudinem contineret &c. jam nego paucioribus potuisse creationem fieri. Inanis illa crisis videtur, quam hic exercet noster; quousque se extendat & in quibus valeat dicti axiomatis veritas, docere aggreditur, semper illud obtinere negat, probatque negationem illam argumento ab opere creationis desumto, hactenus bene: sed quid hoc sibi vult creationis vocem ita distinguere ut aliquando significet simplicem productionem rerum, aliquando illam quæ non tantum potentiam &c. quasi creatio unquam per se aliud quid, quam simplicem rerum denotet, ex nihilo, aut inhabili materia, productionem? quasi etiam concessa altera illa significatione, ultro disputari adhuc possit, an compendiosiore via agere potuerit Deus? talia enim in illa vocis notione includit Wolzogius ut simul non probet, sed ponat, quod quæritur. Quod autem rem ipsam concernit, in foveam ipse incidit, dum ita audacter pronunciat, ac si Deus, aliter si cuncta fecisset, quam fecit, sapientia ejus non eluxisset, ordinis exemplum, laboris & quietis similitudinem non reliquisset. An tu novisti quomodo Deus agere debuerit, ut quam maxime sapientiam, vel alias, demonstraret perfectiones suas? an tu tibi tanta præsumis, ut de infinito & infiniti Entis fine determinare quicquam, absque ejus revelatione, audeas? Non bene hic Cartesii memorem fuisse te, sat scio. Postquam Deo placuit sic agere, fateor, jam sic sapientissime omnia facta undecunque apparent, sed an non & idem accidisset, si Deo aliter agere visum fuisset? Quid si centum, quid si duos, tres, quatuor dies illi operi dedisset, an minus sapientia luceret? vel deesset ordinis exemplum? Quid si uno die omnia sic ordinate produxisset? nonne stupenda patuisset potentia, sapientia eluxisset? Quis es ô homo qui Deo ponas & figas terminum modumque? Uti Cartesius alibi concedit, fieri posse, ut alii, diversis plane hypothesibus, æque feliciter naturæ Phænomena explicent, quam à se putat explicata, sic & nullus dubito, quin alio plane & ab isto longè diverso, ordine, Deus potuerit rerum produxisse mirabilem istam universita-tem, sapientia interim sua, juxta cum aliis perfectionibus, non minus, quam nunc elucescente; Nisi velit ex mundi Deique consideratione colligi posse, non simul non uno die, sed successive, sed diversis diebus Creationem perfectam fuisse. Quod revera ex ipsius discursu colligere datur, ratio etenim docet, Deum procul omni dubio, omnia tali ordine fecisse quali maxime eluceret sapientia &c. Hæc autem Judice Wolzogio non ita eluceret nisi successu temporis & variis diebus peracta fuisset rerum productio. Placet mihi quod alibi {*}Amyraldus, de Adamo & quidem inte-
units.tr: They rightly call it a commonplace axiom, that saying of the philosophers, that what can be done by fewer means is done in vain by more. Wolzogius advises that it be used in a sound sense, and he illustrates it with an example: creation, to which the most wise and powerful Artificer devoted, in truth, the whole six days. He then takes up the question whether this axiom applies here, and he makes a strange fuss over it. The word "creation," he says, needs to be freed from ambiguity. If we want it to mean the simple production of things, there is no doubt that God could have accomplished it in a shorter time. But if by creation we understand that production of things in which God wished to display not only his power but also his wisdom, which would be a pattern of order for us and would contain a likeness of labour and rest, and so on, then I deny that creation could have been done in fewer days. This inquiry of our author seems empty. He sets out to teach how far the axiom extends and where its truth holds. He denies that it always holds, and he proves the denial by an argument drawn from the work of creation. So far so good. But what does he mean by distinguishing the word creation in such a way that it sometimes means the simple production of things and sometimes that which displays not only power and so on? As if creation ever meant anything other than the simple production of things, out of nothing or out of unsuitable matter! As if, even granting that other meaning, it could still be debated whether God could have acted by a shorter route! Wolzogius packs so much into the notion of that word that he does not prove what is in question, he simply assumes it. As for the matter itself, he falls into a pit when he so boldly declares that if God had made all things otherwise than he did, his wisdom would not have shone forth, and he would not have left a pattern of order or a likeness of labour and rest. Do you know how God ought to have acted, so as to demonstrate most fully his wisdom or his other perfections? Do you presume so much that you dare to determine anything about the infinite and the end of the infinite Being without his revelation? I am quite sure you were not well remembering Descartes here. Once it pleased God to act thus, I admit that all things made in this way appear most wisely made from every side. But would the same not have happened if God had preferred to act otherwise? What if he had given that work a hundred days, or two, three, four? Would his wisdom shine less, or would the pattern of order be lacking? What if he had produced all things so orderly in a single day? Would not his power have appeared wonderful, and his wisdom have shone forth? Who are you, O man, who sets limits and boundaries for God? As Descartes elsewhere concedes, it may be that others, on quite different hypotheses, explain the phenomena of nature as happily as he thinks he has explained them, so I too doubt not that God could have produced this marvellous universe in a quite different order, far removed from this one, while his wisdom, together with his other perfections, shone no less than it does now. Unless Wolzogius wants it to follow from the consideration of the world and of God that creation could not have been perfect if it had been done not all at once, not in one day, but successively, over different days. And indeed this is what one can gather from his own reasoning. For reason teaches that God, beyond all doubt, made all things in such an order that his wisdom would shine most brightly, and so on. Yet in Wolzogius's judgement, his wisdom would not have shone so brightly unless the production of things had been carried out over time and across various days. I like what Amyraldus says elsewhere, about Adam and indeed about integrity.

units.la: {*} Amyraldus, de Adamo & quidem integro, Opera Dei perfecta fuisse ex diebus ipsis, ex eorum contemplatione colligere homo nequivit. Adeo enim nulla sunt argumenta distributionis partium creationis in sex dies, ex quibus id certo cognosci possit, ut postquam Moses illius tam exerte meminit, Augustinus tamen, & nonnulli alii, mundum uno die, unoque temporis veluti momento, creatum fuisse crediderint. Quamobrem si quid ea de re primus homo cognovit quod ex contemplatione operum divinorum desumtum dici queat, id ex eo habuit duntaxat, quod Deus dicitur quievisse septimo die eumque diem sanctificasse. Quietem enim illam & septimi diei sanctificationem, Adamo incognitam fuisse, verisimile non est. Utique observationis Sabbathi usque a primordio rerum, vestigia sunt non obscura neque leviter impressa &c. Quid, annon millena in rerum natura occurrunt; quæ breviori via, minorique mediorum apparatu perfici potuissent, salva tamen, omnimoda, divinæ perfectionis declaratione ac manifestatione? Nos ista regula, in iis, quæ nobis peragenda incumbunt, regat dirigat-que, absit ut Deo ullam legem unquam præfigamus, ut sapientissimum potentissimumque illud numen, mentis nostræ cancellis includamus. Superiori exem-plo, sententiam suam explicaturus, alterum subjun-git; creationi, redemtionis opus, & in eo etiam, non putat obtinere illud axioma, de quo disputat, videtur enim fieri ipsius judicio potuisse, ut, absque tanto molimine gens Christiana conderetur: potuisset statim mortem obire Christus, ut statim plene servaretur omne nomen Christianum. Bene agit quod & in eo, illi regulæ, Deum subducat, male autem, quod re-demtionis longe aliam, quam creationis, rationem esse, non probe adverterit; etiam in eo, quod, sicuti creatio, uno momento, perfici potuit, ex rei ipsius constitutione, sic redemtio moram per se re-quirat; nisi obedientiam vitæ, quam activam vocant Theologi, abesse & uno momento nasci morique, sufficere potuisse velit. Ego tam audax non ero, ut quicquam, temere me divinis, abditisque Dei penetralibus, ingerens, proferam. Sit in voluntatem Dei nobis ultima in hisce, & sufficiens, analysis. Occulta reseras imprudenter, quando absque ulla revelatione ex cerebro tuo tanta definis, cum dicis, potuisse sim-plicius nobis tradi Christum. Id nos fatemur, sed tum non tam perfecte nobis traditus fuisset. Unde hoc habes Wolzogi, nisi sic per gradus, nisi tali ordine revelasset Christum Deus, cum non ita perfecte nobis revelandum fuisse aut tradendum? An tu scis, aeque perfectam Christi cognitionem, alio modo acquiri, nobis per absolutam Dei potentiam impossibile esse? ubi tua modestia Wolzogi? ubi ingenium, aut eruditio Theologo digna? qua solius sunt arbitrii divini, nil certi possunt in re habere, inquis alibi. Cujus dicti jam plane oblitus videris.
units.tr: {*} Amyraldus, on Adam and indeed on Adam in his integrity: man could not have gathered from the days themselves, or from contemplating them, that the works of God were perfect. For there are so few arguments for dividing the parts of creation into six days, by which this could be known with certainty, that although Moses mentions it so clearly, Augustine and several others nevertheless believed that the world was created in one day, and in a single moment of time, as it were. Therefore, if the first man knew anything about this from the contemplation of the divine works, which could be stated, he had it only from the fact that God is said to have rested on the seventh day and to have sanctified that day. For it is not likely that Adam was ignorant of that rest and of the sanctification of the seventh day. Indeed, traces of the observance of the Sabbath are visible from the very beginning of things, and not faintly impressed. What? Do not countless things in nature occur which could have been accomplished by a shorter route and with less apparatus of means, while still preserving the full declaration and manifestation of the divine perfection? Let this rule guide and direct us in those things which we are bound to carry out. Far be it from us to prescribe any law to God, or to enclose that most wise and most powerful deity within the limits of our mind. Having explained his view by the earlier example, he adds another: he thinks that the axiom under discussion does not hold for the work of redemption, and in that, as for creation, it seems that in his judgement Christ might have died at once, so that a Christian nation might have been founded without such great effort, Christ could have died at once, so that the whole Christian name would immediately be fully preserved. He does well in withdrawing God from that rule here as well, but he does badly in not properly noticing that the reason for redemption is quite different from that for creation. Just as creation could have been completed in a single moment from the very constitution of the thing, so redemption by its nature requires time, unless he wants to hold that the obedience of his life, which theologians call active, could be absent and that being born and dying in a single moment would have been enough. I will not be so bold as to rashly thrust forward anything of my own into the hidden sanctuaries of God. Let the ultimate and sufficient analysis of God's will be left to us in these matters. You unwisely unlock secrets when, without any revelation, you lay down from your own brain such great things, when you say, Christ could have been handed down to us more simply. We admit that, but then he would not have been handed down to us so perfectly. Where do you get this, Wolzogius, unless God revealed Christ step by step, in such an order, because he was not to be revealed or delivered to us so perfectly otherwise? Do you know that it is impossible, by God's absolute power, for us to acquire an equally perfect knowledge of Christ by another way? Where is your modesty, Wolzogius? Where is the mind or the learning worthy of a theologian? Things which depend solely on the divine will can have nothing certain in them, you say elsewhere. You seem to have quite forgotten that saying.

units.la: Theologi nullo discrimine vapulant sic judicis instar, pro authoritate, Quanquam hic quoque nimio plus sibi permiserint saepe Theologi, non una vice, sed saepius reos hic vides bonos Theologos. Nollem ita contemtim omnes simul exagitatos a te Theologos, Pastores Ecclesiae, Wolzogi, Theologiae nec Doctor, nec Professor; censoria autem potestate te, in illos simul omnes, non armarunt, tui Domini, personam licet tibi imposuerint non contemnendam. Nominasses reos, ne injuste omnes uno ferirentur ictu. Sed crimen Theologorum audiamus, quid tandem illud sit, in quo nimium sibi permiserint, hi cum non satis magnifice de Dei verbo se existimare posse crediderint, quid in eo vitii est, cum verbum Dei sit? at saepe mysteria finxerunt, ubi nulla voluit esse Spiritus Sanctus, tandemque nusquam facile consistente religione, singulis fere punctis aliquod subesse horrendum arcanum sibi sibi persuaserunt. Judæis scio, tantum, non in proverbium abiisse, Rabbini illud, nullum in lege Iota esse, à quo non pendeant montes doctrinarum, Papistas, & inter eos, Mystica, ut vocant, Theologia sectatores, plus quam par est, in sensibus anagogicis, tropologicis, allegoricis, excogitandis sibi indulgent, prementes in eo, sed male aliquot Patrum, maxime Origenis, vestigia. Reformati morem istum detestati, nimium reverentiæ, Scripturæ sacræ ex-hiberi, quamvis nunquam sint conquesti; sensum literalem sectati sunt, mysteria locis, non ficta inge-rentes, vel aliunde arcessentes, sed ex locis sedula cura venantes quærentes & quidem in sedibus singula quantum possunt propriis. Quosnam ergo ita nota-sti? Judæos credo, aut Pontificios, at illos non ita absolute Theologos dixerit accuratus scriptor & di-lucidus. Reformatos autem, posito quod aliqui sub-inde, hunc aut illum locum, non satis magnas ob ra-tiones, allegoricum putaverint, ita tamen spretos abjecteque habitos indiscriminatim quis ferat? Scili-cet ut placeant nova, priora omnia oportet sordeant. Quicquid Cartesiani syderis influxum non redolet, fœtet. Dogmaticos cum Elenchticis, antea non satis dilucidos, vel in maximi momenti negotio, vidi-mus; nunc explanationum, commentariorum, quos dicimus, scriptores, nimium sæpe sibi permisisse di-cit, pronunciat Wolzogius, omni, qua honor Or-thodoxis constet illibatus, omissa limitatione. Ast & sui obliviscitur, etenim paulo ante, magnifice de mi-nimis, quæ in scriptura exstant, prædicat; facere de-bet summa Dei sapientia, inquit, ut credamus non sine mente vel minimos apices esse exaratos. Qui lusum schacchicum scripturæ similem docuit Wolzogium, ea de re sic habet, * Baco Verulamius: Sic interpretan-da Scriptura, ut intelligamus, complecti eas, non solum totaliter aut collective, sed distributive, etiam in clau-sulis sulis[?] & vocabulis singulis, innumeros doctrina rivulos & venas ad Ecclesiæ singulas partes, & animas fide-lium irrigendas. Hæc concoquet Wolzogius, non est Theologus qui loquitur. Et revera quod peculiari Divinæ providentiæ cura servatur, quidni, simili cum attentione hominis pensitetur minimum in sacris Jota? Sed opinionum portenta, ex eo orta dicit Wolzogius. Ea detestamur, simul autem Ortho-doxos Theologos exemtos volumus crimine, & li-beros.
units.tr: Theologians are beaten without any distinction, as if by a judge, on his authority: Although here too theologians have often allowed themselves too much. Not once but often you see good theologians accused here. I would not have wished you, Wolzogius, who are neither a doctor nor a professor of theology but a minister of the Church, to castigate so contemptuously all the theologians together. Your masters have not armed you with censorial power over all of them at once, though they have given you a persona not to be despised. You should have named the guilty, so that not all were struck with one blow unjustly. But let us hear the crime of the theologians, and what it finally is in which they have allowed themselves too much: when they believed that they could not esteem the word of God highly enough. What fault is there in that, since it is the word of God? But they have often invented mysteries where the Holy Spirit wished there to be none, and, since religion can hardly stand firm anywhere, they have persuaded themselves that almost every point conceals some dreadful secret. I know that among the Jews the saying of the rabbis, that there is no iota in the law from which mountains of doctrines do not hang, has passed into a proverb. The Papists, and among them those who follow what they call mystical theology, indulge themselves more than is fitting in devising anagogical, tropological and allegorical senses, pressing in this the footsteps, though badly, of some of the Fathers, above all Origen. The Reformed, detesting that custom, have shown the holy Scripture far too much reverence, although they never complained of it. They pursued the literal sense, and they brought out mysteries from the passages, not invented or dragged in from elsewhere, but sought out from the passages with careful attention, and indeed from the words in their own places as far as they can. Whom, then, have you noticed in this way? The Jews, I suppose, or the Papists. But an accurate and lucid writer would not call those men theologians in such an unqualified way. As for the Reformed, granted that some of them now and then thought this or that passage allegorical for reasons that were not very strong, can anyone bear that they are all thus despised and set aside indiscriminately? Clearly, so that new things may please, all the earlier things must be made to look shabby. Whatever does not smell of the influence of the Cartesian star stinks. We have seen that the dogmatic writers, and the elenctic writers, were not sufficiently clear before, even in a matter of the greatest importance. Now Wolzogius says that the writers of explanations and commentaries, as we call them, have allowed themselves too much, and he says so without any limitation, so that the honour of the Orthodox is left entirely unharmed. But he forgets himself, for a little earlier he praises magnificently the smallest things that are in Scripture: the highest wisdom of God ought to make us believe, he says, that even the smallest strokes were written not without purpose. Someone who taught Wolzogius that the game of chess resembles Scripture holds this view about the matter. Bacon of Verulam says: Scripture is to be interpreted so that we understand that it embraces these things not only totally or collectively, but distributively, even in the clauses and single words, and irrigates the individual parts of the Church and the souls of the faithful with countless streams and veins of doctrine. Wolzogius will digest this, but it is not a theologian who speaks. And indeed, if what is preserved by the special care of divine providence is weighed with similar attention by man, why not even the smallest iota in holy things? But he says these are monstrous opinions arising from this. We detest such opinions, but at the same time we want the Orthodox theologians to be freed of the charge and to be free.

units.la: Pagina 192. Certitudinem requirit ab interprete, ut ipsa quoque fides quæ pendet ab interpretatione, sit perinde certa. Optime. Sed hanc certitudinem negat convenire novo interpreti: itidem in se bona hæc thesis est, audiamus probationem: Exercitator enim à clara distinctaque perceptione quæ solius sit veritatis, omnem derivat persuasionem; sit ita, at hic te tuimet ipsius deprehendo adversarium, idem ipse doces, idem Velthuisius: videris sane ita meditationum tuarum gurgite submersus fuisse, ut subinde in extasin collapsum te præcedentium & sequentium ceperit oblivio. Hic totam Paradoxi molem, eo disjicis ictu, quoniam claram distinctamque perceptionem, quæ solius veritatis sit, requirit ad persuasionem producendam: pagina autem 201. idem serio contendis, loqueris de Theologica & Philosophica rationis & revelationis persuasione & dicis, si sit vere persuasio, à veritatis orta cognitione fuerit, veritas autem omnis sibi semper constat, ergo & persuasio. Agnosce thesin tuam Wolzogi, revera tua est, inde concludis tu adversarii tui incertitudinem, sed ego te lubricum esse, omnique interpretationis certitudine destitutum, eadem ratione conficio. Certitudinem non habet Paradoxi Interpres, sic tu, pag. 192. quia à clara distinctaque perceptione quæ solius sit veritatis omnem derivat per-suasuasionem. Certitudinem non habet Wolzogii Interpres, sic ego, nam ipso judice, si sit vere persuasio, à veritatis orta cognitione fuerit. Aliis argumentis eges, aliis pugnant & vincunt Reformati. Vereor autem ne concedas consequens, nimirum nullam tibi certitudinem esse, saltem in iis quæ præter paucissima illa fundamentalia in sacris extant, hoc aperte profiteris pag. 251. Nam in cateris, sic scribis, de fundamentalibus iisque paucissimis dixeras, non agnosco ullum infallibilem interpretem. Candide profecto & generose sed sceptixῶς. Iterum te in contradictione deprehendo, non agnoscis præterquam in fundamentalibus ullum infallibilem interpretem, hoc est interpretationis normam, de ea enim loqueris, rogo autem an ea, quæ præter fundamentalia, ex sacris te didicisse & docere constat, fide recipias, iisque credas nec ne? rationis non sunt, ergo proprie non sunt scientiæ objectum, doces autem ea quæ dicimus, ergo non solum ea autumas, aut pro opinionibus habes; restat itaque, ut credas, imo credis; jam pergo, fides debet niti certissimo & infallibili fundamento, sic ipse Paradoxum oppugnas pag. 192. at p. 251. Præterquam in fundamentalibus nullum agnoscis infallibilem interpretem, absque interprete nihil ex sacris ex tua sententia constat, ergo præter fundamentalia eaque paucissima nihil credis. Habes quod expedias Wolzogi, en te Scepticismi, præterquam in perpaucis, tuis convictum verbis. Eas jam & Theologos omnes increpa, Dilucidus es, illi non satis hactenus tales.
units.tr: Page 192. He requires of the interpreter that the faith itself, which depends on interpretation, be equally certain. Excellent. But he denies that this certainty belongs to the new interpreter. Again, this thesis is good in itself. Let us hear the proof: for the examiner derives all persuasion from a clear and distinct perception, which belongs only to truth. Granted, but here I catch you as your own adversary. You yourself teach this very thing, and so does Velthuisius. You must indeed have been so submerged in the whirlpool of your meditations that forgetfulness of what precedes and follows has seized you, as if you had fallen into an ecstasy. Here you overthrow the whole mass of the Paradox with a single blow, since it requires a clear and distinct perception, which belongs only to truth, to produce persuasion. Yet on page 201 you seriously maintain the same thing. You speak of the persuasion of reason and of revelation, both theological and philosophical, and you say: if it is truly persuasion, it must have arisen from a cognition of truth; but all truth is always consistent with itself, therefore persuasion is too. Recognise your own thesis, Wolzogius; it really is yours. From it you conclude the uncertainty of your adversary, but I, by the same reasoning, show that you are unstable and destitute of all certainty of interpretation. The interpreter of the Paradox has no certainty, so you say on page 192, because he derives all persuasion from a clear and distinct perception, which belongs only to truth. The interpreter of Wolzogius has no certainty, so I say, for by his own judgement if it is truly persuasion, it must have arisen from a cognition of truth. You need other arguments; the Reformed fight and conquer with other arguments. I fear, however, that you will concede the consequence, namely that you have no certainty at all, at least regarding those matters in Scripture that lie outside the few fundamental articles. You openly profess this on page 251. For in other matters, so you write, speaking of the fundamental and very few matters, I do not acknowledge any infallible interpreter. Frankly and generously indeed, but sceptically [σκεπτικῶς]. Again I find you in contradiction. You acknowledge no infallible interpreter except in fundamentals, that is, no norm of interpretation (for it is of this that you speak). But I ask whether you accept by faith those things which, beyond the fundamentals, you are known to have learned from Scripture and to teach, and whether you believe them or not. They are not matters of reason, and so are not properly the object of science; yet you teach what we say, so you do not merely hold them as opinions. It remains, then, that you believe them; indeed you do believe. Now I proceed: faith must rest on a most certain and infallible foundation, as you yourself assail the Paradox on page 192. But on page 251 you acknowledge no infallible interpreter apart from the fundamentals; without an interpreter, by your own view, nothing from Scripture is established. Therefore, beyond the fundamentals, and those very few, you believe nothing. You have a way out for Wolzogius: behold, you are convicted by your own words of Scepticism, except in a very few matters. Now denounce them all, the theologians too! You are clear; they, so far, are not so clear.

units.la: Philosophiam non minus accurate tradit, quam Theologiam nostèr disputator. Regno illam suo spoliat & de Principatu suo dejicit, ut huic suus maneat honor & eminentia, vis autem scire quo argumento id præstiterit? sensibus detraxit divinas veritates & sic rem probe egit. Haec sunt ipsius verba. Quare totum illud de Philosophia possemus omittere, quia regno eam suo spoliavimus, at qua ratione? quo modo? cum veritates illas sensibus detraximus. En soliditatem, en subtilitatem Wolzogianam{1} sensibus detractæ sunt illæ veritates, ergo injusto dejecta principatu est Philosophia, non id expectaveram, ab homine, Cartesii placitis addicto, qui à sensibus non solum, sed & ipsa imaginatione sese abstrahens, pura mente, intellectu puro, meditari & Philosophari, jam dudum didicisse debuerat. Gassendus corpus dicebatur Cartesio, tu autem quam corporeus, quam crassus ipsi dicereris, si te audiret, ea quæ à sensibus remota sunt, vel iis subducta, aut detracta, Philosophiæ itidem subducta detractaque pronunciare? An talem Philosophiam te docuit Cartesius, aut Aristoteles, an vero tua, si non ignorantia, saltem socordia &, sit venia verbo, inadvertentia? Age, tu Philosophiam ultra sensus & sensualia nondum didicisse te profiteris sicque sensibus detracta veritas, Philosophia tua detracta erit necessario. Verum subtilem illam & divinam Philosophiam quis non mirabitur? Sed probare debueras, ignorat negatque Paradoxus: imo omnes, qui Philosophiæ naturam vel mediocriter noverunt, contrarium statuunt. Credo equidem aliud agenti hoc excidisse. Porro, an ita Philosophiæ principatum de ponte dejecerit, prout Theologum Reformatum decet, ad calcem hujus scripti videbimus. Hic Orthodoxus videri vult & propterea tam longè valere jubet Philosophiam: at præterquam, quod imprudenter & non absque insigni prodita ignorantia id præstet, non serio agere posthac convincendus est, nisi protestatio valeat, quæ actui contraria est.
units.tr: Our disputant hands down philosophy no less carelessly than theology. He strips it of its kingdom and casts it from its principate, so that theology may keep its own honour and eminence. But do you want to know by what argument he accomplished this? He took the divine truths away from the senses, and in this way he handled the matter well. These are his own words: Wherefore we could omit that whole discussion about philosophy, because we have despoiled it of its kingdom; but on what ground? In what way? Since we have taken those truths away from the senses. Behold the solidity, behold the subtlety of Wolzogius! The truths have been taken away from the senses, therefore philosophy has been cast down from its principate unjustly. I did not expect this from a man devoted to the opinions of Descartes, who, withdrawing himself not only from the senses but even from the imagination, should long since have learned to meditate and philosophise with a pure mind and pure intellect. Gassendi was called the body of Descartes, but how corporeal and crude you would seem to him if he heard you pronounce that what is remote from the senses, or withdrawn and taken away from them, is likewise withdrawn and taken away from philosophy! Did Descartes or Aristotle teach you such a philosophy, or is it rather your own, the product, if not of ignorance, at least of sloth and, to use the word with pardon, of inadvertence? Come now, you profess that you have not yet learned philosophy beyond the senses and sensible things, and so truth taken away from the senses means your philosophy is necessarily taken away. But who will not marvel at that subtle and divine philosophy? Yet you ought to have proved it, and the Paradox denies it. Indeed all who have known even moderately the nature of philosophy maintain the opposite. I believe, to be sure, that this slipped out of you while you were doing something else. Further, whether he has cast down the principate of philosophy from its bridge in the manner befitting a Reformed theologian, we shall see at the end of this writing. Here he wishes to appear orthodox, and therefore bids philosophy such a long farewell. But apart from the fact that he does this imprudently and not without a notable display of ignorance, he is not to be convinced that he is acting seriously hereafter, unless a protestation may stand which is contrary to the deed.

units.la: Pagina 195. Historiam Philosophicam in transfi-tu, ab ipso lectam, videmus. Academicorum & Scepticorum sensa sic refert, illos dixisse probabili tantum argumentatione in utramque partem de omnibus disputari; hos, ulterius progressos, omnia esse inania arguisse quæ de rerum scientia traduntur. Noverat Wolzogius Cartesium passim Scepticismi ab Anti-cartesianis accusari, & animus erat sequente pagina, in cælum evehere Cartesii Philosophiam. Cavet itaque prudenter, ne, ut Cartesianismi, sic & Scepticismi habeatur reus. Hunc in finem nobis describit Scepticos & quidem sic describit, ut quam maxime Cartesianismus, differre à Scepticismo, appareat. Scepticos quod attinet, ex Cartesio hoc habet Wolzogius quod narrat, qui fingit eo dementiæ venisse Scepticos, ut vel sensibus etiam in vitæ actionibus regendis non crediderint. Contrarium autem sustinet ut in ipsa Philosophia, sic præsertim in Historia Philosophorum versatissimus Clarissimus Gassendus. Video & Vogelsangium virum Doctissimum, hanc causam tractasse in suis adversus Paradoxum disputationibus, earumque contra Johan. De Bruin Vindiciis. Fuse autem quæ huc pertinent deducit Schook singulari de Scepticismo tractatu. Quare huic labori supersedeo.
units.tr: Page 195. We see that he has read the philosophical history in passing. He reports the views of the Academics and Sceptics in this way: that the former said that all things are disputed on both sides only by probable argument; the latter, going further, argued that everything handed down about the science of things is empty. Wolzogius knew that Descartes was everywhere accused of Scepticism by the Anti-Cartesians, and his intention on the following page was to exalt the philosophy of Descartes to heaven. So he takes prudent care not to be held guilty of Scepticism, as of Cartesianism. To this end he describes the Sceptics for us, and describes them in such a way that Cartesianism appears as far removed as possible from Scepticism. As far as the Sceptics are concerned, Wolzogius has this from Descartes, who pretends that the Sceptics came to such madness that they did not trust even the senses in regulating the actions of life. But the most learned and most distinguished Gassendi, most versed both in philosophy itself and especially in the history of the philosophers, maintains the contrary. I see also that Vogelsang, a most learned man, has treated this cause in his disputations against the Paradox, and in his Vindications against Johannes de Bruin. Schook, in his singular treatise on Scepticism, sets out at length what pertains to this. Therefore I forgo this labour.

units.la: Pagina 197. Post repetitum, Paradoxi verbis, Cartesii elogium, Philosophiam Cartesianam amplectitur non solum, sed & tam manifestæ, tam certæ veritatis esse, audacter asserit; ut, si vel solam nominasset Philosophiam, qua satis indicatur veram intelligi & naturæ congruentem, omnis curiosus indagator veritatis per quascunque ambages fuisset tamen sua sponte tandem ad Cartesianam revolutus. Audax pronunciatum & imprudens. Vere hæc Donatistarum genium redolent, quamquam in eo differentia sit, quod illi Theologiam respiciebant, dum hi de Philosophia loquuntur. Ponam {*}Danæi verba de Dona-tistis, tiftis, Se autem, suumque cœtum, & qui sibi consen-tirent solos esse veros [Episcopos] Philosophos. De reliquo terrarum orbe, [Dei Ecclesiam] veram Phi-losophiam periisse. Non referam Doctissimorum vi-rorum, de Cartesianis dogmatis, contraria judicia, jam dudum enim major Cartesianorum pars inter ab-dicata præjudicia, simul omnem Doctorum homi-num, qui ante Cartesium floruerunt, existimatio-nem, exuerunt. Et mirum non est, tantum enim temporis, meditationibus illis suis, insumere videri volunt, ut legendis aliorum scriptis nihil superfit. Quin & Cartesium imitantur, si literarum studia prorsus relinquant: capiantque consilium nullam in po-sterum quærendi scientiam, nisi vel quam in seipsis, vel in vasto mundi volumine poterunt reperire. Sic-que magis, ut existimat Cartesius, in veritatis co-gnitione promovebunt, quam si in libris evolvendis, vel literatorum sermonibus audiendis omne tempus con-sumpsissent. Ars autem cum ignorantes omnes ini-micos habeat, quid mirum, quæ non legantur, ea non placere, aliorum scripta? Hinc Aristotelem & omnes simul Peripateticos ne titivilitio emunt, na-ris tanto emunctioris, hodierni Philosophastri, per transsennam modo Cartesiana viderint Mysteria. Ar-tis est, omnia scripta, scriptores omnes, studiosorum manibus eripere, ut sola placeant, quæ unus scripsit Cartesius, aut pauci lucis filii. Cartesii sane reperta, inquit modo laudatus Vogelsangh, disciplinam Physicam & Ontologicam quod attinet, perpauca esse, probatu facillimum puto, si hoc jam ageretur. Tantum ferme aliorum inventa compilavit atque digessit, nonnullis addidit, quædam corrupit. Mihi autem, etsi ingeniose quædam à Cartesio inventa non negem, imo magna cum delectatione ejus scripta, præsertim principia, legerim & à D. Joh. de Bruyn privatim explicata audiverim, non tolerandum videtur detur, eousque ejus Philosophemata extolli, ut qui ferio & cum cura veritatem investigare velit, di-cendus sit tandem necessario, ad Cartesianam istam perventurus sapientiam. Sic per tot secula curiosos veritatis indagatores nullos, vel Philosophiam Car-tesianam, jam ante Cartesium, cognitam fuisse, ne-cesse est. Curiosus enim veritatis indagator, tan-dem ad eam revolvitur, quascunque licet per amba-ges; ambages, quae omnem, Philosophorum, omnis aetatis, multitudinem, hactenus absorbserunt, trans-versos egerunt. Nec fuit ante Cartesium, qui hunc ambagum Oceanum, curiosus ut fuerit, pernatare potuerit; Delio isto natatore egebat humanum ge-nus, cujus opera ex immenso gurgite, per gyros & vortices, tandem in lucem protraheretur nondum cognita veritas. In puteo fuit latuitque. O miram hominum mentem! sic solent, qui moderationem crepant, qui praejudicia abdicata volunt, aliis esse infensissimi, & maxima praejudiciorum copia labo-rare. Omnes Ecclesiae Patres, omnes Philosophi, Reformatae Ecclesiae Doctores omnes, tantum non merentur, hoc homine judice, ut indagatores veri-tatis curiosi, id est diligentes & seduli, dici debeant, Cartesianam enim Philosophiam, ad quam per quas-cunque tandem ambages fuissent sua sponte revoluti, non invenerunt. Hi saltem, quotquot hodie Carte-siana non amplectuntur, curiosi veritatis indagato-res non sunt. An nescis bone Vir, quid Cartesius de suis ipse statuat hypothesibus? Juxta eas feliciter qui-dem explicata esse naturae Phaenomena, fieri tamen posse, ut alio plane modo, aliis hypothesibus idem praestetur. Adeo ut necesse non sit, curiosum verita-tis indagatorem, sponte ad Cartesiana revolvi. Pos-set enim forsan excogitare hypotheses, a Cartesianis longe diversas, & juxta illas, rerum naturam, aeque explicare consequenter & perspicue: quod fieri posse non inficiatur Cartesius. Imo tantum, meo judicio, abest, ut novæ Cartesii methodo, quam palam hic profitetur Wolzogen, veritatem scrutanti sit insisten-dum, ut potius nihil magis vitandum putem, quam Cartesium in studiorum methodo sectari. Valde paucis Cartesio ipso teste, expediet eam imitari. Nam vel hoc unum, ut opiniones omnes quibus olim fuimus im-buti deponamus, non unicuique est tentandum. Sum-mam si vis, eorum, quæ adversus Cartesianam Phi-losophandi Methodum dici possunt: adi ea, quæ Cla-rissimus Daniel Voet, de Recentiorum quorundam Philosophandi Methodo, aliisque Disputationibus protulit: & statim rerum cognitionem, in majore, ab ipso, non solum non esse collocatam certitudine, sed & palam ad inextricabilem Scepticismum stratam viam, deprehendes. Non quod Cartesianos Scepti-cos esse judicem, & perpetuis dubitationibus inhæ-rentes: sed casu, non ex Philosophiæ Cartesianæ ge-nio, evenire, si quicquam habeant certi. Permulti homines, nihil plane in tota vita percipiunt satis recte, ad certum de eo judicium ferendum. Non tamen de omnibus dubitant, multa putant, infirmo quamvis fundamento nixi, se certo novisse. Sic & forsan cum Cartesianis se res habet. Regulam dictat Cartes istam, certum esse, nihil nos unquam falsum pro vero admis-suros, si tantum iis assensum præbeamus, quæ clare & distincte percipimus: lubricam autem & minus tutam eam esse jam antea demonstravimus. Nec melioris notæ esse deprehendo, quas alibi, ut fundamentales, veritatem scrutaturo sibi, præfixas fuisse docet. 1. Utnihil unquam veluti verum admitteret, nisi quod certo & evidenter verum esse cognosceret, hæc autem eadem cum superiore difficultate laborat: 2. Ut difficultates, quas esset examinaturus, in tot partes divideret, quot expediret ad illas commodius resolvendas. At dum non-dum rei cognitionem acquisivit, unde hoc ipsi constabit, in tot, non autem in plures, paucioresve partes istam difficultatem dividendam esse? Unde jam facta divisione, dividendum omne exhaustum? unde commodius non dividi posse, constabit? Næniæ profecto, nescio quid velint, quibus hæc oracula tantum non audiunt. Nihil revera dicitur. 3. Ut cognitiones omnes quas veritati quærenda impenderet certo semper ordine promoveret; incipiendo scilicet à rebus simplicissimis & cognitu facillimis, ut paulatim & quasi per gradus ad difficiliorum & magis compositarum cognitionem ascenderet, in aliquem etiam ordinem illas mente disponendo, quæ se mutuo ex natura sua non præcedunt. Bene omnia, sed Cartesianos ista quid juvant? jam enim omnibus abjectis, depositis, pro falsis habitis, unde noverint, cognoscendi dari ordinem. simpliciora dari & minus simplicia? porro unde noverint, inter simpliciora, & minus simplicia, discrimen? dic sodes, unde id hauriet, qui nihil novit, qui cuncta pro falsis habet? Viden' sic te ex dubitationis, in quem te abjecisti, gurgite, non emergere? non dari ubi figas pedem? Miror profecto hominum insaniam. 4. Postremo, ut tum in quærendis mediis, tum in difficultatum partibus percurrendis, tam perfectè singula enumeraret & ad omnia circumspiceret, ut nihil à se omitti esset certus. Sed quæso, quid ille de mediis, de quærendis mediis novit, quid de difficultatibus, de partibus quid, ille qui jam cuncta ex animo delevit suo? qui omnia pro falsis habet? adhucdum an Deus, an ipse sit, ignorans? talem enim requirit Methodus Cartesiana. Deinde semper hærebis animo an omnia enumeraveris, an nihil eorum quæ circumspicienda erant omiseris. Nam clarè quidem, & distinctè esse aliquid cognoscendum, ac nihil esse prætermittendum quo minus clare, & distinctè cognoscamus id, quod ut verum defendimus, id neque novum, neque dubium est, neque regula, quasi tibi propria, est tibi ipsi vindicanda:
units.tr: Page 197. After repeating the words of the Paradoxist, he not only embraces Cartesian philosophy but also boldly asserts that it is of so manifest and certain a truth that, if he had merely named philosophy, by which it is sufficiently indicated that the true and nature-conforming philosophy is meant, every curious seeker after truth would in any case have been brought back of his own accord to the Cartesian philosophy, however many detours he took. A bold and rash pronouncement. These words truly smell of the spirit of the Donatists, although there is this difference, that they spoke of theology while these men speak of philosophy. I will set down Danaeus's words about the Donatists: They alone, and those who agreed with them, are the true [bishops] philosophers. In the rest of the world, [the Church of God] true philosophy has perished. I will not record the contrary judgements of learned men about the Cartesian doctrines, for the greater part of the Cartesians have long since cast off their prejudices and, at the same time, have cast off all esteem for the teachers who flourished before Descartes. And this is no wonder, for they wish to appear to have spent so much time on those meditations of theirs that nothing is left over for reading the writings of others. Indeed they imitate Descartes if they abandon the study of letters altogether and resolve to seek no knowledge in the future except what they can find either in themselves or in the vast volume of the world. And so, as Descartes thinks, they will make more progress in the knowledge of truth than if they had spent all their time turning over books or listening to the talk of scholars. But since art has all the ignorant as its enemies, what wonder is it that they do not like the writings of others which they do not read? Hence they buy up Aristotle and all the Peripatetics together for a trifle, and the modern little philosophers, of a far keener nose, seem to see the mysteries of Descartes only through a chink. It is the trick of this art to snatch all writings and all writers out of the hands of students, so that only those things which Descartes alone, or a few sons of light, have written may please. That the discoveries of Descartes, says the Vogelsang just quoted, as far as the Physical and Ontological discipline is concerned, are very few, I think would be easily proved if that were now the task. He has mostly only collected and arranged the discoveries of others, added some of his own, and corrupted certain things. For my part, although I do not deny that Descartes made some ingenious discoveries, and although I have read his writings, especially the Principles, with great pleasure and have heard them explained privately by Mr. Johan de Bruyn, it does not seem tolerable that his philosophemes should be so extolled that whoever wishes to investigate truth seriously and carefully must necessarily be said at last to arrive at that Cartesian wisdom. Thus it is necessary that, through so many ages, there were no curious seekers of truth, or that Cartesian philosophy was known even before Descartes. For the curious seeker of truth is at last brought back to it, by whatever detours; detours which have hitherto swallowed up and driven off course the whole multitude of philosophers of every age. Nor was there anyone before Descartes who, however curious he was, could swim across this ocean of detours; the human race needed that Delian diver, by whose labour the truth, not yet known, would be drawn up into the light from the immense whirlpool, through eddies and vortices. It lay hidden in a well. O marvellous mind of man! So it is that those who cry up moderation, who want prejudices cast off, are most hostile to others and labour under a very great store of prejudices. All the Fathers of the Church, all the philosophers, all the teachers of the Reformed Church, in this man's judgement, scarcely deserve to be called curious, that is diligent and earnest, seekers of truth, since they did not find the Cartesian philosophy, to which they would have been brought back of their own accord by whatever detours. At least those who today do not embrace the Cartesian doctrines are not curious seekers of truth. Do you not know, good sir, what Descartes himself says about his own hypotheses? That by them the phenomena of nature are indeed explained happily, but that it may happen that the same thing is achieved in a quite different way, by other hypotheses. So that it is not necessary for a curious seeker of truth to be brought back spontaneously to Cartesian doctrines. For he might perhaps devise hypotheses far different from the Cartesian ones, and by them explain the nature of things equally consistently and clearly; which Descartes does not deny can be done. Indeed, in my judgement, the new method of Wolzogen, which he openly professes here, is so far from needing to be followed by one who searches for truth that I think nothing should be avoided more than following Descartes in the method of study. It will be worth the trouble to imitate it in very few respects, Descartes himself being witness, for this one thing alone, that we lay aside all the opinions with which we were once imbued, is not to be attempted by everyone. If you want the sum of what can be said against the Cartesian method of philosophizing, consult what the most distinguished Daniel Voet has put forward about the philosophizing method of certain recent writers, and in his other disputations; and at once you will perceive that the knowledge of things, placed in the greater part, is not only not founded on certainty, but that the road has been openly laid to an inextricable scepticism. Not that I judge the Cartesians to be sceptics, cleaving to perpetual doubts, but that it happens by chance, not from the genius of Cartesian philosophy, if they have anything certain. Many people, in the whole of life, perceive nothing quite rightly enough to pass a sure judgement on it. Yet they do not doubt about everything; they think many things, though resting on a weak foundation, to be known by them with certainty. So perhaps it is also with the Cartesians. Descartes lays down this rule: that it is certain that we shall never admit anything false as true, if we give assent only to those things which we perceive clearly and distinctly; but I have already shown that this rule is slippery and not very safe. Nor do I find that those things which he says were prescribed to himself, as fundamental, by one who searches for truth, are of better quality: 1. That he would never admit anything as true unless he knew it to be certainly and evidently true, but this labours under the same difficulty as the previous one; 2. That he would divide the difficulties he was about to examine into as many parts as would be useful for resolving them more conveniently. But while he has not yet acquired knowledge of the thing, how will it be clear to him that this difficulty must be divided into so many parts, and not into more or fewer? And once the division is made, how is the whole to be divided up exhaustively? How will it be clear that it cannot be divided more conveniently? These are surely mere trifles, and it is unclear what they mean, since these oracles hardly even hear themselves. Nothing is really being said. 3. That he would advance all the cognitions he devoted to seeking the truth in a certain order, beginning, that is, from the simplest things and those most easily known, so that he would gradually, as it were step by step, ascend to the knowledge of the more difficult and more compounded things, arranging in his mind, in a certain order, those things which by their nature do not precede one another. All very well, but how do these precepts help the Cartesians? For once everything has been rejected, set aside, and held as false, how will they know that there is an order of knowing, that some things are simpler and others less simple? Further, how will they know the distinction between the simpler and the less simple? Tell me, please, from where will he draw it who knows nothing and holds everything as false? Do you see how you do not rise out of that whirlpool of doubt into which you have thrown yourself? That there is nowhere to set your foot? I truly marvel at the madness of men. 4. Lastly, that both in seeking the means and in running through the parts of the difficulties he would enumerate each thing so perfectly and look around at everything so carefully that he would be certain nothing had been omitted by him. But I ask, what does he know of the means, of the seeking of means, what of the difficulties, of the parts, he who has now wiped everything clean from his mind, who holds everything as false, who is still ignorant whether God exists, or whether he himself exists? For this is what the Cartesian method demands. Then you will always remain in doubt in your mind whether you have enumerated everything, or whether you have omitted none of the things that ought to have been looked into. For that something is to be known clearly and distinctly, and that nothing is to be passed over by which we may not know clearly and distinctly that which we defend as true, is not new, nor doubtful, nor a rule that is, as it were, your own, to be claimed for yourself:

units.la: Sed quia experimur nos fuisse tam sæpe deceptos, in iis, quæ visi alias nobis fuimus clare, & distincte cognosce-re, postquam nihil prorsus omisimus eorum, quæ ad cognoscendum clare, distinctèque esse necessaria arbitrati sumus; ideo superest Methodus tradenda, quam si olim habuissemus, non fuissemus decepti, & quam si habeamus in posterum, futuri obnoxii deceptioni non simus. Et ne forte dicatur fuisse olim omnia circumspicienda accuratius, quippe, quod non satis circumspecta fuerint, ipso eventu probatum fuisse: Patet id ipsum esse, quod quæritur, quomodo nempe agnosci possit, quandonam fuerint omnia satis circumspecta, vel non; Nam ut prius per decem annos credidi fuisse omnia à me accuratissime circumspecta, & exacto tandem decennio animadverti quidpiam defuisse; ita possum putare jam circumspexisse me omnia, ac pari modo decipi, & in deceptione perseverare non modo toto decennio, sed etiam toto vita decursu: unde & requiro adhuc Methodum, qua constet omnia esse vel non esse à me accuratissime circumspecta. Ex quo fit, ut nisi eam tradas, jure exsibilare Scepticos non possis, qui longe melius, quam tu, præjudicia exuunt, quando in rebus ad naturales speculationes pertinentibus, non statim ut tu, in alia præjudicia sese conjiciunt. Occurrit locus Cartesii, quo hanc difficultatem se sensisse videre est, quam sic tollere conatur. Nec obstat quod sæpe simus experti alios deceptos fuisse in iis quæ Sole clarius se scire credebant: Neque enim unquam advertimus, vel ab ullo adverti potest, id contigisse iis qui claritatem suæ perceptionis à solo intellectu petierunt, sed iis tantum qui vel à sensibus, vel à falso aliquo præjudicio ipsam desumpserunt. Ista dementati sunt homines, ut quicquid Cartesius profert, solidum videatur non solum, sed illi se opponere audax facinus & horrendum. Pueri jam & quorum manus heri aut nudius tertius ferulæ subjectæ sunt, Aristoteli & quotquot fuerunt præcedentium sæculorum, Philosophis, imo Theologis, in faciem volent & barbam evellicent radicitus, belle se gerunt belluli. Per Cartesianos igitur mihi liceat placide Cartesii dicta, ad incudem vocare. Ea erat difficultas, requiri normam ac Methodum qua juvante sciam an clara, quam puto claram esse, istius e. g. hæc perceptio, perceptio, sit nec ne, falluntur enim quotidie &c. Respondet Cartesius: id non contigit iis, qui claritatem suæ perceptionis, à solo intellectu, petierunt, sed iis, qui vel à sensibus, vel à falso aliquo prajudicio ipsam desumpserunt. Quis ita bardus, ita præjudiciis occæcatus esse potest, ut hic nodum intactum, non solutum esse, non palpet? Concedatur enim Cartesio totum quod petit, redit statim eadem difficultas, experimur enim non fuisse tam sæpe deceptos, etiam, dum perceptionis nostræ claritatem, vel à solo intellectu petere putavimus, nihilque magis, quam sensuum fallaciam, aut seductionem præjudiciorum devitare voluimus: quare jam iterum Methodus, quam si olim habuissemus, non fuissemus decepti, & quam si habeamus impostorum, futuri obnoxii deceptioni non simus, Cartesianis tradenda restat. In Resp. ad Obj. sec. videtur velle solvere istum nodum, sic ibi. In iis autem quæ sic non possunt explicari, nempe in maxime claris, & accuratis nostris judiciis, quæ si falsa essent, per nulla clariora, nec ope ullius alterius naturalis facultatis possent emendari, plane affirmo nos falli non posse. Sed breviter qui scis an non ope alterius alicujus naturalis facultatis possit emendari & emendandum sit, quod jam certum autumas, ipso facto? emendari non posse sæpius putasti, quæ tamen emendata vidisti postea, unde jam constat, idem & in isto, & in illo, & in reliquis, non futurum? Deinde unde noveris te tum clare quicquam percipere, ut non corrigi posse, ab aliqua facultate tua, videri debeat? Viden' te non evadere, vel isto figmento? te verba dare & nihil præterea? Ejusdem farinæ est, quod in fine paginæ occurrit. Hac autem persuasio si tam firma sit ut nullam unquam possimus habere causam dubitandi de eo quod nobis ita persuademus, nihil est quod ulterius inquiramus, habemus omne quod cum ratione licet optare. Ac si dice-res, quando persuasio tam vera est, ut deprehendi nunquam possit esse falsam, aut ut non possit esse falsa; bene, vera est, quando vera est. At normam volo, methodum volo, qua sciam me rem sic percipere vel non percipere. Viden' jam multo molimine nihil actum. Sic pasti & saturi redeunt qui hic sapien-tiam quærunt. Nec absurditatem minuit, si dicant jam, antequam se dubitationi dederet, Cartesium istas regulas posuisse, sic enim de seipso narrat, postquam vero me his regulis instruxissem, illasque reservassem, quantum ad reliqua quibus olim fueram imbutus, non dubitavi quin mihi liceret OMNIA ex animo meo DELERE. Ut verum fatear, non video ista Wei-gelianorum Schwenkfeldianorumque deliriis, sa-niora esse. 1. Quomodo enim potest regulas & qui-dem semper retinendas sibi fingere, dum nihil hacte-nus novit, imo dum viam ad primam veritatem quæ-rendam, parat? Postea enim demum deprehendet & inveniet, Archimedeum illud inventum quod, Schoo-kio teste, quasi Delphici Apollinis responsum agnosci volunt. Quod ipsis est primum cognitum, cognoscendorumque principium & prora. 2. Cum jam de-prehenderit, se sæpissime falsum, vel in iis, quæ cer-tissima, & à falsitatis omnis specie remotissima videbantur, ideoque omnia pro falsis habenda, donec firmis fundamentis eorum nixa constaret veritas, unde certus est se & in hisce non falli, vel saltem postea falsitatem non deprehensurum? quid ergo restat, quo nixus hisce regulis fidat? posset enim accidere, certus ad minimum nondum est non fore, ut & istæ regulæ deprehendantur salsissimæ. 3. Stultum videtur supponere, Clare quicquam & distincte unquam posthac percipiendum esse, difficultates dari easque orituras, & quo modo superandas & multa alia, dum nihil, dum nulla veritas adhucdum detecta sit: nisi primo suo principio, Cogito ergo sum, quicquam velint esse prius. 4. Puerile est, figere & refigere, jam multa novit, stipulatur, figitque, quæ paulo post refigenda erunt; ex animo enim delenda omnia, nec est quod hasce regulas excipiat, nisi in cognoscendi ordine millena, quæ hisce regulis comprehenduntur, primum suum principium antevertere & præcedere largiter, at contradictorie, concedat. 5. Contradicunt hæc omnia, tolluntque se mutuo, prima enim regula vult, nihil ut verum unquam NB. unquam vel nunc vel alio tempore admitti, nisi quod certò & evidenter cognosceret. Rogo igitur, an, dum ponit figitque sibi istas regulas, eas pro veris habeat nec ne? pro veris dicet procul dubio: Iterum rogo quoniam pro veris eas habet, an earum omnes difficultates jam rite diviserit, easque omnes & singulas certo ordine, à faciliori ad difficilius semper pergendo, examinaverit & quidem tam perfecte ut nihil se ullibi omisisse certus sit? si neget, jam subvertit primum petitum, quo vult, nihil unquam pro vero admitti, nisi quod clare & distincte perceperit, hæc enim omnia, ad claræ & distinctæ perceptionis conscientiam requiruntur. Si affirmet, jam multa clare & distincte intelligit, ante erutum vel primum principium, imo dum viam ad primam cognitionem sternit, multa jam cognita supponit. Deinde, posito, te istarum regularum rectitudinem jam clare & distincte videre, non potes tamen iis acquiescere, qui postea demum deprehendes, verum esse, quicquid clare & distincte percipitur, detecta sc. demum ista bonitate & perfectione Dei, cui, ex Cartesii placito, repugnat mentem tem esse homini inditam, qua, si quid clare percipe-ret, falleretur. Pro vero sumit, quod verum esse, per Methodi suae rationem, scire repugnat; non enim, quamvis clare forsan aut distincte percipiam, scio id eo ipso verum esse, quoniam clare & distincte perceptum, verum esse, postea demum, ea Idea Dei, colligit Cartesius. Ac tandem, quid est quod te ad quaerendam veritatem, ad regulas, methodos, eum in finem excogitandas, invitet, adigat? Veritatis amor? nescis hactenus an detur ulla veritas; veritatis enim regula, qua, quid sit verum, scias, nondum reperta est. An falsitatis odium? odisse non potes, cujus notitiam nondum habes: falsitas autem an de-tur, & quid sit, ignoras hactenus, qui veritatem non-dum repperisti. Praesertim, cum, ex tua Methodo, prius sciendum sit, quid sit res, antequam inquirere debeas, aut scire queas, an sit res: necesse est, ut, de veritatis aut falsitatis ullius existentia, nihil scias, hoc est, an verum vel falsum, item an veri vel falsi notitia detur, aut dari possit nec ne, quoniam quid sit, ex propria hypothesi nondum novisse convince-ris. Quod autem esse, imo ne quidem esse posse aut non posse, ignoras, quomodo id te moveat?
units.tr: But because we have experienced that we were so often deceived in those things which we had thought we knew clearly and distinctly, even after we had omitted nothing that we judged necessary for knowing clearly and distinctly, a method remains to be delivered: if we had once possessed it, we would not have been deceived, and if we possess it in future, we will not be liable to deception. And lest anyone say that all things were formerly examined more carefully, since it was proved by the outcome itself that they had not been examined carefully enough: this is clearly the very question, namely how it can be recognised when all things have been sufficiently examined or not. For just as I believed for ten years that I had examined everything most carefully, and at the end of that decade noticed that something was lacking, so I may think now that I have examined everything, and be deceived in the same way, and persevere in the deception not only for a whole decade but for my whole life. Hence I still require a method by which it may be established that all things have or have not been examined by me most carefully. From this it follows that, unless you hand it over, you cannot rightly hiss off the Sceptics, who cast off prejudices far better than you do, since in matters pertaining to natural speculation they do not at once throw themselves into other prejudices as you do. There is the passage of Descartes where one sees that he felt this difficulty, and he tries to remove it thus. Nor does it stand in the way that we have often experienced others to have been deceived in those things which they believed they knew more clearly than the sun: for we never notice, nor can anyone notice, that this has happened to those who sought the clarity of their perception from the intellect alone, but only to those who derived it from the senses or from some false prejudice. Men have been so dazed that whatever Descartes puts forward seems not only solid, but a bold and horrible crime to oppose him. Boys whose hands were placed under the ferule yesterday or the day before, and who are just beginning, fly at Aristotle and all the philosophers of previous centuries, indeed at the theologians, to the face, and tear out their beards by the roots, behaving like little beasts. Let me therefore, among the Cartesians, calmly call Descartes' sayings to the anvil. The difficulty was this: a norm and method is required by whose help I may know whether a clear perception (such as this perception of mine, which I think is clear) is clear or not, for men are deceived every day, etc. Descartes replies: this has not happened to those who sought the clarity of their perception from the intellect alone, but to those who derived it from the senses or from some false prejudice. Who can be so dull, so blinded by prejudices, as not to feel that this knot is untouched and unsolved? For grant Descartes all that he asks, and the same difficulty returns at once: we experience that we were not so often deceived even when we thought we sought the clarity of our perception from the intellect alone, and wished to avoid nothing more than the fallacy of the senses or the seduction of prejudices. Therefore the method, by which if we had once possessed it we would not have been deceived, and by which if we possess it in future we will not be liable to deception, still remains to be delivered by the Cartesians. In his Reply to the Second Objections he seems willing to solve this knot, thus: In those things, however, which cannot be explained in this way, namely in our most clear and accurate judgements, which, if they were false, could not be corrected by any clearer thing nor with the help of any other natural faculty, I plainly affirm that we cannot be deceived. But briefly, how do you know that it cannot be corrected with the help of some other natural faculty, and that it need not be corrected, when you now assert it as certain by the very fact? You have often thought that things could not be corrected, and yet afterwards you saw them corrected; from which it is now clear that the same will not happen in this case, and in that, and in the rest? Next, how do you know that when you then perceive something clearly, it ought to appear uncorrectable by any faculty of yours? Do you see that you do not escape, even by this fiction? That you are only playing with words and nothing more? Of the same kind is what occurs at the end of the page: But if this persuasion is so firm that we can never have any cause to doubt what we so persuade ourselves of, there is nothing further to inquire into; we have everything that with reason we may wish for. And if you were to say, when the persuasion is so true that it can never be detected as false, or so that it cannot be false: good, it is true when it is true. But I want a norm, I want a method, by which I may know that I perceive a thing so or do not perceive it. Do you see now that nothing has been achieved with much effort? So those who seek wisdom here return fed and satisfied. Nor does it lessen the absurdity if they now say that Descartes laid down these rules before he gave himself up to doubt; for he thus speaks of himself: but after I had furnished myself with these rules, and reserved them, as far as the remaining things with which I had formerly been imbued, I did not doubt that I might be allowed to DELETE ALL things from my mind. To tell the truth, I do not see that these are any saner than the delusions of the Weigelians and Schwenkfeldians. 1. For how can he feign for himself rules, and indeed rules always to be retained, when he knows nothing as yet, indeed while he is preparing the way to the first truth to be sought? For only afterwards will he discover and find that Archimedean invention which, as Schookius testifies, they wish to be recognised as the response of the Delphic Apollo: what is first known to them, the principle and prow of all knowing. 2. Since he has now discovered that he was most often mistaken, even in those things which seemed most certain and most remote from every appearance of falsity, and therefore that all things must be held false until the truth, resting on firm foundations, is established, whence is he certain that he is not deceived in these also, or at least that he will not discover falsity in them later? What then remains on which he may lean and trust these rules? For it could happen that he is not certain, at least as yet, that these rules too will not be discovered to be most false. 3. It seems foolish to suppose that anything will ever afterwards be perceived clearly and distinctly, that difficulties exist and will arise, and how they are to be overcome, and many other things, while nothing, while no truth has yet been detected: unless they want something to be prior to their first principle, I think, therefore I am. 4. It is childish to fix and refix; he already knows many things, stipulates and fixes, things which shortly after must be refixed; for all things must be deleted from the mind, and there is nothing that these rules may except, unless, in the order of knowing, he concedes, but contradictorily, that the thousand things comprehended by these rules precede and come before their first principle by a great deal. 5. All these things contradict and cancel one another, for the first rule wills that nothing ever be admitted as true, NB. ever, either now or at another time, except what he knows certainly and evidently. I ask, therefore, whether, while he lays down and fixes these rules for himself, he holds them to be true or not? He will undoubtedly say that he holds them true: I ask again, since he holds them true, has he already duly divided all their difficulties, and examined them all and each in a certain order, always proceeding from the easier to the more difficult, and that so perfectly that he is certain he has omitted nothing anywhere? If he denies it, he now overturns his first premise, by which he wills that nothing be admitted as true unless he has perceived it clearly and distinctly, for all these things are required for the consciousness of clear and distinct perception. If he affirms it, then he already understands many things clearly and distinctly before the truth is brought out, or even the first principle, indeed while he is paving the way to the first knowledge, he already presupposes many things as known. Further, granted that you now see clearly and distinctly the rectitude of those rules, you cannot nevertheless acquiesce in them, since you will discover only afterwards that whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived is true, namely when that goodness and perfection of God has been detected, to which, according to Descartes' opinion, it is repugnant that a faculty should be placed in man by which, if he perceived anything clearly, he would be deceived. He assumes as true what, by the reasoning of his own method, it is repugnant to know to be true; for although perhaps I perceive clearly or distinctly, I do not know by that very fact that it is true, since Descartes only afterwards infers that what is clearly and distinctly perceived is true, from that idea of God. And finally, what is it that invites and compels you to seek the truth, to devise rules and methods for that end? The love of truth? Hitherto you do not know whether any truth exists at all; for a rule of truth, by which you might know what is true, has not yet been found. Or the hatred of falsity? You cannot hate that whose notion you do not yet have; but whether falsity exists, and what it is, you hitherto do not know, since you have not yet found the truth. Especially since, according to your Method, one must first know what a thing is before one ought to inquire, or be able to know whether it is a thing at all: it is necessary that you know nothing of the existence of any truth or falsity, that is, whether there is something true or false, and likewise whether knowledge of truth or falsity exists or can exist or not, since you are convicted by your own hypothesis of not yet knowing what it is. But how does it move you that you do not know whether it is, or even whether it can or cannot be?

units.la: Largiter agamus, ponantur istae regulae, seponan-tur nunc & ex animo deleantur omnia, dubitatio-nis abyssus una nos absorbeat, jam dubito, jam hae-reo, nihil novi, nec Deum, nec me, nec caelum, nec terram &c. ubi jam tabula post naufragium? quis manum porriget, quo evadam tandemque aliquid certi deprehendam? Jam novem anni mihi elapsi sunt, jam dies, hebdomadas, menses aliquot in Car-tesianis Meditationibus insumpsi, rationum Cartesia-narum seriem & nexum comprehendere curavi, quan-tum potui sedulo. At omni scientia vacuo, quis pri-mam mihi guttam instillabit? Ostendit, Vir Clar.olim Praeceptor meus, Daniel Voet, nihil superesse,
units.tr: Let us grant it. Let these rules be laid down, let all things be set aside and wiped from our minds, let the abyss of doubt swallow us: now I doubt, now I hesitate, I know nothing, neither God, nor myself, nor heaven, nor earth, and so on. Where then is the plank after the shipwreck? Who will stretch out a hand, by what means shall I escape and at last grasp something certain? Already nine years have slipped away from me, already I have spent days, weeks and several months on the Cartesian Meditations, and have taken pains to grasp the series and connection of the Cartesian reasonings as diligently as I could. But who will drop the first drop into me, empty as I am of all knowledge? My former teacher, the distinguished Daniel Voet, has shown that nothing is left,

units.la: quo pag. 232. quo isti Philosophi Scepticismi vitent Syrtes & ex isto gurgite salvi redeant, hoc modo: 1. dicit, hanc Methodum nos deducere ad Scepticismum naturali lumine non superandum, circa existentiam tum cau-sarum secundarum naturalium tum operationum ea-rundem 2. ad Scepticismum ne quidem revelatione divina tollendum.
units.tr: (see p. 232) how those philosophers of scepticism may avoid the quicksands and come safe back out of that whirlpool, in this way: 1. he says that this method leads us to a scepticism which cannot be overcome by natural light, concerning the existence both of secondary natural causes and of their operations; 2. and a scepticism which cannot be removed even by divine revelation.

units.la: Sic disserit; ut, ex eo quod Deus variis modis me-diantibus variis causis omnino similes potest produ-cere effectus, incertus es, à qua causa præcise effectus hic processerit; ita ex eo, quod Deus quos in natura observamus effectus, immediate producere potest, incertus es an ulla, præter eum, extra te, detur causa secunda. Porro, ut de causis, sic & de effectis, an existant, incertus es, motus enim fibrillis nervo-rum tuorum impressus, quo causarum secundarum deprehendis operationes, imprimi tibi à potentissimo quodam posset genio, multo magis à Deo. Utique, quemadmodum ex eo, quod effectus similes à variis possint procedere causis secundis, colligis nos dubios esse, an ab hac potius quam ab illa causa fluant, ita & hic de motione in organis tuis sensoriis idem dici pos-set, sicque incertus es, an ullæ extra te in rerum na-tura res, earumque effectus existant. Excipies. Hoc pacto Deum deceptorem fore. Resp Non Deum, sed te tuimet ipsius deceptorem fore, quippe qui ju-dicas, simulac mentem tuam affici percipis, eam actionem à sensibili quo, revera præter te existente, proficisci, cum potius tuum judicium hic suspendere debuisses, cogitando, mentem tam ab imaginariis quam à veris posse affici. Pergo & probo te juxta hanc Methodum, etiam incertum esse, an ullæ ejus-modi motiones in organis tuis sensoriis, adeoque an ullæ operationes in corpore tuo, reperiantur: Nescis enim, an à veris fibrillarum motibus, an vero ab imaginariis, id est quos tibi imaginaris, afficiaris, con-sequensequenter an ulli motus revera fibrillis impressi sint nec ne. Tandem, ne quicquam tibi relinquam, osten-dam te, ne quidem cogitationis tuæ certum esse, cognitionis enim cognitio, quoniam fit per actum mentis alium, supra priorem reflectentem, nescis autem an non mens tua, ab alio afficiatur, dum per actum directum hunc actum reflexum productum putas; ut sensus, sic & mens ipsa, à quodam Spiritu posset ita affici, ut cogitationis alterius, actus hic, actus reflexus non fit, sed falso solum à potentissimo deceptore productus: vides quidem cogitationis alicujus in mente speciem, sed unde constat, illam esse alicujus cogitationis tuæ speciem, non autem impressionis Diabolicæ aut potentissimi deceptoris fœtum. Non nego cogitantem existere, aut cognoscentem reflexe, aut dubitantem, de existentia actus præce-dentis cogitare, verum nego cognoscentem, ut putat, reflexe, eo ipso certum esse, se reflexionem prioris cujusdam cogitationis suæ intueri, posset enim in eo mens falli, & pro actu suæ mentis reflexo sumere, qui falsam ejus præ se ferret speciem. Deinde actus re-flexus suimet cum non sit cognoscitivus, in ejusdem iterata reflexione, præterquam quod sic daretur pro-cessus in infinitum, eadem superest difficultas. Quod-nam ergo, quo stes, tibi restat punctum? Certitudi-nem, demonstrationem firmam, prodere deberent, eam præ reliquis jactantes. Hactenus modo laudatus D. Voet.
units.tr: He argues thus: just as, because God can produce wholly similar effects by various means and through various causes, you are uncertain from which cause precisely this effect has proceeded, so, because God can produce immediately the effects we observe in nature, you are uncertain whether any secondary cause exists outside you apart from him. Further, as with causes, so with effects, you are uncertain whether they exist; for the motion impressed on the little fibres of your nerves, by which you perceive the operations of secondary causes, could be imprinted on you by some most powerful genius, much more by God. Indeed, just as from the fact that similar effects can proceed from various secondary causes you conclude that we are doubtful whether they flow from this cause rather than that, so the same could be said here of the motion in your sense organs, and thus you are uncertain whether any things outside you exist in the nature of things, and their effects. You will object: in this way God would be a deceiver. I reply: it would not be God but yourself who would be the deceiver of yourself, since you judge, as soon as you perceive your mind to be affected, that this action proceeds from a sensible cause which really exists apart from you, whereas you ought rather to have suspended your judgment here, considering that the mind can be affected by imaginary things as well as by true ones. I go further and prove that, by this method, you are also uncertain whether any such motions exist in your sense organs, and so whether any operations take place in your body: for you do not know whether you are affected by true motions of the fibres or by imaginary ones, that is, those you imagine, and consequently whether any motions have really been impressed on the fibres or not. Finally, lest I leave you anything, I will show that you are not even certain of your own thought, for the knowledge of knowledge, since it comes about through another act of the mind reflecting upon the earlier one, you do not know whether your mind is not itself affected by another, while you think, through a direct act, that this reflexive act has been produced; just as the senses, so the mind itself could be so affected by some spirit that this act of reflection is not an act of another thought, but only falsely produced by a most powerful deceiver: you indeed see the appearance of some thought in the mind, but how do you know that it is the appearance of one of your thoughts and not the offspring of a Diabolical impression or of a most powerful deceiver? I do not deny that the thinking subject exists, or that it knows reflexively, or that, doubting, it thinks about the existence of the preceding act; but I deny that the knowing subject, as he supposes, is by that very fact certain that he is looking at the reflection of some earlier thought of his own, for in this the mind could be deceived and take for a reflexive act of its own what bears a false appearance of it. Moreover, since the reflexive act is not itself cognitive, the same difficulty remains in its repeated reflection, apart from the fact that in this way there would be an infinite regress. What, then, is the point on which you may stand? They ought to produce certainty and a firm demonstration, boasting of them above the rest. Thus far the aforementioned Voet.

units.la: Candide & generose victas dat manus Henricus Regius, qui, Cartesiana Methodo, veritatem post-quam investigaverat, Scepticismum, naturali via in-vincibilem esse aperte profiteri non erubescit. Sic enim causam dedit. Neque etiam est, quod Sceptici-smus naturalis, sive ex natura sequens nobis objiciatur.
