Quicunque enim omnipotentem & liberrimum cognoscit Deum, & imbecillitatis humanæ mentis sibi satis est conscius, talem omnium rerum verisimilitudinem, vel Scepticismum naturalem, si ita libeat appellare, qualem proposuimus, negare non potest. Et probabilis sola moralis verisimilisque datur rerum extra mentem existentium certitudo. Vana itaque & inanes eorum sunt gloriationes, qui ex natura apodicticam & indubitabilem rerum scientiam se habere, vel habere posse, jactant; cum ex ea supra verisimilitudinem nihil quicquam, ut ex dictis patet, haberi queat. Ergo ad divinam revelationem, certitudinem quæsiturus, fugit, inde Deum esse creatorem omnium, qui causas secundas produxerit, iis operandi facultates indiderit, cum tali intellectu, voluntate, sensibus, hominem creaverit &c. edocendus. Sed unde ipsi constat de Scriptura quicquam, cum sine sensibus, quibus non tuto creditur, percipi ea non possit? Internam revelationem si jactas, unde illusione Diabolica non agitari se alii, vel sibi probabit? Deinde præter alia absurda. 1. Si sensuum etiam ac naturalium ex Sacris petenda certitudo est, Sacramentorum institutio (absit blasphemia dicto) ridicula foret & inutilis. Nam incertum per æque incertum, aut certum per minus certum stabiliretur. 2. Gentiles ex visibilibus ad ἀναπολογησίαν [?] instrui non potuissent, contra Rom. 1. &c. Eant nunc & omnia in dubium vocent Carte-siani, bene Philosophaturo vel existentiam Dei in dubium vocandam, imo ut falsam habendam, blasphe-me doceant. Ego putem, præterquam, quod phrases similes sint intolerandæ, rem ipsam summo absque scelere effectam dari non posse. Ex inferno prodiisse censent, & lugent pii, dubitationes de Deo, quotquot vel in vehementissimis tentationibus sibi suboriri deprehendunt. Desperatæ causæ signum est & imprudentiæ manifesta professio, quod in tot gyros & anfractus sese flectant novi Philosophi, quotiescunque hæc, de dubitatione, regula defendenda venit.
units.tr: Frankly and nobly Henricus Regius gives up the struggle as one defeated; having investigated the truth by the Cartesian method, he is not ashamed to declare openly that scepticism, invincible by the natural way, is no threat. For he gave the case thus: Nor is it an objection that natural scepticism, or scepticism arising from nature, follows. For whoever knows God to be omnipotent and most free, and is sufficiently conscious of the weakness of the human mind, cannot deny that such a likelihood of all things, or natural scepticism (if one likes to call it so), as we have proposed, exists. And the only certainty of things existing outside the mind is probable, moral and likely. Vain and empty therefore are the boasts of those who claim to have, or to be able to have, from nature an apodictic and indubitable knowledge of things; since, as is clear from what has been said, nothing beyond likelihood can be had from it. Therefore, seeking certainty, he flees to divine revelation, by which he must be taught that God is the creator of all things, who produced secondary causes, endowed them with faculties of operation, and created man with such an intellect, will, senses, and so on. But how is it certain to him anything about Scripture, since without the senses, in which we do not safely believe, it cannot be perceived? If you boast of an internal revelation, how will he prove to himself or to others that he is not being disturbed by Diabolical illusion? Furthermore, besides other absurdities: 1. If the certainty even of the senses and of natural things is to be sought from the Sacred Scriptures, the institution of the sacraments (let me say it without blasphemy) would be ridiculous and useless; for the uncertain would be established by the equally uncertain, or the certain by the less certain. 2. The Gentiles could not have been instructed from visible things to be without excuse [?], contrary to Romans 1, and so on. Let them now go and call everything into doubt, these Cartesians, teaching blasphemously that the existence of God is to be called into doubt, even held to be false, in order to philosophize well. I think that, apart from the fact that such phrases are intolerable, the thing itself cannot be done without the greatest wickedness. The godly think that doubts about God, however many of them they find arising in themselves even in the most violent temptations, come from hell, and they lament them. It is a sign of a desperate cause and a manifest profession of imprudence that these new philosophers turn themselves in so many circles and windings whenever this rule of doubting comes to be defended.

units.la: Multi eorum, Criticorum quærentes umbram, sub hac & illa vocis significatione delitescere. De Deo, de rebus fidei nil dictum prætexere, vitæ actiones excipere. Distinctionum alias hostes, multas distinctiones, limitationes, restrictiones; à numero, à duratione, à subjectis, ab objectis fingere. Jam assensum cohibere simpliciter, jam inter extrema quorum neutrum satis constat ambigere, jam aliud quid significatum velle. Necdum enim certi quid ea de re novi Mystæ statuerunt. Sed quorsum ista incogitata dictio, quæ mille technis excusari, palliarique habeat necesse? blasphemum sonat, dubitandum de omnibus, imo blasphemum statuit, quisquis hoc statuerit. Video, ut crudam istam de dubitatione sententiam leniret, res fidei, quæ semper apud ipsum potissimæ fuerunt, sibi reservatas semper docere Cartesium. Quæ verba satis esse putant, quibus inculpata sistatur & innoxia, sequuntur dubitatio, homines Cartesiani: ipse Cartesius, alta voce sibi injuriam fieri clamat ab iis, qui scribunt ipsum docuisse, de Dei existentia esse dubitandum, monebo hic, inquit, me nunquam etiam do- cuisse de omnibus esse dubitandum, vel similia, quæ à calumniatoribus imperitis aliquando mihi objecta sunt; sed omnia ista expressissimis verbis rejecisse &c. Quis jam crimen istud huic intentabit? Sane nihil si scripsisset, verbis deberetur multa fides, scripta autem si conferantur, vereor ne quisque sit judicaturus, hanc protestationem actui contrariam, atque ipso jure nullam esse. Paucis referam quid alibi tradat & an id quod hic se docuisse negat, non apertis verbis ab ipso doceatur videre lubet. Cartesii discipulos si ad partes vocarem, fuit qui blasphemas istas voces chartæ illinire ausus est, serio & ordine philosophaturo existentia Dei in dubium est revocanda, hoc est, dubitandum est an Deus, ens summe perfectum, existat: Nam cum de nulla re adhuc pro certo possumus affirmare quod existat, istat, quoniam non habemus de ulla cogitationem cer-tam & inconcussam, de qua ne minima quidem ratio dubitandi sit reliqua, certe nulla nobis est necessitas, nulla nos movent rationes, quæ pro certo nos cogant concludere Deum existere. Imo omnes opiniones nostras, utile erit aliquamdiu habere pro falsis. At quererentur injuriam fieri Præceptori, cui discipulorum imputentur verba. Vide an meliora sint quæ scripsit Car-tesius: Cum semel in vita de iis omnibus dubitare studendum dicit, in quibus vel minimam incertitudinis suspicionem reperiemus. Quin & illa etiam utile erit habere pro falsis. Utique, inquit Schulerus, quamplurima fidei Mysteria & Sacræ Scr. dicta pro falsis habenda erunt, quia de eorum plurimis sæpissime vel Doctissimos dubitare constat. Si forsan quis putet, quædam Cartesio talia esse, in quibus ne minima quidem incertitudinis suspicio reperiatur, ac proinde multa, quædam saltem, à dubitatione excipi: conferat ille sequentia, sic ipse, Dubitamus etiam de reliquis, quæ antea pro maxime certis habuimus; etiam de Mathematicis demonstrationibus, etiam de iis principiis, quæ hactenus putavimus esse per se nota. Putas Deum excipi? perge, Sic autem NB. rejicientes illa omnia, de quibus aliquo modo possumus dubitare, ac etiam falsa esse fingentes; facile quidem supponimus, NB. nullum esse Deum, nullum cælum, nulla corpora &c. hæc cognitio Ego cogito ergo sum est omnium prima & certissima. NB. hæc est prima quæ cuilibet ordine philosophanti occurrit. Physicum fateor, istud principiorum opus est, res istas illuc proprie non pertinere ne fortassis excipiant, solet enim ridicula Claubergius quæsita inter Cartesii scripta distinctiuncula, multas amoliri difficultates, vel potius subterfugium quærere. Quod sane perquam frivolum esse non est quod demonstrem. Age igitur domesticam & propriam hujus rei sedem, Meditationes videamus. Sic sonat primæ ti-tulus. tulus. De iis quæ in dubium revocari possunt. Statim in capite ista occurrunt, funditus omnia in vita semel esse evertenda. Quod ne absurdum videatur, sic omnes opiniones certas & incertas evelli funditus, satis erit, inquit, ad omnes rejiciendas, si aliquam rationem dubitandi in unaquaque reperero. Nec ideo singula erunt percurrenda: aggrediar statim ipsa NB. principia quibus illud omne quod olim credidi niteba-tur. ——— Sed tandem cogor fateri NB. nihil esse ex iis quæ olim vera putabam, de quo non liceat dubitare, idque non per inconsiderantiam, vel levitatem, sed NB. propter validas & meditatas rationes, ideoque etiam ab iisdem, non minus quam ab aperte falsis, accurate deinceps assensionem esse cohibendam, si quid certi velim invenire. Imo opiniones omnes aliquamdiu omnino falsas, imaginarias que esse fingam. Fatetur dixisse se, nihil esse de quo non liceat dubitare. Omnes simul & semel opiniones tanquam falsas rejiciendas. Cogito &c. primo innotesceret. Adde quæ ex secunda Medi-tat. citavi Strict. XV. ad Libr. 1. Plura ex Methodo adferrem, nisi illam Exotericam solum, Meditationes vero & Principia maxime Acroamatica esse, ex Claubergio didicissem. Putem quoque ista sufficere, ut lectori appareat, an hæc tot artificiosas admittant limitationes, vel an absolutissima dicenda potius, universalissimaque Cartesiana dubitatio. Varia sunt quibus se evasurum putat Cartes & post eum Cartesiani, præcipue autem Clauber gius, qui mira confidentia adversarium suum aggreditur; quoniam ergo eo deventum est, paucis videamus, quid rei tantis ver-borum ampullis subsit: dum autem propius Clauber-giana considero, vana apparent. Ad quinque capita omnia referenda erunt. I. Cartesium referre non sua sed Scepticorum sensa: sic Cartes, sic Clauberg. II. Res fidei fuisse exceptas, quam exceptionem præ reliquis urget & declarat Clauberg ius adductis diversis similitudini. tudinibus : una sic sonat. Pono me habere scriptum eximium, quod clare satis possim legere ad lumen Solis diurnum, sed velim explorare, an idem illud legere, etiam valeam ad lumen Lunæ. Quis hic dicat me revocare in dubium meridianæ lucis claritudinem, eo quod dubitem atque inquiram num idem objectum conspici possit lumine stellarum? Similiter ratione nos pro certo semper ponimus Deum esse &c. quatenus haec scripta legimus in libro S. Script. hoc non obstante, initio Philosophiæ quærimus, an quoque in libro naturæ &c. III.
units.tr: Many of them, hunting for a hiding place like critics, take shelter under this or that meaning of a word. They pretend that nothing has been said about God or the matters of faith, and they confine themselves to the actions of life. Enemies of distinctions themselves, they invent many distinctions, limitations and restrictions, by number, by duration, by subjects and by objects. Now they simply withhold assent, now they waver between extremes neither of which is sufficiently established, and now they want something else to be meant. The new Mystics have not yet settled anything definite on this matter. But why must this thoughtless expression, which needs a thousand artifices to excuse and cloak it, be used? It sounds blasphemous: that everything must be doubted. Indeed, whoever lays this down states a blasphemy. I see that Descartes, to soften this crude opinion of doubt, teaches that matters of faith, which have always been of chief importance to him, have always been reserved for himself. Thinking these words enough to make the charge harmless and innocuous, the Cartesian doubters follow him. Descartes himself cries out loudly that he is being wronged by those who write that he taught that the existence of God must be doubted: I will here note, he says, that I never taught that everything must be doubted, or anything similar, which unskilled slanderers have sometimes objected to me; but I rejected all such things in the most express words, etc. Who will now bring this charge against him? Certainly, if he had written nothing, much trust would be due to his words; but if his writings are compared, I fear that anyone will judge this protestation to be contrary to his action and of no legal force at all. I will briefly report what he teaches elsewhere, and I am glad to see whether what he here denies having taught is not taught by him in plain words. If I were to summon the Cartesian disciples to the field, there was one who dared to smear these blasphemous words on paper: in a serious and orderly philosophizing, the existence of God is to be called back into doubt, that is, it must be doubted whether God, a being most perfect, exists; for since we can as yet affirm for certain of no thing that it exists, and since we have no certain and unshaken thought about anything, of which not even the smallest reason for doubting remains, surely there is no necessity for us, no reasons move us, which compel us to conclude for certain that God exists. Indeed, it will be useful for some time to hold all our opinions to be false. But they will complain that an injury is done to the Teacher, when the words of his disciples are imputed to him. Let us see whether what Descartes wrote is better: Since, he says, it must be studied once in life to doubt all those things in which we find even the smallest suspicion of uncertainty. Nay, it will also be useful to hold even those things as false. Certainly, says Schuler, very many mysteries of faith and sayings of Holy Scripture will have to be held as false, because it is established that the most learned men very often doubt many of them. If perhaps someone thinks that some things are such for Descartes that not even the smallest suspicion of uncertainty is found in them, and therefore that many things, at least some, are excepted from doubt, let him compare the following, where he himself says: We doubt also of the rest, which we previously held as most certain; also of the mathematical demonstrations, also of those principles which hitherto we have thought to be known through themselves. Do you think God is excepted? Go on: Thus, rejecting all those things of which we can in some way doubt, and even feigning them to be false, we easily suppose, NB, that there is no God, no heaven, no bodies, etc.; this knowledge I think, therefore I am is the first and most certain of all. NB, this is the first that occurs to anyone philosophizing in order. I grant that this is the work of a physicist, and that those things do not properly belong there, lest perhaps they be excepted; for Clauberg is accustomed to seek out a ridiculous little distinction among Descartes's writings, to remove many difficulties, or rather to look for an escape. Surely there is no need for me to prove that this is very frivolous. Come then, let us look at the proper and domestic seat of this matter, the Meditations. The title of the first sounds thus: On those things which can be called into doubt. Immediately in the chapter these occur: all things in life must be overturned once from the foundations. Lest this seem absurd, all opinions, certain and uncertain, are thus to be uprooted from the foundations: it will be enough, he says, for rejecting all, if I find some reason for doubting in each. Nor therefore will single things have to be run through; I will at once attack the very principles NB on which all that I once believed rested. ——— But at last I am compelled to confess that NB there is nothing among those things which I once thought true about which it is not allowed to doubt, and this not through carelessness or levity, but NB on account of valid and considered reasons, and therefore that assent must afterwards be carefully withheld from these also, no less than from those openly false, if I wish to find anything certain. Indeed, I will feign that all opinions are for some time altogether false and imaginary. He confesses that he said there is nothing about which it is not allowed to doubt. All opinions are to be rejected at once and together as false. I think, etc. would become known first. Add what I cited from the second Meditation in Strictures XV on Book 1. I would bring forward more from the Method, but I learned from Clauberg that only the Method is exoteric, while the Meditations and the Principles are most esoteric. I think these things are also enough to show the reader whether this doubt admits of so many artificial limitations, or whether it should rather be called absolute and most universal Cartesian doubt. There are various ways by which Descartes, and after him the Cartesians, especially Clauberg, who attacks his opponent with wonderful confidence, think they will escape. Since we have come to this, let us see briefly what lies under such bombast of words. But when I consider Clauberg more closely, his arguments appear vain. All of them can be referred to five heads. I. That Descartes does not refer his own opinions but those of the Sceptics: thus Descartes, thus Clauberg. II. That matters of faith were excepted, which exception Clauberg presses above the rest and sets forth by various similitudes; one of them runs thus: I suppose that I have an excellent writing, which I can read clearly enough by the light of the day sun, but I wish to test whether I can also read the same by the light of the moon. Who here would say that I call into doubt the clearness of the midday light, because I doubt and inquire whether the same object can be seen by the light of the stars? Similarly, we always assume by reason that God exists, etc., insofar as we read these things in the book of Holy Scripture; nevertheless, at the beginning of philosophy we ask whether also in the book of nature, etc. III.

units.la: Non Principia sed conclusiones solum in dubium vocatas, id innuit Cartes. Loc. ad Strict. XV. Libr. I. Citat. Non notiones simplices, sed complexas & ex aliis erutas ait Clauberg. IV. Dubitationem istam solum veritatis contemplationem concernere, non praxin vitæ. V. Tandem, nihil esse aliud præterquam cohibere assensum, non præcipitare judicium, donec res bene constet. Obtestor lectorem, ut, nullo partium studio actus, sequentia serio mecum ad animum re-vocet. Ad Primum ista respondeo. 1. Hanc exce-ptionem non convenire cum aliis Cartesii dictis : si enim Scepticorum quasi referens argumenta, sic agit, unde I. Jactata tam prolixe hujus dubitationis, eva-cuationis &c. difficultas? Vereor, ait Cartes, ne hoc ipsum quod suscepi, tam arduum & difficile sit. Nam vel hoc unum, ut opiniones omnes deponam &c. Sed laboriosum est hoc institutum: sic alibi. An Scepticorum argumenta referre, eaque examinare tibi tanti est? II. Periculum? quod tantum est, ut valde paucis expediat imitari, ut nulli auctor esse velit, ut simile quid aggrediatur. Quod enim, ait apposite D. Voet. quæso periculum in objectionibus Scepti-corum referendis? cum jam alii ante nos eas retule-rint, iisque responderint; III. Tantum temporis requisitum? IV. ab iis tanquam ab aperte falsis assen-sionis cohibitio? non enim hoc requirit objectio, ut thesin meam pro falsa aliquamdiu serio habeam.
units.tr: Descartes indicates that not principles but only conclusions are called into doubt (Descartes, letter on Strictures XV, Book 1, cited). Clauberg says not simple notions but complex ones drawn from others. IV. That this doubt concerns only the contemplation of truth, not the practice of life. V. Finally, that it is nothing other than withholding assent, not hastily passing judgment, until the matter is well established. I beg the reader, moved by no zeal for either side, to call the following seriously back to mind with me. To the first I answer these things. 1. This exception does not agree with other sayings of Descartes: for if he is reporting the arguments of the Sceptics, as it were, how is it that, I. the difficulty of this doubt, its evacuation, etc., is so boastfully extolled at such length? I fear, says Descartes, that this very thing which I have undertaken is so arduous and difficult. For this one thing alone, that I put away all opinions, etc. But this undertaking is laborious: thus elsewhere: Is it worth so much to you to report the arguments of the Sceptics and to examine them? II. Is there a danger? It is so great that it is expedient for very few to imitate, so that no one wants to be the author, so that he might attempt something similar. For what danger, asks Voet aptly, is there, I beg, in reporting the objections of the Sceptics, since others before us have already reported them and answered them? III. Is so much time required? IV. Withholding of assent, as if from things openly false? For the objection does not require that I seriously hold my thesis false for some time.

units.la: 2. Non convenire cum Claubergio: qui dicit I. se- mel tantum & quidem II. in initio, Philosophiam incipienti, id agendum III. atque perexigua dura- tione. Si enim, ut Scepticorum objectio, dubitatio ista movetur, quid causae, quod tam breviter ac semel, idque solum jam Philosophari inchoanti ea injungatur? An semel tantum, an incipientibus solum Scepticorum argumenta proponenda? vide qui se mutuo tollant intricatae nugae. 3. Non convenire cum reliquis exceptionibus, non cum secunda, nam & de rebus fidei, non tertia, nam & de principiis, de notionibus simplicibus, non quarta, nam & de rebus agendis dubitant Sceptici, qui res humanas eo usque negligebant, ut ne se in praecipitia conjicerent, ab ami- cis deberent asservari, ait Cartes. Non item cum quinta, Sceptici enim non cohibebant assensum donec clare & distincte rem perciperent; sed semper. Dubitabant enim, ut dubitarent, ait Cartes. Concludo igitur nullius momenti esse primam illam exceptionem. Ad secundam properaus dico 1. Ponamus te id velle, constet interim, constare queat, sua revelationi certitudo: an igitur Ethnico, qui nullam fortasse agnoscit revelationem supernaturalem, licitum est id de quo quaeritur? ille igitur absque peccandi periculo de Deo &c. dubitare poterit? 2. si tantum intendatur, quod ait Clauberg, supposita rerum revelatarum certitudine, an & ex natura quaedam constent, tentare, certe res ea tanti laboris non est. Neque 3. tanti periculi. 4. Qui ergo ista de dubitatione verba, Scepticorum objectiones dici poterunt? qui non alius generis certitudinem quaerunt, dum negant omnem. 5. Quid ni & sic de rebus agendis dubitari poterit? satis enim prospectum foret ex sacris, ne in foveam, in ignem sese conjiceret, homo qui ita dubitat. 6. Absurde etiam principia, notiones simsimplices excipis ; quoniam & de illis hoc modo dubitaretur tutissime. 7. Res fidei exceptas si velint serio , qui pote, ut absoluta dubitatio, in contemplatione veritatis , admittatur Cartesio : eaque tanta , utplus aequo diffidentia indulgeri non possit ? quandoquidem non rebus agendis sed cognoscendis tantum incumbit, qui sic dubitat. Alterutrum enim sequitur aut verita-tis contemplationem ad fidem nullo modo pertinere, aut & de rebus fidei licitum esse ut dubitetur univer-sis: quorum unum, crassum Papismum, fidem carbonaria absurdiorem & cum Bellarmino per summam ignorantiam describendam nobis reponit; alterum exceptionem à Cartesio factam subvertit. 8. Dei existentia proculdubio etiam res fidei est, Hebr. xi. ea autem, inter alia, etiam à Cartesio in dubium vo-catur. Bilem hoc movet Claubergio, exempla enim similia proferri solummodo ad odium lectoris in Carte-sianos concitandum, queritur. At tacuissent ista, si objecta noluissent: sero sapiunt, vel defendenda vel revocanda quae exciderunt. Sed adhibita non fuerunt à Cartesio quando de dubio pro falso habendo est locu-tus. Quare igitur odii concitandi, non potius falsum allegas & citandi adversariis tuis animum exprobras Claubergi? scilicet vere id dici non poterat, non ignorasti procul dubio quid dixerit Cartesius. Postquam ad dubitationem istam magno & molesto la-bore pervenerat, sic infit, nec quidem adhuc satis sciam utrum sit aliquis Deus. Examinare debeo an sit Deus, hac enim re ignorata &c. Sic autem rejicien-tes illa omnia, de quibus aliquo modo possumus dubita-re, ac etiam falsa esse fingentes; facile quidem suppo-nimus, nullum esse Deum, nullum [?]calum, nulla cor-pora. Luculentissimus locus est, qui occurrit in Epi-stolis, sic ibi disserit, rogatus an unquam liceat de existentia Dei dubitare, respondet, si quis dubitationem hanc sibi proponat sicuti medium perveniendi ad clarioclariorem cognitionem veritatis, hic quod maxime pium & honestum est agit. Qua fronte igitur scribit, exemplum illud à Cartesio non esse adhibitum, quando de dubiis pro falso habendis est locutus? agnosce ista verba & erubesce. Tenet ipsum hujus conscientia, metuque correptus, sequentibus verbis latebras quaerit, eo sensu quem fingit adversarius: eo sensu, non licit, id pro falso habendum Cartesius. Quis tandem ille sensus? eo sensu, quo caelum non esse, corpora non esse supponit. Vide locum quem citavi & patet. Eo sensu, misera cavillatio, eo sensu, quo difficile, quo laboriosum, quo periculosum, quo semel licitum est, ex Cartesii & tua hypothesi: Si ille bonus & utilis[?]ve; periculosum define, semel licitum, laboriosum esse vociferari define. Ista autem non lubet hac occasione prosequi ulterius. Non soli Peripatetici, non soli Scholastici, distinctionibus evadunt. 8. Dum sensuum fides ita vacillat, imo pro nulla habetur, unde fidei erit certitudo, dum nec auribus fidis, nec oculis, quid verbum, quid Sacramenta revelabunt, significabunt? 9. Haec conditio thesin tuam evertit necessario, vis dubitare de existentia rerum corpora-rum, idque data opera, serio & obstinate in ea meditatione defixus; omnium opinionum vacas eversioni: [?]que ex fide, quam sartam rectamque fingis, interim corpora esse, existere, creata esse, constat. Tandem subvertit haec exceptio, quintam. Dubitatio enim si talis assensus solum cohibitio sit, cer-te[?], aut in rebus fidei temere agendum erit, iisque antequam de earum certitudine clare quicquam constet, as[?]sentiendum, aut à dubitatione non removendae.
units.tr: 2. He does not agree with Clauberg, who says (1) that this doubt is to be raised only once, and indeed (2) at the beginning, for one who is starting philosophy, and (3) that it should last only a very short time. If this doubt is raised as the Skeptics' objection, what reason is there that it should be imposed so briefly and only once, and only on one who has just begun to philosophize? Are the Skeptics' arguments to be put forward only once, or only to beginners? See how these entangled trifles cancel each other out. 3. He does not agree with the remaining exceptions. Not with the second, for doubts also arise about matters of faith. Not with the third, for doubts also arise about principles and simple notions. Not with the fourth, for the Skeptics doubt also about things to be done: "The Skeptics, who neglected human affairs to such an extent that they had to be kept by their friends so that they would not throw themselves over precipices," says Descartes. Nor is he right about the fifth, for the Skeptics did not withhold assent until they perceived the matter clearly and distinctly; they always did so. For they doubted in order to doubt, says Descartes. I conclude, therefore, that the first exception carries no weight. I come now to the second, and I say: 1. Let us suppose you want this, but meanwhile let it be granted that the certainty of revelation is established, or can be established. Is it then lawful for a pagan, who perhaps recognizes no supernatural revelation, to doubt the matter in question? Could he then doubt about God, etc., without danger of sinning? 2. If it is only intended, as Clauberg says, that, assuming the certainty of revealed truths, one should try to see whether some things are also established from nature, then certainly that task is not of such great labour. Nor is it of such great danger. 3. 4. What, then, can those words about doubt, or the Skeptics' objections, properly mean? For those who seek no other kind of certainty, while they deny every kind, are not doubting in that sense. 5. Why should it not also be possible to doubt about things to be done in this way? For Scripture would sufficiently provide that a man who doubts in this way does not throw himself into a pit or into fire. 6. You also absurdly except principles and simple notions, since one could doubt about these in this same way, most safely. 7. If they seriously want the exceptions concerning matters of faith, how can Descartes admit an absolute doubt, "in the contemplation of truth," and one so great that "no more distrust than is fitting can be indulged", since the one who doubts in this way is occupied not with things to be done but only with things to be known? For one of two things follows: either the contemplation of truth has no connection at all with faith, or it is lawful to doubt all matters of faith as well. The first of these sets before us a gross Papism, which, with Bellarmine, describes faith by the greatest ignorance, more absurd than a charcoal-burner's faith; the second overturns the exception made by Descartes. 8. The existence of God is undoubtedly also a matter of faith (Heb. 11), and yet this is among the things that Descartes, among others, calls into doubt. This stirs Clauberg's bile: "similar examples are brought forward only to stir up the reader's hatred against the Cartesians," he complains. But he would have kept silent about these things if he had not wanted to raise the objections; too late he becomes wise, either to defend or to recall what has slipped out. "But they were not applied by Descartes when he spoke about holding the doubtful to be false." Why, then, do you allege what is false, and reproach Clauberg with stirring up hatred against your opponents, rather than just citing the passage? Clearly it could not be said truthfully; without doubt you were not ignorant of what Descartes said. After he had come to this doubt with great and troublesome labour, he begins thus: "I do not yet know well enough whether there is any God. I must examine whether there is a God, for while this is unknown &c. Thus, rejecting all those things about which we can in any way doubt, and even pretending that they are false, we easily suppose that there is no God, no heaven, no bodies." The passage that occurs in the Letters is most clear. There he argues thus, when asked "whether it is ever lawful to doubt the existence of God": he replies that "if anyone proposes this doubt to himself as a means of coming to a clearer knowledge of the truth, he does what is most pious and honourable." With what face, then, do you write that Descartes did not apply that example when he spoke about doubts to be held as false? Acknowledge these words and blush. His own conscience holds him, and, seized with fear, he seeks a hiding place in the following words: "in the sense which my opponent invents: in that sense," it is not lawful for Descartes to hold it as false. What, pray, is that sense? In that sense in which he supposes that there is no heaven and no bodies. See the passage I cited, and it is plain. "In that sense," miserable quibbling; "in that sense" in which it is difficult, laborious, dangerous, and once permitted, according to your and Descartes' hypothesis: if he calls it good and useful, define it as dangerous; if he calls it permitted once, define it as laborious. I do not wish to pursue these matters further on this occasion. Not only the Peripatetics and the Scholastics escape by distinctions. 8. While the trustworthiness of the senses so wavers, indeed is held to be nothing, whence will there be certainty of faith, when neither trustworthy ears nor eyes, nor what the Word or the Sacraments reveal or signify, can give it? 9. This condition necessarily overturns your thesis. You want to doubt the existence of corporeal things, and that deliberately, "fixed earnestly and stubbornly in that meditation; you are free for the overthrow of all opinions"; and yet, from the faith which you feign to be whole and right, it is established that bodies exist, are, and have been created. Finally, this exception overturns the fifth. For if doubt is merely the withholding of such assent, then either in matters of faith one must act rashly and assent to them before anything is clearly established about their certainty, or they must not be removed from doubt.

units.la: Tertiam sic refuto 1. Si vera est prima exceptio, ista necessario falsa est, Sceptici enim æque de principiis, æque notionibus simplicibus dubitant ac de reliquis.
units.tr: I refute the third exception thus. 1. If the first exception is true, this one is necessarily false, for the Skeptics doubt principles and simple notions just as much as the rest.

units.la: Ridicula est haec exceptio, nondum enim novi [?]quid sit simplex quid complexa notio, quid principium, quid conclusio? imo an sit, an detur, au[?] conclusio aut principium &c. praesertim cum quae[?] stio quid sit, solvi debeat, Cartesianorum jussu, ant[?] quaestionem an sit res: se quoque mentemque suan[?] nondum quid novit, quid ille de notione simplic[?] aut complexa? 3. Contraria est illi universalitati[?] quam probatam dedimus. 4.Pugnat cum exsertis ver[?] bis Cartesii. Quid cum circa res Arithmeticas ve[?] Geometricas aliquid valde simplex & facile considera[?] bam, ut quod duo & tria simul juncta sint quinque[?] equidem de iis dubitandum esse postea judicavi, po[?] tuisset enim mihi mens indita esse ut etiam circa illa qu[?] manifestissima viderentur deciperer. Et alibi opinionum[?] suarum eversioni vacaturus, omnes rejiciendas dici[?] aggrediar statim NB. ipsa principia. Quas jam notic[?] nes simplices excipiet Claubergius. Excipiendas[?] censet, Philosophum suum corrigat, doceatque agen[?] cautius. Enumeret istas notiones simplices. Quic[?] quid sit, hoc certum est, ille mentis actus, quo no[?] tiones simplices apprehenduntur, posset tibi a mal[?] gno genio forsan, aut saltem aliunde quam a re ip[?] esse inditus, sicque incertus es, an non fallaris, dur[?] putas, istam, exempli gratia, simplicem notionem[?] menti tuae obversari revera, maxime cum nec mer[?] tis tuae tibi constet hactenus existentia, quae illarur[?] sit subjectum notionum. 5. Et si istam exceptioner[?] admitterem, quid jam porro? in simplicem appre[?] hensionem, cum, ex vestra sententia, verum non ca[?] dat vel falsum, sequitur nullam, vel hac exceptior[?] admissa, excipi a dubitatione veritatem, sicque c[?] omnibus veritatibus complexis, ut Deum existere, t[?] esse, praeter te quicquam dari, dubitandum, quc[?] tanto conatu removendum a vobis, ut falso imp[?] Ctum censetis. Quarta ejusdem farinae est, ad praxi[?] vitae enim si scepsin[?] transferendam negas 1. In omn[?] saltem veritatis contemplatione eam concedis. 2. A[?] que hactenus quamdiu sic dubitas, Academicis nullo modo melior videris, quos tamen Scepticis annu-merandos rite censet Cartesius & Wolzogius, diffe-rentiæ licet nonnihil invenire inter ipsos detur: sic autem Academici, minus etsi auderent affirmare se se rerum verarum vera visa percipere, impellebantur tamen æque certo visis probabilibus ad agendum, ac si vera illa esse indubitanter cognovissent, & in tantum distabant à Pyrrhoniis, teste Amyraldo, Schoo-kio aliisque. Sicque evanescit fi&ta illa, quam tanto-pere jactatis, vos inter & Scepticos omnes, in dubi-tatione vestra differentia. Praxin enim vitæ, æque ac vos, in incerto omnem non posuerunt Academici. Estis ergo pares. 3. Pyrrhonios vero si respiciam, cadit prima exceptio; ea enim totum dubitationis negotium, objectionem dicit Scepticorum esse, quorum si istos, quos Pyrrhonios dicimus, putas, absurde vitæ praxin excipis, illam enim æque ac veritatis contemplationem incertam esse voluerunt, ex sensu Cartesii, stulti mortales. 4. Ipsa veritatis contemplatio, per se, praxeos, ut ita loquar, pars est, Tenemur enim scire cognoscenda, non minus quam facienda facere. 5. Ut taceam absurdam fore vitæ praxin, quæ veritatis orbata cognitione est, ac si in tenebris sine omni face quis tuto incederet. Quintam quod attinet, eam & vocis significatio & priores exceptiones sponte tollunt. Aliud etiam quid eos velle luce meridiana clarius est. E diverticulo autem in viam redeundum tandem. Satis enim ad refutandas futiles istas tergiversationes erunt quæ diximus. Superesset, ut jam generalis hujus dubitationis evincerem & demonstrarem, inutilitatem atque absurditatem; sed ἀὐλογαπάτ[?]κτοι[?] in eo apparent Cartesiani. Quorsum enim tanta, ad restringendam limitandamque excogitassent, nisi de absurditate istius dubitationis abunde essent convicti? Modicum tractatum illa Claubergio extorsit circumspecta anxietas. Ægre autem si quis ferat contradictiones à me Cartesio impactas esse, is plura, quibus eæ probentur specimina, facili negotio, si id nunc ageretur, colligi posse resciscat. Unicum impræsentiarum sufficiet, quod & tam palpabile est, ut præteriri non debeat. Uno loco se egisse negat, quod tamen se egisse alibi asserit. Animæ immortalitatem se probasse gloriatur hisce verbis bis: Et quia non eodem modo ipsis (de Scepticis, vel potius Academicis loquitur & Atheis) apparet Deum existere, mentemque humanam esse immortalem; ideo his ne quidem in praxi tanquam veris utendum putant, nisi prius sibi probata fuerint, rationibus magis certis, quam sint ulla ex iis ob quas apparentia omnia amplectuntur. Quæ cum NB. à me sic probata sint & NB. à nemine ante me &c. Alio autem loco se nihil de immortalitate animæ scripisse refert. Sic sonant verba. Cur de immortalitate animæ nihil scripserim, jam dixi in Synopsi mearum Meditationum: Quod ejus ab omni corpore distinctionem satis probaverim, supra ostendi. Quod vero additis, adversarios alloquitur, ex distinctione animæ à corpore non sequi ejus immortalitatem; quia nihilominus dici potest illam à Deo talis naturæ factam esse ut ejus duratio simul cum duratione vitæ corporeæ finiatur, fateor à me refelli non posse. Non nimis tuto proinde ipsi fidimus, odiosam illam dubitationem quando amoliri satagit, loco ex Not. ad Programm. ante citato: verba enim si ponderes paulo penticulatius, non rotunde candideque, sed subdole negari deprehendes impactum crimen: non enim inficiatur se unquam dubitasse, aut dubitare conatum esse; sed solum, se non dubitasse cum illas meditationes conscriberet: at hoc non objicitur, negare debuisset, se in illis meditationibus non agere Historicum, ac enarrare quid sibi aliquando acciderit, ut sibi accidisse dicit Tract. de Methodo, exserte enim inibi atetur[?] se dubitasse, quanquam non ut dubitant Scepti-ci; dubitasse se revera cum Scepticis innuit, sed duratione ac fine suam à Scepticorum differre prætexit dubitationem. Dubitavit igitur revera de omnibus, sed non semper, non ut dubitaret. Vela contraho, alias forsan, Deo volente & negotiis laboriosi ministerii id ferentibus, de hisce aliisque novæ Philosophiæ Mysteriis latius. Hæc videbantur omitti non posse, ut appareat absque omni ratione, Cartesianæ Philosophiæ laudes, ita largiter emetitum esse Wolzogium.
units.tr: This exception is ridiculous. For I do not yet know what a simple notion is, or what a complex one is, what a principle is, or what a conclusion is. Indeed I do not know whether a conclusion or a principle exists, or is given, and so on, especially since the question of what a thing is must be solved, by the order of the Cartesians, before the question of whether a thing exists. Does he himself, or his mind, yet know what he is, or what he thinks about a simple or complex notion? 3. It is contrary to that universality which we have proved. 4. It conflicts with the express words of Descartes. When I was considering something very simple and easy about arithmetical or geometrical matters, such as that two and three added together make five, I later judged that even these should be doubted, for my mind could have been created in such a way that I was deceived even about those things which seemed most manifest. And, intending to turn to the overthrow of his opinions, I shall at once attack the principles themselves, which are to be rejected. NB. Which simple notions will Clauberg except? He thinks they should be excepted. Let him correct his philosophy and teach us to act more cautiously. Let him list those simple notions. Whatever it is, this is certain: that act of the mind by which simple notions are grasped may have been put into you by an evil genius, perhaps, or at least from somewhere other than from the thing itself. And so you are uncertain whether you are not deceived when you think that this simple notion, for example, truly presents itself to your mind, especially since the existence of that thing which is to be the subject of the notions is not yet certain to you, even by your own reasoning. 5. And even if I were to admit this exception, what next? In simple apprehension, since, by your opinion, truth or falsity does not arise, it follows that either no truth is excepted from doubt, or, with this exception admitted, truth is excepted from doubt. And so, with all complex truths, such as that God exists, that you are, and that nothing exists apart from you, must be doubted; and this, which you think is falsely imputed to you, you yourselves strive so hard to remove. Of the same kind is the fourth. For if you deny that the doubt should be transferred to the practice of life, 1. you at least concede it in every contemplation of truth. 2. And as long as you doubt in this way, you seem in no way better than the Academics, whom Descartes and Wolzogen nevertheless rightly count among the Sceptics, although some difference between them may be found. For the Academics, although they would not dare to affirm that they perceived the true appearances of true things, were nonetheless driven by probable appearances to act with no less certainty than if they had known those things to be true beyond doubt; and, as Amyraldus, Schoockius and others testify, they differed so much from the Pyrrhonists. And so that fiction which you make so much of, the difference between you and all the Sceptics in your doubt, vanishes. For the Academics did not place the whole practice of life in uncertainty, as you do not. You are therefore equals. 3. But if I look to the Pyrrhonists, the first exception falls; for it says that the whole business of doubt belongs to the objection of the Sceptics. If you think those whom we call Pyrrhonists are such, you absurdly except the practice of life; for they wished it, as well as the contemplation of truth, to be uncertain, in the sense of Descartes: foolish mortals! 4. The contemplation of truth itself, in itself, is part of practice, so to speak. For we are bound to know what is to be known no less than to do what is to be done. 5. Not to mention that the practice of life would be absurd if it were deprived of knowledge of the truth, as if someone walked safely in darkness without any torch. As for the fifth, both the meaning of the word and the earlier exceptions remove it of their own accord. What they wish by it is clearer than the midday light. But we must at last return from the byway to the road. For what we have said will be enough to refute these futile evasions. It would remain for me now to prove and demonstrate the uselessness and absurdity of this general doubt; but the Cartesians betray their error plainly ([ἀὐλογαπάτ[?]κτοι[?]]). For why would they have devised such a great effort to restrict and limit it, unless they had been abundantly convicted of its absurdity? A careful anxiety wrung a modest treatise from Clauberg. If anyone takes it badly that I have charged Descartes with contradictions, let him learn that, if that were the present purpose, many more examples proving them could easily be gathered. One is enough for now, and it is so palpable that it ought not to be passed over. In one place he denies that he has done what he yet asserts elsewhere that he has done. He boasts twice, in these words, that he has proved the immortality of the soul: And because it does not appear in the same way to them (he speaks of the Sceptics, or rather the Academics and Atheists) that God exists and that the human mind is immortal, they think that these things should not even be used in practice as true unless they have first been proved by reasons more certain than any of those by which they embrace all appearances. Since these things have been NB. proved thus by me, and NB. by no one before me, etc. In another place, however, he reports that he has written nothing about the immortality of the soul. The words sound thus: Why I have written nothing about the immortality of the soul I have already said in the Synopsis of my Meditations: that I have sufficiently proved its distinction from every body, I have shown above. But what you add, that by addressing our opponents you do not infer its immortality from the distinction of the soul from the body, because it may nevertheless be said that God made it of such a nature that its duration ends together with the duration of bodily life, I confess I cannot refute. We therefore do not trust him too much when he strives to remove that hateful doubt by the passage cited earlier from the Notes on the Programme. For if you weigh the words a little more carefully, you will find that the charge is denied not frankly and candidly but craftily. For he does not deny that he ever doubted, or tried to doubt; he only denies that he doubted when he was writing those meditations. But that is not what is objected to him. He ought to have denied that in those Meditations he was not acting as a historian and narrating what had once happened to him, as he says happened to him in the Treatise on Method. For there he expressly admits that he doubted, though not as the Sceptics doubt. He hints that he really doubted along with the Sceptics, but pretends that his doubt differs from theirs in duration and end. He therefore did doubt about all things, but not always, and not so that he might doubt. I draw in my sails, perhaps to speak more fully, God willing, and if the labours of my laborious ministry allow, about these and other mysteries of the new philosophy. These points seemed not to be omitted, so that it may appear that Wolzogen, without any reason, so lavishly measured out the praises of the Cartesian philosophy.

units.la: Pagina 198. Postquam tantopere laudasset Philo-sophiam Cartesianam, abusum ejusdem in Paradoxo suo corrigit, sicque captata occasione, à magno præjudicio Philosophiam istam suam liberandam credidit, ne forsan vitium illud, quo laborat Paradoxus, qui illotis manibus Philosophiam Theologiæ ingerit, imo magistram creat, Cartesio male cedat, aut ejus Philosophiæ detrimento sit. Cartesius è contra, Wolzogio teste, Philosophiam non uno loco scripsit in Theologiæ provinciam irruere non debere, dixitque sæpissime, recordantibus amicis, hoc quidem esse spirituale adulterium si miscentur communi thalamo ratio humana & sapientia divina. Sic ab isto crimine est omnino innocens. Bona verba, sed quibus veritas aut sinceritas an non defit, sequentia incertum reddunt, quando id, de rebus solum, non de Interpreta-tione Scripturarum intelligendum, suspicatur Wolzogius: ac si rationem humanam cum sapientia divina communi thalamo non misceat, qui eam à rerum examine, non autem Scripturæ interpretatione arcet, sed ipsi concedit magnam saltem partem. Nec etiam eo sensu hisce inhæret Wolzogius, qui omnia nihilo excepto rationi examinanda tradit, & maxime Paradoxum oppugnaturus, aliquas res & veritates solum rationis imperium respuere docet, ut in se-quenquentibus patebit. Ista vero primariam concernunt controversiam, illa quod attinet, novimus quam serio, quam saepe iteratis protestationibus idem inculcaverint Cartesius & post eum Cartesiani, eorumque Coryphaeus Claubergius. Quod autem minorem fidem inveniant, vel in hoc negotio, duo sunt quae faciant, praeter ea quae attulit Revius, 1. Contraria Cartesii verba, quorum quaedam exhibebo, quae, tantum abest, ut Philosophiam à Theologiae sacrario arcendam serio consuerit, ut potius incomparabiles fructus huic ab illa certo expectandas promiserit, quod absque illius ad istam applicatione fieri, est impossibile. Deponat praejudicia & ista legat lector candidus, sic Cartesius. Quantum ad Theologiam, cum una veritas alteri adversari nunquam possit, esset impietas timere, ne veritates in Philosophia inventae iis quae sunt de fide adversentur: hactenus bene, verum Philosophice non deprehendi Theologice falsum. Loca Scripturae cum citat, aut explicat Cartesius, id tantum juxta Claubergium agit, ne ipsius Philosophia Theologiae contradicere credatur, sicque putat retundi ea, quae Revius, Cartesio Theologiae involatae & cum Philosophia mixta crimen impingens, profert. At plura dicit Cartesius, ut, quicquid protestentur, clament, spondeant, fidem tamen, qui Theologiam tutam à Cartesio promittunt, non merentur Cartesiani, nisi detrahatur Cartesio fides & suorum moliminum exactior notitia, sic enim dicta prosequitur: Atque omnino profiteor nihil ad religionem pertinere, quod non aeque, ac etiam magis facile explicetur per mea principia, quam per ea quae vulgo recepta sunt. Ecce nihil ad religionem pertinet, quod non magis facile per sua principia explicet &c. Pergat; Famæ[?] hujus rei mihi videor specimen dedisse satis luculentum, in fine meae Responsionis ad quartas Objectiones, circa quaestionem in qua omnium difficillime PhiloPhilosophia cum Theologia solet conciliari: (Missati-cam Transubstantiationem respicit.) Et idem NB. in aliis quibuslibet, si opus sit, præstare paratus sum. Imo eo provehitur, ut putet bonam, quid? nullam meliorem rationem esse ad Hæreses minuendas, quam si veræ opiniones, quales meas esse, sic verba sonant, jam probavi, recipiantur. Qui Hæreses, principiorum suo-rum Philosophicorum ope, minuendas, omnes quæ-stiones Theologicas explicandas promittit, facilius, quam ante hac factum sit? næ ille à Theologia belle arcet cohibetque Philosophiam. Hæc si legerit Wol-zogen mirum quod plane contrarium, adeoque con-tradictionem, tribuat Cartesio. 2. Cartesianorum quotidiana praxis id non minus perspicuum reddit. Claubergius de dubitatione agens, Bezam, Catechi-smum, Spanhemium, Perkinsium vel ipsum Augusti-num ad partes vocat, non alio fine, quam, ut ne à Theologia arcendam putemus Cartesianæ Philoso-phiæ Methodum. Plurimi autem, qui Cartesianis pla-citis addicti sunt, non loquor de omnibus, plurimi inquam eorum, in multis Theologiæ capitibus ex professo novaturiunt, vel saltem decessores carpendi, cuncta corrigendi, ansam sibi datam autumant. Ne alios jam irritem, (quanquam non timeam, quisquis sit, qui Ecclesiæ pacem novitatibus turbare aut Ec-clesiæ Doctorum, Scriptorumque publicorum, hono-rem, nomen, argumenta, phrases, audacter carpe-re, corrigere non veretur) Wolzogius & Velthuisius exemplo sint, qui quantum Cartesiana Methodo im-buti, in novorum conceptuum inventione profece-rint, abunde docent. Omnibus autem, laudem enim istam illi non denegandam existimo, palmam præri-pere voluisse videtur, Celeberrimus ille Lambertus Velthuisius, cujus dogmata subinde, hoc ipso tractatu refelluntur, vel saltem, quia sua absurditate saepissime corruunt, referuntur.
units.tr: Page 198. After praising the Cartesian philosophy so highly, he corrects its abuse in his Paradox, and, seizing the opportunity, he believed that his philosophy must be freed from a great prejudice. He feared that the fault from which the Paradox suffers, namely that of forcing philosophy upon theology with unwashed hands and even making it the mistress, might reflect badly on Descartes or harm his philosophy. Descartes, on the contrary, according to Wolzogen, wrote in more than one place that philosophy ought not to rush into the province of theology, and he said very often, as his friends recall, that it is indeed spiritual adultery if human reason and divine wisdom are mixed in the same marriage bed. So he is wholly innocent of that charge. These are fine words, but whether they lack truth or sincerity is uncertain from what follows, since Wolzogen suspects that this must be understood of things only, not of the interpretation of Scripture. As if one who keeps reason away from the examination of things but not from the interpretation of Scripture did not mix human reason with divine wisdom in the same bed, while still granting it at least a large part. Nor does Wolzogen adhere to these words in the sense in which he hands over everything to reason's examination without exception; and when he is about to attack the Paradox above all, he teaches that some matters and truths reject the rule of reason alone, as will appear in what follows. But these points concern the main controversy. As for the other point, we know how earnestly and how often, with repeated protestations, Descartes and after him the Cartesians, and their leader Clauberg, have pressed the same thing. That they win less credit even in this matter, there are two reasons, besides those which Revius has brought forward. (1) Descartes's own contrary words, some of which I shall set out. These show that he was so far from seriously wishing philosophy to be kept away from the sanctuary of theology that he rather promised from it incomparable fruits for theology, which cannot be achieved without applying it to theology. Let the candid reader lay aside his prejudices and read these words, says Descartes: As far as theology is concerned, since one truth can never oppose another, it would be impiety to fear that truths discovered in philosophy might conflict with those things which are matters of faith: so far, so good; but for philosophy, he does not perceive what is false theologically. When Descartes cites or explains passages of Scripture, he does so only in line with Clauberg, so that his philosophy is not believed to contradict theology; and he thinks that the charge which Revius brings, namely that Descartes has broken into theology and mixed it with philosophy, is thereby refuted. But Descartes says more, so that, whatever the Cartesians protest, proclaim or promise, that they keep theology safe from Descartes, they do not deserve to be trusted, unless Descartes's credit is withdrawn and a more exact knowledge of his undertakings is had. For he continues these words thus: And I openly declare that nothing pertains to religion which cannot be explained just as easily, or even more easily, through my principles than through those commonly received. Behold: nothing pertains to religion which he does not explain more easily through his own principles, and so on. Let him go on: I think I have given a sufficiently clear sample of this matter at the end of my Reply to the Fourth Objections, concerning the question on which philosophy is most difficult to reconcile with theology (he refers to the mystery of transubstantiation). And I am ready to do the same, nota bene, in any other cases, if need be. Indeed he goes so far as to think that there is no better way of reducing heresies than if true opinions, such as mine, as the words sound, are now accepted, and I have already proved them. Who promises that heresies may be reduced by means of his philosophical principles, and that all theological questions may be explained more easily than before? Surely he keeps philosophy well away from theology and holds it back. If Wolzogen has read these things, it is strange that he attributes to Descartes something plainly contrary and therefore contradictory. (2) The daily practice of the Cartesians makes this no less clear. Clauberg, when treating of doubt, calls Beza, the Catechism, Spanheim, Perkins, and even Augustine, to his side, for no other purpose than that we should not think the Cartesian method is to be kept away from theology. Yet very many of those who are devoted to Cartesian opinions (I do not speak of all, but very many of them) in many heads of theology deliberately bring in novelties, or at least believe that they have been given an occasion to censure their predecessors and correct everything. To say nothing more of others (though I do not fear, whoever he may be, who dares to disturb the peace of the Church with novelties, or who does not hesitate boldly to censure and correct the honour, name, arguments, and phrases of the Church's teachers and public writers), Wolzogen and Velthuysen are examples, who abundantly show how far they have progressed in devising new concepts, having been steeped in the Cartesian method. Of all of them, for I think that praise is not to be denied him, the most celebrated Lambert Velthuysen seems to have wished to snatch the palm, whose doctrines are refuted from time to time in this very treatise, or at least are reported, since they very often collapse through their own absurdity.

units.la: Quoniam autem, Strictura, ad priorem librum, quarta, mentionem feci multiplicium Velthuisii errorum, en aliquot specimina quibus dicta mea probem.
units.tr: Since, however, in my Critique of the first book, the fourth, I made mention of the manifold errors of Velthuysen, here are some specimens by which I shall prove what I have said.

units.la: In antecessum notari debet, valde honorifice ab ipso excipi Reformatos Theologos, Sic alicubi, postquam narraverat Janseniistarum, de Christi morte, sententiam, perplexe, inquit, loquuntur: & aliquando non videntur plus de illa docere, quam quod mors Christi in se spectata fuerit sufficiens pretium omnibus hominibus redimendis: quod tamen reipsa redemtio pro omnibus facta non sit. Quæ fuit doctrina NB. plurium Calvinistarum in Synodo Dordracena — à qua plurimi in Gallia Calvinistæ remoti sunt. Ita ut pauci Calvinistæ inter omnes sectas illam profiteantur. Sic ibi passim Calvinistas nominat Reformatos, non magis, quod sensa[?] attinet, scilicet hisce, quam Arminianis addictus aut aliis. Nullo partium studio laborat vir prudentissimus. At non melius veritati studet Reformatæ, quam honori Reformatorum, sic enim paulo post. Existimamus, posita creatura libera, ilico talem relationem inter Deum & illam creaturam nasci, ut, quamdiu Deus eam ut viatorem regere velit, bonum — nunquam necessariam causam habeat: & bonum quidem, non prædeterminantem gratiam; aut Dei destinationem intendentis aliquod bonum absolute in homine efficere. Et ideo dicimus quod Deus tales per gratiam suam credituros prævidet; neque illam fidem producit ut medium à se proficiscens. Et ita hoc sensu prædestinationem juxta præscientiam tuemur. Quatenus Deus neminem destinat ad vitam nisi sub conditione fidei, bonorum operum, & perseverantia in ambobus. Nam respectu illius liberi, quod in omnibus actionibus moralibus reperitur: & propter quod illæ actiones creaturæ liberæ actiones vocantur, & laude atque præmio, vituperio & poena digna æstimantur, repugnat, à Deo absolute aliquid destinari ad quod obtinendum moralis homihominis actio debet intercedere. Et idem illud liberum impedit ut concipiamus gratiam Dei prædeterminantem & physico modo operantem. Et paulo inferius: Alioquin credimus Deum omnium salutem velle; neminemque, ut reprobum, in suo decreto considerare quam qui gratiam suam respuerit: quam omnibus sufficientem, qua potuissent converti, offert. Deinde — Hoc tantum ab aliis discrepantes, quod à multis gratia resistatur, qua potuissent converti si voluissent. — — Et revera falluntur, qui arbitrantur gratiam ideo minorem aut minus efficacem esse, cui resisti potest, illa, cui non potest resisti. Et cum docemus cum aliis Deum omnium salutem velle, docemus quod suppeditatio sufficientium mediorum, quibus omnes salvari possunt, profecta sit ab amore Dei erga genus humanum. Et docemus in ipso tractatu, id sufficere, ut proprio loquendi modo Deus omnium salutem velle dicatur. Et tali modo tuemur gratiam universalem & mortem Christi pro omnibus &c. Atque ista quidem omnia habet Præ-satio. Librum ipsum inspiciamus & pauca delibemus. Consequentiis verba non gravabo, sola per se orthodoxo lectori displicebunt. Voluntati repugnat passive se habere. Decretum nos salvandi, etiam à periculo corporis, est conditionatum, sicut supra docuimus de termino vitæ. Illa pars ordinis, scilicet inter ea quæ fiunt vel non fiunt, quam creatura libera per peccatum sibi occupat, Dei voluntatem decernentem antecedit. Nullo decreto comprehendendus est hominis lapsus aut permissio lapsus, sequuntur enim per accidens ad alias res decretas, quibus intercedentibus post se novum decretum constitui requirunt. Postquam orthodoxam Calvini aliorumque sententiam, non quidem ex vero, sed pro more suo, declarasset, illos enim designari ipse novit & circumstantiæ docent, non dantur enim alii quibus simile quicquam impingatur, sic loquitur eodem libro pag. 75. Qui hujusmodi decretorum ordinem constituit, Regem sceleratum & tyrannum facit, & dignum qui omnibus infamia notis posteritati seculorum tradatur. Sic statuit pag. 89. omni viatori suppeditanda Deo incumbere media sufficientia, quae natura sua homini sufficiunt ad sectandam virtutem; quaeque tantum effectu careant propter malum libertatis usum. In eo autem Pelagianos superat quod illa media non vocanda sint gratia. Quoniam nisi isthaec media reipsa sufficientia essent, ut homo posset, si vellet, iis sibi a peccato cavere, sanctitas & amor Dei erga creaturam rationalem talia officia non imperarent: nec libertas in agendo esset de natura creaturae & actionum moralium. Neque ulla tam copiosa, tamque magna est gratia, quin homo, si velit, eam eludere possit, eamque pervertere, hoc est, homo semper manet Dominus suarum actionum. Dicimus itaque, media illa generalia quae Deus erga omnem creaturam rationalem depromit, non ideo non sufficientia vocanda, quia per eam homo sibi tantum cavere potest si velit. Nam, ut dixi, nulla gratia ulterius procedit. Et si homo vellet, etiam per illam gratiam vellet, eodem modo, quo per gratiam majorem. Major enim & minor gratia in hoc non dif-ferunt, quod major penitius se insinuet singulari alicui voluntatis actui, aut quod minor, si per eam vellemus, minus operaretur circa actum aliquem singula-rem voluntatis quam major. Et quamvis una gratia major sit quam altera, una tamen non est minus suffi-ciens quam altera. Libertas voluntatis, non obstante ejus inclinatione ad malum, ut semper manet eadem, sic & potentia reparandi illam infirmitatem, illa potentia nunquam augetur aut minuitur. Hoc fundamento innituntur[?] omnes admonitiones &c. qui-bus locus esse non potest, si illa potentia non mane-ret. Et explicans quomodo Deus in voluntatem agat quoties bonum operatur, physicum influendi modum omnem removet & sic disserit. Quoties autem talia menti obversantur, aut occasiones praebentur, quibus menti obversari possunt, propter quæ tanquam rationes justas & æquas voluntas bonum vult: & illa præterea talia sunt, ut nos, nostræ infirmitatis conscii, illa non nisi favore & gratia Dei habere possimus; id NB. vocatur fieri per gratiam. En gratiam Velthuisianam. Existimo do-ctrinam Theologorum in Belgio, qua negant gratiam universalem, cum Dei candore & sinceritate consistere non posse: neque conciliari posse cum sequentibus loquendi modis ex Scriptura petitis ———
units.tr: It should be noted at the outset how very honourably he receives the Reformed theologians. So somewhere, after he had recounted the view of the Jansenists on Christ's death, he says: they speak obscurely, and sometimes they do not seem to teach more about it than that the death of Christ, considered in itself, was a sufficient price for redeeming all men, which nonetheless was not in fact a redemption made for all. This was the doctrine of NB. many Calvinists at the Synod of Dort, from which very many Calvinists in France have withdrawn, so that few Calvinists among all the sects profess it. Thus he everywhere calls the Calvinists simply "the Reformed," no more attached, so far as these matters go, to these views than to the Arminians or others. That most prudent man labours under no partisan zeal. Yet he is no more concerned with the truth of the Reformed faith than with the honour of the Reformed, for shortly afterwards he says: We hold that, a free creature being posited, there straightway arises such a relation between God and that creature that, as long as God wishes to govern it as a wayfarer, it never has a necessary cause for good, and indeed not a predetermining grace, nor a good that God's intending destination brings about absolutely in man. And so we say that God foresees such people as will believe through his grace, and he does not produce that faith as a means proceeding from himself. In this sense we uphold predestination according to foreknowledge: insofar as God destines no one to life except under the condition of faith, good works, and perseverance in both. For with respect to that freedom which is found in all moral actions, and on account of which those actions are called free actions of a free creature and are judged worthy of praise and reward, blame and punishment, it is contrary to reason that anything should be destined absolutely by God for which the moral action of man must intervene in order to be obtained. And that same freedom prevents us from conceiving of a grace of God that predetermines and works in a physical manner. And a little further down: Otherwise we believe that God wills the salvation of all, and in his decree he regards no one as reprobate except him who has rejected his grace, which he offers sufficient for all, by which they could have been converted. Further: we differ from others only in this, that by many grace is resisted, by which they could have been converted if they had willed. And indeed those are mistaken who think that grace to which one can resist is for that reason smaller or less effective than that to which one cannot resist. And when we teach with others that God wills the salvation of all, we teach that the supply of sufficient means by which all can be saved has issued from the love of God towards the human race. And we teach in that same treatise that this suffices for God to be said, in the proper manner of speaking, to will the salvation of all. And in this way we uphold universal grace and the death of Christ for all, etc. All these things the Preface contains. Let us look at the book itself and examine a few points. I will not burden the reader with the consequences; they will displease the orthodox reader on their own. It is contrary to the will to be passive. The decree that we be saved, even from bodily danger, is conditional, just as we taught above concerning the term of life. That part of the order, namely among those things that are done or not done, which the free creature seizes for itself through sin, precedes the will of God decreeing. No decree comprehends the fall of man or the permission of the fall; for these follow by accident upon other things decreed, and to these, with other things intervening, they require a new decree to be established. After he had set forth, not indeed truthfully but in his own fashion, the orthodox view of Calvin and others (for he knows whom these terms designate, and the circumstances show it, since there are no others to whom anything of the kind could be imputed), he speaks thus in the same book, page 75: Whoever establishes this order of decrees makes God a wicked and tyrannical king, and one worthy to be handed down to posterity with infamous marks of every kind. He lays down on page 89: It lies upon God to supply to every wayfarer sufficient means, which by their nature suffice for man to pursue virtue, and which lack only effect because of the evil use of freedom. He surpasses the Pelagians in this, that these means are not to be called grace. For unless these means were in fact sufficient, so that man, if he wished, could guard himself from sin by them, the holiness and love of God towards the rational creature would not command such duties, nor would freedom in acting belong to the nature of the creature and of moral actions. Nor is any grace so abundant and so great that a man, if he wishes, cannot elude it and pervert it; that is, man always remains master of his own actions. We say therefore that those general means which God offers to every rational creature are not for that reason to be called non-sufficient, because through them a man can guard himself only if he wishes. For, as I said, no grace goes further. And if a man wished, he would wish through that grace in the same way as through a greater grace. For a greater and a lesser grace do not differ in this, that the greater penetrates more deeply into some single act of the will, or that the lesser, if we were to will through it, would work less upon some single act of the will than the greater. And although one grace is greater than another, one is not on that account less sufficient than another. The freedom of the will, notwithstanding its inclination to evil, remains always the same, and so too the power of repairing that weakness; that power is never increased or diminished. All admonitions etc. rest upon this foundation, and they could have no place if that power did not remain. And explaining how God acts upon the will whenever he works good, he removes every physical mode of influence and argues thus: Whenever such things present themselves to the mind, or occasions are offered by which they can present themselves to the mind, on account of which the will, as on just and equal reasons, wills the good; and moreover such things are of a kind that we, aware of our weakness, can have them only by the favour and grace of God; this NB. is called being done through grace. Behold the Velthuysian grace. I hold that the doctrine of the theologians in Belgium, which denies universal grace, cannot be consistent with the candour and sincerity of God, nor can it be reconciled with the following ways of speaking taken from Scripture ———

units.la: Quia ex illorum Doctorum sententia, Deus non tantum non omnibus media sufficientia suppeditavit quibus salus obtineri possit: sed &c. Sæpius re-sistimus illi gratiæ, per quam potuissemus salvari, si voluissemus: & per quam potuimus velle. Multi hoc vel illud fecissent, si Deus eos in iis circumstantiis constituisset Luc. x. 13. Act. vii. 51. &c.
units.tr: For according to the view of those teachers, God has not only not supplied all men with sufficient means by which salvation can be obtained, but etc. Often we resist that grace by which we could have been saved, had we willed, and by which we were able to will. Many would have done this or that, had God placed them in such circumstances. Luke 10:13; Acts 7:51, etc.

units.la: Quæ loca docent gratiæ sufficientiam; nihilque ei de-fuisse, quare homines se ea convertere non potuissent.
units.tr: These passages teach the sufficiency of grace, and that nothing was lacking to it on account of which men could not have been converted by it.

units.la: Quamdiu aliquis ut viator consideratur, tam diu non est reprobus. Nomen reprobi & reprobationis ubique sumitur pro homine gratiam oblatam contumaciter repudiante. 1 Cor. ix. 29. 2 Cor. xiii. 5. Hebr. vi. 8.
units.tr: As long as someone is considered as a wayfarer, so long he is not reprobate. The name of reprobate and of reprobation is everywhere used for a man who stubbornly rejects offered grace. 1 Cor. 9:29; 2 Cor. 13:5; Heb. 6:8.

units.la: Venit Christus ut omnes salvaret. 1 Tim. ii. 6. 1 Cor. xv. 22. Hebr. ii. 9. Tit. ii. Rom. i. 5. Omnibusque in illum finem sufficientia confert auxilia, sufficientemque gratiam. Et ita mors Christi fuit efficax pro omnibus: quatenus morte Christi effectum est, ut Deus omnes homines peccatores, & reatui obnoxios, quando se convertunt, & in Chri-stum credunt, sine poena dimittere, & pro sibi gratis atque delectis habeat: quatenus illa mors per rationem pœnalis satisfactionis effecit ut ratio ex attributo justitiæ Dei fluens, non flagitet, ut peccatores ipsi puniantur. Cum autem multi pereant, se-quitur etiam multos perire, pro quibus Christus mortuus est. In primo tamen momento conversionis, homo non est considerandus ut mortuus, & ut passive se habens. Sic totum Pelagianismum palam, reponit atque hic Wolzogio orthodoxiae tenax est; Paradoxus autem, nihil habet, quod vel lineam referat veri Velthuisii. Ego econtra heterodoxum dico & Velthuisium & Wolzogium ea approbantem & omnes quotquot talia dogmata docent ac defendunt, judicet Ecclesia Reformata ex verbo Dei, imo judicavit in suis Catechismis & confessionibus Synodique Dordracenae canonibus & condemnavit ea, quae scribentem vidimus Velthuisium. Sed aliquid adhuc taedii devorandum erit.
units.tr: Christ came that he might save all. 1 Tim. 2:6; 1 Cor. 15:22; Heb. 2:9; Titus 2; Rom. 1:5. And to that end he confers sufficient helps and sufficient grace on all. And thus the death of Christ was efficacious for all: inasmuch as through the death of Christ it was brought about that God, when they turn and believe in Christ, forgives without punishment all men who are sinners and liable to guilt, and holds them as his own and chosen; inasmuch as that death, by the manner of a penal satisfaction, has brought it about that the reason flowing from the attribute of God's justice does not demand that the sinners themselves be punished. Since, however, many perish, it follows also that many perish for whom Christ died. At the first moment of conversion, however, man is not to be considered as dead, and as passively disposed. Thus he openly rebuilds the whole of Pelagianism, and here he is tenacious of orthodoxy with Wolzogen; but his paradox has nothing that even reflects a line of the true Velthuysen. For my part, I call heterodox both Velthuysen and Wolzogen, who approve these things, and all who teach and defend such dogmas; let the Reformed Church judge them by the Word of God. Indeed, it has judged them in its Catechisms and Confessions and in the canons of the Synod of Dort, and it has condemned those things which we have seen Velthuysen writing. But some further weariness must still be endured.

units.la: Videamus libellum de Poena; nam & illic plurima occurrunt, quae genium Pelagianum aut similem redolentia, notari debent. Ut, quod habet de moralitate. Omnis moralitatis ratio cessat, quando poena e medio tollitur. Quare quæso[?] furari diceremus peccatum; reddere unicuique suum, virtutem: si putaremus ea post se nullam poenam aut præ-mium habere. Qui gratiam universalem negant, sic argumentari solent: pro quibus debitum solutum est illi absolvi debent reatu: si solutum pro omnibus, ergo omnes debent reatu solvi, ergo omnes salvari; sed quia omnes non salvantur ideo statuendum pro omnibus non esse satisfactum. Hujusmodi argumentationes nullum pondus habent. Deus hominem peccaturum praviderat ante suum decretum. Est hoc per se notum & inter notiones primas recensendum: neminem culpandum nisi qui voluntarie peccat. Manifestum est Deum vitiosos habitus nec odisse nec punire. Constare existimo 1. neminem propter peccatum alterius respectu justitiae divinae naturalis reum constitui, aut poenam proprie dictam subire. bire. 2. Adami peccatum ita Adamo soli adscriben-dum, ut ejus posteritas, quæ tum temporis nondum exstabat, nullo modo in criminis societatem venerit, aut venire potuerit. 3. Posteritatem Adami nec mor-tis, nec reliquarum calamitatum tam spiritualium quam corporalium participem esse, quia rei in Ada-mo. Posteri Adami non fiunt rei, quam per proprium suum actuale peccatum: quatenus in utero matris mens se à Deo avertit. Concedendum puto, men-tem in utero pro modulo usus rationis, bona & ma-la quædam cognoscere, quæ ipsam per culpandam negligentiam aut fugiunt, aut contra quæ sciens pec-cat. Manifesto sequitur nos etiam in utero matris peccare. Quæ sequuntur ex Tractatu altero de Prædest. desumta sunt. Objectum electionis est ho-mo illa morali qualitate fidei affectus. Omnis vo-luntas excludit sua natura impotentiam, qua non possit omnia velle. Gratia NB. tantum est conside-randa tamquam in voluntatem reipsa jam volentem constitutam; & non ex non volente volentem facien-tem. Nullus gratiam qua regeneramur aut perse-veramus aliter concipere debet, quam quæ possit re-pudiari. Infideles, imo reprobi, & qui sunt deleti ex libro vitæ ——— etiam sibi polliceri possunt Deum eos nunquam in hac vita deserturum sua gratia, sed ipsum iis semper ea gratia præsentem fore, qua con-vertantur & se conversuri sunt, modo eam gratiam non abjiciant. Reliqua, quæ in hac de gratia & prædestinatione doctrina creditu sunt necessaria etiam ratione ita nota sunt, ut tanquam notiones primæ in-fixæ sint hominum menti. Quæstiones, An omnis homo viator possit se convertere? An hominibus suf-ficiens suppeditetur gratia? Utrum resistibiliter an irresistibiliter gratia operetur? An homo se habeat pas-sive in regenerationis primordiis? An Deus faciat hominem velle? An prædeterminet voluntatem ho-minis? minis ? An non sit de natura gratiae ut faciat homi-nem velle ? An qui convertuntur non convertantur gratia efficaciori ea, cui non conversi resistunt ? sunt quaestiones, quas movere, & iis sententiam suam inter-ponere aeque absurdum est ac quaerere cujus figurae, aut coloris sit anima: & definire illam esse rubram aut viridem, rotundam aut quadratam. Et sic finit bel-lulum istum tractatum. Sufficerent quidem ista, ad probandam hominis heterodoxiam, specimina; ve-rum ne reliqua neglecta conqueratur, ad Initia Pri-mae Philosophiae transeo; nec iis etiam quicquam refutationis addam, sunt enim ita posita omnia, ultro & per se ut Heterodoxiam suam prodant & falsitatem; quamquam si plura velit, per Dei gratiam in antidotis praescribendis, quam ille in venenis porrigendis, minus largi non erimus. Hac vice solum audiamus praeclara dogmata. Immensitas ante creationem cor-porum Deo attribui non potest. Fundamentum omni-praesentiae divinae, est summa illa eminentia Dei, qua omnes res corporales ab ipsi dependent. In precibus est causa quare Deus destinarit quosdam periculo eripere. Deus, eo, quod per accidens aliquem causarum ordi-nem sequitur, existente, pergit alia ordinare. Sorte ludicra victum quaerere rem licitam & laudabilem ju-dico. An Deus nolit mentem nostram amplius existe-re, quando jam post corporis destructionem sensu & imaginatione uti non potest; id ex mentis contempla-tione nobis innotescere non potest. Intellectione proprie dicta nunquam peccatur. Nomen vitae male de brutis usurpatur. Statuendum id tantum Deo competere, aut non competere, quod ratio Deo inesse aut non inesse dictat. Quis non videt veritati & justitiae Dei repu-gnare aliquem viatorum numero habere: legere regere: praemia & poenas proponere ─── nec tamen illi, quem ita regis, id reliqui fecisse, ut se possit convertere. Ex putido, quem de jure Ecclesiasticorum scripsisse fertur libello, hæc habe, quæ genuinam libertini cujusdam imaginem referre multis videbuntur. Omnis docentium authoritas nihil aliud est quam opinio majoris scientiæ conjuncta cum probitate. Quemadmodum hoc vulgo contingere videmus, in omnibus aliis artificibus, qui alicujus artificii vulgo magis periti existimantur. Externam religionem quæ tota corporalis est solam curant Ecclesiastici, idque solo Prodeorum jussu, non internam. Porro [illegible, ~5 letters] Apostolis, imo vel ipso Christo factas persecutiones, justas fuisse, jam discere potest qui velit. Fingit quidam jussum divinum, de hoc aut illo annunciando obtigisse, dicitque, si Prodiis de Dei patefacientis jussu non con-stiterit, quamvis etiam quis forte annunciare jussus sit; Rationi Naturali sive Deo per eam imperanti nihil adversi eos commissuros sed etiam pie rectéque annunciationes istas prohibituros.
