Recte igitur Galliarum Rex, aliique, Reformatorum Pastoribus silentium imponunt, eosque, annunciantes verbum Dei & veram Religionem, puniunt aut pellunt: Non enim Regi constat, Dei jussu illos loqui, quos persequitur. Quemadmodum Pilatus & Judæorum primates Dominum gloriæ, Stephanum, Petrum & reliquos Apostolos factaque iis jussa non agnoscebant. Ut jam, quicquid Apostoli, quicquid Christus Dominus, aut ejus fideles ministri, Pilato, Judæorum præfectis & deinceps Imperatoribus ac Principibus invitis egerint ad hominum aliorum institutionem & conversionem, pro peccato habendum sit. Tremor occupat artus! Statuit enim Prodeos adeo Jure Civitatis (prodivino, vel etiam divino dicere liceret) dominari, ut quidvis ipsis manifesto taciteque volentibus, NIHIL, ipsis invitis sive manifesto taciteque vetantibus, agere, facere, præsertim in alios cives, civibus liceat: O Antichristianismi Politici promachum! ô intolerandæ tyrannidis propugnatorem nequissimum! tale jugum Belgis imminet, si ex sensu isto res gerendae aliquando erunt. Non no- stri Magistratus, non libertatis à Tyrannide, Hi- spani Prodei, vindices, ista, sed tyranni, pro vero sument rectoque: ut & illud, quod ad calcem hu- jus foetidi libelli cunctis subditis credendum injun- git. Omnia Prodiis licere, sibi autem ipso jure nihil licere & hinc ipsum Deum Optimum Maximum in Prodiis suis in omnibus & per omnia obsequuntur. Tanta quippe aequitas ab hoc homine expectanda non videtur, quantam, de Judaici populi seniori- bus sperari posse censebant Apostoli, dicentes: An justum sit, in conspectu Dei, vobis potius auscul- tare, quam Deo, ipsi judicate. Daniel sese turpis idoli venerationi opponendo, Paulus adversus E- phesiorum Dianam graviter intonando, omnes de- nique Confessores & Martyres sub Imperatoribus & Papis Paganae aut Papanae idololatriae resisten- do, deque iis, invitis Prodiis, concives erudien- do, heu quantum hoc judice, commiserunt sce- lus! quam justas dederunt poenas! Adderem ejus- dem furfuris quaedam ex Belgice scriptis specimi- na, ut quod, an Deus sua essentia sit omniprasens aut ubique; an Deo quicquam novi, aliquid in tem- pore efficiendo, accedat; aut an aliquid de novo velle, Dei beatitudini repugnet; an Dei decreta sint condi- tionalia: quod illa inquam Scriptura Textibus cla- ris aut perspicuis non contineantur. Quod Scriptura & Ratio sint regula fidei. Ecclesia non habet jus, instar judicis sub ratione poenae, Apostatas Disci- plina Ecclesiastica castigandi. Potestas Clavium cum vera Ecclesia data sit, nullusque judex sit, qui de- cidat quaenam sit vera Ecclesia, nulla etiam proin- de sibi eam jure arrogare potest. Verum neque Pa- stores, neque ullum collegium jus habet, diversum sentientes corripiendi, aut iis, ad communionem ea- que que commoda, quae membris competunt, admissionem denegandi. Cujus contrarium vim conscientiis in-fert. Hoc axioma, quod ultimum est in executione,id primum est in intentione, absurde ponitur; quoniam Deum & homines Tyrannos facit injustos atque hypocritas. Se ipsum occidere non debere moralenon est. Sed nauseam moveret lectori, si plura, ex tam putidis lacunis hausta, absque addito antidoto, apponerem, & necesse forsan aliquando erit, eodem idiomate, piis omnibus, fidisque patriae nostrae incolis ac Magistratibus hujus novi Antichristianismi specimina exhibere; nisi desinant, insulsos & maleferiatos ejusmodi foetus in lucem protrudere, homines mundani. Atque ista quidem hactenus. Si autem breves vindicias prioribus (Specimen calumniarum vocat) similes edere velit, hoc sciat, nihil me, praeter veritatis studium, adversus ipsum incitasse; idemque me, quoad vivam, Deo volente, incitaturum, ad veritatis & pietatis, pro virium modulo, causam agendam, tam privatim, quam publice. In quarum neutram si quis incurrat, nihil is nimis magnificum de obedientia Magistratibus debita mihi dixerit. Deo quae Dei sunt, & Caesari quae Caesaris. Quoniam vero candide & aperte secum agi vult Velthuisius, neque judicia, sive Politica, sive Ecclesiastica, declinare. Bene est. Judicet una-que in Belgio Synodus, judicet Theologica cujuscunque Academiae Reformatae facultas. Aperte eum exsupra positis, erroris non unius, sed plurium reum dico & scribo. En culpam sibi, prout voluit, impactam, en judices minime spernendos. Legibus enim, sic loquitur, & causa in hoc negotio me nullibi inferiorem fore confido. Excerpta illa bona fide posui, neque pluribus egent, per se satis perspicua. Ut circumstantias requiri, non nisi fri-
units.tr: Let us look at his little book on punishment, for there too many things occur that smell of Pelagianism or something like it, and they must be noted. For example, what he says about morality: The whole rationale of morality ceases when punishment is removed from the picture. Why, I ask, would we call theft a sin, or the giving of each his due a virtue, if we thought that these things carried no punishment or reward after them? Those who deny universal grace argue in this way: for those for whom the debt has been paid, the guilt ought to be released; if payment was made for all, then all ought to be released from guilt, and so all should be saved; but since not all are saved, it must be held that satisfaction was not made for all. Arguments of this kind carry no weight. God had foreseen man as going to sin before his decree. This is known in itself and must be counted among the first notions: no one is to be blamed except the one who sins voluntarily. It is plain that God neither hates nor punishes sinful habits. I think the following must be agreed: (1) no one is made guilty, with respect to natural divine justice, because of another's sin, nor does anyone undergo punishment properly so called. (2) Adam's sin is so to be ascribed to Adam alone that his posterity, which at that time did not yet exist, in no way came, or could come, into fellowship in the crime. (3) Adam's posterity does not share in death or in the other calamities, spiritual as well as bodily, because they are guilty in Adam. Adam's posterity become guilty only through their own actual sin, insofar as in the mother's womb the mind turns itself away from God. I think it should be conceded that the mind in the womb, according to its measure, knows certain good and evil things by the use of reason, which it either shuns through culpable negligence or, knowingly, sins against. It clearly follows that we sin even in our mother's womb. What follows is taken from his second treatise on predestination. The object of election is man, affected by that moral quality of faith. Every will by its nature excludes an impotence by which it could not will everything. Grace is to be considered only as established in a will that is already actually willing, and not as making a non-willing will into a willing one. No one ought to conceive of the grace by which we are regenerated or persevere in any other way than as something that can be rejected. Unbelievers, indeed reprobates, and those who have been blotted out of the book of life, can also promise themselves that God will never forsake them in this life by his grace, but that he will always be present to them with that grace by which people are converted, and by which they are about to be converted, provided they do not cast that grace away. The remaining matters that must be believed in this doctrine of grace and predestination are so known even by reason that, as first notions, they are fixed in the human mind. The questions: Can every man who is a wayfarer convert himself? Is sufficient grace supplied to men? Does grace work resistibly or irresistibly? Is man passive in the first beginnings of regeneration? Does God make man will? Does he predetermine the human will? Is it not of the nature of grace to make man will? Are those who are converted not converted by a more efficacious grace, the one to which the unconverted resist? These are questions, and to raise them and to interpose one's opinion on them is as absurd as to ask what shape or colour the soul has, and to define it as red or green, round or square. And so he ends this little treatise. These specimens would indeed suffice to prove the man's heterodoxy; but lest he complain that I have neglected the rest, I pass on to the Beginnings of First Philosophy. Nor will I add any refutation to these, for everything is so set forth that it betrays his heterodoxy and falsity of its own accord and by itself. Yet if he wants more, we will not be too sparing, by God's grace, in prescribing antidotes, since he has been so lavish in offering poisons. For now let us only listen to his excellent doctrines. Immensity cannot be attributed to God before the creation of bodies. The foundation of God's omnipresence is that supreme eminence of God by which all corporeal things depend on him. In prayers the reason why God has determined to rescue some from danger is a cause. God, because he follows by accident some order of causes, while it exists, goes on ordering other things. I judge it a lawful and praiseworthy thing to seek a livelihood by a playful lot. Whether God is unwilling for our mind to exist any longer, when after the destruction of the body it can no longer use sense and imagination, cannot be made known to us from the contemplation of the mind. Strictly speaking, one never sins by understanding. The name of life is wrongly used of brutes. It is to be laid down that only that belongs or does not belong to God which reason dictates to belong or not to belong to God. Who does not see that it is contrary to the truth and justice of God to have someone among the number of wayfarers, to read, to rule, to propose rewards and punishments, and yet not to have given to him whom you so rule the means by which he could convert himself? From the foul little book which he is said to have written on the law of ecclesiastics, take these things, which will seem to many to present the true likeness of a certain libertine. The authority of teachers is nothing other than the opinion of greater knowledge joined with integrity, just as we see happen commonly in all other craftsmen who are thought by the common people to be more skilled in some craft. Ecclesiastics attend only to external religion, which is wholly bodily, and that only by the command of the Prodei, not to the internal. Furthermore, [illegible] anyone who wishes can learn that the persecutions made against the Apostles, indeed against Christ the Lord himself, were just. He invents a divine command about announcing this or that, and says that if it has not been established by the Prodei that a command of God who reveals himself has been given, even if someone perhaps has been ordered to announce, they will not commit anything adverse against Natural Reason, or against God ruling through it, but will rather forbid such announcements as pious and right. Rightly, therefore, the King of France and others impose silence on ministers of the Reformed, and punish or expel those who announce the Word of God and the true religion; for it is not clear to the King that those whom he persecutes speak by God's command. Just as Pilate and the chief men of the Jews did not acknowledge the Lord of glory, Stephen, Peter and the other Apostles, or the commands given to them. So whatever the Apostles, whatever Christ the Lord, or his faithful ministers have done, against the will of Pilate, the prefects of the Jews, and afterwards the emperors and princes, for the instruction and conversion of other men, must be held to be a sin. A tremor seizes the limbs! For he lays down that the Prodei rule by the right of the state (we might even call it a divine right) to such an extent that whatever they manifestly or tacitly wish, nothing may be done or made by citizens, especially towards other citizens, if they manifestly or tacitly forbid it, even against their will: O champion of political Antichristianity! O most wicked defender of intolerable tyranny! Such a yoke hangs over the Belgians if ever matters are to be conducted according to this sense. These are not our magistrates, not the Spanish Prodei, avengers of liberty from tyranny; these are tyrants, and they would have it taken as true and right, as also that which at the end of this stinking little book he enjoins all subjects to believe: that everything is permitted to the Prodei, but that by their own right nothing is permitted to themselves, and hence they obey the most Good and Great God in all things and through all things in their Prodei. Indeed, such fairness is not to be expected from this man as the Apostles thought could be hoped for from the elders of the Jewish people, saying: Is it right in the sight of God to obey you rather than God? You judge. Daniel, by opposing himself to the shameful worship of an idol; Paul, by thundering vigorously against the Diana of the Ephesians; finally all the confessors and martyrs who resisted pagan or papal idolatry under emperors and popes, and instructed their fellow citizens against the will of the Prodei: alas, how great a crime, in this man's judgment, they committed! How just the punishments they received! I would add some specimens of the same rubbish from things written in Dutch, such as that whether God's essence is omnipresent or everywhere; whether anything new comes to God by producing something in time, or whether to will something new is repugnant to the blessedness of God; whether God's decrees are conditional: these things, I say, are not contained in Scripture in clear or perspicuous texts. That Scripture and Reason are the rule of faith. The Church has no right, as a judge under the aspect of punishment, to chastise apostates by church discipline. Since the power of the keys was given together with the true Church, and there is no judge who may decide which is the true Church, no one can therefore claim it for himself by right. Yet neither ministers nor any college has the right to rebuke those who think differently, or to deny them admission to communion and the advantages that belong to members. The contrary inflicts violence on consciences. This axiom, that what is last in execution is first in intention, is absurdly laid down, since it makes God and men tyrants, unjust and hypocritical. That one ought not to kill oneself is not a moral matter. But it would make the reader sick if I were to set out more, drawn from such filthy sewers, without an added antidote; and perhaps at some time it will be necessary, in the same idiom, to exhibit to all the pious and faithful inhabitants of our fatherland and to the magistrates specimens of this new Antichristianity, unless worldly men cease to thrust such insipid and ill-fermented offspring into the light. And so far for these things. But if he wishes to publish brief vindications similar to the earlier ones (which he calls Specimen of Calumnies), let him know that I have stirred myself against him with nothing but zeal for the truth; and that, God willing, as long as I live I shall be stirred to plead the cause of truth and piety, according to the measure of my powers, both privately and publicly. If anyone runs into neither of these, he will not say anything too grand to me about the obedience owed to magistrates. Render to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. But since Velthuysen wishes to be dealt with frankly and openly, and not to decline judgments, whether political or ecclesiastical: well and good. Let one synod in Belgium judge, let the theological faculty of any Reformed academy judge. I say and write openly that he is guilty, as above, not of one error but of many; behold the guilt imputed to him, as he himself wished, behold judges not to be scorned in the least. For, he speaks thus, I trust that in this affair my cause will nowhere be inferior to his laws. I have set out those excerpts in good faith, and they need no more, being clear enough in themselves. As for the circumstances, which are to be required, I shall not...

units.la: Specim. Retorsi pag. 6. vole forte excepturus sit. Subterfugia frustra quæ-ret, frustra cum Reformatis consensum prætendet, aut communione sua probatum dare conabitur. Dis-sensum manifestissimum vidimus, quem in bonam partem sumere, quantumvis eum palliaverit, vel ideo quod Reformatos, ut à se diversos, sæpissime, Cal-vinianorum nomine characteristico, non sine probro insigniverit, vix poterit vel indulgentissimus.
units.tr: Specimen Retorsi, p. 6. He will perhaps wish to make an exception. He will seek escapes in vain, and in vain will he pretend agreement with the Reformed or try to show that they approve his communion. We have seen a most manifest dissent, which he could hardly, however kindly he might be disposed, take in a good sense, however much he has tried to disguise it, not least because he has so often branded the Reformed, as if they were different from himself, with the distinguishing name of Calvinists, and not without reproach.

units.la: JOHANNIS VANDER WAEYEN Pro VERITATE, ET GENUINA REFORMATORUM SENTENTIA, Adversus LUDOVICUM WOLZOGIUM, DISCEPTATIONIS LIBER SECUNDUS, Principis Controversiæ , eorumque quæ illam spectant uberiorem Tractationem Continens.
units.tr: JOHN VANDER WAEYEN, For the Truth and the Genuine Opinion of the Reformers, Against LUDWIG WOLZOGEN, Second Book of the Dispute, Containing a Fuller Treatment of the Principal Controversy and of Those Matters That Pertain to It.

units.la: Priori libro, minùs orthodoxè, minùs prudenter & perspicuè dicta, sparsim notavi & refutavi. Nunc ea, quæ Controversiæ primariæ cardinem concernunt, breviter expediam. Absque circuitione statim quod res est dicam. In eo versatur Princeps difficultas quid tandem sit, quod Scripturam legenti persuadeat, aut persuadere debeat, hunc sensum hisce verbis designari. Benè Wolzogius p. 95. id quærimus, quò persuadea-tur de vera interpretatione, nondum certus Interpres, sive lector, & horum verborum, in hisce circumstantiis, hunc sensum esse quid me doceat?
units.tr: In the first book I noted and refuted here and there things said less orthodoxly, less prudently and less clearly. Now I shall briefly settle the matters that concern the hinge of the primary controversy. Without circumlocution, I shall say at once what the matter is. The chief difficulty lies here: what is it that persuades, or ought to persuade, the reader of Scripture that this sense is signified by these words? Wolzogen rightly says on p. 95: we ask by what means one is persuaded of the true interpretation while the interpreter, or reader, is not yet certain; and, given these words in these circumstances, what teaches me that this is the sense?

units.la: Hac de re cum Pontificiis & Socinianis disputat Ecclesia Reformata; quorum priores Ecclesiæ dicta-minii id officii deferunt, ita ut quicquid Ecclesia de hujus aut illius loci sensu dixerit, id pro vero illius sensu ab omnibus indubitatâ fide recipi debeat: interea quid pro Ecclesia, quid pro ejus dictamine habendum & tenendum sit, hactenus ignorant Cadmæi fratres.
units.tr: The Reformed Church disputes this matter with the Papists and the Socinians. The former assign to the dictate of the Church this office, so that whatever the Church has said about the sense of this or that passage must be received by everyone with undoubted faith as its true sense. Meanwhile, the Cadmean brothers have so far not known what is to be held and regarded as the Church's, and what as its dictate.

units.la: Sociniani autem rationi humanæ cuncta judicanda tradunt: docentes, rationem naturalem normam esse & regulam omnis Interpretationis. Reformati utrisque contradicentes, Scripturam ipsam suæ Interpretationis indicem, legem, normamque infallibilem dicunt atque unicam, & Spiritum S. in Scriptura loquentem solum Controversiarum Judicem.
units.tr: The Socinians, however, hand over all things to be judged by human reason, teaching that natural reason is the norm and rule of all interpretation. The Reformed, contradicting both, say that Scripture itself is the index, law and infallible and sole norm of its own interpretation, and that the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture is the sole judge of controversies.

units.la: Omnia autem clarè enodanda, & lectori exhibenda, videntur. Cúmque verear, ne ambitiosum sit, pro maximorum virorum, imò Catholicæ Ecclesiæ, sententia dicere volentem, in totum Theologorum ordinem dictaturæ eminentiam mihi arrogare, quantum potero ipsorum premam vestigia non solùm, sed & loquar verbis. Omnes enim & tantos Heroes spernere non possum, accusare autem & prostituere si quis præsumat, illum non contemnere non possum maximè. Utinam modestiorem hic se præbuisset Wolzogius! non enim ipsius intererat, tantum de omnium Reformatorum & nomine & gloria delibasse, ut jam Lutherus, Calvinus, Whitakerus, Junius, Perkinsus, Chamierus: & quotquot recenter tristi fato Ecclesiæ erepti, Rivetus, Walæus, Gomarus, Altingius, Spanhemius, Crocius, Amyraldus, Dallæus, Hoornbeekius: aut superstites athletæ, Voetius, Maresius, Essenius, Arnoldus, magnoque Patri cognomine & virtutibus par, Fridericus Spanhemius, sancta & veneranda Capita; ut illi, inquam, posthac, non dilucidæ, imo confusæ obscuræque, tractationis, & quidem in tanti momenti negotio, rei audiant.
units.tr: Yet all things seem to need to be clearly explained and set before the reader. And since I fear it may be presumptuous, when I wish to speak for the opinion of the greatest men, indeed of the Catholic Church, to arrogate to myself the eminence of dictatorship over the whole order of theologians, I shall, as far as I can, follow in their footsteps and speak in their very words. For I cannot despise all such great heroes, and if anyone presumes to accuse and disparage them, I certainly cannot refrain from rebuking him. Would that Wolzogen had shown himself more modest here! For it was not in his interest to detract so much from the name and glory of all the Reformers: Luther, Calvin, Whitaker, Junius, Perkins, Chamier; and all those recently snatched by the sad fate of the Church, Rivet, Walaeus, Gomarus, Alting, Spanheim, Crocius, Amyraut, Daillé, Hoornbeeck; or the surviving athletes, Voetius, Maresius, Essenius, Arnold, and the great Father's namesake and equal in virtue, Frederick Spanheim, holy and venerable heads. So that these men, I say, should hereafter hear of a matter of such weight treated not clearly but confusedly and obscurely.

units.la: Non equidem tibi, istud tam imprudentis dictaturæ arrogans exercitium, Wolzogi, invideo, miror magis & detestor. Honorificum est à tantis viris nunquam discedere, nisi cogat necessitas, sed nec sine verecundia & modestia.
units.tr: I, for my part, do not envy you, Wolzogen, that arrogant exercise of such imprudent dictatorship; I rather marvel at it and detest it. It is honourable never to depart from such great men unless necessity compels, but not without reverence and modesty.

units.la: Hoc autem negotium quod attinet, nullam hactenus rationem vidi, quæ Wolzogium ad dissensum istum, & obscuritatis iteratam exprobrationem toti Ecclesiæ objiciendam, cogere debuerit. Viderunt procul dubio viri sagacissimi, æquè perspicuè ac Wolzogius, totam religionem in discrimen venire, & ingentem causam esse, quæque omnium eorum qui Scripturarum stant ju-dicio, discidia contentionesque involvat, omnesque vastæ eruditionis sagacissimique ingenii nervos non segniter intenderunt, ut tanti momenti causa non curaretur minùs accuratè aut perspicuè, quam solidè. Nec ipsis felix defuit, per Dei gratiam, successus.
units.tr: As for this matter, I have so far seen no reason that ought to have compelled Wolzogen to that dissent, and to the repeated reproach of obscurity to be thrown at the whole Church. Without doubt the most sagacious men saw, just as clearly as Wolzogen, that the whole religion is brought into peril, and that it is a great cause which involves the discords and contentions of all who stand by the judgment of the Scriptures, and they did not idly strain every sinew of their vast learning and most acute wit, so that a cause of such weight would be treated not less soundly than accurately and clearly. Nor, by the grace of God, did success fail them.

units.la: Ita ut mirari satis non possim, eruditionem dicam an perspicuitatem, an vero Scripturæ tam prolixè demonstratam ab ipsis, potentiam. Neminem saltem novi ex supra nominatis, quem non multò accuratius magisque methodicè, perspicuè, solidè & orthodoxè, hanc eandem quæstionem pertractasse, demonstrare possim, quam eam pertractavit Wolzogius. Condonabit igitur lector, si præ ingenti Patrum veneratione, ipsorum verbis copiosius utar: Glòriæ ducam, non meis sed Calvini, sed Zanchii, sed Chamieri dictis loqui, totamque absolvere controversiam. Sic ipsis honos stabit suus, quem me illibatum præstare voluisse, videant posteri, ringant licet novaturientes.
units.tr: So I cannot sufficiently marvel whether to call it their learning, their clarity, or rather the power of Scripture, so amply demonstrated by them. At least I know of none of the above-named whom I could not show to have treated this same question far more accurately and more methodically, clearly, soundly and orthodoxly than Wolzogen did. The reader will therefore forgive me if, out of great reverence for the Fathers, I use their words more fully. I shall count it a glory to speak not in my own words but in those of Calvin, of Zanchi, of Chamier, and so to finish the whole controversy. Thus their honour will stand as its own, which I have wished to render unimpaired; let posterity see it, though the innovators may grumble.

units.la: Ad rem ipsam accedo. Hypotheses vero quædam præmittendæ erunt,
units.tr: I come now to the matter itself. Certain hypotheses must, however, be premised.

units.la: 1. Totam Scripturam ab amanuensibus Spiritus Sancti, hoc in omnibus eos dirigente, infallibiliter conscriptam esse; ne minutissimis quidem, si quædam ita vocare fas sit, exceptis: omnis enim, & quæcunque particula divinitùs est inspirata 2. Tim. 3.
units.tr: 1. That the whole of Scripture was written down infallibly by the amanuenses of the Holy Spirit, who directed them in all things; not even the smallest particles excepted, if one may call some things so, for every and each particle is divinely inspired (2 Tim. 3).

units.la: 2. Eam esse perfectam, sufficientem & absolutam fidei, morumque per omnia Ecclesiæ secula, regulam & normam. Aut si hæ phrases figuratæ, etiam in hoc negotio, videantur Wolzogio, quanquam Paulus Canonem dicat, & hæ figuræ, ut alibi ipse de aliis dicit, non obscuram, sed claram, sed nitidam reddant orationem, nihilominus aliis verbis utar; hoc volo, Scripturam omnia illa tradere, continere, dictare, quæ facienda sunt, aut credenda.
units.tr: 2. That it is the perfect, sufficient and absolute rule and norm of faith and morals for all the ages of the Church. Or if these phrases seem figurative to Wolzogen, even in this matter, although Paul calls it a canon, and such figures, as he himself says elsewhere of others, make speech not obscure but clear and bright, I shall nevertheless use other words: I mean that Scripture delivers, contains and dictates all those things which are to be done or believed.

units.la: 3. Ita scriptam esse ut intelligi per se queat ab iis, quorum causâ scripta est, & in quantum ipsorum causâ scripta est.
units.tr: 3. That it is written in such a way that it can be understood of itself by those for whose sake it was written, and insofar as it was written for their sake.

units.la: 4. Ea autem claritate & perspicuitate, ut in tanta rerum Majestate, ne cogitari quidem possit illustrior, nedum adhiberi:
units.tr: 4. And with such clarity and perspicuity that, given so great a majesty of the matters, a clearer could not even be conceived, let alone employed.

units.la: 5. Eumque in finem Deum usum esse verbis & modis dicendi, eâ notione, quâ ista in lingua usurpari & sumi possunt & ex circumstantiis & collatione debent. Hinc Bisterfeldius Perspicuitatem Scripturæ definiens, eam talem esse dicit, ut per eam judiciosæ collationis beneficio, à facultate præditis fructuosè intelli-gi queat.
units.tr: 5. And to this end God has used words and modes of speaking in that sense in which those expressions can and must be taken, from usage in that language and from the circumstances and comparison. Hence Bisterfeld, defining the perspicuity of Scripture, says that it is such that by the benefit of judicious comparison it can be understood fruitfully by those endowed with the faculty.

units.la: 6. Ita ut in genere Canonis, normæ, principii fidei & morum, sibi & per se sufficiens sit, omni tempore. Potest enim sapientem reddere ad salutem 2. Tim. iii. sic ut nullo alio extrinseco adjumento, aut supplemento opus habeat.
units.tr: 6. So that, in general, as the canon, norm and principle of faith and morals, it is sufficient in itself and by itself at all times. For it can make the wise unto salvation (2 Tim. 3:15), so that it has no need of any other extrinsic help or supplement.

units.la: Hisce præmissis, quædam, ut accuratè & perspicuè agam, explicanda veniunt, quorum sæpissimè in hac materia mentio facienda erit: Usus loquendi, ratio humana, Philosophia, & Interpretari seu Interpretatio.
units.tr: With these things premised, certain matters must be explained if I am to treat them accurately and clearly, and these will very often have to be mentioned in this subject: the usage of speech, human reason, philosophy, and interpretation or interpreting.

units.la: 1. Usum loquendi quod attinet; ex instituto verba significant & rerum copia & hominum inertia aliaque ambiguitatem sæpe pariunt, ut notat Wolzogen, multis tamen ea de re dissertationem instituere non erat necesse. Præsupponitur enim quamcunque linguam, ad conceptus, quantum salus, quantum utilitas, & voluntas omnipotentis & omnisapientis requirunt, exprimendos, sufficere. Deumque lin-guâ humanâ utentem eâ uti intelligibiliter, id est, ut institutum, crebrâque locutione verbis inditus charac-ter, & significandi potestas requirunt. Id tamen sacræ Paginæ singulare est, quod, ea quæ hominis captum superant, tradens, sibi peculiarem à rebus ipsis & authore habeat characterismum, qui ex ipsa Scri-ptura unicè addiscendus videtur & noscendus: Sed novit, quisquis vel in transcursu nostrates legerit Theologos, usum istum semper in hoc negotio præ-supponi. Alias enim Scriptura non esset Scriptura, nisi verbis, ex usu significantibus, scripta extaret. Verba autem singula quid significent, dum usus communis docet, sciendum est eorundum, in oratio-ne junctorum, aliam planè rationem esse. Sic enim ex ejus authoris, qui iis uti solet, Phraseologia, optimè innotescent. Nec inficior aliorum, qui forsan de ea-dem re & eodem tempore scripserunt, scripta huic operi etiam inservire posse. Id tamen mihi extra du-bium est, sapientissimum Deum, tali fidei & vitæ nor-mâ Ecclesiam donasse, quæ sibi, & per se, in isto genere sufficiat abundè. Quorsum plura? dum scribo, dum scribens intelligor, videt lectOr quid usus sit, de quo sermo est. Præsupponunt eum in Scriptura, & à parte Scripturæ non excludunt Theologi, quan-do scripturam dicunt Script. Interpretem, ut post-hac videbimus; & patebit frustra esse Wolz. si putet miri inventi gloriam illi debere, qui usum loquendi tanti faciendum, ex ipso audiant.
units.tr: 1. As regards the usage of speech: by appointment, words signify; the abundance of things, the sloth of men and other causes often produce ambiguity, as Wolzogen notes. Yet there was no need to set out a long dissertation on this. For it is presupposed that any language is sufficient to express the concepts which salvation, utility, and the will of the omnipotent and omniscient God require, and that God, using human language, uses it intelligibly, that is, in the way that the character imposed on words by convention, repeated usage and the power of signifying require. Yet this is peculiar to sacred Scripture: in delivering things that surpass human capacity, it has its own characteristic from the things themselves and from the Author, which seems to be learned and known solely from Scripture itself. But whoever has read even in passing our own theologians knows that this usage is always presupposed in this matter. For otherwise Scripture would not exist as Scripture, unless it stood written in words signifying according to usage. Yet while common usage teaches what individual words signify, it must be known that the case is quite different for words joined together in speech. For thus their meaning will be best learned from the phraseology of that author who is accustomed to use them. Nor do I deny that the writings of others, who perhaps wrote on the same matter at the same time, can also serve this work. Yet it is beyond doubt to me that the most wise God has given the Church a norm of faith and life which suffices abundantly in this kind by itself and through itself. Why say more? While I write, and while I am understood as I write, the reader sees what usage is, of which we speak. Theologians presuppose it in Scripture, and do not exclude it on Scripture's part, when they call Scripture the interpreter of Scripture, as we shall see hereafter. It will be plain that Wolzogen is wrong if he thinks the glory of a marvellous discovery is owed to him who, as the matter itself shows, holds the usage of speech in such high esteem.

units.la: II. De ratione humana sciendum, eam hic sumi posse, vel pro mente nostra seu intellectu, seu fa-cultate judicandi, seu anima rationali, omnium co-gitationum Principio ac subjecto: vel pro regulis, veriveritatibus, seu innatis, seu inde naturaliter eductis, juxta quas judicamus. Quae excultae & in ordinem digestae Philosophiam suppeditant, scientiam illam quam naturalis intellectus de naturalibus habere potest ex natura: Insita principia veri excutiendo, & illarum ope naturalia contemplando. Similia, etsi praeposterè, (in initio enim haec tradere debuerat) habet Wolzogen. P. 153.
units.tr: II. Concerning human reason, it should be noted that the term can be taken here either for our mind or intellect, or for the faculty of judging, or for the rational soul, the principle and subject of all our thoughts; or for the rules and truths, whether innate or naturally drawn from them, by which we judge. When these are cultivated and arranged in order, they supply philosophy, that knowledge of natural things which the natural intellect can have from its nature, by examining the implanted principles of truth and contemplating natural things with their help. Wolzogen has similar material on p. 153, though out of order, since he should have presented it at the beginning.

units.la: Qualis autem in homine sit ratio superstes post lapsum, nunc videndum. Principia insita si intelligas, dari quaedam adhuc reliqua, certum est, & docet Apostolus, iisque nos Dei aliquam cognitionem habere, experitur naturalis conscientia. Inde etiam multa, quae bonum & malum morale spectant, absque ulla exterius superveniente nova revelatione, cognosci posse, statuunt Theologi Reformati: at notiones innatae, sicut eaedem non sunt, quae erant ante lapsum, quia corruptae, & offuscatae, quanquam simile quid exciderit Wolzogio p. 154, sic omnia quae inde eliciuntur simul congesta, rudera solùm sunt praeclari quondam aedificii, & ad salutem obtinendam, aut quicquam, quod fidei attinet mysteria, ex sese investigandum, minimè sufficiunt. Imo quae veritates naturales vulgò audiunt, incertas, lubricas, modo non magnam partem falsas, esse, nullus dubito. Non nimium standum vulgaribus & communibus Philosophiae, & rationis placitis, vel sententiis receptis: plures enim sunt tam inaccuratae, incertae, ambiguae, falsae, ut multum molestiarum & errorum inferant orbi, atque Disciplinis: adeo ut praestaret multas plané abolitas, vel saltem reformatas & castigatas, quam ut authoritatem suam ultra tantam possiderent, ingrave veritatis omnis praejudicium, potissimum religionis, vel super ea controversorum.
units.tr: Now we must consider what kind of reason remains in man after the fall. If you mean the implanted principles, it is certain that some remain, as the Apostle teaches, and natural conscience shows that through them we have some knowledge of God. The Reformed theologians also hold that many things concerning moral good and evil can be known from these principles without any new revelation coming from outside. But the innate notions are not the same as they were before the fall, because they are corrupted and clouded. Although something similar has slipped from Wolzogen on p. 154, all that is drawn from them, once gathered together, is only the rubble of a once splendid building, and is quite insufficient for obtaining salvation or for investigating by itself anything that pertains to the mysteries of faith. Indeed, I have no doubt that many of the natural truths commonly so called are uncertain and slippery, and, unless a large part of them is false, at least not sound. We must not lean too heavily on the common and ordinary opinions of philosophy and reason, or on received views; for many are so inaccurate, uncertain, ambiguous and false that they bring much trouble and error upon the world and upon the disciplines. It would be better to abolish many of them altogether, or at least to reform and correct them, than to let them keep their authority beyond what is right, to the great prejudice of all truth, especially of religion and of the controversies concerning it.

units.la: Quòd autem ad subjectum, & facultatem ipsam ejus intrinseca corruptio probè etiam notanda venit. Non quod ejus essentiam, & substantiam, ut ita loquar, diversam post lapsum esse putem ab ea quæ ante lapsum fuerat: sed quod homo justitia originali per peccatum orbatus, jam eousque corruptus fit & debilitatus, ut ne quidem lumine residuo bene uti, aut insita cognitionis semina elicere, principia appli-care & scintillas reliquiasque cognitionis rite colloca-re possit: Ut de præjudiciis, aliisque per modum nebulæ, objectum inter & ipsam facultatem quasi in-terpositis, facultatem offuscantibus, objectum circumsidentibus, mediumque quasi adiaphanum red-dentibus, nihil dicam. Reformati enim Wolzogio hac in parte oculariores & accurati magis, corruptionem intellectus ponunt non solum, 1. In confusione & occasu, sit venia verbis, obliteratione & quid ni dele-tione innatæ Adamo sapientiæ, quâ ex insitis sibi principiis & congenitis, representamina rerum, ideas, species, cogitationes, cognitionemque rerum tam credendarum quam faciendarum elicere aptûs fuisset: Ita ut de isto lumine præter confusas quasdam scintillulas, nihil nunc habeat reliqui. Sed & 2 in multitudine præjudiciorum, perversarum opinionum, & non actuali solùm & præmeditatâ malitiâ, aut, per naturam evitabili socordiâ, acqui-sitorum; sed corruptæ naturæ vitio, ex confusa confusarum offuscatarumque luminis reliqui scintillularum rutilatione, sponte sese objicientium & repræsentantium. Unde naturæ vitio multi errores, & perversæ opiniones nobis subrepunt. Vix aliter ac si per aërem vaporibus ex fætido & fæculento fundo ascendentibus, densoque fumo obsessum, viden-dum tibi quicquam offeratur: Non congruam isti objecto speciem te percepturum, certus sum. 3. Re-stat præterea ipsius facultatis debilitatio, ineptitudo, imo mors spiritualis. Rem autem totam ut brevi complectar; hominem finge, qui non solum propter Solis absentiam, sed & vaporibus repletum aërem & adiaphanum, oculorum denique non hebetudinem, ac ut ita loquar, debilitationem, sed privationem, facultatis saltem videndi amissionem, non videt: quod facultas salva, lucente Sole, per aëra vidisset commodè: habebis vivam hominis naturalis, corruptique intellectus & in eo rationis imaginem. Amisit enim homo non tantum notitiam actualem, sed & oculus ejus excæcatus est ait Bodius ad Eph 1.17. adeoque rerum Spiritualium ne capax quidem natura ejus intellectus, non magis ac cæci oculus luminis aut coloris incapax est. Contra perversam eorum & sacrilegam sententiam, qui vitium illud originis ad inferiores animæ facultates restringunt & ablegant; cum in intellectu cæco perversoque resideat ipse ma-li fons & scaturigo.
units.tr: As to the subject and the faculty itself, its inner corruption must also be carefully noted. I do not think that its essence and substance, so to speak, after the fall is different from what it was before the fall. Rather, man, deprived of original righteousness through sin, has become so corrupted and weakened that he cannot even make proper use of the remaining light, nor draw out the seeds of implanted knowledge, nor apply principles, nor rightly arrange the sparks and remnants of knowledge. I say nothing of prejudices and other things which, like a kind of mist, stand between the object and the faculty itself, clouding the faculty, surrounding the object, and making the medium, as it were, opaque. For the Reformed, being more attentive and exact than Wolzogen in this matter, place the corruption of the intellect not only (1) in the confusion and decline, if I may so put it, indeed in the blotting out and, why not say, the deletion of the wisdom innate in Adam, by which he would have been fit to draw from his implanted and inborn principles the representations, ideas, images, thoughts and knowledge of things, both those to be believed and those to be done. So that, apart from some confused sparks, he now has nothing of that light left. But also (2) in the multitude of prejudices and perverse opinions, which are acquired not only by actual and premeditated malice, or by a folly avoidable through nature, but through the defect of corrupt nature, out of the reddening of the confused and clouded sparks of the remaining light, which present themselves and offer themselves of their own accord. Hence many errors and perverse opinions creep upon us through the defect of nature. It is almost as if, when the air is filled with vapours rising from a fetid and muddy bottom, and dense smoke besieges it, something is set before your eyes to be seen: I am certain you will not perceive an appearance suited to that object. (3) There remains, moreover, the weakening, the unfitness, indeed the spiritual death of the faculty itself. To sum up the whole matter briefly: imagine a man who does not see, not only because the sun is absent, but because the air is filled with vapours and is opaque; and who, finally, has not merely a dullness or, so to speak, a weakening of the eyes, but a privation, that is, the loss of the faculty of seeing. The faculty, if intact, would have seen comfortably through the air when the sun shone. You will have a picture of the natural man, of the corrupt intellect and of the image of reason in him. For man has lost not only actual knowledge, but his eye has been blinded, says Bodius on Eph. 1:17, and so his nature, the intellect, is not even capable of spiritual things, just as the eye of the blind is incapable of light or colour. This is contrary to the perverse and sacrilegious opinion of those who restrict and banish that original defect to the lower faculties of the soul, since the very source and fountain of evil resides in the blind and perverse intellect.

units.la: Hinc ad restituendam hac in parte Dei imaginem, non solùm objecti propositionem, medii, ut ita loquar, serenitatem & claritatem seu nebularum discussionem quandam requirunt; sed & in subjectum facultatemque ipsam, novæ vitæ, virtutis & principii spiritualis & supernaturalis, quâ intus elevetur, vivificetur, infusionem. Per primum, verbum legitimè propositum; per alterum, falsarum præconceptarumque opinionum discussionem; per tertium denique, lumen illud intelligunt & facultatem vitamque spiritualem & supernaturalem, qua homo, conceptibus ex sacris de sacris & circa sacra legitimè & congruè formandis demum adaptatur, huc ap-plicandum quod p 103. res ipsa talis esse debet ut cognoscere possint. Quatuor ponit Amesius, quæ cum jam dictis coincidunt. Objectum cognoscibile. 2. Subjectum vel organon cognoscens. 3. Lumen deferens & deducens objectum ut recipiat. 4. Lumen disponens ac elevans subjectum ut recipiat: quod postremum dicit esse præcipuè de quo contenditur & vocat virtutem supernaturalem naturalem quâ mens elevetur, lumen etiam spiritua-le, &c. Quare in homine per Christum reparando oportet ante omnia mentem ipsam sive intellectum renovari, ac praeterea lumen ipsum cognitionis per Euang splendo-rem infundi immittique: quia in cognoscente requiritur proportio, utique entia, in quibus non est ista capacitas, non possunt cognoscere illa, quae vim suam excedunt. ergo, sensus non cognoscit Spirituale; facultas naturalis non elevata non cognoscit supernaturalia. Eousque hanc ineptitudinem exaggerat Theologus maximi nominis, ut Apostolum docere dicat, ita esse comparatum hominem animalem, ut quae Spiritus Dei sunt, nequeat cognoscere, quemadmodum si Bestiam dicas cognoscere non posse quae hominum sunt. Per rationem igitur naturalem intelligimus si pro facultate sumatur, intellectum caecum, id est videndi aptitudine orbatum & Spiritualiter cum toto homine mortuum; si vero pro notionibus, axiomatibus inde deductis, confusas offuscatasque illas residui luminis scintillulas cum veritatibus inde elicitis. Sed latius haec postea discutienda, & adversus Wolzogium vindicanda erunt.
units.tr: Hence, to restore the image of God in this respect, what is needed is not only the proposal of the object, the clearing, so to speak, of the medium, or a certain dispersal of the mists; but also the infusion into the subject and the faculty itself of a new life, virtue and principle, spiritual and supernatural, by which it is raised up within, made alive, and fitted at last to form concepts from sacred things, about sacred things and in relation to them, rightly and fittingly. Here applies what is said on p. 103: the thing itself must be such that they can know it. Amesius sets out four things which coincide with those already mentioned: (1) the knowable object; (2) the knowing subject or organ; (3) the light conveying and leading the object so that it may be received; (4) the light disposing and raising the subject so that it may receive. He says the last is chiefly what is in dispute, and calls it a supernatural virtue, a natural power by which the mind is raised, also a spiritual light, etc. Therefore in man who is to be restored through Christ, the mind itself or intellect must first of all be renewed, and besides this the very light of knowledge must be poured in and sent in through the splendour of the Gospel; for in the knower a proportion is required, since beings in which there is no such capacity cannot know those things which exceed their power. Therefore the sense does not know the spiritual; the natural faculty, unless raised, does not know the supernatural. The theologian of greatest name exaggerates this unfitness so far that he says the Apostle teaches that the natural man is so constituted that he cannot know the things of the Spirit of God, just as if you were to say that a beast cannot know the things of men. Therefore by natural reason we understand, if it is taken for the faculty, the blind intellect, that is, deprived of the aptitude for seeing and spiritually dead together with the whole man; but if it is taken for the notions and axioms deduced from it, those confused and clouded sparks of the remaining light together with the truths drawn from them. But these matters will be discussed more fully later and defended against Wolzogen.

units.la: III. Tertium denique quod explicandum restat, interpretatio est & interpretari. Interpretatio est vel verbalis, quae proprie versio dicitur, vel realis sive exegetica: quae distinctio probe hic notanda venit, ut recte monet ipse Paradoxus citatis hunc in finem Chamiero aliisque. Prior ab usu sermonis pendet praecipue, de posteriori autem, qua veri sensus explicatio quaeritur hic, sermo est. Quod si animadver-tisset Wolzogius, tam crassum errorem perpetuo non errasset, ut usum verborum, quo sola versio perficitur, in hoc negotio tantum non unicum interpretationis medium dixisset. Videndum quid Orthodoxi, quid Wolzogius, de quo summo jure usur-pes, quod alicubi Cicero, Interpres eget Interprete. Multa enim hac de re, & per ambages, Wolzogius. Gloriosum putat, inter eum qui alteri explicat, aut Interpretatur, distinctionem & differentiam à se notatam esse, quam solidè antea vidimus. Interpretari autem si roges quid sit, jam authoris mentem, jam sensum verborum, non mentem authoris eruere, Wolzogio interpretari est. Sed quid attinet hic ire per ambages, plana est veritas & aperta, potuerit Scriptor ignorare quis sit verborum usus, aut alienata mente contrarium scribere ejus, quod intendebat. Quid hæc ad Scriptores sacros? & esto tandem, ac in iis obtineat quod dicis, non quæritur quid Jeremias, quid Ezechiel, sciverit nec ne, quo animo aut quâ mente scripserit; sed quid Deus per Ezechielis, per Jeremiæ verba significatum voluerit, aut non voluerit: Quidque non per illa dictum esse credere debea-mus. Amanuenses sint diversi, idem auctor Deus est. cumque in Deo nunquam, ut rectè notas, Separata ea mentis significatio sit, quâ nobis judicium exhibet quod ha-bet de rebus ipsis, ab ea, quâ quid nobis voluit patefa-ctum verbo suo, quia nil potest nobis verbo suo detegere quod non ipse tanquam verum judicet, nec tale judicet quicquam, quod nen revera sit tale &c. Verborum igitur rectum sensum, cum mente, si. non ama-nuensis, authoris saltem, congruere, certum est semper, in sacris. Quorsum igitur tantus apparatus ad Interpretem definiendum, scilicet non accuratè non clarè id hactenus perceptum erat; Interpretari est, sic jam antehac Theologi, clarè genuinum sensum enuntiare, (sive jam sibi quis, sive alii hoc præstet, perinde est) & genuinus sensus, est loquentis scribentis-ve expressa notio: quæ cum à mente Dei nunquam discrepet, optimâ ratione veritas hic Logica cum Ethica dicitur semper coincidere, nec est quod Wol-zogen illud in Paradoxo carpat: ferre non possum, inquit, veritatem Ethicam, transferri ad veros sensus, quos exponere debet Interpres, scio quod, se hactenus de Dei sermone nondum loqui, subdat. at quorsum isti circuitus? Sensus verborum cum mente Dei, & Dei, cum sensu, mens, dum congruit, ut supra fassus es.
units.tr: III. Finally, the third thing that remains to be explained is interpretation and to interpret. Interpretation is either verbal, which is properly called translation, or real or exegetical. This distinction must be carefully noted here, as Paradoxus himself rightly points out, citing Chamier and others to this end. The former depends chiefly on the usage of speech; the latter, by which the explanation of the true sense is sought, is what is at issue here. If Wolzogen had noticed this, he would not have fallen so grossly and constantly into error, as to say that the use of words, by which translation alone is accomplished, is almost the only means of interpretation in this business. We must see what the Orthodox think and what Wolzogen thinks, a man whom you may rightly mock with what Cicero says somewhere: The interpreter needs an interpreter. For Wolzogen speaks much and in roundabout ways on this matter. He thinks it a glorious thing that a distinction and difference between one who explains to another and one who interprets has been noted by him, which we have seen solidly refuted earlier. If you ask what it is to interpret, Wolzogen's answer is: to draw out now the author's mind, now the sense of the words, but not the author's mind. But why go round about here? The truth is plain and open: the writer could have been ignorant of the usage of words, or, with his mind turned aside, have written the opposite of what he intended. What has this to do with the sacred writers? And even if it be so, and what you say holds in them, the question is not what Jeremiah or Ezekiel knew or did not know, nor with what intention or mind they wrote; but what God meant or did not mean to be signified through the words of Ezekiel and Jeremiah, and what we must believe was not said through them. The amanuenses may be different, the author is one, God. And since in God, as you rightly note, that meaning of the mind by which he presents to us the judgment he has about things themselves is never separate from that by which he has wished to reveal something to us in his word, because he cannot reveal to us in his word anything which he does not himself judge to be true, nor judge anything such which is not really such, etc. Therefore it is always certain in sacred matters that the right sense of the words agrees with the mind of the author, if not of the amanuensis. Why, then, such a great display to define the interpreter, as if this had not hitherto been perceived accurately and clearly? To interpret is, as theologians have said before now, to state clearly the genuine sense (whether someone does this for himself or for another, it makes no difference); and the genuine sense is the expressed notion of the speaker or writer. Since this never differs from the mind of God, it is for the best reason that the logical truth here is said always to coincide with the ethical truth, and there is no reason for Wolzogen to carp at this in the Paradoxa. I cannot bear, he says, that ethical truth be transferred to the true senses which the interpreter ought to set forth; he adds that he has so far not yet spoken of the word of God. But why these circlings? The sense of the words agrees with the mind of God, and God's mind, as far as it agrees, agrees with the sense, as you yourself have confessed above.

units.la: Hisce ita praelibatis, Quaesiti & Controversiae sta-tus ponendus erit accurate: quod pro perspicuitate sua & novae Methodi ἀκριβείᾳ[?] negligit non solum; sed & contemnit, ut minimè necessarium aut utile in hoc negotio, noster: benéne enim & ex vero, an perperam id explicuerit, nil id, Judice Wolzogio, facit ad quaestionem magnopere. Sic decebat, ne aut parum, aut nihil à Paradoxo distare Wolzogium pateret: nec etiam hactenus videre potui quisnam paradoxum inter, & Wolzogium sit verae controversiae status; jam enim cum adversario idem, nunc ab ipso diver-sum quid, sentire diceres. Quare, quod de Reformatis Theologis habet, ipsi saepe accidit, ut nec sua defendat nec oppugnet aliena: hinc forsan est quod ita largiter, turpem licet, captatam nihilominus Paradoxo, novitatis cedat gloriam; controversiae enim statu posito, in omnibus Socinianis, praecipue illo qui edidit, Brevem Disquisit. contra Valeria-num &c. sententiam reipsa eandem reperisset, ejus-que apud nostros solidam refutationem. Maximam semper in Controversiae statu fingendo operam posue-runt, quotquot seriò unquam simul & solidè sese veritatis adversariis opposuerunt. In hoc etiam nego-tio, id præ multis requiritur: sic enim sententiae di-vortium cernitur, & vis argumentorum percipitur clarius.
units.tr: Having thus first set out these matters, the status of the question and the controversy must now be stated precisely. Our author neglects this, and even scorns it, as neither necessary nor useful in this business, for the sake of its clarity and of his new method accuracy [ἀκριβείᾳ]. For, in Wolzogen's judgement, whether he has explained it well and from the truth, or wrongly, is nothing to the question, and makes little difference to it. That was not fitting, lest it appear that Wolzogen differs little or not at all from the Paradox. Nor have I until now been able to see what the true status of the controversy is between the Paradox and Wolzogen. For you say that he now agrees with his opponent, now holds something different from him. Therefore, what he says about the Reformed theologians happens to him often, so that he defends neither his own views nor attacks those of others. Hence perhaps it is that he so freely yields to the Paradox the glory of novelty, though it is a shameful thing he has sought. For had he stated the controversy, he would have found the same view in all the Socinians, especially in the author of the Brief Inquiry against Valerianus, and its solid refutation among our own people. All who have ever seriously and solidly opposed the adversaries of the truth have always taken the greatest pains in stating the controversy. In this business too, this is required above all: for thus the divergence of the opinions is seen, and the force of the arguments is perceived more clearly.

units.la: Non quaeritur hic, quid me, hujus & illius vo-cis, sigillatim sumtæ, significationem docere de-beat. Id enim de singulis, si viva, cujus illa vox est, lingua fit, quotidianus usus; sin minus, Lexicon, pristini usus index, præstabit facilè. Quod pro-prie versionem spectat & interpretationem verbalem, quam vocant laxo vocis significatu, ut vel ex Paradoxo discere potuit. Deus verborum ista, qua utitur lingua, significationem, quam habent, praesupponit, iisque ex isto usu significantibus, utitur, & quidem taliter constructis, ut Scripturam ipsam conferenti, consideranti, prout decet, constare id sufficienter queat; ita ut per has aut illas causas, mutato quamvis aliquantulum verborum usu, nihilominus quid hoc aut illud velit, ex usu adhuc, & ipsa Scriptura satis innotescat. Nec omittendum etiam, de quo dubitari non potest, ne unquam canon esse non possit, aut inutilis evaderet hic Scripturae thesaurus, sapienter a Deo semper & potenter cautum esse: sicque illius respectu in intelligibilis fieri haud potuit. Nec in eo nobis tricas faciunt praecipue, aut nodos nectunt, adversarii: ut mihi fluctus in sympulo excitasse videatur, tam multa, super hoc negotio & anxie scribens Wolzogius: hoc praesupponendum res ipsa postulat, eo ipso enim quod de Interpretatione Scripti divini disputas, illud intelligibiliter scriptum esse praesupponitur, & verbis ex usu significantibus. Quod enim de Homonymia, & ambiguitate verborum, copiose nimis effudit Paradoxus, refutari debuit brevibus, non imitationi inservire. Videat Lector quae viri Clar. Essenius, Disp. de Conscientia, & Vogelsangh illi homini opposuere. Quas in singulis separatim sumtis, difficultates enumerat Paradoxus, universus contextus solvit vel ipso, sua praxi, teste ἀυτακαλακείτω[?].
units.tr: Here the question is not what I ought to teach about the meaning of this or that word taken singly. For that is a matter of daily usage for each word, if the language to which the word belongs is living; if not, a lexicon, the index of earlier usage, will readily supply it. This concerns properly the version and the verbal interpretation, which they call the loose sense of the word, as the Paradox himself could learn. God, in the words he uses, presupposes the meaning that they have in the language, and he uses words that signify by that usage, and indeed constructed in such a way that this can be sufficiently established for one who compares and considers Scripture itself, as is fitting. So that, for whatever reasons, even if the usage of words has changed somewhat, what this or that means is still sufficiently known from usage and from Scripture itself. Nor must we omit what cannot be doubted: that God has wisely and powerfully provided that the canon could never be unusable, or this treasure of Scripture become useless, and so it could not become unintelligible with respect to it. Nor do our adversaries, especially, make difficulties or tie knots in this matter. Wolzogen, writing so much and so anxiously on this business, seems to me to have stirred up a storm in a teacup. The matter itself requires this to be presupposed: for by the very fact that you dispute about the interpretation of a divine writing, it is presupposed that it has been written intelligibly, and in words that signify by usage. As for what the Paradox has poured out too copiously about homonymy and the ambiguity of words, it should have been refuted briefly, not imitated. Let the reader see what the distinguished Essenius, in his disputation On Conscience, and Vogelsang have set against that man. The whole context resolves the difficulties that the Paradox enumerates in each thing taken separately, as his own practice witnesses [ἀυτακαλακείτω].

units.la: Hoc proprie est hic differendum, quid tandem sit, quod me convincat horum verborum, sic simul junctorum, hunc sensum esse, hoc loco: ex: gratia super illo Textu Joh. 1. 1. non disquiritur quid per se significet vox ἀρχὴ, quid Θεὸς, quid λόγος, sed quid ista enunciatio ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, aut quid vox ἀρχὴ, cujus ex usu constat significatio, sigillatim quando ponitur, significet, in hac verborum serie, aut, ut Wolzogii verbis utar, qua tandem ratione sc: per modum objecti motus, apud ani-mum meum statuere pro certo possim. hunc sensum cum hac oratione copulandum esse. Recte hactenus; sed ab eo subjuncta vide. Nec magna foret in eo definiendo diffi-cultas, inquit, si certa essent & indubitata verborum signa: horum signorum sufficeret generalem habere cog-nitam institutionem, ut quae mens eorum in singulis esset, haberemus explorate Perceptum; Et post nonnulla de ambiguitatis causis, omnis disputationis suae materiam in eo contineri dicit. Siccine, bone vir, de singulis verbis, quid velint, tu solum disputas? singulorum non fixa significatio, tibi tantam parit molestiam? aut obscure loqueris, aut veritatis, aut tui immemor. Lege quae scripsti, libro sequente; Nec enim in Inter-pretatione orationis, quid in se valeant verba, sed quid hic valere debeant, examinatur; multum enim interest inter significationem vocabuli, quod solutum spectatur ab omni oratione, & in prima tantum origine sua; & inter illam ejusdem vocabuli significationem, quando in media comparet oratione, varia constructione, multisque cir-cumstantiis determinatum. Idem dicendum de partibus quibusdam orationis, quae sensum aliquem continere pos-sunt, integrisque propositionibus, quae si seorsim sumantur aliud longe significent, quam si toti orationis corpori intertextae cohaereant cum antecedentibus. Tunc enim a materia, a scopo, ab aliis rebus quamplurimis sensum accipiunt ab eo diversum, quem per se habere possent. Sed hoc NB. non moratur Interpretem: is enim, non sectatur illum sensum, quem soluta vocabula, senten-tiaeque separatae possunt habere, nisi Lexicon forte scribat, aut Logica praecepta velit exemplis illustrare. Inquirit sensum, qui eo loco, videatur elici posse. viden aliam plane belli sedem esse, & locum ubi congredi debeas, etiam te ipso judice? Indubitatam igitur fixamque verborum significationem quaerere, non unicus in hoc negotio labor dicendus erat, de seorsim & fi-gillatim sumtis illic loqueris, ut ex ambiguitatis & difficultatis, quas inibi tradis, causis, liquido patet.
units.tr: What is to be argued here is this: what finally convinces me that this sense is the sense of these words so joined together, in this place? In the case of that text John 1:1, the question is not what the word ἀρχὴ, or θεὸς, or λόγος signifies in itself, but what the statement ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος means, or what the word ἀρχὴ, whose meaning is known from usage, signifies when it is placed singly in this series of words. Or, to use Wolzogen's words, by what reasoning, namely by way of the object moving my mind, I can hold it for certain that this sense is to be joined with this sentence. So far, so good. But see what he adds: Nor would there be great difficulty in defining this, he says, if the signs of the words were certain and undoubted: it would be enough to have a general knowledge of the institution of these signs, so that we would have a clearly perceived understanding of what their meaning was in each case. And after some remarks on the causes of ambiguity, he says that the whole matter of his dispute is contained in this. Is it so, good sir, that you dispute only about what each word means, taken singly? Does the unfixed meaning of single words cause you so much trouble? Either you speak obscurely, or you forget the truth, or yourself. Read what you wrote in the following book: For in the interpretation of a sentence, what the words can mean in themselves is not examined, but what they ought to mean here. For there is a great difference between the meaning of a word considered loose from every sentence, and only in its first origin, and that meaning of the same word when it appears in the middle of a sentence, determined by varied construction and many circumstances. The same must be said of certain parts of a sentence, which can contain some meaning, and of whole propositions, which, if taken separately, signify something quite different from what they do when they cohere with the preceding words within the whole body of the discourse. For then they receive from the subject matter, from the aim, and from many other things a meaning different from that which they could have in themselves. But take note: this does not delay the interpreter, for he does not pursue the meaning which loose words and separate sentences can have, unless perhaps a lexicon is being written or logical precepts are to be illustrated with examples. He seeks the meaning which seems to be capable of being drawn out in that place. Do you see, even by your own judgement, that there is a quite different seat of the war, and a place where you ought to join battle? So it was not the sole labour in this business to seek the undoubted and fixed meaning of words. You speak there about things taken separately and singly, as is clear from the causes of ambiguity and difficulty that you set out there.

units.la: Manet igitur hic controversia status; quid tandem sit,quod me per modum objecti certum reddat, hujus orationis illum esse sensum, non alium. Dicam quid statuant Reformati, Spiritum Sanctum in Scriptura loquentem, & Scripturam explicantem, id facere per modum judicis sententiam ferentis. Spiritus S. Judex est, norma & praescriptum ipsa Scriptura.
units.tr: So the status of the controversy remains here: what finally makes it certain to me, by way of the object, that the sense of this sentence is this one and not another. I will say what the Reformed hold: that the Holy Spirit, speaking in Scripture and explaining Scripture, does this by way of a judge pronouncing sentence. The Holy Spirit is the judge; the norm and rule is Scripture itself.

units.la: Totum autem negotium ut bene & ex Reformatorum genuino sensu rite intelligatur, sciendum est, ut in omni cognitione, sic & in intellectione Scriptura, requiri subjectum capax, objectum, & legitimum utriusque contactum. Sic & hic quaerenti quid ad Scripturæ genuinam requiratur intellectionem, respondendum erit requiri. 1. In subjecto, homine intellecturo, non solum dispositionem quâ homo aptus sit & dispositus ad illud in Scriptura videndum: capax quasi, ad illud capiendum, necessum enim est ut perceptio sit rei & cognoscenti & cognoscendæ, & mutuæ ipsarum habitudini ac statui, proportionalis: dico proportionalis, neque enim necesse est ut cognoscens in omni cognitione sit æquale cognoscendo; potest esse majus & minus; sed requiritur, sufficiens aptitudo & quasi capacitas, ut cognoscens possit efficaciter cognoscendi similitudinem in se habere. Sed & istius dispositionis excitatio, applicatioque legitima. Res ipsa, ait Wolzogen, talis esse debet, ut cognosci possit; mens oculusve ita affecti ut cognoscere possint; denique relatio id postulat, ut rebus istis cognoscendis applicata mens illas revera percipiat. 2. In objecto intelligendo quod Scriptura est, nihil praeter ipsam Scripturam, ut in hypothesibus dictum est. de hoc loquuntur Reformati cum Scripturam Scripturae dicunt Interpretem. Objectum illud sibi sufficere ad ingenerandum quantum ab objecto requiri potest, sui intellectionem veram & legitimam, à Deo denique intentam. Scripturam cum Scriptura legitimè collatam ,non posse falsam , imò eam demum posse veram detegere, docere, dictare, (per modum objecti sc ) & certam Interpretationem : de utroque tam quod à parte subjecti, quam quod à parte objecti requisitum dixi, videamus latius.
units.tr: Now, so that the whole matter may be rightly understood, and in accordance with the genuine sense of the Reformed, we must recognise that, as in every knowledge, so also in the understanding of Scripture, three things are required: a capable subject, an object, and a lawful contact between the two. So here, to one who asks what is required for the genuine understanding of Scripture, the answer must be that the following are required. (1) In the subject, the man who is to understand, not only a disposition by which he is fit and disposed to see that in Scripture, capable, as it were, of grasping it; for it is necessary that perception be proportional both to the thing perceived and to the one perceiving, and to their mutual relation and state. I say proportional: for it is not necessary that the knower in every knowledge be equal to the thing known; the one may be greater or less than the other; but sufficient aptitude and, as it were, capacity is required, so that the knower can effectively have the likeness of the thing known in himself. There is also the stirring up and lawful application of this disposition. The thing itself, says Wolzogen, must be such that it can be known; the mind or eye must be so affected that they can know; finally, the relation demands that the mind, applied to those things to be known, actually perceives them. (2) In the object to be understood, which is Scripture, nothing beyond Scripture itself, as was said in the hypotheses. The Reformed speak of this when they say that Scripture is the interpreter of Scripture. That object is sufficient for itself to produce, as far as can be required from an object, a true and lawful understanding of itself, and finally one intended by God. That Scripture, lawfully compared with Scripture, cannot be false, but can rather disclose, teach and dictate the true and certain interpretation (by way of the object, namely) — let us examine more widely both what I have said is required on the side of the subject and what on the side of the object.

units.la: Subjectum quod attinet, ejus ineptitudo natu-ralis, præsertim in hoc negotio , negari, aut dissimu-lari, aut minui à Reformato non debet: segniter autem & languidé, procul omni dubio, nimis , de ea loquitur, qui segnitiem & languorem, eam , cum Wolzogio, vocaverit: nisi, quod mortuum est, languidum & segne dici queat: vivit qui segnis est, quamvis inertissimè; vitæ majus exercitium solum & major incitatio requiritur in eo qui se languori de-dit: dum mortuus interim vita indigeat nova, motûs novo principio. Jllo Pelagiani, & quidem crassiores, hoc verò modo Reformati loquuntur & quidem ex sacris. Peccatum mors est animæ. Quid ni sese excitare posset languidus? quid ni allaborans, torporem excuteret? quid? Oculos nobis esse negat Apostolus, nihil homo in spiritualibus comprehendit. Quid, ita? an quia per ignaviam negligit? imo, etiamsi enitatur, nihil potest: & ne culpa hujus detur hominis animalis desidiæ & negligentiæ, ubi animalis homo conatur ad cognitionem pertingere regni Christi frustra laborat, ubi de rebus Spiritus disputat, garrit, ubi pronunciat, mentitur &c. sic isti heroes olim absque omni sane ob-scuritate. Languor sæpe etiam & segnities pios corripit, tum excitandus solum est segnis, non vivificandus mortuus, quæ immane quantum distant! Non sufficit hic, mentis aciem obtusiorem dicere, non membranam intellectus oculo obductam cogitare, salva intus videndi facultate. Sed oculum effossum spiritualiter, se videndi facultate destitutum, orba- tum statuere, orthodoxorum est. Hinc non perse- ctionis gradu sed toto genere differunt, quae a natura prodeunt & homine naturali, ab iis quae ex principio supernaturali elicit homo regenitus. Vix aliter quam ut operationes reliquorum animantium, quamvis subtilissimae, nihilo minus, cum iis, quae a mente hominis proficiscuntur, collatae, defectum facultatis rationalis arguunt: hac similitudine utitur ante me, vir Clarissimus. Necessarium igitur est, ut novum intellectui superinfundatur lumen, potentia, principium, quod sit vita in intellectu, olim per peccatum mortuo, quo intellectus elevetur & coaptetur ad recipiendum, objectum spirituale modo convenienti. Quod si non requiratur, vicirent Pelagiani, homo ψυχικὸς, atque σαρκικὸς, poterit per se apprehendere objecta spiritualia, ait idem Theologus. De lumine illo disponente subjectum & elevante, sola disceptatio est.
units.tr: As for the subject, its natural inability must not be denied, concealed, or diminished by a Reformed writer, least of all in this matter. Without doubt, he speaks of it far too sluggishly and feebly who, with Wolzogen, has called it sluggishness and feebleness, unless what is dead can be called feeble and sluggish. Whoever is sluggish still lives, however inertly; a greater exercise of life and a stronger stimulus are needed only for one who has given himself over to feebleness, whereas the dead need a new life and a new principle of motion. The Pelagians, and especially the cruder ones, speak in this way; but the Reformed speak in another way, and indeed from Scripture. Sin is the death of the soul. Why should the feeble not be able to rouse himself? Why should he not, by labouring, shake off his torpor? The Apostle denies that we have eyes: man comprehends nothing in spiritual things. What, so? Is it because he neglects through idleness? No, even if he strives, he can do nothing; and lest the fault of this be laid on the sluggishness and negligence of the natural man, where the natural man tries to reach the knowledge of the kingdom of Christ, he labours in vain; where he disputes, chatters, and pronounces about the things of the Spirit, he lies, &c. So those heroes once spoke, without any sane obscurity. Feebleness and sluggishness often also seize the pious; then the sluggish man only needs to be roused, and the dead man must not be made alive: how immeasurably different these things are! Here it is not enough to say that the edge of the mind is somewhat blunter, or to think that a membrane has been drawn over the eye of the intellect while the faculty of seeing remains intact within. It belongs to the orthodox to say that the eye has been spiritually put out, that the man is deprived of the faculty of seeing, and is blinded. Hence they differ not in degree of perfection but in whole kind: the things that proceed from nature and the natural man, and those that the regenerate man brings forth from a supernatural principle. Just as the operations of the other animals, however subtle, nevertheless when compared with those that proceed from the human mind, prove a defect of the rational faculty: this comparison is used before me by that most distinguished man. It is therefore necessary that a new light, power, and principle be poured into the intellect, which is life in the intellect, once dead through sin, by which the intellect is lifted up and fitted to receive the spiritual object in a suitable way. If this were not required, the Pelagians would win, and the psychic and fleshly man could apprehend spiritual objects by himself, says the same theologian. Concerning that light which disposes the subject and raises it up, there is only a dispute.

units.la: Sed praeter illud principium infusum, ad ejus excitationem, qua actus ejus eliciantur, requiritur nova perpetuo S. Spiritus attingentia & influxus novus, quo intus vi sua facultatem illam regenitam & elevatam excitat, applicat &c. Ita ut si, e. gr. hoc momento intellectus regenitus & supernaturali illa virtute donatus, ad individuum hunc aut illum actum excitandus fit, nova semper, ad illum signatum actum egeat Spiritus S. praeexcitatione & concursu gratioso: sicut in naturalibus, id nostri docent, de communis providentiae agendi modo, circa omnem motum naturalem. Nec hoc meum est quod dico, Cloppenburgio id debet lector. Adeoque inquit ille in Spiritu esse dicimur, quando per efficacem Spiritus Sancti operationem, vivimus vitam novam, simili phrasi, qua dicimur naturae universali beneficio, in Domino vivere, moveri & esse Act. xvii. 25, 28. non enim solum per suum Spiritum afflat mentibus donum sapientiae, sed etiam efficit ut actu sapiamus: hoc est, non solum au-ctor est actus primi (ut loquuntur Philosophi) sed etiam actus secundi: ut oculus actu videat aliquid, duo in ipso requiruntur: primum facultas videndi: sed hoc non est satis: nam etiam cum dormimus, & in tenebris, facultatem tenemus. Ergo, ut etiam mens nostra res divinas atque coelestes actu cognoscat; non sat habet, vi praedita sit dono sapientiae, sed opus illi est; ut lumine Sp. Sancti affecta, illuminata, permota in actum secundum deducatur. sic Zanchius & post eum Bodius, ex Dei dono & S. S. operatione dependet, tum donum ipsum habituale, tum ejus usus & exercitium, quod in actuali cognitione consistit.
units.tr: But besides that infused principle, for its stimulation, by which its acts are brought forth, there is required a new and perpetual touch and influx of the Holy Spirit, by which, acting within by his power, he stirs up, applies, and so on that regenerate and raised faculty. So that if, for example, at this moment the regenerate intellect, endowed with that supernatural power, is to be roused to this or that particular act, it always needs a new prior stirring and gracious concurrence of the Holy Spirit for that particular act; just as in natural things, our people teach concerning the common manner of divine providence working in every natural motion. Nor is this my own doctrine that I am saying; the reader owes it to Cloppenburg. Accordingly he says: we are said to be in the Spirit when, by the effectual operation of the Holy Spirit, we live a new life, in a phrase similar to that by which we are said, by the universal benefit of nature, to live, move and be in the Lord (Acts 17:25, 28). For he not only breathes into minds through his own Spirit the gift of wisdom, but also brings it about that we actually become wise: that is, he is not only the author of the first act (as the philosophers put it) but also of the second act. As for the eye actually seeing something, two things are required in it: first the faculty of seeing; but this is not enough, for we also hold the faculty even when we sleep and are in darkness. Therefore, so that our mind may also actually know divine and heavenly things, it is not enough that it be endowed with the power of the gift of wisdom; it needs, being affected by the light of the Holy Spirit, to be illuminated and moved, and led into the second act. So Zanchius, and after him Bodius: it depends on the gift of God and the operation of the Holy Spirit, both the habitual gift itself, and its use and exercise, which consists in actual knowledge.

units.la: Subjecti ineptitudinem uti minuendam non esse statuunt Reformati, sic objecti in suo genere perfectionem & sufficientiam defendunt serio & solide in hoc negotio. Ita ut quaerenti, quid illud sit, quod me, per modum objecti, movere, persuadere debeat, Deum hac enunciatione, istis verbis, per se ex usu linguae, seorsim & sigillatim intelligibilibus, hoc & non aliud significasse, responderi debeat Scripturam esse, seu hoc ipso loco clarissime id intellectui objicientem, seu aliunde ex aliis locis huic facem accendentem: hic jam congredi partes videas. Philosophiam id praestare voluit tenebrio. Wolzogen rationem, usum loquendi & Spiritum S. Neuter ex veritate, ex Reformatorum sensu neuter. Tenebrio-nem aliis committimus qui jam dudum malesanum ipsius commentum refutarunt abunde; Maresium puto, Essenium, Arnoldum, Vogelsangh, Ser-rarium: nos Wolzogium examinabimus. Tribus ille hanc Provinciam dari debere statuit: sed nullum eorum respuet, suo sensu, Socinianus, aut cum ipso Paradoxus.
