Nullum etiam non requirit Reformatus, sed suo quodque loco & ordine & modo: quandoquidem vero de objecto quaestio est, ut vocabula normæ, & regulæ, in hoc negotio, (quanquam judice Wolzogio figuratæ nimis,) occurrentes, docent: docet & Wolzogius p. 91. cum dicit quæri quidnam potissimum id esset, quo, qui ratione uteretur, adduci posset ac deberet, ut de veritate alicujus Interpretationis se persuaderi pateretur. nam & qui sibi est Interpres aliqua certe ratione movetur; & qui aliis inservit, eandem adhibere potest:- ita ut vi rationis allatæ debuisse convinci, si nil vitii contraxissent ipsi, cognoscatur: quæ- rit aliquid quod me per modum rationis movet aliquid quod si sit bene perspectum, non possimus de sensu dubitare; aliquid denique quod nos instar facis ducit, ut ad evidentiam perveniamus, & quidem tali modo ut res ipsa, ut ipsa oratio nos ducere possunt. Quæ certe id agunt per modum externe objecti, & in eo ordine, quæ per modum facis ducunt, sicut res, sicut oratio ducere potest, Spiritum recenset, & de ejus efficientia disputat laxè: sed palàm nimis oscitantiam suam prodit Wolzogen. De subjecto ejusque aptitudine si ageretur aliter se haberet res ista. Nunc autem de objecto & per modum objecti externe propositi agente & ducente face dum disserit,turpiter hallucinatur,dum hic etiamSpiritum recenset & de eo ratiocinatur tanto molimine. Spiritus Sancti etiam, cum circa objectum versor & de objecto differo,mentio facienda est,fateor, sed in tantum solùm, in quantum Scripturæ author est & in ea ut Judex suam prodidit sententiam: excusandum vero Wolzogium, si quis judicet, quia Paradoxus qui refutandus erat, latè de Sp. S. disserit, ejusque in nos operatione: illi regero, Paradoxum in eo graviter errasse, dum ab objecto turpi, εἰς ἄλλο γένος μετάβασις, ad subjectum devolvitur ipsius disfertatio. Scripturam Scripturæ Interpretem, aut Sp. S. in Scriptura loquentem esse Controversiarum omnisque Interpretationis Judicem, dixerant Reformati; hanc in sententiam insurgit impotens jactator, tor, & multis de Spiritus illuminatione hac & illa garrit homo ψυχικὸς, πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχων. Reformatos porro obscuritatis insimulans quasi hæc non bene di-stinguant: Cum de rationis sufficientia & viribus fa-cultatis ratiocinantis loquitur, tum Spiritus requisi-ta virtus removenda erat & vendicanda intellectui cum suis insitis notionibus sufficientia & virtus: cum autem Scripturæ Interpretem Scripturam dicunt Ref. procul omni dubio, seposito subjecto, de ob-jecto disputant, & ejus interpretandi normam quæ-runt & regulam, ut alibi fatetur Paradoxus: & Spi-ritum S. per Scr. & in ea Judicem Interpr. quando statuunt, nihil aliud re ipsa dicunt: adhuc de obje-cto loquuntur. Spiritum S. authorem & ideo in ea loquentem audiunt, Interpretantem agnoscunt, sed non aliter ac Optatus Milevitanus ait, si fuerit inter fratres (post Patris mortem) contentio nata, non itur ad tumulum; sed quæritur Testamentum: & qui tumulo quiescit, tacitus de tabulis loquitur. Sic quando Jurisconsultus Imperatorem hanc aut illam legem explicare dicit, nihil dicit diversum ab eo, qui legem unam dicit explicare aliam: ut impudentem malitiam aut ignorantiam videas in Paradoxo qui Whi-takerum & Scarpium ab aliis singulare quid statuere facit & præter Script. Spiritui authoritatem Inter-pretandi dum tribuunt, à reliquis Reformatis dis-sentire dicit: non intelligit aut dissimulat veram Re-form. sententiam infrunitum caput. Quod si fuisset probè à Wolzogio notatum, non habuisset ipsum er-roris discipulum Paradoxus, non sequacem: potuis-set, quæ de Spiritu S. perversa docet adversarius, refutasse, sed suo ordine & loco. Est subjecti elevatio, excitatio, applicatio, ut & post factam sic ex Scriptura Interpretationem superveniens quædam istius verita-tis per Sp. in nobis obsignatio: sed jam circa obje-ctum versamur. At quoniam sic poscit Wolzogiana methomethodus, audiamus quibus interpretandam Scriptu-ram committat. Et quia Spiritus prima mentio facta, ejus quidem vis & efficacia duplex esse potest, altera soluta, libera, animos hominum ipsa per se movens, nec ullis al-ligata rebus extra se positis: altera rebus adstricta, perque illas demum exerens sese: prior illa virtute immediata mentes afficit; mediata tantum posterior, illa extraordinaria, hæc ordinaria. Perplexa omnia, quid? an nunquam immediatè tuam afficit mentem Spiritus & excitat ad operationes spirituales? non videris intelligere quid velint Reformati, omnes motus, omnia dictata ad Scripturæ normam & amussim exigenda, & an cum ea conveniant nec ne probanda; non autem, nullos motus, operationes Spiritus S. nullas à fidelibus percipi & recipi immediate & de Scriptura ne quidem tum cogitantibus: imò sæpius ad Scr. lectionem, ad preces, aliaque incitantur immedia-tè. Túne igitur omnem afflatum internum negas? túne ista ut pugnantia opponis? imo vero, si verba ponderentur, dubium linquit lectorem, an, præter objectivam propositionem, ullam Spiritus Sancti in ipsam mentem operationem admittat: efficit, inquit, Spiritus ut mens perspiciat quibus confirmetur: & alibi, id tantum facit ut mens nostra perspicere ea possit sine nube, quæ in ipso insunt Scripturæ contextu: eadem sanè & plura dicent Pelagiani. Efficit, ais, Spiritus S. ut mens &c. sed quali operatione, quo modo? externè solum istud objectum perceptibiliter proponendo, an vero intus etiam ipsum subjectum disponendo habitualiter, ad actum excitando, & deinceps contactum in genere causæ primæ efficiendo? De orthodoxia me dubium reddis tua, dum omnem negas afflatum internum,& illum demùm Spiritum agnoscis, quem in ipsa invenis Scriptura, non eo sensu, quod nullum alium agnoscas, quàm de quo loquitur Scriptura, cujus motus congruunt Scripturæ; sic enim me sponte adstipulantem habeamong; sed est aliquid, quod. in Scriptura est, quo viso & perspecto non potes dubitare de sensu, aliquid quod præ mentis corruptione quadam videre non possumus: quod revera nihil aliud est, quam palam ad objectum relabi, omnia unicè in objecto quaerere, & in objecti propositione externa totam ponere illuminationem Spiritus: imò illud omne quod per operationem Spiritus Sancti, intelligis opponis iis operationibus, quibus intus tem[?] affiat, quales negas & explodis unà omnes: hinc tam parce alibi, aliquas Spiritui partes tribuis, & quidem ob Scripturarum præcipuè singularem quandam naturam: singulari quadam constitutione Scripturæ. Ponamus enim vel in summa ignorantia demersum peccatorem, possetne ita loqui Deus, ut vel ab ignorantissimo intelligeretur. Siccine in revelationis modo tibi hæret aqua, potuisset ita loqui ista Mysteria regni cœlorum ut intelligeretur ab ignorantissimo, absque indita nova peccatori vita, modo proponendi modus exter-nus & à parte objecti, id est Scripturæ, alius & talis sit? mira narras, quasi diceres Solem tam fortiter vibra-re radios potuisse, ut etiam à cæcis perciperentur. egregiè sanè. Nec plura petent Pelagiani, ut mediis moralibus sua constet, possibilis saltem, efficacia. Sed hæc multùm correcta videas alibi, vi quoque Spi-ritus confirmari in hisce quæstionibus dicis. Sic satis tenuiter, at quænam sunt illæ quæstiones, in quarum decisione tam parce Spiritum agere putat Wolzogen, sunt illæ 1. quamobrem credamus has esse Scripturas. 2. quamobrem hunc statuamus & non alium Scripturæ sensum. Quæ non in authoritatem Dei refunduntur & fidei sunt, sed plane alterius naturæ: nec enim tam pro-pe Deum attingunt: ad hominem referuntur, & res humanas, aut ab ipsius constitutione materiæ pendent. Mira Theologemata. Candidè dicam, aut meticulosè falsa doctes[?], aut intricatè & absque sensu vera: expedias te ipse, si potes: facem nos ducentem quæris alibi, & quidem eo modo, uti res ipsæ, uti oratio ducunt, atque hîc aliquid esse dicis, quod à Sp. proficisci posse intelligitur, (quam benè autem hîc, dum facem quærit, de Sp. agat, notatum est antea) sed planè illud removes, ita ut in castra Fanaticorum transeant, qui hîc à Sp. quicquam expectant. Ipse autem, te ipso teste, Fanaticus jam audies. pag. enim 50 & 51. nonne idem quærebas, quod hîc tibi fax dicitur? imo idem; illic enim rem illam de quâ ante, illic & ista tria ponis & quidem ut facem, ut rem quâ tu perceptâ & visâ non poteras dubitare de sensu; & multa ibidem videri vis tribuere Spiritui, jam Fanaticismum Ludovicus exprobrat Wolzogio: quocunque te vertas, à contradictione te non liberabis, ut facem enim hic, Spiritum qui expectat, Fanaticus est, ibi multum sub eodem formali tribuis Spiritui. Rem si intelligis & rectè de ea sentis, ad quid tanta confusio? ubi nunc ista Methodus? noli posthac aliis obscuritatem impingere: sed puto, inquies, mentis constitutionem talem esse, at de mentis constitutione dum agis, quid ad istam usus, cujus oratio, quid ratio, cujus res ipsa objectum est? quid Spiritum removes? sed resipiscens operas Spiritum inter & usum ac rationem partiri videris, ut saltem aliquid sit Spiritui reliquum, dicis mentis constitutionem talem esse, ut multa cernere non possit sæpissimè, quibus opus habet ut persuadeatur, id non negabunt Pelagiani, modo ne ipse neges, quid enim mentis constitutionem culpas? potuisset enim ita constituta Scriptura esse, ut in summa ignorantia demersum peccatorem, ejus sensus non fugisset, ut dicis p. 172. & sic Scripturarum constitutio aliquo egebat auxilio: quid dicis? multa cernere non posse natura hominem quibus &c. id est, pervidere sæpe cœlestem veritatem non potest quia cæcus, sic explicas te p. 167. Ergo quædam cernere aliquando, cœlestem veritatem pervidere aliquando potest cæcus, egregiè! ex sensu Reformatorum nihil spiritualiter, nihil rite percipit, ut nihil videt qui cæcus est; sed de salutari & vera jam perceptione loqueris, dum Spiritum requiris, & illius respectu dices, hominem solummodo multa cernere non posse, sæpe cœlestem veritatem pervidere non posse? Idem ultro dabunt omnes Pelagiani: præsertim, si ita illum Spiritus efficaciam descriptam videant, ut in eo vim exerat Dei Spiritus qui illuminare mentes nostras dicitur, non quod novum lumen iis infundat, quod omne in ipsa radiat Scriptura, sed quia mentis vitia tollit ut videre illud lu-men queat. Novum lumen certè nobis non infundit, si pro veritatibus sumas, quas omnes in Scr. habemus quæ unica lux est, scilicet in genere normæ, regulæ, facis: sed hic circa subjectum, circa mentem ejusque constitutionem versaris, & dicis, quod novum illi non infundatur lumen, attamen Spiritus mentis tollit vitia, imo excitat inertem animum, ad verum scopum ducit, & per illas semitas ducit, quibus tandem perveniat ad salutarem interpretationis veritatem, faciatque omnia illa quæ requiruntur ad hanc veluti actionem animæ. bona verba sed 1. quæ vitia? segnitiem & languorem p. 64. nubem quandam p. 130. errores & præjudicia p. 172. opiniones anticipatas, desidiam p. 250. imo cæcitatem, sed non totalem, quaque homo multa solum non cernere potest, sæpe non pervidere cœlestem veritatem p. 167. moderatè satis omnia, nec Pelagianos sic offendes? 2. Quali operatione? & quomodo ista tolluntur vitia? non per infusionem novi luminis p. 153. non igitur per immediatam realem aut hyperphysicam attingentiam, sed est aliquid in Scriptura quo persuadear p. 64. omne in objecto est, quod de illuminatione nostra: hinc non specie sed gradu solum differre ipsi videtur cognitio & lumen hominis naturalis & regeniti, quid enim aliud illæ phrafes? non ita attendit, non ita scrutatur, qui hoc Sp. non excitatus, non NB eos facit progressus nec NB semper veritatem assequitur. Ac alibi cum explicat qualem lucem agnoscat praeter & supra naturalem, aliam non memorat quam illam, quae objectiva dicitur Theologis: sic enim P. 134. alterius generis est lux rationis, alterius lumen testimoniorum, aut aliorum indi-ciorum quibus de rei veritate erudior. Viden' supra ratio-nem agnoscit aliud, testimoniorum id est objecti-vum lumen, nihil ultra. Nec mirum est, ortho-doxus enim ille Senior multis hoc contendit, non esse diversi generis in regenitis quam irregenitis lu-men aliquod, nimirum concipi sic ab ipso non potest, ergo non est. Imo addit Wolzogius sufficere lumen naturale, ut ad ea attendat, ex quibus pendet intelli-gentia. P. 65. tale quid ad interpretationem requirit solum, quo NB non regenitus, per internam illu-minationem jam elevatus, sed quo, qui ratione utere-tur, adduci posset & deberet, ut de veritate alicujus interpretationis se persuaderi pateretur, est aliquid in ver-bo, dicis, quo persuadeor, at si Amesio credis, non plus quam moralis vis, est illa vis, quae per verbum derivatur, si vero ex Velthuisio, quem, tamen orthodoxum dicit Wolzogen, haec latius vellem deducere, recoctus tandem revivisceret Pelagianismus.
units.tr: The Reformed hold that the unfitness of the subject must not be diminished in any way, but they defend with earnestness and solidity the perfection and sufficiency of the object in this matter. So when someone asks what it is that must move and persuade me, by way of the object, they must be answered that God, in this utterance and in these words, which taken singly and separately by ordinary usage are intelligible, signified this and not something else: namely, that it is Scripture, which in this very place sets this plainly before the understanding, or else kindles a torch for it from other passages. Here you may now see the parties meeting. Philosophy wished to supply this to the blind man: Wolzogen assigns it to reason, to the usage of speech, and to the Holy Spirit. Neither of these, from the truth or from the sense of the Reformed, is right. We leave Tenebrio to others, who long ago have thoroughly refuted his mad invention: Maresius, I think, Essenius, Arnoldus, Vogelsang, Serrarius. We shall examine Wolzogen. He lays down that this office must be given to three things, but he will reject none of them in his own sense, being a Socinian, or in company with himself a paradox. Nor does the Reformed man require none of them, but each in its own place, order and manner. For since the question concerns the object, as the words "norm" and "rule," occurring in this matter, show (although, in Wolzogen's judgment, they are too figurative), so Wolzogen also teaches, on p. 91, when he says that the question is what it was, by which one who uses reason could be led and ought to be led, so as to allow himself to be persuaded of the truth of some interpretation. For one who interprets for himself is certainly moved by some reason, and one who serves others can use the same; so that it is recognised he ought to have been convinced by the force of the reason alleged, had they not themselves contracted some fault: he asks for something that moves me by way of reason, something which, if it is well perceived, we cannot doubt the sense; finally something which leads us as a torch, so that we arrive at evidence, and indeed in such a way that the thing itself and the speech itself can lead us. These things certainly work by way of the external object, and in that order which leads as a torch, as the thing, as the speech can lead; and he recounts the Spirit and disputes loosely about his efficacy; but Wolzogen plainly betrays his great drowsiness. If the matter were concerned with the subject and its aptitude, the case would be otherwise. But now, while he discourses about the object and about the torch that leads, set forth externally by way of the object, he shamefully goes astray, since here too he recounts the Spirit and reasons about him with such great effort. I confess that mention must be made of the Holy Spirit when I am dealing with the object and discussing the object, but only so far as he is the author of Scripture and has declared his judgment in it as Judge. But if someone judges that Wolzogen should be excused because the Paradoxer, who was to be refuted, discourses at length about the Holy Spirit and his operation in us, I reply to him that the Paradoxer has gravely erred in this, since his discourse slides from the object to the subject, a shameful transition into another genus. The Reformed had said that Scripture is the interpreter of Scripture, or that the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture is the judge of controversies and of all interpretation; against this opinion the impotent boaster rises up, and the psychic man, not having the Spirit, chatters much about this and that illumination of the Spirit. Moreover, accusing the Reformed of obscurity, as though they did not distinguish these things well: when he speaks of the sufficiency of reason and the powers of the faculty that reasons, then the power required of the Spirit ought to have been removed, and sufficiency and power claimed for the understanding with its innate notions; but when the Reformed say that Scripture is the interpreter of Scripture, they undoubtedly, setting aside the subject, dispute about the object, and seek its norm and rule of interpreting, as the Paradoxer elsewhere admits; and when they lay down that the Holy Spirit through Scripture and in it is the Judge of interpretation, they say in fact nothing other than this: they are still speaking about the object. They acknowledge the Holy Spirit as author and therefore as speaking in it, they recognise him as interpreter, but not otherwise than Optatus of Milevis says: "If a dispute has arisen among brothers after the father's death, one does not go to the tomb, but the will is sought; and he who rests in the tomb speaks silently from the tablets." Thus when a jurist says that the Emperor explains this or that law, he says nothing different from one who says that he explains one law by another. So you may see the shameless malice or ignorance of the Paradoxer, who makes Whitaker and Scarpius hold something singular apart from the others, and says they dissent from the rest of the Reformed when they attribute to the Spirit an authority of interpreting besides Scripture. He does not understand, or he dissembles, the true opinion of the Reformed, which is an extremely foolish head. But if Wolzogen had noted this properly, the Paradoxer would not have been his pupil in error, nor his follower; he could have refuted what the adversary teaches perversely about the Holy Spirit, but in its own order and place. There is an elevation, excitation and application of the subject, and also a certain sealing of this truth in us by the Spirit, which comes after the interpretation of Scripture has been made; but now we are dealing with the object. But since Wolzogen's method demands it, let us hear to whom he commits the interpretation of Scripture. "And since the power and efficacy of the Spirit has been mentioned first, it can be twofold: one loose, free, moving minds of men by itself, and bound to no things placed outside itself; the other bound to things, and putting itself forth through them at last: the former affects minds by immediate power; the latter only mediately; the former extraordinary, the latter ordinary." All these things are confused. What? Does the Spirit never immediately affect your mind and excite it to spiritual operations? You do not seem to understand what the Reformed mean: that all motions and all dictates are to be measured by the rule and line of Scripture, and whether they agree with it or not must be tested; not that no motions or operations of the Holy Spirit are perceived and received immediately by the faithful, nor that they do not even think of Scripture at the time; indeed they are more often immediately stirred to the reading of Scripture, to prayers and other things. Do you then deny every inward breathing? Do you set these up as contrary? Indeed, if the words are weighed, they leave the reader in doubt whether, apart from the objective proposition, he admits any operation of the Holy Spirit upon the mind itself. "The Spirit," he says, "brings it about that the mind perceives by what it is confirmed," and elsewhere, "he does only this, that our mind may perceive those things without a cloud which are in the very context of Scripture"; the Pelagians will certainly say the same and more. "The Holy Spirit brings it about," you say, "that the mind &c." But by what operation, in what manner? Does he do this only by proposing that object externally and perceptibly, or also by disposing the very subject within habitually, exciting it to act, and thereafter bringing about contact in the manner of a first cause? You make me doubtful of your orthodoxy, when you deny every inward breathing and acknowledge only that Spirit whom you find in Scripture itself; not in the sense that you acknowledge no other than the one of whom Scripture speaks, whose motions agree with Scripture (for so you would have me as a willing supporter); but "there is something in Scripture which, once seen and perceived, you cannot doubt the sense of; something which, on account of a certain corruption of the mind, we cannot see." This is really nothing other than openly sliding back to the object, seeking everything solely in the object, and placing the whole illumination of the Spirit in the external proposition of the object. Indeed, everything that you understand to be done by the operation of the Holy Spirit you oppose to those operations by which he breathes within, which you deny and explode together with all of them; hence elsewhere you grant the Spirit only "some parts," and that too chiefly on account of a certain singular nature of the Scriptures, by a singular constitution of Scripture. "For let us suppose a sinner sunk even in the greatest ignorance: could God speak in such a way that he might be understood even by the most ignorant?" Does the water stick to you so much in the mode of revelation? Could these mysteries of the kingdom of heaven have been spoken so that they might be understood by the most ignorant, without a new life infused into the sinner, if the external mode of proposing, on the side of the object, that is of Scripture, were otherwise and such? You tell marvels, as if you said the sun could vibrate its rays so strongly that they would be perceived even by the blind. Very fine indeed. The Pelagians will ask nothing more, so that their moral means may stand, at least possible, and efficacious. But you may see these things much corrected elsewhere, where you say that these questions are confirmed also "by the power of the Spirit." So, rather thinly; but what are those questions, in whose decision Wolzogen thinks the Spirit acts so sparingly? They are these: 1. why we believe these to be Scriptures; 2. why we hold this and not another sense of Scripture. These are not referred to the authority of God and are not matters of faith, but are plainly of another nature: for they do not touch God so nearly; they are referred to man, and depend upon human affairs or upon the very constitution of matter. Wonderful theologisms. I will say candidly: you teach things that are either timidly false or intricately and without sense true. Extricate yourself, if you can. You seek elsewhere a torch leading us, and indeed in the way that the things themselves, that the speech leads, and you say that here there is something which can be understood to come from the Spirit (how well, however, while he seeks the torch, he speaks of the Spirit has been noted before); but you remove it plainly, so that they pass over into the camp of the Fanatics, who here expect anything from the Spirit. But you yourself, by your own testimony, will now be heard as a Fanatic. For on pages 50 and 51, were you not seeking the same thing that is here called a torch for you? Indeed the same; for there you set down that thing of which we spoke before, and there you set down these three things too, and indeed as a torch, as a thing which, once perceived and seen, you could not doubt the sense of; and you wish to attribute much to the Spirit in the same place under the same formal aspect. Ludovicus already reproaches Wolzogen with Fanaticism. Whichever way you turn, you will not free yourself from contradiction: for here the Spirit, whom the torch expects, is a Fanatic, there you attribute much to the Spirit under the same formal aspect. If you understand the thing and rightly judge of it, why such confusion? Where is that method now? Do not hereafter lay obscurity at the door of others. But, you will say, I think the constitution of the mind is such; yet when you speak of the constitution of the mind, what does use have to do with it, whose speech it is, or reason, whose thing is the object? Why do you remove the Spirit? But, returning to your senses, you seem to divide the work between the Spirit and use and reason, so that at least something remains for the Spirit; you say that "the constitution of the mind is such that it very often cannot discern many things, which it needs to be persuaded of." The Pelagians will not deny this, provided you yourself do not deny it; for why do you blame the constitution of the mind? "For Scripture might have been so constituted that the sense would not have escaped a man sunk in the greatest ignorance," as you say on p. 172; and so the constitution of Scripture needed some help. What do you say? "That man by nature cannot discern many things, by which &c.," that is, "often cannot see through heavenly truth because he is blind," so you explain yourself on p. 167. Therefore the blind man can sometimes discern some things, and sometimes see through heavenly truth: excellent! According to the sense of the Reformed he perceives nothing spiritually, nothing rightly, just as one who is blind sees nothing; but you are speaking of a saving and true perception now, while you require the Spirit, and in regard to him you will say that man can only "not discern many things," and "often cannot see through heavenly truth"? All the Pelagians will readily grant the same, especially if they see the efficacy of the Spirit described thus: that "the Spirit of God, who is said to illuminate our minds, exerts his power in this, not by pouring into them a new light, since all of it shines in Scripture itself, but because he removes the faults of the mind so that it may be able to see that light." Certainly he does not pour a new light into us, if you take as truths those which we all have in Scripture, which is the only light, namely in the general sense of norm, rule and torch; but here you deal with the subject, with the mind and its constitution, and you say that a new light is not poured into it; yet the Spirit "removes the faults of the mind, indeed stirs up the sluggish soul, leads it to the true goal, and leads it along those paths by which it may at last arrive at the saving truth of interpretation, and does all those things which are required for this, as it were, action of the soul." Good words; but first, what faults? "sloth and languor," p. 64; "a certain cloud," p. 130; "errors and prejudices," p. 172; "anticipated opinions, idleness," p. 250; indeed "blindness," but not total, since "man can only not discern many things, often cannot see through heavenly truth," p. 167. Are you not offending the Pelagians by describing everything so moderately? Second, by what operation? And how are these faults removed? "Not by the infusion of a new light," p. 153; so not by an immediate real or hyperphysical touching, but "there is something in Scripture by which one may be persuaded," p. 64. Everything is in the object, which is for our illumination; hence the knowledge and light of natural man and of the regenerate seem to differ to him not in kind but only in degree; for what else do those phrases mean? "He does not attend thus, he does not search thus, who, not stirred up by this Spirit, does not make these advances, nor always attains the truth." Note well. And elsewhere, when he explains what light he acknowledges beyond and above the natural, he mentions no other than that which is called objective by the theologians; for thus on p. 134: "The light of reason is of one kind, the light of testimonies, or of other indications by which one is better taught the truth of a matter, is of another." You see he acknowledges something above reason, namely the objective light of testimonies, and nothing beyond. Nor is it surprising: for that orthodox Senior (Ludovicus) contends that there is no light of a different kind in the regenerate than in the unregenerate; that is to say, it cannot be conceived by him in this way, therefore it is not so. Indeed Wolzogen adds that natural light is sufficient to attend to those things on which understanding depends. On p. 65 he requires only something of this kind for interpretation: that by which one who uses reason, not regenerate and not yet raised up by inward illumination, could be led and ought to be led, so as to allow himself to be persuaded of the truth of some interpretation. There is something in the word, you say, by which I am persuaded; but if you believe Amesius, that power is no more than moral, and that power which is derived through the word is such; but if from Velthuysen, whom Wolzogen calls nevertheless orthodox, I should wish to draw out these matters more widely, Pelagianism, revived and warmed up again, would at last come to life.

units.la: Sic tortuosis istis scripti Wolzogiani jam paragratis viis, quid tandem de ipsius sensu & sententia mihi videtur, breviter exponam. 1. Nihil eum hactenus de corruptione, per peccatum, aut restauratione per gratiam quicquam dixisse, quo non magis emphati-cum & veritati vicinius apud Remonstrantes & Semi-pelagianos invenias. 2. Ac proinde nullibi sufficienter & perspicue demonstratam ipsius orthodoxiam: quod praecipue hoc seculo, hisce temporibus, in ista con-troversia, fieri debuerat, praesertim à Severo isto Catone, qui omnes tam acri obscuritatis notâ pro authoritate dignos[?] censet. 3. Non pauca docere, quæ falsa & veritati & orthodoxis, tam quoad verba quam qnoad sensum, quantum ex hoc dilucido tractatu videri potest, contraria esse probabimus. Dico quantum ex hoc tractatu patet, posset enim resipiscens aut meliora addere, aut mirum in modum ista palliare, sed quantum ex isto tractatu conjici potest, falsa esse dico & Phrasiologiam & rem ipsam quod attinet Heterodoxa; speciminis gratia enumerabimus aliquot ex Wolzogio theses & ventilabimus, antequam ad rei apicem perveniamus.
units.tr: Having now traced those tortuous paths of Wolzogen's writing, I will briefly set out what I think of his meaning and opinion. 1. So far he has said nothing about corruption through sin or restoration through grace that you could not find more emphatically and more closely to the truth among the Remonstrants and Semi-Pelagians. 2. Consequently, his orthodoxy is nowhere sufficiently and clearly demonstrated. This should have been done especially in this century, in these times, in this controversy, and especially by that stern Cato, who judges everything marked with such sharp obscurity unworthy of authority. 3. I will prove that he teaches not a few things which, both in words and in sense, are contrary to the truth and to orthodoxy, so far as can be seen from this clear treatise. I say "so far as this treatise shows," for a penitent man could add better things or soften these remarkably. But as far as can be conjectured from this treatise, I say the things are false, and as regards both the phraseology and the matter itself they are heterodox. By way of sample, I will list some of Wolzogen's theses and examine them before we reach the heart of the matter.

units.la: 1. Prima est, immediatas omnes operationes Sps. Sancti nunc cessare, non immediate mentes nostras affici, ut vidimus supra ex P. 58. hinc ita ipsi displicet afflatus, vocis internæ & similium mentio, imo eos, qui ista crepant, Fanaticis annumerat, & Enthusiastas dicit. Virtute immediata affici ipsi extraordinarium est quod etiam nunc plane cessat. At priusquam alios Enthusiasmi accusares, discere debuisses, quid sit fanaticum, quid Enthusiastam esse. Immediatis revelationibus, aut Scripturæ præferendis aut æquiparandis, ad earum amussim saltem non exigendis, qui fidunt & eas jactant tales Enthusiastas habendos scio; sed afflatum internum omnem, immediatam Sp. inspirationem, vocem internam omnem proscribere, nunquam ausus est, nisi qui Libertinus, saltem carnalis. Quid vetat idem intus & exterius revelari, quid jam revelatum denuo obsignari? Spanhemius etiam, ubi contra Enthusiastas agit, sic statum format controversiæ, urumpræter vel extra Scripturam & ex peculiaribus Enthusiasmis, & privatis revelationibus petenda sit norma sive credendorum sive faciendorum? nunquam autem nostri aut afflatum internum, aut vocem internam, aut immediatam inspirationem rejecerunt, modo Scriptura manserit fidei non solum morumque norma unica, sed & amussis, ad quam &
units.tr: 1. The first is that all the immediate operations of the Holy Spirit now cease, and our minds are not immediately affected, as we saw above from p. 58. Hence he dislikes the mention of an afflatus, an inner voice and similar things. He even counts among the fanatics, and calls enthusiasts, those who harp on such things. To be affected immediately by power is something extraordinary, which indeed now plainly ceases. But before you accused others of enthusiasm, you should have learned what is fanatical and what it is to be an enthusiast. I know that those who trust in immediate revelations, and either set them above Scripture or equate them with it, or do not even require them to be measured by its rule, are rightly to be regarded as enthusiasts. But to banish every inner afflatus, every immediate inspiration of the Spirit, every inner voice, is something only a libertine, or at least a carnal man, has ever dared to do. What forbids the same things to be revealed both inwardly and outwardly, or what forbids what has already been revealed to be sealed again? Spanheim too, when he argues against the enthusiasts, frames the state of the controversy thus: whether the rule of what is to be believed or done is to be sought beyond or apart from Scripture, and from peculiar enthusiasms and private revelations? Yet our people have never rejected an inner afflatus, an inner voice, or immediate inspiration, provided Scripture remains not only the sole rule of faith and morals but also the measure to which all the ... (Disput. Antianabapt. disp. xvi, §. vi) ... of any spirit and mode of operation must be exactly tested.

units.la: Reformatorum de ea sententia & dicta. Disput. Antianabapt. disp xvi. §. vi. dictamina cujuscunque Spiritus, & modus operandi, exigantur exactè. Atque adeo clarè demonstras quam hospes sis in scriptis Reformatorum, quam ignoti ipsorum juxta Scripturam termini & loquendi modi, ni forsan omnes jam Fanatici, exorto novo lu-mine, deprehendantur. Sed audiamus: distinguenda, ait Spanh: inspirationes privatae, quae & originaliter & subjectivè tales, à talibus subjectivè tantum. Illae non damnandae, nemo enim fidelis qui non ejusmodi inspira-tiones habeat: istae vero damnandae. Imo potest Deus extraordinariè inspirare singulare lumen, gratiam, ze-lum, iis qui ordinarias vocationes funguntur in Ecclesia. Verum ut ne videatur solum largiri, Deum id posse, concedit dari, hodieque saepe, praeter motus ordina-rios Spiritus, etiam extraordinarios in filiis Dei,& lumen tale, vide autem quomodo probandi, nego tales motus esse raptus Enthusiastarum, quippe qui contrarii sunt declara-tioni Spiritus in verbo Scripto. At Sp. Dei non est ita & non 2 Cor 1.18. hoc si retineatur, dicit peccari falsa hypothe-si, si quis dicat omnes inspirationes extraordinarias a nobis damnari quin nemo verè pius est, qui tales non persentiscat saepe in corde suo. Haec audi, qui ista negas ridesque. At Spanhemium Virum summum si spernas, aut for-tassis, hujus aevi Enthusiastico malo, correptum putes, (sciat autem lector pios fere nunc carnalibus Enthusiastas dici.) Calvinum audi, Musculum, & fi-miles, illi sic loquuntur, sic sentiunt, ut libello isto Judice, Fanatici sint, unà omnes. Si Spiritus afflatum internum mentem Dei, testis instar, aperientis rides, Hemmingium rides, qui in 1. Cor. 11:16. hac voce utitur hunc in modum. Accipere Sp. Dei, inquit, est eo Sp. afflari, qui nos ad Deum usque subvehat, cujus vi sc: scrutemur & intelligamus salutis nostrae Mysterium, alioqui impervestigabile. Calvinum rides, sic ille ad 1. Joh. 11: 17. Apost. significat se nihil quicquam proponere quod non ultra illis, NB juggerat Dei Sp. . . . . hoc dicit quo plus authoritatis suæ Doctrinæ conciliet: dum ejus NB subscriptionem quisque in corde suo reperit digito Dei insculptam, Bucerum rides qui de Anagocicis Interpretationibus alibi differens eo progreditur, ut putet à solo Spiritu in cordibus fidelium eas doceri solidè, audiamus an non forsan Enthusiasmos doceat vir pientissimus. Ab Anagocicis Interpretationibus mihi temperavi quod ... cognita Historia quisque ipse, subducente Spiritu, illas sibi facile formet. Quæ enim solidæ sunt & animum valent pascere, illæ solius Spiritus, docentis in Sanctorum pectoribus, opus sunt: & alibi sic lo- quitur, Spiritus est afflatus Dei in nobis, energia & vis divina. Episcopius hac de re, antequam ita crasse Pelagianizabat, non malè. Secunda Sp promissi actio, inquit, est motio, ἐνέργεια, agitatio, seu inspiratio quædam arcana & imperceptibilis, per quam Sp. sive animus credentium alacer, idoneus, atque agilis redditur. Actio hæc primum & potissimum circa mentem occupatur, & quidem aut immediatè, per illustrationem & illuminationem ejus in veritatis cognitione: aut mediatè per objectorum obscurorum elucidationem, impedimentorum amotionem, specierum novarum oblationem, mediorum ad firmandas species suppeditationem &c. Hinc Synodus Ar-ausicana illuminationem & inspirationem Sp. S. negantem Hæretico falli statuit spiritu, & veteris Ecclesiæ judicio, requiri præter doctrinam, inspirationem Sp. S. quam vocat occultam, internam mirabilem, ineffabilem, & veram in corde revelationem Vossius author est. Quid? nonne Spiritus testificatur Spiritum veracem esse? nonne testificatur cum nostro Spiritu nos Dei filios esse? non sufficit Reformatorum phrases carpere, ipsam Scripturam tandem corrigent, hodiernæ lucis filii. Palinodiam canat Simeon, aut redeat & de exorta nunc demum luce fundat carmina. Calvinum audi novelle scriptor; necesse est Deum, non mortua tantum litera litera magistrum & Doctorem esse, sed arcano Spiritus in- stinctu Sic necesse est Enthusiastam[?] esse, a Spiritu vero si quid acciperemus deberet voce quadam interna, heu quantus Fanaticismus judice Wolzogio! nos compellare Sanctus Spiritus. Vapulet Paraeus, Spiritus Dei, ait ille, ducit nos dupliciter, foris per verbum, intus per lucem, inclinationes, motus infusos secundum verbum. Imo novam revelationem vocare non veretur Calvinus. Vapulet jam Musculus, qui pro sua simpli-citate sic disserit, si quaeras, inquit, quare nequeat animalis homo cognoscere ea quae sunt Sp Dei, respondet, Apost. sc: quia Spiritaliter dijudicantur. Quid est Spi-ritaliter aliquid fieri? est ex sententia, instinctu & judicio Sp. fieri. --- spiritaliter res divinas cognoscere est eas cognoscere judicio, dictu, & illuminanime Sps. sicut animaliter aliquid vel rationaliter cognoscere, est ex judicio rationis cognoscere Imo praecipuum locum assignat internae revelationi, alibi. Ita enim, ait, comparati sumus, ut licet intus per revelationem caelestis gratiae doceamur, quae sit veritas, Christi nihilominus plurimum adferat roboris, si etiam auribus nostris accesserit vox verbi Dei, idem adferens, quod intus traditum est per revelationem Spiritus Sancti. Scitè admodum Hemmingius Tolle Spiritum à verbo, & remanet mortua litera. Tolle verbum à Spiritu, non amplius remanet Spiritus Dei, sed Sathanae potius. Verbum internum à Reformato defendi si nescis, adi Spanhemium & disce θεοδίδακτον[?] demum esse in cujus animo Deus verbum internum producit, praeter externum{1}, quod audiunt ab hominibus, unice quippe necessarium ad salutarem istius auditionem. Hinc Christus Joh. XVII. verba quae dedisti mihi, dedi iis, id est non per solum externum ministerium in eorum aures posui, nam hoc modo verba sua dederat etiam Pharisaeis, quibus praedicaverat; sed dedi iis per Sp. meum, in eorum corda insculpendo. atque hoc est verè audire Christum intus docencentem : & paulo ante, alii, inquit, praeter externum ministerium intus quoque Christum audiunt & in illo ac per illum docentur. Ipse Jesuita Lorinus hic veritati cedit, haud dubium inquit, quinper fe Joannes velit significare unctionem internam, nec gratiae quidem justi-ficantis, sed doni intellectus, quo vulnus ignorantiae curetur, & ut Gregorius interpretatus est, allocutionem intimae inspirationis, quae humanam mentem contingendo sublevat. Afflatus & inspirationes immediatas omnes pii te docebunt. Conscientias tracta & cum Spirituali-bus, (ringant mundani, sic vocantur ab Apostolo,) consuetudinem cole, eos visita, & disces quae hacte-nus ignoras. Jngenuè dicam, pudore me suffudit Socinianus Smalcius, quippe qui impuro suo scripto de Divinitate Christi, longè melius hosce agnoscit Sp. Sancti motus, quam ullibi Wolzogius, sic ibi homo alias πνϑματόμαχος. Accidit etiam nobis ipsis sæpenumero ut ardentiores ad omnia pietatis officia simus quam alias sumus : & tamen illud quomomodo vel nobis vel aliis accidat nescimus. De Modo quo datur Sp. S. loquitur. Quid? an nunquam immediatè te movet Spiritus, gemitus in te ciet inenarrabiles? nunquam audisti Dominum tibi, in te, loquentem? nunquam consolationem Spiritus de adoptione tua, de Spi-ritus veritate testimonium nunquam percepisti, au-divisti? magister es in Jsraele & illa ignoras Wolzogi? imo rides & exsibilas? Judicas sanè de eo quod nescis. Nam nisi ipse Spiritum ita per instinctum, per afflatum,in te agentem habeas,ineptus es qui judices Spiritu-ales: & hæc jam ride, sed noveris, Spiritum Christi, quem ignominia afficis, vivere. Nemo animalis potest dijudicare, æstimare & cognoscere Spiritalem hominem, ut est Joh. iii. Sp spirat ubi vult, & vocem ejus audis, & nescis unde veniat aut quo vadat, sic est omnis, qui natus est ex Sp. spiritalem enim esse, spiritaliter intellige-re, spiritaliter vivere, talia sunt, quæ non possunt ra-tiotionis judico comprehendi, ideo illud a nemine judicatur non est universaliter de omnibus, sed de iis tantum accipiendum, qui non sunt spirituales. De Spiritus interna sug-gestione dixerat Calvinus de subscriptione digito Dei in corde insculpta dixerat, & subdit, eos ad Spiritus examen revocat, qui solus est idoneus Doctrinae Censor & approbator; deum eam cordibus obsignat ut sciamus Deum loqui. Piorum experientiae quotidianae refragaris apertissime qui ad preces, aliaque saepius pietatis exercitia, excitatos se testantur, imo Spiritus S. nonsolum juvat infirmitatem nostram, sed precandi formulam dictat, ait Aretius. Jmo cuncta a Sp. petunt, expectant, quotquot se, nisi a Sp. agantur, Christi non esse credunt. Quantus Enthusiasta Bucerus hodie audiret, sic ille ad Matth: x. 13. pro Euangelio responsurus suis cogitationibus non nitatur, & Spiritus facundiam ad fore non dubitet: caeterum ut Spiritum orare tamen debet, ita animum ad plectrum Spiritus per eundem Spiritum formare, pia praemeditatione officii est. Spiritus qui loqui in nobis dignatur, idem & cogitare, & meditari solet. Nec minor ipse Calvinus, preces excitat, inquit, & precum motus: scimus enim Sp. S. precum nostrarum esse authorem & impulsorem: ac sine illius instinctu, ne os quidem nobis ad Deum patere. Fides etiam est inspiratio Spiritus Sancti ex sententia Ecclesiae Scoticanae Confess. Art. xii. Fidem dicimus esse sanctam inspirationem, item resipiscentiam, etiam omnes motus sanctos homini subiorientes dicimus esse, sanctas inspirationes, ait Tuissus. Divini est muneris cum & recte cogitamus & pedes nostros a falsitate tenemus, dicebat olim Ecclesia, & nemo habet de suo nisi mendacium & peccatum. Quorsum se dedunt Spiritui, quorsum illius ductum tantopere desiderant? Spiritus reminiscentiae quid an non immediate agit, an non ipsam mentem nostram attingit? quando in periculis & tentationibus etiam ea quae alioqui nobis ex verbo Dei sunt notissima, sæpe non occurrunt, nisi à Sp. S. suggerantur, verba sunt Joh. Gerhardi. Deus per Sp. sublevat fideles illud ipsum eis in memoriam revocando, quod antea audivere. Socinianò ipso teste, certè nimis arctè Christo uniti sunt fideles, quam ut Spiritus eos nunquam immediatè, per internum afflatum nunquam tangat. Totum Ecclesiæ corpus, singulaque Ecclesiæ membra à Christo, qui est caput, accipiunt vitam, motum & totum alimentum, quo augentur & incrementum capiunt: quemadmodum etiam ab eodem suam habent originem, suum esse, & ut sint membra tali capiti adglutinata---tam verè ac realiter vita ac motus, sed spiritualis, alimentum ac incrementum, sed spirituale, à Christo in nos derivantur, sed per ejus Sp. uti etiam à capite corporis nostri in membra fluit vita, motus & alimentum quo vivimus & adolescimus: ut enim hoc significaret Apostolus, non usus est simili corporis Politici, sed corpois Physici. Hinc juxta Sp. ambulare Hemmingio est juxta motus Sp. S. vivere. Wolzogio autem, similia si quis diceret, næ ille Fanaticus habebitur. Taceant nunc de Spiritus diversis & variis motibus; νεωτερισμα[?], quibus quid Spiritus, quid caro dictet, quid pro carnis, pro Sp. divini afflatu motuque quid tenendum, probari possit, anxiè ne inquirant, frustra est. Exorto novo lumine dispelluntur & deteguntur hæ præstigiæ; Fanatici sunt qui sic concionantur, sic scribunt, qui ista crepant Enthusiastæ omnes. Infantes cogita, quibus semen fidei inditum & sanctificationis; in illis etiam non continenti influxu, non immediato contactu, sed mediatè semper fidei semen conservat & fovet? quali afflatu, quali revelatione, quali influxu, qui in infantia in Domino moriuntur à Sp. S. preparati sunt? Tedet me cum Reformato disputare de re tam certa & perspicua. Miros animorum motus, amoris incendia, gaudii ineffabilis in corda per Sp. effusiones, cælestes delicias, ebrietates, osculaquid referam? ram? quid manna occultum? quid novum nomen? frustra hæc omnia, modo non clarè & distinctè percipiantur, dum interim mundo ridicula fore, solis piis nota, cunctis vero ineffabilia, dudum ex Scriptura docti sumus. Utinam hæc non tam aliunde docti & in conjectura prospicientes, quam in nobis experti sciamus, intelligamus! Sed regeres forsan, me elenchum ignorare, & te de istis Sp. S. motibus non loqui, nihil determinare, sed tantum quid Sp. in Scripturæ intellectione præstet explicare voluisse. Quod credi forsan posset, ni omnes immediatas operationes, omnes afflatus internos rejecisses absque ulla limitatione: & quid si credam, nihil tamen ad te excusandum, nam etiam in Scripturæ intellectione, Spiritus immediatè mentem tangit, suo afflatu; ut ex aliis audivimus jam supra, præterquam enim, quod menti novum habituale lumen indere, illud principium continuo influxu conservare, ut & ad singulos actus novo contactu excitare debet, quò totum illud quod producitur, totus ille actus, sit Spiritus Sancti, in genere causæ primæ, & hominis in genere causæ secundæ: sicque æque ista signata e. gr. intellectio Spiritui tribuenda erit, quam ad preces incitatio, aliique quos forsan concedere videri velles motus. At porro post elicitam e. g. hanc aut illam, circa certam veritatem, congruam intellectus actionem, nullam Spiritus S. sæpe supervenientem suavem & immediatam obsignationem, qua mira certitudine, animo ulterius certioretur veritas ista, didicisti? claram perceptionem ejusque conscientiam ait Paradoxus tuus, neutram vero quomodo peragat in piis Sp. novit. Quanquam, quod ad istam obsignationem attinet, non semper æqualem & eundem agendi modum, aut gradum observet S. Sp. quod enim Publicè in Scriptura S. judicat S. Sp. id ipsum privatim in cordibus fidelium confirmat, quisquis hoc negat, Spiritum Christi non habet, sed Spiritum hujus mundi. Sic magnus Thologus : plura alibi idem author, de Obsignatione beneficiorum Dei agens, sic disserit. Obsignatio be- neficiorum Dei interna, est, quæ fit per testimonium internum in corde uniuscujusque verè credentis. Testi- monium illud internum est geminum: unum Spiritus nostri, alterum S. Sancti. Illud est conscientia nostra per sanguinem Christi mundata quæ nobis testatur quod filii Dei simus; hoc vero est revelatio interna per Sp. Sanctum fidelibus facta, dum corda nostra perfundit ineffabili quodam sensu &c. En internum testimonium, revelationem internam, & quidem à conscientiæ testimonio diversam : Et ne minus hunc Polani locum, quia de beneficiis loquitur, quadrare putes, quia de veritatibus nobis sermo est: scias utriusque, hoc respectu, rationem, non diversam sed eandem esse, res per se clara est. Jmo veritas est quæ obsignatur, dum credenti revelat quod filius Dei sit: & majus quid est, quam si veritatem, in Scriptura explicitè positam, intus, per talem revelationem, obsignari statuerem: veritas enim hæc, non nisi per consequentiam ex sacris haberi potest, sicque non solum, ut primo intuitu, sed & in quamtum per consequentiam ex sacris deducitur, superveniente tali interna revelatione, Polano teste, obsignatur. Annon autem simile etiam circa Scripturæ veritates admittat internum testimonium, ex ipso Polano audire lubet, sic ille alibi, internum de Scrip- tura testimonium, est revelatio interna Spiritus Sancti, qui nos per internum afflatum ita docet in cordibus nostris, quo efficaciter persuadeat &c. & paulo post, omnia vera fidei dogmata à Sp. Sancto in cordibus nostris obsignantur Joh. xv. 13. & Papisticum esse dicit, statuere hoc internum Sp. testimonium (revelationem, afflatum etiam vocaverat, à quibus tantopere abhorret Wolzogen,) ad Scripturarum cognitionem non pertinere, hinc est, quod mundani, sapientiam suam ita de throno dejectam & conculcatam non ferentes, adversus Dei servos ita petulanter insurgant, dicant modo, hoc omnes non intelligitis, hoc solum capiunt quibus datum est &c. & Enthusiastæ erunt: Scio quid præcedenti anno hac de re quidam antisabbathicus cum Velthuisio de usu Rat.p. 138. scripserit. Ridet illos, qui nisi Sp. intus doceat, revelet &c. auditores capere non posse, quæ proponuntur, clamitant, sed quandoquidem sanni & sarcasmi placent istis hominibus, bene est, Augustinus ipsis deridendum sese itidem propinat, sic enim ille, Sonus verborum nostrorum aures percutit, magister intus est. Nolite putare, quemquam hominem discere ab homine. Admonere possumus per strepitum vocis nostræ: si non sit intus qui doceat, inanis sit strepitus noster. Adeo fratres vultis nosse? numquid non sermonem istum omnes audistis? Quam multi hinc indocti exituri sunt? Quantum ad me pertinet, omnibus locutus sum: sed quibus unctio illa intus non loquitur, quos Spiritus S. intus non docet, indocti redeunt. Magisteria forinsecus adjutoria quædam sunt & admonitiones. Cathedram in cælo habet, qui corda docet. De Domino dico ubi illius inspiratio & illius unctio non est, forinsecus inaniter perstrepunt verba. Similia habet Gregorius Homil. xxx. in Euang. Nisi idem Spiritus cordi adsit audientis, ociosus est sermo Doctoris. Non ergo docenti homini tribuat, quod ex ore docentis intelligit, quia, nisi intus sit, qui doceat, Doctoris lingua exterius in vacuum laborat: per vocem non instruitur, quando mens per Sp. non ungitur. Sic quoque Beda. hosce rideant, Heidanum sannis excipiant, Virum satis Celebrem, sic enim ille cælestem sapientiam considerat, ut aut occulta nobis semper remanere debeat, aut immediata Spiritus revelatione acquiri. Christus discipulorum aures externa voce verberans, Spiritu suo internas mentis tis aures perforat; sine quo externas aures perforare non solum inutile, sed etiam noxium foret. Hinc docemur, nullam cujusque Doctoris esse, seu notitiam rerum cælestium, seu facultatem dicendi, seu sanctimoniam, seu denique quicquid est, quod in Ecclesiæ Doctore exoptari possit, quod non tantum nobis non prosit, sed vel non obsit etiam, nisi dona illa Deus spiritu suo fæcunda-verit & fructuosa reddiderit. Cum enim servatoris Christi dona & ἰκανότης perfectissima hominibus non commodent, nisi à Spiritu S. irrigentur, & perpluantur, næ nos ipsos fallemur, si ab aliorum doctrina fructum & messem sine Spiritus operatione præstolemur. Sic Cartwrichtus, qui quantus fuerit Heereboordio, docet præfixa operi dedicatio. Sine Spiritu enim arcana Spiritus quærere, ni-hil est aliud, quam sine luce videre velle. Non mirum est ergo, si non tantum inter eos, qui extra septa Ecclesiæ vagantes in errore versantur, tot reperiantur qui S. Scr. sensus prorsus alienos affingunt: sed etiam si inter illos, qui in Ecclesiæ communione externa vivunt, & se profitentur verbi Dei auditores, imo & scrutatores, non pauci sint, qui corticem sæpe mordentes, spiritus medullam non assequantur, ait Rivetus. Jam dicas Spiritum nihil dictare, id tantum facere ut mens nostra perspicere ea possit sine nube quæ in ipso insunt Scripturæ Textu, nunc interpretationis omnem certitudinem ab usu expectandam doce; aliquam si diceres, aut omnem, sed in suo genere, non ita absurdum foret; sed nullo alio sensu, inconcussam concedis explicationis certitudinem, quam quatenus, præter id, quod usus suppeditat, à ratione confirmatur sæpissime, ab interiori Sp. afflatu diceret Calvinus. Sed Spiritui aliquid saltem tribuit Wolzogen: & à Sp. corroboretur plerumque, sed fallitur, qui se jam ex Reformatorum sensu dictam modo obsignationem à Wolzogio concessam videre putat, non enim per revelationem, testimonium, afflatum internum, quæ ad Enthu-siastas fiastas[?] ablegat, hoc ejus sensu agit Sp. sed mentes nostras solum ita defæcando, ut sine ullo impedimento omnem pervidere interpretationis veritatem possint, hoc sensu inconcussam certitudinem admitto. Aliud quid dixerat Po-lanus, aliud quisque Orthodoxus, à Deo, sic Bodius, imposterum ita pendeamus, ut sensum & apprehensionem omnem, ut cognitionem & aspectum omnem rerum illarum cœlestium, omnem denique in fide, sapientia, & alia quavis virtute salutari progressum, nec hominum industriæ, & in docendo solertiæ, nec nostris ipsorum laboribus, sed ejus unius efficaci gratiæ acceptum feramus, ejus arcanæ virtuti & persuasioni imputemus. Confen-tit Calvinus. Virtutis suæ afflatu, de Dei Sp. loquitur, divinam nobis vitam sic inspirat, ut non jam agamur ipsi à nobis, sed ejus actione & motu regamur: ut si quæ sunt in nobis bona, fructus sunt gratiæ ipsius, nostræ vero sine ipso dotes, mentis sint tenebræ cordisque perversitas. Lubet adscribere insignem locum Bodii, quo quid Spiritui tribuatur à Reformatis graphicè depingit. Vita Dei, inquit, nempe quam pii ut tales vivunt, appellatur, non quod Deum authorem habeat, quomodo vitam omnem à Deo esse diximus, verum potius quod à Dei præsentia gratiosa per Spiritum suum in nobis habitantis NB immediatè promanet; & ejus voluntati conformis sit, per Spiritum Sanctificationis, qui est vitæ nostræ vita, & animæ nostræ anima. Sicut enim hæc vita naturalis ab animæ rationalis præsentia & unione illa personali cum corpore immediate promanat atque dependet, estque vel illud esse viventis, quod ex animæ cum corpore conjunctione nascitur, vel proxima & præcipua animæ functio sive operatio in corpore, per quam tum corpori vegetationem, motum, sensum, impertitur; tum in homine ratiocinatur, appetit, intelligit; atque ita omnium viventis, qua vivens est, actionum principium est; Ita etiam vita illa nova & Spiritualis, à Spiritus S. præsentia & gratiosa in nobis habitatione promanat; estque vel novum illud esse quod habemus in Christo Jesu, simulatque ipsi per fidem insiti sumus, & Spiritus ipsius facti participes, de quo loquitur Apostolus 1. Cor. 1. 30. Sed ex ipso vos estis in Christo Jesu, qui factus est nobis à Deo &c. inquiens; h. e. in Christo J. vos novum [esse] novam vitam, novam (ut ita dicam) conditionem, exi-stentiam, naturam, una cum nova illa generatione acce-pistis. (Nam ut alias inquit idem, si quis est in Christo, est nova creatura: vetera praeterierunt, ecce nova facta sunt omnia) vel ipsa Spiritus S. in cordibus nostris efficax operatio, qua novum sensum, motum, affectum in nobis producit, nosque ad novas & Spirituales actiones, Dei voluntati conformes, idoneos reddit, ita ut hac nova vita donati alia plane sapere & sentire, alia plane quaerere & curare, alia prorsus eligere atque diligere, alius denique affici, moveri, delectari incipiamus, quam quae nos antea capiebant atque tangebant, quamdiu vitam tantum animalem viveremus. Quilibet fidelis habet verum ac spirituale Urim & Thummim in pectore suo, nempe luci-dissimum ardentissimumque modo indicatum summi Sacer-dotis Di. N. J. C. Spiritum. Rom. viii. 9. 14. Gal. iv. 6. quilibet etiam fidelis est Sacerdos, qui & consuli & consulere potest Apoc. 1. 6. Nimirum ardens instansque precatio est Catholica illa Jesu Christi per Urim & Thummim interrogatio cui ipse per ineffabilem lucem invictumque motum & impulsum priorum consulentium conscientiae ita respondet, ut de officio suo certi & de salutari eventu sint securi. Haec disce Wolzogi. Necesse non est in hisce diutius morari. Quid ex Wolzogii scripto objici adversus jam disputata queat, videamus.
units.tr: Of the Reformers' view on this, and what they said. Disputation against the Anabaptists, disp. 16, §6: the dictates of every kind of Spirit, and the manner of its working, must be examined exactly. And so you clearly show how much of a stranger you are to the writings of the Reformers, and how unknown to you are their terms and modes of speaking, unless perhaps everyone is now found to be a Fanatic, now that a new light has risen. But let us hear him: distinguish, says Spanheim, private inspirations, which are such both originally and subjectively, from those that are such only subjectively. The former are not to be condemned, for no believer is without inspirations of this kind; but the latter are to be condemned. Indeed, God can extraordinarily inspire a singular light, grace, and zeal in those who discharge the ordinary callings in the Church. But so that he may not seem to grant only that God can do this, he concedes that it is given, and often today, besides the ordinary motions of the Spirit, also extraordinary ones in the children of God, and such a light. See, however, how he proves it: I deny that such motions are the raptures of the Enthusiasts, since they are contrary to the declaration of the Spirit in the written Word. But the Spirit of God is not so, and not 2 Cor. 1.18. If this is retained, he says, it is an error from a false hypothesis if someone says that all extraordinary inspirations are condemned by us, since no one is truly pious who does not often perceive such things in his heart. Hear this, you who deny and mock these things. But if you despise Spanheim, a man of the highest rank, or perhaps think him seized by the Enthusiastic disease of this age (let the reader know that the pious are now almost always called carnal Enthusiasts), hear Calvin, Musculus, and their like. They speak so, they think so, that by this little book's judgment they are all Fanatics together. If the Spirit reveals the inward breathing of God's mind, as a witness, you mock; you mock Hemmingius, who uses this expression in 1 Cor. 11:16 in this manner: to receive the Spirit of God, he says, is to be breathed upon by that Spirit, who carries us up even to God, by whose power we may search out and understand the mystery of our salvation, which otherwise could not be investigated. You mock Calvin, who, on 1 John 11:17, says of the Apostle that he sets forth nothing that is not further impressed upon them by the Spirit of God (NB) ... he says this so that he may win more authority for his doctrine, while everyone finds its subscription in his heart, inscribed by the finger of God (NB). You mock Bucer, who, writing elsewhere about anagogical interpretations, goes so far as to think that they are solidly taught only by the Spirit in the hearts of believers. Let us hear whether this most pious man perhaps does not teach Enthusiasm. I have refrained from anagogical interpretations, because, once the history is known, each person, with the Spirit leading him, easily forms them for himself. For those that are solid and able to feed the soul are the work of the Spirit alone, teaching in the breasts of the saints. And elsewhere he speaks thus: The Spirit is the breathing of God in us, the energy and divine power. Episcopius on this matter, before he began to Pelagianize so crudely, did not write badly: The second action of the promised Spirit, he says, is motion, [ἐνέργεια], agitation, or a certain secret and imperceptible inspiration, through which the Spirit, or the mind of believers, is made lively, fit, and agile. This action occupies the mind first and foremost, and indeed either immediately, through the illumination and enlightenment of it in the knowledge of the truth; or mediately, through the elucidation of obscure objects, the removal of hindrances, the offering of new species, the supplying of means to strengthen the species, etc. Hence the Council of Orange, denying the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, decided that one is deceived by a heretical spirit, and that by the judgment of the ancient Church, besides doctrine, the inspiration of the Holy Spirit is required, which it calls hidden, inward, wonderful, ineffable, and the true revelation in the heart; Vossius is the author. What? Does not the Spirit testify that the Spirit is true? Does He not testify with our spirit that we are children of God? It is not enough to pick at the phrases of the Reformers; the sons of today's light will in the end correct Scripture itself. Let Simeon sing a palinode, or let him return and pour out songs about the light that has at last risen. Hear Calvin, the new writer: It is necessary that God be not only a teacher and instructor by the dead letter, but also by a secret instinct of the Spirit. So it is necessary that we be Enthusiasts. If we were to receive anything from the Spirit, it would have to be by a certain inward voice, alas, how great the Fanaticism by the judgment of Wolzogen! The Holy Spirit addresses us. Let Paraeus be scourged: The Spirit of God, he says, leads us in two ways, outwardly through the word, inwardly through light, inclinations, and motions infused according to the word. Indeed, Calvin does not hesitate to call it a new revelation. Let Musculus now be scourged too, who, in his simplicity, argues thus: If you ask, he says, why the natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit of God, he answers, that is, the Apostle, because they are judged spiritually. What is it for something to be done spiritually? It is to be done according to the mind, instinct, and judgment of the Spirit. ... To know divine things spiritually is to know them by the judgment, dictation, and illumination of the Spirit, just as to know something animally or rationally is to know it by the judgment of reason. Indeed, he assigns the chief place to inward revelation elsewhere: For we are so constituted, he says, that although we are taught inwardly, through the revelation of heavenly grace, what the truth is, nevertheless the voice of God's word, if it also reaches our ears, brings much more strength, bringing the same thing that has been delivered inwardly through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Hemmingius has said it very well: Take the Spirit away from the word, and the dead letter remains. Take the word away from the Spirit, and it is no longer the Spirit of God, but rather Satan's. If you do not know that the inward word is defended by a Reformed writer, consult Spanheim, and learn [θεοδίδακτον] that he is taught by God in whose mind God produces the inward word, besides the outward one that they hear from men, which alone is necessary for the saving hearing of it. Hence Christ, John 17: the words which you have given me, I have given to them, that is, I did not place them in their ears only through the outward ministry (for in this way He had given His words also to the Pharisees, to whom He had preached); but I have given them through My Spirit, engraving them in their hearts. And this is truly to hear Christ teaching within. And a little before: Others, he says, besides the outward ministry, hear Christ inwardly also, and are taught in Him and through Him. The Jesuit Lorinus himself yields to the truth here: there is no doubt, he says, that John wishes to signify an inward anointing, not even of justifying grace, but of the gift of understanding, by which the wound of ignorance is healed, and, as Gregory interpreted it, an address of inward inspiration, which, by touching the human mind, raises it up. Pious men will teach you all about immediate afflatuses and inspirations. Deal with consciences and keep company with the spiritual (let the worldly mock; they are so called by the Apostle); visit them, and you will learn what you have hitherto not known. To speak frankly, the Socinian Smalcius has made me blush with shame, for in his impure writing on the Divinity of Christ he acknowledges these motions of the Holy Spirit far better than Wolzogen anywhere, although there he is otherwise a [πνευματόμαχος]. It also happens to us ourselves very often that we are more ardent for all the duties of piety than we otherwise are; yet how this happens to us or to others we do not know. He speaks of the manner in which the Holy Spirit is given. What? Does the Spirit never move you immediately, stir up unutterable groanings in you? Have you never heard the Lord speaking to you, in you? Have you never perceived or heard the Spirit's consolation about your adoption, the testimony of the Spirit's truth? Are you a teacher in Israel and ignorant of these things, Wolzogen? Or rather do you laugh and hiss? You judge surely about what you do not know. For unless you yourself have the Spirit working in you by such instinct and such afflatus, you are unfit to judge spiritual men. Laugh at these things now, but know that the Spirit of Christ, whom you dishonour, is alive. The natural man cannot judge, estimate, and know the spiritual man, as it is in John 3: the Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, and you do not know where it comes from or where it goes; so is everyone who is born of the Spirit. For to be spiritual, to understand spiritually, to live spiritually, are such things that cannot be comprehended by the judgment of reason; therefore that saying, that it is judged by no one, is not to be taken universally of all, but only of those who are not spiritual. Calvin had spoken of the inward suggestion of the Spirit, of the subscription of the finger of God engraved in the heart, and he adds: he calls them back to the examination of the Spirit, who alone is a fit censor and approver of doctrine; God seals it in their hearts so that we may know that God speaks. You openly contradict the daily experience of the pious, who testify that they are stirred to prayer and to other exercises of piety very often; indeed the Holy Spirit not only helps our weakness, but dictates the form of prayer, says Aretius. Nay, all who do not believe themselves to belong to Christ unless they are led by the Spirit seek and expect everything from the Spirit. How Enthusiastic Bucer would sound today, who thus, on Matthew 10:13, says: He who is to answer for the Gospel must not rely on his own thoughts, and must not doubt that the Spirit will supply eloquence in the moment; yet he must pray to the Spirit, and by the same Spirit prepare his mind for the plectrum of the Spirit, which is a pious preparation for the duty. The Spirit who deigns to speak in us is also accustomed to think and meditate. Calvin is no less: he stirs up prayers, and the motions of prayer, he says, for we know that the Holy Spirit is the author and impeller of our prayers, and without His instinct not even our mouth is open to God. Faith too is an inspiration of the Holy Spirit, according to the Confession of the Scottish Church, Art. 12: We say that faith is a holy inspiration; likewise repentance; and we say that all holy motions arising in man are holy inspirations, says Tuissus. It is a gift of God both when we think rightly and when we keep our feet from falsehood, the Church once said, and no one has anything of his own except lies and sin. Why do men give themselves over to the Spirit, why do they so greatly desire His guidance? Does not the Spirit of remembrance act immediately, and touch our very mind? When in dangers and temptations, even those things which are otherwise most familiar to us from the Word of God often do not come to mind unless they are suggested by the Holy Spirit: these are the words of John Gerhard. God, through the Spirit, raises up the faithful by recalling to their memory that very thing which they heard before. By the testimony of the Socinian himself, the faithful are certainly too closely united to Christ for the Spirit never to touch them immediately, never through inward breathing. The whole body of the Church, and each member of the Church, receive life, motion, and all nourishment from Christ, who is the head, by which they are increased and grow; just as they also have from the same Christ their origin, their being, and that they are members joined to such a head ... so truly and really life and motion, but spiritual; nourishment and growth, but spiritual, flow to us from Christ, but through His Spirit. Just as life, motion, and nourishment, by which we live and grow, flow from the head of our body into the members; for the Apostle, in order to signify this, did not use the likeness of a political body but of a physical body. Hence, according to the Spirit, to walk is for Hemmingius to live according to the motions of the Holy Spirit. But for Wolzogen, if someone said similar things, he would be considered a Fanatic. Let them now be silent about the diverse and various motions of the Spirit, [novelty], by which it may be proved what the Spirit dictates and what the flesh dictates, and what is to be held as from the divine breathing and motion of the Spirit as opposed to the flesh; it is in vain that they anxiously inquire. With a new light risen, these illusions are dispelled and exposed; those who preach so, who write so, who crow these things, are all Enthusiasts. Think of infants, in whom the seed of faith and of sanctification has been placed; does not the Spirit preserve and cherish this seed in them always, not by a continuous influx, not by immediate contact, but mediately? By what breathing, what revelation, what influx were those prepared by the Holy Spirit who die in infancy in the Lord? I am weary of disputing with a Reformed man about a matter so certain and so clear. Shall I recount the wonderful movements of souls, the burnings of love, the inexpressible joy poured into hearts by the Spirit, heavenly delights, intoxications, kisses? What of the hidden manna? What of the new name? All these things are in vain unless they are perceived clearly and distinctly, while meanwhile we have long since learned from Scripture that they will be ridiculous to the world, known only to the pious, and ineffable to all. Would that we might know and understand these things not so much as learned from elsewhere and foreseen by conjecture, but as experienced in ourselves! But perhaps you would reply that I do not know the point at issue, and that you are not speaking of these motions of the Holy Spirit, determining nothing, but wished only to explain what the Spirit achieves in the understanding of Scripture. This might perhaps be believed, were it not that you rejected all immediate operations and all inward afflatuses without any limitation. And even if I were to believe it, it would not excuse you at all, for even in the understanding of Scripture the Spirit touches the mind immediately by His breathing; as we have heard from others above. For besides pouring a new habitual light into the mind, and preserving that principle by continual influx, He must also stir it up to each act by new contact, so that everything that is produced, the whole of that act, is of the Holy Spirit as first cause in general, and of man as second cause in general. And thus that particular intellection, for example, will be attributed to the Spirit just as much as the incitement to prayer, and the other motions which you might seem willing to concede. But further, after this or that congruous act of the intellect has been elicited, concerning some certain truth, have you not often learned of a sweet and immediate sealing by the Holy Spirit coming upon it, by which the soul is further assured of that truth with wonderful certainty? Your Paradox speaks of clear perception and its consciousness, but how the Holy Spirit accomplishes neither in the pious, it does not know. Although, as far as that sealing is concerned, the Holy Spirit does not always observe an equal and the same manner or degree of acting, for what the Holy Spirit judges publicly in Scripture, the same He confirms privately in the hearts of the faithful; whoever denies this does not have the Spirit of Christ but the spirit of this world. So says the great theologian. The same author, speaking more about the sealing of God's benefits, argues thus: The inward sealing of God's benefits is that which is effected by the inward testimony in the heart of each one who truly believes. That inward testimony is twofold: one of our spirit, the other of the Holy Spirit. The former is our conscience, cleansed by the blood of Christ, which testifies to us that we are children of God; the latter is the inward revelation made to believers by the Holy Spirit, while it pours our hearts full with a certain ineffable sense, etc. Here is the inward testimony, the inward revelation, and indeed one different from the testimony of conscience. And lest you think this passage of Polanus less apt because it speaks of benefits, while our discussion concerns truths, know that the reason in both respects is not different but the same; the matter is clear in itself. Indeed it is the truth that is sealed, while it reveals to the believer that he is a son of God; and it is something greater than if I were to maintain that a truth explicitly set down in Scripture is sealed inwardly by such a revelation. For this truth can be had only by consequence from the sacred writings, and so it is sealed by such an inward revelation, according to Polanus, not only as at first sight but also insofar as it is deduced by consequence from the sacred writings. But let us hear from Polanus himself whether he admits a similar inward testimony also concerning the truths of Scripture. He says elsewhere: The inward testimony concerning Scripture is the inward revelation of the Holy Spirit, who teaches us in our hearts through an inward breathing, so that He effectively persuades, etc. And a little after: all the true dogmas of faith are sealed in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, John 15:13. And he says it is Papistical to hold that this inward testimony of the Spirit (he had also called it revelation and afflatus, things from which Wolzogen shrinks so greatly) does not pertain to the knowledge of the Scriptures. Hence it is that worldly men, unable to bear their wisdom so cast down from its throne and trampled, rise up so insolently against the servants of God, and say only: you all do not understand this, they alone grasp this to whom it has been given, etc., and they will be Enthusiasts. I know what a certain anti-sabbatarian wrote on this matter the previous year, together with Velthuysen, on the use of reason (p. 138). He mocks those who, unless the Spirit teaches inwardly, reveals, etc., cry out that hearers cannot grasp what is proposed; but since jests and sneers please these men, it is well that Augustine offers himself to them also for mockery in the same way. For thus he says: The sound of our words strikes the ears; the teacher is within. Do not think that anyone learns from a man. We can admonish by the noise of our voice; if there is not within one who teaches, our noise is empty. Do you, brethren, wish to know so much? Have not you all heard this sermon? How many will go out from here untaught? As far as I am concerned, I have spoken to all; but those in whom that anointing does not speak within, whom the Holy Spirit does not teach within, return untaught. Outward teachings are certain helps and admonitions. He who teaches hearts has his chair in heaven. I speak of the Lord: where His inspiration and His anointing is not, the words resound outwardly in vain. Gregory has similar things in Homily 30 on the Gospel: Unless the same Spirit is present to the heart of the hearer, the teacher's discourse is idle. Therefore let us not ascribe to the teaching man what he understands from the mouth of the teacher; for unless there is within one who teaches, the teacher's tongue labours outwardly in vain: he is not instructed by the voice when his mind is not anointed by the Spirit. Bede likewise. Let them mock these men; let them pelt Heidanus with jeers, a man famous enough. For thus he considers heavenly wisdom: it must either always remain hidden from us, or be acquired by an immediate revelation of the Spirit. Christ, striking the ears of the disciples with an outward voice, pierces their inner ears of the mind with His Spirit; without which to pierce the outward ears would be not only useless but even harmful. Hence we are taught that there is nothing in any teacher, whether knowledge of heavenly things, or ability to speak, or holiness, or, in short, whatever can be desired in a teacher of the Church, which not only does not profit us but may even harm us, unless God has made those gifts fruitful and productive by His Spirit. For since the gifts of the Saviour Christ and most perfect [ἱκανότης] are of no use to men unless they are watered and drenched by the Holy Spirit, we would certainly deceive ourselves if we awaited fruit and harvest from the doctrine of others without the working of the Spirit. So Cartwright, who was, as the dedication prefixed to the work shows, a great man to Heereboord, teaches: For to seek the secrets of the Spirit without the Spirit is nothing else than to wish to see without light. It is no wonder, then, if not only among those who, wandering outside the fences of the Church, live in error, so many are found who attach senses wholly foreign to Holy Scripture, but also if among those who live in the outward communion of the Church and profess themselves hearers, indeed searchers, of the Word of God, there are not a few who, while often biting at the bark, do not reach the marrow of the spirit, says Rivetus. Now you may say that the Spirit dictates nothing, but only does this, that our mind may perceive without cloud those things which are in the very text of Scripture; and now you teach that all certainty of interpretation is to be expected from use; if you said some certainty, or all certainty but in its own kind, it would not be so absurd; but in no other sense do you concede an unshakable certainty of explanation than insofar as, besides what use supplies, it is very often confirmed by reason, as Calvin said from the inward breathing of the Spirit. But Wolzogen does ascribe something at least to the Spirit: and it is for the most part strengthened by the Spirit; but he is mistaken who thinks he sees already, in the sense of the Reformers, that the sealing just mentioned is conceded by Wolzogen; for he does not mean by the Spirit an act of revelation, testimony, or inward afflatus, which he sends off to the Enthusiasts; in this sense the Spirit acts only by purging our minds so that they can, without any hindrance, perceive the whole truth of interpretation; in this sense I admit an unshakable certainty. Polanus had said one thing, and every orthodox writer another.
