From God, thus Bodius: henceforth we should so depend that we bear every sense and apprehension, every knowledge and insight into those heavenly things, and every progress in faith, wisdom, and every other saving virtue, not to the industry of men or their skill in teaching, nor to our own labours, but to the acceptance of His alone effectual grace, and impute it to His secret virtue and persuasion. Calvin agrees. Speaking of God's Spirit, he says: by the breathing of His power He so breathes divine life into us, that we are no longer driven by ourselves, but are ruled by His action and motion; so that if there are any good things in us, they are fruits of His grace, while our own endowments apart from Him are darkness of mind and perversity of heart. I should like to add an outstanding passage of Bodius, in which he vividly portrays what the Reformed attribute to the Spirit. The life of God, he says, that is, the life which the pious live as such, is so called not because it has God as its author, as we have said that all life is from God, but rather because it flows immediately from the gracious presence of God dwelling in us through His Spirit (NB), and is conformed to His will through the Spirit of sanctification, who is the life of our life and the soul of our soul. For just as this natural life flows immediately from the presence of the rational soul and its personal union with the body, and depends on it, and is either the being of the living thing, which arises from the conjunction of soul and body, or the proximate and chief function or operation of the soul in the body, by which it imparts to the body growth, motion, and sense, and in man reasons, desires, and understands; and thus is the principle of all the actions of the living thing, insofar as it is living; so too that new and spiritual life flows from the presence of the Holy Spirit and His gracious indwelling in us; and it is either that new being which we have in Christ Jesus, as soon as we are implanted in Him by faith and made partakers of His Spirit, of which the Apostle speaks in 1 Cor. 1:30: "But of Him are you in Christ Jesus, who was made unto us from God," etc.; that is, in Christ Jesus you have received a new life, a new condition, as it were, a new existence and nature, together with that new generation (for as the same says elsewhere: if anyone is in Christ he is a new creature; old things have passed away, behold, all things are made new); or it is the efficacious operation of the Holy Spirit in our hearts, by which He produces in us a new sense, motion, and affection, and makes us fit for new and spiritual actions conformed to God's will; so that, endowed with this new life, we begin to taste and feel other things altogether, to seek and care for other things altogether, to choose and love other things altogether, and in short to be affected, moved, and delighted otherwise than we were moved and touched before, as long as we lived only an animal life. Every believer has a true and spiritual Urim and Thummim in his breast, namely the most bright and burning Spirit of our high priest, our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 8:9, 14; Gal. 4:6). Every believer is also a priest, who both can be consulted and can consult (Rev. 1:6). Indeed, that Catholic inquiry of Jesus Christ through the Urim and Thummim is an ardent and insistent prayer, to which He Himself responds, through an ineffable light and an invincible motion and impulse, to the consciences of those who first consult Him, in such a way that they are certain of their duty and secure about the saving outcome. Learn this, Wolzogen. There is no need to dwell on these things any longer. Let us see what can be objected from Wolzogen's writing against what has already been argued.

units.la: 1. Illa ratio agendi (sc. per afflatum quendam in-ternum, immediatam revelationem, instinctum, de hisce enim loquitur ut vidimus) nunc nulla est, haec Thesis; audiamus rationem, non possunt de illa gloriari, nisi qui Enthusiastarum furore correpti insaniunt. Sic satis modeste, jam moderatum te & tui similes credant qui velint. 1. Solennis ista est Remonstrantium, Lutheranorum, Socinianorum & Papistarum calumnia. Episcopius eousque provehitur, ut inter-num Sp. S. testimonium de Scr. divinitate sarcastice tradutraducat. Quod an Wolzogio etiam displiceat ex hoc libello nullibi patet. Hoc loco autem, si non Episcopii discipulus, saltem ipsi Paradoxo non plane dissimilis videtur, ut enim illius verbis alibi Cartesii laudes praedicat, sic hic non mollioribus dicteriis proscindit Reformatos. Nec sufficit solum Enthusiastas nominasse. Rem ipsam, quam culpat, Reformatorum esse probatum est, eosque à Paradoxo suo tanta cum acerbitate Enthusiasmi ne semel quidem excusat ut postea notabitur. 2. Ignoras utrorumque sensum, aliud enim est principium doctrinale & regula objectiva à fidei efficiente causa, dicit Marefius Jesuitæ, idem tecum nobis objicienti. In illo genere nullum præter Scripturam agnoscimus, immediatas licet hujus operationes, afflatus, instinctus doceamus: vide quæ antea ex Spanhemio allata sunt. Quid ni adscribo quæ habet Whitakerus adversus Duræum? Nihil ergo, sic ille, opus fuit, ut tam multa hic Luthero & Calvino de novis quibusdam Enthusiasmis objiceres, in quo quis non videt à quo hoc Sp. profectum sit? Deum precor ut hanc tibi blasphemiam ignoscat. Joh. XIV. 26. 1. Joh. II. 20. 27. 1. Cor. II. 14. 10. Jes LI. 16. ex his per spicuum est, eundem Sp. qui in prophetis atque Apostolis locutus est, in nostris etiam mentibus hanc Dei vocem obsignare.
units.tr: 1. That method of acting (namely, through some inward inspiration, immediate revelation, or instinct; for they speak of these things, as we have seen) does not exist now, is your thesis. Let us hear the reason: only those seized by the frenzy of the Enthusiasts can boast of it. Let those who wish to believe it think you and your like moderate in saying so. This is the familiar slander of the Remonstrants, the Lutherans, the Socinians and the Papists. Episcopius goes so far as to mock the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning the divinity of Scripture. It does not clearly appear from this booklet whether Wolzogen also disapproves of this. Here, if not a disciple of Episcopius, he at least seems not wholly unlike his Paradox, for just as he praises Descartes in Episcopius's words elsewhere, so here he tears into the Reformed with no gentler taunts. Nor is it enough to have named them Enthusiasts. The thing he blames has been shown to belong to the Reformed, and he does not once excuse them from the charge of Enthusiasm, with such bitterness does he assail them in his Paradox, as will be noted later. 2. You are ignorant of the meaning of both sides. "A doctrinal principle and an objective rule are one thing, and the efficient cause of faith is another," says the Jesuit Maresius, who raises the same objection against us as you do. In the former sense we acknowledge nothing except Scripture, although we teach that its immediate operations, inspirations and instincts exist; see what was cited earlier from Spanheim. Why should I not add what Whitaker has against Duraeus? "There was therefore no need," he says, "for you to raise so many objections here against Luther and Calvin concerning certain new Enthusiasms. Who does not see from whom this has come? I pray God to pardon you this blasphemy. John 14:26; 1 John 2:20, 27; 1 Cor. 2:14; Isa. 51:16. From these it is plain that the same Spirit who spoke in the prophets and apostles also seals this voice of God in our minds."

units.la: 2. Actum tum de Scr. de interpretandi labore & mediis esset. nam eo delabi istam sententiam necesse putas, ut post habitis omnibus iis quae vel leges interpretandi orationem, vel res ipsas examinans ratio afferre possent luminis ad impetrandam assensionem, Spiritus credatur oraculo quodam pronunciare &c.
units.tr: 2. The whole matter of interpreting Scripture and the means of doing so would then be at an end. For you think it necessary to sink to this opinion: that after all the considerations which either the rules of interpreting speech or reason, examining the things themselves, could offer as light for winning assent have been set aside, the Spirit is to be believed to pronounce by some oracle, etc.

units.la: In Fanaticorum somnia haec quadrant, non ea quae à te, ac si talia essent, rejecta vidimus: est enim immediata operatio, est inspiratio interna, quam etsi tu omnem rejicis, hisce opponendam non esse certum est. Nos enim non separamus Sp. S. à Scriptura, mediisque eam interpretandi, non opponimus, sed subordinamus. Principaliter à Sp. S. fluit cognitio, judicium. Organicè à Scriptura, verba sunt Joh. Crocii. mutuo enim quo-dam nexu Dominus verbi Spiritusque sui certitudinem inter se copulavit: ut solida verbi religio animis nostris in-sideat, ubi affulget Sp. qui nos illic Dei faciem contem-plari faciat: ut vicissim nullo hallucinationis timore Spiritum amplexemur, ubi illum in sua imagine, hoc est in verbo recognoscimus, -- eundem Sp. cujus virtute verbum administraverat, submisit, qui suum opus efficaci verbi confirmatione absolveret, in hunc modum Christus Discipulis duobus sensum aperiebat: non ut abjectis Scripturis per se saperent: sed ut Scripturas intelligerent. Spiritum non extinguendum monet Paulus, sed & non spernendas Prophetias: hanc conciliationem longe amicissimam dum non percipis, rejicis, & opponis subordinanda. Helvetiorum confessio tibi os obturet ita sophisticanti. Neque arbitramur, sic Viri Cordatissimi, praedicationem illam externam tanquam inutilem ideo videri, quoniam pendeat institutio verae religionis ab interna Spiritus illuminatione. Qui enim intus illuminat idem dixit praedicate &c. Peccatur,ait Spanhemius,elencho oppositorum, nec enim inspirationes internae opponendae sunt Scripturae S. & institutioni quae ex ea habetur, sed componendae cum ea. Imo,ut dicam quod res est,ipse En-thusiastarum, sic argumentando, praemis vestigia, illi enim ex interna revelatione adversus externam, à Sp. adversus Scripturam argumentari solent, quod tu, lucem objectivam à subjectiva, revelationem internam ab externa discriminare & inter se utramque componere nescius, imitaris. Putas tu pios, quibus de in-terno afflatu coram Deo saepe modestè gloriandi datur occasio, putas tu illos Scripturam spernere, interpretandi laborem susque deque habere? minimè: illi enim, postquam gustarunt, maximè deside-rant. Profecto quae hominem interiorem concernunt, hoc seculo multi ignorant, & interim contemnunt, rident & detestantur. Utinam gustarent manna illud absconditum illi, de quibus merito cum Camerone dici potest: quod miseri sint homines qui aliorum sensum ex suo ipsorum ingenio metiuntur; vel enim (si quis eorum vitam paulò attentius consideret) homines sunt omnibus cooperti probris, vel boni quidem viri, si eorum mores ad justitiæ externæ & civilis normam exigantur, cæterum vim istam Spiritus nec senserunt unquam, nec vero cupiunt persentiscere; imò vero subsannant & irridٜent eos qui se eam sensisse profitentur. Tu quidem sic, ego (inquiunt) aliter sentio. Nempe hoc illud est, si Evangelium nostrum tectum est, tectum est iis qui pereunt. &c. 2. Cor. iv. 3
units.tr: These are the dreams of fanatics, and they do not fit the things which you have rejected, as if such things existed. For it is an immediate operation, an inward inspiration, and although you reject every such inspiration, it is certain that it is not to be opposed to these. For we do not separate the Holy Spirit from Scripture, nor set him against the means of interpreting it, but subordinate him to it. Knowledge and judgement flow principally from the Holy Spirit; organically from Scripture, these are the words of John Crocius. For the Lord has joined the certainty of his Word and of his Spirit to one another by a kind of mutual bond, so that the solid religion of the Word may dwell in our minds where the Spirit shines forth, who causes us to contemplate the face of God there; and conversely, that we may embrace the Spirit without any fear of delusion where we recognise him in his own image, that is, in the Word. The same Spirit by whose power he had administered the Word sent forth, to complete his work by the effective confirmation of the Word. In this way Christ opened the sense of the Scriptures to the two disciples, not so that they might be wise apart from the Scriptures, but so that they might understand the Scriptures. Paul warns us not to quench the Spirit, but neither to despise the prophecies. While you do not perceive this most friendly reconciliation, you reject it and set against it what ought to be subordinated. Let the Confession of the Helvetic Churches stop your mouth, you who thus sophisticate: "Nor do we think, most judicious men, that external preaching is therefore seen as useless because the establishment of true religion depends on the inward illumination of the Spirit. For he who illumines within is the same who said, Preach, etc." There is a fault, says Spanheim, against the rule of opposites: "for inward inspirations are not to be set against Holy Scripture and the teaching which is had from it, but are to be brought into agreement with it." Indeed, to say what is the case, you follow the very footsteps of the Enthusiasts in arguing thus. For they are accustomed to argue from inward revelation against outward, from the Spirit against Scripture; and you, not knowing how to distinguish the objective light from the subjective, inward revelation from outward, nor how to reconcile the two, imitate them. Do you suppose that the godly, to whom the occasion is often given of modestly boasting before God of an inward inspiration, despise Scripture and treat the labour of interpreting it with indifference? By no means: for having tasted, they desire it most of all. Certainly many in this age are ignorant of the things that concern the inner man, and meanwhile they scorn, mock and detest them. Would that they might taste that hidden manna! Of such people it may rightly be said with Cameron: "Wretched are those men who measure the sense of others by their own disposition; for either (if one considers their life a little more carefully) they are men covered with every reproach, or indeed good men, if their morals are judged by the standard of external and civil justice. Yet they have never felt that power of the Spirit, nor do they desire to perceive it; rather they sneer at and mock those who profess to have felt it. You, they say, feel one way, I feel another. Surely this is the case: if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who perish, etc." 2 Cor. 4:3

units.la: 3. Obtendi potest, Immediatam revelationem in multis Apostolis necessariam fuisse, veritates enim multas non potuerunt certas credere, nisi testimonio nixi Sp. extraordinario: illa singularia Spiritus edocuit Apostolos sine ullis Scripturis, quæ nullis adhuc Scripturis continebantur; immediata autem revelatio nunc nulla est. Hæc quæ virtute immediata mentes afficit, est extraordinaria nec omnibus fidelibus aut omni tempore concessa. Resp.
units.tr: 3. It may be objected that immediate revelation was necessary for many apostles, for they could not believe many truths with certainty unless they rested on an extraordinary testimony of the Spirit. The Spirit taught the apostles those singular things without any Scriptures, since as yet they were contained in no Scriptures; but immediate revelation does not exist now. That which affects minds by immediate power is extraordinary, and is not granted to all the faithful or at all times. Answer:

units.la: 1. quid hoc sibi velit, quid non in omnibus, sed in multis saltem, extraordinariam infallibilemque Sp. operationem attribuat Apostolis, vidimus priori libro. 2. Notandum hæc eadem sic fere Heidano opposita ab Episcopio, ita ut, si unquam Belgicum scriptum sua lectione Wolzogius dignatus fuerit, videritque hoc Episcopii, ex eo defumta videri ista possint. Sic Episcopius, revelationem Sp. Apostolis factam, iisque omnibus, quos in initio, ad Evangelium Judæis & gentibus prædicandum, immediatè vocabat, respiciunt verba Apostoli 1. Cor. 11. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. &c. Illam autem revelationem, iis factam, immediatam fuisse nemo dubitat -- primi annunciatores futuri cum essent - sed similem singulis fidelibus obtingere absurdè concluditur. Simili autem aut potius eidem nodo ut eundem adhibeam cuneum, tran-scribam quæ Heidanus Episcopo & simul nostro Wolzogio, solidè & doctè reposuit. Belgicum nitorem versio mea non exprimet, rem ipsam quamvis & dicta fideliter. Hæc quidem est, ait, Sociniano-rum quorundam in ista verba commentatio, sed nulli ratione innixa, & ab Apostoli scopo tota discrepans, nam sapientia quæ non est hujus mundi, nec Primatum hujus mundi, quam plerique Ethnicorum Philosophi, summique Judæorum Scribæ & magistri, quamvis ab Apostolis ipsis propositam & externè revelatam, non potuerunt capere, sed ut scandalum detestati sunt & ut stultitiam rejeceruut: non solis Apostolis, sed & cunctis credituris interna Sp. revelatione innotescere necesse est: sicuti enim ut percipiatur & recipiatur hujus mundi sapientia, mundi accepisse Spiritum satis est: ita Spiritu, qui ex Deo est, vers. 12. ad talis supernaturalis cognitionis egemus receptionem, aliud est humanam sapientiam doctum, θεοδίδακτον [?] autem esse, aliud est.
units.tr: 1. What this means, and why he attributes an extraordinary and infallible operation of the Spirit to the apostles not in all, but at least in many, we have seen in the first book. 2. It should be noted that these same points are opposed almost in the same way by Episcopius to Heidanus, so that if Wolzogen ever deigned to read a Dutch writing and saw this of Episcopius, these things may seem to be taken from it. Thus Episcopius: "The revelation of the Spirit made to the apostles, and to all those whom he at first called immediately to preach the Gospel to Jews and Gentiles, is what the words of the Apostle regard, 1 Cor. 2:6–10, etc. But that this revelation, made to them, was immediate, no one doubts, since they were to be the first announcers; but it is absurdly concluded that a similar one falls to each of the faithful." Now, to drive the same wedge into the same knot, I will transcribe what Heidanus solidly and learnedly replied to the Bishop and at the same time to our Wolzogen. My translation will not express the Dutch elegance, though it renders the matter itself and the words faithfully. "This," he says, "is the commentary of certain Socinians on those words, but it rests on no reason and wholly departs from the Apostle's purpose. For the wisdom which is not of this world, nor the rulers of this world, which most of the Gentile philosophers and the chief scribes and teachers of the Jews could not grasp, though it was proposed by the apostles themselves and revealed outwardly, but they abhorred it as a stumbling-block and rejected it as foolishness: this must be made known not only to the apostles but to all who are to believe, by inward revelation of the Spirit. For just as it is enough, in order that the wisdom of this world be perceived and received, to have received the spirit of the world, so we who have the Spirit that is of God (v. 12) need the reception of such supernatural knowledge. It is one thing to be taught human wisdom, and another to be God-taught [θεοδίδακτον]."

units.la: Sapientia Dei quæ in mysterio est, quæ occulta est, quam nemo Principum hujus seculi cognovit, à nemine sola revelatione cognosci potest, sed ad eam interna Sp. revelatio necessaria est. Quid an illa sapientia solummodo Apostolis mysterium occultum est, piis autem reliquis non item? imo multo magis. Mysterium Dei & quidem occultum, non nisi à Deo detegi potest aut revelari: idque Deus non aliter, quam per suum perficit Spiritum.
units.tr: The wisdom of God, which is in a mystery, which is hidden, which none of the rulers of this age knew, can be known by no one through revelation alone, but the inner revelation of the Spirit is necessary for it. Is that wisdom a hidden mystery only to the Apostles, and not likewise to the other pious? Much more so. The mystery of God, and indeed a hidden one, can be uncovered or revealed only by God, and God does this only through his own Spirit.

units.la: Hinc est quod Judæis in lectione V. pac[?]ti non retectum maneat velamen: quod tam diu durare necesse est, donec, postquam se ad Deum converterint, ab iis velamen illud tollatur. Hoc autem, quî aliter quam per Spiritum fiat? Dominus jam est Spiritus: qui Spiritu illo donatus, eum solus dispensat & dat cui & quando & quantum lubet: & ubi Sp. Domini est ibi libertas. Hæc Sapientia igitur, occulta Judæis, non quod V. T. non legant, industriâ enim quam in eo ponunt, pudori Christianis sint oportet: sed quia Dominum non habent illum, qui Spiritum largitur solus, liberamque, qua Regni Cælorum Mysteria intelligant, mentem. 2 Cor. iij. 14, 15, 16, 17. Hinc Christus Matt. xi. 11. vobis datum est nosse Mysteria Regni Cælorum, illis vero non est datum. Quemadmodum & Patri gratias agebat Matth. xi. 25. Gloriam tibi do Pater Domine cæli & terræ, quod hæc occultaveris à sapientibus & intelligentibus: & ea retexeris infantibus. quod autem, quî sic? quia Filius, qui Patrem solus novit, & cui omnia à Patre sunt tradita, etiam per Sp. id ipsis revelare non voluit.
units.tr: Hence it is that the veil remains unremoved for the Jews when the Old Testament is read; it must remain as long as they do not turn to God, and until that veil is taken away by him. But how could this happen except through the Spirit? The Lord is now the Spirit, and he alone, having been endowed with that Spirit, dispenses and gives it to whom, when and how much he pleases, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. This wisdom, then, is hidden from the Jews, not because they do not read the Old Testament (for the diligence they put into it ought to shame Christians), but because they do not have the Lord, who alone gives the Spirit, and a free mind by which they might understand the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. 2 Cor. 3:14, 15, 16, 17. Hence Christ says, Matt. 11:11, "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given." Likewise he gave thanks to the Father, Matt. 11:25, "I give you thanks, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants." But why is this so? Because the Son, who alone knows the Father, and to whom all things have been handed over by the Father, did not wish to reveal these things to them even through the Spirit.

units.la: „Talem etiam hanc nobis sapientiam describit Apostolus, ut, nisi immediatè nobis per Spiritum reveletur, „nullum aliud ulli homini medium, quo ad hanc cognitionem pertingat, superfit. Quod nemo Principum hujus seculi cognovit; quodque oculus non vidit, nec in mentem hominis venit unquam, („quæ præter, nullæ aliæ viæ, „quibus ad cognitionem, naturali modo, perveniamus) „illud aut occultum nobis semper remanere debet aut immediata Spiritus revelatione acquiri.
units.tr: „The Apostle also describes this wisdom in such a way that, unless it is revealed to us immediately through the Spirit, no other means remains for any man by which he might attain this knowledge." "That none of the rulers of this age knew; and that eye has not seen, nor has it ever come into the mind of man" (apart from which there are no other ways by which we attain knowledge in a natural manner), that must either always remain hidden from us or be acquired through the immediate revelation of the Spirit.

units.la: Ideo Apostolus versu 10. Nobis autem Deus ea retexit per Spiritum suum. Idque sequente ratione confirmatur. Quod enim nemo novit, aut novisse potest, nisi Dei Spiritus, id nemo vel revelat vel revelare potest, præterquam Dei Spiritus. Sed hanc in Mysterio occultam Dei sapientiam, nemo novit nisi Sp. Dei, qui omnia scrutatur etiam profunditates Dei. Quis enim hominum novit ea quæ sunt hominis, nisi Spiritus hominis qui est in eo? ita etiam quæ sunt Dei nemo novit, nisi Spiritus Dei. versf. 11. vel an hæc, postquam Apostolis revelata sunt, jam non sunt profunditates Dei, ut quisquam ea novisse præter Spiritum Dei possit? Quæ autem ista sunt quæ revelat Spiritus? suntne talia quæ Apostolis quidem, Christianis vero reliquis non item, sint necessaria? est autem sapientia illorum quæ præfinierat Deus ante secula, ad nostram gloriam antequam Mundus erat. versf. 7. quæ paravit Deus iis à quibus diligitur versf. 9. quæ Deus nobis gratificatus est. versf. 12. Illis autem cunctis Spiritus revelatio competit, quibus ista quæ revelantur competunt. Ea vero non solos ApostoApostolos, sed & omnes fideles respiciunt. Vel an homo ille spiritualis, qui omnia bene discernit, dijudicat, à nemine autem judicatur, sint soli Apostoli, & non unusquisque fidelium, & quidem in quantum, naturali homini, qui non percipit ea quæ sunt Sp. Dei, quia ipsi stultitia sunt, neque ea potest percipere, quia spiritualiter dijudicantur, opponitur? Spiritualis homo qui omnia discernit & dijudicat, is est qui Sp. revelationem adeptus est. Omnes autem regeniti & fideles sunt iste homo spiritualis. Ergo omnes revelationem illam Spiritus acceperant: non soli Apostoli. Optimè Paulus 1 Cor. xij. 3. neminem posse dicere Jesum Dominum, nisi per Sp. Sanctum.
units.tr: Therefore the Apostle says in verse 10, "But God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit." This is confirmed by the following argument. What no one knows, or can know, except the Spirit of God, no one reveals or can reveal, except the Spirit of God. But no one knows this hidden wisdom of God in the mystery, except the Spirit of God, who searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man that is in him? So too no one knows the things of God, except the Spirit of God (v. 11). Or, now that these things have been revealed to the Apostles, are they no longer the depths of God, so that anyone could know them apart from the Spirit of God? What, then, are those things that the Spirit reveals? Are they such things as are necessary for the Apostles but not likewise for the other Christians? Yet that wisdom is one which God ordained before the ages for our glory, before the world was (v. 7); which God has prepared for those who love him (v. 9); which God has graciously given to us (v. 12). Now the revelation of the Spirit belongs to all those to whom the things revealed belong. And these things concern not only the Apostles but all the faithful. Or is the spiritual man, who judges all things well and is judged by no one, opposed to the natural man, who does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, because they are foolishness to him and he cannot perceive them, since they are judged spiritually? The spiritual man who discerns and judges all things is the one who has obtained the revelation of the Spirit. But all the regenerate and faithful are this spiritual man. Therefore all have received that revelation of the Spirit, not the Apostles alone. Paul rightly says, 1 Cor. 12:3, that no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quænam vero ratio restat, quapropter hæc immediata revelatio Sp. Apostolis, ut sciant ea quæ Dei sunt, & sapientiam illam in Mysterio occultam, necessaria sit, præ reliquis fidelibus? etenim Christus cum Apostolis suis & Discipulis versans, viva voce eos quæ ad salutem necessaria alios docerent, docuit. Quid loquebantur Apostoli præter id quod audiverant, quod viderant oculi ipsorum, quod spectaverant & manus ipsorum contrectaverant de Sermone illo vitæ? 1 Joh 1.1. Spiritus autem immediata revelatio, ut aliis, quæ de verbo vitæ audiverant & viderant, prædicarent, dum requirebatur: quid ni æque ea necessaria iis, qui ea ex illis audiebant? vel an Apostolis magis necessaria erat revelatio, ut intelligerent, quæ ipsis à Christo dicebantur, quam fidelibus, ut ab Apostolis prædicata perciperent? Si immediatè à Spiritu S. doceri debuerunt Apostoli, quæ postea Ecclesius[?] tradiderunt: sequitur aut omnia viva voce non docuisse Christum, aut, nisi interna accedente illuminatione Sp. S. externam non sufficere traditionem.
units.tr: But what reason remains why this immediate revelation of the Spirit should be necessary for the Apostles, so that they might know the things of God and that wisdom hidden in the mystery, more than for the other faithful? For Christ, dwelling with his Apostles and disciples, taught them by the living voice what was necessary for salvation, so that they might teach others. What did the Apostles speak of, except what they had heard, what their eyes had seen, what they had looked upon and their hands had handled, concerning that Word of life? 1 John 1:1. But if the immediate revelation of the Spirit was needed, so that they might preach to others what they had heard and seen of the Word of life, why should it not be equally necessary for those who heard these things from them? Or was revelation more necessary for the Apostles, so that they might understand what was said to them by Christ, than for the faithful, so that they might perceive what was preached by the Apostles? If the Apostles had to be taught immediately by the Holy Spirit the things they later handed down to the churches, it follows either that Christ did not teach everything by the living voice, or that, unless the inner illumination of the Holy Spirit is added, outward tradition is not sufficient.

units.la: Hanc ob causam Euangelium ministerium Spiritus dicitur 2 Cor: iij. non quod propterea, ut vellet Episcopius, alia interna revelatio non requiratur, contrarium patet in Lydia[?] Joh. vi. 44, 45, &c. & deinde quid si intellectionem inde acquiri posse largiremur, internam tamen requireret revelationem ulterior applicatio. Sed quod ei Spiritus dum fidelibus aut electis vocationis momento & deinceps dispensatur, comitetur &c. quia Spiritum dare voluit, non sub legis dispensatione, nec Philosophiæ, aut alterius cujuscunque verbi, sed Euangelii &c. & tandem istud caput concludens sic finit. Epistolam Christi esse, non atra-mento inscriptam sed Spiritu Dei vivi, in tabulis carneis cordis, non est verbi effectus, quia Apostolis inspirati. Rursus voluntatis Dei in carneis cordis nostri tabulis inscriptio NB est interna & immediata Sp. S. operatio: sed Epistolam Christi esse, est inscriptio voluntatis Dei, in carneis cordum tabulis. Ergo Epistolam esse est effectum internae & immediatae operationis Sp. Sancti. Sic jam adversus Episcopium simul & adversus Wolzogium vindicatas vide immediatas Spiritus operationes; easque, impru-denter licet negante Wolzogio, omnibus fidelibus & quidem omni tempore concessas non solùm, sed & ita necessarias, ut sine iis Epistola Christi esse nequeant.
units.tr: For this reason the Gospel is called the ministry of the Spirit, 2 Cor. 3, not because, as Episcopius wished, no other inner revelation is required on that account; the contrary is plain from John 6:44, 45, etc. And then, even if we were to grant that understanding can be acquired from it, a further application would still require an inner revelation. But this Spirit is dispensed to the faithful or the elect at the moment of calling and thereafter, and accompanies them, etc., because he wished to give the Spirit, not under the dispensation of the law, nor of philosophy, or of any other word, but of the Gospel, etc. And finally, concluding this chapter, he ends thus: That we are the epistle of Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, on the fleshly tables of the heart, is not the effect of the word, because it was inspired in the Apostles. Again, the writing of the will of God on the fleshly tables of our heart NB is an inner and immediate operation of the Holy Spirit; but that we are the epistle of Christ is the writing of the will of God on the fleshly tables of the heart. Therefore being the epistle is the effect of the inner and immediate operation of the Holy Spirit. Thus, now, see the immediate operations of the Spirit vindicated both against Episcopius and against Wolzogen; and these, although Wolzogen imprudently denies it, are granted to all the faithful, and indeed at all times, and are so necessary that without them the epistle of Christ cannot exist.

units.la: Nec solis, ut putat, Apostolis, sed æque omnibus necessarias; ad inaudita enim prædicanda Mysteria non magis, quam ad millies audita intelligenda, percipienda rite, requiri internam, immediatam revelationem, à Veterano nunc docetur Theologo, omnem evadendi rimam, Pelagianis olim, tam felicitèr præcludenti, quam solidè. Ride nunc & rejice internam immediatam revelationem & si id honori ducas, Episcopio similem dicam Wolzogium, utrumque ab Heidano profligatum, conculcatum: sin minus, te ipse explica nunc irretitum, & define te turpi prædicatione omnes perspicuitate superantem gloriari, qui confusè concepisti & scribsisti aut He-terodoxè, en probaturum me id ulterius si necesse sit, offero lubens & intrepidus. Nihil enim tanto hiatu dignum postquam præstitisti, terribilis esse desiisti. Ignosce lector si omnium nostrorum Theologorum vituperium minus tolerem, veneratio tantorum vi-rorum me tenet. At instas & dicis, immediatè si ageret, deberet per modum novi testimonii vel argumen-ti se insinuare. Verum si testis sit testimonium dicere proproculdubio id agit Dei Spiritus, quid? dicitur testa-ri Rom: viii. & de veritate testari: sed non, ais, per no-vum testimonium: vel putas novum, hoc est, quod no-vam vel diversam à revelatâ in Sacris veritatem pro-fert, vel quod eandem novo confirmat, illustratque testimonio, mente aliquando de Scriptura ne quidem cogitante. Obscurè satis, sed expediam, illud si intelligi à Lectore velis, omnem immediatam reve-lationem, afflatum, non debueras dixisse; hoc vero nega & Heterodoxus es.
units.tr: And these are necessary not only for the Apostles, as he thinks, but equally for all. For to proclaim unheard-of mysteries requires an inner, immediate revelation no more than to understand and rightly perceive things heard a thousand times. This is now taught by a veteran theologian, who closes off, as happily as solidly, every crevice of escape that the Pelagians once used. Laugh now and reject the inner immediate revelation; and if you count it an honour, I will say that Wolzogen is similar to Episcopius, both struck down and trampled by Heidanus. But if not, now explain yourself, caught in your own net, and cease to boast that you surpass everyone in clarity with that shameful preaching, you who have conceived and written confusedly or heterodoxly. Here I offer, gladly and fearlessly, to prove this further if it is necessary. For, after you have produced nothing deserving so great a gape, you have ceased to be terrible. Pardon me, reader, if I cannot bear the reproach of all our theologians with much patience; reverence for such great men holds me back. But you press on and say that, if it acted immediately, it ought to insinuate itself by way of a new testimony or argument. Yet if the witness is to give testimony, without doubt the Spirit of God does this; why? It is said to bear witness in Rom. 8, and to testify to the truth. But, you say, not by a new testimony. Or do you think of "new" as meaning that it brings forth a truth different from or other than what is revealed in the Scriptures, or that it confirms and illustrates the same truth with a new testimony, while the mind perhaps does not even think of Scripture? I have said this obscurely enough, but I will explain it if you wish the reader to understand it: you ought not to have said that every immediate revelation is an inspiration; but deny this, and you are a heterodox man.

units.la: 2. Afflatus, vox interna & quæ de iis habes, nihil faciunt ad rem: distinguimus in ordinariam & extraordinariam; nam cum Spiritus à spirando, à flando dicatur, quis spirituales, qui Spiritu ducuntur I Cor: II. Rom. viii. inspirationes, afflatus per-sentiscere ordinariò, negabit, nisi qui eos à Spiritu duci, regi ordinariò negaverit?
units.tr: 2. As for afflatus and inward voice, and what you say about them, none of it bears on the matter. We distinguish between ordinary and extraordinary (inspiration). Since the Spirit is so named from breathing and blowing, who will deny that spiritual people, who are led by the Spirit (1 Cor. 2; Rom. 8), ordinarily perceive inspirations and promptings, unless he also denies that they are ordinarily led and governed by the Spirit?

units.la: 3. Non credis autem sed rides, quod Spiritus oraculo credatur quodam pronunciare, ita hæc verba intelligenda &c. sed ride quantum lubet; imò Spiritus hoc dictat, Spiritus hoc immediate dictat & nisi tibi immediate id dictet, carnalis es, nunquam vel unicam veritatem ritè vides, sicuti immediatè, hoc est, actione ad ipsam usque mentem pertendente, efficaciter non excitatus, nunquam boni quid præstabis. Imo immediatè, nec tamen absque medio, omni respectu, sed morali sed instrumentali, causa principali, medium (ut ita loquar) penetrante & sic hyperphysica vi ad ipsam mentem pertendente. Nec est quod Oraculi vox, nobis piaculum fit, audiunt certè, si ita vis, Dei, non idolorum oracula Christi oves, interne, immediatè, audiunt & externè: & tandem quid si & in ipsis somniis obtingere, etiam post Apostolo-rum longè tempora, inspirationes, afflatus, piis posse, quid si quotidie id evenire dixerint Theologi? In explicatione Decimi præcepti insomniis etiam peccari probatur, quid ni ex principio illo supernaturali etiam de nocte & in somniis optimæ cogitationes, inspirationesque, hoc agente Spiritu, suboriri queant? Practicos consule & videbis non frustra hæc dici. Ego, ut inclinationes peccaminosas, præsertim quæ peccata in deliciis vocant, sic & spiritualis internique hominis magis aut minus vividum in his aut illis statum hinc dignosci sæpe posse nullus dubito.
units.tr: 3. You do not believe, but laugh at, the claim that one must trust a certain oracle of the Spirit to pronounce that these words are to be understood thus, etc. Laugh as much as you like. Indeed the Spirit dictates this, the Spirit dictates this immediately. Unless he dictates it to you immediately, you are carnal, and you will never rightly see even a single truth, since, unless you are roused effectively by an action reaching to the mind itself, immediately, that is, you will never accomplish anything good. Indeed, immediately, yet not without a means, in every respect, moral and instrumental: the principal cause penetrates the means (so to speak) and so reaches the mind itself by a hyperphysical power. Nor is there any reason why the voice of an oracle should be a sacrilege for us. Certainly, if you like, the sheep of Christ hear the oracles of God, not of idols, inwardly and immediately, and also outwardly. And finally, what if inspirations and promptings can happen to the godly even in dreams, even long after the time of the apostles? What if theologians have said that this happens every day? In the explanation of the Tenth Commandment it is proved that sins are committed even in dreams. Why, then, should not the best thoughts and inspirations arise by night and in dreams from that same supernatural principle, the Spirit acting? Consult practical writers and you will see that these things are not said in vain. I have no doubt that, just as sinful inclinations, especially those which they call sins of pleasure, can often be discerned, so too the more or less lively state of the spiritual and inner man in this or that condition can often be discerned from them.

units.la: Hoc etiam sensu aliquando pia anima, sponsa Christi, dormit animo interim vigilante. Pios roga quanti faciant γνωρίσματα dispositionis tam naturalis quam spiritualis, quæ inde desumere se posse sciunt: peccaminosa somnia, (ut viscidi humores talis unde prodeunt, fundi) cordis indices sæpe sunt: sic è contra gaudere solent pii, quando evigilantes & quæ vel somniarunt examinantes, bonorum motuum [co-piam in corde suo fuisse vident. Quid ni & sic Davidem renes docuerunt? non decet autem Pastores illius incertos esse, quod piis omnibus, quotquot aliquo vitæ Spiritualis majori tanguntur sensu, expertum est, tam sæpe tam certò. Applica huc Analogicè quæ alibi de somnio Zuinglii Spanhemius, qui extraordinariam in eo suggestionem agnoscens, nihil minùs tamen quam Enthusiastis favet, refutat eos solidè & perspicue vir summus. Ex inspiratione extraordinaria, immediata, probari putabant suos Enthusiasmos, sic autem respondet Spanhemius.
units.tr: In this sense also the godly soul, the bride of Christ, sometimes sleeps while her mind is awake. Ask the godly how highly they value the signs (gnōrismata) of disposition, both natural and spiritual, which they know they can draw from these things. Sinful dreams, like the thick humours from which they arise, are often indications of the heart. Conversely, the godly are wont to rejoice when, waking and examining even what they dreamed, they see that there was an abundance of good motions in their heart. Why should David's kidneys not have taught them this as well? Ministers, however, ought not to be uncertain about it, since all the godly who are touched by any greater sense of spiritual life have found it to be so often and so certain. Apply here, by analogy, what Spanheim says elsewhere about Zwingli's dream. Recognising an extraordinary suggestion in it, yet by no means favouring the Enthusiasts, this great man refutes them solidly and clearly. They thought that their Enthusiasms were proved by extraordinary, immediate inspiration. Spanheim replies as follows.

units.la: I. Peccari falsa suppositione, omnes inspirationes extraordinarias à nobis damnari. At NB nemo verè pius est, qui tales non persentiscat sæpe in corde suo. Scrutemur jam coram Domino, excutiamus nos Wolzogi,
units.tr: I. They commit the error of a false supposition, that we condemn all extraordinary inspirations. But note: no one is truly godly who does not often perceive such things in his heart. Let us now examine ourselves before the Lord, let us search ourselves, Wolzogen.

units.la: II. Peccatur elencho παρὰ [?]τὸ ἐπομένον & partium. Bona fuit suggestio extraordinaria loci Exod: xij. quæ obtigit Zuinglio in somno: Ergo inspirationes, quas jactant Enthusiastæ, sunt vel bonæ vel licitæ. Ratio disparitatis est, NB quia nec novum Dogma Zuinglio suggestum fuit, sed probatio dogmatis jam ab ipso traditi & propugnati ex Scriptura. Enthusiastæ verò & nova dogmata tradunt, & extra Scripturam sibi credi volunt. Somnium istud Zuinglii ἀπόπεμπτον[?] fuisse patet, & ex occasione, & ex materia suggesta, & ex sancta ejus applicatione ad dogma verissimum adstruendum.
units.tr: II. They commit the fallacy of the consequent and of parts (para to epomenon). The extraordinary suggestion of the passage in Exodus 12, which came to Zwingli in sleep, was good. Therefore the inspirations which the Enthusiasts boast of are either good or lawful. The reason for the difference is this, note: because no new dogma was suggested to Zwingli, but a proof from Scripture of a dogma already taught and defended by himself. The Enthusiasts, however, deliver new dogmas, and wish to be believed apart from Scripture. That dream of Zwingli's was plainly sent (apopempton) both from the occasion, from the matter suggested, and from its holy application to establishing a most true dogma.

units.la: Superpondium si velit, Walæus & plures optimæ notæ Theologi, nullam rationem esse putant, etiam omnes extraordinarias de rerum eventibus Propheticas revelationes negandi, è contrà, salva modo & intacta si maneat, quam ex Scriptura habemus, fidei morumque doctrina, illi nihil addatur, nihil detrahatur; quod ad particularia facta, aut eventus futuros attinet, sic loquitur, non velimus plane negare, quin tale quid quibusdam post Apostolorum tempora contigerit, aut adhuc contingere possit: nam multarum prædictionum complementum videtur id confirmare, & nullus quod sciam Scripturæ locus in contrarium produci potest. Idem alibi Spanheim. Tantum abest ut immediatas omnes Spiritus operationes, revelationes negaverit Reformatorum Schola.
units.tr: If someone wishes to add more, Walaeus and several other theologians of the highest reputation think there is no reason to deny even all extraordinary prophetic revelations of future events, provided that the doctrine of faith and morals which we have from Scripture remains intact and untouched, with nothing added and nothing taken away. As far as particular facts or future events are concerned, he speaks thus, we would not wish to deny altogether that something of this kind has happened to some after the time of the apostles, or may still happen: for it seems to confirm the fulfilment of many predictions, and no passage of Scripture, so far as I know, can be produced to the contrary. Spanheim says the same elsewhere. So far is the Reformed school from denying all immediate operations and revelations of the Spirit.

units.la: 4. Nec sic victas dabit manus, imo facile se eva-furum fortassis cogitabit, modo excipiat, nihil tamen nostris magis familiare esse & tritum, quam negare, quas & ille negat, immediatas revelationes. Resp. probationem non peto; jam dudum Heidanum & alios vidi immediatas revelationes afflatus &c. communes negare simul & ponere, cum negant Verbo usum instrumentalem, normalem vindicant & tales immediatas negant inspirationes, quarum veritates, non ex Sacris petitæ & primùm doctæ, nec cum iis consentientes, quarum modus & conditio non congruit iis, quæ de Sp. operatione norma ista tradit & amussis. Concedunt autem & ponunt dari immediatas inspirationes & revelationes non solum, sed & absolutè necessarias esse, ut jam paulo ante vidimus, tum ob subjecti conditionem, tum, ne instrumento mo-rali verbo transcribatur quod efficienti principali Spiritui vindicandum, tum, ne Spiritus in suis operationibus quicquam præjudicii patiatur. Maneat dictatorum modique dictandi norma S. Scriptura. Quæ autem posterioris sunt generis, tu aut negas, aut intelligi non potes. Omnem dixisti: hoc visus es velle, operationem Spiritus non afficere nisi mediatè ipsam mentem, quod, hoc sensu, totum reponit Pelagianismum. Per medium operatur, ita tamen ut ipse Sp. intellectu (novo nunc vitæ Spiritualis principio informato, elevato,) immediatè, hyperphysice & irresistibiliter, ipsa illa penetret præcordia, & penetralia suis vibret radiis, idque in prima mentis illuminatione non solum, sed & in singulis regeniti intellectus actibus; Præter lucem objectivam, distinctio est Spanhemii, requiritur lux subjectiva, ut in prima novæ vitæ infusione, sic in singulis ejus, circa veritates revelatas, actibus spiritualibus. Nec aliter esse potest, quin tota de Providentiâ, gratiâ & concursu Theologia destruatur: cui adde, quod Spiritus mentem jam ita dispositam sæpius immediatè, & quidem de verbo aut ullo medio nihil cogitantem (hæc soluta, libera actio quid ni, contra id, quod tu p. 58. dici potest?) attingat, moveat, afflet tam quoad intellectum, quam quoad voluntatem &c. imo tota vita Spiritualis & quilibet ejus motus aliquod, licet interveniente medio externo,immediatum Spiritus attactum requirit,afflatum, tum,operationem,inspirationem: nam omnes motus san-ctos, homini subiorientes, dicimus esse sanctas inspirationes. Quid de hisce sentias, si Orthodoxus sis, eloquere ut intelligi queas, nec enim te gravare ultra culpam velim, publicè potius Palinodiam canerem, sed juxta scriptum illud tuum judico: de eo enim jam quæstio est, an verum, an tam perspicue verum dicat.
units.tr: 4. Nor will he yield his hands so conquered. Indeed he will perhaps think he can easily escape, provided he takes this exception: that nothing is more familiar and commonplace among our people than to deny immediate revelations, which he too denies. I reply that I do not ask for proof. I have long since seen Heidanus and others both deny and affirm at once immediate revelations, inspirations, and so on, which are common. When they deny to the Word an instrumental, normal use, and claim it for themselves, they deny such immediate inspirations whose truths are not first sought from and taught by the Scriptures, nor agreeing with them, and whose mode and condition do not fit what that rule and standard hands down about the Spirit's operation. Yet they also concede and affirm that immediate inspirations and revelations exist, and indeed are absolutely necessary, as we have just seen: partly because of the condition of the subject, partly so that nothing that belongs to the principal efficient Spirit is transferred to the moral instrument, the Word, and partly so that the Spirit suffers no prejudice in his operations. Let Holy Scripture remain the norm both of what is dictated and of the mode of dictating. As for those of the latter kind, you either deny them or cannot be understood. Every you have said: this you seemed to want, that the operation of the Spirit affects the mind only mediately. In this sense it entirely restores Pelagianism. He works through a means, yet in such a way that the Spirit himself, with the intellect now informed and raised by the new principle of spiritual life, immediately, hyperphysically and irresistibly penetrates those very inmost parts and makes its rays vibrate in the innermost recesses. And this happens not only at the first illumination of the mind, but in each single act of the regenerate intellect. Besides the objective light, Spanheim's distinction is that the subjective light is required, both at the first infusion of the new life and in each of its spiritual acts concerning revealed truths. It cannot be otherwise, or the whole theology of providence, grace and concurrence would be destroyed. Add to this that the Spirit, touching, moving and inspiring a mind already so disposed, often does so immediately, and indeed while thinking of no Word or any means at all (this free, unconstrained action, why not, can be said against what you say on p. 58?). Both as to the intellect and as to the will, and so on. Indeed the whole spiritual life, and every one of its motions, requires some immediate touch, inspiration, and operation of the Spirit, even though an external means intervenes: for we say that all holy motions arising in man are holy inspirations. What you think of these things, if you are orthodox, declare so that you may be understood. I would not want to burden you further with guilt; I would rather publicly sing a palinode. But I judge according to your own writing. For the question now is whether it is true, or whether he says what is so plainly true.

units.la: 5. Quintum quod pro Wolzogio facere videtur & multis in ore est argumentum, habet p. 63. quod semel hac via aperta, præterquam quod res ipsa non pa-tiatur hanc insaniam, jam actum sit de religione, nec ullam habituri simus aliam, quam quæ libidine malitiosorum hominum, vel melancholicorum imaginatione fuerit obtrusa. Pronum est enim cuique Spiritum crepare, nec quisquam potest ulla oratione obstinatum confutare. Quo ruis Wolzogi? quibuscum tibi res sit scire aveo, modò ipse scias. Enthusiastas petis, sed an non de Interpretatione Scripturæ agis & quidem cum iis, qui ejus Interpretationem quærunt? eorum autem neminem novi, qui tam periculosè de Spiritu sentiat, ut inde tanta rerum confusio metuenda sit; Enthusiastæ Scripturam spernunt, ubi ipsis obesse videtur rident, de Interpretatione non multum laborant, Scripturam enim Alphabetariis committentes, hanc vitæ fideique normam non sic agnoscunt. Tu autem adversus illos disputas, qui tecum, de Scriptura-rum Interpretatione anxii, hanc regulam admittunt, quo facto impossibile est ut eo eatur, ut tota vertatur religionis facies. Quod autem pronum sit unicuique Sp. crepare. ad id Respondeo 1. idem esse quod omnes veritatis adversarii in hoc negotio objicere solent, ut ad objectionem primam notatum est, 2. Quod eadem difficultas sit in ista Philosophiæ tuæ Regula, pronum est enim unicuique, claram crepare & distinctam perceptionem, quis enim Philosophorum, sibi idem, quod Cartesius, non imaginatus est? arro-ganter quamvis satis, suam certitudinem, imo omnis erroris evitandi potentiam jactet: non putem tamen omnes ab ipso immodestia superari, sed eadem qua ille superbia repletos fere fuisse. Non minus certus sibi visus est & tutus Aristoteles, quam Cartesius. Hic clare & distinctè sua percipit, idem & dicet prior: nonne igitur eadem hic tuæ Philosophiæ objici possent ? cogitas autem fortassis, rationis normâ adhibita, litem istam finiri posse, modo homines, quibuscum rem habeo, rationem non exuant ; optime, sed an hic non agis cum iis quos praesupponis Scripturam ut normam recipere : cur hic istas, quas nectis, non solvis tricas ut in tua Philosophia, sic & in Theologia ? utrosque ad normale suum mittens principium. 3, Scriptura, quippe Deus seducentes Spiritus exorituros noverat, nobis media suppeditavit, quibus fit ut frustra id crepent omnes, qui non verè Spiritum intus habent, praedixit enim non solum venturos tales Spiritus, sed & sese ut normam unicam fidei & morum commendavit, & unicuique Spiritui tui non credere, sed probare jussit omnes ; regulam insuper, ad quam omnia cujuscunque Sp. dictamina, & operandi modus, tutò exigi possit, suppeditans.
units.tr: 5. The fifth argument, which seems to favour Wolzogen and is on the lips of many, he states on p. 63: once this way is opened, apart from the fact that the matter itself does not allow such madness, religion is finished, and we shall have no other than that which has been forced on us by the lust of malicious men or the imagination of the melancholy. For it is easy for anyone to boast of the Spirit, and no one can refute an obstinate man by any argument. Where are you running, Wolzogen? I long to know with whom you have to deal, provided you yourself know. You attack the Enthusiasts, but are you not really dealing with the interpretation of Scripture, and that with those who seek its interpretation? I know none of them who thinks so dangerously about the Spirit that such great confusion of things is to be feared from him. The Enthusiasts despise Scripture; where it seems to stand in their way, they laugh at it; they do not labour much over interpretation, for they leave Scripture to the alphabet-men and do not acknowledge it as the norm of life and faith. You, however, dispute against those who, anxious about the interpretation of the Scriptures, admit this rule with you; once this is done, it is impossible that it should go so far as to change the whole face of religion. As for the claim that it is easy for anyone to boast of the Spirit, to this I reply: (1) it is the same objection that all adversaries of the truth are wont to raise in this matter, as was noted in the first objection; (2) the same difficulty attaches to your rule of philosophy. For it is easy for anyone to boast of a clear and distinct perception. Which of the philosophers has not imagined for himself what Descartes did? He boasts, arrogantly enough, of his certainty, indeed of his power to avoid every error. I do not think, however, that all have been overcome by his immodesty; rather, they were almost filled with the same pride that he was. Aristotle seemed to himself no less certain and safe than Descartes. He clearly and distinctly perceives his own things, and the former will say the same. Could not then the same objections be raised against your philosophy here? But perhaps you think that, once the norm of reason is applied, that dispute can be ended, provided the men with whom I have to deal do not strip off reason. Very good; but are you not here dealing with those whom you presuppose to accept Scripture as the norm? Why do you not here untie these knots, as in your philosophy, so also in theology, sending them back to their own normal principle? (3) Scripture, since God knew that seducing spirits would arise, has supplied us with means by which it comes about that all who do not truly have the Spirit within them boast in vain. For it foretold not only that such spirits would come, but also commended itself as the sole norm of faith and morals, and it commanded everyone not to believe every spirit, but to test them all. Moreover, it supplies a rule to which all the dictates of any spirit, and his mode of operating, can safely be referred.

units.la: Nec ista nihili sunt, etiamsi forsan de Scripturae Interprete nondum constare & proinde Sp. ad eam exigi nondum posse dixeris. Vel enim, cum quo res est, Scripturam ut divinitus nobis datum Canonem agnoscit, vel rejicit: si istud, alio plane modo cum ipso agendum, Scriptura enim donec ab ipso admittatur, frustra de ejus Interprete disputas, adversario de eo nullo modo sollicito ; si autem illud, jam cogitur, quod ambo praesupponimus, fateri Scripturam intelligibiliter nec contradictorie scriptam esse & quidem hominibus. Dicat jam Spiritum suum Interpretem esse, facilè talis retundetur superbia, ni contradi-ctoriam & Barbaram, id est non intelligibilem, faciat Scr. quod foret contra hypothesin. Sed loquantur Venerandi senes, qui pro sapienti & spirituali sua perspicacia hanc viderunt; & sustulerunt difficultatem. Unus pro omnibus erit Calvinus, sic loquitur Vir Dei.
units.tr: Nor are these things nothing, even if you say that the interpreter of Scripture is not yet agreed upon, and that the Spirit therefore cannot yet be tested against it. For either he accepts Scripture as the canon given to us by God, or he rejects it. If he rejects it, we must deal with him in a completely different way, since you dispute in vain about Scripture's interpreter while he does not admit Scripture, and so he has no concern about its interpreter at all. But if he accepts it, he is compelled to confess what we both presuppose: that Scripture was written intelligibly and without contradiction, and indeed for men. Let him now say that his own Spirit is the interpreter. Such pride will be easily refuted, unless he makes Scripture contradictory and barbarous, that is, unintelligible, which would be contrary to our hypothesis. But let the venerable old men speak, who by their wise and spiritual insight saw this and removed the difficulty. One will stand for all: Calvin, that man of God, speaks thus.

units.la: Ergo cum Dei nomen obtendunt Spiritus fallaces, ex Scrip-turis inquirere convenit, an res ita habeat. Modo pium a nobis studium adhibeatur cum humilitate & modestia, [?]derit Spiritus discretionis, qui seipsum in Scripturis loquentem, tanquam fidus interpres, exponat. Adscri-bam quaedam huic facem accendentia, quae habet ibidem ad versum 1. Qui respondent, verbum Dei regulam esse ad quam exigi oportet quicquid in medium proferunt homines, neque illi nihil dicunt, neque totum. Concedo probandas esse verbo Dei doctrinas: verum nisi adsit Spiritus prudentiae, nihil aut parum proderit verbum Dei habere ad manum, cujus interpretatio nobis non constabit. Quemadmodum, exempli gratia, aurum igne aut lydio lapide probatur: sed ab iis qui artem tenent. Nam imperitis, nec lapis Lydius, neque ignis usui esse poterit. Ergo ut simus idonei judices necesse est nos Spiritu discretionis donari & dirigi. Quod ad eos qui Sp. Sancto aguntur ii possunt Dei vocem agnoscere, ait Whitakerus, ut quis amicum quicum familiarissime & diutissime vixerit ex voce solet agnosce-re. Nulli enim notior est amici quantumvis charissimi ac familiarissimi sermo, quam Dei est sanctis servis suis, quibus familiarissime utitur, quosque pro amicis suis habet. -- Quibus haec peregrina vox est aut incognita, eorum non sunt illuminatae mentes a Spiritu, quibuscunque inest, ait Polanus, iis certum & notum esse potest, si & divinitus afficiat eos intus in cordibus ipsorum & divinis testimoniis externis, id est, Scr. S. consentiat. Eodemque modo & aliis, hunc aut illum Spiritum habere, innotescere posse docet. Unde se mutuo agnoscunt veri Discipuli Christi, unde alii de aliis colligunt quod Spiritu S. sint illuminati, quod ab illo gratiose regantur, inde etiam testimonium illud internum aliis innotescit. Ut autem videas & objectam esse nostris saepe, & solutam difficultatem, quam moves, Amyraldum audiamus, haec accuratissime expedientem. Ideone inquit quia obstinata & cedere nescia ingenia ex opinione semel concepta nulla ratione deduci possunt, sequetur inter eos & vere sapientes, qui ratione freti permanent immoti in proposito, nulnullum discrimen inter esse? Nonidcirco sapiens se ratione duci certo sentiet, quia capitones illi, suas etiam se rationes habere arbitrantur? & alibi. Nec tamen hic deficimur, Scriptura etenim illa descripsit accuratissimè vim Spiritus, qui doctrinæ ac veritatis interventu in cordibus humanis operatur. Si quis igitur est qui vim eam persentiscat (persentiscunt autem omnes verè Christiani) absolutissima quadam conformitate cum Scriptura congruentem (nam quod in aliis languidior & remissior Paulo, in aliis vividior apparet, conformitatis veluti ductus & lineamenta haud abolet) esne qui dubitare possit eundem illum esse Doctorem qui mentem intus aperit, & docet extrinsecus? Si Tenebrioni, multum de inexplicabili hujus Spiritus, harum operationum natura & modo, aliquid regerendum putat Wolzogius: Sciat Manna istud abscönditum esse, & ne in mentem quidem venisse homini. Naturalis autem, quod cæcutiens hic multa garriat, mirum non est. Nec facile cæcum instrues de coloribus. Et quid si ipse, qui eo Spiritu donatus est, explicare id minime queat, quid sit & quomodo operetur? Est tamen quod etiam pro minimis Christi Discipulis, hæc sententibus quidem, explicare tamen non valentibus, reponi potest. Egregie hac de re idem Amyraldus: fateor, quod in antecessum removeri debet, illum, de illa operatione Sp. qua de Scripturæ divinitate ut mens persuadeatur opus est, loqui; verum & in reliquis, de quibus disputari posseт, eadem ratio est, ab inexplicabilitate si probationem quis velit desumere; quapropter huc optime quadrant, quæ hunc in modum disserit Vir Doctissimus.
units.tr: Therefore, when false spirits put forward the name of God, it is fitting to inquire from the Scriptures whether the matter stands so. If a pious zeal is brought to this by us with humility and modesty, the Spirit of discernment will be present, who will set himself forth as a faithful interpreter, speaking in the Scriptures. I will add some remarks that kindle a torch here, which he gives in the same place at verse 1. Those who answer that the Word of God is the rule to which everything men bring forward must be brought, say neither nothing nor everything. I grant that doctrines are to be proved by the Word of God; but unless the Spirit of prudence is present, it will profit little or nothing to have the Word of God at hand, whose interpretation will not be settled for us. Just as gold is tested by fire or by the touchstone, but by those who have the skill, for neither the touchstone nor fire will be of use to the unskilled. Therefore, that we may be fit judges, it is necessary that we be endowed and directed by the Spirit of discernment. As for those who are moved by the Holy Spirit, they can recognise the voice of God, says Whitaker, just as one usually recognises from the voice a friend with whom he has lived most intimately and for the longest time. For no one knows the speech of even the dearest and most intimate friend better than God's speech is known to his holy servants, whom he uses most intimately and holds as his friends. -- To those for whom this voice is strange or unknown, their minds are not illumined by the Spirit, says Polanus, in whom it is present. It can be certain and known to them if he also affects them inwardly in their hearts and through the divine external testimonies, that is, if it agrees with Holy Scripture. And in the same way he teaches that it can be made known to others whether this or that man has this or that Spirit. Hence true disciples of Christ recognise one another; hence others infer from one another that they are illumined by the Holy Spirit and graciously ruled by him; and hence that inward testimony also becomes known to others. But that you may see both that this difficulty you raise has often been urged against us and that it has been resolved, let us hear Amyraldus, who settles these matters most accurately. Does it follow, says he, that because obstinate minds that cannot yield cannot be drawn by any reasoning away from an opinion once conceived, there is no difference between them and truly wise men who, relying on reason, remain fixed in their purpose? Does the wise man feel certain that he is led by reason merely because those stubborn fellows think they too have their reasons? & elsewhere. Nor, however, are we left at a loss here, for Scripture describes most accurately the power of the Spirit who works in human hearts through the intervention of doctrine and truth. If there is anyone who perceives that power (and all truly Christian people do perceive it), agreeing with Scripture in the most perfect conformity (for although in some it appears feebler and more relaxed than in Paul, and in others more vivid, it does not wipe out the outlines and lineaments of conformity), can anyone doubt that he is the same Teacher who opens the mind from within and teaches from without? If Wolzogius thinks he must reply to the Tenebrio about how inexplicable this Spirit is, and about the nature and manner of these operations, let him know that this manna is hidden and has not even entered the mind of man. That this blind man chatters on so much, being a natural man, is no wonder. Nor is it easy to instruct a blind man about colours. And what if he himself, who has been endowed with that Spirit, is quite unable to explain what it is and how it works? Yet something can be replied even on behalf of the least disciples of Christ, who indeed feel these things but are unable to explain them. Amyraldus says excellently on this matter: I admit, as must be set aside at the outset, that he speaks of that operation of the Spirit by which the mind must be persuaded of the divinity of Scripture; but the same reasoning applies to the rest that might be disputed, if anyone wishes to derive a proof from their inexplicability. Therefore what that most learned man argues in this manner fits here very well.

units.la: Sane si respiciamus ad subjectum & constitutionem ipsius facultatis, proportione multo minus est hominum qui possint ea ponere dilucidè, quibus argumentis commoti credant se esse ratione præditos, seseque mente completi quæ cum ratione consentanea sunt, quam qui possint inter verè Christianos fidei suæ rationes dicendo explanare. Ideone ergo destituti sunt à ratione & inter bestias relegandi? ideone mente non utuntur ad vitæ munia obeunda? ideone minus boni cives sunt aut quod boni sunt minus est bonæ eorum menti rectæque rationi imputandum? haud magis merito sanè quam si quis idcirco pessima valetudine uti dicatur, quia nescit enucleare disertè, positane sit ratio bonæ valetudinis in exquisita humorum corporis temperie, an omnino sit ulla humorum in corpore temperies. Quem-admodum igitur usus bonæ valetudinis satis est ad vita suaviter fruendum & ejus muneribus rite fungendum: quod supra est, pertinet ad Physicorum & Medicorum accuratiorem disciplinam. Sunt ergo cum in animo tum in corpore plurimæ seu facultates, seu facultatum consti-tutiones, quarum usus esse potest expeditissimus atque valentissimus, tametsi quæ sit earum natura, qui motus & agendi ratio, plane qui iis felicissimè utuntur, verbis declarare non possit, -- imo ita, de qua loquitur Scrip-turæ spiritualis cognitio, etiam quæ paulo confusior movet, ut & magna voluptate perfundat, & ita penitus insideat animo nulla ut ratione revelli possit. Unde fit ut cum vaferrimus insidiator diabolus - verè credentibus et-iamnum ubique laqueos tendat; nec non homines profani, quantum possunt, simulato Numinis contemtu, & nescio quam vim vel ingenii vel animi inusitatam jactan-tes - lacessiverint disputationibus - magna Philosophorum nomina venditaverint; nihil tamen promovere potue-rint adversus eos qui verè & ex animo Deo in verbo suo loquenti crediderunt. Fingens enim & plane insuperabilis est ea vis quæ eos semel è regno tenebrarum in regnum D. N. J. C, transtulit. Possunt quidem isti luci interdum offuciæ quædam offundi: at eas splendore suo discutit. Potest mens sic affecta in Sophistarum strophis, tanquam in vinculo hæsitare: at eas vel sua vi disrumpit, vel dissolvit solo contentu, hæc est victoria quæ vicit mundum, nempe fides nostra. Quoniam major est, ait Johannes Spi-ritum habentibus, qui est in vobis quam qui in mundo.
units.tr: Indeed, if we look to the subject and the constitution of the faculty itself, there are far fewer men, in proportion, who can clearly set out the arguments by which they are moved to believe that they are endowed with reason and that their minds are filled with things consonant with reason, than there are who can explain the grounds of their faith when speaking among true Christians. Are they therefore destitute of reason and to be relegated among the beasts? Do they therefore not use their mind to perform the duties of life? Are they therefore worse citizens, or, if they are good, is that to be imputed to their good mind and right reason any less? Surely no more justly than if someone were said to be in very poor health because he cannot clearly explain whether good health consists in an exquisite balance of the bodily humours, or whether there is any balance of humours in the body at all. Just as the use of good health is enough for enjoying life pleasantly and fulfilling its duties properly, while what goes beyond this belongs to the more exact discipline of natural philosophers and physicians, so there are in both mind and body many faculties, or constitutions of faculties, whose use can be most expedient and most powerful, even though those who use them most happily cannot declare in words what their nature is, or what their motion and manner of action are. Indeed, the knowledge of spiritual things of which Scripture speaks, even that which stirs a little more confusedly, both suffuses the soul with great delight and so deeply inheres in the mind that by no reasoning can it be torn away. Hence it comes that although the most crafty deceiver, the devil, still spreads snares everywhere for those who truly believe, and profane men, as far as they can, with feigned contempt for the Deity, boasting of some unusual power of wit or spirit, have assailed them with disputations and bandied about the great names of philosophers, yet they have been able to achieve nothing against those who have truly and from the heart believed in God speaking in his word. For that power which once transferred them from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ is both effective and altogether insuperable. Certainly some clouds may sometimes be cast over that light, but it disperses them by its own brightness. A mind so disposed may hesitate in the snares of the sophists as if in a bond, but it either breaks them by its own power or dissolves them by mere contact; this is the victory that overcame the world, namely our faith. Because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world, says John to those who have the Spirit.

units.la: 6. Procul omni dubio, cum nihil à se magis alie-num esse videri velit, quam ab Ecclesia Reformata palam dissentire, injuriam sibi a me factam esse conqueretur Wolzogius, imo se ne latum quidem unguem à nostris discessisse testabitur. Quod quam nulla specie, nisi actui contraria protestetur, quod ad primariam de Interprete controversiam, fieri queat, in sequentibus videre dabitur. Hanc vero quæstionem quod attinet, sentiat quid velit, hoc assevero, nullibi ita apertè, ita clare, in toto illo perspicuo tractatu, extare quidpiam, quod satisfacere justæ suspicioni posit. Sæpissimè enim phrases culpat, sententias rejicit, vel saltem rejicere videtur, Reformatis usitatissimas, indubitatas, ut luce clarius jam demonstravimus. Quid autem erit quapropter sic agens, dum argumenta interim, dum sententiam Reformatorum, in causa principali turpiter deserit, dum nondum enucleatè satis hactenus tractata aggreditur novamque promittit lucem, quid inquam erit, quod ab omni suspicione ipsum liberet? dum tam intricatè saltem, & languide loquitur; ut, si omnia quæ paulo ἐμφατικώτερον[?] videri possent & veritati propinquiora ex toto libello congesseris, nihil dictum ab eo statim pateat, quin similia, modo non plausibiliora, hinc inde à Pontificiis, Remonstrantibus, imò Socinianis dicta, absque anxia inquisitione, offendas. Jmo si ex terminis & dicendi modis judicari debeat, quid dicet si multos ex ipso Pelagio didicisse videri posse convincatur. Corruptionem quandam mentis statuit & depravationem. Nec rectè ducitur mentis oculus; nec si vel duceretur recta via multis impedimentis præpeditus, videre tamen acutè posset, tanta autem hæc calamitas vel exaggeratâ oratione propositá demum reperitur; ut neque per se excitentur mentes nostræ segnes & languore peccati demissæ; neque ubi agere incipiunt, quo debeant tendere perspiciant; neque si vel si vel hoc viderint, qua via pergere debeant, tenent. Quid hic sodes, quo non magis emphaticum quid proferant Pelagiani? nec tam parum lectoris judicio fido, ut, me non explicante, eum hoc videre imò palpare non posse putem. Quicquid subjectum concernit, est languor, segnities, quâ per se excitari ne-queat, quo autem tendere, qua via pergere debeat, ut perspicere detur, verbum sanè per se sufficit. Illustratio autem, quæ sequitur, talis est, ut non principii in subjecto, sed viæ sed normæ diversitas, omne discrimen, inter naturalem & à Spiritu du-ctum, penitus exhauriat. Et sicut, hæc sunt verba, in percipiendis scientiis, quanquam bona mens credatur, æqualiter inter mortales distributa, tamen quia di-versa via ac ratione utuntur, videas alios aliis multum præcellentes sapientia: ita licet homines sint suis animi facultatibus æque præditi omnes, aliter proficit qui Spiritu Dei ducitur, aliter qui eo destituitur -- qui non eos facit progressus nec semper assequi veritatem potest. Hanc ergo vim hic tribuimus Spiritui S. ut excitet inertem animum. Quis hinc aliud quid extunderet, quam, sicut scientiarum humanarum sic & divinarum re-spectu, æqualem esse subjectivam aptitudinem, & unum si alter superet, id à diversitate viæ quam ingreditur ortum ducere omnem, nisi quod in spiritualibus, iners præterea excitetur animus. Impe-dimenta (quatuor forsan illa, quæ numerat Episcopius, Negligentiam, Præjudicia, affectum, & malitiam,) enim cum removet Sp. hoc tantum facit ut discussis nebulis possim clarè animadvertere &c. dat igitur, & sic dat, posse. Pelagium video plura concedere & tribuere gratiæ; quanquam enim antea omne virtutis divinæ auxilium spreverat, postea tamen paulatim gratiam quoque interiorem adjunxit, per quam intellectus illuminaretur, addo & per quam voluntas nonnihil afficeretur, unde, referente Augustino, qui certè supra verum non laudavit adversam sententiam, quam, & speciosissimè propositam, refutare intendera, non in lege, sic vocant externam omnem revelationem, tantum gratiam, quippe immeritis patefactam, sed in Dei esse adjutorio & adjuvare nos Deum per revelationem suam, dum NB cordis nostri oculos aperit, dum nos multiformi & ineffabili dono gratiae caelestis illuminat, neque id modo profitetur, verum etiam ipsam possibilitatem voluntatis & operis Deum gratiae suae adjuvare semper auxilio & Deum operari velle in nobis dum revelatione sapientiae in desiderium Dei stupentem suscitat voluntatem, dum nobis suadet omne quod bonum est. Nec abludunt hodierni Pelagiani aut Semipelagiani, Bellarminus non magis parce quam Pelagius, modo ne superet omnia quae scripsit hic, (de sensu enim ejus & sequuturis forsan retractatione, aut correctione, jam nihil,) Wolzogius. Concedit non posse hominem sine speciali illustratione credere Mysteria fidei, nec posse hominem solus naturae viribus ad gratiam recipiendam ullo modo se praeparare. Posse dum à Deo esse dicit Wolzogen, dubium relinquit an actione quadam solum morali (quando morale dico, Remonstrantium sensu istam vocem sumo, scio enim longe aliter & melius eam usurpari à Camerone) an alia à morali toto genere diversa id fiat. Impedimentorum remotionem unicè requirere videtur. At nihil notius quam semper à Pelagianis concessum esse, à Deo posse dari;sed quale auxilium & an ad singulos actus necesse sit, disputatum est. posse donavit, qui hoc posse adjuvat ait Pelagius. Plura autem dicit Wolzogius Sp. facit ut iis argumentis persuadeamur, quia mentem ad id apte disponit. excitat enim non solum inertem animum sed & ad verum scopum ducit & per illas semitas, quibus tandem perveniat ad salutarem interpretationis veritatem, faciatque omnia illa quae requiruntur ad hanc veluti actionem animae. animæ. Hæc nondum sufficiunt, non enim dicis an moralem, objectivum, an vero Hyperphysicum, subjectum reali influxu actuque attingentem & immediatum ducendi modum intelligas nec ne. Jmo necdum post te relinquis Pelagianos. Cordis enim, inquiunt illi, nostri oculos aperit, dum nobis, ne præsentibus occupemur, futura demonstrat, dum Diaboli pandit insidias, dum nos multiformi & ineffabili dono gratiæ cælestis illuminat. Qui hoc dicit gratiam tibi videtur negare? Remonstrantes, sic de mente, mens hominis sc. irregeniti est, salutiferâ cognitione destituta, impotens ex se ad concipienda ea quæ Euangelio specialiter, revelantur. Hominem, dicunt, salvificam fidem non habere à se, neque ex viribus liberi arbitrii, quandoquidem in statu apostasiæ & peccati nihil boni, quod quidem verè bonum sit, à se & ex se cogitare potest: hanc Dei gratiam, (Wolzogen omnia putat dicta, dum omnia illa, quæ requiruntur ad hanc, sed solum, veluti actionem animæ, Deum suo ductu facere largitur) esse principium progressum & complementum omnis boni, eò usque ut ne homo quidem regenitus absque præcedente ista, sive præveniente, prosequente & cooperante gratia bonum cogitare, velle aut peragere possit. Et quod magis est irresistibiliter intellectum illuminari volunt. Cunctis Wolzogianis ista sunt speciosiora. Nec corrigit in calce libri primi, dicit enim, posse quem verè interpretari Scripturam in multis, qui nulla sit singulari Spiritus efficacia adjutus. Fidelium autem hoc speciale privilegium est, ut auxilio divino, sicubi opus est, nunquam destituantur. Nondum quale putet, aut cujus naturæ, quantæque efficaciæ auxilium explicans: deinde addit, quando opus est, quod non levem suspicandi rationem suppeditat, quasi non semper, sed aliquando, auxilio isto pium egere velit. Cum ipse Pelagius ultro largiatur nos pro ineffabili Dei benignitate quotidiano muniri auxilio. Remonstrantes etiam regenitos, absque præexcitante &c. gratia, nihil posse statuunt. Casu vero factum nescio quo, ut hæc ultima verba, quibus quam efficacissimè potuisti, sententiam tuam proposuisti, fere coincidant, cum iis, modo ne superentur ab iis, quæ alibi Socinianus in simili causa. sic Smalcius: Potest igitur homo planè multum præstare absque ista Spiritus S. singulari opera. Utitur autem Deus auxilio isto suo singulari ad juvandum fideles: - Sic etiam quotiescunque opus est fidelibus, toties istud auxilium Deus habet paratissimum: & eo, si quid defit hominibus vere probis, illud totum supplet. Nollem igitur Reformatos omnes accusasse obscuritatis, antequam Pelagium & Socinianos veritate dictorum, saltem puritate, superassem. Quod si posthac præstiteris, habebis me candoris tui amatorem, imo præconem.
