Utinam ita scripsisses, ut licet Scripturam se explicare ipsam neges, scriptum tuum sua se explicatione ab omnis Heterodoxias saltem suspicione immune præstare potuisset! intricatam tuam obscuritatem lubens prætermisissem.
units.tr: 6. Beyond all doubt, since Wolzogius would have it appear that nothing is further from him than openly dissenting from the Reformed Church, he will complain that I have done him an injustice, and he will even testify that he has not departed a single nail's breadth from our people. How he can do this, unless he professes it in a way that contradicts his actions, will be seen in what follows, in the chief controversy concerning the Interpreter. As for that question, let him feel what he wishes. I assert this: nowhere in that whole transparent treatise is there anything stated so openly and so clearly that it could satisfy a just suspicion. For very often he finds fault with phrases, rejects opinions, or at least seems to reject them, which are most common and undoubted among the Reformed, as we have already shown more clearly than light. But what will there be that frees him from all suspicion, when he, acting in this way, meanwhile shamefully abandons the arguments and the opinion of the Reformers on the principal issue, when he takes up a matter not yet sufficiently explained so far and promises a new light? What, I ask, will there be? He speaks so intricately and feebly that, if you gathered from the whole little book everything that might seem a little more emphatic [ἐμφατικώτερον] and closer to the truth, nothing said by him would at once be evident; you would instead find similar things, though not more plausible, said here and there by Papists, Remonstrants, and indeed Socinians, without any anxious inquiry. Indeed, if he ought to be judged by his terms and modes of speaking, what will he say if it is shown that he appears to have learned much from Pelagius himself? He establishes a certain corruption and depravity of the mind. The eye of the mind is not rightly led; nor, even if it were led by the right way, hindered by many obstacles, could it see sharply. Yet this calamity is found, even with the matter stated in exaggerated speech, so that our minds are neither roused of themselves, being sluggish and sunk in the languor of sin; nor, when they begin to act, do they perceive where they ought to tend; nor, even if they see this, do they keep to the way by which they ought to proceed. What here, pray, do the Pelagians propose that is more emphatic? Nor do I think the judgment of the reader so weak that, without my explaining, he cannot see, indeed feel, this. Whatever concerns the subject is languor and sloth, by which it cannot be roused of itself; but that it may be given to see where to tend and by what way to proceed, the word surely suffices by itself. The illustration which follows, however, is such that it entirely exhausts every distinction between the natural and the one led by the Spirit, not in a difference of principle in the subject, but in the difference of way and rule. And just as, these are his words, in perceiving the sciences, although a good mind is believed to be distributed equally among mortals, yet because they use different ways and methods, you see some far excelling others in wisdom: so although men are all equally endowed with the faculties of their soul, he who is led by the Spirit of God progresses differently from him who is deprived of him, who does not make such advances nor can always attain the truth. Therefore we attribute this power here to the Holy Spirit, that he may rouse the sluggish mind. What would anyone draw from this other than that, with respect to human sciences and divine ones alike, the subjective aptitude is equal, and if one surpasses the other, this arises entirely from the diversity of the way it enters; except that in spiritual matters the mind is moreover sluggish and must be roused? For when the Spirit removes the impediments (perhaps those four which Episcopius enumerates: negligence, prejudices, affection, and malice), he does only this: that, the mists having been dispelled, I can notice clearly, and so on. He gives, therefore, and so gives the power. I see Pelagius conceding and attributing more to grace. For although before he had scorned all the help of divine power, afterwards he gradually added inner grace also, through which the understanding would be illumined; I add, and through which the will would be somewhat moved, whence, as Augustine reports, who certainly did not praise the opposing opinion beyond the truth, though he intended to refute it, though it was most splendidly proposed: not in the law, for so they call all external revelation, only grace, surely bestowed on the unworthy, but it is in the help of God, and God helps us through his revelation, while, NB, he opens the eyes of our heart, while he illumines us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace. He not only professes this, but also the very possibility of the will and of the work, God always helping with the aid of his grace, and God willing to work in us, while by the revelation of wisdom he rouses the will amazed into a desire for God, while he persuades us of everything that is good. Nor do today's Pelagians or Semipelagians differ. Bellarmine is no more sparing than Pelagius, provided he does not surpass in everything he has written here (for about his meaning, and about the retraction or correction that perhaps followed, there is now nothing to say), and Wolzogius likewise. He concedes that man cannot believe the mysteries of faith without special illumination, nor can man in any way prepare himself to receive grace by the powers of nature alone. That he can, while Wolzogen says it is from God, leaves it in doubt whether it is done by some action merely moral (when I say moral, I take the word in the sense of the Remonstrants, for I know it is used far differently and better by Cameron) or by some other kind entirely different from the moral. He seems to require only the removal of impediments. But nothing is better known than that it has always been conceded by the Pelagians that the ability can be given by God; what kind of help, and whether it is necessary for individual acts, has been disputed. He has given the ability who helps this ability, says Pelagius. But Wolzogius says more: the Spirit brings it about that we are persuaded by those arguments, because he aptly disposes the mind to this. For he not only rouses the sluggish mind but also leads it to the true goal, and through those paths by which at last it may reach the saving truth of interpretation, and he makes all those things which are required for this, as it were the action of the soul. These things do not yet suffice, for you do not say whether you understand the moral, objective mode, or the hyperphysical one, touching the subject with real influx and act and leading it immediately, or not. Indeed, after you the Pelagians are not left behind. For they say, he opens the eyes of our heart, while he shows us future things, lest we be occupied with present ones, while he unfolds the snares of the devil, while he illumines us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace. Does he who says this seem to you to deny grace? The Remonstrants, on the mind: the mind of man, that is, of the unregenerate, is destitute of saving knowledge, unable of itself to conceive those things which are specially revealed in the Gospel. Man, they say, does not have saving faith from himself, nor from the powers of free will, since in the state of apostasy and sin he can think nothing from himself and of himself that is truly good: this grace of God (Wolzogen thinks everything has been said, while he grants that God by his leading does all those things which are required for this, but only as it were the action of the soul) is the beginning, progress and completion of all good, to such an extent that not even a regenerate man can think, will or perform good without this preceding, accompanying and cooperating grace. And what is more, they want the understanding to be illumined irresistibly. These statements are more attractive to all the Wolzogians. Nor does he correct this at the end of the first book, for he says: he can truly interpret Scripture in many matters who is not aided by any singular efficacy of the Spirit. But this special privilege belongs to the faithful, that they are never deprived of divine help wherever there is need. He does not yet explain what kind of help he thinks it is, or of what nature and how great its efficacy. Then he adds when there is need, which provides no slight ground for suspicion, as if he would have the pious need that help not always but sometimes. Yet Pelagius himself freely concedes that we are fortified by daily help through the ineffable goodness of God. The Remonstrants also state that the regenerate, without a preceding exciting grace and so on, can do nothing. But by some chance I do not know, these last words, with which you proposed your opinion as efficaciously as you could, nearly coincide with those which the Socinian says elsewhere in a similar case; so Smalcius: Man can therefore do very much without this singular work of the Holy Spirit. God uses this his singular help to aid the faithful. So also as often as the faithful have need, so often God has this help most ready; and if anything is lacking to men truly upright, he supplies all of it by it. I would not, therefore, have accused all the Reformed of obscurity before you had surpassed the Pelagians and Socinians in the truth of what is said, or at least in its purity. If you do so hereafter, you will have me as a lover, indeed a herald, of your candour. Would that you had written in such a way that, though you deny that you explain Scripture itself, your writing could by its own explanation have shown itself free at least from suspicion of every heterodoxy! I would gladly have passed over your intricate obscurity.

units.la: Coronidis loco, ut, quod ventilamus controversiæ caput, finiam, notandum est, omnia quibus Enthu-siasmum & Fanaticismum impetivit dicteria Wolzo-gius, si res penitius paulo consideretur, in Refor-matos revera dicta esse, nisi quid Reformati, quid Enthusiastæ doceant, ignorasse se fateatur. Agit cum iis, ut antea posuit, qui Scripturam fidei co-lunt morumque normam,& adversus eos quiScriptu-ræ Interpretem omni labore & industria genuinum quæri & audiri volunt, utpote à cujus decisione controversiæ, tota pendeat religio. Inter illos vero, qui Spiritum ita crepent, sic Wolzogen pro dictio-nis nitore, nulli sunt, nisi Reformati cum Luthe-ranis purioribus. Nam qui Enthusiastæ hactenus au-diunt & Fanatici, aut Scripturam rejectant omnem, aut saltem alphabetariis solum relinquunt. Hi omne suum odium, sic de minus turbulento istorum gene- re Hoornbeek, in S. Script. evomunt, eam simpli- cem literam, elementum, Alphabetum criminantur, solis pueris, non adultis & spiritualibus, quales ipsi sint scilicet, imperandum & praescribendum, Spiritum suum ajunt verum Dei verbum, normam Scripturae, imo apertis frontibus in Scripturam incurrunt, eam pe- tulanter repudiant, contemnunt. Denique verbum scriptum non simpliciter sequendum, sed Spiritum ejusque afflatus etiam contra Scripturam volunt. Hinc de Schwenkfeldo, quem Lutherus & Melanchton Stenkfeld vocant, testatur Historicus, eum novam religionis ideam, sed verbo Dei sepositio, venditasse, ut, referente Calvino, soliti fuerint blasphemare Scr. S. & Scriptores ejus sacros. Apud eos Paulus vas con- fractum erat; Petrus abnegator Dei; Johannes ado- lescens stolidulus; Matthaeus fenerator. Si quis plura velit consulat Crocii Antiweig Clariss. Viros Hoorn-beek in Sum. Controv. & Georgium Hornium, per anagrammatismum, Honorium Reggium de statu Ecclesiae Anglicanae aliosque; & primo intuitu, quanti Scripturam faciant, quantopere quam prolixe eam spernant simul & eos qui Scripturae adhaerent & judicium normale indeaccersunt, videri poterit. Quis jam non certus sit, eos tanti Scripturam non facere, ut, anxie de Interprete solliciti, de eo disputent? Re-formati ergo supersunt unice, qui Spiritu S. tanto-pere egent, ei tam multa deferunt. Hos oppugna-vit Wolzogen. Quod si neget, probet praeter illos alios dari, qui Scr. ut dictum est, admittentes, de Interprete disputantes, Spiritum crepent. Non inficior de Scripturae vera clavi, de Mystica, spiritua-li sua interpretatione, etiam Weigelium, Jacobum Boehme, aliosque quandoque haec & illa profudisse, sed & certum est. 1. Eos hoc dicis causa agere. 2. In Scripturâ normae & regulae eminentiam minime agnoscere, quod tamen in suis, quibuscum agit Wolzogen, posuit. 3. Scripturam fere ab ipsis solum usurpari καθ' ἄνθρωπον adversus literalistas, Psychicos, Scripturarios, & ad amoliendum universale odium, cui se Scr. contemtu omni expositos experiebantur. Quandoquidem autem de Enthusiastis & Fanaticis bene multa scripsit & quidem concitatione animo Wolzogen, exponam ipsi quid de Enthusiastis didicerim, ut inde innotescat quinam Enthusiastis propiores haberi debeant, præ illis qui ab Enthusiastis longissimè & toto cælo diversi, tantum Scripturæ normali usui tribuunt, ut omnis Spiritus, sive naturalia doceat, sive quæ religionem concernunt, qui Scripturæ aut contrariatur, aut amussim declinat, ipsis impurus sit & Fanaticus; optimè horum mentem explicuit Vir Clarissimus & Doctissimus, D. Johannes Valkenier, cujus judicio, quisquis Mosis aut Davidis & Sanctorum Prophetarum oracula in dubiâ & indecisâ Philosophorum lite circa rerum primordia, cælorum spatia, siderum motus, humanæ mentis operationes, brutorumque vitam non consulit, artis suæ hostis æstimatur. Novi alios, qui, si non in supernaturalibus, saltem in naturalibus, Spiritus sui, Gas-sendi phrasin respicio, dictamina tantopere efferunt, ut Scriptura potius, non dogmatizare in naturalibus, secundum erroneam vulgi opinionem loqui, imò verbale mendacium subinde proferre dici debeat, quam ut Spiritus illius dictamina vel tantillum flectantur. Quid? ipsum Wolzogium mox Rationi in multis, imò fere in omnibus, Ducis Normæque in Scripturæ Interpretatione fasces & sceptrum deferentem videbimus. Quis jam in Scripturæ reverentia, aut juxta dictamina sui Spiritus detorsione, longius abest à Fanaticis? Si plura velis? Enthusiastas, Fanaticos novi, qui omnia ante docta & cognita oblivioni tradenda discipulos docent, sic de iis Bohemus. Novi, qui de omnium rerum veritate, priusquam ad certam cognitionitionem ullam venire queant, dubitandum suis in-culcant, donec ita certi evadant, ut nihil dubitationis vel diffidentiae reliquum sit. Hanc unam ex primariis Nicolai Stork, Thomae Munceri &c. regulis fuisse author est Chemnitius. Enthusiastas novi, qui Me-thodum, qua res omnes, ita ut in iis nunquam errent, disci posse, jactitant. Scripsit Weigelius, homo in-fanus, librum, cui titulus, Captura aurea, hoc est, ad res omnes absque ullo errore agnoscendas, multis doctissi-mis incognita, attamen omnibus scitu necessaria. Enthu-siastas novi, qui omnia antehac scripta contemnunt, rident, qui ex insita luce meditando cuncta deduci volunt. Quakeris nihil usitatius est, quam libros spernere, vituperare scripta, introversionem, ut vo-cant, ad lucem quam intus habent, attentionem clamare, in homine omnium rerum species, omnium artium & scientiarum semina fingere. Hinc omnem ex se ipso cognitionem excitandam, excu-tiendam. Fratres Rosex Crucis erant, qui omnes scientias, omnes disciplinas restituendas sua methodo somniabant. Enthusiastas novi, qui omnium argumen-ta rident, exsibilant, interim meliora non substituentes hominem sibi committunt. Enthusiastas denique novi, qui se filios lucis esse gloriantur, qui quocunque absque ulla reverentia suisque deque habent. Dum inte-rim ne unicum ex tota secta sua proferre queant, qui disciplinas restitutas jam, aut multum in melius mutatas ostenderit. Velim id etiam ex hodiernis doceri novaturientibus, qui sane ab Enthusiastarum pollicitationibus non longe absunt, quaenam ex dis-ciplinis primariis tantam lucem adepta sit, ut novae huic luci quicquam debeat hactenus: tantum abest ut alia disciplinarum orta facies appareat, Thrasonice licet jactata a Velthusio: non sine magna totius or-bis literariae & manifesta contumelia dicam an injuria, nimirum sapientiae studium jejunis & minutis ingeniis hactenus relictum fuisse. Theologiam tantopere ab ipsis correctam non video. Iurisprudentes, Medicos rogo & idem de suis testantur. Sed Philosophiam nunc alio splendore coruscantem mundus adspicit. Fateor, nullum fere seculum fuisse, nisi forsan ferrea illa excipias, quo non ab ingeniosis aliquid excogitatum novi sit. Nec Cartesio laudem suam detractam velim, multa in illius scriptis, ingeniose inventa, aut ab aliis dicta, ad suas hypotheses translata esse, negari non potest. Philosophicam amo libertatem, nec majoris facio, qui Aristotelem, quam qui Cartesium caeco amplexantur impetu. Hoc velim, Scripturae & Theologiae suam manere praeminentiam. Dogmata Philosophica, in hanc normam infallibilem incurrentia, rejici, aliorum scripta & inventa manibus nostris non extorqueri, non contemni. Displicet item, aliquos, quod tamen Philosophiae huic, quam non intelligunt, impactum nolim, postquam in istam lucis scholam delati fuerunt, eo venisse arrogantiae, ut, dum veterem Logicam exscribunt maximam partem, eo ineptiorem ad disciplinas omnes esse unumquemque dixerint, quo in Logica hactenus usitata doctior evaserit, nisi forsan suam stupiditatem nimiae pristinae Logices cognitioni imputare velint, fluctuantes & dubitantii fratres. Imo ut inhumanis dicteriis erga Venerandos & pientissimos Praeceptores non peperce-rint miseri, qui, absque contradictionum addito nitore, vix disputationem scribere docti sunt.
units.tr: By way of a conclusion, to finish this main point of the controversy: it must be noted that, if one considers the matter a little more closely, everything Wolzogen has hurled as insults at enthusiasm and fanaticism has in fact been said against the Reformed, unless he admits he does not know what the Reformed teach and what the enthusiasts teach. He deals with those who, as he said earlier, honour Scripture as the rule of faith and of conduct, and who want the genuine interpreter of Scripture sought and heard with all diligence and effort, since the whole of religion depends on his decision in the controversy. Among those who boast of the Spirit in the way Wolzogen, with his polished phrasing, describes, there are none except the Reformed and the purer Lutherans. For the enthusiasts and fanatics we have heard of hitherto either reject Scripture altogether or at least leave it to the alphabetarians alone. They pour out all their hatred (to use Hoornbeek's words about the less turbulent members of that group) against Holy Scripture. They call its plain letter an elementary alphabet, to be imposed and prescribed only on children, not on the mature and spiritual, which is evidently what they themselves are. They say that their own spirit is the true Word of God and the rule of Scripture; indeed, with their faces uncovered, they run straight against Scripture and wantonly repudiate and despise it. Finally, they want the written word not simply to be followed, but the Spirit and its inspirations even against Scripture. Hence the historian testifies of Schwenckfeld, whom Luther and Melanchthon call Stenkfeld, that he peddled a new idea of religion, but a setting aside of the Word of God, so that, as Calvin reports, they were accustomed to blaspheme Holy Scripture and its sacred writers. Among them Paul was a broken vessel; Peter a denier of God; John a foolish youth; Matthew a usurer. If anyone wants more, let him consult Crocius's Antiweigelius, the most distinguished men Hoornbeek in his Summa Controversiarum, and Georgius Hornius, who by anagram calls himself Honorius Reggius, on the state of the English Church, and others. At first glance it can be seen how highly they value Scripture, and how greatly and at length they scorn it, along with those who cling to Scripture and seek from it the normative judgment. Who is not now certain that they do not value Scripture so highly that they anxiously worry about its interpreter and dispute about him? The Reformed alone, therefore, remain, who so greatly need the Holy Spirit and ascribe so much to him. It is these whom Wolzogen has attacked. But if he denies this, let him prove that there are others besides them who, while admitting Scripture as we have said, and disputing about the interpreter, boast of the Spirit. I do not deny that Weigel, Jacob Boehme, and others have at times poured out this and that about the true key of Scripture, its mystical and spiritual interpretation; but this too is certain: (1) they do this for the sake of appearance; (2) they hardly acknowledge the pre-eminence of Scripture as a rule and norm, although Wolzogen has laid this down for his own people, with whom he deals; (3) Scripture is almost only used by them according to man [καθ' ἄνθρωπον] against the literalists, the psychici, and the scripturists, and in order to remove the general hatred to which they found themselves exposed through contempt for Scripture. Since, however, Wolzogen has written much about enthusiasts and fanatics, and indeed with an agitated mind, I shall set out for him what I have learned about enthusiasts, so that it may become clear who ought to be regarded as nearer to the enthusiasts, in comparison with those who are far removed from the enthusiasts and wholly different from them, yet ascribe so much to the normal use of Scripture that every spirit which either teaches natural things or matters concerning religion, and which either opposes Scripture or deviates from its line, is in their eyes impure and fanatical. The most distinguished and learned man, Mr. Johannes Valkenier, has expressed well the mind of these men, and in his judgment whoever does not consult the oracles of Moses or David and the holy prophets in the doubtful and undecided dispute of the philosophers about the beginnings of things, the spaces of the heavens, the motions of the stars, the operations of the human mind, and the life of beasts, is considered an enemy of his own art. I know others who, if not in supernatural matters, at least in natural ones (I am looking at the phrase of Gassendi concerning his own Spirit), so extol their own dictates that Scripture ought rather to be said not to teach doctrine in natural matters, but to speak according to the erroneous opinion of the common people, and even at times to utter a verbal lie, than for those dictates of their Spirit to be bent even a little. What? We shall soon see Wolzogen himself handing over the fasces and sceptre of leader and norm in the interpretation of Scripture to Reason in many things, indeed in almost all. Who is now further from fanatics in reverence for Scripture, or in twisting it to the dictates of his own spirit? Do you want more? I know enthusiasts and fanatics who teach their disciples that all things previously taught and known must be consigned to oblivion, as Boehme says of them. I know those who impress upon their followers that one must doubt the truth of all things before they can arrive at any certain knowledge, until they become so certain that no doubt or distrust remains. The author Chemnitz says that this was one of the chief rules of Nicolas Storch, Thomas Müntzer, and others. I know enthusiasts who boast of a method by which all things can be learned so that they never err in them. Weigel, an insane man, wrote a book entitled The Golden Capture, that is, for recognising all things without any error, unknown to many most learned men, yet necessary for all to know. I know enthusiasts who scorn and laugh at all writings produced hitherto, and who want everything to be deduced by meditation from the light implanted within. Nothing is more usual among the Quakers than to despise books, to disparage writings, and to cry out for an introversion, as they call it, to the light they have within, and to imagine in man the forms of all things and the seeds of all arts and sciences. Hence all knowledge is to be stirred up and shaken out of oneself. The Brothers of the Rosy Cross were those who dreamed that all sciences and all disciplines were to be restored by their method. I know enthusiasts who laugh at and hiss at all arguments, and who, while substituting nothing better, entrust themselves to man alone. Finally, I know enthusiasts who glory that they are sons of light, and who hold everything in contempt and without any reverence, both their own and that of others, while not one of their whole sect can produce a single example of a discipline already restored or greatly improved. I would like those modern innovators, who are certainly not far from the promises of the enthusiasts, to show from today's examples which of the primary disciplines has gained so much light that it owes anything hitherto to this new light. Far from it: a different face of the disciplines has appeared, although Velthuysen boasts of it in a swaggering way. Not without great insult to the whole literary world, and I may say injustice, the study of wisdom has hitherto been left to meagre and petty minds. I do not see theology so greatly corrected by them. I ask the jurists and physicians, and they likewise testify the same about their own fields. But the world now beholds philosophy shining with another splendour. I admit that there has been almost no age, except perhaps that iron one, in which something new has not been devised by some ingenious person. Nor would I wish to deprive Descartes of his praise; it cannot be denied that many things ingeniously discovered in his writings, or said by others, have been transferred to his hypotheses. I love philosophical freedom, and I do not esteem more highly those who embrace Aristotle with blind impetuosity than those who do so with Descartes. This I would wish: that Scripture and theology keep their pre-eminence. Philosophical doctrines which run against this infallible norm should be rejected; the writings and discoveries of others should not be wrested from our hands or despised. It also displeases me that some (though I would not wish them to be struck by this philosophy, which they do not understand) after they have been brought into that school of light have come to such arrogance that, while they copy out most of the old Logic, they have declared that each person is the more unfit for all the disciplines the more learned he has become in the Logic hitherto in use; unless perhaps these wretched wavering and doubting brethren wish to attribute their own stupidity to an excessive knowledge of their former Logic. Indeed, the wretches have not spared even their venerable and most pious teachers with inhuman insults, although they have hardly learned to write a disputation without the polish of added contradictions.

units.la: χ̓ ταῦτα μὲν δ᾽ ἢ ταῦτα. [?]
units.tr: "These things indeed, or these." [χ̓ ταῦτα μὲν δ᾽ ἢ ταῦτα.] [?]

units.la: 2. Hactenus de prima ista Wolzogiana thesi dixi-mus. Sequitur secunda, primae vicina & connexa: ita enim, ut in toto religionis negotio, sic praesertim in iis quae Pelagianas controversias spectant, comparata res est, ut plura sibi invicem connexa semper incedant juncta simul pari passu nexuque, & unum eorum rejici non possit, aut stabiliri, quin mox secundum & tertium simul & rejiciatur aut stabiliatur, non mirum igitur erit, postquam ita titubantem in veritatis doctrina, imo labentem vi-dimus Wolzogium, eundem sæpius inpingentem offendere. Immediatas, illo quo dictum sensu, Spiri-tus sancti operationes afflatusque quanti faciat, pro-ut ex illo libro nosse datur, jam novimus. Omnem etiam novi luminis infusionem negat, nullumque, præter id quod in Scriptura radiat, lumen dari asse-rit. Sic sonant verba, de mentis constitutione dixe-rat, & hic vim suam exerit Dei Spiritus qui illuminare mentes nostras dicitur, non quod novum lumen iis in-fundat, quod omne in ipsa radiat Scriptura. Idem plane Velthuisen de Usu Rat. p.70 nobis gratia no-vum lumen non inserit. Jam supra monuimus, verum hoc esse, si de veritatibus loquereris, quas omnes in Scriptura agnosco collocatas, nec alias a novo quodam lumine expectandas, sed falsum, quoniam de ipsius mentis constitutione, illiusque corrigendæ modo agis: Sic enim dixeras, paulo ante, mentis nostræ constitutio talis est a natura, ut multa cernere non possit sæpissimè quibus opus habet ut persuadeatur. Et hic, in constitutionis nimirum correctione, vim suam, dicis, exerit Dei Spiritus, qui &c. mentis igitur constitutio corrigitur, sed non per in-fusionem novi luminis. Affici concedis, sed non per novi luminis infusionem. Nec crimen heterodoxias amo-lieris, etiam si omnia, quæ alibi veritati propiora, hac de re, hinc inde, dicta collegeris. Quod ne absque gravi ratione à me dici videatur, aut imme-ritò, sequentia mecum considera paulo pensiculatius.
units.tr: 2. So far I have discussed this first thesis of Wolzogius. The second follows, close to the first and connected with it. For, as in the whole business of religion, so especially in those matters that concern the Pelagian controversies, the situation is such that several connected propositions always go forward together, step by step and bound together, and one of them cannot be rejected or established without the second and third being rejected or established at once. It is therefore no surprise that, having seen Wolzogius so unsteady in the doctrine of truth, indeed sliding, we now find him stumbling again and again. We already know how much he values the immediate operations and inspirations of the Holy Spirit, in the sense in which that book allows them to be understood. He also denies any infusion of new light and asserts that no light is given except what shines in Scripture. Those are his words, which he had spoken about the constitution of the mind: and here the Spirit of God, who is said to illuminate our minds, exerts his power, not because he pours new light into them, since all of it shines in Scripture itself. Velthuysen says exactly the same in On the Use of Reason, p. 70: grace does not insert new light into us. Earlier I pointed out that this is true if you are speaking of the truths, all of which I acknowledge to be contained in Scripture and not to be expected from some new light; but it is false, since you are dealing with the constitution of the mind itself and the way it is to be corrected. For you had said a little earlier: the constitution of our mind is such by nature that it often cannot perceive many things it needs in order to be persuaded. And here, in the correction of that very constitution, you say: the Spirit of God exerts his power, who etc. So the constitution of the mind is corrected, but not by the infusion of new light. You concede that it is affected, but not by the infusion of new light. Nor will you remove the charge of heterodoxy, even if you gather together all the statements, here and there, that come closer to the truth on this point. So that no one thinks I say this without serious reason, or unjustly, consider the following with me a little more carefully.

units.la: I. Hic propriam sedem fuisse rotundæ & candidè dicendi quid res sit, versatur enim in examine eorum quæ de lumine & illuminatione Spiritus S. Refor-matos statuere dixerat Paradoxus Cap. xiv. hic dicen-dum dum erat, hic explicandum, quid ipsi hæreret animo. Non illa igitur respicienda quæ alibi in transi-tu ponunutur, cum ex professo hic de isto negotio agens, omne infusum in mentem lumen neget. 2. Priori libro de eadem re, & quidem in propria sede, non meliora inveniri p. 63. 64. 65. 3. Nullibi ita clarè asserit, ac quidem hic rejicit, de quo loquimur, lumen & illuminationem. 4. Nullibi ita emphaticè, ut Heterodoxos superet. 5. Adde quod hoc ipso loco, qui Wolzogio præ manibus, Reformatæ Ecclesiæ sententiam rejiciendam, ut Enthusiasticam, dixerat Paradoxus, Wolzogio interim eam nec vindicante, nec explicante, imo ne quidem ejus vindicias ab Enthusiasmo tentante;quapropt-ter eundem ipsi cum Reformatis sensum esse quis credat?noverat procul dubio,quiHeterodoxias crimen impactum sibi quæritur, compendiosiori via, quam Orthodoxæ doctrinæ amplexu, candidâque & aperta vindicatione, ita receptæ veritatis, iri non posse. Quod tantum abest ut egerit, ut potius, nihil dicendo, si non vadimonium turpiter deseruerit, divinandum saltem quid sentiat reliquerit. Refert quædam à Paradoxo ad eruendam quasi mentem nostram dicta, p. 255. & sic respondet. Equidem hanc veniam lubens do Exercitatori ut inquirat in sensus nostros, qui sanè etsi sint omnium Reformatorum iidem, non iisdem tamen verbis aut eadem orationis claritate exprimuntur. Tu autem, an, non impetrata venia, quid Reformati sentiant, quid tu, eloqui clarè non audes? Quorsum enim neutrum eorum quæ dixerat Paradoxus eligis? aut quod tertium detur, non explicas? Quorsum, quid tu Reformatorum putes esse, non profers? & eorum sensa ab Enthusiasmi calumniosè simul & ignoranter à tenebrione impacto crimine non liberas, imo ne verbo quidem? Hoc omne est quod prodis. Sed omnes tamen & Scripturam agnoagnoscunt sui Interpretem, & Spiritum auxilium imperant ut confundi minimè cum Scriptura Sp. oporteat ex eorum sen-tentia. Quam frigide? ite deferbuisti Wolzogi, qui tam alta voce Clementissimis tuis Dominis, qui tibi perso-nam quam sustines imposuerunt, ob Ecclesiam Walo-nicam injuria affectam testabundus advocabas in capi-te, ut in calce Ecclesiæ Reformatæ, quasi ab illa diver-sam tibi commisissent Reformati proceres, causam ita turpiter deserere debueris? Imo sic proponis ipsorum sententiam, ut nec à Socinianis, nec ab ipso tuo Para-doxo dissentiat Ecclesia Reformata: illi enim & Scripturam agnoscunt & Spiritus auxilium imploran-dum non negabunt, nec etiam cum Scriptura con-fundent Spiritum, ut notum est, vel ex Exercitatore, intelligat enim claram & distinctam perceptionem per Sp. internam revelationem, necdum idem cum ipsa Scriptura, sed diversum quid intelligit. Quid jam Reformati? nihil præter id quod Sociniani, quod ipse paradoxus? Non possum, quin semper mihi suspicionem suboriri patiar, quotiescunque ita titubantes, ita latebras quærentes, offendo veritatis quasi defensores, ut te nunc deprehensum teneo, Wolzogi, quanquam satis gloriosè te jactantem.
units.tr: I. This is the proper place for speaking frankly and candidly about what the matter is. For here he is engaged in examining what the Paradoxus said in chapter 14 that the Reformed hold concerning the light and illumination of the Holy Spirit. Here one had to speak, and here one had to explain what stuck in his mind. Therefore what he sets down elsewhere in passing is not to be considered, since here, treating this matter deliberately, he denies that any light is infused into the mind. 2. In his earlier book, on the same subject and indeed in its proper place, nothing better is found, pp. 63, 64, 65. 3. Nowhere does he assert so clearly, as he does here, that the light and illumination in question are rejected. 4. Nowhere so emphatically that he surpasses the heterodox. 5. Add that in this very place, where Wolzogius has the Paradoxus before him rejecting the view of the Reformed Church as enthusiastic, Wolzogius neither defends nor explains it, nor even tries to defend it against the charge of enthusiasm. Who would believe that he holds the same view as the Reformed on this point? He undoubtedly knew that by seeking to escape the charge of heterodoxy by a shorter route than embracing orthodox doctrine, he could not succeed. Far from doing so, he has, by saying nothing, left us at least to guess what he thinks, if he has not shamefully deserted his recognizance. He quotes some statements of the Paradoxus, p. 255, as if to draw out our mind, and answers thus: Indeed I gladly grant this indulgence to the Examiner, that he inquire into our opinions, which, though they are the same among all the Reformed, are not however expressed in the same words or with the same clarity of speech. But you, if you have not obtained that indulgence, why do you not dare to state clearly what the Reformed think, and what you yourself think? Why do you choose neither of the things the Paradoxus said? Or, if there is a third option, why do you not explain it? Why do you not set out what you think the Reformed believe? And why do you not free their views, even by a word, from the charge of enthusiasm, a charge that the slanderous and ignorant Paradoxus has fastened on them? This is all you bring forward. But all of them, nevertheless, acknowledge Scripture as its own interpreter, and beg the Spirit for help, so that in their view the Spirit should by no means be confused with Scripture. How coldly you have cooled off, Wolzogius, you who so loudly, in the title, called on your most gracious lords, who imposed on you the role you play, to witness that the Walloon Church had been wronged, and who, as if the leading men of the Reformed had entrusted you with a cause different from that of the Reformed Church, ought to have so shamefully deserted that cause at its end! Indeed, you present their view in such a way that the Reformed Church does not dissent either from the Socinians or from your own Paradoxus. For they acknowledge Scripture, and will not deny that the Spirit's help must be implored; nor, as is well known, do they confuse the Spirit with Scripture, as even the Examiner understands. For he understands a clear and distinct perception through the internal revelation of the Spirit, and not the same thing as Scripture itself, but something different. What then do the Reformed hold? Nothing but what the Socinians hold, what the Paradoxus himself holds? I cannot help being suspicious, every time I find such wavering men, such men seeking hiding places, posing as defenders of the truth. So now I hold you caught, Wolzogius, though you boast quite gloriously.

units.la: 6. Plura habeo, negat noster omnem afflatum in-ternum, immediatam operationem Sp. omnem, quod fieri non potest, quin sponte sequatur, quod hic ponit, non per infusionem novi luminis illuminari mentes. Hoc autem 7. non prætereundum, quod hic error in terminis doceatur à Velthusio, Seniore non solum Ecclesiæ, cujus Wolzogen Pastor est, sed viro qui orthodoxias tenacem gerit animum ita ut sua satis innocentia tutus sit, ex judicio Wolzogii. Ille autem tam crasse, tam turpiter hic, Pelagiani-zat, ut ne quidem ipse Pelagius magis rotunde, sic ille: unum tantum genus luminis mente concipere licet. Regeniti & non regeniti cognitio de rebus & mysteriis fidei non differt luminis ratione, neque illius cognitio est diversum cognitionis genus. Sic Senior Ecclesiae Reformatae. Gratia, quae ad cognitionem salutarem prodest, NB non est lumen, neque nobis, neque Scripturae novum lumen inserit. Item homines non possunt cognoscere Mysteria fidei, quia nolunt, & quia nunquam sine gratia Dei volent: non quod in se non habeant ea cognitionis principia, eamque cognoscendi facultatem, qua ea, quae in Script. traduntur, tantum capiuntur & intelliguntur, ita ut novis principiis aut nova facultate indigeant, sed quia homo animalis ita carnis affectibus ducitur, &c. Sit igitur ista secunda Thesis quam examinare necesse duxi & refutare: Novum lumen in mentes nostras non infundi, sed omne in Scriptura radiare, idque dicendum quando non de veritate revelanda, sed mentis, veritatem recipiendae, constitutione, sermo est. Ego eam falsam esse, Heterorodoxam, Pelagianam dico & Socinianam, conferantur Romonstrantes & Socinani eademque {†}ab ipsis doceri videbis. Dixerat Walaeus Sp. lumine opus esse, ridet ea Episcopius, & falsis sarcasmis exsibilat. Sic alicubi Joh. Stoinski Caetus Racoviensis minister auxilium caeleste accedere fatetur, quo intelligantur rite S. Scr. novas autem qualitates creari, seu produci, non est necesse inquit. Jam supra audivimus, quid Amyraldus de hac Thesi, quid Amesius: quorum ille ista posita Pelagianos vicisse, alter de ea unice disceptari asserit. Quid ego sententiam, exponant, quibuscum mihi eadem est sententia, Reformatorum Theologi.
units.tr: 6. I have more. Our author denies every internal inspiration and every immediate operation of the Spirit, and it cannot be that this does not follow of its own accord from what he puts forward here: minds are not illuminated by the infusion of new light. But 7. this must not be passed over: this error is taught in plain terms by Velthuysen, a senior not only of the Church of which Wolzogius is the minister, but a man who keeps a mind tenacious of orthodoxy, so that he is safe in his own innocence, according to Wolzogius's judgment. Yet Velthuysen so grossly, so shamefully Pelagianizes here that Pelagius himself could not have put it more plainly. He says: the mind can conceive only one kind of light. The knowledge of the regenerate and of the unregenerate concerning the things and mysteries of faith does not differ in respect of light, nor is their knowledge a different kind of knowledge. So says the Senior of the Reformed Church. Grace, which profits for saving knowledge, is not light, NB, and does not insert new light into us or into Scripture. Likewise, men cannot know the mysteries of faith because they are unwilling, and because they will never be willing without the grace of God; not because they lack in themselves the principles of knowledge and the faculty of knowing by which the things set out in Scripture are only grasped and understood, so that they need new principles or a new faculty, but because the natural man is so led by the affections of the flesh, etc. Let this second thesis, which I thought necessary to examine and refute, stand as follows: new light is not infused into our minds, but everything shines in Scripture, and this must be said when the discussion concerns not the revelation of truth but the constitution of the mind that receives the truth. I say that it is false, heterodox, Pelagian and Socinian. Compare the Remonstrants and the Socinians, and you will see that these things are taught by them. Walaeus had said that the Spirit's light is needed; Episcopius laughs at this and hisses at it with false sarcasms. So too somewhere John Stoinski, minister of the Racovian Synod, confesses that heavenly help must come in so that the Holy Scriptures may be rightly understood, but, he says, it is not necessary that new qualities be created or produced. We have already heard above what Amyraut and Amesius thought about this thesis: the former asserts that, once this is laid down, the Pelagians have won, and the latter asserts that the dispute is about this alone. As for my own view, let the Reformed theologians set it out, since their view is the same as mine.

units.la: Et s. novum lumen infusum ab ipsis agnitum videbis. Sic Hoornbeekius Necessario requiritur interna Sp. S. illuminatio & institutio Act. VIII. 31. XVI. 14. nempe, Deus cum verbo suo ulterius penetrat in hominis animum; & Spiritus sui efficacia creat ibi, in mediis adeo tenebris (2. Cor. IV. 6. 1. Cor IV 5. Joh. 1. 5.) principium caeleste novi ac salutaris luminis. Quod est quasi spiritualem facem introducere, qua divinam lucem animus concipit & calorem, quo caelitus inardescat. Luc. XXIV. 32. Rident ista Remonstrantes, & quot-quot conversionem ex nobis, solo verbo adjutis, derivant, non ex Deo & singulari operatione Spiritus: sed male. Episcopius, in judicio de controversia Anabaptistarum, de ordinario medio conversionis Oper. Part. II. Calvinisticum dicit pag. 375. statuere quod homo sit ineptus ad sensum verbi intellectu capiendum, & propterea peculiarem etiam internam inspirationem & operationem Dei accedere oportere, quae hominem ad id idoneum reddat & in hominis intellectu & voluntate sensum illum efficaciter exprimat, infundat aut inspiret. adde pag. 372. & paulo post ait Hoornbeek. Auctor & causa illumina-tionis, quemadmodum jam indicavimus, solus est Deus Ps. cxix. 8. Jes. L. 4. 5. per Verbum Act. xxvi. 17. 18. Rom. I. 17. x. 15. Eph. iii. 9. 2. Tim. i. 19. 2. Cor. iv. 4. &c. & per Spiritum Joh. xvi. 13. Eph. i. 17. Hebr. vi. 4. etenim ab eo solo est veritas credenda; & NB lumen internum, quo videri ac percipi illa potest. 1. Tim. iii. 16. imo talis est illuminatio, ut non solis gradibus, sed, contrarium licet docente Velthuisen, tota specie differat ab ea quae unquam est in non electis, in reprobis. Elevari possunt, sic Tuissus, potentiae naturales ad objectum aliquod supernaturale per habitus quosdam supernaturales, verum potentiarum novarum, quae ipsis inhaerant, capaces omnino non sunt. Habitus supernaturalis intellectum afficiens habet se per modum luminis supernaturalis. Hos autem habitus supernaturales vereor ut admittant adversarii. Splendide & magnificè quidem de ea loquuntur, imo non minori apparatu, quam ipse Wolzogius, eo tamen non contentus Subtilissimus disputator, sic pergit, Gratiam istam supernaturalem quam praedicant, & supra Paradisum efferunt, negant haberi per modum NB infusionis, ut ante hac accepimus ex Arminio, suffragante Corvino; eundem in modum noster Wolzogius, prae-dicat alibi magnifica de Spiritus operatione, sed hic novum in mentem lumen NB infundi negat; pergat jam Tuissus, unde fit, ut infra naturam eam abjiciant, si negant nobis esse inhaerentem; sin inhaerere velint, nec tamen infundi; sequitur nihil omnino eo notari praeter potentiam aliquam naturalem. Nec aliter removeri possunt, quae removenda concedunt impedimenta, nisi per infusum lumen novum; si enim quis impedimenta dixerit, quae mortuum a vitae operatio-nibus, aut caecum a videndo impediant, non aliter sane quam novae vitae infusione & videndi facultatis restitutione, medicinam parari posse ultra largiri debet. Talis autem naturalis homo est & caecus & mortuus spiritualiter: Nec a mortis labe immunis intellectus somniari potest, nisi ab eo qui moribun-dum sed vivum tamen & vitam alicubi palam demonstrantem mortuum finxerit. Non ita ludit Sa-cra Pagina. Jmo tanta hujus veritatis vis est, ut & Pontificiis excidat aliquando, sic Bellarminus Jesui-ta, Omnes nostrae conciones, sed omnia alia nostra signa & prodigia non sufficiunt, ut fidem nostram Ethni-cis & haereticis persuadeamus; nisi Deus ipse Doctor acce-dat, & mentem eorum hoc divino lumine illustret -- Pe-lagiani affirmare non dubitabunt, nos isto lumine non in-digere usque adeo. Hoc est lumen illud, ait Rivetus, quod requirebat Lutherus, sine quo ne jota quidem unum videri possit in Scripturis, id est ea perspicientia quae salutaris est, merito censuit: & Spiritum Sanctum, qui lumen illud indat, inditumque eliciat, excitet, applicetque, esse necessarium docuit, ad totam Scripturam & quamlibet ejus partem intelligendam. Stapletonus, qui alibi dictum Lutheri calumniatur, Relect. Princip. fid. controv. 4. Q. 1. Art. 2. Intellectus, inquit, ut propositae veritati ex fide assentia-tur, induci non potest absque fidei dono, & lumine divinitus infuso, est conclusio de fide, non solum contra Pelagianos veteres, sed & contra quosdam Scholasticos recentiores Durand. Biel. &c.
units.tr: And you will see that they acknowledge a new light infused in the mind. Thus Hoornbeek: The internal illumination and instruction of the Holy Spirit is necessarily required (Acts 8:31; 16:14), namely, that God, together with his word, penetrates further into the mind of man, and by the efficacy of his Spirit creates there, even amid such darkness, the heavenly beginning of a new and saving light (2 Cor. 4:6; 1 Cor. 4:5; John 1:5), which is like introducing a spiritual torch, by which the mind takes in the divine light and a warmth by which it is kindled from heaven. Luke 24:32. The Remonstrants laugh at these things, and all who derive conversion from us, aided only by the word, and not from God and the singular operation of the Spirit; but they are wrong. Episcopius, in his judgment on the controversy with the Anabaptists, on the ordinary means of conversion, Works, Part II, p. 375, says that the Calvinists hold that man is unfit to grasp the sense of the word by understanding, and that therefore a peculiar internal inspiration and operation of God must come in, which makes man suitable for this and effectively expresses, pours in or breathes that sense into his understanding and will. Add p. 372, and a little later he says Hoornbeek: The author and cause of this illumination, as we have already indicated, is God alone (Ps. 119:8; Isa. 50:4–5), through the Word (Acts 26:17–18; Rom. 1:17; 10:15; Eph. 3:9; 2 Tim. 1:19; 2 Cor. 4:4, etc.), and through the Spirit (John 16:13; Eph. 1:17; Heb. 6:4), for the truth to be believed comes from him alone; and NB the inner light by which it can be seen and perceived (1 Tim. 3:16). Indeed, this illumination is such that it differs not merely by degrees, but, although Velthuysen teaches otherwise, in its whole kind from that which is ever found in the non-elect, in the reprobate. The natural powers, says Tuissus, can be raised to some supernatural object through certain supernatural habits, but they are altogether incapable of new powers inhering in them. A supernatural habit affecting the understanding has itself in the manner of a supernatural light. But I fear that our opponents will not admit these supernatural habits. They speak splendidly and magnificently of it, indeed with no less display than Wolzogen himself; yet the most subtle disputant, not content with this, goes on thus: This supernatural grace which they proclaim, and extol above Paradise, they deny is had by way of NB infusion, as we heard earlier from Arminius, with the support of Corvinus. In the same way our Wolzogen, in other places, preaches magnificent things about the operation of the Spirit, but here he denies that a new light is NB infused into the mind. Let Tuissus go on: Hence it follows that if they deny it is inherent in us, they cast down that grace below nature; but if they want it to be inherent and yet not infused, it follows that nothing at all is signified by it beyond some natural power. Nor can the hindrances which they concede must be removed be removed otherwise than by an infused new light. For if someone should call hindrances those things which keep a dead man from the operations of life, or a blind man from seeing, he must surely concede that a remedy cannot be provided otherwise than by the infusion of a new life and the restoration of the faculty of sight. Now such a natural man is both blind and dead spiritually; nor can the understanding be imagined free from the stain of death, unless one has pictured it dead, as one who is dying but still alive and somewhere plainly showing life. Holy Scripture does not play so. Indeed, the force of this truth is so great that it sometimes escapes even the Papists; thus Bellarmine the Jesuit: All our sermons, and all our other signs and wonders, do not suffice to persuade pagans and heretics of our faith, unless God himself as teacher comes and illumines their mind with this divine light... The Pelagians will not hesitate to affirm that we do not so much need that light. This is the light, says Rivet, which Luther required, without which not even one jot can be seen in the Scriptures, that is, that perspicacity which is saving; he rightly judged so; and he taught that the Holy Spirit, who pours in that light and, having poured it in, draws it out, stirs it up and applies it, is necessary for understanding the whole of Scripture and any part of it whatever. Stapleton, who elsewhere slanders Luther's saying, Relectio of the Principles of the Faith, Controversy 4, Q. 1, Art. 2, says: The understanding cannot be induced to assent to a proposed truth from faith without the gift of faith and a light divinely infused; this is a conclusion of faith, held not only against the ancient Pelagians but also against certain more recent Scholastics, Durand, Biel, etc.

units.la: 3. Addunt ne unicum quidem Jota salutariter, verè spiritualiter intelligi posse, sine infuso illo lu-mine. Hoc de Luthero refert & probat Rivetus. Et revera, si actus omnes verè spirituales provenire aliunde, quam ex principio infuso spirituali & su-pernaturali non possunt, procul omni dubio, om-nis illa, quæ ab intellectu producitur operatio, intel-lectio verè spiritualis, oriri etiam non potest, nisi ex habituali illo, quod in intellectu est, eumque spiritualiter quasi vivificat, lumine, eliciatur: sed hac de re postea latius.
units.tr: 3. They add that not even one jot can be understood truly and savingly, or spiritually, without that infused light. Rivetus reports and proves this of Luther. And indeed, if all truly spiritual acts cannot arise from any source other than a spiritual and supernatural infused principle, then undoubtedly every operation produced by the intellect, including every truly spiritual understanding, cannot arise except by being drawn out by that habitual light which is in the intellect and quasi-vivifies it spiritually. But more on this matter later.

units.la: 4. Hinc est, quod, non tam pro naturalis scien-tiæ, quam Spiritus ejusque luminis, majori aut mi-nori copia, majores aut minores in Scripturæ vera intellectione profectus fieri statuant. Homo vetus (verba sunt Polani) seu animalis non potest, capere ea quæ sunt Sp. Dei: Novus in tantum capit, in quantum renovatus est. Nemo prophetias, sic Paræus, intelligere potest absque Spiritu, quo sunt conscriptæ. Hinc NB tantum quisque de sensu Scripturarum assequitur, quantum de Spiritu qui eas inspiravit participat. Nescio igi- tur quem genium sapiant Pelagianumne, an pure naturalem, & mundanum, quæ alibi Medicus, verè sutor ultra crepidam, sic ille, Philosophia in plurimis tantum talemque usum præstat ad assequendum quid Spiritus S. loquatur & doceat in Scriptura, ut quo quis magis artibus & disciplinis ratione & usu repertis instructior accedat ad Scripturæ lectionem, eo paratior est, ad capiendos maximos fructus ex illius lectione: & frustra se fatigabit -- qui omnia ex Scripturæ revelatione eruere nititur. Nec abluit Wolzogius. Nam quos limites, sic ille p. 202 de suo adversario, ponit Interpreti suo, quem pro rerum tantum cognitione quam est, adeptus plus minusve in interpretando posse statuit, non moveo. Verum est, tam signorum quam rerum notitia multum conducit ad feliciorem Scripturæ scrutationem, nec tamen ad Philosophos ea proprie pertinet, aut ex Philosophia arcessenda, ut somniat Medicus, longè aliter summus Philosophus simul & Theologus Bisterfeldius. Utraque, ait ille, rerum puta & verborum notitia, diligenti ac judiciosa collatione ex ipsismet sacris literis sufficienter hauriri potest Ps. xix. 8. cxix. 30. Proverb. 1. 4. Mat. xi. 26. 1. Cor. 1. 26. Nec contrarium evincunt, quæ profert Medicus, furtum enim & odium, vindicta publica quid sit & privata ex sacris disci non posse quis credat? Sed talia habet, quæ tractant res momento-sas & forte necessarias ad salutem, tamen obscurissima sunt, & ex Scriptura lumen accipere non possunt. Quam imprudenter dixit Apostolus Scripturas sapientes reddere nos posse ad salutem 1. Tim. iii. Quare David, PhiloPhilosophia insalutatâ, insipientes sapientes ex Scrip-tura evadere posse dixerit, rogetur Medicus. Egregiam vero Theologiam! etiam ad salutem necessaria obscurissima sunt & ex Scriptura lumen accipere non possunt, refragantibus licet Theologis & Confessionibus quotquot sunt Reformatis. Deinde conducat quantum potest rerum & verborum praerequisita cognitio, praeterquam, quod ex ipsa Scriptura sufficienter hauriatur, etiam ea applicari non potest, nisi postquam, & in quantum dicto quis illustratus est lumine. Optimè ista exequitur Amyraldus, ut in Spiritus, sicille, aequali mensura, qui Hebraici Graecique sermonis ita peritus est, ut ex ipsis fontibus, quod dici solet, haurire possit; aliquanto certior suae cognitionis erit, quam qui cogitur uti translatione quantumvis accurata. Item in pari copia Spiritus qui utitur translatione accuratiore quam qui minus accurata. Vice versa, in objecti propositione pari & impari constitutione facultatis, firmitas assensus non omnino par esse potest. Nam NB qui majorem Spiritus copiam est adeptus, rem clarius videbit, quam qui minorem, tametsi uterque pari linguarum peritia praeditus sit. Quin tanta est in constitutione facultatis posita vis, ut qui translatione uti cogitur, etsi minus accurata, multo majore illustrabitur divinitatis illius, tam in tota Scriptura, quam in cujusvis enunciationis sensu, evidentia, quam qui linguarum intelligentia pollet, multis vero prae altero partibus defi-tur a Spiritu facultatem ipsam illuminante. Utique cum tanta simus ab ortu nostro caligine circumfusi, ut praestantissimi oculatissimique viri sint aperte ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φέγγος ἔχει τὸ καθ' ἡμέραν, ὅτ[?] ἡ ἡμετέρας ψυχῆς ἡ νοῦν ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων[?]. eam laudem nobis, seu nostrae signorum rerumque ex natura acquisitae cognitioni, arrogare falso nec Deo ejusque illuminationi adimere nisi per summum nefas nequimus. Est enim objectum ita sublime ut à mente nostra perfectè comprehendi nequeat, non etiamsi illa careret omni labe. Tantæ sc. rei, creaturæ modus capax non est. Ꝺeo præclarè Petrus de mysteriis Religionis Christianæ verba faciens εἰς ἃ[?], inquit, ἐπιθυμοῦσιν οἱ ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι. Quapropter priusquam lux illa Spiritus assulserit, in summa nostri & rerum quæ ad salutem nostram spectant ignoratione versantibus, vis illa ab ipso Deo deflυxisse censenda est, cujus ope ea comprehendimus quæ sublimitate & excellentia ἡ αὐτὸν θεῖκὸν τῶν μαθημάτων infinito intervallo supereminent. Denique ad eam notitiam accessio magna fieri debet ex nostri comparatione cum iis qui adhuc in nativa omnium ignorantia jacent. Hic enim valet quod Apostolus ait; τὶς σὲ διακρίνει τὶ ἔχεις ὃ οὐχ ἔλαβες. Quum natura nos omnes ex eodem luto corrupto cruentoque finxerit, quæ res labes istas penitus inhærentes eluisse ac novam NB quandam formam in nos introduxisse potis est, nisi supra naturam ipsam constituta? Ꝺd vero multo fiet apertius si reputemus animo quam præstanti ingenio in omni alio rerum genere, quam sagaci prudentia, quam acribus oculis præditi sint in rebus humanis cernendis, plerique eorum quos in tanta luce Euangelii non caligare modo, sed prorsus cæcutire videmus. Diuinam vim qua tam certo perspeximus quæ ne per nebulam quidem à viris cæteroquin maximis perspiciuntur, auxilio divino suppeditatam esse arbitrari par est. Scriptura etiam fidem appellat donum Dei: & testatur nobis gratuito datum esse, ut credamus: & oculos mentis illuminatos nobis obtingere ait a Spiritu revelationis: & quod credimus id tribuit τῇ δωρεᾷ τῆς κρατεως[?] ἰσχύος τῆς Θεοῦ[?]: & credentes appellat τῆς Θεοῦ διδάκτας[?], & quid non? Quod necessaria etiam ad salutem obscurissima dicat, verum est, respectu eorum qui pereunt, nam si Euangelium nostrum tectum est, iis qui pereunt tectum est, non autem propterea, quod, uti Medicus somniat, ex Philosophia solum signorum rerumque notitiam sibi non acquisiuerit, sed quod, omni licet naturali sapientia imbuti & onusti, Spirituali isto careant lumine & à Spiritu intus reve-lante & docente non ducantur; quo non illuminante, in tenebris versatur cæcus & excæcatus peccator, & per suam istam cæcitatem, cum voluntatis natura-li etiam perversitate junctam, non potest non er-rare. Dicam potius verbis gravissimi Theologi, Pe-lagianorum Mallei, Lucerna, inquit ille, fateor est pedibus nostris verbum Dei & quotquot ad salutem pro-movendam conducunt aperte satis in Scripturis tradun-tur: quorum tamen omnium salutaris agnitio atque in-terpretatio non tam hominis ingenio (adde quæ hominis ingenio ex natura eliciuntur) quam Sancti Spiritus illu-minatione deputanda est, pro cujus, NB non pro majori aut minori Philosophiæ notitia, Spiritus sc. varia dispensatione aut denegatione nunc infirmitati hominis succurritur, ut discernat ea quæ Dei sunt, nunc in tenebris & mentis suæ caligine fædum in modum errare permitti-tur. Vides, Spiritus lumine non dispensato & in quan-tum non dispensato, errat necessario quicunque sit, sit licet Philosophus. Philosophiæ operam minister-rialem nullo modo sperno, nec spernere à præcep-toribus doctus sum, acuat illa facultatem naturalem, Hagaris instar, sic Lutherus ejus opem jam dudum considerasse tritum est, serviat Sacræ Theologiæ: verum omnem aut primam in explicanda Scriptura provinciam sustinendo impar est, in subjecto, sit licet caput Philosophotaton, Spiritus lumen du-ctusque ita requiruntur, ut absque iis omnis huma-na sapientia nihil valeat, Scripturas scrutetur licet, qui iis imbutus est. Loquantur venerandi senes. sic Bucerus, alias Philosophiam tantopere laudans ali-bi, Quid jam possit satis magnificum de ea, Scripturæ sc. doctrina dici, qua hæc, beata sc. in Dei agnitione veroque cultu consistens, vita traditur? Omnes Phi-losophi id conati quidem sunt, at solæ arcanæ literæ præ-stitesiterunt: Sed sunt & hæ mortuæ, nihilque docere possunt quum deest Spiritus Christi, qui unus in omnem veritatem inducit. Quare quod hic Psaltes de divina lege encomium cecinit, de ea, ut a mentibus Spiritu superno donatis percipitur, intelligendum est, non ut scripto tantum comprehenditur. Hic autem ubi Spiritus adest, effari non potest, quantum frugis optimæ adferat diligens & sedula Scripturarum & lectio & excussio: ut non injuria Paulus suum Timotheum tantopere incumbere illi voluerit, tantumque fructuum promiserit.
units.tr: 4. Hence they hold that greater or lesser progress in the true understanding of Scripture comes not so much from natural knowledge as from the Spirit and his light, in greater or lesser measure. The old man (these are Polanus's words), that is, the natural or animal man, cannot grasp the things that are of the Spirit of God; the new man grasps them insofar as he has been renewed. No one, so Paraeus says, can understand the prophecies without the Spirit by whom they were written. Hence NB each person grasps of the sense of Scripture only as much as he partakes of the Spirit who inspired it. I do not know, therefore, what spirit they savour of, whether Pelagian or purely natural and worldly, as the Physician (a cobbler going beyond his last, as he says elsewhere) puts it: philosophy contributes, in most matters and only to such a degree, to grasping what the Holy Spirit says and teaches in Scripture, so that the more someone comes to the reading of Scripture equipped with the arts and disciplines discovered by reason and practice, the more prepared he is to gather the greatest fruits from its reading; and in vain will he weary himself who tries to draw everything out of the revelation of Scripture. Nor does Wolzogen wash his hands of it. As to the limits which, as he says on p. 202 concerning his opponent, he sets for his interpreter, whom he holds able to interpret more or less according to how much knowledge of things he has acquired, I do not dispute. It is true that knowledge of both signs and things greatly contributes to a happier examination of Scripture, yet it does not properly belong to the philosophers, nor is it to be drawn from philosophy, as the Physician dreams; far otherwise the most eminent philosopher and theologian at once, Bisterfeld. Both, he says, namely knowledge of things and of words, can be sufficiently drawn from the sacred letters themselves by diligent and judicious comparison (Ps. 19:8; 119:30; Prov. 1:4; Matt. 11:26; 1 Cor. 1:26). Nor do the things the Physician brings forward prove the contrary, for who could believe that theft and hatred, and what public and private vengeance is, cannot be learned from the sacred books? But he has such things as deal with weighty matters, perhaps necessary for salvation, which nevertheless are most obscure and cannot receive light from Scripture. How imprudently the Apostle said that the Scriptures can make us wise unto salvation (2 Tim. 3). Let the Physician be asked why David, without philosophy, could say that the foolish can become wise through Scripture. What an outstanding theology! Even the things necessary for salvation are most obscure and cannot receive light from Scripture, though the theologians and all the confessions of the Reformed object. Further, however much the prior knowledge of things and words may help, apart from the fact that it is sufficiently drawn from Scripture itself, it cannot be applied unless and only so far as one has been illuminated by the light of the word. Amyraldus carries this out admirably: a person who, with an equal measure of the Spirit, is so skilled in the Hebrew and Greek language that he can draw from the very sources, as they say, will be somewhat more certain of his knowledge than one who is forced to use a translation, however accurate. Likewise, with an equal measure of the Spirit, one who uses a more accurate translation [is more certain] than one who uses a less accurate one. Conversely, with an equal or unequal constitution of the faculty in the proposition of the object, the firmness of assent cannot be altogether equal. For NB the one who has obtained the greater measure of the Spirit will see the matter more clearly than the one who has the lesser, although both are endowed with equal skill in languages. Indeed, so great is the power placed in the constitution of the faculty, that one who is forced to use a translation, though less accurate, will be illuminated by a far greater evidence of that divinity, both in the whole of Scripture and in the sense of any statement, than one who excels in knowledge of the languages, but who in many respects is lacking to the other, the faculty itself being illuminated by the Spirit. Since we are so surrounded by darkness from our birth, that even the most excellent and sharp-sighted men are, as Aristotle says, [ὥσπερ τὰ τῶν νυκτερίδων ὄμματα πρὸς τὸ φῶς τὸ μεθ' ἡμέραν ἔχει, οὕτως καὶ ἡ τῆς ψυχῆς ἡμῶν διάνοια πρὸς τὰ τῇ φύσει φανερώτατα πάντων], we cannot ascribe that praise to ourselves falsely, or to our knowledge of signs and things acquired from nature, nor take it from God and his illumination, except by the greatest wickedness. For the object is so sublime that it cannot be perfectly comprehended by our mind, even if that mind were free from every stain. The capacity of a creature is not equal to so great a thing. Peter, speaking excellently of the mysteries of the Christian religion, says [εἰς ἃ ἐπιθυμοῦσιν ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι], "into which the angels desire to look." Therefore, before that light of the Spirit has shone upon us, who dwell in the complete ignorance of ourselves and of the things that pertain to our salvation, that power by which we comprehend those things which surpass all the mathematical sciences by an infinite interval in sublimity and excellence must be judged to have flowed from God himself. Finally, great addition must be made to that knowledge by comparing ourselves with those who still lie in the native ignorance of all things. For what the Apostle says applies here: [τίς σε διακρίνει; τί δὲ ἔχεις ὃ οὐκ ἔλαβες;] "Who makes you to differ? And what do you have that you did not receive?" Since nature has fashioned us all from the same corrupt and bloody clay, can anything but what is set above nature itself wash away those stains that cling so deeply and introduce a new NB form into us? And this will become much clearer if we reflect in our minds with what outstanding talent, in every other kind of thing, with what shrewd prudence, with what keen eyes most of those men are endowed in discerning human affairs, whom we see not merely dimly seeing, but altogether blind in the midst of such light of the Gospel. It is right to think that the divine power by which we have so clearly perceived things which, even through a mist, are not perceived by men otherwise very great, has been supplied by divine help. Scripture also calls faith a gift of God, and testifies that it has been given to us freely that we may believe; and it says that the eyes of the mind are illuminated for us by the Spirit of revelation; and what we believe it attributes [τῇ δωρεᾷ τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος τοῦ Θεοῦ] to the gift of the might of God's strength; and it calls believers [θεοδίδακτοι] taught by God, and what not? That it says the most obscure things are necessary even for salvation is true with respect to those who perish; for if our Gospel is hidden, it is hidden from those who perish. But this is not because, as the Physician dreams, they have not acquired for themselves a knowledge of signs and things from philosophy alone, but because, though steeped in and loaded with all natural wisdom, they lack that spiritual light and are not led by the Spirit teaching and speaking within them; without whose illumination the blind and blinded sinner lives in darkness, and through this blindness, joined also with the perversity of his natural will, he cannot but err. I would rather say in the words of a most weighty theologian, the hammer of the Pelagians: Lamp, he says, I grant that the word of God and whatever contributes to promoting salvation are set forth quite plainly in the Scriptures; yet the saving acknowledgement and interpretation of all these things must be attributed not so much to the ingenuity of man (add what is drawn from man's ingenuity by nature) as to the illumination of the Holy Spirit, by whose NB not by a greater or lesser knowledge of philosophy, that is, the Spirit's varied dispensation or denial, now help is given to human weakness, so that it discerns the things that are of God, and now it is permitted to err foully in darkness and the fog of its own mind. You see, the Spirit's light not dispensed, and insofar as it is not dispensed, whoever he is, even if he is a philosopher, necessarily errs. I by no means despise philosophy as a handmaid, nor was I taught to despise it by my teachers; let it sharpen the natural faculty, as Hagar did, as Luther long ago observed, as is commonly known; let it serve sacred theology. But philosophy, even if it is the chief of philosophers, is by no means equal to undertaking the whole or first task in explaining Scripture; in the subject, the light and guidance of the Spirit are so required that without them all human wisdom is worth nothing, even if he who is steeped in it searches the Scriptures. Let the venerable elders speak. Thus Bucer, who elsewhere praises philosophy so highly. What can be said that is grand enough about the doctrine of Scripture, which hands down this life, the blessed life consisting in the knowledge of God and true worship? All philosophers have indeed attempted this, but the hidden letters alone have accomplished it. Yet these too are dead and can teach nothing when the Spirit of Christ, who alone leads into all truth, is lacking. Therefore, what the Psalmist sang in praise of the divine law must be understood of it as it is perceived by minds endowed with the superior Spirit, and not merely as it is comprehended in writing. Where the Spirit is present, however, it cannot be told how much excellent fruit the diligent and earnest reading and searching of the Scriptures brings; so that Paul was not wrong to want his Timothy to labor so earnestly at it, and promised such fruits.

units.la: At vero NB nullis id rationibus ita ut experimento percipi potest: quan-quam pio homini, vel præsens Psaltis encomium, aut Pauli elogium quod adduximus, vel Moscheh testimonium Deut. iv. 6. satis probent nullum esse scripti genus quod vel dignitate, vel fructu ulla ex parte divinæ Scripturæ, quam jure vocamus, conferri queat.
units.tr: Indeed NB this cannot be perceived by any arguments as it can by experience; yet to a godly man the Psalmist's present praise, or the testimony of Paul which we have adduced, or the witness of Moses in Deut. 4:6, sufficiently prove that there is no kind of writing which can in any respect be compared with Holy Scripture, which we rightly call divine, either in dignity or in fruit.

units.la: Sed, ut dixi, NB experientia hic omni ratione potior est: ea pios animos ita Scripturæ arcanæ de Deo nostro ubique præclare testanti, & de ejus nos voluntate erudienti addicit, sic reddit affectos, ut plane comparatos se sentiant uti de se Vates in sequentibus canit. Desiderabilia præ auro &c. verf. 11 & 12. Sentiunt siquidem hi quam adversetur huic felicitati omnis naturæ nostræ sensus & conatus. Nihil siquidem est quod Dei apertius & potentius admoneat, judiciorum & operum ejus rationem plenius explicet, quam Sacræ Scripturæ: non tamen quibusvis, sed timentibus Deum, & Spiritu cælesti præditis. Expertus sum &c. Finge tibi aliquos, qui ratione naturali utuntur tanquam principio, ad maximam, quæ per naturam acquiri potest, venisse verborum rerumque cognitionem, & quid in Scripturæ intellectione præstituri sint, quoniam Theologi, te scilicet autocrato- rice id dictante, admodum falluntur & nimium sibi assumunt, cum hujusmodi controversias, quomodo sc. in Adamo omnes peccasse, concupiscentia peccatum dici queat, determinare volunt quamvis si ullum, hoc saltem ex sacris, à Theologis unicè expediendum negotium judicaturus sit omnis cui sanum sinciput non deerit, quoniam autem Theologi nimium sibi assumunt, (Medico Theologos inter & Philosophos judice) audiatur aliquis non ex fæce Theologorum aut ex gregariis Philosophis, sed vir qui summus audiit hactenus & incomparabilis Philosophus, qui etiam præjudicia deponere, rationes ponderare didicerat & docuit Baco Verulamius, qui quantus Heereboor-bio aliisque fuerit, longum foret enarrare, sic ille ad calcem Tractatus, quem de Augmentatione Scientiarum inscripsit, ad Jacobum Regem. Restat adhuc Theologia Sacra, sive inspirata. Veruntamen si eam tractare pergamus, exeundum nobis, intrandum putat Medicus pro sua sc. Philosophica aut Medica religione, è navicula rationis humanæ. Neque enim sufficient amplius Stellæ Philosophiæ, quæ hactenus præcipue nobis affulserunt. Itaque par foret, sic modestè summus Philosophus, silentium quoque in hac re colere. Et, tantummodo de modo informationis dum tractat, exempla subjungere, præcepta dare detrectat. Sed Theologis relinquemus. Qui nostro Palæmone judice nimium sibi assumunt, etiam, quomodo in Adamo omnes peccasse, quomodo concupiscentia peccatum dici queat, determinare cum volunt; fungi sc. isti Theologi. Pudeat te immodestum, superbum caput! pergat Verulamius, Prærogativa Dei totum hominem complectitur: nec minus ad rationem, quam ad voluntatem humanam extenditur: ut homo scilicet in universum se abneget & accedat Deo. Quare, sicut legi divinæ obedire tenemur, licet reluctetur voluntas, ita & verbo Dei fidem habere, licet reluctetur ratio. Etenim, si ea duntaxat credamus, quæ sunt rationi nostræ consentanea, rebus assentimur non auctori. Quæ verba ita placuere Heidano, ut ea adoptaverit & sua fecerit. Et quamvis Theologos spernat Medicus, producam eorum verba ut videat Aphilosophos non esse quos contu-melia afficit. Heidanus docet fidei esse rationi praescri-bere, & id facere, ut ne sit opus ratione. Atqui tan-tum abest ut rationi aliqua praerogativa hic debeatur, ut contra Christus gratias agat Patri, quod absconderit hæc ab intelligentibus & sapientibus, & revelarit νηπίοις in-fantibus. Matth. xi.25. Unde & Discipulis suis dixit ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε, ἢ γίνησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία, οὐ μὴ εἰσελθητε εἰς βασιλείαν θεοῦ Matth. XVIII. 3. Vult plane hos instar infantium suscipere Regnum Dei. Quin Deus praeteritis sapientibus, potentibus & nobilibus secundum carnem, quae stulta sunt mundi & infirma, & ignobilia & contemtibilia, & ea quae non sunt, elegit, ut ea quae sunt aboleret, uti ne gloriatur ulla caro coram eo I. Cor. I. 27. 28. Neque tan-tum injuria fit Deo, sed & homini ipsi, cum talis illi ἱκανόυς[?] adscribitur, cui nullo modo par est, & quam sustinere non potest. Cum enim ipsa ratio per peccatum ob-tenebrata sit, quod horrenda illa ignorantiae profunditas, cum qua mundum istum ingredimur, testatur, & quae nos a pueritia obsidet, certe si lumen quod in nobis est tenebrae sunt, ipsae tenebrae quantae erunt? Mat. VI.23. Ex ista densissima tenebrarum caligine omnis error huma-nae vitae proficiscitur, qui omnes filios Adam tenebroso quodam sinu suscipit: unde cum multis praejudiciis à veri cognitione avertamur, nunquam iis liberari possimus, nisi ab illo illuminemur, qui est lux Mundi, & via & veritas & vita, Joh. XIV At quomodo tenebrae judi-cent de luce & lumine? Et quomodo sapientiam Dei pos-set justificare homo, cui illa est stultitia? Et quomodo verbo crucis aedificari ad salutem posset, qui ad illud im-pingit & offendiculum patitur? Quis NB à tam stulto Judice rectam sententiam expectet. Unde quo quis ma-jorem, audi Medice, sapientiam praefert, & majore ratione niti videtur, eo iniquior Euangelio reperitur, ni-mirum non capit animalis homo ea quae sunt Sp. Dei: stultitia siquidem illi sunt, nec potest cognoscere, eo quod spirituaspiritualiter dijudicantur. 1. Cor. 11. 14. Quare monet Apostolus 1. Cor. 111. 18. ut ne quis se ipsum fallat: si quis videtur sibi sapiens esse inter vos in seculo hoc, stul-tus fiat, ut reddatur sapiens. Etenim sapientia hujus Mundi stultitia est apud Deum. Quid circa Mysteria & à mero beneplacito pendentia ratio sibi arrogare possit? non-ne plane intellectus noster captivandus & subjiciendus Deo? An forte quæ aliter homini videtur, & ratio secus de iis quæ revelata sunt judicat, alium sibi Deum & aliam voluntatem ejus finget? Et tu bone vir tantum rationi, tantum Philosophiæ tuæ tribues? ut etiam res momentosas & forte ad salutem necessarias etiam ob-scurissimas dicas & ex Scriptura lumen accipere non posse. Divam Philosophiam de iis consulendam: tibi for-san evenit, quod Boëthius fingit, hæc tecum im-mediatè egit & dictavit ista oracula. Hæc feres Wol-zogi, hunc Virum Orthodoxias tenacem animum gerere scribes, ipse plane contrarium sentire videris, ita te de fundamentalibus loquentem audivimus, ut absque omni cura & industria (quippe tanta per-spicuitate tradita quæ omnem legenti dubitatio-nem, primo statim intuitu, eximat) percipi posse putes, sicuti vidimus Libro priori hæc jam concilia si potes: Quid ego velim pro me dicat Nobilissimus Sadeel, sic ille at nos de Theologia ex principiis Thologicis disputandum esse, ex ipsa Theologia didicimus, & ita faciendum esse, vel ex ipsa analytica disciplina affirma-mus, qua vetat μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος [?] & vagari ex-tra orbem illius scientiæ de qua disserendum susceperis. Porro cum Theologia sit supra omnes scientias, eam subjici principiis Philosophicis non ineptum modo verum etiam iniquissimum est atque indignilsimum. Tantum abest ut ex Scriptura etiam quæ necessaria sunt, lumen non accipere non solum non possint sed & ex Philosophia illud expectare debeant. Nec enim opus habere divinam Scripturam humana sapientia rectè, ex Sadeelis judicio, dixit Chrysostomus, qui etiam ait Magnum esse periculum res fidei committere humanis rationibus. In Scriptura Sacra enim, Augustino teste, quid tenendum & quid fugiendum sit, plenè invenitur. Ut autem agnoscat Medicus quantum differat à viris Theologis, unum adhuc audiat Musculum graviter hoc negotium & pie per-tractantem. Quid ergo, ait, hic relinquitur viribus rationis in cognoscendis rebus Christianæ fidei? scilicet duobus verbis, velut fulminibus, prosternitur omnis conatus sapientum huius mundi in rebus Dei. Nec potest, inquit, cognoscere. Ergo ubi animalis homo conatur ad cognitionem pertingere regni Christi, frustra laborat, ubi de rebus Spiritus disputat, garrit, ubi pronunciat, mentitur, ubi in religione statuit, temerarius est, ubi docet, seducit, ubi sectatores reperit, perdit. Quare? quia non potest cognoscere. Quid igitur expectabimus in fidei Christianæ negotio decisionem animalium? Hæc in Velthusio vera esse, vereor ne nimis aperte videat lector, qui pius est.
