Quia ergo intellectus noster natura sua sicut luminis non est: & præterea tot præjudiciis & erroribus ex singulari dispositione est irretitus; quid aliud est rationis naturalis (& illa, in tam multis, juxta Velthusium principii vices obtinet) nisus, in religionis negotio, quam religiosa quædam insania, imò verius irreligiosa stultitia, & rationale delirium. Et quoniam hic de cognitione eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei loquitur, spi-ritaliter res divinas cognoscere, est eas cognoscere judicio, ductu, & illuminatione Sp. sicut animaliter cognoscere, est NB ex judicio rationis cognoscere. Idem ergo est ac si diceret, animalis homo non potest cognoscere ea quæ sunt Sp. Dei, quoniam non animaliter NB & cum judicio ra-tionis dijudicantur, sed ex instinctu, iudicio, ductuque Spiritus. Et hoc verbo in loco utitur, ut indagationes & scrutinia Philosophorum traducat & rejiciat, doceatque impossibile esse ut hac via perveniatur ad cognitionem eorum quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, eo quod illa non rationis sed Sp. Dei judicio & scrutinio cognoscantur. Video ex Sociniano-rum lacunis haustam exceptionem nobis obtrudi à Medico, ut sic vis istorum locorum enervetur & Reformatorum tela irrita sint adversus Pestilentissimam Hæresin Socini & Pelagii. Objicit sibi locum 1. Cor. 1. 19. 26. & Respondet, id intelligendum tantum de præjudiciis, non de vera cognitione, notandum autem 1. hominem hic ex professo agere adversus Reformatos, qui passim, juxta alia, etiam hoc loco, adversus Socinianos pugnant & Pelagianos, videsis Episcopium aliosque, ipse Paradoxus, quem refutare videri vult Medicus, agit cum adversariis adversus Orthodoxos, hi enim soli ex hisce & similibus rationis humanæ naturæ probant ineptitudinem ad percipienda dijudicandaque ea quæ religionem Christianam spectant. 2. Subdolè agit, dum, reticens optima nostrorum argumenta ex locis magis emphaticis desumta, hoc unicè vellicat. 3. Re ipsa idem statuit cum adversariis, imo cum Paradoxo exercitatore, eo enim utriusque redit evasio, ut negent, hic in veræ sapientiæ præjudicium statui quicquam. Sic Paradoxus, Apostolum non sapientiam veram, sed apparentem designare patet ex scopo. de Præjudiciis, non de vera cognitione, dixit Velthuisen, sic bene inter ipsos convenit dum rixari videri volunt. 4. Nullo modo probat quod dicit; verum est, prejudiciis multos transver-ros agi, veram sapientiam nullibi rejectam esse in sacris: propterea & magni eam facimus, sed in suo genere, præterquam enim, quod frustra plerumque vera prætexatur & jactetur sapientia, non possumus non præjudiciis à veri cognitione, Heidano judice, averti, donec ab illo illuminemur qui est lux mundi. Sapiat, quantum potest homo, naturaliter, aptus nondum est, imo ineptus, qui salutis doctrinam rite percipiat, nisi intus facultas ipsius, indito novo lumine, relevetur & ad percipienda quæ sunt Spiritus Dei adaptetur, hoc volunt nostri, hoc docet Apostolus. Hic per sapientiam intelligit Apostolus quicquid comprehendere potest homo tam naturali ingenii facultate quam usu & literis atque artium scientia adjutus: nam mundi sapientiam Spiritus sapientiæ opponit, proinde quicquid intelligentiæ in hominem cadit absque Spiritus sanĉti illustratione, id sub mundi sapientia continetur. Eam totam dicit infatuatam esse à Deo, hoc est damnatam stultitiæ. Interim tamen notandum est quod non simpliciter damnat Paulus aut naturalem perspicaciam hominis, aut prudentiam usu & experientia collectam, aut cultum ingenii literis comparatum, sed hoc totum NB ad percipiendam spiritualem sapientiam nullius momenti esse asserit. Sic Calvinus, ita ut merito & hunc locum non Theologastris tantum, sed etiam gravissimis Theologis passim in ore esse dicere potuisset Paradoxus, nec facile eorum vim Medicaster quis evitabit aut Philosophaster. Nec est quod miremur, Carnis enim sapientia, inquit Paulus, sic notæ, quæ in Bibliis Junii & Tremellii, nihil certi, ne in suis quidem rebus constituit, nedum ut aliena id est spiritualia discernat. Homines etiam in suis naturalibus, non sunt præditi ea facultate, qua res spirituales dignoscuntur (quæ facultas est adventitia) perinde est ac si diceret, mirum non esse cæcos non judicare de coloribus, quum oculorum luce careant, ac proinde lux sit illis pro tenebris. Bezæ sunt verba. Et revera non multum est quod ex natura discimus, ut eo ad tanta percipienda capaces reddi posse nos ullo modo credendum putem, Humana sapientia enim, quod, ad cognoscendum Deum, etiam per creaturas, ob vitiatam naturam, parum idonea sit, citra controversiam est, teste Musculo. Exultet in Utopia, noster Medico Philosophus, & multa de imaginaria verae sapientiae ubertate, cui & ipsa Scriptura tantum debeat, ut ne quidem in necessariis ad salutem clare satis instruat, nisi adjutrice Diva Philosophia. O crassum Socinianismum! Mitto blasphemiam, nec enim refutatione eget, sic Medicus: Philosophia in multis principium est, & tantum talemque usum præstat ad assequendum quid Spiritus S. loquatur & doceat in Scriptura, ut quo quis magis artibus &c. Multoque is felicior erit in Scrip-turæ interpretatione, compendiosioremque inibit rationem, quam is qui destitutus talium artium & disciplinarum ido-nea cognitione, omnia ex Scripturæ revelatione eruere niti-tur. Idque etiam in necessariis & fundamentalibus, sunt enim loca quæ tractant res momentosas & forte ne-cessarias ad salutem, tamen obscurissima sunt, & ex Scrip-tura(en crassissimum Papistam!) lumen accipere non possunt. Quos tandem in sinu fovebit errores Ecclesia, quas feret blasphemias? ô tempora! Utinam videant quibus cordi veritas & expergiscant.
units.tr: But, as I said, NB experience here outweighs every argument. It so inclines pious minds toward the hidden Scripture, which everywhere proclaims our God gloriously and teaches us his will, and so affects them that they feel themselves truly disposed as the Psalmist sings of himself in the following verses: "More to be desired than gold" and so on, verses 11 and 12. For they feel how opposed to this happiness is every sense and effort of our nature. Indeed, there is nothing that warns us of God more plainly and powerfully, or explains the reasons of his judgments and works more fully, than Holy Scripture. Yet this holds not for everyone, but for those who fear God and are endowed with the heavenly Spirit. I have experienced it, etc. Imagine some people who use natural reason as their principle, who have reached by nature the greatest knowledge of words and things that can be acquired, and consider what they will achieve in understanding Scripture. Since the theologians, as you certainly dictate in your self-appointed authority, are greatly mistaken and claim too much for themselves when they want to settle such controversies as how all sinned in Adam, and how concupiscence can be called sin. Yet if any question is to be settled solely from the sacred writings by the theologians, it is one that every man of sound mind will judge belongs to them. But since the theologians claim too much for themselves (the physician being judge between the theologians and the philosophers), let us hear someone not from the dregs of the theologians or from ordinary philosophers, but a man who is the greatest and, until now, incomparable philosopher, who had learned and taught to set aside prejudices and weigh reasons, Bacon of Verulam. It would be a long task to recount how great he was to Heereboord and others. Thus he writes at the end of his treatise on the Advancement of Learning, addressed to King James: There remains still Sacred Theology, or inspired theology. Yet if we proceed to treat it, we must leave, thinks the physician, according to his own philosophical or medical scruple, the little boat of human reason. For the stars of philosophy, which have hitherto shone upon us chiefly, will no longer suffice. Therefore it would be fitting, so modestly says the greatest philosopher, to keep silence in this matter also. And while he treats only the manner of instruction, he refuses to add examples or to give precepts. But we shall leave this to the theologians. Who, in our Palaemon's judgment, claim too much for themselves, even when they wish to determine how all sinned in Adam, and how concupiscence can be called sin; those theologians, that is, are doing their job. Shame on you, immodest, proud head! Let Verulam continue: The prerogative of God embraces the whole man, and extends no less to reason than to the human will, so that a man denies himself entirely and draws near to God. Therefore, just as we are bound to obey the divine law even when the will resists, so too we must have faith in the Word of God even when reason resists. For if we believe only those things which agree with our reason, we assent to things, not to the Author. These words so pleased Heidanus that he adopted them and made them his own. And although the physician despises the theologians, I shall quote their words, so that he may see that those he insults are not unphilosophical. Heidanus teaches that faith must prescribe to reason, and do so in such a way that there is no need of reason. Yet far from reason being given any prerogative here, Christ on the contrary gives thanks to the Father that he has hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants [νηπίοις]. Matt. 11:25. Hence he also said to his disciples: Unless you turn and become like little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of God [ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε, ἢ γίνησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία, οὐ μὴ εἰσελθητε εἰς βασιλείαν θεοῦ], Matt. 18:3. He plainly wills that such men receive the Kingdom of God as infants do. Indeed, God, passing over the wise, the powerful and the noble according to the flesh, chose what is foolish, weak, base and despised in the world, and things that are not, that he might bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh may glory before him, 1 Cor. 1:27, 28. And an injury is done not only to God, but also to man himself, when such sufficiency [ἱκανόυς?] is ascribed to him, for which he is in no way fit and which he cannot bear. For since reason itself is darkened by sin, as that dreadful depth of ignorance with which we enter this world bears witness, and which besets us from childhood, if the light that is in us is darkness, how great will that darkness itself be? Matt. 6:23. From this most dense mist of darkness every error of human life proceeds, which receives all the sons of Adam into a certain shadowy bosom. Hence, since we are turned away from the knowledge of truth by many prejudices, we can never be freed from them unless we are illumined by him who is the light of the world, and the way, and the truth, and the life, John 14. But how shall darkness judge concerning light and lumen? And how could man, to whom the wisdom of God is foolishness, justify it? And how could one be built up unto salvation by the word of the cross, who stumbles at it and suffers offence? Who, NB, would expect a right judgment from so foolish a judge? Hence, the more a man, hear, physician, prefers his own wisdom and seems to rest on greater reason, the more he is found to be opposed to the Gospel; for the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness to him, nor can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned, 1 Cor. 2:14. Therefore the Apostle warns, 1 Cor. 3:18, that no one deceive himself: if anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. What can reason claim for itself concerning mysteries that depend on the mere good pleasure of God? Must not our intellect plainly be taken captive and subjected to God? Or perhaps, if reason judges otherwise of what is revealed than it seems to man, will it fashion for itself another God and another will of his? And do you, good man, attribute so much to reason, so much to your philosophy, that you say even weighty matters, and perhaps necessary to salvation, and even most obscure, cannot receive light from Scripture. The divine Philosophy must be consulted about them. Perhaps it happens to you what Boethius pretends: this divine Philosophy dealt with you directly and dictated these oracles. You will bear this, Wolzogen; you who write that this man has a mind tenacious of orthodoxy, you yourself seem to think quite the opposite. We have heard you speak of fundamentals in such a way that you think they can be perceived without any care or effort (since they are delivered with such clarity that they remove every doubt for the reader at first glance), as we saw in the former book. Can you reconcile these things? Let the most noble Sadeel speak for me; thus he: We have learned from theology itself that theology must be disputed from theological principles, and we affirm that it must be done so even from the analytic discipline itself, which forbids passing over into another kind [μεταβαίνειν εἰς ἄλλο γένος?] and wandering outside the orbit of that science about which you have undertaken to discourse. Moreover, since theology is above all sciences, to subject it to philosophical principles is not only unfitting but most unjust and most unworthy. So far is it from being the case that Scripture cannot give light even in necessary matters, that they ought to expect it from philosophy. For, as Chrysostom rightly said, divine Scripture has no need of human wisdom; he also says that it is a great danger to entrust matters of faith to human reasonings. For in Holy Scripture, as Augustine testifies, what is to be held and what is to be avoided is fully found. So that the physician may recognise how far he differs from the theologians, let him hear one more, Musculus, who treats this matter gravely and piously: What, then, he says, is left here to the powers of reason in knowing the things of the Christian faith? In two words, like thunderbolts, every effort of the wise of this world in the things of God is cast down. He cannot, he says, know them. Therefore where the natural man tries to attain the knowledge of the kingdom of Christ, he labours in vain; where he disputes about the things of the Spirit, he chatters; where he pronounces, he lies; where he decides in religion, he is rash; where he teaches, he seduces; where he finds followers, he destroys. Why? Because he cannot know. What then shall we expect in the business of the Christian faith from the decision of natural men? I fear that the reader who is pious will see too clearly that these things are true in Velthuysen. Since, then, our intellect by its nature is not of light, and moreover is entangled in so many prejudices and errors through a singular disposition, what else is the effort of natural reason (and in so many matters, according to Velthuysen, it takes the place of a principle) in the business of religion, than a certain religious madness, or rather an irreligious folly, and a rational delirium? And since he speaks here of knowing the things of the Spirit of God, to know spiritually is to know those things by the judgment, guidance and illumination of the Spirit, just as to know naturally is NB to know from the judgment of reason. It is therefore the same as if he said: the natural man cannot know the things of the Spirit of God, since they are not discerned naturally, NB, and by the judgment of reason, but by the instinct, judgment and guidance of the Spirit. He uses this word in this passage so as to set aside and reject the inquiries and investigations of the philosophers, and he teaches that it is impossible to reach the knowledge of the things of the Spirit of God by that way, since those things are known not by the judgment and scrutiny of reason but of the Spirit of God. I see that an objection drawn from the sewers of the Socinians is thrust upon us by the physician, so that the force of these passages may be weakened and the weapons of the Reformed made void against the most pestilential heresy of Socinus and Pelagius. He objects to himself 1 Cor. 1:19, 26, and answers that it is to be understood only of prejudices, not of true knowledge. But note, first, that this man here acts expressly against the Reformed, who everywhere, as on other passages, so also in this place, fight against the Socinians and Pelagians; see Episcopius and others. The paradox itself, which the physician wishes to seem to refute, deals with adversaries against the Orthodox; for these alone from such passages, and similar ones, prove the unfitness of human nature to perceive and judge those things that concern the Christian religion. Second, he acts deceitfully, while, keeping silent about our best arguments drawn from the more emphatic passages, he merely nips at this one. Third, in fact he holds the same as the adversaries, indeed as the paradoxical exerciser himself, for the escape of both comes to this, that they deny that anything is settled here to the prejudice of true wisdom. So Paradoxus, and Velthuysen said, that the Apostle plainly designates not true but apparent wisdom, from the scope of the passage, concerning prejudices, not true knowledge; thus they agree well among themselves while they wish to seem to quarrel. Fourth, he in no way proves what he says. It is true that many are led astray by prejudices, and that true wisdom is nowhere rejected in the sacred writings; therefore we also hold it in high regard, but in its own kind. For apart from the fact that true wisdom is for the most part vainly pretended and boasted of, we cannot but be turned away from the knowledge of truth by prejudices, in Heidanus' judgment, until we are illumined by him who is the light of the world. Let man be wise as much as he can by nature, he is not yet fit, nay, he is unfit, to receive the doctrine of salvation rightly, unless his own faculty within is raised up by a new light implanted and adapted to perceive the things of the Spirit of God. This our men want, this the Apostle teaches. Here the Apostle understands by wisdom whatever man can comprehend, aided both by natural faculty of mind and by use, letters and knowledge of the arts. For he opposes the wisdom of the world to the wisdom of the Spirit; therefore whatever understanding falls to man without the illumination of the Holy Spirit is contained under the wisdom of the world. He says that all of it has been made foolish by God, that is, condemned to foolishness. Meanwhile it must be noted that Paul does not simply condemn either the natural acuteness of man, or prudence gathered by use and experience, or the cultivation of mind acquired by letters, but he asserts that all this NB is of no weight for perceiving spiritual wisdom. So Calvin, so that Paradoxus might rightly have said that this passage is on everyone's lips, not only of the little theologians but of the most serious theologians too; nor will any medicaster or philosophaster easily escape their force. Nor is it to be wondered at: For the wisdom of the flesh, says Paul, thus noted in the Bibles of Junius and Tremellius, establishes nothing certain, not even in its own affairs, much less does it discern the things of others, that is, the spiritual. Men too, in their natural state, are not endowed with that faculty by which spiritual things are discerned (which faculty is adventitious), just as if he said it is no wonder that the blind do not judge of colours, since they lack the light of the eyes, and therefore light is to them as darkness. These are Beza's words. And indeed it is not much that we learn from nature, so that I should think we can in any way be made capable of perceiving such great things, for human wisdom, as to knowing God, even through creatures, is, on account of our corrupted nature, very unfit; there is no controversy about this, says Musculus. Let our philosopher the physician rejoice in his Utopia, and in many things about the imaginary abundance of true wisdom, to which Scripture itself owes so much that it does not clearly enough instruct even in matters necessary to salvation, unless Divine Philosophy helps. O crass Socinianism! I pass over the blasphemy, which needs no refutation, says the physician: Philosophy is in many respects a principle, and renders such great and such service in attaining what the Holy Spirit says and teaches in Scripture, that the more one is versed in the arts etc., and the happier he will be in interpreting Scripture, and will enter upon a shorter method, than he who, lacking the suitable knowledge of such arts and disciplines, strives to draw out everything from the revelation of Scripture. And this also in necessary and fundamental matters, for there are passages which treat matters of weight and perhaps necessary to salvation, yet they are most obscure, and cannot receive light from Scripture (behold the crassest Papist!). What error will the Church at last cherish in its bosom, what blasphemies will it bear? O the times! Would that those to whom truth is dear might see and awaken!

units.la: 5. Quintum, quod Reformatorum mentem emphatice explicat, est, quod ne quidem piis & qui jam à Spiritu S. illuminati sunt & lumine interno donati, vel ad minimum verè spiritualis intellectio-nis actum sufficere doceant, nisi, præter continuam, habitualis illius gratiæ potentem & gratiosam conser-vationem, novo ad singulos actus influxu seu afflatu excitentur, quo actum intellectionis eliciant. Nihil, si de providentia, de gratia, de hominis dependentia Reformatorum sententiam rite perpen-deris, magis indubitatum esse potest. Sed antea hac de re sufficienter egimus. Notandum, inquit Cart-wrightus, inter recentiorum Interpretum principes à Polyandro collocatum, cui consentiebat Heere-boordius, qui exactum ejus ingenium, subactum judicium, & singularem in S.S. sensu eruendo dex-teritatem magnis laudibus efferendam censuit, Notandum, inquit ille, non tantum cæcos & infideles my-steria regni non percipere sine Sp. operatione, sed ne pios quidem ipsos, quamtumvis Spiritu Sancto imbutos, eo-que opus habere Dei Spiritum suppliciter petere, nisi velint inanes à concionibus redire: quod ut hoc loco, sic etiam sæpe in Apostolis experti sumus: nam nisi adsit Spiri-tus, Scripturæ utcunque explicatæ veluti clausus & obsignatus liber sunt. Sic & Apostoli ab optimo quidem magistro rite & abunde docti fuerant: nisi tamen indigerent Spiritu veritatis qui eorum mentes hac ipsa doctrina, quam ante audierant, erudiret, non ullum expectare juberentur. Si quod petimus a Deo: deesse nobis confitemur, & ipse in eo quod promittit, nostram arguit inopiam: nemo jam fateri dubitet se tantum ad intelligenda Dei mysteria valere, quantum ejus gratia fuerit illuminatus. Qui sibi plus intelligentiae tribuit, eo caecior est &c.
units.tr: 5. Fifthly, which sets out the Reformers' mind emphatically, they teach that not even the pious, who have already been illuminated by the Holy Spirit and endowed with inner light, or at least the act of truly spiritual understanding, is enough for them unless, besides the continual, habitual, powerful and gracious preservation of that grace, they are also roused by a new influx or inspiration for each individual act, by which they bring forth the act of understanding. If you weigh the Reformers' view of providence, grace and man's dependence rightly, nothing can be more certain. But we have already dealt with this matter sufficiently. It should be noted, says Cartwright, who is placed by Polyandrus among the leading recent interpreters, and whom Heereboord agreed with, judging that his exact talent, trained judgment and singular skill in drawing out the sense of Scripture deserve great praise: It should be noted, he says, that not only the blind and unbelieving do not perceive the mysteries of the kingdom without the operation of the Spirit, but not even the pious themselves, however much they are imbued with the Holy Spirit, and they need to ask God's Spirit humbly, unless they want to return empty from sermons. We have often found this to be so in the apostles, as we do here: for unless the Spirit is present, Scripture, however explained, is like a closed and sealed book. Thus the apostles too had been rightly and abundantly taught by the best of teachers; yet unless they needed the Spirit of truth to instruct their minds in this very doctrine which they had heard before, they would not have been bidden to wait for anything. If we confess that we lack what we ask of God, and he, in what he promises, proves our poverty, let no one now hesitate to confess that he is worth only as much in understanding God's mysteries as he has been illuminated by his grace. Whoever attributes more understanding to himself is the blinder...

units.la: 6. Inde est quod tam prolixe in hoc negotio commendent preces & suspiria ad implorandam Sp. S. illuminationem & revelationem. Duo quidem ad recte intelligendas S. S. summe sunt necessaria: Oratio & Meditatio: & magis tamen oratio valet quam studium. Nemo enim prophetias intelligere potest absque Spiritu quo sunt inspiratae. Hinc tantum quisque de sensu script. S. assequitur, quantum de Spiritu, qui eas inspiravit, participat. Tantum vero de Sp. participat, quantum ejus a Deo impetrat. Tantum vero ejus a Deo impetrat, quantum precibus ad Deum ardenter invigilat. Haec unica hodie tot dissensionum, (audiat haec Veltkhuisen, cum suis Philosophastris) est causa circa Scripturarum sensus, quod plerique interpretes vel orando vel meditando vel utroque deficiunt. Huc facit, quod cum Deus ipse sit interpres verborum suorum, non potest quis ad eorum sensum attingere, quem ille non manu ducit. Proinde necessarium est, ut qui huic studio se applicat per orationem ad Deum accedat. Si ergo a Dei Spiritu proprie discere debemus, quae sit mens Domini, maxima erit temeritas, si quis lege & voluntate Dei contempta, putet sibi diligentiam & industriam suam sufficere. Sic omnes Reformati. Quid autem Wolzogium moverit, ut, ubi preces praecipue commendandae erant, earum nullam fere mentionem faciat ullibi, conjectu difficile videtur, nisi Spiritus auxilio non semper, non tantopere nos egere putet, aut forsan nimis tritum preces commendare & pietatis exercitia Quia eo jam delabimur, non possum non exscribere, quæ alibi habet Bisterfeldius. Oratio, ait ille, (hic) est religiosa voluntatis nostræ coram Deo repræsentatio, ut nobis Spiritum suum sanctum largiatur. Matt. vii. 7. Luc. xi. 9. Jac. i. 5. Pf. li. 12. 13. cxliii. 10. Hæc est certissima panacea & panchrestum, quo omnes animi morbi curantur: instructissimum armamentarium, quo omnia impedimenta removentur, omniaque instrumenta ac media procurantur; accommodatissimum vas quo Aqua illa viva, Spiritus S. hauritur ac retinetur. Joh. iv. 10. 14. Unde pius sacrarum literarum studiosus NB plus orando quam meditando proficit. Complectitur autem hæc oratio deprecationem, ut Sp. S. ineptitudinem nostram tollat & facultates nostras reformet ac transformet; petitionem, ut eadem conformet, informet ac præformet: ac gratiarum actionem, ut pro sensu usuque nobis concesso Deum laudemus. Eph. vi. 18. Huic orationi opponitur precum neglectus, quo quis vel plane non orat, vel non eo modo graduque quo oportebat; quod peccatum est fons omnis incogitantiæ, ignorantiæ, nequitiæ & inertiæ. Tentatio, quæ est hominis fidelis externarum internarumque afflictionum Spiritus igne, facta probatio. 1. Petr. i. 6. Jac. i. 2. insignem vim habet in germano Scripturæ sensu, vivoque ejus usu eruendo. Congruus etiam requiritur interpretantis status, qui est religiosa, adeoque omnimoda & omnigena, totius hominis ad sacrarum literarum studium, applicatio. Joh. Hulsemannus Theologus Lutheranus, tanti, in hoc negotio, hoc exercitium pietatis fecit, ut de studio Theologico agens, ex professo doceat, quid Oratia ista, quanta ejus necessitas, quodnam ei tempus commodum. Optimam precandi rationem esse quam hic & nunc Sp. S. ex verbo Dei homini in memoriam revocat, aut indit. Statam autem si quis desideret, refert, inter alias formulas, hanc Thomæ Aquin. ex Cassandro, cujus hic majorem partem inferere lubuit. O Benig-nissime Pater, Creator ineffabilis, qui verus fons & luminis & sapientiæ, ego indigus peccator tibi supplico devotus digneris diffundere super intellectus mei tenebras claritatis tuæ radium, & duplicem in qua nati sumus removere privationem, peccatum sc. & ignorantiam. ---- O Sp. Sancte Deus, dator munerum, da mihi intelligendi acumen, retinendi capacitatem, introspectandi subtilitatem, addiscendi facultatem &c. imo inquit in margi-ne Hulsemannus Oratio est ipsum studium Theologicum. Pientissimam hac de re qui velit instructionem, Zanchium adeat, Polanum, aliosque, imo vix ullus, qui, etsi in transitu solum & brevissimè Script. tractet interpretationem, preces non laudet & efferat, vide inter alios Venerandum Præceptorem meum Essenium; Wolzogen nihilominus, in earum commendatione ita parcus est, ut, dum integrum de ea materia tractatum scribit, earum vix ullam mentionem injiciat. Quantopere, huic labori intentus dum erat, orationi incubuerit, si quis hinc colligat, næ ille parum de Wolzogiana præsumet pietate.
units.tr: 6. Hence it is that they commend prayers and sighs so lavishly in this business, for imploring the illumination and revelation of the Holy Spirit. Two things indeed are supremely necessary for rightly understanding Holy Scripture: prayer and meditation; and yet prayer is worth more than study. For no one can understand the prophecies without the Spirit by whom they were inspired. Each person grasps the sense of Holy Scripture only so far as he shares in the Spirit who inspired it. But he shares in the Spirit only so far as he obtains him from God. And he obtains him from God only so far as he devotes himself ardently to prayer to God. This alone is the cause, in our day, of so many disagreements about the senses of Scripture (let Veltkuysen hear this, with his little philosophers), namely that most interpreters fail either in prayer, or in meditation, or in both. To this point: since God himself is the interpreter of his own words, no one can reach their sense unless he is led by the hand. Therefore it is necessary that whoever applies himself to this study should approach God through prayer. If then we ought to learn properly from the Spirit of God what the mind of the Lord is, it will be the greatest rashness if anyone, despising the law and will of God, thinks that his own care and industry are enough. So all the Reformers. But what moved Wolzogen, when prayers above all ought to have been commended, to make almost no mention of them anywhere, is hard to guess, unless he thinks that we do not need the help of the Spirit so much, or not at all, or perhaps that it is too hackneyed to commend prayer and the exercises of piety. Since we are now coming to that point, I cannot refrain from copying out what Bisterfeld says elsewhere. Prayer, he says, is the religious presentation of our will before God, that he may bestow on us his Holy Spirit. Matt. vii. 7. Luke xi. 9. James i. 5. Ps. li. 12, 13. cxliii. 10. This is the most certain panacea and cure-all by which all diseases of the mind are healed: the most fully equipped armoury by which all hindrances are removed and all instruments and means are procured; the most suitable vessel by which that living water, the Holy Spirit, is drawn and kept. John iv. 10, 14. Hence the pious student of the sacred letters NB makes more progress by praying than by meditating. This prayer embraces, first, a petition that the Holy Spirit may remove our incapacity and reform and transform our faculties; second, a request that he may shape, inform and pre-form us in the same way; and third, thanksgiving, that we may praise God for the sense and use granted to us. Eph. vi. 18. Opposed to this prayer is the neglect of prayer, by which a man either does not pray at all, or does not do so in the manner and degree that he ought; this sin is the source of all thoughtlessness, ignorance, wickedness and sloth. Temptation, which is the trial of a faithful man by the fire of external and internal afflictions, has a remarkable power in drawing out the true sense of Scripture and its living use. 1 Pet. i. 6. James i. 2. A fitting condition of the interpreter is also required, namely a religious application, and therefore a complete and all-embracing application of the whole man to the study of the sacred letters. Johann Hülsemann, a Lutheran theologian, so valued this exercise of piety in this business that, when treating of theological study, he teaches expressly what prayer is, how great its necessity is, and what time is suitable for it. He holds that the best way of praying is what the Holy Spirit now brings to a man's memory or implants from the word of God. If anyone wants a fixed form, Hülsemann gives, among other formulas, this one of Thomas Aquinas from Cassander, of which I have chosen to insert the greater part here. O most kind Father, ineffable Creator, who are the true fountain of light and wisdom, I, a needy sinner, devoutly beg you to deign to pour over the darkness of my understanding a ray of your brightness, and to remove the double privation into which we were born, namely sin and ignorance. ---- O Holy Spirit, God, giver of gifts, give me sharpness of understanding, capacity to retain, subtlety in looking within, facility in learning, etc. Indeed, says Hülsemann in the margin, prayer is itself the theological study. Whoever wants the most devout instruction on this matter should consult Zanchius, Polanus and others; indeed hardly anyone, even one who treats the interpretation of Scripture only in passing and very briefly, fails to praise and extol prayer. See among others my venerable teacher Essenius. Yet Wolzogen is so sparing in commending it that, while he writes a whole treatise on that subject, he hardly brings any mention of it into it. If anyone infers from how little he prayed while he was occupied with this work, he will assume that Wolzogen has little piety.

units.la: Hactenus, me non tam rationes quam quidem authoritates adhibuisse lubens fateor, nec etiam unicè de veritate disceptamus sed & cum veritate, Reformatorum genuinus sensus investigandus erat, simulque quam parum Wolzogio cum iis conveniat, quam perspicuè omnia, quæ hanc causam spectant, à Viris Doctissimis jam ante nos pertractata fuerint demonstrandum; eorum præcipue gratia, qui dum authorum lectionem vituperari audiunt, postquam suis aut præceptorum suorum meditationibus & institutionibus nimium indulserunt, se solos sapere & jam demum exortam lucem esse, suaviter somniant, supina interim ignorantiâ, eorum quæ summi viri tradiderunt scriptorum monumenta, fædum in modum laborantes. Argumenta autem, quæ infusum illud probent novum lumen, multa fatis habent & solida nostri. Lumen hoc spirituale necessarium esse contendimus 1. quia nihil agit ultra suum genus; atque adeo naturale lumen intellectus, nullam proportionem idoneam habet ad spirituale objectum. Ratio enim humana, aut intellectus humanus, verba sunt Mus-culi, in causa regni Dei non est id, quod in oculis corporis est facultas videndi: cui satis est si lux externa offeratur... At ratio in causa religionis caeca est ut ad objecta Euangelicæ lucis magis stupeat, nisi per operationem Spiritus Sancti aperiatur, hinc est quod nemo NB minus est lucis Christi capax, quam qui sunt in hoc mundo sapientes ac prudentes. Hic autem Spiritus, sic Marefius, qui lumen illud fidei accendit in mentibus nostris, absque quo tam impossibile est nos assentiri principiis fidei super-na-turalibus, quam impossibile est bruta ratione destituta assentiri principiis naturalibus (quo simili etiam utitur Bellarm. Conc. de Lum. fidei) non est privatus Sp. sed communis omnium fidelium Rom. viii. 8. 1 Cor. ii, 12. 1 Joh. ii. 20..... nominatim 1 Cor. ii. 15. ubi Tirinus per spiritualem hominem intelligit eum, qui per internum lumen fidei a Sp. S. sibi infusum, capit, intelligit, judicat, dijudicat omnia. Accurate illa explicat Strangius, sic ille Cæcitas & excæcatio proprie dicuntur de oculis corporeis, & metaphoricè transferuntur ad mentem seu facultatem intellectivam quæ est quasi oculus animæ. Ad visum requiritur & lumen internum oculis insitum, & externum à lucido corpore promanans. Cæcitas est privatio luminis interni. Cui lumen deest externum, privatur quidem actu videndi, cui vero internum deest, privatur potentia videndi, quantum ad organum spectat. Sic ex naturali cæcitate & ineptitudine infusi luminis necessitatem probat vir Doctissimus. 2. Alterum ex adventitia deducitur excæcatione, quam probè à naturali distinguendam docet Strangius loco citato, sic autem Amesius: secundo inquit, quia obscuritas magnana tam privationis, quam perversitatis accessit ad na-turalem illum defectum, ἐσκοτισμένοι ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ, ἀπηλ-λοτριωμένοι τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν οὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς. Eph. iv. 18. & v. 8. 3. quia Scriptura apertis verbis testatur, apertionem cordis (τότε διήνοιξεν αὐτῶν τὸν νοῦν τοῦ συνιέναι τὰς γραφάς. Luc. xxiv. 25.) spiritum revelatio-nis Eph. i. 17. & novum quendam intellectum a Deo donatum (νοῦ ἀλλὰ λέγω[?], inquit Paulus Timotheo 2. Eph. ii. 7. δώη γὰρ σοι ὁ κύριος σύνεσιν ἐν πᾶσι[?]) omnino necessaria esse, etiam NB praeter & ultra patefactionem illam objecti quae in verbo fit. Huc respicit Calvinus quando duplicem illuminationem ab Apostolo poni dicit, unam Euangelii, alteram arcanam. Ideoque recta Dei cognitio, sapientia, ipsi est, quae humani ingenii captum longe superat: quamque ideo adipisci nemo potest nisi arcana Spiritus revelatione. Non vult solum mentem nostram novi infusione luminis elevari, sed & intellectui sic capaci, rem istam a Spiritu indi, idem, quod in Scriptura est, objectum immediate repraesentari, quod probe notandum, & ad praecedentem quae-stionem spectat. Huc ea quae Musculus alibi: Dei cognitio, inquit, quae per exercitium Scripturarum est tantum, sine singulari revelatione magis opinio est quam scientia.
units.tr: So far I gladly confess that I have used authorities rather than arguments, nor are we disputing only about truth, but the genuine sense of the Reformers was to be investigated along with the truth, and at the same time it had to be shown how little Wolzogen agrees with them, and how clearly all the matters that concern this cause have already been treated by the most learned men before us. This is for the sake especially of those who, when they hear the reading of authors disparaged, after they have indulged too much in their own meditations and in the teachings of their teachers, sweetly dream that they alone are wise and that the light has at last dawned, while in the meantime, through their supine ignorance, they wretchedly neglect the written monuments of the highest men. Our arguments, however, which prove that this infused new light exists, have plenty of solid support. We contend that this spiritual light is necessary, first, because it does nothing beyond its own kind; and so the natural light of the intellect has no suitable proportion to a spiritual object. For human reason, or the human intellect, as Musculus says, in the cause of the kingdom of God is not what the faculty of seeing is in the eyes of the body, for which it is enough that external light be offered... But reason is blind in the cause of religion, so that it is rather amazed at the objects of the gospel light, unless it is opened by the operation of the Holy Spirit; hence it is that no one NB is less capable of the light of Christ than those who are wise and prudent in this world. Moreover, this Spirit, says Maresius, who kindles that light of faith in our minds, without whom it is as impossible for us to assent to the supernatural principles of faith as it is impossible for a brute devoid of reason to assent to natural principles (Bellarmine uses a similar comparison in his book on the light of faith), is not private to some, but is common to all the faithful. Rom. viii. 8. 1 Cor. ii. 12. 1 John ii. 20... especially 1 Cor. ii. 15, where Tirinus understands by the spiritual man him who, through the inner light of faith infused into him by the Holy Spirit, grasps, understands, judges and discerns all things. Strangius explains this exactly, thus: Blindness and blinding are properly said of the bodily eyes, and are transferred metaphorically to the mind or intellective faculty, which is as it were the eye of the soul. For sight both the inner light inborn in the eyes and the external light coming from a luminous body are required. Blindness is the privation of inner light. Whoever lacks external light is indeed deprived of the act of seeing; but whoever lacks inner light is deprived of the power of seeing, so far as the organ is concerned. In this way the learned man proves the necessity of the infused light from natural blindness and incapacity. Second, it is deduced from the adventitious blinding, which Strangius, in the passage cited, teaches must be carefully distinguished from the natural; so too Amesius: secondly, he says, because the darkness of great perversity as well as of privation has been added to that natural defect, [ἐσκοτισμένοι ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ, ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν οὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς] having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them. Eph. iv. 18; v. 8. Third, because Scripture testifies in plain words to the opening of the heart ([τότε διήνοιξεν αὐτῶν τὸν νοῦν τοῦ συνιέναι τὰς γραφάς] Luke xxiv. 45) and to the spirit of revelation (Eph. i. 17), and to a certain new understanding given by God (Paul says to Timothy, [νόει ἃ λέγω], 2 Tim. ii. 7; [δώη γὰρ σοι ὁ κύριος σύνεσιν ἐν πᾶσι], Eph. ii. 7) are altogether necessary, and NB even beyond and above that revelation of the object which is made in the word. Calvin has this in view when he says that the Apostle sets down a twofold illumination, one of the gospel, the other secret. Therefore the right knowledge of God, that is wisdom, far surpasses the capacity of the human mind, and so no one can attain it except by the secret revelation of the Spirit. He wants not only our mind to be raised by the infusion of a new light, but also that this thing be impressed by the Spirit on an understanding so capable, and that the same object which is in Scripture be presented to it immediately, which must be carefully noted and bears on the preceding question. To this belongs what Musculus says elsewhere: The knowledge of God, he says, which comes through the exercise of the Scriptures alone, without a special revelation, is more an opinion than knowledge.

units.la: 4. Quia hoc Sanctos obtestari & supplicare Deum videmus Pf. cxix. 18. 27. 73. &c. Quas preces nefariè illi abrogant, qui luminis hujus interni abolent necessitatem, multo magis, qui omnem ejus negat existentiam.
units.tr: 4. Because we see that the saints call upon and entreat God (Ps. 119:18, 27, 73, etc.). Those who abolish the necessity of this inward light abrogate these prayers wickedly, and much more those who deny its existence altogether.

units.la: 5. Huc accedit etiam, quod contra-sentientes, tam fidei quam respipiscentiae, & obedientiae originem in ipsa natura, necesse est ut collocent: Nam objecti lumen nihil huc adferre potest, priusquam recipiatur & actu fiat ἐμφύλον, receptionem vero naturae acceptam referre necesse habent, si (quod faciunt) naturalem intellectum harum rerum capaces satis statuant.
units.tr: 5. It follows also that those who think otherwise must locate the origin of faith, repentance and obedience in nature itself. For the light of the object can contribute nothing here before it is received and actually becomes innate [ἐμφύλον]. And they must attribute its reception to nature, if (as they do) they hold that the natural intellect is capable enough of these things.

units.la: 6. Si non opus sit superinfuso lumine facultati intellectivae, sed sufficeret tantum clara veritatis propositio, ut ajunt in script. Synod. Art. 3 & 4. p. 164. Remonstrantes, ad intelligendas Scripturas; non magis animalis homo caecutiret in capiendis mysteriis Regni Dei, quam rudis discipulus in capiendis Acroamaticis, & disputationibus Metaphysicis & Logicis Aristotelis; & ad discendum Organon Aristotelis opus esset unctione Christi, & collyrio Sp S. & Spiritu sapientiae & revelationis. Nam in his maximè opus est clara veritatis propositione. 7. Quia tota corruptio in voluntate est à mentis obscuratione; & si haec obscuratio non sit tanta, ut opus sit superinfuso lumine Dei; jam animalis homo poterit non tantum capere; sed etiam rectè dijudicare, probare, velle & facere, quae sunt Spiritus Dei. 8. Consideretur modo mortis & caecitatis spiritualis natura. Mors certè & caecitas absque indito lumine non pelluntur. 9. Et revera vis illa Dei qua regeneratio perficitur & nova creatio, frustra tantopere à sacris scriptoribus praedicaretur, imo frustra regenerationis, struftra creationis nomine exprimeretur, nisi novae cujusdam vitae novi motus, principii, includeret productionem, quae respectu intellectus infusum merito appellamus lumen, & inditum : ------- 10. Denique nullum lumen, qualitas, potentia, facultas, ut ita loquar, nulla in intellectum si infundatur, necesse est, superfit[?] potentia credendi in homine naturali, modo adsit Gratia Pelagii, objecti propositio: Quascunque enim excitationes aut incitationes tandem fingas, nisi infusam gratiam lumenque statuas, credendi, ut intelligendi potentiam, homini corrupto, reliquam fingis necessario. Non video quid dictis objici queat à Wolzogio nisi palam nostra castra deserens, ad gratiae simul & Ecclesiae Orthodoxae transeat adversarios. Quod scrupulum aliquem injicere lectori posset hisce tribus complectar.
units.tr: 6. If there were no need for light poured over the intellective faculty, but a clear proposition of truth sufficed for understanding the Scriptures, as the Remonstrants say in the Synod's writing, Art. 3 & 4, p. 164, then natural man would be no more blind in grasping the mysteries of the Kingdom of God than a raw student is in grasping the Acroamatic works and the metaphysical and logical disputations of Aristotle. Learning the Organon of Aristotle would then need the anointing of Christ, the eye-salve of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit of wisdom and revelation. For in these matters above all a clear proposition of truth is needed. 7. Because all corruption of the will arises from a darkening of the mind; and if this darkening is not so great that God's inpoured light is needed, then natural man will be able not only to grasp but also to judge rightly, to prove, to will and to do the things that are of the Spirit of God. 8. Let us consider the nature of spiritual death and blindness. Certainly death and blindness are not driven away without an inborn light. 9. And indeed that power of God by which regeneration is accomplished and new creation would be preached in vain by the sacred writers so much, and would be expressed in vain by the names regeneration and creation, unless it included the production of a certain new life and a new motion and principle, which with respect to the intellect we rightly call an infused and inborn light. ------- 10. Finally, if no light, quality, power, faculty, so to speak, is infused into the intellect, it must necessarily be that the power of believing remains in natural man, provided the grace of Pelagius, that is the mere proposition of the object, is present. For whatever excitations or incitements you then imagine, unless you posit an infused grace and light, you necessarily imagine that the power of believing, like the power of understanding, remains in corrupt man. I do not see what Wolzogen can object to these statements except to desert our camp openly and pass over to the adversaries of grace and of the Orthodox Church at once. Three points will be enough to remove any doubt that might trouble the reader.

units.la: 1. Primum erit, Wolzogium Heterodoxias non satis praegnantes ob rationes accusari in hoc negotio, eum diversis locis simile quid docere. Verum Responspondeo 1. Me Wolzogio de professa orthodoxia li- benter gratulaturum, si aliquando palam eam pro- fiteatur & explicatè, tantum enim ad minimum, jam superius dicta, efficient, ut, nisi manifestissi- mè sese explicet & sententiam summam cum claritate proponat, merito suspicione gravandus sit porro.
units.tr: 1. The first will be that Wolzogen is accused in this matter of heterodoxies not pregnant enough, because in various places he teaches something similar. But I answer: 1. I would gladly congratulate Wolzogen on his professed orthodoxy, if he ever professed it openly and explained it. For at the very least the things said above will bring it about that, unless he explains himself most plainly and sets out his main view with clarity, he is rightly to be burdened with suspicion from now on.

units.la: 2. Nego ex Wolzogii isto scripto quicquam produci posse, cui non simile quid, imo quo non magis, saltem æque, emphaticum quid invenias, apud professos Ecclesiæ simul & gratiæ hostes. Ipsi Sociniani pro- testantur injuriam sibi fieri, rationis absque divina illustratione ineptitudinem non agnoscere si dicantur. Nullibi Wolzogius tam exertè, tam signatè preci- bus commendandis incumbit, toto hæc tractatu, ac quidem supra nominatus Joh. Stoinski, qui pesti- lentissimo, Socianorum Crelli & Schlightingii commentariorum operi binis voluminibus in folio edito, Epistolam præmisit Liminarem ; sic ille, post-quam plurima in Scripturam interpretaturo requisi-verat, subdit, speciosè satis, nisi assiduis & ardentibus precibus auxilium cælitus impetret, vix est, cur sibi eam, de qua loquimur, dexteritatem, pollicere audeat. Nec plus sibi tribuat, quam ei divina benignitas largita est. & pag seq. de Spiritu loquitur qui penetralia S. paginæ introspicit. Crellius explicans quid sit homo spiritualis, est, inquit, qui non solum Spiritu Dei præditus est, sed etiam ejus ductum sequitur, & à Spiritu isto totus pendet, & alibi, Spiritus Dei ab ipso promanat & influit in homines. Quorum unum tamen infundi nobis & indi qualitates quasdam negantem audivimus antea, alter peculiare aliquod donum infundi negat. De Jona Schlightingio refertur, eum ad calcem Comment. in Epist. ad Philemona, hæc verba scripsisse. Finivi per eandem Domini nostri Jesu Christi gratiam, quæ cum Spiritu meo fuit. Ardentissimas etiam preces requirit Brenius homo Socinianus, mentem à Spiritu illustratam demum approbare spiritua-lem Christi doctrinam. Jmo Spiritum qui impertitur nobis, revelatorem vocat cælestis sapientiæ. Velthu-sius, qui infusum istud lumen negat non solum, sed tanto molimine oppugnat, nihilominus alicubi etiam Spiritui aliquid defert. Quapropter justa suspicio, sic nondum prudentiorum animis eximetur, præsertim cum Velthusii Orthodoxiam predicet tantopere Wolzogen. 3. repetantur ea quæ ante ad similem exceptionem dixi.
units.tr: 2. I deny that anything can be produced from this writing of Wolzogen to which you cannot find something similar, or indeed something more emphatic, or at least equally so, among the professed enemies of the Church and of grace. The Socinians themselves protest that an injury is done to them if they are said not to acknowledge the inability of reason without divine illumination. Nowhere does Wolzogen so vigorously and so pointedly devote himself to commending prayers as throughout this whole treatise. And indeed Johannes Stoinski, mentioned above, who prefaced a introductory letter to the most pestilential work of the Socinians, the commentaries of Crellius and Schlichting, published in two folio volumes, says, after he had asked for very many things for one who would interpret Scripture, and speaks quite splendidly: unless he obtains help from heaven by assiduous and ardent prayers, there is little reason why he should dare to promise himself that skill of which we speak. Nor let him attribute to himself more than the divine kindness has granted him. And on the following page he speaks of the Spirit who looks into the innermost parts of holy Scripture. Crellius, explaining what a spiritual man is, says: he is one who not only is endowed with the Spirit of God, but also follows his guidance, and wholly depends on that Spirit; and elsewhere: the Spirit of God flows forth from him and pours into men. We heard earlier that the one denies that certain qualities are infused into us and innate, and the other denies that any peculiar gift is infused. It is reported of Johannes Schlichting that at the end of his commentary on the Epistle to Philemon he wrote these words: I have finished with the same grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was with my spirit. The Socinian Brenius also requires most ardent prayers, so that the mind, illuminated by the Spirit, at last may approve the spiritual doctrine of Christ. Indeed, he calls the Spirit who is imparted to us the revealer of heavenly wisdom. Velthusius, who not only denies that infused light but attacks it with such great effort, nevertheless somewhere also ascribes something to the Spirit. Therefore a just suspicion will not yet be removed from the minds of the more prudent, especially since Wolzogen so loudly proclaims the orthodoxy of Velthusius. 3. Let those things be repeated which I said earlier against a similar objection.

units.la: 2. Secundum quod obtendi posset, est, providam adversus Enthusiasmum curam anxios reddidisse Wolzogium & Velthusium, sc. ne Enthusiastae etiam audiant, quos tam longe à superstitione animi & animarum tyrannide abesse audivimus. Evenit nostro Medico quod sæpius Circumforaneis erronibus & artis Medicæ ignaris agyrtis, qui humores expellere dum satagunt, nimis vehemente purgatione, cum fæcibus simul vitam abigunt: aut venæsectione pletoræ aut corruptioni aut nimiæ fermentationi sanguinis quasi opem laturi, nimia exinanitione[?] spiritus simul omnes viresque ægroto subtrahunt, eumque placida quidem at certa necant morte. Hinc nullibi aut in Pastore aut in Seniore concitatiorem offendas animum, affectus vehementiores quam ubi ad Enthusiastas ventum est, confer quæ ea de re dixi antea. Hypochondriacos autem ita excipit Medicus ut contagio nescio quo præ nimio calore & particularum motu caput ipsi affectum & lolliginis succum, jam non in Hypochondriis subsidentem, sed cerebrum versus præ nimia crebraque minimarum particularum agitatione & affectuum quasi vortice quodam, raptos & delatos verear. Quotiescunque Pastores eorumque de docendi munere speciali prærogativâ sibi demandato jactantiam videt, parum à rabie abesse videtur, gratulor mihi quod tam longè remotus ab ipsius vivam morsibus. Eadem cura jam dudum vexavit Remonstrantium, Socinianorum, Mundanorum, etiam Prophanorum & Libertinorum animos, antea jam id probatum dedimus. Appositè Tuissus. Hactenus obstupui ad dilutam illam assistentiæ Spiritus explicationem quam verbo tribuunt isti Theologi; nunc tandem aliquando mysteria sua recondita produnt; nempe ne motus aliquos Enthusiasticos introducant, ideo sibi cavent, & lectoribus suis cautum esse volunt, ne aliam assistenti Spiritui operationem tribuant, quam quod sensum verbi mentibus hominum imprimat; quod tamen si Spiritu tribuendum sit, etiam in omnibus Gentilium declamationibus Panegyricis locum habebit, etiam in ipsis Diaboli suggestionibus; ut videas lector (quod & diligenter advertas velim) quam splendidè se gerant & magnificè; dum assistentiam Spiritus amplificant, nihilo tamen efficacius sese exerentem in Euangelio, quam in moralibus Ethnicorum institutis, in orationibus Panegyricis, in ipsis Diaboli suggestionibus. --- Ne scilicet alias Enthusiastici nescio qui motus introducantur. Nec tamen cooperationem Spiritus ad actum fidei puto pro motu habent Enthusiastico. Et cur quæso determinationem Sp. ad actum fidei, addo ego illuminationem internam & determinationem ad intellectionis unumquemque actum, & conversionem motum aliquem Enthusiasticum esse volunt, potius quam cooperationem? Sed de Enthusiasmo antea actum est.
units.tr: 2. The second thing that might be put forward is that Wolzogen and Velthusius have made their provident care against Enthusiasm anxious, namely lest the Enthusiasts too should listen, whom we have heard to be so far from superstition of mind and from tyranny over souls. It happens to our Physician as it often happens to itinerant quacks and charlatans ignorant of the medical art. While they are busy expelling humours with excessive purging, they drive out life together with the dregs; or, as if to bring help against plethora, corruption or excessive fermentation of the blood by bloodletting, by excessive draining of the spirit they take away from the sick man all his strength, and kill him with a calm but certain death. Hence nowhere do you find a more agitated mind or more vehement affections in a Pastor or an Elder than where one comes to the Enthusiasts; compare what I said about this earlier. Physicians receive hypochondriacs in such a way that I fear that, by some contagion from excessive heat and motion of particles, the head is affected, and the juice of the cuttlefish, no longer settling in the hypochondria but carried toward the brain, is borne off and carried away by excessive and frequent agitation of the smallest particles and by a kind of whirlpool of the affections. Whenever he sees Pastors boasting of the special prerogative of teaching entrusted to them, he seems hardly far from rage; I congratulate myself that I am so far removed from its living bites. The same anxiety has long vexed the minds of the Remonstrants, the Socinians, the worldly, and even the profane and Libertines; we have already shown this earlier. Tuissus aptly says: Hitherto I have been astonished at that diluted explanation of the assisting of the Spirit which these theologians attribute to the Word; now at last they reveal their hidden mysteries: namely, lest they introduce some Enthusiastic motions, they take care, and want their readers to be on guard, not to attribute to the assisting Spirit any operation other than that it impresses the sense of the word on human minds. But if this is to be attributed to the Spirit, it will also have its place in all the panegyric declamations of the Gentiles, and even in the very suggestions of the Devil. So you may see, reader (and I would like you to notice this carefully), how splendidly and magnificently they conduct themselves while they magnify the assistance of the Spirit, which nonetheless exerts itself no more effectively in the Gospel than in the moral institutions of the Gentiles, in panegyric orations, and in the very suggestions of the Devil. --- Namely, lest some Enthusiastic motions of I know not what kind be introduced. Nor do I think they regard the cooperation of the Spirit to the act of faith as an Enthusiastic motion. And why, I ask, do they wish the determination of the Spirit to the act of faith (I add: the inner illumination and determination to each act of understanding) and the conversion to be some Enthusiastic motion, rather than cooperation? But concerning Enthusiasm it has been treated before.

units.la: 3. Tertium est, argumentorum illa, tam solide & firmiter concatenata series & copia, quam ita largitur profudit Medicus. Verè de eo dicitur, quod in Paradoxo notat Celeberr. Marefius, pari loco habet scientiam Philosophicam & fidem, lumen naturale & revelatum. Hæc Thesis est: neque illa cognitio, loquitur de naturali, est aliud genus luminis, quam illius cujus est cognitio rerum spiritualium, Vis rationem? sic pro sua nova Methodo Medicus nulla ratione aliter conconcipere licet. Ita solet plerumque argumentari, & fungi tales dantur, qui nec Philosophos nec Theologos genuinos unquam legerunt, quibus interim oracula fundere videtur iste, magnus sc Philosophus. Sed pergat. Nam quandoquidem hic sermo est de cognitione vera, nulla ratione concipere licet; quomodo cognitio alicujus rei vera, possit esse tenebrae: at bone vir quis unquam ullam cognitionem veram, aut absolute, aut in quantum vera est, tenebras dixit? nemo tam bardus est, quanquam tacitè aliis tantam stupiditatem imputare studeas. An nescis distinguere genus à genere, spirituale à naturali, regenitum ab irregenito? an non potest esse, vera rerum naturalium, terrenorum, quaedam cognitio, qua non obstante, respectu spiritualium, spiritualis quo ea concipiuntur modi homo ejusque intel-lectus dicantur tenebrae? & mente excaecati? quasi lectusdicantur tenebrae? & mente excaecati? quasi naturaliter vivens, spiritualiter mortuus & à vita Dei alienatus dici, nequeat? quasi quaedam naturalia, terrena dicit Velthuisen, verè per naturam cognoscentes, mentè excaecati dici non possint? Verum falleris vehementer, aut Ephesii omni modo mortui, eorumque Doctissimi omni modo amentes, ex tua sententia fuerunt ante conversionem: erant enim, Apostolo judice, non obstante vita naturali mortui spiritualiter, & non obstante etiam vera quorundam terrenorum cognitione, olim mente excaecati, imo tenebrae. Quorsum igitur haec verba, sc. ut ne alia, praeter τὸ[?], non licet concipere, desit ratio: cum utraque cognitio tam spiritualium quam rerum terrenarum sit à Deo, sit veritas, sit regula ad quam homines rectè vitam suam componunt &c. quid inde? nihil aliud, quam, quod naturaliter verum est illud revera verum esse & merito pro vero haberi. At longe aliud quid hinc extundet Medicus. Propter eadem, inquit, rationes unum tantum luminis genus mente concipere licet. Nisi lapidem Philosophorum invenisses, procul dubio fugerent te istiusmodi proces-sus. Quis vortex te circumagit? an forsan Saturni sit, an alterius erratici syderis, dicant, qui vorticum tuorum norunt gyros, Utraque cognitio à Deo est, in quantum vera est, concedo; utraque veritas, in quantum a Deo, concedo; utraque vitæ regula, in quantum vera & justa, concedo; quid autem jam porro? ergo tantum unum genus luminis, utrumque à Deo ergo utrumque idem: Weigelium legisti procul dubio. Homo est à Deo, bestia est à Deo, ergo unum & idem &c. sic fere insanus ille Enthusiasta. Sumamus objecta scientiæ humanæ, tam terrena, quam cælestia, & videamus quid ex tuis fundamentis de iis concludendum sit, utraque à Deo, utraque vera &c. ergo tantum unum genus objectorum: egregie! sic omnia idem, quia à Deo, modo vera. Conveniunt fateor in aliquo tertio, sc. quod utrum-que lumen, lumen sit. Sic forsan aliquo respectu, ejusdem generis, dici possent. At quæ in aliquo su-periori genere, quodam respectu, conveniunt, ea nihilominus, si descendamus paulò inferius, toto ge-nere differre possunt. In genere entis conveniunt Deus & homo, vermis & Angelus, quæ tamen ge-nere differre, non negabit nisi insanus. Vel si ita pla-cet, sufficiet dixisse quod specie differat à naturali, de quo disputamus, habituale, infusum lumen. Can-dide profiteris D. Doctor te ne tanti quidem facere Logicam Peripateticam aut Ramæam, quæ alias, genus summum & subalternum, aut species quid sint, te docuisset facili negotio. Restat adhuc nodus satis durus, sic pergit, quibus etiam hoc argumentum addere lubet. Quod, cum cognitio vera sit adæquatio conceptus, sive judicii conformitas cum re, de qua conceptus formatur, aut de qua judicatur, tam ineptum & frivolum est docere diversitatem & multitudinem lu-miminum, quam diversitatem adæquationum, aut diversam, judiciorum confirmitatem cum re, de qua judicium formatum est. Hæc sc. argumenta ista sunt Apo-dictica quæ à Theologia aliena esse arbitrantur te Judice Theologi, quapropter & frustra evidentia argumento-rum cum iis pugnes. Rem habet cum Theologis, ideoque argumenta etiam profert non Apodictica, sic iis morem gerit vir modestus & ab argumentis Apodicticis sibi magno molimine temperat. Et quia frustra cum iis evidentibus pugnatur, obscuris eos aggreditur, ut mirari subiret lucis filium, tam densa caligine circumfusum, in prælium tanquam in scenam prodiisse, nisi cum Theologis ipsi rem esse, aut potius spiritualibus quibusdam Pastorculis, iterato inculcasset. Ex ungue Leonem. Hic saltem ita clare & distincte scribis, ut quid ipse velis ignorasse te putem. Cognitio vera est adæquatio conceptus cum re, in conceptu autem, sive apprehensione simplici quoniam etiam rei adæquatio esse possit, vel non adæquatio, ut ita loquiar, hoc est rem per eam repræsentari uti est, vel aliter quam est, necesse est etiam in simplicem apprehensionem veritatem cadere & falsitatem, si verum sit, quicquid rei adæquatum est:quod, quo modo rationi congruat nec ne, nunc non determino, sodalis autem tuus & amicus Joh.de Bruin cum plurimis aliis in sim-plicium apprehensione nullum errorem locum habere posse, docet, ergo & nulla veritas, quod tibi adversatur. Ut autem clare loquaris, duo dicis adæquationem sc. conceptus, sive judicii; quæ si diversa tibi significent, sequitur, aut apprehensionem simplicem conceptum dici non posse, aut in apprehensionem simplicem veritatem cadere & falsitatem, illud contra Etymologiam, hoc contra amicum tuum. Si vero declarativè sumas pro eodem, tum omnis conceptus adæquatus etiam simplex, nam & ille conceptus est, actus judicii statuitur, quod absurdum. Aliud est, & magis generale conceptus, quam judicium, multa enim concipiuntur, de quibus non judicamus. Ut ex hypothesibus tuis clare loquaris, dic potius, adæquatio conceptus complexi & judicii cum re est cognitio vera, hoc est vera cognitio est ve-ra. Sed transeat. Hæc argumenti vis est: ineptum & frivolum esse, docere diversitatem & multitudinem adæquationum, ergo & luminum. Notandum est. 1. Te actua-lem cognitionem, ipsam intellectionem, mentis istum actum, confundere cum suo principio. conf. p. 14. Aliud enim est mens ab ejus actione; aliud mentis lumen, quod principii qualitativè instar mentem evehit, elevat &c. aliud actio, intellectio, cognitio, à mente sive illuminata sive non illuminatâ elicita. 2. Eandem rem, idem objectum, à diversis, pro diversitate recipientium & concipientium, aut potius pro diversitate principii quo unum est receptivum alterius, id est, aptitudinem habet rem illam recipiendi sibique de hac aut illa re conceptum formandi, unde oritur cognitio, diversas fieri ejusdem rei repræsentationes seu adæquationes & quidem necessario. Sic autem sese res habet in hoc negotio, deest in uno aptitudo subjecti, deest qualitas illa spiritualis, quæ adest in altero, quo posito, aliter fieri non potest, quin alia sit & alia ejusdem rei repræsentatio, prout aliter subjectum dispositum & aptum vel ineptum est, tam quoad aptitudinem & recipiendi principium, quam, exinde resultantem, diversum percipiendi modum. Hoc oppugnare debuisset, non præterire, non dissimulare. Quoniam autem Philosophari lubet Velthusio, videamus an hanc sapientiæ Velthusianæ abyssum' pervestigare detur. Nunc autem ut specimen habeas tuæ soliditatis, videasque, vires tuæ & molimina quo subvertantur, novas machinas non requiri, exscribam quædam ex
units.tr: 3. The third point is the series and abundance of arguments, so firmly and solidly linked, which the physician pours out so lavishly. What Maresius, the distinguished man, notes in his Paradox is truly applicable here: he places philosophical knowledge and faith, natural light and revealed light, on the same level. This is the thesis: that natural knowledge (he speaks of the natural kind) is no different kind of light from that whose object is the knowledge of spiritual things. Do you ask for a reason? According to his new method the physician says it is in no way possible to conceive otherwise. That is how such men usually argue, and there are people who have never read genuine philosophers or theologians, yet to whom he seems to pour out oracles, this great philosopher of his. But let him go on. Since here we are speaking of true knowledge, it is in no way possible to conceive how a true knowledge of anything could be darkness. But, good sir, who has ever called any true knowledge darkness, whether absolutely or insofar as it is true? No one is so dull, although you tacitly try to impute such stupidity to others. Do you not know how to distinguish genus from genus, spiritual from natural, the regenerate from the unregenerate? Can there not be some true knowledge of natural and earthly things, which, nevertheless, in relation to spiritual things, is called darkness, and the man and his understanding, in the way they conceive spiritual things, are called blinded in mind? Is it that a man living naturally and dead spiritually, and alienated from the life of God, cannot be so called? Is it that certain natural and earthly things, which Velthuysen says are known truly through nature, cannot be said to be blinded in mind? You are gravely mistaken. Either the Ephesians were wholly dead, and their most learned men wholly mad, by your opinion, before their conversion. For, according to the Apostle, they were spiritually dead despite their natural life, and blinded in mind, indeed darkness, despite the true knowledge of certain earthly things. Why, then, these words, that (so that nothing else, beyond [τὸ?], may not be conceived) there is no reason: since each knowledge, both of spiritual things and of earthly things, is from God, is truth, is the rule by which men rightly order their lives, etc. What follows from this? Nothing except that what is naturally true is really true and rightly held to be true. But the physician will draw something quite different from this. For the same reasons, he says, it is possible to conceive only one kind of light in the mind. Unless you had found the philosophers' stone, such procedures would surely escape you. What whirlpool is spinning you around? Let those who know the circuits of your whirlpools say whether it belongs to Saturn or some other wandering star. Each knowledge is from God, insofar as it is true, I grant; each truth, insofar as it is from God, I grant; each rule of life, insofar as it is true and just, I grant. But what then follows? Therefore only one kind of light, since both are from God, therefore both are the same. You have undoubtedly read Weigel. Man is from God, a beast is from God, therefore one and the same, and so on. That is nearly how that madman, the Enthusiast, argues. Let us take the objects of human knowledge, both earthly and heavenly, and see what must be concluded about them from your foundations: both from God, both true, etc. Therefore only one kind of object. Splendid! So everything is the same, because from God and merely true. I admit they agree in some third thing, namely, that each light is light. So perhaps in some respect they could be said to be of the same kind. But things that agree in some higher genus, in some respect, may nevertheless, if we descend a little lower, differ in their whole genus. Within the genus of being, God and man agree, and worm and angel agree, yet no one but a madman would deny that they differ in genus. Or, if you prefer, it will be enough to say that the habitual, infused light differs in species from the natural light we are discussing. Frankly, Doctor, you confess that you do not think much of Peripatetic or Ramist logic, which would have taught you with little effort what the highest and subordinate genus are, or what species are. There remains a fairly hard knot, he goes on: to which I also wish to add this argument. Since true knowledge is the adequation of a concept, or the conformity of a judgement with the thing of which the concept is formed or about which a judgement is made, it is as absurd and frivolous to teach a diversity and multitude of lights as it is to teach a diversity of adequations, or a different conformity of judgements with the thing about which the judgement is formed. These arguments, he says, are apodictic arguments, which the theologians think alien to theology, in your judgement, theologians, wherefore you fight in vain against them with evident arguments. He has to do with theologians, and so he also brings forward arguments that are not apodictic. Thus the modest man accommodates them, and with great effort refrains from apodictic arguments. And because it is in vain to fight with them using evident arguments, he attacks them with obscure ones, so that one would be surprised that a son of light, wrapped in such thick darkness, came out into battle as if onto a stage, had he not repeatedly reminded us that the matter concerns theologians, or rather certain spiritual little shepherds. You recognize the lion by its claw. Here, at least, you write so clearly and distinctly that I think you do not know what you yourself mean. True knowledge is the adequation of a concept with a thing. But since in a concept, or simple apprehension, there can also be an adequation of the thing, or not an adequation, so to speak (that is, whether the thing is represented through it as it is, or otherwise than it is), it is necessary that truth and falsity fall even on simple apprehension, if true is whatever is adequate to the thing. Whether this agrees with reason or not, I do not now determine. But your companion and friend Joh. de Bruin teaches, with very many others, that no error can have a place in simple apprehensions, therefore also no truth, which is contrary to you. Moreover, to speak clearly, you say two things, adequation, namely, of concept or of judgement. If these signify different things to you, it follows either that simple apprehension cannot be called a concept, or that truth and falsity fall on simple apprehension, the former against etymology, the latter against your friend. But if you take them declaratively as the same thing, then every adequate concept is also simple, for it too is a concept, while the act of judgement is established, which is absurd. The concept is one thing, and more general than judgement, for many things are conceived about which we do not judge. To speak clearly from your hypotheses, rather say: the adequation of a complex concept and judgement with the thing is true knowledge, that is, true knowledge is true. But let that pass. The force of the argument is this: it is absurd and frivolous to teach a diversity and multitude of adequations, therefore also of lights. It must be noted: 1. You confuse the actual knowledge, the intellection itself, this act of the mind, with its principle (see p. 14). For the mind is one thing, its act another; the light of the mind, which qualitatively raises and elevates the mind as its principle, is one thing; the act, the intellection, the knowledge, elicited from the mind whether illuminated or not, is another. 2. The same thing, the same object, is received in different ways by different recipients and conceivers, or rather according to the diversity of the principle by which one thing is receptive of another, that is, has the aptitude to receive that thing and to form a concept of this or that thing, from which knowledge arises. So many different representations, or adequations, of the same thing necessarily arise. Now the matter stands thus in this business: in one there is lacking the aptitude of the subject, that spiritual quality is lacking which is present in the other. Given this, it cannot happen otherwise than that the representation of the same thing is one thing in one case and another in the other, according as the subject is otherwise disposed and apt or inept, both as to the aptitude and principle of receiving and, resulting from this, as to the different mode of perceiving. This is what you ought to have attacked, not passed over or dissembled. But since it pleases Velthuysen to philosophise, let us see whether it is possible to search out this abyss of Velthuysian wisdom. Now, however, so that you may have a specimen of your solidity, and see that your strength and efforts are overthrown, and that no new machines are needed, I shall copy out certain passages from the First Philosophy of Bisterfeld, which will suffice to dispel these clouds of multiplicity, so to speak, of adequations, thrown at us. I pass over the reproof of your wording, for adequate concepts are not many, even if true. Thus he says every being is perceptive, that is, every being is apt...

units.la: Philosophia Prima Bisterfeldii, quæ sufficient ad dispellendas hasce, de multiplicitate, ut ita loquar, adæ-quationum, nobis objectas nebulas. Verbi reprehensionem praetermitto, adaequati enim multi non sunt conceptus, licet veri. Sic ille omne ens est perceptivum, id est, omne ens est aptum natum, entis similitudinem in se habere. Sic quaelibet substantia, etiam inanimata & simplex, est perceptiva. Quodlibet enim corpus recipit radios seu efficacias cujuslibet corporis, in proportionali sphaera activitatis siti, & quidem tum suae, tum recepti naturae convenienter --- Quia cognitio, est perceptio, & quidem vitalis, necessum est ut sit rei, & cognoscenti & cognoscendae, & mutuae ipsarum habitudini & statui proportionalis, & quia in cognoscente requiritur proportio, utique entia, in quibus non est ista capacitas, non possunt cognoscere illa quae vim suam excedunt. Ergo sensus non cognoscit spirituale; Facultas naturalis non elevata non cognoscit supernaturalia, nec supernaturaliter. Diversitatem subjectivae dispositionis & principii, quo apti sumus percipere, docuimus, quam, modi percipiendi, necesse est, ut sequatur diversitas; nec tamen diversitatem aut multiplicitatem adaequationis videt Medicus. Subdit vero haec sequentia. Et in die quo judicabit Dominus de rebus occultis hominum ex Evangelio suo, tunc improbos non alio lumine suae impietatis convincet quam quo sancti in vita aestimarunt quid sui esset officii: 2. Cor. v. 21. Rom. ii. 15. Non percipio sane quid velis, visne Deum juxta aliam normam tunc non judicaturum, quam quae nunc vivendi regula data & aliquatenus conscientiae a natura insculpta est? bene habet, concedo: sed quid hoc ad rhombum, de lumine & dispositione & aptitudine subjecti loquimur. Velan hoc vis, idem lumen, eadem insita justi rectique cognitio naturalis, quae impios tum convincet, piis jam officii index est? hoc quidem in tantum verum est, in quantum naturalis Synteresis piis aeque ac impiis communis est. At qui haec ferient hunc scopum? Revera principium petis turpissime, hoc enim est quod quaeritur, an non aliud fit in fidelibus ac in infidelibus lumen, quo hic illuminati illic judicandi erunt. Quod Scripturæ ista loca attinet, dicis causa ea addita videntur, ego saltem nescio quid ex iis extundere velis, unus enim juxta opera, alter ex conscientiæ testimonio, utrosque judicandos asserit. Dum autem locum Rom. II. 15. huc pertrahis, præter conscientiam ut à natura omnibus inest gentibus & id quod ea per se dictat, nihil admittere videris. Hæ sunt præmissæ, sic sonat conclusio. Proprie itaque loquendo, lumen non est varium, sc. dispositio, habitus, qualitas subjecti, non est varia, licet res, quæ cognoscuntur, sint diversæ, spirituales & terrenæ. Multum largiris, res sunt diversæ, quis autem ex rerum, quæ menti objiciuntur, diversitate, unicè aut præcipuè argumentatus est? subjecti, dispositionis qualitativè diversitas bene considerata, & inde percipiendi varius modus, ea sunt, quæ luminis diversitatem requirant & arguant præcipuè, manente licet eadem formali cognitionis ratione, quam in convenientia conceptus cum re positam dixeras. Eandem angeli speciem recipiebat Asinus, eandem Bileam, utriusque receptionis veritas consistebat in convenientia speciei visibilis cum objecto, nec tamen non differebant specie, utriusque visionis & principium & modus. Alias vero, quid ni lumen Diaboli, à lumine fidelium, ab Angelorum, non differet? ubivis enim manet eadem formalis ratio, sc. conceptus ista adæquatio &c. Pariter, inquis, non ideo luminis discri-men est introducendum, quia facultas mediorum est di-versa. Quid audio, media cognitionis acquirendæ, ea & suas facultates habent? Quis etiam inde rursus aut unicè aut præcipuè rationes deducit?
