Revelari procul dubio quædam potuissent, quæ mera naturali, qualem nunc habemus, potentia, absque ullo superindito principio capere potuisset homo peccator, non igitur quod revelata sunt quæ capienda, sed quod talia revelata quæ absque eo infuso habitu recipi nequeant, hoc est quod statuunt Reformati, quodque, tam ex subjecti, quam objecti consideratione, abundè probant. Hinc non mediorum facul-tas, quod nihil est dicere, sed recipientis cognoscentis facultas diversa est, cujus diversitatem sequitur modi perceptionis diversitas: quæ necessario luminis habitualis inferunt diversitatem, imo per se ponunt. Nec inficias eo ex propositionis diversitate primario hanc diversitatem non inferri. Revelationis vero veritatem non aliter quam per artificialia argumenta constare posse, ita laxè, falso dicitur; etenim Deus immediatè aliquid ita revelare posset, ut statim, uno obtutu quasi, constaret, istud Deum loqui, à Deo dictari. An visionibus inspirationibus fidem non nisi artificialibus argumentis permotos adhibuisse credis prophetas? Sicuti sensibus sua se objecta ita sæpe ingerunt, ut ex illo attactu statim percipiantur, non implorato artificialium argumentorum subsidio, sic etiam mens aliquando, quid ni affici possit, explicet disputator: si verba & quidem scripta adhibeantur, medium intervenit quidem artificiale, sed percepto, per illud medium, eo, quod significare Deus instituerat, fides jam non in signa sed authoritatem resolvitur Dei: obsignatio etiam Spiritus interna, testimonium illud de quo Rom. viii. quibus argumentis artificialibus totum nitatur docere velim. Simile quod fingis non probat, ut notum est. Quoniam autem ipse alibi te refutas; te cum te ipso committere satis erit, sic enim Deus multis modis suam voluntatem manifestavit: --- unus est quo ἐμέσως[?] mentem hominis instruit, & quidem aliquando absque loquela & signis; per se in mente hominis excitat cognitionem. Necdum satis argumentorum; pergis, neque diversitatem luminis introducit, quod nos aliter atque aliter afficimur ex cognitione alicus rei, si modo cognitio rei sit æque clara & evidens. Quid ni addis, modo cognitio sit eadem? sic enim poneres quod in quæstione est, à qua absurditate non longe abes. Deinde aliter & aliter affici ab eadem re duo possent, ut toto genere differat ejusdem rei in uno ab eâ quæ in alio est receptio, & subjecti recipientis conditio. Lumen profers Solis, sed radios & calorem emittat in vividam simul & aridam, mortuam quam dicimus, arborem, nonne specie differet ejusdem luminis in hac & in illa receptio. Cæcum simul & videndi facultate prædi-tum, idem offendat Solis lumen, cadaver & vivum corpus idem calor, & vide, quanta, subjecti recipien-tis, receptionisque, apparitura sit diversitas. Cognitio,ais, Euangelica eadem est, sive unus ea cognitione imbutus, idem quo ad mores maneat, qui erat ante fidem, & alter eo lu-mine ita afficiatur, ut in imaginem Dei transformetur. Quod verba, tot hæreses, judicet Ecclesia Refor-mata ex Dei verbo, idem fateor cognitionis obje-ctum, sed eadem cognitio, quanta insania! ergo cui Euangelium stultitia est, illi, eadem erit cogni-tio cum eo cui est potentia Dei ad salutem. Dia-bolus sic eandem nobiscum Euangelii cognitionem habet, Animalis cum Spirituali, cui non est datum nosse, cum eo cui datum, occæcato cum illumi-natis, omnibus quippe aliquo modo innotuit Euan-gelium. Quo ruis dementiæ homo animalis? (spiri-tuales enim contemtim alios appellitas) sed aliud ad-huc virus in his verbis detegendum, homines fir[?]is eosdem quo ad mores, qui erant ante fidem: quale[?]m[?] fingis fidem? putasne veram fidem non purificare corda Act. xv. 1. Joh. iii. Christum ut Sanctifica-torem non apprehendere? sed quorsum ista tibi? non intelligis satis scio. Nisi forsan fides etiam eadem tibi sit, quæ temporalis dicitur, quæ Historica, cum ea, quam salvificam vocamus. Et certe si, quæ de cognitionis luminisque eadem natura somnias, sive pios sive impios, regenitos aut irregenitos tibi objiciant, si ea, inquam, rité ad animum revocentur, necessario idem de fide concludendum patebit statim, quod tu de cognitione fingis, eandem specie omnibus esse, quid ni & Diabolis quoniam & credere dicuntur, nec video quid ex tua hypothesi in contrarium dici possit. Hæc tu concoquere potes Wolzogi, in Ecclesiæ membro, in Seniore. O veritatis! O pietatis! o Ecclesiæ fortem deplorandam! Sic superba mundi sapientia dominabitur, obtestor omnes quotquot supersunt veritatis amatores & vindices, ut legant, ut videant, quid à Velthusio & aliis ejusdem farinæ hominibus, Ecclesiæ, pietati, veritati expectandum sit, oppressio, contumelia, devastatio. Et anseres aliquando Capitolio profuerunt maximè. Utinam per me minimum Christi servum & in Ecclesiæ excubiis positum vigilem expergiscant viri Docti, Pii; quò prece, quò calamo, quò ore & tota armatura spirituali se hisce objiciant periculis! Necesse erit, ut & plebs Christiana, malorum conscia, non ignoret, quanti fiat veritas. Præcipuè autem id fieri posset, si Belgico idiomate exponerentur, hujus, similiumque, fætidi & perniciosissimi errores. Tales enim alit qui Socinianos superent, quod vel ex iis, quæ diximus, probari potest. Illi enim de cognitione de fide vix talia, de Spiritus operatione longè speciosiora, tradunt.
units.tr: Bisterfeld's First Philosophy, which will suffice to dispel those clouds of multiplicity, so to speak, of adequations, thrown up against us. I pass over the criticism of his wording, for adequate concepts are not many, though they are true. Thus he writes: every being is perceptive, that is, every being is by nature fitted to have in itself the likeness of a being. So any substance, even inanimate and simple, is perceptive. For every body receives the rays or efficacies of any body situated within its proportional sphere of activity, and indeed in a manner suited both to its own nature and to that of what it receives --- Because cognition is perception, and indeed vital perception, it must be proportional to the thing and to the knower, and to their mutual relation and state; and because proportion is required in the knower, beings in which this capacity is absent cannot know those things which exceed their power. Therefore sense does not know the spiritual; a natural faculty not raised up does not know supernatural things, nor does it know them supernaturally. We have taught the diversity of the subjective disposition and of the principle by which we are fitted to perceive; and necessarily a diversity of the modes of perceiving follows from it. Yet the physician does not see any diversity or multiplicity of adequation. He adds, however, the following: And on the day when the Lord shall judge the hidden things of men by his Gospel, then he will convict the wicked by no other light of their impiety than that by which the saints in life judged what their duty was: 2 Cor. 5:21. Rom. 2:15. Frankly, I do not perceive what you mean. Do you want to say that God will not then judge by any other norm than the rule of living now given, and in some measure engraved on conscience by nature? Very well, I concede it; but what does this have to do with the point? We are speaking of light, and of the disposition and aptitude of the subject. Do you mean that the same light, the same innate natural knowledge of right and wrong, which will then convict the impious, is already a guide to duty for the pious? This is true to the extent that natural synteresis is common to the pious as well as the impious. But do these arguments hit the mark? Really you beg the question most shamefully, for this is exactly what is in dispute: whether the light in believers is not different from the light in unbelievers, by which the one are illuminated and the others are to be judged. As for those passages of Scripture, you cite them, it seems, for show; I at least do not know what you wish to extract from them, for the one asserts that each will be judged, the one by works, the other by the testimony of conscience. But when you drag in Rom. 2:15, you seem to admit nothing beyond the conscience that is in all Gentiles by nature, and what it dictates of itself. These are the premises; the conclusion reads thus: Properly speaking, therefore, light is not varied, namely the disposition, habit and quality of the subject is not varied, although the things which are known are diverse, spiritual and earthly. You concede a great deal: the things are diverse. But who has argued, solely or chiefly, from the diversity of the things presented to the mind? It is the qualitative diversity of the subject and its disposition, rightly considered, and the varied mode of perceiving that follows from it, which chiefly require and prove a diversity of light, even though the formal ground of cognition remains the same, which you had placed in the agreement of concept with thing. The ass received the same image of the angel, and so did Balaam; the truth of each reception consisted in the agreement of the visible species with the object, and yet the principle and the mode of each vision differed in kind. Otherwise, why would the light of the devil not differ from the light of believers, or from that of angels? For everywhere the same formal ground remains, namely that adequation of concept, and so on. Likewise, you say, a distinction of light should not be introduced on the ground that the faculty of the means is diverse. What do I hear? Do the means of acquiring knowledge have faculties of their own? And who again deduces arguments from this, solely or chiefly? Certainly some things could have been revealed which a sinful man could grasp by mere natural power, such as he now has, without any superadded principle. Therefore it is not because the things to be grasped are revealed, but because such things are revealed as cannot be received without that infused habit, that the Reformed hold this, and they prove it abundantly from the consideration of both subject and object. Hence it is not the faculty of the means, which is to say nothing, but the faculty of the receiving knower that is diverse, and the diversity of the mode of perception follows from its diversity; and these necessarily imply, indeed in themselves posit, a diversity of habitual light. Nor do I deny that this diversity is not primarily inferred from the diversity of the proposition. But that the truth of revelation can exist in no other way than by artificial arguments is said loosely and falsely; for God could reveal something immediately in such a way that at a single glance, as it were, it is established that God speaks and that it is dictated by God. Do you think the prophets were moved to faith by visions and inspirations and used nothing but artificial arguments? Just as objects often impose themselves on the senses so that they are perceived at once from that contact, without calling for the aid of artificial arguments, so too the mind can sometimes be affected in the same way. The disputant explains: if words, and indeed written words, are used, an artificial medium does intervene; but once that which God had appointed to signify has been perceived through that medium, faith is no longer resolved into the signs but into the authority of God. So too is the internal sealing of the Spirit, that testimony of which Rom. 8 speaks. I would like to teach what artificial arguments the whole rests on, but I cannot. The similar thing you invent proves nothing, as is well known. Since you refute yourself elsewhere, it will be enough to set you against yourself, for God has made his will known in many ways: ... one is that by which he instructs the mind of man immediately [ἀμέσως], and indeed at times without speech and signs; by himself he excites cognition in the mind of man. Nor are there yet enough arguments; you go on: nor does it introduce a diversity of light, that we are affected in one way and another by the knowledge of some thing, provided the knowledge of the thing is equally clear and evident. Why do you not add: provided the knowledge is the same? For in that way you would assume what is in question, and from such an absurdity you are not far away. Next, two things might affect the same thing differently, so that the reception of the same thing in one differs wholly in kind from that in another, and likewise the condition of the receiving subject. You offer the light of the sun; but if it sends its rays and heat upon a living tree and upon a dry tree, which we call dead, does not the reception of the same light differ in kind between this and that? Let the same sunlight fall upon a blind man, and upon one who is also endowed with the faculty of sight; let the same heat fall upon a corpse and a living body; and see how great a diversity of receiving subject and of reception will appear. Evangelical cognition, you say, is the same, whether one imbued with that knowledge remains in the same morals as he was before faith, and another is so affected by that light that he is transformed into the image of God. As for the words, let the Reformed Church judge from God's Word how many heresies they contain; I concede the same object of knowledge, but the same knowledge? What madness! So for one to whom the Gospel is foolishness, the knowledge will be the same as for one to whom it is the power of God unto salvation. The devil thus has the same knowledge of the Gospel as we do. The animal man has it along with the spiritual man, to whom it is not given to know, along with him to whom it is given; the blinded along with the enlightened, for the Gospel has in some way become known to all. Where are you rushing, animal man, in your madness? (For you contemptuously call others spiritual.) But there is yet another poison to be uncovered in these words: men [remain] the same in morals as they were before faith. What kind of faith do you imagine? Do you think true faith does not purify the heart (Acts 15:1; John 3), and does not lay hold of Christ as Sanctifier? But why do you say these things? I know well that you do not understand them. Unless perhaps faith is for you also the same as what is called temporal, historical faith, the same as that which we call saving. And certainly, if the things you dream about the nature of cognition and light, whether of pious or impious, regenerate or unregenerate, are rightly recalled to mind, it will immediately be evident that one must conclude the same about faith as you feign about cognition: that it is the same in kind for all. Why not for devils too, since they are said to believe? I do not see what can be said against this on your hypothesis. Can you digest these things, Wolzogen, as a member of the Church, as an elder? O truth! O piety! O deplorable state of the Church! Thus proud worldly wisdom will hold sway. I beseech all who remain lovers and defenders of the truth to read and see what is to be expected from Velthusius and others of the same stamp: for the Church, for piety, for truth, oppression, contumely and devastation. And geese have sometimes been of the greatest use to the Capitol. Would that through me, the least servant of Christ, placed on watch in the Church, learned and pious men might be roused and throw themselves into these dangers with prayer, with pen, with voice and with the whole spiritual armour! The Christian populace, aware of its troubles, will also necessarily not be ignorant of how much the truth is worth. This could be done especially if the foul and most pernicious errors of these men, and of others like them, were set out in the Dutch language. For such men as surpass the Socinians nourish such errors, as can be proved even from what we have said. For they hand down about cognition and faith hardly anything of the kind, and about the operation of the Spirit things far more specious.

units.la: Tertium sequitur errorum Wolzogianorum caput, quod est de Scripturæ, liceat sic Barbarè loqui, intelli-gibilitate. Reformati ita Scripturam divino jussu in-stinctuque exaratam esse docent, ut clarè & perspicuè menti illuminatæ, quæ creditu factuve necessaria sunt, offerat. Nec opus est id multis probare. Locorum communium scriptores, inter perfectiones, perspicuitatem referent, ad unum omnes. Scripturam itaque volunt, ejusque in necessariis sensum, rite intelligi posse, diverso quamvis modo: aliter enim homo naturalis videt, spiritualis aliter, vel eandem licet veritatem videat uterque. Recipiens quippe unumquodque recipit pro suo modulo. Principio diverso, potentia diversa, quæ prædita sunt, diverso etiam modo agere debent necessario. Sic & hic sese res habet, idem quando repræsentatur homini naturali objectum, ac spirituali, uterque idem necessario recipit, at pro suo quisque modulo; spiritualis, qua talis, spiritualiter; naturalis è contra naturaliter. Hoc volunt Orthodoxi, quando sensum Grammaticum & literalem solum, non vero vero spiritualem percipere statuunt hominem animalem. Eundem licet sensum, veritatem eandum [?] percipiant, quippe diverso tamen modo, atque ex diverso agunt principio. Regenitum vero ac illuminatum, potentiæ naturali infuso habitu gaudentem, sicque in aliam, ut ita loquar, activitatis sphæram translatum, eum recipere spiritualiter. Non enim, quod in transcursu notandum, eventum, Reformati quando ita phrasin instituunt, eos unicè vel præcipue respicere putandum est, ac si salutaris perceptio, quæ & quia solummodo cum salute nexum habet, dicatur, specie quamvis ab alia illa, quæ non salutaris evadit, non diversa: quemadmodum Remonstrantes de salvifica & salutari fide perperam philosophantur; principium agens, agendique diversum plane modum respiciunt. Ut, licet cum irregenito idem videat regenitus, ut talis, (potest enim subinde, partim adhuc corrupto intellectu, Spiritus gratia actuali tantisper ipsum non excitante, minus bene ac spiritualiter agere, aut quidquam recipere) ex alio tamen & diverso agens principio, modo etiam plane diverso, spirituali ac salutari, id videat, quod irregenitus modo naturali, non salu-
units.tr: The third chief error of the Wolzogians follows, concerning the intelligibility of Scripture, if I may put it so barbarously. The Reformed teach that Scripture was written by divine command and inspiration in such a way that it presents clearly and plainly to an enlightened mind what must be believed or done. There is no need to prove this at length. The writers of common places (loci communes) all, without exception, count perspicuity among the perfections of Scripture. They therefore hold that Scripture, and its sense in necessary matters, can be rightly understood, though in different ways: the natural man sees one way, the spiritual man another, even when both see the same truth. For whatever receives, receives according to its own measure. Since the faculties are endowed with different principles, they must necessarily act in different ways. So it is here as well: when the same object is presented to the natural man and to the spiritual man, each necessarily receives the same thing, but each according to his own measure. The spiritual man, as such, receives it spiritually; the natural man, on the contrary, naturally. This is what the Orthodox mean when they hold that the natural man perceives only the grammatical and literal sense and not the spiritual sense. Though both perceive the same sense and the same truth, they do so in different ways and from different principles. The regenerate and enlightened man, who enjoys a natural power infused with a habit, and who has thus been transferred into another sphere of activity, so to speak, receives it spiritually. We must note in passing that when the Reformed frame their language this way, they should not be thought to have in view only, or chiefly, the saving perception, as if it were called saving only because it is joined with salvation alone, and as if it were not different in kind from that other perception, which does not turn out to be saving. The Remonstrants philosophize wrongly about saving and salutary faith in this way: they look only at the acting principle and at a manner of acting that is entirely different. So, although the regenerate man sees the same thing as the unregenerate man, as such (for at times, his understanding being still partly corrupt, and the Spirit not stirring him by actual grace for the moment, he may act less well and less spiritually, or receive nothing), he nonetheless sees it from another and different principle, and in an entirely different, spiritual and saving manner, what the unregenerate man sees in a natural and not a saving way.

units.la: Eundem ... eandum: possibly printing error for eandem, as printed. tari videt. Jmo, vel pauciora intelligat quam naturalis, spiritualiter tamen ea intelligit ac salutariter. Cumque sensu quoque & gustu quodam spirituali, in res ipsas quasi intromittatur, eaeque ipsi vicissim quasi ingerantur, hinc experimentalis illa oritur & suavissima cognitio. Ita ut, res omnis si penitius ponderetur, diversa plane appareat quae nobis, cum Pontificiis singillatim, ab ea, quae cum Pelagianis in universum omnibus intercedit controversia. Cum illis etenim seorsim consideratis, (in posteriori controversia idem quippe cum reliquis Pelagianis faciunt) in loco de Scriptura quando disputatur, de ejus perspicuitate discrimen est, & quidem objectiva proprie. Nimirum, an in se talis sit, ut intelligibiliter piis & regenitis propohat[?], ea, quae sciri ab ipsis aut peragi debent. Adversus Pelagianos autem, de salutari Scripturae perceptione quando disputamus, subjecti, hominis vires, aptitudo, facultas proprie in disquisitionem veniunt. Quare & ii qui subjecti, seu mentis ineptitudinem naturalem, ejusque, per infusum lumen, gratiam, viresque supernaturales, elevationem, vivificationemque non rite concipiunt, necessario cæspitare ac errare in isto negotio deprehenduntur. Optime hanc Reformatorum mentem & distincte exprimit Triglandius.
units.tr: Indeed, he understands fewer things than the natural man, yet he understands them spiritually and savingly. And since he is, as it were, drawn into the things themselves by a sort of spiritual sense and taste, and those things in turn are, as it were, impressed upon him, this experiential and most sweet knowledge arises. So that, if the whole matter is weighed more carefully, the controversy that we have with the Papists, taken one by one, appears entirely different from that which we have with the Pelagians in general. For with the Papists, considered separately (in the later controversy they do the same as the other Pelagians), when we dispute in the locus on Scripture, the difference concerns its perspicuity, and properly its objective perspicuity: namely, whether in itself it is such that it intelligibly sets before the pious and regenerate the things that they ought to know or do. But when we dispute with the Pelagians about the saving perception of Scripture, it is properly the powers, aptitude and faculty of the subject, of man, that come into question. Therefore those who do not rightly grasp the subject, that is, the natural incapacity of the mind, and its elevation, vivification, and supernatural powers and grace through infused light, are necessarily found to stumble and err in this business. Triglandius expresses this mind of the Reformed excellently and distinctly.

units.la: Non, inquit Episcopius, satisfaciet, sc. Censor Walaeus, si dicat, Scripturam claram quidem esse, sed non nisi iis, qui speciali efficacis gratiae lumine a Spiritu Dei collustrantur, ut eam possint intelligere. Quod id tantundem sit atque hastam abjicere, & in castra Pontificiorum, jam olim solenniter ac sponte deserta, redire. Sic ista confundit Apologista. Respondet Triglandius. Pudeat arrogantem illum ac fastuosum magistrum tam crassae ignorantiae. An illa fuit de perspicuitate Scripturae inter Pontificios & Reformatos controversia, quod Pontificii statuerint tenebras mentis nostrae tantas esse, ut, propter eas, homo naturalis S. Scripturam intelligere non queat, sed opus habeat interna & supernaturali illuminatione Sp. Sancti, cujus contrarium statuerint Reformati? Pontificii docent, Scripturam per se, & sua ratione loquendi, obscuram esse: quod negant Reformati, dicentes eam perspicuè & clare tradere ea quæ &c. Præclare ista antehac tractavit Heidanus. Sed Catechumenis notum est, quantum ista distent. Con-geramus jam, & conferamus, qnæ hac de re Wol-zogius.
units.tr: Episcopius says: "It will not satisfy him," that is, the censor Walaeus, "if he says that Scripture is indeed clear, but only to those who are illuminated by the Spirit of God with the special light of efficacious grace, so that they can understand it. For this is just as much as to throw away the spear and return to the camp of the Papists, which was long since solemnly and willingly deserted." Thus the apologist confuses these things. Triglandius replies: "Let that arrogant and haughty master be ashamed of such crass ignorance. Was the controversy between the Papists and the Reformed about the perspicuity of Scripture of this kind: that the Papists held that the darkness of our mind is so great that, on account of it, the natural man cannot understand Holy Scripture but needs the inward and supernatural illumination of the Holy Spirit, which the Reformed hold to be false? The Papists teach that Scripture is obscure in itself and by its manner of speaking; the Reformed deny this, saying that it delivers plainly and clearly the things that etc. Heidanus has treated these matters admirably before now. But it is known even to catechumens how far these positions differ. Let us now gather together, and compare, what Wolzogius has said on this matter."

units.la: I. Errat in eo, quod Reformatorum, de perspi-cuitate Scripturæ objectiva, immerito culpet senten-tiam. Ne quisquam ante Wolzogium ad istam ma-teriam rite satis & accurate scripsisse crederetur, quicquid dictum à decessoribus erat, aut scriptum, rejicere necesse fuit, saltem corrigere. Theologi, de Scripturis statuunt, quod in se sint perspicuæ in iis quæ sunt ad salutem necessaria. Bene, sic Theologi, sic Optimi & quidem omnium seculorum, cum Augustino enim asserimus Deum ita attemperasse stilum & Phrasin scripturæ sanctæ, ut quæcunque continent fidem & mores vivendi, spem scilicet & charitatem, aperte in scripturis posita inveniantur &c. Non est abscondita in Scripturis veritas, sed obscura iis qui quærere nolunt, inquit Chrysostomus, & alibi. Quod lumen est oculo, id est lex Dei menti nostræ. Luculentissimè autem in Poster. ad Thess. ii. Hom. iii. Cap. 4. Omnia clara sunt & plana ex scripturis divinis, quæcunque necessaria sunt, manifesta sunt. De objecto loqui Patrem con-stat, subjecti aptudinem alibi requirens. Mysteria, inquit in Matth. Hom. xxii. sacræ Scripturæ non cognoscunt perversa corda, in quibus non requiescit Spiritus veritatis. Hæc Calvinus, Zanchius, Martyr. Hæc omnes Ecclesiæ Orthodoxæ profitentur. Tanti autem ista non sunt Wolzogio, ut in eorum gratiam, vel unicum verbum, non castigatum dimittat. Sic enim pro sua authoritate & perspicacia. Verbum minus commodum videtur, quia perspicuitatem vocant eam &c. Quid si vocula magis commoda, verbum magis commodum usurpari potuisset, an res cum recta est & sensus verus, imo divinus, ne tanti quidem tantorum virorum valet authoritas, ut vel unum jota impunitum per te maneat? O inexorabilem Catonem dicam an Aristarchum! Non debebat ignorare Ecclesia, quantum Wolzogiano deberet acumini & accurationi. Scriptura tandem tribunal criticum forumque Philosophorum non declinabit. Quid garris? verbum minus commodum dicis, quo scriptura perspicua esse praedicatur. Lumen est Scriptura, lux est, lucerna & quid non Davidi. Et tamen verbum minus commodum videtur? splendet propheticum verbum, illuminat caecos lex Dei, perspicuitas tamen ei commode non tribuitur. Sic propriis conceptibus suaviter irretitum, Scripturae universae cepit oblivio. Majoris momenti causa est, quam ut castra prodere, quam ut praevaricari debueris. Pontificii, in cassum hactenus & minus accurate de Scripturae perspicuitate disputasse nostros, si dixerint; quid tandem regereret Wolzogius? Nihil, nisi, fateor, verbum minus commodum, in hunc usque diem adhibuerunt nostri. At anguis in herba latet, videri vult verbo minus addictus & phrasi, sed absque veritatis, absque sensus praejudicio. Sic enim exerte. Neque hic video quid in sensu reprehendi possit. In verbo reprehendendum saltem aliquid. Verbum minus commodum. Neque vel in verba tenemur jurare doctorum aut decessorum. Sed Resp. 1. Verbum scripturarium est, imo ἐμφατικώτερος[?], in isto negotio, & magis perspicuitatem exprimentia, scriptura ipsa adhibet. Sic imprudenter in Sp. S. crisin exerces tuam, Lux enim, lumen, lucerna, & quidem splendens, amplius quid quam perspicuum sonant. 2. Posito commodiorem forsan vocem excogitari potuisse, an non debita tot tantorumque nominum veneratio, aliud quid, quam intempestivam suggerere poterat reprehensionem? 3. Et salsissimè imò ineptissimè dicitur, Verbum illud minus commodum, non solum, quod Scriptura similia & efficaciora in isto negotio adhibeat, sed & res ipsa id poscere certum sit, ut paulo post videbimus. 4. Fucum facis si phrasin solum displicere dicas, nisi, quod facilè crediderim, ipse quid sentias nondum certus sis. Altius paulo verba tua repetamus. 1. Non verbum solummodo, sed rem ipsam, ipsam Reformatorum sententiam aperte rejicis, vel hoc ipso, quem citavi, paragrapho. Verbum, inquis, minus commodum videtur: ratio autem quam addis, in re ipsa te dissentire, sufficienter evincit, non enim vocem commodiorem substituis, quod faciendum, si verbum unicè displiceret, fuisset procul dubio; sed rem ipsam corrigis, quia, dicis, perspicuitatem vocant eam, quæ primam tantum habet perfectionem, tres tu necessarias dixeras, ut aliquid perspicuum merito diceretur, unam solum habet Scriptura, non igitur verbum minus commodum, sed ipsa sententia minus vera, saltem minus commoda declaratur. Et tantum abest, tuo judicio, recte rem ipsam exposuisse hactenus Reformatos, ut perspicuum dixerint, id, quod per rerum naturam perspicuum esse, imo vel concipi non potest, nisi duo ultro addantur, quarum rationem non habuerunt. Non enim intelligis, quæ phrasis stylo ac sensu Cartesiano vehementer negat & removet id, quod intelligi negatur, perspicuitatem, nisi eum simul intelligas, qui percipiat. Imo omnis in sensu hæc perspicuitas posita est, quem sensum concipere ne quidem potes, nisi sit qui sentiat: Fateris autem Theologos de eo, quod in objecto est, loqui; necesse igitur est, statuas, illos perspicuum dixisse, quod perspicuum non est, hoc est, in re ipsa esse palam hallucinatos. Imo vere dicam, inquis, hæc quæ de re cognoscenda, quam unice à Reformatis respici in capite hujus pag. dixeras, quæque de eo qui cognoscit, dixi, nil NB ad intimam naturam perspicuitatis faciunt. Sic quod Reformati, id nihil ad rem. At vide subtilitatem, tria requiruntur ut perspicuitatis naturam comprehendamus, ait pag. seq. Hic autem duo eorum nihil ad intimam naturam perspicuitatis faciunt. En, non verbum, sed rem ipsam culpas maximè. 2. Vitium, quamvis le-vius, vitium tamen cum Paradoxo, incurrisse dicis nostros Theologos. 3. Quid? exerte ponis Thesin Theologis illis contrariam, perspicuitas omnis, & quidem procul dubio, est relativa, nullam absolute di-ctam exhiberet sermo perspicuitatem, si rerum naturæ responderet accuratissimè. Sic elenchum formas egregie, nec unquam apertiori via Paradoxum tuum aggrederis, quam hic Theologos Reformatos, tota cælo te diversos profiteris, bene est, larvam detraximus, nec jam de verbo, de phrasi, lis est, perspicuitas non nisi relativa docetur. Sermo autem, qui, licet vel ipso fatente, [Reformatorum omnium sermo sit, attamen si, non, (quod solum verbi correctionem inferret) commodior, sed, quod rem ipsam evertit, rerum naturæ congruus foret, nullam nobis absolute dictam exhiberet perspicuitatem. 4. Thesin contrariam explicat & confirmat aliquot argumentis. Explicatio ista est, sunt enim in omni hac perspicuitatis materia minime miscenda confusis cogitationibus tria, res ipsa quam perspicuam dicimus, is qui illam percipit, & rei istius ad mentem ejus qui illam intuetur appulsio. Probatio occurrit p. 104. 106. quam postea ad partes vocabimus.
units.tr: He is wrong to blame the Reformers unjustly for their view of the objective perspicuity of Scripture. Lest anyone think that no one before Wolzogius has written on this subject properly and accurately, he has had to reject, or at least correct, whatever his predecessors said or wrote. Theologians hold that Scriptures are in themselves perspicuous in those things which are necessary to salvation. Good; so the theologians hold, and the best of them, indeed of all ages. For with Augustine we assert that God so tempered the style and phrasing of holy Scripture that whatever it contains concerning faith and morals, namely hope and charity, is found plainly set down in the Scriptures, etc. The truth is not hidden in the Scriptures, but it is obscure to those who are unwilling to seek it, says Chrysostom, and elsewhere: What light is to the eye, that the law of God is to our mind. Most clearly, however, in his Homily 3 on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, chapter 4: All things that are necessary are clear and plain from the divine Scriptures; whatever is necessary is manifest. It is plain that the Father is speaking of the object, while elsewhere he requires the fitness of the subject. The mysteries of the sacred Scripture, he says in his Homily 22 on Matthew, are not known by perverse hearts, in which the Spirit of truth does not rest. These things Calvin, Zanchius and Martyr teach, and all the orthodox Church professes them. Yet these things are of so little weight to Wolzogius that, for their sake, he will not let pass even a single word without censure. For thus, by his own authority and sharp-sightedness: The word seems less suitable, because they call it perspicuity, etc. What if the more suitable little word, a more suitable word, could have been used? Is the matter not right and the sense true, indeed divine, and does not even the authority of so many great men avail, so that not one jot is left unpunished by you? O inexorable Cato, shall I call you, or Aristarchus! The Church ought not to have been ignorant of how much it owes to Wolzogius's keenness and accuracy. Scripture, after all, will not avoid the critical tribunal and the forum of the philosophers. What are you babbling about? You say the phrase less suitable word by which Scripture is said to be perspicuous. Scripture is light, it is a lamp, and what not, says David. And yet the word seems less suitable? The prophetic word shines, the law of God gives light to the blind, yet perspicuity is not suitably attributed to it. Thus, pleasantly ensnared by his own conceptions, he has forgotten all of Scripture. This matter is of too great importance for you to betray the camp or to desert. If our men have argued about the perspicuity of Scripture hitherto in vain and too carelessly, what then would Wolzogius reply? Nothing, unless, I admit, a less suitable word, which our men have used down to this day. But the snake lies hidden in the grass: he wishes to appear attached to the word and the phrasing rather than to the truth, and without prejudice to truth and sense. For he states openly: Nor do I see here what can be found fault with in the sense. There is at least something to find fault with in the word: a less suitable word. Nor are we bound to swear to the words of teachers or predecessors. But I reply: (1) The word is scriptural, indeed more emphatic, in this business, and Scripture itself uses words that express perspicuity more. So you rashly exercise your criticism on the Holy Spirit, since light, lumen, lamp, and indeed shining, sound like more than perspicuous. (2) Granted that a more suitable word might perhaps have been devised, would not the due reverence for so many and so great names have suggested something other than an untimely censure? (3) And it is said most wittily, or rather most foolishly, that that word is less suitable, not only because Scripture uses similar and more effective words in this matter, but it is certain that the thing itself demands it, as we shall see shortly. (4) You make a smoke-screen if you say only that the phrasing displeases you, unless, as I readily believe, you are not yet certain what you yourself think. Let us repeat your words a little more deeply. (1) You openly reject not merely the word but the thing itself, the very view of the Reformers, by this very paragraph which I have cited: The word, you say, seems less suitable; but the reason you add shows sufficiently that you dissent in the matter itself. For you do not substitute a more suitable term, which would undoubtedly have been the right course if you had simply disliked the word; instead you correct the thing itself, because, you say, they call it perspicuity, which has only the first perfection. You had said that three are required for something to be rightly called perspicuous; Scripture has only one. Therefore it is not the word that is less suitable, but the very view that is declared less true, or at least less fitting. And so far are the Reformers, in your judgment, from having rightly explained the thing itself, that they called perspicuous what cannot by the nature of the thing be perspicuous, or even be conceived, unless two further things are added, the reason for which they did not consider. For you do not understand, a phrase that in the Cartesian style and sense strongly denies and removes what is denied to be understood, perspicuity, unless you understand at the same time him who perceives it. Indeed all this perspicuity is placed in the sense, which you cannot even conceive unless there is someone who senses. But you admit that the theologians speak of what is in the object; it is necessary, therefore, that you hold that they called perspicuous what is not perspicuous, that is, that they were manifestly mistaken in the thing itself. Indeed I will say truly, you say, these things which I said about the thing to be known, which you had said the Reformers alone regard at the head of this page, and what I said about the one who knows, make nothing NB to the inner nature of perspicuity. So what the Reformers say is nothing to the point. But see the subtlety: three things are required if we are to grasp the nature of perspicuity, you say on the following page; yet here two of them make nothing to the inner nature of perspicuity. Behold, it is not the word but the thing itself that you chiefly blame. (2) You say that our theologians have fallen into a fault, though a lighter one, namely a paradox. (3) What then? You openly lay down a thesis contrary to those theologians: all perspicuity, and certainly undoubtedly, is relative; speech would present no perspicuity absolutely said, if it answered most precisely to the nature of things. Thus you cleverly construct an elenchus, and never approach your paradox by a more open route than here, while you profess the Reformed theologians to be wholly different from you. Good, we have torn off the mask, and the dispute is no longer about the word or the phrasing: perspicuity is taught only as relative. But the speech which, although, even by your own confession, it is the speech of all the Reformers, nevertheless, if it were not more suitable (which would bring only a correction of the word), but, which would overturn the thing itself, were congruous with the nature of things, would present to us no perspicuity said absolutely. (4) You explain and confirm the contrary thesis by several arguments. The explanation is this: for in all this matter of perspicuity, three things must not be mixed up in confused thoughts: the thing itself which we call perspicuous, the one who perceives it, and the application of that thing to the mind of the one who looks at it. The proof comes up on pages 104 and 106, which we shall summon to the parties later.

units.la: In omni illo discursu sane nihil sani est.
units.tr: There is certainly nothing sound in that whole argument.

units.la: Primo, mentem Theologorum nondum didicisti, vel in tritissima illa materia. Deinde rem ipfam confundis. Tertio falsum doces. Singula brevi- bus ad oculum demonstrabo.
units.tr: First, you have not yet learned the mind of the theologians, even in that most familiar matter. Second, you confuse the thing itself. Third, you teach what is false. I shall demonstrate each point briefly and plainly.

units.la: Theologorum nostrorum mentem quod attinet, ac sententiam, ea sic se habet. In se, ait Maresius, Scriptura est dilucida, utpote à Patre luminum profecta, qui dici nequit vel noluisse vel non potuisse clarius loqui, unde dicitur lucerna, lux &c. Pertendimus Scripturam in se perspicuam esse & claram. Luculentur Coccejus. Quandoquidem in Scripturis est Canon, & μόρφωσις τῆς γνώσεως ἢ ἡ ἀληθείας & ἀποκάλυψις ἡ δικαιοσύνης τῆ θεοῦ [?]; necesse est, eam habere suam claritatem & perspicuitatem. Nihil, sic paulo post, enim impedit, eam esse claram atque perspicuam & hominem nihilominus esse τυφλὸν, ἀνόητον [?] ἢ ἀσύνετον. Quippe uti liber naturae clare &c. Et bene distinguunt, quae tu confundis, objecti percipiendi & subjecti percipientis considerationem: sic, ut solet, accurate Spanhemius. Scriptura se luminosam formaliter & illuminantem effective profitetur. Imo dolet Sophistis eam nimis esse claram. Nec obscuritas quae in subjecto, transferanda in objectum. Docte & Graviter Vir summus M. Bucerus. Porro si divinae, inquit, Scripturae integrae sunt & simplices, ut doceant etiam rudiores sapientiam, si rectae & planae sunt, ut illuminent oculos, si erudiunt ad salutem, si ad omnem docendi rationem utiles sunt, quid praeterea requiras vel lucis vel certitudinis? Quid inesse tali Doctrinae obscuri & ambigui possit suspicari? Quamobrem, si non modo alicubi, sed multis in locis Scr. impingas; id tibi, non Deo attribuito, quo nemo potest docere benignius, atque adeo dilucidius & certius. Ideo ne dicamus solem obscurum, quia intueri eum oculis noctuae non valent, aut non certum tenere cursum quia imperiti eum non percipiunt. Antithesin Wolzogianam & Velthusianam in exemplari, Episcopio, sic lego. Statum controversiae, inquit ille, non recte ponitur ab iis qui quaerunt. I. An Scriptura sacra absolute & in se considerata non sit clara, perspicua, ac dilucida?
units.tr: As for the mind and opinion of our theologians, it stands thus. In itself, says Maresius, Scripture is clear, as it proceeds from the Father of lights, who cannot be said either to have been unwilling or unable to speak more clearly; hence it is called a lamp, a light, etc. We maintain that Scripture is in itself perspicuous and clear. Cocceius shows this most plainly: Since in the Scriptures there is the canon, and the formation of knowledge, or of truth, and the revelation of the righteousness of God [as printed: μόρφωσις τῆς γνώσεως ἢ ἡ ἀληθείας & ἀποκάλυψις ἡ δικαιοσύνης τῆ θεοῦ], it must have its own clarity and perspicuity. For nothing, as he says shortly after, prevents it from being clear and perspicuous while man is nevertheless blind [τυφλὸν], foolish [ἀνόητον] or unintelligent [ἀσύνετον]. Indeed, as the book of nature is clear, etc. And they rightly distinguish what you confuse: the consideration of the object to be perceived and of the subject that perceives. So, as he usually does, Spanheim distinguishes accurately: Scripture professes itself to be formally luminous and effectively illuminating. Indeed it grieves the Sophists that it is too clear. Nor is the obscurity which lies in the subject to be transferred to the object. Learnedly and gravely, the most eminent man M. Bucer: Furthermore, he says, if the divine Scriptures are whole and simple, so that they teach wisdom even to the less learned; if they are straight and plain, so that they enlighten the eyes; if they instruct to salvation; if they are useful for every manner of teaching, what more could you require of light or certainty? What obscurity or ambiguity could one suspect in such doctrine? Wherefore, if you stumble not only somewhere but in many places in Scripture, you must attribute that not to God, by whom no one can teach more kindly and therefore more clearly and certainly. Thus we should not call the sun dark because owls cannot look at it with their eyes, nor because the unskilled do not grasp its course. I read the Arminian and Episcopian antithesis in the copy as follows: The state of the controversy, he says, is not rightly set down by those who ask: (1) whether Holy Scripture, considered absolutely and in itself, is not clear, perspicuous and lucid?

units.la: Quis enim id quaerat? imo quis id asserat, si eam claram, dilucidam, ac perspicuam esse non intelligat? Nemo Solem clarum, aut lucem perspicuam adserere potest, nisi claritatem solis & lucis perspicuitatem viderit. Caeco Sol etiam clarus non est. Praeter ea quae superius ex Maresio audivimus, haec porro ex ejusdem adversus Anonymum Disput iii. Thesi vii. addam, ut, quem olim magistrum coluit, nunc sese reprehendisse agnoscat. Sic ille, pessimè philosophatur de orationis obscuritate & perspicuitate, dum utramque semper facit relativam, sed idem Wolzogius hac in re cum Paradoxo, pergat Maresius, ut Sol in se semper est lucidus, licet non luceat omnibus. NB Temerariae hujus censurae causa fuit Anonymo, ac proinde etiam Wolzogio, eandem cum Paradoxo in Reformatos stringente, quod nequirit distinguere inter obscurum aut perspicuum in se & absolute ab eo quod obscurum est nobis & quoad nos. Igitur perspicuitas est attributum absolutum Scripturae. Difficultatem à Wolzogio motam, jam dudum removerunt nostri: primam nimirum perfectionem solum in Scriptura esse, juxta quam, binae aliae adhuc, ut perspicuitas habeatur, requirantur. Quaenam est illa perfectio, quam concedit Wolzogen? ita Scr. scriptas esse ut nihil desit orationi, eorum, quae conferre debet ad perspicuitatem. At bone vir, sic & in re ipsa ignorantiam tuam prodis egregie. Nihil enim ultra intelligunt Theologi, quando Scripturam in se perspicuam dicunt. Spe-ctanda[?] haec virtus (de perspicuitate sic loquitur, in consummatissimo illo Theologiae Systemate, Essenius) distincte, tum objective in se; tum quo modo subjective in hominibus recipiatur. Objective Scripturam in se, aut in suo systemate, claram esse dicimus ac perspicuam, ut Sol in se clarus est, etiamsi caecus eum suo vitio videre non possit. Non enim agimus, sic adversus Pontificios Alexander Morus, de obscuritate subjecti
units.tr: Who would ask that? Indeed, who would assert it, if he did not understand that Scripture is clear, plain and perspicuous? No one can assert that the sun is bright, or that light is perspicuous, unless he has seen the brightness of the sun and the perspicuity of light. Even the sun is not bright to a blind man. Besides what we heard earlier from Maresius, I will add these points from the same man's Disputatio 3, Thesis 7, against the Anonymous, so that Wolzogius may acknowledge that he is now rebuking the man whom he once honoured as his teacher. Thus he writes: he philosophizes very badly about the obscurity and perspicuity of speech, since he always makes both relative. But the same Wolzogius, Maresius goes on, in this matter agrees with the Paradox: as the sun is always bright in itself, even though it does not shine for everyone. NB: The cause of this rash criticism was the Anonymous, and therefore also Wolzogius, who likewise attacks the Reformed with the Paradox, because he cannot distinguish between what is obscure or perspicuous in itself and absolutely, and what is obscure to us and in relation to us. Therefore perspicuity is an absolute attribute of Scripture. Our men long ago removed the difficulty raised by Wolzogius, namely that there is only one perfection in Scripture, the first, and that two others are still required before perspicuity can be had. What is that perfection which Wolzogen concedes? That Scripture is so written that nothing is lacking in the discourse of those things which it ought to contribute to perspicuity. But good sir, in this you betray your ignorance of the matter itself most clearly. For theologians understand nothing more when they call Scripture perspicuous in itself. This virtue is to be considered (Essenius speaks thus about perspicuity in that most complete theological system) distinctly, first objectively in itself, and then in what way it is received subjectively in men. We say that Scripture is clear and perspicuous objectively, in itself or in its system, as the sun is bright in itself, even if a blind man cannot see it because of his own defect. For, as Alexander Morus says against the Papists, we are not dealing with the obscurity of the subject

units.la: Essen Systém. part. 1. de Script. §. XLIII. XLIV. Morus Causa Dei p. 186. jecti sive ignoratione personarum, sed de obscuritate in objecto, seu Scripturarum. Hoc ergo demum quaeritur, an modus docendi ita sit obscurus &c. In eo tibi haeret aqua, quod perspicuitatem objecti, confusa cogi-tatione, a perspicientiae, aut perspectionis actu non distinxeris, quae longe tamen diversa sunt, si rem penitius consideres. Tria requiris ad perspicuitatem. Res ipsa talis esse debet ut cognosci possit; mens oculusve ita affecti ut cognoscere possint; denique relatio id postu-lat, ut rebus istis cognoscendis applicata mens illas revera percipiat. Erras gravissime vel in elementis Theologiae ac Philosophiae. Ac si, cum de objecto agi-tur, ad ejus perfectionem, id omne requiram, quo sine, hujus aut illius actio, circa illud forsan exeri non potest. Perspectionis, ut ita loquar, actus, ista requirit, non autem objecti, liceat hic verba formare, perspicibilitas, quam in hoc negotio con-siderant Theologi. Quis enim eos tam stupidos credat, ut ista distinguere demum a Wolzogio docendi putentur. Si de perspecta loqueremur oratione, recte tria concurrisse diceres, perspicuum autem hic, non perspectum significat, sed perspectibile. Sic-que falleris plus quam perspicue. Non tibi autem soli, sed & Seniori tuo res ista cordi fuit. Argu-menta, quibus omnis absoluta in objecto claritas tollatur, conquisiviistis [?], a quorum viribus tamen non est quod mali quicquam timeat Ecclesia Ortho-doxa. Alii Heroes in ista veritate excolenda desuda-runt, quam ut ipsorum sensa a Velthusio aut Wol-zogio falsitatis convincantur. Sic Wolzogen. Non ideo, dixerat quamombrem Theologis in se perspi-cua scriptura diceretur, non ideo, inquit, magis per-spicua dicenda fuerit oratio, quam rubrum diceremus fluentem in venis sanguinem, qui nullis oculis objicitur; aut frigidam in ultimum septentrionem projectam nivem, quae neminem unquam ullo horrore percussit. In sensu sunt ista omnia posita. Ubi pudor Wolzogi? antea defensurus videbaris, quos hic non deseris solum, sed risu sarcastico exsibilare non erubescis. Quid sanguinis rubor, quid frigus nivis? ludis in re seria. Prodis communem causam aperte. Hoc vult Paradoxus, hoc negant Reformati, quod tu concludis. Et illud tandem Orthodoxum scriptum erit, at rationes examinemus, tanti sane ponderis, ut easdem ex Pastoris ore Echi instar iterum ingeminaverit gravissimus Senior, sed aliquantulum aucto verborum numero. Sic ille, neque illud lumen re ipsa in rebus est, non magis quam sensus caloris, aut calor est in igne, & frigus in glacie. Et, si non darentur tales sensus in quibus caloris & frigoris ideae excitantur (quae ideae proprie sunt color & frigus) non esset calor aut frigus in natura: quemadmodum non esset dolor in natura, si non esset homo, qui doloris capax est. Nam quemadmodum dolor non dicitur esse in gladio aut cultro, quo vulnus inflictum est, ita nec calor, nec frigus est in igne & glacie. Sic in re cognoscibili non est lumen, sed est apta ut nobis excitet per facultatem intellectus lumen, hoc est cognitionem. Nihil itaque, nec res, nec sermo, in se proprie clarum aut perspicuum dicitur, sed ut refertur ad intellectum. Ineptissima sane argumentatio, nec meliora de hoc homine sperat lector. Resp. 1.
units.tr: Essen, System, part 1, on Scripture, §§ XLIII, XLIV; Morus, Causa Dei, p. 186. ...subject, or with ignorance of persons, but with obscurity in the object, that is, in the Scriptures. So this is the question: whether the mode of teaching is so obscure, etc. You are stuck here, because in a confused train of thought you did not distinguish the perspicuity of the object from the act of perceiving or perspecting, which are very different if you consider the matter more deeply. You require three things for perspicuity: the thing itself must be such that it can be known; the mind or the eye must be so disposed that they can know it; finally, the relation requires that the mind, applied to those things to be known, actually perceives them. You err most gravely, even in the elements of theology and philosophy. For if, when we are speaking of the object, I require for its perfection everything without which the action of this or that power cannot perhaps be exercised upon it, I am confusing things. Those conditions belong to the act of perceiving, so to speak, not to the object; and the theologians in this discussion consider the perspicibility of the object, if I may coin the word. Who would believe them so stupid as to be thought to need Wolzogius to teach them to distinguish these things? If we were speaking of a discourse that has been perceived, you would be right to say that three things concur; but here perspicuum means not what has been perceived but what can be perceived. So you are mistaken more than plainly. This matter was dear not only to you but also to your Senior. You have sought out arguments by which all absolute clarity in the object is removed, but the Orthodox Church has no reason to fear anything bad from their strength. Other heroes have laboured to cultivate this truth so well that their views cannot be refuted as false by Velthusius or Wolzogius. Thus Wolzogen: It does not follow, he had said, that Scripture should be called perspicuous in itself by theologians, that the speech should be called more perspicuous than we would call blood red as it flows in the veins, which is not presented to any eyes, or snow thrown into the farthest north, which has never struck anyone with any chill. All these things are posited in the sense. Where is Wolzogius's shame? You seemed about to defend those men, and now you not only abandon them but are not ashamed to hiss at them with sarcastic laughter. What has the redness of blood to do with it, or the cold of snow? You are joking about a serious matter. You openly betray the common cause. This is what the Paradox maintains, and this is what the Reformed deny, though you conclude it. Finally, it will be written as Orthodox, but let us examine the arguments, which are of such weight that the most serious Senior repeated them, like an echo, from the mouth of this Pastor, though with a somewhat increased number of words. Thus he: That light is not in things in reality, any more than the sensation of heat is; nor is heat in fire, and cold in ice. And if there were not such senses in which the ideas of heat and cold are excited (which ideas are properly colour and cold), there would be no heat or cold in nature; just as there would be no pain in nature if there were no man capable of pain. For just as pain is not said to be in the sword or knife with which the wound was inflicted, so neither heat nor cold is in fire or ice. So in a knowable thing there is no light, but it is apt to excite light in us through the faculty of the intellect, that is, knowledge. Therefore nothing, neither a thing nor a speech, is said to be properly clear or perspicuous in itself, but only as it is related to the intellect. This argument is certainly most inept, and the reader can hope for nothing better from this man. Reply 1.

units.la: Reformatae sententiae ab hoc Pastore & Seniore nuncium aperte mitti. Quam si iterum videre lubeat consulatur Maresius loc cit. 2. Paradoxam deinde sententiam, argumentorum loco, hoc & illo simili illustrant. Nimirum, non aliter concipientibus viris summis, praeter sententiae declarationem, absque ratione petitur quicquam. 3. Quod autem dolendum, quaecunque proferunt viri Clarissimi, tam longe a thesis suae absunt probatione, ut eam funditus potius evertant. Agedum, percurramus singula & retorqueamus. Rubeus non est sanguis, non frigida nix aut glacies. At vides conclusionem di-rectè condradicturam exertissimis Scripturæ dictis, quæ Scripturam in se lucidam dicunt. Pono dein-ceps, sanguinem hoc momento à me videri, ni-vem tangi, visum deinde mihi & tactum deficere, an statim sanguis desinet esse ruber & nix frigida? mirabile somnium. Quid tibi lux est, quid color, quid frigus? nonne particularum motus & modus & quies, tria ista juxta Cartesium perficiunt? nec enim lubet cuncta transcribere, remoto sensu, an definit motus & pressio globulorum æthereorum quæ lumen constituunt, an nulli si darentur sensus, nulla daretur istorum globulorum agitatio? De co- lore idem dici potest, qui est luminis, secundum glo- bulorum ejus æthereorum processus, & circumvolutionis proportionem, modificatio. Nemo sit qui colorem vi- deat, sit rubeus e. gr. qui fit cum globuli multo celerius circumrotantur, quam procedunt. Visio ista desinat, an simul desinet partium illa dispositio, globulorum agitatio? & si ista numero desinat, an non, de Phi- losophia vestra, altera ocyus existet. Quid? Scrip- turæ hoc directè adversatur. Nisi enim fallat Moses, lucem & tenebras ante ullos sensus fuisse credendum est. Lux erat primo die creata juxta Mosen. At lu- men in rebus non est, in sensu sita sunt omnia. Nimi-mirum Moses referat quomodocunque velit, sic docet ratio, cui, si Velthusius vera dicat, non mi-nus tuto quam ipsi Deo credimus. Quis ferat superbiam, quis arrogantiam istorum hominum? Sol non est lucidus, nisi videatur, ignis non est calidus, id est minimarum particularum non est varia agitatio, in eo enim consistit calor juxta novitios, quando non sentitur. Nugæ tantis viris indignæ. Perspicuitas scripturæ, est proprietas insita, quam & semper reti-net, homo licet illuminatus sit nec ne: quamvis, non illuminato homine, istam claritatem idem non videat. Plane quemadmodum Sol in sese clarus est & lucidus, homo sive claudat oculos, sive aperiat, sive caecus sit, sive videre possit: illa enim hominis diversitas Solem nec lucidum reddit nec obscurum. Verba sunt Heidani, à Paradoxo cum elogio authoris citata, adversus Episcopium. Rem totam sic concipiebat Lutherus; Ut res ipsas, referente id Withakero, positas in luce diceret, & obscuritatem potius in nobis quaerendam esse: idque rectissime probat, ait Withakerus, testimonio Pauli 2. Cor. iii. 14, 15, 16. & iv. 3. illustratque si-militudine solis & diei quorum utrumque etsi clarissimum, caeci tamen minime vident. Sole, inquit, aut die nihil illustrius; at caecus ne Solem quidem adspicit, & sunt qui lucem etiam ipsam fugiant. At lumen, ait Velthuisen, reipsa in rebus non est, non magis quam sensus caloris, aut calor est in igne. Delirat Medicus, sensum caloris quis unquam in igne finxit, vel an in se calidum esse, Cartesiano modo loquar, an ista agitatione particularum in aqua aliisque excitata, idem tibi erit ac caloris sensum habere? Si calorem, maximam committens & crassissimam abusionem, pro sensu caloris sumas, finita disputatio est, sensus enim absque sensu non est: at quid tandem nugari est, si hoc non est. Non quaeritur, an ignis calidus sit, caloris sensu, ita ut ignis calorem sentiat, quis enim praeter istum Medicum sic unquam deliravit? sed an accidens illud, quod Peripatetici, aut particularum talis agitatio, quam Cartesiani, calorem vocant, non insint rebus, etiam ante & citra omnes sensus: illud negasse, illud refutasse debueras. Cum umbra igitur strenue dimicat gloriosus miles, quando dicit, si non darentur tales sensus in quibus caloris ideae excitantur (quae ideae proprie sunt calor & frigus) non esset calor & frigus in natura. Non esset ullius animalis calefactio & frigefactio, non esset caloris sensus, bene, sed de eo non disputamus. Ideae, quid audio, ideae in sensibus excitatae proprie sunt calor & frigus. frigus. Ineptiorem Philosophum unquam vidit? Fricanda ista si forent, ignorantiæ Velthusianæ fæ-tore replerent omnia. Ideæ istæ unde bone vir? Ideæ istæ, an sunt ipsissimus particularum motus quiesve? Iterum, ideæ, an sunt ipse calor, ipse frigus? sal-leris. Nequidem receptionem caloris, ejusve sen-sationem si respicias, verum loqueris. Idea enim ipsa sensatio non est. Sic solent clarè & distincte phi-losophari hodierni vates. Quemadmodem, sic largiter similia fingit, quæ per somnium in alembico isto distillata pro argumentis vendit noster Chymicus, non esset in natura dolor, si non esset homo, qui doloris capax est. Omne simile claudicat. Dolor aperte sen-sationem, receptionem, in subjecto ponit, non item calor, lux, frigus, quorum longè diversa est ratio. Non sentias tu cultri aciem, non hellebori vires, acutus tamen in se culter est, & cerebrum purgat helleborus. Dolor non est in gladio, fateor, sed dolorem excitare, ut instrumentum, aptus est. Tandem per ambages in viam è diverticulo redit noster. Sic in re cognoscibili non est lumen, hoc est, actu non illumi-nat aliquem, sed est apta ut nobis per facultatem intel-lectus lumen excitet. Illam aptitudinem in suo genere ponimus in Scriptura, nihil præterea, quid igitur est quod oppugnas? dicis perspicuum, clarum, lucidum id dicendum non esse? rem ipsam concedis, unicum illud restat, quod adversus omnem usum, imò directè contra exertissima scripturæ dicta, phrasi & dictione abutaris. Sed tamen in sensu ista, in perceptione posita omnia, inquit Wolzogius, sicque tria requiruntur: neque enim aliter licet concipere. Ergo, &c. Argumentum in forma juxta Methodum novissimam. Sive tu concipias, sive non concipias mihi perinde est. Ad perspicientiæ ad perspectionis, ut ita loquar, actum, ista tria requiruntur, non autem, ut objecto sua constet objectiva perspicibilitas, qua aptum est, à subjecto capace, sic recipi. Finge Scripturam ante omnes homines exstare, an sic desinet esse perspicua, hoc est, scripta intelligibiliter? Sic causa cadimus, adversus Pontificios de Scripturarum in se perspicui-tate quoties disputamus. Saltem durae & absurdae abusionis convicti, aliter post hac loqui, scribere aliter debebimus. Strenue communem causam agit Walonicus concionator. Pacem init cum suo Paradoxo, is enim contra Magnum inter Reformatos Theologum, sic Heidanum vocat ingratus & turpis laudator, nihil ultro contendit, quam, quod pro sua moderatione, invita licet tota Ecclesia, concedit noster, Scripturam in se claram aut perspicuam di-cendam non esse. 2. Confunduntur subjecti & ob-jecti consideratio. 3. Se ipse jugulat Wolzogius, loca quaedam obscura, atque ambigua esse concedit. Deum obscuritatis aliquid in verbo suo reliquisse, & alibi. Quae perspicuitatis ratio est, eandem & obscuritatis putat. Atque inde concludit, Paradoxum in idem cum nostris vitium incidisse, & absolutam posuisse Scripturae perspicuitatem, eadem vero illatio valet adversus nostrum.
units.tr: The Reformed view is plainly being sent back to us by this Pastor and Elder. If he cares to see it again, let him consult Maresius, loc. cit. 2. Then, in place of arguments, they illustrate their paradoxical view with this and that similar example. Indeed, since such eminent men conceive it in no other way, nothing is sought beyond the bare declaration of the view, without reason. 3. What is to be lamented is that everything these most distinguished men put forward stands so far from proving their thesis that it rather overturns it utterly. Come, let us go through each point and turn it back. Red is not blood, nor is cold snow or ice. But you see that this conclusion directly contradicts the most explicit sayings of Scripture, which call Scripture itself clear. Next I assume that at this moment I see blood and touch snow, and that then sight and touch fail me: will blood at once cease to be red and snow cold? A marvellous dream. What is light to you, what colour, what cold? Do they not, according to Descartes, consist in the motion, the mode and the rest of particles, those three things? For I do not wish to transcribe everything: with sense removed, does the motion and pressure of the ethereal globules which constitute light cease, or, if there were no senses, would there be no agitation of those globules? The same can be said of colour, which is a modification of light according to the course and the proportion of rotation of its ethereal globules. No one sees colour, say red, which arises when the globules spin around much more quickly than they advance. Will that vision cease, or will that arrangement of parts and agitation of globules cease at the same time? And if the latter ceases in number, will not, by your philosophy, another exist more swiftly? What? This is directly opposed to Scripture. For unless Moses deceives, we must believe that light and darkness existed before any senses. Light was created on the first day, according to Moses. But light is not in things; all things lie in sense. Naturally, let Moses report however he likes; reason teaches thus, which, if Velthusius speaks truly, we believe no less safely than God himself. Who can bear the pride, who the arrogance of these men? The sun is not bright unless it is seen; fire is not hot, that is, there is no varied agitation of the smallest particles in it, for according to the novices heat consists in this when it is not felt. Trifles unworthy of such great men. The perspicuity of Scripture is an inherent property, which it always retains whether or not the man is enlightened, although, when a man is not enlightened, he does not see that clarity. Just as the sun is in itself clear and bright, whether a man closes his eyes or opens them, whether he is blind or can see: for that diversity in man makes the sun neither bright nor dark. These are the words of Heidanus, cited from the Paradox with praise of its author, against Episcopius. Luther conceived the whole matter thus: that the things themselves, as Withaker reports it, were placed in the light, and that the obscurity is rather to be sought in us; and this he proves most correctly, says Withaker, by the testimony of Paul, 2 Cor. iii. 14, 15, 16 and iv. 3, and illustrates it with the likeness of the sun and day, both of which, however bright, the blind do not see at all. The sun or day, he says, is nothing more illustrious; yet the blind man does not even look at the sun, and there are those who flee even the light itself. But light, says Velthuysen, is in reality not in things, no more than the sense of heat is, or heat is in fire. The physician raves. Who ever imagined a sense of heat in fire? Or, to speak in the Cartesian manner, is being hot in itself the same to you as having a sense of heat, when this agitation of particles is excited in water and other things? If you take heat, committing a very great and very gross abuse, as the sense of heat, the discussion is over, for a sense is not without sense; but what then is trifling, if this is not? The question is not whether fire is hot with a sense of heat, so that fire perceives heat (for who besides that physician has ever raved in this way?), but whether that accident which the Peripatetics call heat, or that agitation of particles which the Cartesians call heat, is not in things, even before and apart from all senses. You ought to have denied that, you ought to have refuted that. So the boastful soldier fights strenuously against a shadow when he says: if there were no such senses in which the ideas of heat are excited (which ideas properly are heat and cold), there would be no heat and cold in nature. There would be no heating or cooling of any animal, there would be no sense of heat. Good, but we are not disputing about that. Ideas, what do I hear, ideas excited in the senses are properly heat and cold, cold. Has anyone ever seen a more inept philosopher? If those things were to be rubbed, they would fill everything with the stench of Velthusian ignorance. Those ideas, from where, good man? Are those ideas the very motion or rest of particles? Again, are they heat itself, cold itself? You are mistaken. Indeed, if you look even at the reception of heat or its sensation, you speak truly, for the idea is not itself sensation. So the modern prophets are accustomed to philosophize clearly and distinctly. As, thus he lavishly feigns similar things, which our chemist sells as arguments, distilled in this alembic in a dream: there would be no pain in nature if there were no man capable of pain. Every likeness limps. Pain plainly places sensation and reception in the subject; not so heat, light or cold, whose reasoning is quite different. You would not feel the edge of a knife or the powers of hellebore, yet the knife is sharp in itself, and hellebore purges the brain. Pain is not in the sword, I grant, but it is suited to excite pain, as an instrument. Finally, after roundabout ways, our man returns to the road from the byway. Thus in a knowable thing there is no light, that is, it does not actually illuminate anyone, but it is suited to excite light in us through the faculty of the intellect. We place that aptitude, in its own kind, in Scripture, nothing more. What, then, is it that you attack? You say that it should not be called perspicuous, clear, bright? You concede the thing itself; only one thing remains, which you misuse against all usage, indeed directly against the most explicit sayings of Scripture, in phrase and wording. But yet all these things, all that is placed in sense, in perception, says Wolzogen, and thus three things are required: for we cannot conceive otherwise. Therefore, etc. An argument in the form of the newest method. Whether you conceive it or not is all the same to me. For the act of perceiving, of perception as I may put it, these three things are required; but not that the object should have its objective perspicuity, by which it is fit to be received in this way by a capable subject. Suppose Scripture existed before all men: would it cease to be perspicuous, that is, written intelligibly? Thus we fall in our cause whenever we dispute against the Papists about the perspicuity of Scripture in itself. Once convicted of harsh and absurd abuse, we shall have to speak differently from now on, and write differently. Walonicus the preacher strenuously defends the common cause. He makes peace with his Paradox; for against the great Reformed theologian, whom he calls Heidanus, the ungrateful and shameful praiser, he contends for nothing beyond what our man, for all his moderation, concedes even though the whole Church be against it: that Scripture is not to be called clear or perspicuous in itself. 2. The consideration of subject and object is confused. 3. Wolzogen cuts his own throat: he concedes that certain places are obscure and ambiguous, God has left something of obscurity in his word, and elsewhere: he thinks the same reasoning that holds for perspicuity holds for obscurity. And from this he concludes that the Paradox has fallen into the same fault as ours, and posited an absolute perspicuity of Scripture; yet the same inference holds against ours.

units.la: Quid tandem te potuit, Wolzogi, eò perducere socordiae, ut, in tanti momenti negotio, cum Vel-thusio, cum Paradoxo tuo, quam cum Ecclesia Ca-tholica consensum profiteri malueris?
units.tr: What, Wolzogen, could have led you into such carelessness that, in a matter of such importance, you preferred to profess agreement with Velthuysen and your Paradox rather than with the Catholic Church?

units.la: 2. Secundus sequitur Wolzogii in isto negotio error; dum Scripturae perspicuitatem vel potius hu-manas vires eo extendit, ut de impiis dicat; Certum enim est, etiamsi aliquando videant quamcunque veritatem, quae exhibetur in Scriptura, saepe tamen illos non videre ullam salutarem, & perinde in aliis percipiendis caecutire. Dicit, Impios aliquando videre quamcunque veritatem, quamcunque si sumat pro omni, profusam liberalitatem erga ipsos probat certissime: at huc redit, quam nunc respicio, difficultas, quo-modo, modo, quo principio acti, videant homines impii, idem enim licet videant subinde, eodem modo tamen non vident, neque eodem acti principio. Hinc sensum spiritualem ipsos non penetrare, Grammaticum solummodo percipere, docent nostri. Salutaria quidem vident & spiritualia, sed naturaliter. At sæpe non vident ullam salutarem veritatem, inquit Wolzogen. Qui ista cum prioribus cohæreant ego non percipio. An dum ponis quamcunque, remo-ves omnem salutarem, ita ut, dum quamcunque videant, nullam tamen videant salutarem? Si dicas te videndi modum ac principium spectare, ut aliter videant, licet omne videant: tunc non debueras dicere, eos sæpe nullam salutarem videre; sed salu-tariter eos non videre. Uti nec eos sæpe sic non videre, ac si unquam ipsis ulla salutaris obtingeret per-ceptio, sed nunquam salutariter videre. Hæc si errore careant & heterodoxia, vehementer saltem in-tricata sunt & obscura. Eandem limam produnt Theologicam, quæ sequuntur. Rationes tradit, quare veræ significationes non occurrant impiis. Ig-norantiam narrat, tenebras vocari dicit, obfirmatum-que de iis in errore prædicari animum. Utrum conatur evincere? impiis non occurrere unquam veros sensus, an verò occurrere quidem, sed sæpe non salutariter? si prius, deficit in probatione, posito enim, quod ignorantiâ laborent naturali, quod sint tenebræ, imo vel obfirmatum gerant in errore animum, nondum tamen sequitur, eos nullam vel salutarem veritatem videre: quæ, omnibus istis non obstantibus, videri tamen in multis potest, sed pro modo, pro conditione videntis, naturaliter, animaliter &c. Qui tenebrarum princeps, & ab omni vera luce remotissimus, Jesum tamen ille servatorem esse videt. Quid? homo naturalis, sive præter naturales facul-tates nihil habeat, sive aliqua, reprobis etiam communi, spiritus illuminatione ultro gaudeat; nullam- ne ille veritatem in Verbo Dei videre posset, quidem salutarem? In reprobum sensum traditi qui sunt, omnium illos veritatum statim oblitos somnias, easque in Verbo videre postea non valere? Vel in ipso inferno, in extremis tenebris demersis, super- erit veritatum quidem salutarium cognitio quae- dam. Peccatorum conscientia hoc requirit, in iis, qui Dominum gloriae spreverunt & rejecerunt contra conscientiam. Nimis liquidum est quod dicimus, quam ut plura addere necesse sit. Posterius si probare animus fuit: Thesis saltem, quam demonstrandam sumis, manca & intricata est, modo non falsa sit & heterodoxa. Quid enim? an saepe non vident salutariter? an igitur unquam vident salutariter? Priori sensu disquiritur quid videant, hoc vero, quo modo, quonam principio acti: spirituali autem & supernaturali non donati, impossibile est ut ullam veritatem, eamque unquam videant, aut videre possint spiritualiter, salutariter &c. quamdiu novo, novae vitae, principio non informantur. Vel an putas, unum eundemque hominem, aliquando salutariter viden- di facultate pollere, aliquando ea plane orbatum esse? actus quidem subinde, fateor, exerit non principium illd[?] spirituale, semen tamen in nobis manet. Nisi fortassis apostasiam doceas, si non finalem, ad minimum totalem.
units.tr: 2. Wolzogen's second error in this matter follows. He extends the perspicuity of Scripture, or rather human powers, so far that he says of the impious: For it is certain that even if they sometimes see whatever truth is set forth in Scripture, they often do not see any saving truth, and in the same way they are blind to other things that are to be perceived. He says that the impious sometimes see whatever truth there is. If by "whatever" he means every truth, he proves most certainly a lavish generosity towards them. But the difficulty I now address comes back to this: in what way, and from what principle of action, do impious men see? For they may see the same things at times, yet they do not see them in the same way, nor from the same principle of action. From this our people teach that they do not penetrate the spiritual sense and perceive only the grammatical sense. They do see saving and spiritual things, but in a natural way. But often they do not see any saving truth, says Wolzogen. I do not understand how this coheres with what came before. Do you mean that, while you say "whatever," you remove every saving truth, so that, although they see whatever truth, they see no saving truth? If you say that you are concerned with the manner and principle of seeing, so that they see differently even though they see everything, then you should not have said that they often see no saving truth, but rather that they do not see it savingly. Nor should you have said that they often do not see in this way, as if any saving perception ever came to them, but that they never see savingly. If these things are free from error and heterodoxy, they are at least very intricate and obscure. Theological mistakes of the same kind follow. He gives reasons why true meanings do not occur to the impious. He describes ignorance, says it is called darkness, and says that a mind hardened in error is predicated of them. Which does he try to prove: that true senses never occur to the impious, or that they do occur, but often not savingly? If the first, he fails in the proof. For granting that they labour under natural ignorance, that they are darkness, or even that they bear a mind hardened in error, it still does not follow that they see no saving truth at all. Despite all these things, such truth can be seen by many, though according to the manner and condition of the one seeing: naturally, animally, and so on. The prince of darkness, most remote from all true light, nevertheless sees that Jesus is the Saviour. What then? Whether a natural man has nothing beyond natural faculties, or whether he rejoices in some enlightenment of the spirit, common even to the reprobate, could he not see some truth in the Word of God, even a saving one? Are those who have been given over to a reprobate mind immediately forgetful of all truths, so that they are not able to see them afterwards in the Word? Even in hell itself, plunged into the deepest darkness, there will remain some knowledge of saving truths. The consciousness of sins requires this in those who have spurned and rejected the Lord of glory against their conscience. What we say is too plain to need more words. If he intended to prove the latter, then at least the thesis he undertakes to demonstrate is maimed and intricate, unless it is false and heterodox. For what? Do they not often see savingly? Then do they ever see savingly? In the former sense the question is what they see; but the question of how, from what principle they act, is another matter. Those not endowed with a spiritual and supernatural principle cannot see any truth, or ever see it, or be able to see it spiritually or savingly, for as long as they are not formed by a new principle of new life. Or do you think that one and the same man is sometimes endowed with the faculty of seeing savingly and sometimes is wholly deprived of it? I admit that the spiritual principle does not always act, yet the seed remains in us. Unless perhaps you teach apostasy, if not final, at least total.

units.la: 3. Tertium erroris, in negotio de Scripturae per- spicuitate, specimen occurrit p. 172. Singularem quandam istic loci Scripturae constitutionem narrat, qua fit, ut, omni hominis culpa longe remota, homo saepe relinquatur de sensu dubius. Statuitque posito vel in summa ignorantia demerso[?] peccatore, posse sane ita loqui Deum, ut vel ab ignorantissimo intelligeretur.
