De scripturae perspicuitate ab una, & hominis impotentia ab altera parte quid sentiat, haec verba clare innunt; nunt; de illa, non solum, clariorem esse posse, sed ita claram, ut ejus objectiva claritas sufficiens futura fuisset, quò ignorantissimus peccator ad intelligentiam sufficientem pervenire potuisset. Nescio quid velit author, videat lector & spernat intricatissimas in re seria nugationes. Vis igitur gratiam objectivam, quam vocant, sufficere posse? ac hominem non ita cæcum esse, quin veritatem, nunc, præ nimia Scripturæ obscuritate, non percipiendam, ab homine percipi potuisse, magis perspicuè & clarè modo scripsisset Deus. Crassum illa & stupidum Pelagianismum olent, in quantum peccatoris cæcitatem respiciunt, de qua antea; Papismum vero, in quantum culpa nimis magna in Scripturam, ut non satis claram, devolvitur. Subinde enim omnem continet obscuritatis causam ex sensu Wolzogii.
units.tr: 3. A third instance of error in the matter of the perspicuity of Scripture occurs on page 172. There he describes a certain peculiar constitution of Scripture by which it comes about that, with all human fault far removed, a man is often left in doubt about the sense. And he holds that even when a sinner has sunk into the greatest ignorance, God can certainly speak in such a way that He would be understood even by the most ignorant. These words clearly indicate what he thinks about the perspicuity of Scripture on the one hand and human impotence on the other: that Scripture could be not only clearer, but so clear that its objective clarity would have been sufficient for the most ignorant sinner to attain sufficient understanding. I do not know what the author wants. Let the reader see and despise these most intricate trifles in a serious matter. Do you want to say that so-called objective grace can suffice, and that man is not so blind that God could have spoken more plainly and clearly, so that the truth, which now cannot be perceived because of the excessive obscurity of Scripture, could have been perceived by man? These words smack of gross and stupid Pelagianism, insofar as they concern the blindness of the sinner, mentioned above; and of Papism, insofar as the great fault is thrown upon Scripture for not being clear enough. For he always places the whole cause of obscurity in the sense of Wolzogen.

units.la: 4. Quartum superest, quod Pelagianismi suspicio-nem merito augeat. Explicaturus ante hac totum perspicuitatis negotium, tria requirebat author; unum à parte objecti, alterum à parte subjecti, de-nique hujus & illius debitum contactum. Quæ jam in antecessum notavimus; sed subjectum cum depingit, ita agit jejunè ut nihil supra: in intelligentibus, inquit, hoc sigillatim requiritur, ut sint gnari omnium earum legum quibus orationis universa compages constricta tenetur. Nec in eo, qui nec stultus sit, nec præpeditus aliqua animi perturbatione, aliove impedimento, quicquam ultra desiderandum putem. Quid hinc aliter elici datur, quam unam Wolzogio, quod ad rei summam, cum Socinianis & Remonstrantibus mentem esse? nimirum, Lectores omnes, communi quidem sensu & judicio præditos, quantum satis est, mentem sacrorum librorum assequi posse, modo præjudicio, vana confidentia, aliisque pravis affectibus, sese occæcari non sinant. Quibus verbis, quoniam Spiritus S. nullam faciunt mentionem, D. D. Professores nihil quam Pelagianifmum recoqui, merito, ait Triglandius, censuerunt. In eodem luto haeret noster, non enim decebat ita perspicuitatem Scripturae exponere, tria ad perspicuitatem requirens Wolzogius primo de perspicuitate ejus, pro suo more, quid dixerat, secundo jam de percipiente ipsi sermo est, non decebat autem ita perspicuitatem exponere, ait Hoornbeekius, ut in secundo capite, de modo vel medio Scripturam intelligendi, hoc omitteretur, quodsemper Protestantes in hac cum Pontificiis disputatione exigunt, gratia nempe, & illuminatio Sp. S. maxime cum, id distinctam hoc loco controversiam cum Socinianis facere, non lateret illos, de Remonstrantibus agit, qui de Socinianismo suspectos se fecerant, nisi etiam hac ratione suum consensum clam, an aperte, declarare fuisset animus. Praeter ista, quae modo ex Wolzogio audivimus, haec sunt quae suspectam ejus in hac controversia Orthodoxiam reddunt jurene an injuria, candidum lectorem penes judicium esto.
units.tr: 4. There remains a fourth point, which rightly increases the suspicion of Pelagianism. Wishing to explain the whole matter of perspicuity beforehand, the author required three things: one on the side of the object, another on the side of the subject, and finally the due contact of the one with the other. We have already noted these in advance. But when he depicts the subject, he does so so meagrely that he says nothing further: In those who understand, he says, this is required one by one: that they know all the laws by which the whole structure of speech is bound. And I think nothing further should be desired in one who is neither foolish nor hindered by any disturbance of mind or other impediment. What else can be drawn from this than that Wolzogen's mind, as to the whole matter, agrees with the Socinians and Remonstrants? Namely, that all readers, endowed indeed with common sense and judgement, can grasp the meaning of the sacred books as far as is sufficient, provided they do not allow themselves to be blinded by prejudice, empty confidence, and other wicked affections. In these words, since they make no mention of the Holy Spirit, the Professors of D. D. rightly judged, says Triglandius, that they were merely reheating Pelagianism. Our author sticks in the same mud. For it was not fitting to set out the perspicuity of Scripture thus: Wolzogen, requiring three things for perspicuity, first said, in his own manner, what he had said about its perspicuity; second, he now speaks of the perceiver himself. But it was not fitting to set out the perspicuity thus, says Hoornbeeck, that in the second chapter, concerning the mode or means of understanding Scripture, this should be omitted, which Protestants always require in this dispute with the Papists, namely grace and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, especially since this point makes a distinct controversy with the Socinians here, and it would not escape them; he speaks of the Remonstrants, who had made themselves suspected of Socinianism, unless the author had also wished to declare his consent in this way, secretly or openly. Besides those things we have just heard from Wolzogen, these are the points that make his orthodoxy in this controversy suspect. Whether justly or unjustly, let the judgement rest with the fair reader.

units.la: 1. Illa quae superius de Articulorum fundamentalium perspicuitate ex ipsius libello congessimus. Unum repetam locum, credimus semper ea quae salus nostra exigit ut sciamus, esse obvia & ita clara, ut ab omnibus intelligi possint. 2. Illa quae superius ab ipso adversus infusum novum lumen dicta audivimus, quae cum ista controversia tam arcte cohaerent, ut lumen infusum negari non possit, quin naturali intellectui Scriptura pervia statuatur, aut plane Barbara. 3. Quae ante hac adduximus loca p. 65. 134. &c. quorum primus expresse statuit sufficere lumen naturale, ut ad ea attendat, ex quibus pendet intelligentia. Nil equidem magis emphatice, vel a Sociniano dici posset, 4. Velthusii, cujus Orthodoxiam praedicat noster, aperta hujus erroris professio: sic ille, impotentia tantum morali impeditur homo, quo minus mysteria fidei cognoscere possit. Non enim in se non habet ea cognitionis principia, eamque cognoscendi facultatem, qua ea quae in Scriptura traduntur, tantum capiuntur & intelligun-tur, ita ut novis principiis aut nova facultate indigeat. &c. Vis Socinianam thesin, sic eam proponit Maccovius. S. Scriptura perspicua est, ita ut solius intellectus auxilio intelligi queat. Status igitur Controversiae inter Reformatos & Wolzogium idem est, ac Reformatos inter & Socinianos ac Remonstrantes. Hoc volunt Orthodoxi. Quamvis Sp. S. ea quae ad salutem necessaria sunt, apertis planisque verbis ita exprimat, ut homo animalis intelligere interdum possit quid Verba ista & phrases indicent: Oportet tamen ut accedat Sp. S. lumen internum, quo, non tantum capiat homo quid verbis, & loquendi modo Grammaticè indicetur, verum etiam spiritualiter &c. Quod jam, sic Heida-nus adversus Episcopium, cum quo idem dicit Wolzogen, ipsius sententiam attinet, qua statuit ita perspicuam Scripturam esse, ut omnis, etiam irregenitus, quisquis tandem sit, modo sanum ipsi sinciput, & a praejudiciis liber, ac destinata malitia, mentem Spiritus absque ulla S. Sancti interna illuminatione percipere possit; praeterquam quod cum experientia, piorum praxi, ac eo quod passim scriptura inculcat, pugnet; in eodem statu cum regenitis homines collocantur irregeniti. Tenebrae non capiunt lucem: neque regni Dei mysteria intelligunt nisi quibus datum est. Nemo verbum Dei audire, hoc est intelligere & credere, potest, nisi qui ex Deo est: cum sapientia carnis inimicitia sit adversus Deum. Animalis homo ψυχικὸς[?]: Chrysostomus, intelligit quidem vocabula & aliquot sententias: spiritualem vero eorum sensum percipere, & fidem eis habere non potest, sed manet ei liber clausus. Cum homo animalis audit, Christum mortuum esse &c. verba quidem percipit, quid sit mori, mori pro aliquo, quid suscitari ex mortuis &c. sed spiritualem sensum non assequitur, -- quia non potest cognoscere: nempe ob luminis defectum in mente, & pravitatem in corde. Hanc ἀδυναμίαν[?] etiam supra attigit. Verba sunt Paraei. Atque ut in notis quibusdam, sic Cartwricht, ad occultandos sensus excogitatis, iidem characteres ab iis percipiuntur, ab illis ne degustantur quidem. Aut si quis multos simul alloquens eo sermone uteretur qui iis cognitus, illis ignotus est. Cum igitur dono hoc fiat si quis Scripturae & Mysterii regni particeps sit, ejus intelligentiam NB nullo humano acumine percipi posse in promtu est: Acies enim oculorum nostrorum eo non poterit penetrare. Absque Spiritu omnia vel apertissime dicta, parabolae & aenigmata erunt; & liber ipse tanquam clausus & septem sigillis obsignatus videbitur. Ratio humana in causa Regni Dei non est id, quod in oculis corporis est facultas videndi: cui satis est, si lux externa offeratur, per quam rerum discrimina pandantur. Sic enim comparata est ut capax sit objectorum. At ratio in causa religionis sic est caeca ut ad objecta Euangelicae lucis magis etiam stupeat & obscuretur, nisi per operationem Sp S. aperiatur, Hinc est NB quod nemo minus est lucis Christi capax quam qui sunt in hoc mundo prudentes ac sapientes. Lubet adscribere pia & vere divina ad hanc rem dicta, ab incomparabili Viro, M. Bucero. Quid mirum, inquit, si in divinis scriptis, quae plane novum requirunt homi-nem, mentem illustratam divinitus, quae praeterea humanae rationi & naturae vitiatae penitus adversantur, labantur & hallucinentur, qui carne adhuc & sanguine gravantur? Ne igitur quod vitii inest nobis a mentis nostrae imbecillitate, a tempore precandi, a remissa nostri ad placita Dei consecratione, divinis ipsis libris, ipsique adeo Spiritui S. adscribamus. Quis enim hic vivens non sentit in se spiritum carnis spiritui Christi gravissime adhuc repugnare, ac saepe numero praevalere? Quis audet etiam gloriari, se ad lectionem sanctorum Bibliorum Sp S. unicum eorum certum interpretem, votis invocasse satis ardentibus? Quis denique ausit gloriari se faciendis Dei praeceptis plene addixisse? At nisi tria haec adsint tibi, animus faciendi quae legeris omnino confirmatus, preces pro Sp.interprete Scripturarum ardentes, & represso Sp.car-nis, mens Sp. S. auscultans quam religiosissimè, non ex eorum numero es qui Dei sapientiam vere diligunt. Ad percipiendam Philosophiam cœlestem, his duabus rebus opus est, ingenio intelligendi & studio. Ingenio, inquam, sed novo ac cœlesti: nam quantacunque valeant homines ingenii per-spicacia naturali, NB si non etiam donentur spiritu rege-nerationis, sicut non prima principia Theologiæ, ita ni-hil ejus solidè possint percipere. Animalis homo, id est, qui Sp. novo filiorum Dei non afflatur, non potest percipere, quæ sunt Sp. Dei, inquit Apostolus. Stultitia illi sunt, nec potest cognoscere: nam spiritualiter dijudicantur. Hinc Dominus Petro, finem legis summumque caput divinarum scripturarum confesso, ipsum sc. Christum esse, filium Dei vivi, dicebat: Beatus es Simon Bar-iona, quia non caro & sanguis, id est NB naturalis luminis vis revelavit tibi, sed pater meus qui in cælis est. Ex his & similibus clarissimis testimoniis Sp. S. evidentissime sanè cognoscitur, homines quantumvis alias ingeniosos & studiosos, NB nihil tamen prorsus posse in divinis literis rectè & planè intelligere, nisi illuminati sint mente, luce cœlesti, & donati Sp. novo, Sp. Dei, Sp. veræ sapientiæ. Quocirca mirum non est, tam multos ingenio & doctrina præstantissimos viros, ut olim, ita & hoc seculo, veram Scripturarum intelligentiam non posse assequi, adeo esse aliena ab illi mente, ut eam plerique eorum acerrimè oppugnent. Nituntur enim isti NB ratione sua, sunt sapientes in oculis suis, sunt ex illis sapientibus & prudentibus, quibus pater cœlestis regni Mysteria abscondit, vacant timore Dei, qui initium est sapientiæ. Alium hæc Spiritum referunt, quam profana hodie multorum scripta. Tales legeres Wolzogi, tales pervolveres authores. Utinam vestigia premeremus virorum, quorum memoria Deo piisque grata est & pretiosa! Longe aliter illi de Scriptura, de viribus humanis, de Spiritus denique lumine, philosophantur. Wol-zozogium Velthuisium in alia plane euntes hic offendimus. Sic tandem pristina Theologia, veritas, quæ juxa pietatem est, abolenda & ex recordatione hominum, per istos homines, delenda, novitatibus, meditationibus propriis indulgendum erit unicè. O quam in rebus cælestibus percipiendis sumus stupidi natura & bardi! Cum enim cætera omnia, tametsi cognitu difficillima, in intimis terræ quasi penetralibus abstrusa, infinitis spaciis à nobis dissita, aut propria industria, aut duce magistro percipiamus; cum terræ, maris, cæli magnitudinem animo & disquisitione assequamur; cum solis, stellarum mensuram, cum corporum cælestium motus comprehensa habeamus; naturæ secreta rimentur; cum in artibus inveniendis miri artifices esse comperiamur: tamen NB ne minimum regni cælorum Mysterium percipere rite possumus. Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ Dei. 1 Cor. 11. 14. Ps. xiv. 2, 3. Rom. iii. 11. 1 Cor. 11. 9. Si sapientia & ingenio humano percipi possent, quis non videt plures sapientes & nobiles ad religionem veram aggregatos iri, quam fatuos & ignobiles. Huc 1 Cor. 11. 11, 12. Quod quidem adeo verum est, ut ne improbi quidem ipsi mysteria regni percipiant ad eorum auctiorem condemnationem, nisi cælitus ea accipiant Hebr. vi. 4. tantum abest ut salutariter percipiant. Neque vero hoc ad illos duntaxat speƈtat, qui Sp. S. destituti sunt & extranei, sed & ad illos pertingit, qui S. S. & cognitione Script. aliquousque imbuti sunt. Sic de Gregorio Thaumaturgo seu Neocæsariensi, in ejus vita, Nyssenus Gregorius. Καταλαμβάνει δὲ ἡ ἐςω-τα λόγον [?] &c. latina exscribam prout versa sunt à Vossio Tungrensi præfecto, apprehendit autem firmum ac stabile verbum fidei. quod non redundanti aliqua verborum curiositate, & artificiosis argumentorum nexibus confirmatur: sed per simplicitatem verborum ex æquo adnunciatur omnibus: quod eo ipso, quod sit supra fidem, vim fidei faciendæ habet. Nam si id, de quo sermo habetur, ejusmodi esset, ut humanarum cogitationum viri-bus comprehenderetur, nihil a Graecanica sapientia differ-ret, nam & illi quodcunque comprehendere potuerint, illud quoque esse opinantur. Quoniam autem supernam illam naturam quae rebus praesidet universis, cogitationes & rationes humanae assequi ac comprehendere nequeunt: ideo fides in locum rationum succedit, ad ea, quae ratio-nem & comprehensionem superant, sese extendens. Socra-tis authoritate permotus, hanc orationem Nysseni esse credit Sculteus. Varia licet a Vossio laudentur, quae suppositia probavit Perkinsus & post eum Rivet, Argumenta thesin Orthodoxam probantia, brevita-tis causa omittam, hac vice Wolzogii ab Ortho-doxis cum Velthusio suo dissensum demonstrasse, eorumque cavillationibus ivisse[?] obviam, sufficiet. Plura habet Clar. Hoornbeekius Opere adversus So-cin. Tomo Primo, Libro Primo. Praetereundum autem non est, quod Zanchius tam late diffusam hominis doceat corruptionem, tantamque cæcita-tem esse, ut ne quidem scientiae theoreticae, & artes tam liberales, quam mechanicae ab hominibus etiamsi velint & conentur assequi, ex natura, aut ex generali influxu (ut vocant) absque speciali Dei auxilio, unquam sint consequendae. Varia adversus orthodoxam veritatem objiciuntur ab adversariis, verum frustra, ut fuse id docuit Hoornbeekius: Neque multum diversa aut validiora sunt, quae sparsim Wolzogio excide-runt. Quaedam ab impiis cognosci, veritatem illos videre saepissime, proximum praecedente articulo, quomodo verum & quousque verum sit, explicui, ita ut nihil inde pro sua sententia evincat. Naturaliter enim & Grammatice solum capiunt, quae percipi ab impiis Orthodoxi concedunt. Neque eo evadendi rimam Wolzogio aperiunt, licet excipiat fortassis, se etiam de nuda loqui [illegible, ~9 letters], qui de Scripturae per-spicuitate sententiam suam exponit, non de fide, aut obe-dientia. dientia. Sic Remonstrantes in sua Apologia. Re-spondet autem Hoornbeekius, quid ni enim eidem nodo eundem adhiberem cuneum? Illa distinctio, sive distinctus modus cognoscendi, non a fide & obedientia est, quae sequitur post cognitionem quasi non in ipsa quoque cognitione attendendus sit. Ipsa cognitio æque etiam indiget novo spirituali principio, ac fides & conver-sio. Neque vel ad minimum intellectus circa Scrip-turam actum bene eliciendum, magis ex nobis ipsis sumus idonei, quam ad actus fidei & conversionis. Ex-erté id docet Apostolus. 2 Cor. iii. 5. Et tandem, de percipiente loquitur Wolzogius p. 105. atque sic in ipsa cognitione, & ratione cognoscendi, ut sacras Scripturas cognoscat homo quantum satis est, requiritur, plus quam nudum percipere sensum Grammaticum; Ideoque & fucus patet, quem præ-tendunt Remonstrantes, aut præte ndere cum ipsis posset Wolzogius, de fide & obedientia nec vola nec vestigium in declaratione est, nec locus de iis agendi hic erat. Quia in declaratione jam egerant de tali intelligentia Script. quantum satis est. Wolzogius eodem argumento convinci facile potest, non quidem eadem verba habet, sed Synonyma: nobis sufficit ea firmiter tenere quæ neces-sitate quadam ad salutem requiruntur. Quæ ita clara sunt atque obvia ut ab omnibus intelligi possint. Sic Wolzogius: certe ovum non magis ovo simile est, quam in hac causa Remonstrantibus Wolzogius.
units.tr: 1. I will repeat one passage from what I gathered earlier from his little book on the clarity of the fundamental articles: "We believe that those things which our salvation requires us to know are always so obvious and so clear that they can be understood by all." 2. What we heard earlier from him against an infused new light is so closely bound up with this controversy that it cannot be denied that the light is infused unless Scripture is held to be open to natural understanding, or else is plainly barbarous. 3. The passages we have cited before (pp. 65, 134, etc.), the first of which expressly states that "the natural light is sufficient for attending to those things on which understanding depends," could hardly be put more emphatically, even by a Socinian. 4. Here is the open profession of this error by Velthuysen, whose orthodoxy our author proclaims: "Man is hindered only by a moral impotence from knowing the mysteries of faith. For he does not lack in himself the principles of knowledge and the faculty of knowing by which the things handed down in Scripture are grasped and understood, so that he does not need new principles or a new faculty," and so on. You see the Socinian thesis; Maccovius sets it out thus: "Holy Scripture is perspicuous, so that it can be understood with the aid of the intellect alone." The state of the controversy between the Reformed and Wolzogen is therefore the same as between the Reformed and the Socinians and Remonstrants. This is what the Orthodox maintain: "Although the Holy Spirit expresses those things that are necessary for salvation in plain and open words, so that the natural man can sometimes understand what the words and phrases indicate, nevertheless the inward light of the Holy Spirit must be added, by which man grasps not only what is indicated grammatically by the words and mode of speech, but also spiritually," and so on. Heidanus says this against Episcopius, with whom Wolzogen agrees on the point of his opinion, namely that Scripture is so clear that every man, even the unregenerate, whoever he is, provided only that he has a sound head, is free of prejudices, and is not set on malice, can perceive the mind of the Spirit without any inward illumination of the Holy Spirit. This conflicts not only with experience, with the practice of the pious, and with what Scripture repeatedly urges, but also with the fact that unregenerate men are placed in the same state as the regenerate. "Darkness does not comprehend the light; nor do they understand the mysteries of the kingdom of God unless it has been given to them. No one can hear the word of God, that is, understand and believe it, unless he is of God, since the wisdom of the flesh is enmity against God." The natural man (ψυχικός) understands indeed the words and some sentences, as Chrysostom says, but he cannot perceive their spiritual sense or have faith in them; the book remains closed to him. When the natural man hears that Christ is dead, etc., he grasps the words, what dying is, dying for someone, what rising from the dead is, and so on, but he does not attain the spiritual sense, because he cannot know it, namely on account of the lack of light in the mind and the perversity of the heart. [ἀδυναμία] He touched on this inability above. These are the words of Paraeus. And just as in certain notes devised to conceal meanings, the same characters are perceived by some and not even tasted by others, or as if someone addressing many at once used a language known to some but unknown to others, so, since this is a gift given to those who share in Scripture and in the mystery of the kingdom, its understanding, I say, cannot be grasped by any human acuteness, as is plain: the sharpness of our eyes cannot penetrate it. Without the Spirit, all things, even those said most openly, will be parables and riddles, and the book itself will seem closed and sealed with seven seals. Human reason, in matters of the kingdom of God, is not like the faculty of sight in the eyes of the body, for which it is enough that external light be offered by which the differences of things are laid open. For reason is so constituted that it is able to take in objects. But in religion reason is so blind that, when faced with the objects of the Gospel light, it is made even more dull and obscured, unless it is opened by the operation of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is indeed the case that no one is less capable of the light of Christ than those who are prudent and wise in this world. I am pleased to add the pious and truly divine words on this matter of the incomparable man, Martin Bucer. "What wonder," he says, "if in the divine writings, which plainly require a new man, a mind divinely illuminated, and which moreover are utterly opposed to human reason and to corrupted nature, those who are still weighed down by flesh and blood stumble and go astray? Let us therefore not ascribe to the divine books themselves, and to the Holy Spirit himself, the faults that lie in us from the weakness of our mind, from our neglect of prayer, and from our slack dedication to the purposes of God. For who here in this life does not feel in himself that the spirit of the flesh still strongly resists the Spirit of Christ and often prevails? Who dares even to boast that he has called upon the Holy Spirit, the only certain interpreter of the holy Bible, with sufficiently fervent prayers? Who, finally, would dare to boast that he has fully devoted himself to doing God's commands? But unless these three things are present in you: a determination to do what you have read, fervent prayers to the Holy Spirit as interpreter of the Scriptures, and a suppressed flesh with a mind listening most devoutly to the Spirit, you are not among those who truly love the wisdom of God. To grasp heavenly philosophy two things are needed: a gift of understanding and zeal. A gift, I say, but a new and heavenly one. For however sharp men may be by natural talent, unless they are also given the Spirit of regeneration, they cannot grasp anything of theology solidly, nor even its first principles. The natural man, that is, one who is not inspired by the new Spirit of the sons of God, cannot perceive the things of the Spirit of God, says the Apostle. They are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, for they are judged spiritually." Hence the Lord said to Peter, who had confessed that the end of the law and the chief point of the divine Scriptures was Christ himself, the Son of the living God: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood, that is, the power of natural light, has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven." From these and similar most clear testimonies it is evident beyond doubt that men, however otherwise gifted and studious, nevertheless can grasp nothing at all rightly and plainly in the divine letters unless they are illuminated in mind by heavenly light and given the new Spirit, the Spirit of God, the Spirit of true wisdom. Wherefore it is no wonder that so many men most excellent in talent and learning, as in former times so also in this age, cannot attain the true understanding of the Scriptures, being so alien to that mind that most of them most fiercely attack it. For these men rely on their own reason; they are wise in their own eyes; they are among those wise and prudent to whom the heavenly Father has hidden the mysteries of the kingdom; they are without the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom." These words describe a different spirit from that of the profane writings of many today. You would read such things in Wolzogen, such things you would find in his authors. Would that we might tread in the footsteps of those men whose memory is pleasing and precious to God and to the pious! Those men philosophize about Scripture, about human powers, and finally about the light of the Spirit in a quite different way; here we find Wolzogen going in a completely different direction from Velthuysen. Thus at length the ancient theology, the truth which accords with piety, is to be abolished and, through these men, erased from the memory of men, and we shall have to indulge solely in novelties and our own speculations. O how stupid and dull we are by nature in perceiving heavenly things! For while we grasp all other things, however most difficult to know, hidden in the inmost recesses of the earth, far removed from us by infinite spaces, either by our own industry or with a master as guide; while we measure with mind and inquiry the greatness of earth, sea and sky; while we have comprehended the measure of the sun and stars and the motions of the heavenly bodies; while we search out the secrets of nature; and while we find ourselves to be wonderful craftsmen in inventing arts: nevertheless we can rightly perceive not even the smallest mystery of the kingdom of heaven. "The natural man does not perceive the things of God" (1 Cor. 2. 14; Ps. 14. 2, 3; Rom. 3. 11; 1 Cor. 2. 9). If these things could be perceived by human wisdom and talent, who does not see that more wise and noble men would be gathered to the true religion than foolish and ignoble ones? To this, 1 Cor. 2. 11, 12. Indeed this is so true that not even the wicked themselves perceive the mysteries of the kingdom, so that their condemnation is greater, unless they receive them from heaven (Heb. 6. 4); so far are they from perceiving them to their salvation. Nor does this pertain only to those who are destitute of the Holy Spirit and strangers to it, but it also reaches those who are, to some extent, steeped in the Holy Scriptures and in knowledge of the Scriptures. So Gregory Nyssen writes of Gregory Thaumaturgus, or of Neocaesarea, in his life: "He apprehends the inner word..." [Καταλαμβάνει δὲ ἡ ἔσω λόγος]. I will copy out the Latin as it was rendered by Vossius of Tongres: "He apprehends the firm and stable word of faith, which is not confirmed by any superfluous curiosity of words or by artificial chains of arguments, but is proclaimed equally to all through the simplicity of words; and this very fact, that it is above faith, has the power of creating faith. For if that of which the discourse treats were of such a kind as to be grasped by the powers of human thoughts, it would differ in no way from Greek wisdom, for they too believe that whatever they can grasp is that. But since human thoughts and reasonings cannot reach or comprehend that supernal nature which presides over all things, faith takes the place of reasonings, extending itself to those things which surpass reason and comprehension." Moved by the authority of Socrates, Sculteus believes this oration to be Nyssen's. Although Vossius praises various arguments, which Perkins, and after him Rivet, proved to be spurious, I shall for brevity omit the arguments that support the orthodox thesis. For the present it will suffice to have shown that the Orthodox have demonstrated Wolzogen's dissent from his Velthuysen, and have gone to meet their cavils. The illustrious Hoornbeek has more in his work against the Socinians, Volume 1, Book 1. Nor must it be passed over that Zanchius teaches the corruption of man to be so widely diffused, and such blindness to be so great, that not even theoretical sciences and arts, liberal as well as mechanical, can ever be attained by men, even if they wish and try, from nature or from general influence (as they call it) without the special help of God. Various objections are raised by the adversaries against orthodox truth, but in vain, as Hoornbeek has thoroughly taught; nor are the things that have slipped from Wolzogen here and there much different or stronger. I have explained, in the immediately preceding article, how and how far it is true that the impious sometimes see the truth, so that they can gain nothing from it for their own opinion. For they grasp only what the Orthodox concede can be perceived by the impious, and that naturally and grammatically. Nor do they open for Wolzogen a crack for escape by this means, though he perhaps objects that he is speaking of mere understanding [illegible, about 9 letters], when he sets out his opinion on the perspicuity of Scripture, not on faith or obedience. So the Remonstrants say in their Apology. Hoornbeek replies: "Why should I not apply the same wedge to the same knot? That distinction, or distinct manner of knowing, is not separate from faith and obedience, which follow after knowledge, as if it were not to be considered also in knowledge itself. Knowledge itself equally needs a new spiritual principle, as do faith and conversion. Nor are we any more competent of ourselves to elicit well even the minimal act of understanding concerning Scripture than we are for the acts of faith and conversion." The Apostle teaches this plainly: 2 Cor. 3. 5. And finally, Wolzogen speaks of the perceiving subject, p. 105, and thus in the very act of knowing and the manner of knowing, a man requires, in order to know the holy Scriptures as much as is sufficient, more than the bare perception of the grammatical sense. Hence the deception the Remonstrants put forward is plain, or Wolzogen could pretend it with them: "Concerning faith and obedience there is neither a sign nor a trace in the declaration, nor was there any place here for treating of them, because in the declaration they had already treated of such understanding of Scripture as is sufficient." Wolzogen can easily be convicted by the same argument; he does not use the same words, but synonyms: "It is enough for us to hold firmly those things which by a certain necessity are required for salvation, which are so clear and obvious that they can be understood by all." So Wolzogen: certainly an egg is no more like an egg than Wolzogen is, in this matter, like the Remonstrants.

units.la: Obscuritatis vero scripturam sic argui ab Ortho-doxis, si forsan putet cum Velthusio. Frequens illa & trita Remonstrantium & Socinianorum quidem cavillatio est, sed nullius monenti. Dudum ex Heidano aliisque id didicimus. Subjecti recipientis imperfectio, objecto non est imputanda. Celeberri-mus ille Pontificiorum victor Withakerus, hanc di-stinctionem ex Luthero proponit his verbis, sane scopum nostrum exactissimè ferientibus. Alia etiam distinctione utitur Lutherus eodem in loco. Ait enim, scripturarum sive claritatem, sive obscuritatem, vel internam vel externam esse, subjectivam dicunt alii vel objectivam, absolutam vel relativam, eodem enim res redit; internam, ipsius cordis scilicet; externam, in ipsis verbis positam. Si de interna scripturae obscuritate vel perspicuitate loquamur, ait, ne unum quidem jota isto modo in Script. perspicuum esse, sine Sp. S. interna luce: omnia enim hac ratione & hoc respectu carni & acumini hominis obscura esse, juxta illud quod habetur Pf. xiv. Dixit insipiens in corde suo non esse Deum. Sin autem externam Scripturae claritatem vel obscuritatem intelligamus, ait, omnia dogmata isto modo clara esse, & in lucem producta. Atque haec quidem di-stinctio est valde necessaria. Et haec certe differentia est inter Theologiam & Philosophiam, quandoquidem ad artes Philosophicas perdiscendas externum tantum naturae lumen requiritur. Sed ut Theologiam recte teneamus, opus est interno lumine Sp. Sancti, quia, quae fidei sunt, sub rationis humanae disciplinam minime cadunt. Atque haec interna claritas est, quae tota a Sp. Sancto fluxit.
units.tr: Orthodox writers argue that Scripture is obscure only if one thinks so with Velthuysen. That is a frequent and hackneyed quibble of the Remonstrants and Socinians, but it is refuted by no one. We learned this long ago from Heidanus and others. The imperfection of the receiving subject is not to be imputed to the object. That most famous victor over the Papists, Whitaker, takes this distinction from Luther in these words, which hit our purpose very precisely: Luther also uses another distinction in the same place. For he says that the clarity or obscurity of the Scriptures is either internal or external; others call it subjective or objective, absolute or relative, for it comes to the same thing. Internal means that of the heart itself; external means that which lies in the words themselves. If we speak of the internal obscurity or perspicuity of Scripture, he says, not even one jot is perspicuous in Scripture in this way and in this respect without the inner light of the Holy Spirit, for all things are obscure to flesh and human acumen in this way, according to what stands in Ps. xiv., The fool has said in his heart, There is no God. But if we understand the external clarity or obscurity of Scripture, he says, all doctrines are clear in this way and brought into the light. And indeed this distinction is very necessary. And this difference certainly exists between theology and philosophy, since for learning the philosophical arts only the external light of nature is required. But to hold theology rightly we need the internal light of the Holy Spirit, because the things of faith do not at all fall under the discipline of human reason. And this internal clarity is what flows wholly from the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Neque sic frustra nobis aut data Scriptura, aut in-dita intellectus facultas est; uti argumentantur Pelagiani, Et cum iis Wolzog. ut videre est ad Libr. I. Str. 6. Non enim eo fine data est, ut ab intellectu naturali & mortuo perciperetur, sed ut ii, quibus daretur principium illud cognoscendi spiritualiter, mysteria inde regni cælorum addiscerent. Novit au-tem, ait Bucerus, Dominus suos, & hi illum, ejus-que hi vocem norunt, his enim Dominus, se, & Pa-trem revelat. Agnoscunt igitur se in Domino invicem, ex certa doctrina verbi & Spiritus Domini: at dicit unusquisque, scio cui credidi. Obsignatur enim veritas Christi in uniuscujusque corde. Itaque certa & indubitata exis-tit divinarum Scripturarum interpretatio, sed in veris Christi Ecclesiis, & apud eos qui vere vivunt in Christo & aguntur ejus Spiritu.
units.tr: Nor, as the Pelagians argue (and Wolzogen with them, as may be seen in Book I, Str. 6), is Scripture given to us in vain, nor is the faculty of understanding implanted in us in vain. For it was not given for this end, that it should be perceived by the natural and dead intellect, but so that those to whom the principle of knowing spiritually is given might learn from it the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. The Lord, however, knows his own, says Bucer, and they know him and know his voice, for to these the Lord reveals himself and the Father. They therefore recognise one another in the Lord, from the sure doctrine of the Word and of the Spirit of the Lord; and each one says, I know whom I have believed. For the truth of Christ is sealed in the heart of each one. Thus the interpretation of the divine Scriptures is certain and indubitable, but it exists in the true churches of Christ, and among those who truly live in Christ and are led by his Spirit.

units.la: Duplicem etiam sensum non fingimus, uti splendidè mentiuntur Remonstrantes, sed ejusdem sensus diversos recipiendi modos, prout diverso agun-tur homines principio. Fuse id, adversus insultatio-nes Apologistae, docent nostri. Ad fidem, fateor, plura requirit quam ad Scripturae intellectum Wol-zogen, majus quippe est, credere quam scire, hinc ad fidem requiri gratiam non negat, sed ad Scr. intellectionem, ut ita loquar, non item. Ad amussim Pelagianam omnia, sic ejus Doctor, Ma-gister Episcopius, nam & is aliquando liberalis est. Aliud est credere aliud intelligere, ad intelligentiam sen-suum perspicuorum, nihil aliud necessarium est, quam vis apprehendendi & percipiendi verba, quibus clare & significanter sensus isti expressi sunt. Ea vis naturalis est, & omnibus ratione recta aut sana praeditis communis in omni statu. Ad fidem vero sive ad adsensum sensibus intellectis adhibendum, sola ista vis non sufficit, &c. Diversa sunt credere & cognoscere, sed & cognos-cere, & cognoscere, diversum esse posse, non advertunt. Imo cognitio hominis naturalis, ab ea, quae in regenito reperitur, magis distat, quam, in eodem homine, fides à cognitione, quarum una tam arcta affinitate cum altera jungitur, ut cognitio non solum pars fidei sit, sed & fides saepe per cognitionem denotetur. Ac profecto cognitio omnis, quae vere cognitio dici meretur, & spiritualis est, non minus, quam fides, Deum ejusque Spiritum authorem habet. Datur enim nosse. Spiritus est sp. revelationis & notitiae. Deoque transcribit Christus omne quod in suis parvulis cognitionis est. Calumniatur tamen audacter & splendidè Velthuisen, quan-do Spiritum nos pro principio fidei ponere refert, aut pal-pabilem docet Pelagianismum. Vel enim significat, nos præter Scripturam aliud principium normale fingere, dictata nimirum Sp. S. atque sic calumniatorem agit. Vel, nos Spiritui sancto causalitatem fidei hyperphysicam, qua ille fidei in nobis effector & author est unicus, transcribere, principio pro causa efficiente prima sumto, si autem hoc sensu ida nobis dici conqueratur, verum dicit, sed Pelagium sic in oppugnando Sp. S. ejusque gratiâ superat immensum. Plura sunt quibus Pastori Senior suppetias hac in controversia ferre voluisse videtur. Ut Medicum decet, in antecessum ex signis[?] diacriticis de natura morbi judicat; Etiam illi, sic pronunciat, in vici-nitate Enthusiasmi versantur, quibus pro concione in ore est, se quidem certa & explorata docere, sed sibi & re-genitis ea tantum esse perceptibilia, aliis autem imper-ceptibilia; & quia Spiritu destituuntur, eos ad illa argumenta cæcutire. Ideo sæpius solent præfari se ea in medium prolaturos, quæ multi ex auditorum numero non possunt intelligere, neque illorum causa se istum sermonem habere, sed spiritualium gratia. Statuo tales non longe abire ab Enthusiasmo. Jam anteà sarcasmum istum re-tudimus. Talem etiam hanc nobis sapientiam describit Apostolus, ut, nisi immediatè nobis per Spiritum revele-tur, nullum aliud ulli homini, quo ad hanc cognitio-nem pertingat, supersit. Quod enim nemo Principum hujus seculi cognovit, illud aut occultum nobis remanere debet aut immediata Sp revelatione acquiri. Verba sunt Hei-dani contra Episcopium. Augustinum, Gregorium Magnum, aliosque sic Enthusiasticè concionantes audivimus. Quid? an in publico cætu non dantur omnis generis auditores? nonne, quibus datum est nosse, quibus dati sunt aperti mentis oculi, quibus Spiritus testificatur, dantur? nonne & alii, quibus Spiritus hujus seculi occæcavit mentes, qui adhuc in errore versantur, cæci, non videntes? An Christus Jesus male & Enthusiasticè auditores suos ita discriminabat? Pastores quod attinet, putasne nullos esse, qui cum Johanne ea quae viderunt, quae audiverunt, quae manibus suis palparunt, proponant? quibus dedit Deus experientiam spiritualem, gustumque eorum, quae aliis annunciant? At surdo narrat fabulam, qui huncce hominem ista doceat. Benedictus sit Deus noster, qui Pastores hactenus Ecclesiae suae superesse voluit, quorum verba mundo peregrina, quorum phrases hominibus animalibus sunt Barbarae, ridiculae, absurdae, dum interim, iidem illi, manifesti sunt, eorumque ministerium piorum praesertim conscientiis & approbatum. Sic Withakerum superius Dureo suo respondentem audivimus. Nihil opus fuit ut tam multa hic Luthero & Calvino de novis quibusdam Enthusiasmis objiceres, in quo quis non videt a quo hoc Spiritu profectum sit? Deum precor ut hanc tibi Blasphemiam ignoscat. Quibus haec peregrina vox est aut incognita, eorum non sunt illuminatae mentes a Spiritu: ait Polanus.
units.tr: Nor do we invent a double sense, as the Remonstrants splendidly lie, but diverse modes of receiving the same sense, according as men are moved by a different principle. Our people have taught this at length against the taunts of the Apologist. I admit that faith requires more than the understanding of Scripture requires from Wolzogen; for it is greater to believe than to know, and so he does not deny that grace is required for faith, but not likewise, so to speak, for the understanding of Scripture. All things are measured by the Pelagian rule, as their teacher, Master Episcopius, says (for he too is sometimes generous). To believe is one thing, to understand another. For understanding perspicuous meanings, nothing else is necessary than the power of apprehending and perceiving the words by which those meanings are clearly and significantly expressed. That power is natural, and common in every state to all who are endowed with right or sound reason. But for assenting to meanings once understood, that power alone does not suffice, etc. Believing and knowing are different, but they do not notice that knowing and knowing can also be different. Indeed the natural knowledge of man is further removed from that which is found in the regenerate than, in the same man, faith is from knowledge; and these two are joined by so close an affinity that knowledge is not only a part of faith, but faith is often denoted by knowledge. And truly all knowledge that deserves to be called true knowledge is spiritual, and has God and his Spirit as its author no less than faith does. For to know is given. It is the Spirit of revelation and of knowledge. And Christ ascribes to God whatever knowledge there is in his little ones. Yet Velthuysen is boldly and splendidly slandered when he reports that we set the Spirit as the principle of faith, or when he teaches that this is plain Pelagianism. For either he means that we invent some other normal principle besides Scripture, namely the dictates of the Holy Spirit, and so he acts as a slanderer; or else he means that we ascribe to the Holy Spirit a hyperphysical causality of faith, by which he alone is the sole effector and author of faith in us, taking principle for the first efficient cause. If he complains that these things are said to us in this sense, he speaks truly, but in thus assailing the Holy Spirit and his grace he far surpasses Pelagius. There are several points on which the elder minister seems to have wished to bring help in this controversy. As a physician should, he judges the nature of the disease in advance from its distinguishing signs: Those too, he pronounces, who in the church have the word of Enthusiasm in their mouth, who say that they teach certain and tested things, but that these are perceptible only to themselves and the regenerate, and imperceptible to others; and because they are destitute of the Spirit, they grope blindly at those arguments. Therefore they often make a preface that they will bring forward those things which many of the hearers cannot understand, and that they do not give this discourse for their sake, but for the sake of the spiritual. I hold that such men are not far from Enthusiasm. Already earlier we have blunted this sarcasm. The Apostle also describes such wisdom to us, so that, unless it is revealed to us immediately through the Spirit, no other means remains by which any man may attain to this knowledge. For what none of the princes of this age has known, that must either remain hidden from us or be acquired by immediate revelation of the Spirit. These are the words of Heidanus against Episcopius. We have heard Augustine, Gregory the Great, and others preaching in such an Enthusiastic manner. What then? Are not all kinds of hearers present in a public assembly? Are there not some to whom it is given to know, to whom the eyes of the mind are opened, to whom the Spirit bears witness? Are there not also others, whose minds the spirit of this age has blinded, who still remain in error, blind and not seeing? Did Christ Jesus wrongly and in an Enthusiastic manner distinguish his hearers in this way? As for ministers, do you think there are none who, with John, proclaim what they have seen, what they have heard, what their hands have handled? To them God has given spiritual experience and a taste of the things they announce to others. But he tells a tale to a deaf man who teaches this man such things. Blessed be our God, who has willed that ministers should hitherto survive in his church, whose words are foreign to the world, whose phrases are barbarous, ridiculous and absurd to animal men, while at the same time those same men are manifest, and their ministry is approved especially by the consciences of the pious. Thus we have heard Whitaker above answering his Durus: There was no need for you to object here so many things against Luther and Calvin about certain new Enthusiasms. Who does not see from what spirit this came? I pray God to pardon you this blasphemy. Those to whom this is a foreign or unknown word do not have their minds enlightened by the Spirit, says Polanus.

units.la: Rationes addit noster Medicus 1. Scripturae dissen-taneum est, ponere aliud impossibilitatis genus in addiscenda & cognoscenda fidei veritate, quam quod in virtutis & pietatis studio se manifestat. Obscurum hoc est, sic mentem suam illustrat. Et Scriptura docet impios tam volentes in ignorantia & errore exitiali versari, quam volentes & sua sponte impietatem sectantur. Non negamus multos affectata ignorantia & maligna laborare, quos & ideo reliquis pejores esse Scriptura innuit: at aliud impossibilitatis genus, sive aliam ignorantiae causam, praeter propriam malitiam nullam esse, certe falso salsius est, & crassissime Pelagianum. Oculos nobis esse negat Apostolus, nihil homo in spiritualibus comprehendit. Quid ita? an quia per ignaviam aut malitiam negligit? imo, etiamsi enitatur, nihil potest, ne culpa hujus detur animalis hominis desidiae & negligentiae, sic Calvinus, sic Musculus, sic Reformati. An non agnoscis oculos nobis deesse, non mortuos nos esse in peccatis Velthusi? vel an illa omnia obicem non po-nunt, nisi nova & actualis malitia ultro superadda-tur? Norunt quid velis, quibus fætent[?] Pelagii fæces. Scripturæ affingis audacter id, cui tota reclamat. Lapsum hominem, natura insipientem, cæcum, mortuum dicit peccatorem & inculcat. Hinc ineptus est ad omne bonum, juxta Catechesin, etiam ad spirituales intellectus actus exerendos. Fuè, internum lumen supernaturale requiri, quo nondum indito, nihil cogitat, nihil percipit peccator spiritualiter, jam antea probavimus, ac proinde hominem per se ineptum esse, faciat quicquid potest; nisi, facienti quod in se est, de congruo gratiam deberi somniet cum Jesuitis noster Medicus. Christus Jesus, nonne exertè docet, aliquibus dari quod non datur omnibus? hoc autem fit ex gratia, sicque ille, cui ista gratia, quam Deus nulli debet, non obtingit, non capit; ac quidem, ob subjecti, per originale peccatum, corruptionem, impossibile est ut capiat My-steria Regni cælorum. Hinc Dominus Judæis ait, Vos non creditis : non enim estis ex ovibus meis. En aliam im-possibilitatis causam.Probavimus alibi, inquit Hoorn-beekius, Spiritus Sancti opem & illuminationem non re-stringi ad difficiliora Scripturæ intelligenda; sed ad omnia & singula sacra requiri. 2. Secunda ratio sic sonat. Etiam illi ipso usu hoc probant, nam de sua sententia & alios erudire nituntur iis argumentis & rationibus, quæ etiam valent in interpretatione scriptoris profani. In docendo, & explicandis rationibus & argumentis suæ fidei, insistunt viam à notissimis, ad quæ intelligenda tam singularem Sp. operationem, tanquam novum lumen non requirunt, ad obscuriora progrediuntur. Quid jam porro? sic concludit: Hac ipsa opera ostendentes se agnoscere suas opiniones suaque dogmata, quæ prosi-tentur iis notionibus niti, & ab iis manare, quas singuli possent percipere sine novo & non omnibus communi lumine. Misera & plus quam puerilis ista est cavillatio. Distinguenda perceptio naturalis à spirituali, quippe toto genere diversa ab una altera, uti superius demonstravimus. Non enim omnem perceptionem, sed spiritualem omnem denegamus homini irregenito Ratiocinationes quibus utimur, media esse credimus, sed moralia, quibus homines illuminentur &, superveniente Spiritus operatione hyperphysica, veritatem intus & spiritualiter percipere apti evadant ac doceantur. Nullam fidei notionem, vel notissimam, absque Spiritus interno lumine perceptibilem credimus & profitemur, Lutheri sententia nobis placet, quam ex Whitakero audivimus, interna claritate ne unum quidem jota perspicuum esse, & verè spirituali modo recipi, absque interna Spiritus Sancti luce, naturali modo, licet eadem forsan veritas, & Grammaticè, uti in Censura Professores Leidenses loqui amant, ab homine naturali percipiatur. Sic agnoscimus nostra iis notionibus niti & Scripturæ dictis, quas, absque lumine regenerantis Spiritus, naturaliter percipere valeat homo animalis, Spiritum non habens; atque eum in finem sic ratiocinationem instituimus, ut morali medio adhibito, per supervenientem Sp. S. hyperphysicam operationem, ad supernaturalem intelligendi aptitudinem perveniant auditores jam animales. Sic & tuas aliasque malas ratiocinationes ad oppugnandam veritatem excogitatas, refellimus, non quod putemus veritatem tibi aut tui similibus spirituali modo perceptibilem esse, sed naturali, neque tamen incassum nos laborare speramus in domino: fieri enim posset, ut tute tandem, post tot tantasque adversus lucem Spiritus scriptas fictasque altercationes stultitiæ tuæ naturalis convictus, sic ad spiritualem, tali morali medio interveniente, per Dei gratiam perducereris sapientiam & illuminatos adipiscereris mentis oculos, quos animitus tibi apprecor: aliis saltem manifesta erit ista ad conscientias veritas, quam docemus, eritque medium pios & spirituales, in fide recepta, adversus tuos aliorumque carnalium perpetuos insultus, muniendi & corroborandi. Instas & dicis sententiam tuam confirmare, quod illi spirituales eo intelligentiores aut minus intelligentes sunt in Theologia, quo instructiores sunt earum rerum scientiis, quas absque illa singulari Spiritus opera comparari posse confitentur. Resp. ı. Dicterium illud quod attinet, in deliciis nobis est, per Dei gratiam, & esse spirituales, & propterea carnalibus ludibrio haberi: neque enim inde tantum nobis periculi imminet, quantum tibi; qui temet à spiritualibus segregando, vel tuo judicio carnalis es. 2. Sed ex Buceri, Musculi, Calvini, Camero-nis, quorum verba superius producta sunt, vel ipsius Apostoli judicio, ineptus es, ad judicium de spiritualibus depromendum. Cæcus garris de coloribus. Spiritualiter spiritualia dijudicantur à spiritualibus. 3. Deinde, quid valeant artes & studia humaniora, ante hac, summos Viros explicantes audivimus, nuperrimè Bucerum. Absque Spiritu nihil valent, imo ineptiores reddunt ad spiritualem perceptionem homines animales. Ubi Spiritu regitur illuminata mens, hæc dona sanctificata, media sunt, in suo genere, sanè non contemnenda, quæque & omni studio sibi comparare nituntur isti spirituales: non enim illi eruditorum spernunt labores, nec sibi soli sapere videntur, cum multis Neotericis. Scientia interim non intumescentes, omnia quippe illa adminicula ulteriori adjumento non esse probe conscii profitentes, quam in quantum spiritu, qui est spiritus modestiæ & vetat altum sapere, sanctificantur & elevantur. Atque sic concedunt spiritualiter magis intelligentem esse, qui sanctificata aliarum rerum sapientia praestat, quam illum qui ista caret, vel rerum quidem scientia, sed quae non fit san-ctificata,pollet. Non negantes interim, Grammaticam illam quam diximus & naturalem percipiendi aptitu-dinem, seu perceptivitatem, hoc termino utitur Bisterfeldius, in suo genere, aliarum rerum scien-tia mediante, extendi. Quae tamen, vel maxime licet aucta, nunquam in aliam perceptivitatis sphæ-ram transfert hominem peccatorem. Haec disce Velt-hufi, sic totum negotium concipiunt homines, qui spirituales esse desiderant, & pro suo modulo.
units.tr: Our physician adds reasons. (1) It is inconsistent with Scripture to posit another kind of impossibility in learning and knowing the truth of faith than that which shows itself in the pursuit of virtue and piety. This is obscure, and it is how he illustrates his own mind. And Scripture teaches that the impious are as much given to ignorance and deadly error as they are to impiety, willingly and of their own accord. We do not deny that many labour under deliberate ignorance and malice, and for that reason Scripture hints that they are worse than the rest. But that there is no other kind of impossibility, no other cause of ignorance, apart from one's own wickedness, is certainly falser than false and grossly Pelagian. The Apostle denies that we have eyes: man comprehends nothing in spiritual things. Why so? Is it because he neglects them through laziness or malice? Indeed, even if he strives, he can do nothing; so the fault is not to be laid on the sloth and negligence of the natural man, so Calvin, so Musculus, so the Reformed. Do you not acknowledge that we lack eyes, and that we are not dead in sins, Velthuysen? Or do those things not place an obstacle unless new and actual malice is freely added? They know what you mean, those whose dregs of Pelagius stink. You boldly ascribe to Scripture what the whole of Scripture opposes. It calls fallen man, ignorant by nature, blind, dead in sin, and it drives this home. Hence he is unfit for every good, according to the Catechism, even for exercising the acts of spiritual understanding. Moreover, we have already proved that an internal supernatural light is required, and without it, the sinner, not yet having been given it, thinks nothing and perceives nothing spiritually. Hence man is unfit of himself, however much he does, unless, as our physician dreams with the Jesuits, grace is owed to him de congruo for doing what is in him. Does not Christ Jesus plainly teach that to some is given what is not given to all? This comes from grace, and so the one to whom this grace, which God owes to no one, does not come, does not grasp it; and indeed, because of corruption of the subject through original sin, it is impossible for him to grasp the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Hence the Lord said to the Jews, You do not believe, for you are not of my sheep. Here is another cause of impossibility. We have proved elsewhere, says Hoornbeek, that the help and illumination of the Holy Spirit are not restricted to understanding the more difficult passages of Scripture, but are required for all and each of the sacred things. (2) The second reason sounds thus: By their very practice they prove this as well, for they strive to instruct others about their opinion by those arguments and reasons which also hold good in the interpretation of a profane writer. In teaching, and in explaining the reasons and arguments of their faith, they keep to the way that starts from the most familiar things, and for understanding these they do not require any special operation of the Spirit as a new light, but proceed to the more obscure. What then follows? He concludes thus: By this very work they show that they recognise their opinions and their doctrines, which they profess, rest on those notions and flow from those which each could perceive without a new light not common to all. This quibble is wretched and more than childish. The natural perception must be distinguished from the spiritual, since they are of a wholly different kind, as we showed above. For we deny not every perception, but every spiritual perception, to the unregenerate man. The reasonings we use we believe to be means, but moral means, by which men are enlightened and, when the hyperphysical operation of the Spirit supervenes, become apt to perceive the truth inwardly and spiritually and be taught. We believe and profess that no notion of faith, even the most familiar, can be perceived without the inward light of the Spirit; we approve the opinion of Luther, which we heard from Whitaker, that not even one iota is clear by inner clarity, and that it is received in a truly spiritual way, and not in a natural way without the inner light of the Holy Spirit, although perhaps the same truth, and grammatically (as the Leiden professors in their Censure like to speak) is perceived by the natural man. Thus we acknowledge that our arguments rest on those notions and on the words of Scripture which the natural man, not having the Spirit, can perceive naturally without the light of the regenerating Spirit; and to that end we frame our reasoning so that, by the moral means applied, the hearers, who are as yet natural, may by the supervening hyperphysical operation of the Holy Spirit arrive at a supernatural aptitude for understanding. So too we refute your and others' bad reasonings devised to attack the truth, not because we think the truth is perceptible to you or to those like you in a spiritual way, but in a natural way; nor do we hope that we labour in vain in the Lord. For it could happen that you yourself, at last convicted of your natural folly after so many great and invented wranglings against the light of the Spirit, might be led through the grace of God to spiritual wisdom, with this moral means intervening, and obtain enlightened eyes of the mind, which I pray for you inwardly. At least to others this truth which we teach will be plain for their consciences, and it will be a means for the pious and spiritual, received in faith, of being fortified and strengthened against your perpetual insults and those of other carnal men. You insist and say that your opinion is confirmed, that those spiritual men are the more intelligent or the less intelligent in theology the more or less they are instructed in those sciences of things which they admit can be acquired without that special operation of the Spirit. Reply. 1. As for that taunt, we delight, by the grace of God, in being spiritual, and therefore in being mocked by the carnal; for we are not in as much danger from this as you are, who, by separating yourself from the spiritual, are carnal by your own judgment. 2. But by the judgment of Bucer, Musculus, Calvin, Cameron, whose words were produced above, or by the very judgment of the Apostle, you are unfit to pronounce a judgment about spiritual things. You blind man chatter about colours. Spiritual things are judged spiritually by the spiritual. 3. Next, what the humane arts and studies are worth, we heard the great men explaining formerly, most recently Bucer. Without the Spirit they are worth nothing; indeed they make men still more unfit for spiritual perception, being natural. Where the enlightened mind is ruled by the Spirit, these gifts, sanctified, are means, in their own kind certainly not to be despised, and the spiritual men strive to acquire them with all zeal; for they do not scorn the labours of the learned, nor do they seem to be wise alone, as many modern men do. Meanwhile, not puffed up by learning, they profess that they are well aware that all those aids are not of themselves sufficient, and they are sanctified and raised up only so far as they are touched by the Spirit, who is the Spirit of modesty and forbids high-mindedness. And so they concede that one who excels in wisdom of other things made holy is more intelligent spiritually than one who lacks such things, or who is strong in knowledge of things but which are not made holy. Not denying, meanwhile, that the grammatical and natural aptitude for perceiving, or perceptivity, which I have mentioned, is extended, in its own kind, by means of knowledge of other things (Bisterfeld uses this term), however greatly it may be increased, it never transfers the sinful man into another sphere of perceptivity. Velthuysen, learn this; men who wish to be spiritual conceive the whole matter thus, each according to his measure.

units.la: 4. Quid diceret Medicus, vel aliarum rerum scien-tiam communi adjuvante providentia & influxu ac-quiri non posse, cum Zanchio si quis statueret, ho-nemque[?] ita in tenebris demersum, ut Spiritus sancti quadam opera & inspiratione gratiosa non adjuvante vel in iis proficere quicquam ipsi impossibile sit? At deberet tum, dicit Medicus, id ex adversariorum sen-tentia obscurum in Theologia vocari, non quod a principiis & notioribus remotius est, sed quod desiderat Spiritus lumen regenitis tantum proprium. Neque rem ipsam, neque adversariorum sententiam intelligit, miserri-mus argumentator. Perspicuitatem ut & obscuri-tatem dicimus internam vel externam esse, seu ob-jectivam aut subjectivam: objectivam perspicuita-tem scripturae vindicamus: id autem, quod sic ob-jective perspicuum est, percipitur pro diversa sub-jecti habitudine & operandi modo, vel Grammati-cè, literaliter & naturaliter, vel spiritualiater & salu-tariter: hoc respectu non ea solum, quae a princi-piis sunt remotiora, sed vel ipsa principia ac notissi-ma quaeque in scriptura, obscura, hoc est, imper-ceptibilia dicimus homini animali seu naturali, quip-pe vel minimum jota, absque Spiritus interno lumi-ne, spiritualiter percipere non valenti. Grammaticè vero atque literaliter & prima principia, & alia plura inde profluentia, suo modo homo animalis potest intelligere, vel ex spiritualium sententia. Stultum vero est quod subdit. Neque illi deberent discere Theo-logiam via vulgari, progrediendo à facilibus intellectu ad minus facilia: sed confuse, prout Spiritus iis sensum adspirat. Quasi isti spirituales mediis non uterentur, iisque tali modo ac serie, qui à Deo, ut gratiæ dispen-satore, sic & ordinis authore sapientissimo, rebus impositus est. Adversus vorticordiam, imo omnem efficacem gratiam,ejusque quamcunque operationem, eodem sophismate insurgunt omnis generis Pelagiani, sed perabsurdè:novimus Deum non confusionis Deum esse, mediaque & causas rerum ordinasse tam reales quam morales; cujus ordinis neglectus,cum pia Spiri-tus sancti expectatione cultuque pugnant exertissimè.
units.tr: 4. What would the physician say if someone, with Zanchius, were to maintain that a man so sunk in darkness that, without some operation and gracious inspiration of the Holy Spirit, it is impossible for him to make any progress even in those things, cannot be helped by common providence and influence to acquire knowledge of other things? But then, says the physician, according to the opinion of our opponents, that ought to be called obscure in theology, not because it is more remote from principles and better-known things, but because it requires the light of the Spirit, which belongs only to the regenerate. The wretched arguer understands neither the matter itself nor our opponents' opinion. We say that clarity and obscurity, both inward and outward, that is, objective or subjective, belong to the perspicuity of Scripture; we claim objective perspicuity for Scripture. But what is thus objectively clear is perceived according to the different disposition of the subject and mode of operation, either grammatically, literally and naturally, or spiritually and savingly. In this respect we say that not only the things which are more remote from principles, but the very principles and all the best-known things in Scripture, are obscure, that is, imperceptible, to the natural or animal man, since he cannot perceive even the least iota spiritually without the inner light of the Spirit. But grammatically and literally, the man of nature can understand the first principles and many others that flow from them in his own way, or according to the sense of the spiritual. It is indeed foolish what he adds: Nor should they learn theology by the common way, progressing from things easy to understand to those less easy, but confusedly, as the Spirit breathes the sense into them. As if those spiritual men did not use means, and that in such a way and order as has been imposed on things by God, the dispenser of grace and also the most wise author of order. Against the (?) heart, indeed against all efficacious grace and every operation of it, all kinds of Pelagians rise up with the same sophism, but most absurdly: we know that God is not the God of confusion, and that he has ordained means and causes of things, both real and moral; neglect of this order fights most strongly with the pious expectation and worship of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Tandem in Remonstrantium castra concedit aper-tè: sic sonant quæ sequuntur. Cum etiam homo hæ-reticus conscius sit suæ pravitatis, per quam volens veri-tatem oppugnat, & affectibus obsequitur, agnoscendum est res fidei etiam reprobis manifestas esse posse, quomodo alioquin hæreticus posset esse convictus in sua conscientia? ejusdem notæ est, quod idem author tradit alibi, sic differens. Et hinc unus idemque error in uno erit hæresis: quam Apostolus inter opera carnis recenset Gal. v. Atque quo cum disputare vetat, verum eum post unam & alteram admonitionem vitandum monet, talis quippe satis apud animum erroris sui convictus est & sanis rationibus prout decet à se locum non dari conscius Tit. III. Idem plane quod urgent Remonstrantes: voluntque hæreticum omnem & semper scientem errare, ita ut hæreticus non sit, qui verum putat, illud in quo errat, probantque eodem Apostoli loco, cujus verba adducit Velthusius: ex eo autem conficit noster, res fidei reprobis manifestas esse posse. Omnia falsa, nihilque sani in his verbis inest. Non jam consequentiam exagitabo, nimirum, an ex eo, quod om-
units.tr: Finally he openly goes over to the Remonstrants' camp. His words are these: Since even a heretic, being aware of his own depravity, by which he wilfully opposes the truth and gives way to his passions, we must acknowledge that matters of faith can be manifest even to the reprobate; otherwise how could the heretic be convicted in his own conscience? The same author says elsewhere, and in the same vein: And hence one and the same error will be a heresy in one person; the Apostle counts it among the works of the flesh, Gal. v. And where he forbids us to dispute with a man, he bids us avoid him after one or two admonitions, since such a man is sufficiently convicted of his error in his own mind, and, being conscious that he is given no place by sound reasons, as is fitting. Tit. iii. This is exactly what the Remonstrants press, and they want every heretic always to err knowingly, so that a man who thinks the truth is not a heretic, though he errs in what he thinks. They prove it from the same passage of the Apostle whose words Velthusius cites, and from it our author draws the conclusion that matters of faith can be manifest to the reprobate. Everything in these words is false, and there is nothing sound in them. I will not now examine the inference, namely whether it follows from the fact that every heretic who errs knowingly

units.la: Gal. v. ⁂ Mark in text: "quam Apostolus" is preceded by an ornamental sign that is not legible as a letter. nis hæreticus sciens erret, sequatur, res fidei ipsis reprobis notas esse posse, peccati enim perpetrandi conscientiam, cum evitandi impotentia, consistere posse commodissimè, certum est: nisi non cunctis solum reprobis, sed vel ipsis Diabolis, scientes quippe illi peccant, errantque, peccati errorisque evitandi, absurdo commento, potentiam tribuas & facultates: Antecedens vero paucis expendere lubitum. Origo quippe perversæ istius lenitatis & moderationis est, quam hodie circa quosvis hæreticos exercendam esse, post Remonstrantes crepant homines munda-ni: Errant enim errores inculpatos, profitentur ac credunt, quæ vera putant, multi eorum qui dicuntur hæretici, nec sunt tamen tales: hæreticus enim nemo est, nisi qui in conscientiâ sua convictus est. Sic Velthusius alibi contendit, eundem errorem in uno hæresin esse, nimirum qui in conscientia convictus est, in altero non item, qui seductus &c. hosce non coercendos docet inibi, aut puniendos, ne quidem pæna minoris libertatis: quod extendendum putat ad omnes errores; quamdiu non perspicuè videmus eos cum malitia junctos esse. Neque an non vel Judæorum vel Idololatrarum errores huc pertineant, determinari facile posse putat. Posset quis gravissimè errare & tamen inter peccatores recensendus non esse, inquit idem. In hoc absurdum absurdorum absurdissimum viros alias nimis quam perspicaces præcipitavit ipsorum Deo, (ecce hujus tui erroris fontem Velthusi, verba viri Doctis-simi refero) quod ipsi perditè depereunt idolum, libertas arbitrii: sic enim cum ratione insaniunt: omne peccatum voluntarium est, liberum est, in voluntate sedem habet; errores vero mentis vitia sunt, non voluntatis; quare errores, nisi voluntarii sint, peccata non sunt dicendi. En quo dementiæ miseros suum perduxit arbitrium! At arbitrio in hoc prælio suppetias fert Philosophia Cartesiana, sic illius fundamentis insistens, alicubi noster Medicus. Recte concludi intellectum nunquam prave intelligere. Et ideo intellectione proprie dicta nunquam peccatur. Causa erroris a voluntate proficiscitur: intellectus autem ab eo vitio plane immunis est. Error semper voluntarius est. Nec aliter statuere possunt quotquot Cartesii cogitatis adhærent. Affirmare enim & negare ipsi non intellectus sed voluntatis est. Vidimus Velthusii cum Remonstrantibus exactissimam in isto negotio συμβι-βασιν, argumenta Reformatorum breviter audiamus. Sic de hæresi Baillius. Num omnis hæreticus erret sciens &c. Hoc Apologistæ asserunt: idem asserit Velthusius & necessario omnis, qui Cartesii, de intellectu & voluntate Philosophemata, amplectitur: nos cum tota Christianorum natione negamus. Pro recta sententia militat locus 2 Thess. ii. 9-13. qui sic sonat. Cujus adventus est ex vi efficaci Satanæ, & cum omni seductione injustitiæ, in iis qui pereunt, ideo mittet iis Deus efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio, ut damnentur omnes qui non crediderunt veritati, sed acquieverunt in injustitia.
units.tr: nis hæreticus sciens erret, sequatur, that matters of faith can be known to the reprobate themselves. It is certainly possible for the consciousness of committing sin to exist together with an inability to avoid it, unless you ascribe to the reprobate, and indeed to the devils themselves, who sin and err knowingly, a power and faculties of avoiding sin and error, which is an absurd fiction. But I am pleased to weigh the antecedent briefly. The origin of that perverse leniency and moderation, which worldly men now clamour after the Remonstrants must be shown to every heretic, is this: they say that many who are called heretics are not such, since they profess and believe their errors blamelessly, taking what they hold to be true. For there is no heretic except one who is convicted in his conscience. So Velthusius argues elsewhere that the same error is a heresy in one man, namely the man convicted in conscience, but not in another who is seduced, and so on. He teaches that such men are not to be restrained or punished there, not even with the penalty of loss of liberty; and he thinks this should be extended to all errors, as long as we do not clearly see them joined with malice. Nor does he think it hard to determine whether the errors of Jews or idolaters belong here too. Someone, he says, could err most gravely and yet not be reckoned among sinners. In this absurdity of absurdities, men otherwise more than sharp-sighted have been hurried headlong by their idol of free will (here is the source of your error, Velthusius; I quote the words of that most learned man): for they madly ruin themselves with this reasoning: every sin is voluntary, free, and has its seat in the will; but errors are faults of the mind, not of the will; therefore errors, unless they are voluntary, are not to be called sins. See to what madness their own will has brought these wretches! But our Medicus, in one place, brings aid to the will in this battle, relying on the foundations of Cartesian philosophy: It is rightly concluded that the intellect never understands wrongly. And so in the strict sense of understanding no one ever sins. The cause of error comes from the will, while the intellect is wholly free from that fault. Error is always voluntary. Nor can all who adhere to the thoughts of Descartes hold otherwise, for to affirm and to deny belongs not to the intellect but to the will. We have seen Velthusius's most exact agreement with the Remonstrants on this matter; let us briefly hear the arguments of the Reformed. Thus Baillius on heresy: Does every heretic err knowingly? The Apologists assert this: Velthusius asserts the same, and necessarily everyone who embraces Descartes's philosophy about intellect and will does too: we with the whole nation of Christians deny it. The passage 2 Thess. ii. 9–13 supports the right opinion, and it reads thus: Whose coming is by the powerful working of Satan, with all deception of unrighteousness, among those who perish; because they did not receive the love of the truth that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.

units.la: Quibus Deus mittit efficaciam erroris, ut credant mendacio, quos Satanas efficaciter seducit, ut non credant veritati, sed acquiescant in injustitia, isti sua dogmata habent pro nimium veris: Atque hæc est sequacium Antichristi cognitio, qui procul dubio errantes sunt & hæretici. Alter locus est 2 Tim. ii. 18, 24, 25, 26. Qui circa veritatem aberrarunt à scopo, & subvertunt quorundum fidem. Servum autem Dei non oportet pugnare, sed cum lenitate erudire eos, qui contrario animo sunt, si forte daturus sit iis Deus resipiscentiam ad agnitionem veritatis, ut sanitate mentis recepta, evadant ex Diaboli laqueo, ab eo facti captivi ad ejus libitum. Inde sic arguo, Hymenæus & Philetus habebant sua dogmata pro veris: Atqui illi erant hæretici. Ergo. Majorem probo. Qui aberrarunt à veritate, veritate, qui non agnoscunt veritatem, quorum animus veritati contrarius est, quorum ipsa mens captiva est in Satanæ laqueo, isti, quæ profitentur dogmata, non vident esse falsa, sed habent pro veris: Atqui hæc omnia Hymenæus & Philetus verbis citatis. Ergo &c. Sic Fannes & Iambres dicuntur etiam mente corrupti & non solum seducentes, sed etiam seducti, atque ut illi, sic & hæretici qui resistebant Apostolis, seducentes quidem, verum etiam seducti erant. Et Christus Mat xxii. 29. dicit, erratis neque Scripturam scientes, neque potentiam Dei. Hinc arguo, errantes etiam fœdissimè nesciebant dogmata sua errores esse &c. Quid? sequetur neminem de hæresi convenire posse coram hominibus, solus enim Deus renes scrutatur. Hoc Ithacus velit, & magno mercentur Atridæ. Hoc ipsum est pessimæ hujus operæ Remonstrantibus aliisque pretium. Hac late patente porta jubent irruere in Ecclesiam hæreticorum omnigenos greges; quos suo isto sinu peramanter excipiunt. Quam immane vero sit hoc ἄτοπον, præter omnium Ecclesiarum omni tempore praxin, præter varios Scripturæ locos, is ipse ad Titum iii. 10. in quo causæ suæ columen consistere putant adversantes, abunde probat. Imo neque erraret hæreticus, cum quæ errores sunt pro erroribus habeat, licet id dissimulet. Et ab omni hæreseos nota absolverentur Manichæi, Ariani, Macedoniani, Vorstius,Socinus, Servetus & quotquot pro summe nefariis hæreticis, vel olim, vel hodie habiti sunt, ni tibi constet istorum interna de suis erroribus persuasio. Denique nudo errori sic nullum inerit vitium. At nullam in eo absurditatem vident Remonstrantes, nullam Velthusius. Quanquam autem boni isti viri in eo nullum inconveniens videant, nostri tamen officii est illud abominari. Nam si in errore nullum est peccatum, certè non tantum quotquot hodie in terris hæretici dicuntur, habendi sunt pro fratribus genuinis, verum etiam Judæis & Turcis pandenda sunt Ecclesiæ adyta: quin & ipse Paganismus adi-tum tum hac ratione postulabit in cælum. Profecto si Socinianis absque omni piaculo, absque ulla salutis jactura negare liceat Christum Deum, blasphemare Sp. S. & ejurare sacrosanctissimam Trinitatem, si Serveti pura est ab omni scelere anima, quanquam in Deum omni blasphemiarum spurcitie ad ultimum usque spiritum debacchatus sit, istos omnes si liberes peccati reatu, hoc nomine, quod quæ miseri eructarunt ex ipsis animæ penetralibus, ex ipsa mentis suæ medulla protulerint, iniquum certè fuerit atriore carbone notasse Judæos vel Turcas, vel Paganos: quorum multi singulis semper seculis parati fuerunt vel sanguine, & vita, testatissimum facere quæ contra Christianos blasphemarent, ea se absque omni hyprocrisi, ex imo cordis, qualequale haberent, fundo proferre, nisi ad istas absurditatum Gorgonas Remonstrantes & Velthusius expalleant, nobis ipsorum durior adamante stuporis plurimum incutiet facies. Tandem scire ex nostro Velthusio velim, an prorsus excusari possit, invincibilis licet sit, ignorantia illa, quæ partem facit peccati originalis inhærentis. Apostolus an non peccavit ante conversionem erroribus circa Christum commissis, quamvis ignorans erraverit? Plura hac de re habet Essenius. Quæstionem istam his verbis proposuit Voetius. An de ratione hæresis sit, ut error fundamentalis contra conscientiam teneatur? Sententia Remonstr. inquit, est in Vindiciis seu Vedelio Rhapsodo L. i. C. i. & x. cum Apolog. Cap. xxiv. quod hæresis speculativa, ut eam vocant, non sit peccatum. Imo proprie non hæresis. Vide hæc commenta eorum abunde in lucem protracta & excussa à Vedelio in arcanis Arminianismi part. iv. L. ii. Cap. 4. & locis ibi cit.
