Certè habuissent hæretici quo sese excusassent, si Velthusii aut Remonstrantium commentum ipsis notum fuisset, iniquè secum agi, innoxium & inculpatum errorem exagitari, quod quantumvis tota errarent terra, mari, cælo,
units.tr: To those to whom God sends the working of error, that they should believe a lie, whom Satan efficaciously seduces, so that they do not believe the truth but take pleasure in unrighteousness, these men hold their doctrines to be too true. And this is the knowledge of the followers of Antichrist, who without doubt are erring and heretical. Another passage is 2 Tim. ii. 18, 24–26: Who concerning the truth have erred from the mark, and overthrow the faith of some. And the servant of God must not strive, but be gentle to all, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those who oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth; and that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will. From this I argue thus: Hymenaeus and Philetus held their doctrines to be true; but they were heretics. Therefore. I prove the major: those who have strayed from the truth, who do not acknowledge the truth, whose mind is opposed to the truth, whose very mind is held captive in the snare of Satan, these do not see that the doctrines they profess are false, but hold them to be true. But all these things were true of Hymenaeus and Philetus, by the words cited. Therefore etc. Thus Jannes and Jambres are said to be corrupt in mind, and not only seducers but also seduced; and like them, the heretics who resisted the Apostles were both seducers and seduced. And Christ says, Matt. xxii. 29: You do err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God. Hence I argue: those who err even most foully did not know that their doctrines were errors, etc. What then? Does it follow that no one can be convicted of heresy before men, since God alone searches the reins? Let Ithacus wish this, and the Atridae pay dearly for it. This very thing is the value of the Remonstrants' and others' worst labour. Under this widely open gate they bid all kinds of herds rush into the Church of heretics, and they receive them most lovingly into their bosom. How monstrous this absurdity is, apart from the practice of all the Churches at all times, and apart from various passages of Scripture, Tit. iii. 10 itself, in which our opponents think the pillar of their cause stands, sufficiently proves. Indeed a heretic would not even be in error, since he holds as errors what are errors, though he pretends otherwise. The Manichaeans, Arians, Macedonians, Vorstius, Socinus, Servetus, and all whoever have been held as most wicked heretics, either formerly or today, would be absolved of every mark of heresy, unless it is established to you that they had an inward persuasion of their errors. Thus a bare error would have no fault in it at all. But the Remonstrants see no absurdity in this, and Velthusius sees none. Although those good men see no inconvenience in it, it is nonetheless our duty to abhor it. For if there is no sin in error, then not only should all who are today called heretics on earth be regarded as genuine brothers, but the inner sanctuaries of the Church must also be thrown open to Jews and Turks; indeed paganism itself will by this reasoning demand entry into heaven. Truly, if it is allowed to the Socinians, without any sin and without any loss of salvation, to deny that Christ is God, to blaspheme the Holy Spirit and to abjure the most holy Trinity; if the soul of Servetus is pure of every crime, although he raged against God with every filth of blasphemy to his last breath; then it would surely be unjust to mark all these men free of the guilt of sin, while Jews or Turks or pagans are branded with a blacker coal, on the ground that what those wretches belched out came from the innermost recesses of their souls and from the very marrow of their minds. Many of the Jews, in every age, have been ready to attest most solemnly, even with their blood and lives, that what they blasphemed against the Christians they uttered from the bottom of their hearts, without any hypocrisy, however they held it. Unless Remonstrants and Velthusius turn pale at these Gorgons of absurdity, their face, harder than adamant, will strike us with great astonishment. Finally, I would like to know from our Velthusius whether that ignorance, though it be invincible, which forms part of inherent original sin, can be wholly excused. Did not the Apostle sin before his conversion by the errors he committed concerning Christ, although he erred in ignorance? Essenius has more on this matter. Voetius proposed the question in these words: Is it of the nature of heresy that a fundamental error is held against conscience? The opinion of the Remonstrants, he says, is in the Vindiciae, or in Vedelius the rhapsodist, book i, chapters i and x, together with the Apology, chapter xxiv: that speculative heresy, as they call it, is not a sin. Indeed, strictly speaking, it is not heresy at all. See their inventions amply brought to light and shaken out by Vedelius in the Secrets of Arminianism, part iv, book ii, chapter 4, and the places cited there. Certainly heretics would have had a way to excuse themselves if the fiction of Velthusius or the Remonstrants had been known to them: that it is unjust for them to be harassed, since their error is harmless and blameless, however much the whole earth, sea and sky err.

VIII. | §. 23 & 24. | §. 1. 22. cælo, procul tamen ab omni hæ-reseos abessent macula: quandoquidem parati essent Deos omnes jurare, etiam san-guinis martyrio testari, sua sibi dogmata sanissima, ve-rissima videri. Hujusmodi tamen errorum excusatio hæ-reticorum ingeniosissimis in mentem nunquam venit. Au-gustinus testis sit, quo nemo magis idoneus in hoc argu-mento produci possit. Nam nemo Patrum diutius in fœdis-simarum hæreseon cæno volutavit. Fatetur is ingenuè, toto Manichæismi sui undecennio firmissimam sese fidem habuisse putidissimis nugis: credidisse ficum veras emittere lacrymas, in cibis angelos corporaliter inclusos, etiam Dei particulas &c. Imo credidit non solum, sed obluctatus ne quidem evasit, sic de se ipse. Novem ferme anni sunt, quibus ego miser illo limo profundi ac te-nebris falsitatis, cum sæpe surgere conarer, & gravius alliderer, volutatus sum; & alibi per idem tempus an-norum novem seducebamur, & seducebamus, falsi atque fallentes. At quoniam Velthusio libuit in castra adversariorum transilire non solum, sed & inde ar-mis hostium Reformatos aggredi, age audiamus quid proferat ad stabiliendum tam putidum errorem. Nihil peccaminosum esse, nisi quod etiam volunta-rium sit, de eo jam disputatur: & istud inculcando tur-piter principium petit Medicus. Præterquam quod peccata inadvertentiæ quæ vocant & multa alia argu-mentorum loco enumerare facillimum foret. Ve-rum Belgico isto Tractatu, putat homines qui in ma-joris momenti fidei articulis errant inter peccatores non re-censeri. Certè Paulus, eodem illo loco quem inibi respicit & alibi citat, contrarium planè innuit, se isto errore graviter peccasse, tantum enim, D. Cocce-jo Interprete, abest ab erroris sui excusatione Apostolus, ut potius hisce verbis culpam suam exaggeret ad summum usque. Innuit enim parum abfuisse quin incideret in peccatum quod remitti non potest. Et certè putidissimè argumentum Apostolicum glossa ista Velthusiana emaemasculatur; in eo enim Apostolus est, ut quam maxi-mè divinæ misericordiæ & gratiæ laudet, prædicet & exaggeret magnitudinem, idque eo præsertim argu-mento, quod & ipsi obtigerit, qui talium tantorumque reus erat. Et quæ tandem magnitudo misericordiæ & gratiæ in eo elucet, si remissus Apostolo dicatur in-culpatus error, qui eum ne quidem peccatoris no-mine dignum fecerat? Vel an blasphemia illa, per-sequutio, & contumelia, etiam post auditam Ste-phani orationem apologeticam peccati nomen non merebatur, quia ignorans Paulus omnia ista patra-verat? En mirabilem scripturæ interpretem! Re-stat locus Tit. iii. ii. quem sæpius in hac materia inculcat. Unde sic Remonstrantes & Velthusius argu-mentantur, loquor iterum verbis Baillii, Omnis αὐτο-κατάκριτος peccat contra sui judicii, suæ mentis expres-sum dictamen: Atqui omnis hæreticus est talis. E. Si negaremus minorem, rueret statim tota fabricæ moles. Nec enim probare possent vel de omnibus vel de plerisque hæreticis loqui Apostolum. At negamus majorem, quam magnis id faciamus authoribus & quanta cum ratione ha-be paucis. Nihil pro ista explicatione Athanasius, Chry-sostomus, Theodoretus, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Hieronymus &c. Chrysostomus nihil aliud ad αὐτο-κατάκρισιν requirit quam perseverantiam in errore post ad-monitiones. Τί ἐστιν; inquit ὧν αὐτοκατάκριτος; ὃ γὰρ ἔχῃς εἰπεῖν τῇ ἀδελφῇ εἶπεν, ἀδελφὲ ἵνα [?] δέτησεν, ὅταν μετὰ τὴν παράκλησιν αὐτὸς ἐπιμένῃ, αὐτοκατάκριτος γίνεται. Hieronymus aperte adversariorum commentum elidit. A se ipso, ait, con-demnatus est, qui semel bisque correctus, audito errore suo non vult corrigi, errare existimans corrigentem; & è contrario ad pugnas & jurgia verborum sese parans eum vult lucrifacere à quo docetur. Verumenimvero, quia novaturientibus sordet auctoritas veterum; probationes audiamus: ac nullam habent, nisi quod forsan aliquam ex ipso vocabulo αὐτοκατάκριτε ingeniosi homines excu-dant: dant : Nullis autem fidiculis aliud inde extorqueas, quam damnatum à se; si ultra premas, omnem sui damnationem, suæ mentis tantum & conscientiæ sententia fieri, omnino negamus sequelam. Nam à genere ad speciem alteram putida est consequentia, nec melior à re ad unum rei modum. Multis potest quis condemnare se ipsum, mente sua, ore suo, opere suo: de posterioribus modis aliquoties scriptura, de primo quantum memini nunquam. Confer Luc. xix. 21. Rom. ii, 1. Hinc Am-brosius, Hieronimus, Augustinus vocabulum Græcum exponunt, &, fortassis ante ipsos, Syrus interpres, ipse condemnat animam suam, uehou hajah naphs-hah: non condemnatur ab anima sua. Condemnat se suo facto, quod Ecclesiæ admonitionem spreverit: ore, quod verbis saltem amplectens omne Dei verbum, sic profiteatur veritates ex quibus convinci queat. En argumentum tuum Velthusi misere prostratum à Viro doctissimo jam ante quam tu id publicè tuum feceras. Sed quoniam quædam adhuc restant magni momenti adversus Wolzogium dicenda, hanc digressionem finio, postquam Wolzogio qualem virum Ortho-doxiæ tenacem dixerit imprudens, in memoriam re-vocavi.
units.tr: Marginal notes, right, top to bottom: 1 Tim. 1.13. | Essen. | Systèm. | Tit. xvi. §. 103. 104. | Voet. | Disp. | Sel. | part. iii. | pag. 744. | Maresi. | Exam. | Disser. | II. Curcell. | Sect. VIII. | §. 23 & 24. | §. 1. 22. Let them be ever so far from every stain of heresy, though they were in all lands, seas and skies. For they would be ready to swear by all the gods, and to attest with the blood of martyrdom, that their own doctrines seem to them most sound and most true. Yet the most ingenious heretics never thought of such an excuse for their errors. Let Augustine be the witness, than whom no one could be produced who is more fit in this matter. For none of the Fathers wallowed longer in the mire of the most foul heresies. He frankly confesses that for the whole eleven years of his Manichaeism he held most firmly to the most putrid trifles: that he believed the fig sheds real tears, that angels are bodily enclosed in foods, that there are even particles of God, and so on. Indeed he not only believed these things, but, struggling against them, he did not even escape, and he speaks of himself thus: For almost nine years, wretched that I was, I rolled about in that slime of the depths and the darkness of falsehood, often trying to rise, and being dashed down more heavily. And elsewhere: For the same nine years we were led astray and led others astray, being false and deceiving. But since Velthusius has chosen not only to leap over into the camp of the adversaries, but also from there to attack the Reformed with the enemy's arms, let us hear what he brings forward to establish so putrid an error. That nothing is sinful except what is also voluntary, is already being argued; and in inculcating this, the physician shamefully begs the question. Not to mention that it would be very easy to list sins of inadvertence, as they call them, and many other things as arguments. But in that Belgic treatise he thinks that men who err in articles of faith of greater moment are not counted among sinners. Surely Paul, in the very passage that he himself has in view and cites elsewhere, plainly hints at the contrary: that he had sinned grievously in this error. For, according to the interpretation of D. Coccejus, the Apostle is so far from excusing his error that rather, in these words, he magnifies his fault to the utmost. For he hints that he had come close to falling into a sin that cannot be forgiven. And truly this gloss of Velthusius most foully emasculates the Apostolic argument. For the Apostle's purpose is to praise, proclaim and magnify as much as possible the mercy and grace of God, and this especially by the argument that it fell to himself, who was guilty of such great offences. And what greatness of mercy and grace would shine forth in this, if the error that had not even made him worthy of the name of sinner is said to be pardoned as blameless in the Apostle? Or did that blasphemy, persecution and insult, even after he had heard Stephen's apologetic speech, not deserve the name of sin, because Paul had committed all those things in ignorance? Behold the marvellous interpreter of Scripture! There remains the passage of Titus 3.10-11, which he often presses in this matter. Hence, so the Remonstrants and Velthusius argue, I speak again in the words of Baillie: Every self-condemned man sins against the express dictate of his own judgment and mind. But every heretic is such. Therefore, if we were to deny the minor premise, the whole mass of the structure would straightway collapse. For they could not prove that the Apostle speaks of all heretics or of most of them. But we deny the major premise, and with how great authorities we do so, and with how much reason, I shall set out briefly. Athanasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome and others say nothing in favour of that explanation. Chrysostom requires nothing else for self-condemnation than perseverance in error after admonitions. "What is it," he says, "to be self-condemned? For what you have to say to your brother, he said, 'Brother, ...' when, after the exhortation, he persists, he becomes self-condemned." Jerome plainly overturns the adversaries' fiction. He is condemned by himself, he says, who, corrected once or twice, having heard of his error, does not wish to be corrected, thinking that the one correcting him is in error; and on the contrary, preparing himself for battles and quarrels of words, he wishes to gain over the one from whom he is taught. But truly, since the authority of the ancients is despised by men who are eager for novelties, let us hear the proofs: and they have none, except what clever men perhaps devise from the very word αὐτοκατάκριτος [autokatakritos]. Yet from no racks can you extract anything from it beyond "condemned by himself"; if you press further, and say that all his self-condemnation is made only by the judgment of his mind and conscience, we utterly deny the consequence. For the inference from the genus to another species is absurd, and no better from the thing to one mode of the thing. A man can condemn himself in many ways: by his mind, by his mouth, by his work. Of the latter modes Scripture speaks several times; of the first, as far as I remember, never. Compare Luke 19.21, Rom. 2.1. Hence Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine explain the Greek word, and perhaps, before them, the Syriac translator, [he himself condemns his soul, uehou hajah naphs-hah]: not [non] is condemned by his own soul. He condemns himself by his deed, because he has spurned the admonition of the Church; by his mouth, because, by at least embracing every word of God in words, he thus professes truths by which he can be convicted. Behold your argument, Velthusius, miserably overthrown by a most learned man already before you had made it your public property. But since some matters of great moment still remain to be said against Wolzogius, I end this digression, after I have called to mind what kind of man Wolzogius, carelessly, called a staunch defender of Orthodoxy.

units.la: JOHANNIS vander WAEYEN PRO VERITATE, & genuina Reformatorum sententia ADVERSUS LUD. WOLZOGIUM DISCEPTATIONIS Liber Tertius, Postremam Controversiam continens & primariam.
units.tr: JOHANNES VAN DER WAEYEN'S THIRD BOOK OF THE DISPUTATION, IN DEFENCE OF THE TRUTH AND THE GENUINE VIEW OF THE REFORMERS AGAINST LUDWIG WOLZOGEN, containing the last and chief controversy.

units.la: ADipsum tandem Wolzogiani libelli nucleum pervenire dabitur. Ut autem tota pateat orationis meæ series, priora breviter revocanda erunt in memoriam. Controversiæ statum ad libri secundi initium delineaturus, prælibanda quædam judicabam & explicanda paucis: & quidem 1 quid usus loquendi, 2 quid ratio. 3 quid interpretari. Statum deinde quæstionis hoc modo formandum esse vidimus: Quid tandem sit, quod me, per modum objecti, certum reddat, aut reddere debeat, hujus orationis illum esse aut hunc sensum, non alium. Quid Reformati, quid utrique, sed diversa via, à veritate discedentes, Pontificii ab una, & Sociniani ab altera parte, hac de re sentiant, uno verbo indicavi. Quoniam verò Wolzogio, per universam, de Scripturæ intelligentia, materiam, fusè exspatiari visum fuerat: Reformatorum de toto isto negotio sententiam, quidque illi, tam à parte subjecti, quam objecti, ut & ad utriusque congruum & legitimum contactum requirant, succinctè explicandi necessitatem mihi incumbere putavi: at congestis collatisque iis, quæ ad eandem mate-riam scripserat Wolzogius, ejus multiplices erro-res, & ab Orthodoxis dissensum detegendi ac re-futandi occasio data fuit inevitabilis: aliquoties in-terim Velthusio etiam ad partes vocato. Sicque de immediata operatione Spiritus Sancti, ejusque su-perinfuso lumine, ut & de Scripturæ intelligibilitate disseruimus; ac, quod præsertim agendum esse con-sultum duximus, Theologorum Reformatorum de iis controversiis sparsim dicta collegimus, defensa ipsorum adversus Enthusiasmi impactum crimen sen-tentia, ut inde patere autumem, quid distent æra lu-pinis. Nunc de primaria controversia quid statuat Wolzogius examinandum restat. Quæritur, quid me per modum objecti, instar regulæ, normæ, du-cis, facisve ducat in Scripturæ interpretatione rea-li, quæsiti sensum in capite huius libri explicatum reperiet lector. Quædam hic usui loquendi, Spiri-tui quædam, quædam rationi tribuit noster. Quam autem præposterè ista sint posita atque explicata, ad oculum demonstravimus. De usu loquendi nihil ultra erat oggerendum[?] Wolzogio, quam, eum tam generalem, seu communem, quam scripturæ pe-culiarem, quando scriptura interpres scripturæ or-thodoxis dicitur, supponi. Imo posito, scripturam intelligibiliter scriptam esse, necesse est, ut verbo-rum significatio grammatica, prout vel usu vel lexi-cis innotescit, præsupponatur: quæ autem cogni-ta non tam realem, quam verbalem interpretatio-nem, seu versionem, producit: ut ejus tam pro-lixa tractatio, præter scopum Wolzogio exciderit, multa verborum & laxa copia nihil revera præstan-ti. Spiritum S. quod attinet, is circa subjectum vim suam exerit, manente unicâ veritatis normâ sacrâ scripturâ, eâque in se perspicuâ & intelligibili, quam quisque salutariter magis aut minus percipit, prout magis vel minus à spiritu ad percipiendum aptus redditur & excitatur; vel naturaliter, prout, in suo genere, se magis vel minus extendit naturalis inintelligentiæ aptitudo. Rationi nunc quid tribuat, age inquiramus. Eo istam in loco collocavit Paradoxus, ut normam dixerit interpretandi summam & infallibilem. Per rationem enim rationis axiomata cum suis conclusionibus sic disposita intelligit, ut philosophiam vocandam censeat: Et certè isto sensu, sive rationem dicas, sive Philosophiam, perinde erit. Hic duo Wolzogio incumbebant: Sententiæ Reformatæ explicatio cum vindiciis, ac adversæ refutatio. In utroque verò prævaricatur. Quod Sole clarius deprehendet, quisquis, positis præjudiciis, partiumque studio, causam cum causa conferre operæ pretium duxerit. Longam veræ sententiæ explicationem ac defensionem non meditor, dabunt eam, & partim præstiterunt, Viri Clarissimi, Maresius, Essenius, Vogelsangh, & ante illos, in præclaro isto opere Hoornbeekius. Uno verbo, hoc volunt Reformati, non rationem, aut Philosophiam, hic enim isti termini idem valent, non Papam, non ullius hominis dictata, sed ipsam Scripturam unicam & summam interpretationis suæ normam esse & amussim. Illa enim demum interpretatio realis est, inquit Sohnius, cum vera Scripturæ sententia ex ipsa Scriptura demonstratur. Illa expositio demum admittenda, quæ Scripturam exponit ex Scriptura, sic Spanhemius. Sic igitur cum nobis Scripturam suam Deus indulgentissimus comparavit, tantaque illustravit perspicuitate, tanta eam demiserit intelligendi facilitate, ad nostram humilitatem, tanta etiam simplicitate & certitudine eam prodiderit, ejus profecto interpretationem germanamque intelligentiam, si qui non omnino ex ipsis divinis scriptis petant, illi homines Deo optimo & in docendo quoque benignissimo patri nostro, anteponunt & sapientia & fide nos ad salutem instituendi: eamque ob rem à vero & salvifico scripturarum sensu ut aberrent quam longissime necesse est. Et ô portentosam perversitatem, atque infandum Domini contemptum: fatentur omnes docti, nullius omnino scriptoris mentem posse in locis difficilioribus dissiciioribus certò cognosci, nisi ex ipsomet, per collationem scilicet obscuriorum locorum cum scopo authoris ac præcipuis ejus præceptis, & cum dictis ea de re aper-tioribus, atque cum phrasi ejus, eosque habemus solos authorum idoneos interpretes, qui hac ratione scripto-res ipsos suorum librorum exhibent dilucidatores. Nec aliam rationem Sancti quoque Patres in explicandis Scripturis sunt secuti, tam in conciliis, universi, quam in privatis suis scriptis singuli. Sic sensum Reforma-tum, inter ipsos Reformatores, quos vocamus, non ultimus, M. Bucerus, exprimit. Sumus autem scripturas, sic Zanchius, ut scitissime docuit Augustinus esse faciendum, per scripturas, explicata prius genuina verborum & locutionum significatione, interpretaturi. Est enim scriptura, id est Sp: Sanctus loquens in scriptura, sui ipsius interpres: quo quis melior inveniri potest? Scripturam esse interpretem sui, si quis neget, insaniat, inquit Chamierus. Hic locus ostendit, inquit Paræus, quomodo Scriptura se ipsam interpre-retur, dum, quæ uno loco concisius aut obscurius dixit, alio loco apertius & pleniusillustrat: modo non desint qui intelligant, inquirant, conferant. Hic est sensus illius, quod hodie contra Papistas urgemus, Scripturam esse sui ipsius interpretem. Et alibi, Manifestum sit, verissimè dici, non esse meliorem Scripturarum divinarum interpretem, quam Scripturas ipsas neque hoc posse negari, nisi à Scripturarum imperitis: quos de re tanta judicare vel audiri non convenit. Quid de ra-tione sentiant nostri, luculenter explicat Hoornbeeckius, his verbis: Quando contra Pontificios, & secundum veritatem tenemus, Solam Scripturam esse fidei normam &c. Scriptura tum opponitur omni alteri normæ, & non hominum placitis, quæ commenta sint solum, sed sive placita sint rationis certæ, quibuscunque; non quod uspiam veritas veritati sit contraria, sed quia veritas fidei & Scripturæ non vult judicari à placito rationis humanæ, vel à quocunque alio, quod eo longe inferius est: Scriptura sui norma est, & interpres, neque eget testimonio humano; non magis ac Christus
units.tr: At last we shall come to the very kernel of Wolzogen's little book. But so that the whole course of my discussion may be clear, the earlier points must be briefly recalled. Intending to set out the state of the controversy at the beginning of the second book, I thought certain preliminary matters had to be explained briefly: namely (1) what the usage of speech is, (2) what reason is, and (3) what interpreting is. I then saw that the state of the question had to be framed in this way: what it is that, by way of an object, makes me certain, or ought to make me certain, that the meaning of this passage is this one and not another. I indicated in one word what the Reformed think about this matter, and what each of the others think, the Papists on one side and the Socinians on the other, both of whom have departed from the truth by different roads. Since, however, Wolzogen had decided to range widely over the whole subject of the understanding of Scripture, I thought it necessary to set out briefly the Reformed view of this whole business, and what is required of the interpreter, both on the side of the subject and on the side of the object, for the proper and lawful contact of each. But when I had gathered and compared what Wolzogen had written on the same matter, an unavoidable occasion arose of detecting and refuting his manifold errors and his dissent from the Orthodox, Velthuysen having been called in as well at several points along the way. So I discussed the immediate operation of the Holy Spirit and his superadded light, and also the intelligibility of Scripture; and, which we judged especially worth doing, I collected what the Reformed theologians have said scattered about on these controversies, defending their view against the charge of Enthusiasm, so that it may be seen, as I hope, how far bronze coins differ from lupins. It remains now to examine what Wolzogen holds about the chief controversy. The question is what it is that guides me, by way of an object, as a rule, norm, guide, or torch in the real interpretation of Scripture; the reader will find the answer explained in the beginning of this book. Our author assigns some things to the usage of speech, some to the Spirit, and some to reason. But how absurdly these things have been put and explained, we have shown plainly. Regarding the usage of speech, nothing more was needed against Wolzogen than to note that it is presupposed when Scripture is said to interpret Scripture for the Orthodox, both the general or common usage and the peculiar usage of Scripture. Indeed, granted that Scripture is written intelligibly, the grammatical meaning of words, as it is known through usage or through the lexicons, must be presupposed. What is known in this way produces not so much a real interpretation as a verbal interpretation or version; so his very lengthy treatment of it has, beside his purpose, come to nothing, a great deal of words and loose talk accomplishing nothing in fact. As for the Holy Spirit, he exerts his power on the subject, with the one norm of truth, Holy Scripture, remaining, which is itself clear and intelligible, and which each person grasps savingly more or less, according as he is made more or less apt and roused by the Spirit to grasp it; or naturally, according as the natural aptitude for understanding extends itself more or less within its own kind. Let us now inquire what he assigns to reason. Paradoxus has placed it in this position, calling it the highest and infallible norm of interpreting. For by reason he understands the axioms of reason with their conclusions so arranged that he thinks it should be called philosophy; and certainly, in that sense, whether you call it reason or philosophy, it will come to the same thing. Here Wolzogen had two tasks: an explanation of the Reformed view with its vindication, and a refutation of the opposing view. In both he goes wrong. Anyone who, setting aside prejudices and partisan zeal, thinks it worth the effort to compare cause with cause will detect this more clearly than the sun. I do not intend a lengthy explanation and defence of the true view; the most illustrious men, Maresius, Essenius, Vogelsang, and before them Hoornbeeck in that excellent work, will supply it, and in part have already done so. In a word, the Reformed want this: not reason, or philosophy (for these terms here mean the same), not the Pope, not the dictates of any man, but Scripture itself is the sole and supreme norm and rule of its own interpretation. For that interpretation is then real, says Sohnius, when the true sense of Scripture is demonstrated from Scripture itself. That exposition alone is to be admitted which expounds Scripture from Scripture, so Spanheim. So when the most indulgent God has furnished us with his Scripture, and has illumined it with such great clarity, has let it down to our humble capacity with such great ease of understanding, and has handed it down to us with such simplicity and certainty, then those who do not wholly seek its interpretation and genuine understanding from the divine writings themselves set men above the best God and our Father, who is most kind even in teaching, and set their own wisdom and faith above him in instructing us to salvation; and for that reason they must wander as far as possible from the true and saving sense of the Scriptures. O monstrous perversity and unspeakable contempt of the Lord! All learned men confess that the mind of no writer whatever can be known with certainty in the more difficult and obscure passages, except from the writer himself, namely by comparing the obscure passages with the writer's purpose and his chief precepts, and with the things said more clearly on the same subject, and with his manner of speaking; and we have only those interpreters of authors who are fit, who by this method show the writers themselves to be the clarifiers of their books. Nor did the holy Fathers follow any other method in explaining the Scriptures, both in the councils, as a whole, and in their private writings, each one. So the Reformed sense is expressed among the Reformers themselves, whom we call not the least, Martin Bucer. Moreover, we must interpret the Scriptures in the way that Zanchius, as Augustine most shrewdly taught, must be done, through Scripture, having first explained the genuine meaning of words and expressions. For Scripture is, that is, the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture, its own interpreter: who could be better? If anyone denies that Scripture is its own interpreter, let him go mad, says Chamier. This passage shows, says Paræus, how Scripture interprets itself, while what it has said more briefly or obscurely in one place it illustrates more clearly and fully in another, provided there are people who understand, inquire and compare. This is the sense of that principle which we now press against the Papists, that Scripture is its own interpreter. And elsewhere: it is plainly true, he says, that there is no better interpreter of the divine Scriptures than the Scriptures themselves; nor can this be denied except by those ignorant of the Scriptures, whose judgment on so great a matter it is not fitting to hear. What our men think about reason is clearly explained by Hoornbeeck, in these words: When against the Papists we hold, and rightly, that Scripture alone is the norm of faith, etc., Scripture is then set against every other norm, and against the opinions of men, which are mere inventions, but whether they are opinions of sure reason, whatever they are; not because truth is anywhere contrary to truth, but because the truth of faith and of Scripture does not wish to be judged by the opinion of human reason, or by anything else that is far beneath it. Scripture is its own norm and interpreter, and it needs no human testimony, no more than Christ does.

units.la: Ioh v. 34. Non ut sui norma sit duntaxat in manifestis, & quæ sunt evidentissimæ veritatis; sed in omnibus æque; quia omnia sua & paria sunt, divina nempe & sacra; ob quam rationem est quod tribunal ea humanum detrectent & contemnant. Non est quæstio an ratio in credendis veniat, ut subjectum, etiam ut instrumentum; duntaxat de tertio; an ut norma, secundum sua dictata, conclusiones & sententiam. Si enim, verba sunt Marcsii, Scriptura est infallibile Dei verbum, & Patris cœlestis testamentum, ipsa ergo nobis sufficienter explicat sensa, mentem & voluntatem supremam summi illius testatoris. Confer ejusdem Systema Loc. 1. & AntiTirinum, Controv. 1. At quorsum plura, quoniam, ut recte notat Clarissimus Coccejus, Notum est, à Reformatis responderi, Scripturam ipsam & Spiritum Sanctum esse judicem Controversiarum, & interpretationis Scripturæ.
units.tr: John 5:34. Not only is it a norm in plain matters, and in those of most evident truth, but equally in all things; since all its matters are alike, namely divine and sacred. For this reason human tribunals shrink from and despise it. The question is not whether reason comes in when things are believed, as subject, or even as instrument (only the third point is at issue), but whether it comes in as norm, according to its own dictates, conclusions and judgment. For if, as Maresius's words go, Scripture is the infallible Word of God and the testament of the heavenly Father, then it itself sufficiently explains to us the meaning, mind and supreme will of that great testator. Compare the same author's System, locus 1, and his Anti-Tirinus, controversy 1. But why say more? As the most illustrious Coccejus rightly notes, It is well known that the Reformed reply that Scripture itself and the Holy Spirit are the judge of controversies and of the interpretation of Scripture.

units.la: Et si publica scripta velis, en Confessionis Scoticanæ verba: Scripturæ interpretationem, neque ad privatam aliquam aut publicam Personam pertinere confitemur, neque ad Ecclesiam aliquam: sed jus & authoritatem hanc esse solius Spiritus Dei, per quem S. Scripturæ literis sunt mandatæ. Cum ergo contingit quod controvertitur pro recto sensu alicujus loci, vel sententiæ Scripturæ aut pro reformatione alicujus abusus in Ecclesia Dei, non tam videndum nobis est, quod homines ante nos, vel dixerunt, vel fecerunt, quam quid Spiritus Sanctus uniformiter, in corpore Sacræ Scripturæ dicat. Hujus, sic de Scriptura loquuntur, in Confessionis suæ summariis, Helvetii, Interpretatio ex ipsa sola petenda est, ut ipsa interpres sit sui. Ergo non alium sustinemus in causa fidei judicem, quam ipsum Deum, per Scripturas Sanctas pronunciantem, quid verum sit, quid falsum, quid sequendum sit, quid vefugiendum. Nihil enim, sic Argentinenses, poterit is veritatis Christianæ, nihil doctrinæ salutaris desiderare, scripturam qui consulere religiose studeat. Concinunt reliqui. Sic Wirtembergici. Vera sententia Scripturæ quærenda est in ipsa scriptura, & apud eos qui divino Spiritu excitati, scripturam per scripturam interpretantur. Sic Patres, purioris Ecclesiæ antistites & membra. Secundum scripturas expositio legitima & sine periculo. Ostensiones, quæ sunt in scripturis, non possunt ostendi nisi ex Scripturis ait Irenæus. Quæ ambiguè & quæ obscurè videntur dici in quibusdam locis sacræ scripturæ, ab iis quæ in aliis locis aperta ac perspicua sunt explicantur. Sunt verba Basilii. Exertissimè vero magnus ille Scripturæ amator ac laudator Chrysostomus. Sacra scriptura, inquit, se ipsam exponit, & neminem errare finit. Quantum ipsi hic Philosophia valeat & ratio alibi clarè exprimit. Singuli, inquit, dicunt, ego verum dico: cui credam nescio, cum utrinque scripturas prætexant. Respondeilli [?], hoc multum pro nobis. Nam si diceremus nos rationibus credere, merito turbareris: sed cum scripturas accipimus, & illæ sint simplices ac veræ, facile tibi fuerit judicare. Sic Ambrosius Gratiano, Nolo argumento credas, sancte Imperator, & nostræ disputationi. Scripturas interrogemus, Apostolos interrogemus, item Prophetas, interrogemus Christum. Sic Augustinus, Ad obscuriores locutiones illustrandas de manifestioribus sumantur exempla. Et ubi apertius sententiæ ponuntur, ibi discendum est, quomodo in locis intelligantur obscuris. Ratio autem contra divinarum scripturarum auctoritatem quæ redditur, quamlibet acuta sit, fallit versimilitudine, vera esse non potest. Non enim illis, sic Cyrillus Alexandrinus, qui temeraria investigatione, humanisque potius rationibus, quam auctoritate scripturæ gaudent, gratia Spiritus veritatem infundit mentibus.
units.tr: And if you want public documents, here are the words of the Scottish Confession: We confess that the interpretation of Scripture belongs neither to any private person nor to any public person, nor to any Church; but this right and authority belongs to the Spirit of God alone, by whom the letters of Holy Scripture were committed. Therefore, when it happens that something is disputed about the right sense of some passage or statement of Scripture, or about the reformation of some abuse in the Church of God, we must consider not so much what men before us have said or done, as what the Holy Spirit says uniformly in the body of Holy Scripture. The Swiss, in the summaries of their Confession, speak of Scripture in this way: Interpretation must be sought from Scripture alone, so that Scripture may be its own interpreter. Therefore we maintain no other judge in the cause of faith than God himself, pronouncing through the Holy Scriptures what is true, what is false, what is to be followed, and what is to be avoided. For, so the men of Strasbourg say, whoever religiously sets out to consult Scripture can lack nothing of Christian truth, nothing of saving doctrine. The rest agree. So the Württembergers: The true sense of Scripture is to be sought in Scripture itself, and among those who, roused by the divine Spirit, interpret Scripture by Scripture. So the Fathers, the bishops and members of the purer Church: "Legitimate exposition is according to the Scriptures and without danger." "The demonstrations which are in the Scriptures cannot be shown except from the Scriptures," says Irenaeus. "Those things which seem to be said ambiguously and obscurely in certain places of Holy Scripture are explained by those things which are open and plain in other places." These are the words of Basil. Most emphatically of all, that great lover and praiser of Scripture, Chrysostom: "Holy Scripture," he says, "expounds itself and does not allow anyone to err." How much weight he gives to philosophy and reason he states clearly elsewhere: "Each one," he says, "says, I speak the truth; I do not know whom to believe, since both sides put forward Scriptures." To them I reply: this is much in our favour. For if we said that we believed on the basis of reasons, you would rightly be troubled; but since we take up the Scriptures, and these are plain and true, it will be easy for you to judge. So Ambrose to Gratian: "Do not, holy Emperor, believe the argument, nor our disputation. Let us question the Scriptures; let us question the Apostles, likewise the Prophets; let us question Christ." So Augustine: "To illuminate more obscure expressions, examples should be taken from the clearer ones. And where opinions are set out more openly, there one must learn how to understand them in obscure passages. But whatever argument is offered against the authority of the divine Scriptures, however subtle it may be, it deceives by its plausibility and cannot be true." For, so Cyril of Alexandria: "The grace of the Spirit does not pour truth into those minds which delight in rash investigation and human reasonings rather than in the authority of Scripture."

units.la: Explicatâ jam Reformatorum sententiâ, videndum, quomodo istam controversiam pertractet, & quid de ea sentiat Wolzogius. Quod ut ordine fiat, duo agenda erunt. Primò examinandus erit Wolzogianus controversiam tractandi, communemque causam defendendi, modus & animus; Deinde ad aliquot theses referenda erit tota ipsius sententia. tentia. Patebitque immeritò & absque omni ratione ad demulcendos lectorum animos subinde eandem cum Reformatis mentem prætendi. Neque erit injuria, de qua conqueratur Wolzogius, si dicam, majorem ipsum inter & Reformatos, quam Paradoxum, sententiarum discrimen dari ac divortium. Tractandi modus, qualemque erga Reformatam sententiam animum gerat, modo sequentia accuratè considerentur, palam constabit. Notandum igitur, sententiam animus, aliquot thesibus demonstratus.
units.tr: The opinion of the Reformed having now been explained, we must see how Wolzogen treats this controversy and what he thinks of it. To do this in order, two things must be done. First, the manner and spirit of Wolzogen in handling the controversy and defending the common cause must be examined; then his whole opinion must be set down in some theses. It will become clear that he has, without any justification and without reason, repeatedly put forward, to soothe the minds of his readers, the same view as the Reformed. Nor will it be unjust, if I say, that Wolzogen, though he complains of it, finds a greater divergence and parting of opinions between himself and the Reformed than between himself and Paradoxus. His manner of handling the matter, and the attitude he bears towards the Reformed opinion, will plainly appear if the following is carefully considered. It should be noted, therefore, his attitude, shown by several theses.

units.la: 1. Primò : Quod statum controversiæ figat & formet nullibi, imo sive ponatur sive non, multum in eo situm non esse dictitet : quod vitium priori libro notavimus ; & revera vereor, ne id studio commiserit, metuens, ut parva nimis & parca deprehenderetur à Paradoxo dissensio : Optimè Clarissimus Hoornbeekius de disputandi modo disserit, in Apparatu ad Confutat. Socinian. inter alia ista huc quadrant, quæ habet pagina 86 & 87. Vitium hoc, inquit, in vulgaribus disputationibus haud leve observo, quod vix bene jactis fundamentis, id est, non discusso ante omnia & accuratè examinato controversiæ statu, quid utraque pars dicat, in quo & quousque consentiat, ubi divellatur, & sententiarum figendum sit divortium, ocyus ad pugnam, ad argumenta utrimque adferenda provoletur. Nos ut certum semper haberemus nobis propositum scopum, quo omnium rationum tela concorditer agerentur, non piguit multa aliquando insumere in indagando controversiæ statu, priusquam ad disputationem perveniretur. Unde factum, ut simul & mens illorum certius constiterit, & mox patefacta vena sit denotandæ in sententia falsitatis, atque argumentorum indicativa. Ego nunquam sollicitus de argumentis sum ; magis autem de sententia pernoscenda : Longe autem, adversus omnem bene disputantium methodum, Wolzogius aliter, idque in negotio, cujus maxime interest, ut bene ponantur limites, & status controversiæ accuratè describatur, quare &, tam à parte illa, quá Pontificii, quam quá Socinianis niani, veritatem istam de Interpretatione Scriptu-rae infestant, Theologos ita sedulo terminos figere, videas, ut vix ullibi majorem invenias ipsorum dili-gentiam : longè autem inquam aliter Wolzogius, Sic enim p. 194. Illum statum controversiae multipli-cem benéne & ex vero, an perperam explicuerit adver-sarius, nil hoc facit ad quæstionem magnopere. Nimi-rum certissimum est, quod dicto loco Hoornbeeki-us, quod in ista prima de mutuis sententiis velitatione, aliquando componatur & evanescat controversia, quæ non erat adeo, ac videbatur; vel devitetur aliqua, aut contrahatur, neque aut illa, aut tam multa est, ac quidem sæpe sibi alii persuadent: Noverat id Wolzogius, adeoque statum quæstionis non ponere accuratè, è re sua esse judicavit. Neque vitio vertendum mihi est, quasi suspicionibus nimis indulgeam; nam ve-ritatis causa, ut castitatis[?], omnem requirit atten-tionem & curam: verùm Velthusius, qui ortho-doxus[?] audit Wolzogio, prodidit arcanum, exerte e-nim ille dubium sese fatetur, an ulla sibi suisque cum Socinianis, ac proinde etiam cum Paradoxo, de in-terpretatione Scripturæ intercedat controversia, nam quicquid garriat homo, sub Paradoxi larva, Li-bertinus aut SemiAtheus, unum reipsa cum Socinia-nis idemque docuit. Quicquid sit, confusionem instituunt dedita opera, ait Hoornb. qui causæ diffidunt: Et si vel socordiæ vel minori cuidam vitio tribuen-dum videri posset, quem nunc culpamus, status controversiæ neglectus, excusari tamen nullo mo-do potest jam subsequens.
units.tr: 1. First: he nowhere sets out or shapes the state of the controversy, but even says that whether it is laid down or not, not much depends on it. We noted this fault in the first book; and truly I fear he did it deliberately, fearing that the dissent would be found by Paradoxus to be too small and slight. The distinguished Hoornbeek discusses the manner of disputing most excellently, in the Apparatus to his Confutation of the Socinians, and among other things what he says on pages 86 and 87 fits here. I observe, he says, that this fault is by no means slight in common disputations: that, with foundations scarcely well laid, that is, without first discussing and carefully examining the state of the controversy, what each side says, where and how far they agree, where they diverge and where the division of opinion must be fixed, they hasten quickly to battle and to bringing arguments on both sides. We, so that we might always have a fixed aim before us, by which the weapons of all reasons would act in harmony, did not grudge sometimes to spend much effort in inquiring into the state of the controversy before coming to the disputation. Hence it came about that both their minds were more surely settled, and soon the vein of falsehood in the opinion was laid open, and the arguments that point it out. I am never anxious about the arguments; I am more concerned to grasp the opinion. But Wolzogen does quite the reverse of every sound method of disputing, and in a matter where it matters most that the limits be well set and the state of the controversy accurately described. Hence, whether from that side where the Papists or from that where the Socinians assail this truth about the interpretation of Scripture, you will see theologians setting their boundaries so carefully that you could scarcely find anywhere greater diligence on their part. But Wolzogen, I say, does quite otherwise. For so he says on p. 194: Whether the adversary has explained that manifold state of the controversy rightly and truly, or wrongly, makes little difference to the question. Certainly it is true, as Hoornbeek says in the passage cited, that in that first skirmish of opposing opinions, sometimes a controversy which was not so great as it seemed is settled and vanishes away, or some part of it is avoided or narrowed, and it is neither that great, nor as many as others persuade themselves. Wolzogen knew this, and so judged it to his advantage not to set out the state of the question accurately. Nor must I be blamed for indulging too much in suspicion; for the cause of truth, like chastity, demands all attention and care. But Velthuysen, who is heard by Wolzogen as orthodox, has let out the secret: for he openly confesses himself uncertain whether any controversy lies between himself and his people and the Socinians, and therefore also Paradoxus, about the interpretation of Scripture. For whatever the man prattles under the mask of Paradoxus, a Libertine or semi-atheist, he in fact taught one and the same thing as the Socinians. Be that as it may, those who distrust their cause create confusion deliberately, says Hoornbeek. And if this neglect of the state of the controversy, which we now blame, could be ascribed to carelessness or some lesser fault, what follows can in no way be excused.

units.la: 2. Quod absque ullo involucro, diversam, ab omnibus etiam Reformatis, & singularem habeat sententiam, ac profiteatur. Sic enim, postquam ad defensionem suæ sententiæ, & solutionem eorum, quæ objecerat Paradoxus, perventum erat, loquitur p. 215. Et hic quidem scribendi finem facere possem, quia & MEAM propositi sententiam, & Paradox-ae meo judicio everti, præsertim cum duæ reliquæ partes, quæ vindicias continent novæ opinionis ab objectionibus, & NB. refutationem ALIARUM sententiarum, me non tangant magnopere. Quænam vero istæ aliæ sententiæ, quas oppugnaverat Paradoxus? quorum obiectiones erant quas solvere conatus fuit Paradoxus? Reformatorum sententia, inter alias, eorumque argumenta, & de hisce ait Wolzogius, quod se non tangant ista magnopere: imo tota sex capita, velitationi suæ cum Reformatis, impendit Paradoxus; & tamen, ea non tangunt Wolzogium: ut finem scribendi hic facere potuerit. Capite Decimo, ex Chamiero, Polano, Wendelino, Walæo, Whitakero, Tileno, Scarpio Reformatorum sententiam proponit; quam Capite undecimo explicat, additis variis adversus eandem obiectionibus: Duodecimo capite Scripturæ loca, Nehem. viii. 9. 1 Petr. 1, 20. à plerisque Reformatis Theologis & bene huc citata, suo modo explicat: Argumenta, non solum præstantissimis Theologis, sed ipsis confessionum formulis, usitata, solvere allaborat cap. xiii. Binis sequentibus capitibus, lumen & illuminationem Sp. Sancti, à Reformatis sic concipi & proponi queritur, ut Enthusiasmi ipsis dicam scribat, eorumque sententiam hac in re etiam refutandam sumat. Et hæc omnia, suâ sententiâ salvâ, intacta prætermisse potuisset noster, quia refutationem continent A L I A R U M sententiarum, quæ me, ait Wolzogius, non tangunt magnopere. Quid hinc aliter, quam aliam sibi sententiam & à Reformatis diversam, gloriari Wolzogium, colligere datur? quid est castra deserere? quid singularitatem, novitatemque affectare, si hoc non est? Unum locum addam, sic paulo post Paradoxum Pontificios, Reformatos, Socinianos, Arminianos aggressum refert: ad quæ frigidè noster: Nos vero contenti nostram proposuisse sententiam, viden', diversa igitur ipsi à Reformatis sententia est. Ne autem Pontificiis ex æquo cum Reformatis addictus videatur, sic propensiori animo hosce præ illis excipit. Et Pontificios quidem quod attinet, ne verbulo quidem eos at-
units.tr: 2. That he holds, without any disguise, an opinion that is different and singular, even from all the Reformed, and professes it. For so, after he had come to the defence of his opinion and the answering of the objections raised by Paradoxus, he speaks on p. 215: And here indeed I could make an end of writing, because both MY proposed opinion and, in my judgment, that of Paradoxus have been overthrown, especially since the remaining two parts, which contain the defence of the new opinion against objections, and NB the refutation of OTHER opinions, do not greatly concern me. But what are those other opinions which Paradoxus had attacked? Whose objections were those which Paradoxus tried to solve? The opinion of the Reformed, among others, and their arguments; and about these Wolzogen says that these things do not greatly concern him. Indeed, Paradoxus devoted six whole chapters to his skirmish with the Reformed; and yet these do not touch Wolzogen, so that he could have made an end of writing here. In chapter ten, from Chamier, Polanus, Wendelin, Walaeus, Whitaker, Tilenus and Scarpius, he sets out the opinion of the Reformed, which in chapter eleven he explains, with various objections added against it. In chapter twelve he handles in his own way the passages of Scripture, Nehemiah 8:9 and 1 Peter 1:20, which most Reformed theologians rightly cite here. In chapter thirteen he labours to solve the arguments commonly used, not only by the most outstanding theologians but also by the confessional formularies themselves. In the two following chapters he complains that the light and illumination of the Holy Spirit are so conceived and put forward by the Reformed that, so to speak, they smack of enthusiasm, and he takes their opinion in this matter also to be refuted. Our author could have passed over all these things, with his own opinion intact and untouched, because they contain the refutation of OTHER opinions, which do not greatly concern me, says Wolzogen. What can be gathered from this, other than that Wolzogen boasts of another opinion for himself, different from the Reformed? What is it to desert the camp? What is it to aim at singularity and novelty, if this is not? I shall add one more passage. A little later he reports that Paradoxus attacked the Papists, the Reformed, the Socinians and the Arminians; to which our author coldly replies: But we, content to have set out our own opinion, you see... So his opinion is different from the Reformed. Lest he should seem to be bound equally to the Reformed and to the Papists, he receives the former, with a more favourable mind, in preference to the latter. And as for the Papists, we do not touch them even with a little word

units.la: Aaa tingimus. Reformatos, quos ita prolixè & petulan-ter oppugnaverat totis sex capitibus Paradoxus, non ita possumus praeterire. Quis sine nausea tepidam le-gat orationem? turpissimam ἀστοργίαν[?] spiritualem (sic peccatum illud, quod erga matrem Ecclesiam committitur, vocare liceat) quis ferat? in homine, sic aestuante & bulliente, Ecclesiae suae Walonicae, imo vel unico ejus Seniori, quicquam quando im-pingitur. At pergat.Etsi nolim eorum opinionem scru-pulofo investigare examine: quot verba, tot probra Ecclesiae adspersa; eorum sententiam non &c. Reformatos putat, quorum opinionem, scrupuloso non di-gnatur examine, scilicet tanti huic viro non est Ec-clesiae honos & decus. At non parce nostris gratifi-catur vir magnus, post exprobatam enim dictionis obscuritatem, & mutuas dissensiones, se idem sentire dicit, non quidem cum eo quod sentiunt, sed ex suis hypothesibus sentire debent Reformati, sic cautissimè prospicit, ne nimis magnam videatur nobiscum profiteri convenientiam, multum enim de Wolzogiani operis honore delibaret, quod pro primo, quod in isto genere recte ab homine & satis-dilucidè scriptum est, haberi vult praeclarus author, si sententiam jam aliis professam solummodo trade-ret, non singularem.
units.tr: We now touch on the Reformed. Paradoxus attacked them so lengthily and insolently, across six whole chapters, that we cannot pass them over so easily. Who can read such a lukewarm speech without nausea? Who could bear such a shameful lack of spiritual affection [ἀστοργίαν], if that is the right name for the sin committed against our mother, the Church? A man who seethes and boils like this cannot let anything be aimed at his Walloon Church, or even at its single elder, without a reaction. But let him go on. "Although I would not wish to examine their opinion with a scrupulous examination": he has cast as many insults on the Church as he has written words, and he says their opinion is not worth such scrupulous examination. Evidently the honour and glory of the Church are not worth much to this man. Yet the great man does not spare our side entirely. After reproaching the obscurity of the Reformed expression and their mutual disagreements, he says he holds the same view. Not, indeed, the view they hold, but the view they ought to hold from his own hypotheses. He takes such careful precautions lest he seem to profess too great an agreement with us, for he would greatly diminish the honour of Wolzogen's work. The distinguished author wishes it to be regarded as the first work written clearly and with reasonable plainness on this subject, which it would not be if it merely set out a view already professed by others rather than an original one.

units.la: Hinc Reformatorum dictis multa impingit cri-mina, non de hujus aut illius Theologi, sed com-muni cunctis sententia agitur, & tamen, non satis dilucidè semper mentem suam aperire, (dum totum interim negotium ipsa luce clarius in singulis no-strorum scriptis expressum exstat) aut non satis di-stinctè rem ipsam nonnulli mente concepisse vel saltem dissentire dicendi sunt. Quod hic autem non omni-bus, sed nonnullis, hoc est aliquibus id imputare videatur, ne fallat lectorem, pagina quinta conse-renda est, & de omnibus dictum esse statim depre-hendet, quod hic aliquibus vitio vertere videri vo-luit noster, illic enim in universum hanc contro-versiam, NEQUAQUAM satis hactenus enu-cleatè cleatè expositam esse, asserit audacter. Et deinde, isti nonnulli, quinam sunt? non è vulgo certe, non gregarii milites, inspice Paradoxum, Chamierum, Polanum, Wendelinum, Walæum, aliosque Cori-phæos, citatos reperies capite decimo, quod respi-cit Wolzogius. Withakerus, Calvinus, Hemmin-gius, Marloratus, similesque heroes ad partes voca-ti erant in sequentibus, eorum tamen sententiam confusa saltem quadam obscuritate à sua diversam pronunciat p. 251. ipsosque obscurè vel non confide-ratè satis locutos fingere audet, pagina sequente, in initio: scommate ex spurcissimo authore mutuato, quodque omni opera ab Ecclesia eorumque Doctoribus amoliri debuisset, causæ publicæ propugnator non fidus.
units.tr: Hence he lays many charges against the sayings of the Reformed. The matter concerns not the view of this or that theologian, but an opinion common to them all, and yet they must be said either not always to have made their meaning plain enough (although the whole business is in fact set out in our writings more clearly than daylight), or some of them not to have grasped the matter distinctly enough in their minds, or at least to have dissented. That he seems to impute this not to all but to "some," that is, to certain individuals, the reader should not be deceived about. Let him set beside it the fifth page, and he will at once discover that the author there boldly asserts that this whole controversy has so far by no means been set out clearly enough, which here he seemed to want to hold against certain people. Moreover, who are these "some"? Certainly not the common people, nor ordinary soldiers. Look at Paradoxus, and you will find Chamier, Polanus, Wendelin, Walaeus and other leaders cited in the tenth chapter, which Wolzogen addresses. Whitaker, Calvin, Hemmingius, Marlorat and similar heroes were summoned to the field in what follows, yet he declares their opinion to differ from his own by a certain obscurity, if not confusion, on p. 251. On the following page, at the beginning, he even dares to pretend that they spoke obscurely or not carefully enough. This is a jest borrowed from a most filthy author, and a supporter of the public cause who is not loyal to it, one who should have been kept away from the Church and its teachers with every effort.

units.la: 4. Non mirum igitur, quod & illorum argu-menta non approbet, sed rejiciat, sed refutet, sed rideat. Retulerat optimas & validissimas, pro vera sententia, nostrorum rationes Paradoxus, has autem non tantum non suas dicit noster, sed nec proba-re eas potest universas, ultimum illud verbum dicis causa additum est, omnes enim non tantum non probat, sed rejicit. Plerasque saltem non ferire sco-pum existimat. Sic agit de singulis pagina sequente. Duo quidem priora argumenta non video quid habeant soliditatis. Ipsa argumenta eorumque authores videamus. Primum Chamieri est, nec tantum Chamiero, sed & aliis usitatum; alterum Withakeri referente Paradoxo: quorum vel nomina tam insolenti audaciæ frænum injicere deberent. Quoniam autem, ruptis istis repagulis, tantos leones vellica-re ausus est novellus disputator, vires ipsius experi-amur, summorum doctorum clientela tuti. Duo argumenta unico ictu disjicit, sic argumentabatur Chamierus. Omnes controversiæ fidei dirimi judica-rique debent à Scriptura; At omnis scripturæ interpre-tatio, est quædam controversia de fide. E. Brevibus, idem fere respondet cum Paradoxo, sic fideli certa-mine dimicat pro causa communi noster. Verissimè dixit olim Lactantius. Quidam non satis cœlestibus literis eruditi, cum veritatis accusatoribus respondere non possent, novam sibi doctrinam sine ulla radice composuerunt. Evenit id nostro Wolzogio, nam primo congressu abjicit hastam, fugit, & orthodoxorum castris armisque relictis, causam dedit probrosissimè. Ipsi forsan evenit, quod de Davide refertur, arma insolita ipsi erant & non usitata. Negaverat, post futiles distinctiunculas, Paradoxus minorem, idem plane Wolzogius, non facit enim, ipso judice, ad fidem interpretatio quicquam nisi remotè. Quo nihil infulsius dici poterat. Quod fidem terminat, fundatque, quod vehiculum rerum credendarum est & quidem divinum, nihilne hoc ad fidem? de quo ex supernaturali principio decisio petenda est; denique cujus decisionem ob dicentis authoritatem amplectimur, nihil hoc ad fidem, nisi remotè? Ludis in generalibus & laxè ac indeterminatè loqueris: forsan, præ metu tanti adversarii, eloqui non audes, quod in mente geris. Disputemus de sensu hujus aut illius loci, sumamus illum qui exstat Psalmi secundi commate septimo, quidnam illud est quod te convincit, illic de filio Dei, ejusque æterna generatione, sermonem esse, nonne ea sunt, quæ Deus in textus circumstantiis, in paralellis, in aliis textibus argumenta posuit, nonne igitur hunc istius loci sensum esse credis, quia Deus istis mediis & signis, homini pro suo cuique modulo perceptibilibus, significat & indicat, hunc, non alium, horum verborum esse sensum? Nonne igitur Deus ipse, nonne ipsa Scriptura interpres, nonne ista interpretatio fide recipienda est? & non res solum, ope istius interpretationis, eruta, sed & ipsa interpretatio? atque hoc volunt Reformati, concludit Chamierus, & frustra velicaiti Wolzogi. At viam tantum ad fidem habet interpretatio, ait, non ipsius fidei quicquam. Est tantum instrumentum, quo ea investigamus, quæ fidei objecto continentur. Sit ita, habeat viam ad res credendas, ad dogmata credenda, & sit isto sensu, instrumen-tum, tum, an tamen credere non debeo & fide recipere istam viam veram viam esse &instrumentum Dei authoritate suspiciendum & adhibendum. Ac si alia, quam divina via, alio, quam divino instrumento, ad divinam grassaremus cognitionem fidemque, verba, fateor, phrasesque, Deo cum homine com-munes sunt, sed Deus cum loquitur & phrasibus verbisque mediis mihi intelligendum præbet, aut se, aut aliud quidpiam, ego rem istam verbis istis signi-ficatam non solum fide divina recipio, sed & verba ista sic sumenda Dei jubet authoritas, ipso quippe se illis, hoc aut illo modo, intelligibiliter manifestan-te. Recta interpretatio, loci modo citati, via est, qua perveniam ad agnitionem istius veritatis, quam, fide divina, & authoritate divina nixus, credo, fi-lium vera generatione ab æterno à patre genitum esse, bene, sed an non & divina authoritas est, quæ te movet hæc verba isto sumere sensu non alio? Locus jam explicatus istam veritatem repræsentat & dictat divinitus; sed & ista verba, istum sensum requirere, nisi etiam divina docear authoritate, tota certè tollitur Christianorum fides, & nihil erit quo convincar. At Deus hic non loquitur, ait pag. 130. ut, quia ille affirmat hunc esse hujus loci sensum, credere debeamus. Quod si faceret per Spiritum suum, ut pertendunt Enthusiastarum patroni, non esset utique removenda fides. Imo revera & perspicuè hic loquitur Deus, nisi, dum divinis suis signis in Scriptura collocatis, nobis intelligibiliter, mentem hanc, non aliam esse, significat, non loqui dicendus: loquitur, & suâ loquelâ, ut ita loquar, Scripturæ sen-sum revera dictat; primo externè, secundo internè. Externè in ipsa Scriptura, & internè per suum Spi-ritum. Docet per scripturas omnia, docet per expositi-onem scripturarum omnia. Veritatis Spiritus invisibi-liter menti insinuat scientiam divinorum. Sunt verba Didymi Alexandrini, de quo alibi Hieronymus ejus discipulus, referente Sixto Senensi, Didymus meus, oculos habet sponsæ de Cantico Canticorum, & illa lu-mine mina, quæ in candentes segetes sublimare præcepit Je-sus. In Scriptura, quæso, nonne ea sunt, quæ te moveant ac persuadeant, modò dicta verba, hoc sensu, non alio, sumenda esse? nonne textus circumstantiæ, nonne aliorum textuum paralellismus, nonne fidei analogia, supposita singulorum verborum significatione, atque intelligibilitate, abundè te hujus aut illius convincunt sensus? Verùm, quis ille est, qui ista in Scriptura, sapientissimâ & imper-scrutabili sapientiâ, sic posuit, nonne Deus est? nonne per ista signa sic nobis sensum illius dicti, adeo-que mentem suam cognoscendam præbet? nonne mentem suam, mediantibus signis intelligibilibus, exprimens, loqui dicendus erit? affirmare, hunc aut illum, hisce verbis, sensum subesse, non est cen-sendus? Sic Deus in Scriptura loquitur, & de sensu pronunciat. Internè autem præterea, idem loqui-tur, & per Spiritum suum, non solum mentem dis-ponendo, excitando, &c. sed & istam veritatem, sic ex tali collatione resplendescentem, intus quidem repræsentando, mentique indendo, ejusque ibi mi-rabilem certitudinem perficiendo, qua pium animum suavissime perfundit. Neque id pertendunt En-thusiastarum Patroni, ut falso docet Wolzogius: vilior enim ipsis Scriptura est, & nimis magnæ ac su-perbæ de spiritu suo imaginationes, quam ut illi ex-plicandæ, hic ipsis multum negotii facessat, non Scripturis explicandis, sed novis rebus dictandis, u-nicè fere intentus. Reformati sunt qui id docent, & quotquot Spiritus Sancti motus, & inspirationes venerabundi recipiunt, ac favent: scientes, Spiri-tum sibi promissum esse, quo in verbi veritate duce-rentur, memores pretiosissimæ promissionis, Joh. xiv. 6, 7. Oraturum Christum ut pater alium advoca-tum mitteret, qui maneret cum ipsis in æternum. Nem-pe Spiritum illum veritatis, quem mundus non potest recipere, quia non conspicit eum, nec novit eum, vos autem inquit D. J. nostis eum, quia apud vos manet, & in vobis erit. Hæc unctio illa est, quæ intus docet. Hic ille, de quo Augustinus, Magister intus est, & ait i-dem, quibus unctio illa intus non loquitur; indocti, re-deunt. Adeo ut, Heidano teste, occulta nobis mane-re debeat caelestis sapientia, aut immediata revelatio-ne, externae superaddita, acquiri. Audi & expende Wolzogi, quae habet magnus Calvinus, sic ille de Spiritu, sic Enthusiasmi crimen amolitur prudentissime. Si rite in Dei schola proficere cupimus, prae-fertim tolerantia opus est, donec patefaciat Spiritus, quod frustra visi sumus saepius legisse vel audisse. Qua-re, ne languescat in nobis discendi studium, vel in de-sperationem labamur, ubi non statim assequimur loquen-tis Christi mentem, sciamus hoc nobis omnibus dici, SPIRITUS tandem SUGGERET quae locu-tus sum. Hanc quidem poenam denunciat, Esaias xxix. 11. Ut sermo Dei sit illis tanquam liber clausus: sed Dominus, hoc etiam modo, plerumque suos humiliat. Ideo patienter ac placide expectandum revelationis tem-pus, nec verbum propterea respuere decet... sequitur irritam & nihil fore externam praedicationem nisi ac-cedat Spiritus magisterium. NB. Duplicem ergo habet Deus docendi modum, nam & hominum ore insonat nostris auribus, & intus Spiritu suo nos compellat: idque facit nunc eodem momento, nunc diversis tempo-ribus, prout illi visum est. Observa autem quaenam sint illa omnia, quorum doctorem fore Spiritum promittit: suggeret, inquit, vel reducet in memoriam quaecunque dixi. Unde sequitur non fore novarum revelationum architectum. Hoc uno verbo refutare licet quaecunque sub praetextu Spiritus in Ecclesiam figmenta ab initio hucusque Satan invexit. Mahometes & Papa commune habent religionis principium, non contineri in Scriptura perfectionem doctrinae, sed quiddam altius revelatum esse a Spiritu. Ex eadem lacuna nostro tem-pore Anabaptistae & Libertini, sic saepe Enthusiastas vocat, sua deliria hauserunt. Atqui impostor est spi-ritus, non Christi, qui extraneum aliquod ab Evangelio commentum ingerit. Spiritum enim Christus pro-mittit, qui Evangelii doctrinam quasi subscriptor con-firmet[?]. firmet. Et paulo ante vers 17. Sic loquitur idem Vir Dei. Ornat spiritum Christus altero titulo, quod sit magister veritatis. Unde sequitur, donec ab eo intus simus edocti, vanitate & mendacio captas esse nostras omnium mentes. Quem mundus non potest accipere. Antithesis ista gratiae excellentiam amplificat, qua Deus non nisi electos suos dignatur. Significat enim non vulgare esse donum quo privatur mundus. Quo sensu etiam Esaias, LIX.2. Ecce tenebrae operient terram, & caligo populos: super te autem orietur Dominus. Eo enim plus meretur laudis Dei misericordia erga Ecclesiam, dum singulari privilegio eam supra totum mundum extollit. Simul tamen Discipulos hortatur Christus ne sensu carnis inflati, ut solet mundus, Spiritus gratiam à se repellant.
units.tr: 4. It is therefore no wonder that he does not approve their arguments but rejects them, refutes them, and laughs at them. Paradoxus had set out the best and strongest arguments of our side for the true view, yet our author says that these are not his own, and he cannot even approve them all. The last word was added for show, since he does not merely fail to approve them all, he rejects them. He thinks that most of them, at least, do not hit the mark. He deals with each one in this way on the following page. The first two arguments, I do not see what solidity they have. Let us look at the arguments themselves and their authors. The first belongs to Chamier, and was in common use not only with Chamier but with others. The second is Witsius's, as Paradoxus reports it. Their names alone ought to put a bridle on such unbridled boldness. Since, however, with those barriers broken down, this novice disputant has dared to pluck at such great lions, let us test his strength, protected by the support of great teachers. He knocks down two arguments with a single blow. Chamier argued thus: All controversies of faith ought to be decided and judged by Scripture; but every interpretation of Scripture is a certain controversy of faith. Briefly, he answers almost the same as Paradoxus, and our author fights for the common cause with a faithful struggle. Lactantius spoke most truly long ago: Some, not sufficiently learned in heavenly letters, when they could not answer the accusers of the truth, composed for themselves a new doctrine with no root at all. This has happened to our Wolzogius, for at the first encounter he drops his spear and flees, and, leaving the camp and arms of the orthodox, he gave up the cause most shamefully. Perhaps what is reported of David happened to him too: the arms were strange to him and not his usual ones. Paradoxus, after some trifling distinctions, had denied the minor premise, and Wolzogius plainly does the same, for interpretation, by his own judgment, does nothing for faith except remotely. Nothing more silly could be said. Does interpretation, which bounds and grounds faith, which is the vehicle of the things to be believed and that a divine one, have nothing to do with faith? Faith is to be sought from a decision made on a supernatural principle; finally, it is the decision whose authority we embrace because of the speaker's authority. Does this have nothing to do with faith, except remotely? You play with generalities and speak loosely and indefinitely. Perhaps, out of fear of so great an adversary, you do not dare to say what you have in mind. Let us dispute about the sense of this or that passage. Let us take the one found in Psalm ii. 7. What is it that convinces you that there the discourse is about the Son of God and his eternal generation? Are these not the things which God has placed in the circumstances of the text, in parallel passages, and in other texts as arguments? Do you not therefore believe that this is the sense of that passage, because God, by these means and signs, which are perceptible to each man according to his own measure, indicates and shows that this, and not another, is the sense of these words? Is it not, then, God himself, Scripture itself as interpreter, and this interpretation that must be received in faith, and not only the thing drawn out by means of that interpretation, but the interpretation itself? This is what the Reformed hold, Chamier concludes, and Wolzogius's struggles are in vain. But interpretation has only a way to faith, he says, and nothing of faith itself. It is only an instrument by which we investigate those things which are contained in the object of faith. Granted, let it have a way to the things to be believed, to the doctrines to be believed, and let it be an instrument in that sense. Yet ought I not to believe, and by faith receive, that this way is a true way and an instrument to be revered and used on God's authority? If we were pursuing knowledge of God and faith by any way other than the divine way, by any instrument other than the divine instrument, then, I admit, the words and phrases are common to God and to man. But when God speaks and, through words and phrases, gives me to understand either himself or something else, I not only receive in divine faith the thing signified by those words, but the authority of God also commands that those words be taken in this way, since he himself makes himself intelligibly manifest by them in this or that way. The right interpretation of the passage just cited is the way by which I arrive at knowledge of that truth which, relying on divine faith and divine authority, I believe: that the Son was begotten by the Father from eternity by true generation. Good, but is it not divine authority that moves you to take these words in this sense and no other? The passage, once explained, sets forth this truth and dictates it divinely; but if these words also do not require this sense, taught by divine authority, then the whole faith of Christians is surely taken away, and there will be nothing by which I can be convinced. But God does not speak here, he says on page 130, so that, because he affirms this to be the sense of this passage, we ought to believe it. But if he did so through his Spirit, as the patrons of the enthusiasts maintain, faith would certainly not be removed. Indeed, God really and plainly speaks here. Unless, while by his divine signs placed in Scripture he intelligibly signifies to us that this is the mind and no other, he is not to be said not to speak. He speaks, and, by his speech, as I may put it, he really dictates the sense of Scripture: first outwardly, second inwardly. Outwardly in Scripture itself, and inwardly through his Spirit. He teaches all things through the Scriptures, he teaches all things through the exposition of the Scriptures. The Spirit of truth insinuates the knowledge of divine things invisibly into the mind. These are the words of Didymus of Alexandria, of whom Jerome his disciple speaks elsewhere, as Sixtus of Siena reports: My Didymus has the eyes of the bride from the Song of Songs, and she has those lights which Jesus commanded to be raised over the white fields. In Scripture, I ask you, are there not those things which move you and persuade you that the words just mentioned must be taken in this sense and no other? Do not the circumstances of the text, the parallelism of other texts, the analogy of faith, once the meaning and intelligibility of the individual words is assumed, fully convince you of this or that sense? But who is he who has placed these things in Scripture with most wise and unsearchable wisdom? Is it not God? Does he not, through these signs, thus present to us the sense of that saying, and so present his mind to be known? Is he not to be said to speak, when, by intelligible signs, he expresses his mind? Is it not to be judged that to affirm that this or that sense lies under these words is folly? So God speaks in Scripture and pronounces concerning its sense. Moreover, he also speaks inwardly, and through his Spirit, not only by disposing and stirring the mind, and so on, but also by presenting within, and impressing upon the mind, that truth shining forth from such a comparison, and by bringing to completion there its wonderful certainty, by which it sweetly fills the pious soul. The patrons of the enthusiasts do not maintain this, as Wolzogius falsely teaches. For Scripture is of less value to them, and their imaginations about their own spirit are too great and proud to be explained by Scripture. Their chief concern is not to explain Scripture, but to dictate new things, and it causes them much trouble here. The Reformed are those who teach this, and all who receive and favour with reverence the motions and inspirations of the Holy Spirit, knowing that the Spirit has been promised to them, by whom they would be led into the truth of the Word, mindful of the most precious promise, Joh. xiv. 6, 7: that Christ would ask the Father to send another Advocate who would remain with them forever. Namely, that Spirit of truth whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him; but you, says our Lord, know him, because he abides with you and will be in you. This is that anointing which teaches within. This is the one of whom Augustine says, The Teacher is within, and says the same, to whom that anointing does not speak within; they are untaught, they go back. So that, as Heidanus testifies, heavenly wisdom must remain hidden from us, or be acquired by an immediate revelation added from without. Hear and weigh what Wolzogius has, what great Calvin says. Thus he very prudently removes the charge of enthusiasm concerning the Spirit. If we desire to make progress rightly in God's school, patience is especially needed, until the Spirit reveals what we have often seemed to read or hear in vain. Therefore, lest the zeal for learning grow cold in us, or we slip into despair when we do not immediately grasp the mind of Christ who speaks, let us know that this is said to all of us: THE SPIRIT at last WILL SUGGEST what I have said. This punishment is indeed threatened, Esaias xxix. 11: that the word of God may be to them as a closed book; but the Lord also in this way often humbles his own. Therefore the time of revelation must be awaited patiently and calmly, nor is it proper to reject the word on that account... it follows that external preaching would be vain and of no effect unless the teaching of the Spirit came with it. NB. God therefore has a twofold mode of teaching, for he both sounds in our ears through the mouth of men, and inwardly urges us by his Spirit; and he does this sometimes at the same moment, sometimes at different times, as seems good to him. But observe what all those things are of which he promises that the Spirit will be the teacher: he will suggest, he says, or bring to memory whatever I have said. From this it follows that he will not be the architect of new revelations. By this one word it is permitted to refute whatever fictions Satan has introduced into the Church under the pretext of the Spirit, from the beginning until now. Mahomet and the Pope have a common principle of religion: that the perfection of doctrine is not contained in Scripture, but that something higher has been revealed by the Spirit. From the same gap in our own time the Anabaptists and Libertines, whom he often calls enthusiasts, have drawn their delusions. And yet it is the spirit of an impostor, not of Christ, that introduces some invention foreign to the Gospel. For Christ promises the Spirit, who would confirm the doctrine of the Gospel, as it were, as a witness. confirm. And a little before, at verse 17, the same man of God speaks thus: Christ adorns the Spirit with another title, that he is the teacher of truth. From which it follows that, unless we are taught within by him, the minds of all of us are captured by vanity and falsehood. Which the world cannot receive. This antithesis amplifies the excellence of grace, which God deigns to bestow only on his elect. For it signifies that the gift of which the world is deprived is not a common one. In this sense Isaiah also says, lx. 2: Behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples: but the Lord shall arise upon you. For the mercy of God toward the Church deserves all the more praise, since he raises it above the whole world by a singular privilege.
