At the same time Christ exhorts his disciples not to reject the grace of the Spirit, as the world does, puffed up with the sense of the flesh.

units.la: SOMNIUM EST TERRENIS HOMINIBUS QUICQUID DE SPIRITU SANCTO PRÆDICAT SCRIPTURA, QUIA RATIONE SUA FRETI, COELESTEM ILLUMINATIONEM DESPICIUNT. TAMETSI PASSIM GRASSATUR HÆC SUPERBIA, QUÆ SPIRITUS SANCTI LUCEM QUANTUM IN SE EST EXTINGUIT: NOS TAMEN PROPRIÆ INOPIÆ CONSCII, SCIAMUS NON EX ALIO FONTE MANARE QUICQUID SANÆ INTELLIGENTIÆ EST. Interea ostendunt Christi verba, nihil, humano sensu, de Spiritu Sancto posse percipi, sed eum cognosci sola fidei experientia. Mundus, inquit, capax non est Spiritus, quia eum non cognoscit: Vos autem cognoscitis eum, quia apud vos manet: Solus ergo Spiritus est qui, in nobis habitando, cognoscendum se praebet, alias ignotus & incomprehensibilis.
units.tr: IT IS A DREAM TO EARTHLY MEN WHATEVER SCRIPTURE PREDICATES OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, BECAUSE, TRUSTING IN THEIR OWN REASON, THEY DESPISE HEAVENLY ILLUMINATION. ALTHOUGH THIS PRIDE RAGES EVERYWHERE, AND SO FAR AS IT IS IN ITS POWER QUENCHES THE LIGHT OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, LET US NEVERTHELESS, AWARE OF OUR OWN POVERTY, KNOW THAT WHATEVER SOUND UNDERSTANDING WE HAVE FLOWS FROM NO OTHER SOURCE. Meanwhile the words of Christ show that nothing concerning the Holy Spirit can be perceived by human sense, but that he is known by the experience of faith alone. The world, he says, is not able to receive the Spirit, because it does not know him; but you know him, because he abides with you. Therefore it is the Spirit alone who, by dwelling in us, presents himself to be known; otherwise he is unknown and incomprehensible.

units.la: Mundi nomine, ait Joh. Gerhardi hic intelliguntur primo sapientissimi, tumentes mundanâ sapientiâ, quos solos mundus veneratur ac suspicit, qui mundano sensu ac judicio, tanquam certissimâ regulâ, omnia metiuntur. 1 Cor. 1. 20, 21.
units.tr: By the name of the world, says Johann Gerhard, are understood here first of all the very wise, puffed up with worldly wisdom, whom alone the world venerates and admires, who measure all things by a worldly sense and judgment, as by the most certain rule. 1 Cor. 1:20, 21.

units.la: Dedisce ergo tandem, à veritate, à Reformato-rum sensu, sub Enthusiasmi terribili umbra, lecto-rem abster rere Wolzogi. Nubes testium est, quo te convincam, id à Reformatis rectè doceri, quod tu pro Euthusiastico somnio censendum putas.
units.tr: Therefore, reader, at last learn from the truth, from the sense of the Reformed, to refrain from being terrified by the shadow of Enthusiasm, as Wolzogen would have you. A cloud of witnesses is there to convince you that what you think should be judged an enthusiastic dream is rightly taught by the Reformed.

units.la: Fide tamen, inquis, non opus est, ut secundum le-ges humanas judicem, hunc sensum huic orationi con-venire. Tu age secundum leges humanas quantum velis, fide tamen creditur & per fidem apprehen-ditur, iste sensus, qui ex verbis eruitur, idque quia mens videt ex natura signorum, talem in iis Deo mentem esse. Ita ut res significata & credenda, recipiatur, ut à Deo tradita, per talia signa, quorum significatum, ex legitima collatione resultans, pro Dei ipsius loquela per fidem recipitur: Et fide, non res ipsa solùm, sed & signorum valor talis esse creditur. Quoniam divina sunt, quae me persuadent, verba, per se sigillatim sic significantia, hoc aut illud significare, prout in hoc aut illo Scripturae loco scripta conjunctim reperiuntur. Atque ista de primo Reformatorum argumento; eodem talo, stat hactenus, etiam secundum illud, quod ex Chamiero & Withakero profert Paradoxus, ut inspicienti ad oculum patebit: neque enim Bellarmi-num, Duraeum, Stapletonum, summos & exercita-tissimos adversarios, ita temere & tam levi armatu-ta accincti, oppugnarunt & expugnarunt illustrif-simi Heroes, ac somniat Wolzogius. Tertium ab analogia ductum argumentum eatenus stringit, quatenus est cognita analogia, inquit, at ipsa debet ante doceri. Cunctorum vindicias non instituatm [?], occuparunt eam operam, viri Clarissimi, modo citati, unicum tamen hic Wolzogio in mentem revocandum censeo: quam pauci articuli, iisque inventu tam obvii, ac se sponte cuivis quasi objicientes, analogiam sibi constituant fidei: ut mirum sit, hic difficultatem poni, in eo, quod prius doceri debeat, quod absque multo labore vel sponte sese ingerat vel inspientis modo lectoris animo, quemadmodum ipse antea de articulis necessariis, qui ἀναλο-γίαν constituunt τῆς πίστεως philosophatus est. At verum est, prius cognoscendam istam analogiam, priusquam reliquae interpretationis regula esse queat; sicuti scientiae cujusdam rudimenta & primas regulas discimus, antequam ad perfectiorem ejusdem scientiae cognitionem ascendamus, veruntamen, non alio principio, ista rudimenta inaedifi-canda sunt, ac fundamenta, quam reliqua totius æ-dificii compages. Sic & hic sese res habet: quamvis prius cognoscenda sit, in sequentibus pro norma habenda, fidei analogia, non tamen aliunde, quam ex ipsa scriptura, petenda est; quae cum clarè eandem proponat, ut pio lectori & scrutatori ex ipsa Scriptura non possit non innotescere, perspicuum evadit omnem interpretandi regulam & normam scripturam esse, quod demonstrandum erat. Quar-tum ex Polano & Alstedio desumtum, non majoris in pretio est nostro censori. Quartum, sic disserit, quod vocem Dei vult audiri, qua clarior aut manifestior nulla esse potest, ego audirem, nisi quaereretur de ipsa voce Dei, quemadmodum ejus claritatem percipiamus, & in quo sita sit haec claritas. Supponunt Reformati lucernam, lucem, imo lucem splendentem scripturam esse, eamque, Solis instar, suo lumine clarissimè videri: noster regerit, de ipsa voce Dei quemadmodum ejus claritatem percipiamus, & in quo sita sit ejus claritas quaeri: ac si quis Solem proprio lumine conspiciendum contendenti regereret, at de solis claritate quaeritur quomodo percipiatur? quis tam stolidè nugantem responsione dignaretur? hoc argumentum supponit istam Scripturæ perspicuitatem & intelligibilitatem, quam ex locis, de quorum sensu dubitari non potest, probarunt antea Reformati Doctores: ista autem intelligibilitate & perspicuitate supposita, non minus sequitur, scripturam per scripturam explicandam, quam solis lumine conspici Solem. Sic feliciter castra Dei, Reformatorum primipilos oppugnat hic Pastor Walonicus. Intumescente autem, inter præ-liandum, animo, reliquas nostrorum copias in triumphum ducendas exercitatori suo tradit; ut miserrimo Ardelioni, non magis; partæ in Reformatos victoriæ quam Velthusio, orthodoxiæ testimonium, denegaturus sit hic Pastor belle Reformatus. Audiamus distribuentem spolia. Quintum, Sextum, Septimum argumentum non stringere cum Exercitatore censeo. Quintum sic habet, quia ipsa scriptura potest sapientem reddere ad salutem 2 Tim. III. 15. &c. Quid autem ad illud Paradoxus? negat consequentiam, neque enim, inquit egregius Thraso, adeo Lyncei sumus, ut videre quea-mus, qui sequatur, S. Script: intellecta hominem ad salutem sapientem reddere potest, ergo est sui interpres. Et hâc responsione elumbe factum est, Judice Wolzogio, nostrorum illud argumentum. Ego autem, non tantum non Lynceos hosce duumviros, sed calpis cæciores esse putem, qui, ita misere dum cavillantur, se, sub certa victoriæ spe, cum summis viris, in arenam descendisse somniare possunt. Quis sic rationem instituit, Scripturam intellectam; facultatem habere, aptam esse, qua ad sapientiam salutarem perveniatur? nemo Reformatorum ita desipuit: Scriptura intellecta, non est medium ad sapientiam, sed ipsa sapientia salutaris. Quoniam igitur Scriptura facultatem habet & aptitudinem in suo genere, sapientem reddendi, sapientiam docendi, necesse est ut & sibi sufficiat, ad propriam interpretationem, qua sine, medium sufficiens ad sapientiam, dicenda non esset, quod est contra Apostolum. Sic argumentantur Reformati & frustra hoc argumentum, junctis cum Paradoxo copiis, impetivit Wolzogius. Æqua facilitate sextum & septimum vindicari posset, sed non est operæ pretium, quia nihil, præter fætidissimi Paradoxi recoctam cramben, apponit noster disputator[?]. Octavum argumentum aliquatenus saltem stringere existimat; multum ipsi debent, præ reliquis magis gratiogratiosè exceptæ, magni Polani manes. Non qui-dem totum quod volunt Reformati evicit Polanus, sed de singulari quorundam locorum interpretatione docuit, scripturam sui interpretandi modum exhibuisse; at bone vir, quæ ratio diversitatis in reli-quis, si scriptura ullibi, quid ni, eadem methodo, ubique sese explicare censenda est, præsertim cum αὐτοκατάκριτῳ[?]·, exemplorum plenam esse scripturam, quibus probetur ipsam per seipsam esse explicandam, fatearis? Hoc volunt Reformati, & isto, & reliquis argumentis, quorsum igitur tuæ cavillatio-nes & prævaricationes Wolzogi? Eo, quod talibus exemplis plena Scriptura est, idem concludunt de reliquis. Nonum argumentum, licet Altingius, Withakerus, Walæus, imo omnes Theologi Reformati eo utantur, omni fundamento caret, ut putat Wolzogius, Deum esse interpretem suæ scripturæ, quia eo nemo melior esse potest, cum suorum verborum sit optimus quisque interpres, non video quo fundamento nitatur. Negamus Deum dici posse proprie Scripturarum interpretem. En aperte toti Reformatæ Ecclesiæ bellum denunciat audax scriptor. Audi Præce-ptorem tuum discipule, hac in causa, nimium dege-ner, sic ille in Tirino castigavit idem, quod tute hic effutiisti. Non esse ipsammet Scripturam, sc: sui interpretem, dixerat Tirinus: Sic autem Jesuitæ, simulque tibi, regerit Vir Clarissimus: Imo Scripturam per Scripturam oportet interpretari. Nec certius Scriptura, quam ex Scriptura potest intelligi, ut non certius cognoscitur Sol, quam per Solem. Quæ hominum quæso istorum insolentia, qui refugiunt judicium Scri-pturæ, quia de Scriptura agitur. Quam esse interpre-tem sui si quis neget insaniat, ait Chamierus. Verissimè enim dicitur, sunt verba Paræi, non esse meliorem Scripturarum divinarum interpretem, quam Scripturas ipsas: neque hoc potest negari, nisi à scripturarum imperitis: quos de re tanta judicare vel audiri non convenit: At licet verum sit unumquemque suorum verborum interpretem optimum esse, non tamen videt qui inde sequatur, Deum esse suorum verborum interpretem. Hoc est, non videt sub genere speciem; verum eo fortius hoc argumentum Wolzogio videri debuerat, quo ille magis humano more verbum suum dedisse Deum docuit; de aliis enim authoribus negari non potest, optime sese ipsos explicare: magis autem, quoniam ipsa Scri-ptura de se hoc innuit, & multis exemplis probat, concedente id, in variis, Wolzogio; Nam exemplo-rum est plena Scriptura quibus probetur ipsam esse per se explicandam, quod re vera idem est, ac si fatere-tur quod hic negat, nimirum Deum dici posse proprie Scripturarum interpretem, hoc est, Deum sacrum illud monumentum, quo nobiscum loquitur, ita at-temperasse, ut quae ambiguè & quae obscure videntur dici in quibusdam locis sacrae Scripturae, ab iis, quae in aliis locis aperta ac perspicua sunt, explicantur, uti id ex Basilio superius audivimus, ultra quod nihil plane petunt, aut concludunt Reformati. Instat autem Wolzogius & dicit, hinc concludi aeque posse, debere oraculo quodam pronuntiare Deum de sensibus Scripturae. Verum qua ratione in mentem suam inducere potuit tantam perversitatem, homo qui inter Reformatos pastor audit, ut tam turpi tam probrosa & ignominiosa consequentia, com-munem illorum causam gravare, non erubuerit? Generale axioma hoc infert, Deum optimum suorum verborum esse interpretem, cui placuit, non fictis oraculis, sed firmo sermone Prophetico & Apostolico nos de sua voluntate, & verbi vero sensu, erudire; ut, quamvis potuerit, noluerit tamen neque necesse sit id extraordinariis oraculis perfici, quod nobis seipso sufficit & per se satis est; scom-ma istud, cum reliquis Papistarum & Sociniano-rum illusionibus, interim nihili facimus. Potuisset Deus vivo oraculo, potuisset per Urim & Thum-mim dictorum suorum mentem explanare, sed voluit, ut per verbum, verbū intelligeretur, & per Scri-pturam Scriptura, ut sic eadem revera nos possit sa-pientes pientes reddere ad salutem. Quid multis? omnis malæ argumentationis fontem detegit noster, aliter enim accidere non potuit, quin omnes isti Theologi debili & vitiosa argumentandi methodo insisterent, argumenta enim, sic magnus noster Theologus, quia ipsa non est satis explorate percepta quæstio, non possunt ex ipsa re esse petita. O deplorandam hactenus Reformatorum ignorantiam! valida argumenta nondum produxerunt ipsorum Coryphæi, nec producere potuerunt, ipsa enim non est satis explorate percepta quæstio. Crediderim profecto nullum unquam Theologorum, qui hanc materiam ex professo per tractarunt, Wolzogio lectum esse, non Chamierum, non Withakerum, non Hoornbeekium, quorum ultimus ita consummate hoc negotium elaboravit, ut unicum illud Libri Primi Socinianismi Confutati Tom. 1. Caput septimum sufficiat quo Paradoxus, cum omnibus Socinianis, & Wolzogius cum suo Velthufio, abunde refutetur. Hoc saltem asseverare ausim, neminem illorum, quos vel sexcentos producere possem, Wolzogium non multis parasangis, vel in hujus quæstionis solida ac dilucida pertractatione, post se relinquere.
units.tr: Yet, you say, it is not necessary to judge by human laws that this sense agrees with this saying. Then judge by human laws as much as you like. Still, this sense, which is drawn out of the words, is believed by faith and apprehended through faith, because the mind sees from the nature of the signs that such is the mind of God in them. So the thing signified and to be believed is received, as delivered by God, through such signs, and the meaning that results from their lawful comparison is received through faith as God's own speech. By faith it is believed that not only the thing itself but also the force of the signs is of this kind. For the words that persuade me are divine, and they signify separately in this way or that, according as they are found written together in this or that place of Scripture. So much for the first argument of the Reformed. It stands so far on the same footing, and also on that which the Paradoxus brings from Chamier and Withaker, as anyone looking at it will see plainly. For the most illustrious heroes did not attack and overcome Bellarmine, Du Rhay, and Stapleton, the chief and most practised opponents, with such rash and light weapons, though Wolzogen dreams that they did. The third argument, drawn from the analogy, is weakened only so far as the analogy is known, he says, but the analogy itself must be taught first. The most distinguished men I have just cited have taken up the defence of all these points, but I think there is one thing here that Wolzogen should be reminded of: how few articles, and those so easy to find, and offering themselves to anyone as if thrown at him, establish for themselves the analogy of faith. So it is remarkable that a difficulty is raised here in what must be taught first, when it either presents itself without much labour or comes into the mind of an attentive reader, just as he himself earlier reasoned about the necessary articles, which make up the analogy of faith [ἀναλογία τῆς πίστεως]. It is true, however, that this analogy must be known before the other rule of interpretation can be, just as we learn the rudiments and first rules of some science before we ascend to a fuller knowledge of it. Yet these rudiments are not to be built on any other principle than the whole framework of the building is built on its foundations. So it is here too: although the analogy of faith, to be held as the norm in what follows, must first be known, it is nevertheless not to be sought from anywhere except Scripture itself. Since Scripture sets it out so clearly, it cannot fail to become known to the godly reader and searcher from Scripture itself. It thus becomes plain that every rule and norm of interpreting is Scripture, which was to be demonstrated. The fourth argument, taken from Polanus and Alsted, is of no greater worth in the eyes of our critic. The fourth, he argues, is that God wishes his voice to be heard. No voice can be clearer or more manifest. I would hear it, were it not asked about the voice of God itself, how we perceive its clarity and in what this clarity lies. The Reformed suppose that Scripture is a lamp, a light, indeed a shining light, and that, like the sun, it is seen most clearly by its own light. Our man replies that it is asked about the voice of God itself, how we perceive its clarity and in what its clarity lies. This is as if someone, insisting that the sun must be seen by its own light, were answered: but is it asked how the clearness of the sun is perceived? Who would deign to answer a man talking such foolish nonsense? The argument presupposes that clarity and intelligibility of Scripture which the Reformed doctors earlier proved from passages whose sense cannot be doubted. Given that intelligibility and clarity, it follows no less that Scripture must be explained by Scripture than that the sun is seen by the light of the sun. So this Walloon pastor happily attacks the camp of God and the Reformed front-line men. But as his spirit swells in the fight, he hands over the rest of our forces to his trainer to be led in triumph. He is going to deny the victory won against the Reformed, as much to that most wretched busybody as to Velthuysen, and to deny the testimony of orthodoxy; this pastor, so well Reformed in name, does so. Let us hear him dividing the spoils. I think the fifth, sixth and seventh arguments should not be dealt with by the examiner. The fifth runs thus: because Scripture itself can make a man wise unto salvation (2 Tim. 3:15, etc.). But what does the Paradoxus say to this? He denies the consequence. For, says this excellent braggart, we are not so sharp-eyed that we can see what follows: the Holy Scripture, once understood, can make a man wise unto salvation; therefore it is its own interpreter. And by this answer, in Wolzogen's judgement, our argument has been made feeble. I, however, think these two men are not only not lynx-eyed but blinder than moles, to imagine that, with a sure hope of victory, they have gone down into the arena against the greatest men. Who reasons like this: Scripture, understood, has the faculty and fitness by which one arrives at saving wisdom? No Reformed man has been so foolish: understood Scripture is not a means to wisdom but saving wisdom itself. Since Scripture therefore has in its own kind a faculty and fitness for making men wise and teaching wisdom, it must also be sufficient for its own interpretation. Otherwise it would not be a sufficient means to wisdom, which is contrary to the Apostle. This is how the Reformed argue, and Wolzogen has attacked this argument in vain, with his forces joined to the Paradoxus. The sixth and seventh could be defended with equal ease, but it is not worth the trouble, since our disputant adds nothing except a reheated scrap of the most stinking Paradoxus. The eighth argument he thinks he at least touches in some degree; the shades of the great Polanus owe him much, as he is welcomed with more favour than the rest. Polanus did not indeed prove all that the Reformed want, but he taught, concerning the particular interpretation of certain passages, that Scripture has shown its own method of interpretation. But, good man, if Scripture is anywhere to be explained by its own method, why should it not be considered to explain itself by the same method everywhere? This is especially so since you must admit that Scripture is full of examples [αὐτοσαφήνεια, self-clarity] by which it is proved that it is to be explained through itself. The Reformed mean this, and by this and their other arguments; why then, Wolzogen, your cavilling and prevarication? Because Scripture is full of such examples, they conclude the same about the rest. The ninth argument, although Altingius, Withaker, Walaeus, indeed all the Reformed theologians use it, lacks all foundation, as Wolzogen thinks: that God is the interpreter of his own Scripture, because no one can be a better one, since each man is the best interpreter of his own words. I do not see on what foundation this rests. We deny that God can properly be called the interpreter of the Scriptures. Here is the bold writer openly declaring war on the whole Reformed Church. Hear your teacher, disciple, in this matter, who is far too degenerate. He rebuked in Tirinus the very thing you have blurted out here. Tirinus had said that Scripture itself is not its own interpreter. The most distinguished man replies to this, and at the same time to you, as he does to the Jesuits: Indeed Scripture must be interpreted through Scripture. Nothing is more certain than Scripture, which can be understood from Scripture, just as the sun is not more certainly known than through the sun. What insolence of these men, I ask, who flee the judgement of Scripture because the matter concerns Scripture! Whoever denies that it is its own interpreter, says Chamier, is out of his mind. For it is most truly said, in the words of Paraeus, that there is no better interpreter of the divine Scriptures than the Scriptures themselves. This cannot be denied except by those unskilled in the Scriptures, whose judgement on so great a matter it is not fitting to hear. But although it is true that each man is the best interpreter of his own words, he does not see what follows from this, that God is the interpreter of his own words. That is, he does not see the species under the genus. Yet this argument ought to have seemed the stronger to Wolzogen, the more he has taught that God gave his word in a human manner. For it cannot be denied that other authors explain themselves very well. But Scripture, since it itself indicates this about itself and proves it by many examples, does so the more; Wolzogen concedes this in various places. For Scripture is full of examples by which it is proved that it is to be explained through itself, which in truth amounts to the same thing as if he confessed what he here denies, namely that God can properly be called the interpreter of the Scriptures. That is, God has so tempered that sacred monument by which he speaks with us, that the things that seem said ambiguously and obscurely in certain passages of Holy Scripture are explained by those things that are open and clear in other places, as we heard earlier from Basil. Beyond this the Reformed ask for nothing and conclude nothing. But Wolzogen presses on and says: from this it can equally be concluded that God ought to pronounce on the senses of Scripture by some oracle. But by what reasoning could a man who is heard as a pastor among the Reformed have put into his head such perversity, and not blushed to burden their common cause with so base, so shameful and disgraceful an inference? He draws from this general axiom that God is the best interpreter of his own words; it pleased him to instruct us about his will and the true sense of his word not by fictitious oracles but by the firm speech of the Prophets and Apostles. So although he could have done otherwise, he did not wish, nor was it necessary, that what suffices for us in himself and is sufficient in itself should be done by extraordinary oracles. We hold this sneer, together with the other mockeries of the Papists and Socinians, as nothing. God could have explained the meaning of his sayings by a living oracle, or by the Urim and Thummim, but he willed that the word be understood through the word, and Scripture through Scripture, so that in truth it can make us wise unto salvation. What more need be said? Our author uncovers the source of all bad argument. Indeed it could not have happened otherwise than that all these theologians should persist in a weak and faulty method of arguing: for arguments, so says our great theologian, cannot be drawn from the thing itself, because the question is not yet sufficiently clearly perceived. O lamentable ignorance of the Reformed until now! Their chief men have not produced strong arguments, nor could they, since the question is not yet sufficiently clearly perceived. I am certain that no theologian who has treated this subject professionally has been read by Wolzogen, neither Chamier, nor Withaker, nor Hoornbeek, the last of whom laboured so perfectly over this business that the single chapter, the seventh of the first book of his Socinianism Confuted (vol. 1), is enough to refute the Paradoxus with all the Socinians, and Wolzogen with his Velthuysen, abundantly. I dare at least to assert this: none of those whom I could produce by the six hundred would fail to leave Wolzogen behind by many leagues, whether in the solid and clear handling of this question.

units.la: §. Quintum notandum erit, quod communi Reformatorum sententiæ in terminis se opponat, eamque argumentis petat, caute subinde prospiciens, ne cum ipsis sentire, vel ulla ratione videatur. Negamus, inquit, Deum dici posse proprie Scriptura interpretem. Deum esse interpretem suæ Scripturæ non video. Satis confectum esse puto, non fuisse huc illud adducendum, quisque suorum verborum optimus interpres. Quod axioma tamen omnes Reformatorum Theologi hactenus pro fundamento posuerunt, & summo jure. Wolzogius è contra, ac si nesciret, quid Reformati sentiant, aut publice ipsis dicam scribere & bellum movere vellet, ad Enthusiastarum familiam pertinere asserit, qui sic loquuntur: hoc statuit omnis Enthusiastarum familia, illi demum hoc axiomate nituntur, quilibet suorum verbo-rum optimus interpres. En omnes Reformatorum Theologos, uno jactu, in Enthusiastarum castra translatos à Wolzogio. Quin prudenter cavet, ne putetur cum iisdem idem sentire: sic pag.206. nec quia facimus interpretationis judicem usum, ideo Deum facimus interpretem. Ac si grande nefas patraret, si Deum statueret Scripturæ interpretem. Quod tamē accuratissimè & verissimè dici, jam antea audivimus.
units.tr: §. Fifthly, it must be noted that he sets himself directly against the common view of the Reformed and seeks his arguments against it, taking care now and then not to seem to agree with them in any way. "We deny," he says, "that God can properly be called the interpreter of Scripture. I do not see that God is the interpreter of his own Scripture. I think it is sufficiently established that this should not have been brought in here: each man is the best interpreter of his own words." Yet all the Reformed theologians have hitherto laid this axiom down as a foundation, and with the fullest right. Wolzogius, on the other hand, as if he did not know what the Reformed hold, or as if he wished to attack them openly, asserts that it belongs to the family of the Enthusiasts, who speak thus: "Every family of Enthusiasts holds this, and they rely on this axiom alone: each man is the best interpreter of his own words." See how, at one stroke, Wolzogius has transferred all the Reformed theologians into the camp of the Enthusiasts! Indeed he takes care, with some prudence, that he is not thought to agree with them: "So on page 206: nor because we use a judge of interpretation do we therefore make God the interpreter." As if he committed a great crime by holding that God is the interpreter of Scripture! Yet we have already heard that this can be said most accurately and most truly.

units.la: Ex supra dictis, satis superque patet, nihil minus quam fidelem & solidam receptæ fidei defensionem, ut & Paradoxi hominis seriam refutationem, à Wolzogio sperandam esse.
units.tr: From what has been said above, it is plain enough and more than enough that nothing less than a faithful and solid defence of the received faith, or a serious refutation of the Paradoxus man's paradox, is to be hoped for from Wolzogius.

units.la: 6. Quare etiam quod sexto loco considerandum venit, adversarium suum stramineis plane, & ficul- neis argumentis, aut plane nullis aggressus est. Præcipuum, quo eum quodammodo stringit, enu-merationem continet eorum, quæ ad veritates, sic vocat, referri ac proinde ad rationis trutinam exigi nequeunt: ut & eorum, quæ licet ad veritates per-tineant, rationem tamen superantes, itidem illius respuant arbitrium. Quæ omnia, etiam sensu Wolzogiano, ultro concedet Paradoxus, nec tamen concedet id quod concludit Wolzogen. Per veritates intelligit Wolzogen axiomata & dictata quædam, ut ita loquar, universalia, factis contradistincta ge-stisque: At facile concedet illo sensu, omnes scri-pturæ sermones, veritates non continere; neque enim tam stultus est, ut omnia quæ longa serie enu-merantur Wolzogio, Historias, Prophetias, Præcepta positiva, Cæremonias, promissa &c. ad talis ge-neris veritates referenda doceat. Hoc vult; omnes veritates, sive axiomaticam habeant, sive historicam veritatem, modo ex textu deriva-ri queant, esse veros sensus; & vice versa, omnes ve-ros sensus, continere veritates, hoc est enuncia-tionem, cujus subjectum verè jungitur cum prædi-cato, aut prædicatum cum subjecto, sive nexus ille sit naturalis, ut in axiomatis generalibus, sive casuaiis[?] seu arbitrarius, ut in historicis & similibus. Ee[?] Wolzogen aliquot paginis solum probat, multa Scripturam continere, quae ad veritates prioris generis, quas unice veritatum nomine designat, referri non possunt, quod Paradoxus nullo modo negabit. Sumamus res gestas Mosis, Christi vitam, Apostolorum actus, putat Wolzogius tam insanum suum Paradoxum esse, ut ea omnia inter talis generis veritates recensenda judicaverit? Nihil certè minus.
units.tr: 6. Hence also what must be considered in the sixth place: he has attacked his opponent with flimsy and frivolous arguments, or with none at all. The chief point with which he somehow presses him is a list of those things which, as he calls them, are referred to truths and therefore cannot be brought to the scales of reason; and also of those things which, though they pertain to truths, nevertheless exceed reason, and which he likewise rejects from the judgment of reason. The Paradoxus man will readily concede all of these, even in Wolzogius's sense, but he will not concede what Wolzogius concludes from them. By truths Wolzogius understands certain axioms and dictates, so to speak, universal, set in contrast to facts and deeds. But the Paradoxus man will easily concede, in that sense, that not all the sayings of Scripture contain truths; for he is not so foolish as to teach that all the things Wolzogius enumerates at length (histories, prophecies, positive precepts, ceremonies, promises, etc.) are to be referred to truths of that kind. His meaning is this: all truths, whether they have an axiomatic or a historical truth, provided they can be derived from the text, are true senses; and conversely, all true senses contain truths, that is, a statement whose subject is truly joined with its predicate, or its predicate with its subject, whether that connection is natural, as in general axioms, or contingent and arbitrary, as in historical and similar statements. Wolzogius, in a few pages, merely proves that Scripture contains many things which cannot be referred to truths of the former kind, which alone he designates by the name of truths; and the Paradoxus man will by no means deny this. Let us take the deeds of Moses, the life of Christ, the acts of the Apostles: does Wolzogius think his Paradoxus so mad that he has judged all these to be counted among truths of this kind? Nothing could be less so.

units.la: Attamen veritates vocat & jure merito Paradoxus, quamvis non ejusdem sint naturae, cum istis, quas axiomaticas vocavimus. Eodem successu, se-cundum illud strenuè contendit Wolzogius, nimi-rum multas veritates esse quae respuant rationis arbitrium; easque esse quae inveniri ratione non pof-sint. Hoc priori libro & nunc iterum pluribus urget noster, sed absque omni necessitate, quoniam non negat hoc Paradoxus, aut ullus Socinianus. Licet enim nihil admitteret, nisi quae symbolo, quod Apo-stolorum vocant, comprehenduntur, plura tamen statim admitteret, de quibus lubens fateretur, quod hic tanto labore ipsi extorquendum putat Wolzogius, dicendo multa in Scripturis esse quae inveniri ratione non possint; non Christi adventus, non ex virgine ortus ejus, non opera & quae illius generis multa enumerari possent. Circa quae, rationi suae nihil praeterea vindicabit Paradoxus aut Socinianorum ullus, quam[?] quod ultro ei tribuit Wolzogius, ea rationem attingere eo usque, ut non esse contra ra-tionem deprehendat. Sic Sociniani. Nos vero ultrò fa-temur plurima esse in religione Christiana, quae ratio-nem superent, & tamen nobis necessariò sint credenda, ob id ipsum, quia, quantumvis rationem superent, tamen in sacris literis prodita exstent, & rationi nostrae, quam superant, sint maximè consentanea. Potest enim aliquid rationem superare, & tamen ei applaudere. Quabia[?] fere sunt omnia, quae in religione, praesertim Christiana, continentur. Haec si novisses, aut considerasses Wolzogi, magno labore te levare potuisses: quid enim probare attinet, quod ambabus ulnis ad-versarii amplectuntur, imo sponte sua ultro prosi-tentur ? Aliud esse supra , aliud contra rationem esse, noverat olim , idem Smalcius , nec te egebant ma-gistro hac in re , eadem tecum loquentes . Atque hæc ad rationis utriusque, quam protulisti, mino-rem pertinent,quam concedunt Socinian cum Pa-radoxo : ad veritates scilicet axiomaticas omnes veros sensus referendos non esse, ut & inter eas dari quæ inveniri ratione non possunt ; quare de ista mi-nore probe inter vos convenit , caduntque omnia, inutilia saltem evadunt , quæ totis sex aut septem paginis , utrimque concessa probando , scripsisti. Absque omni candore hæsce theses oppugnandas ti-bi propositueras p. 143 . omnia quæ traduntur in Scri-pturis ad veritates,scilicet tales , referri posse : & o-mnes veritates quas tradit Scriptura , ratione cognosci posse , id est excogitari. Quas tamen eo sensu , quo eas oppugnas, Paradoxus tuus minimè agnoscet: sed longe alio, uti jam notavimus. Videamus quid ad majorem dicere queant , non contemnendi ad-versarii , Socinianivel Paradoxus. Major ista erit, si in formam redigantur solidissimæ istæ , magnoq; verborum ambitu elaboratæ , probationes , quic-quid non est veritas,ejus Philosophia aut ratio nor-ma esse non potest;negabunt una voce omnes istam majorem. Quamvis enim sensus ille,quem conti-nent verba , ex. gr. quæ historiam Dominicæ pas-sionis complectuntur , non possit referri ad verita-tes illas axiomaticas,quarum subjectum& prædica-tum Wolzogius æterno nexu conjunctum diceret, verus tamen esse debet , saltem ut in eas non incur-rat , sicque ratio semper suum hic exercebit judici-um ; an nimirum ista narratio , quæ alias hoc aut illud significaret, si in isto ponatur significatu, nihil veritati æternæ , quin & iis veritatibus , quas ratio jam antea ex Scripturâ aut sese elicuisse censenda est,contrarium complectatur. Hoc regerent Soci-niani,cui tantum abest, ut quicquam respondere valeas,ut hic, confecto prælio, in iisdem castris con-corditer commoremini. Tu enim rationi circa ea, quæ ad veritates referenda negas, tantum largiris, quantum petunt Sociniani, nimirum quatenus nil continere debent quod cognitæ nobis veritati repugnet; aut quod se ipsum evertat. Imo non inficiari te dicis, quasdam in Scriptura Historias narrari, quæ sic pendent à veritate rerum, ut inde NB. omnem accipere lucem interpretatione possint. Idem plane, secundi argumenti tui, majori propositioni eveniet, negabunt, veritate supra rationem posita, eo ipso illam rationis arbitrio exemtam esse. Quin, nec ipse hoc serio & absolute verum esse credis, ut ex sequuturo, sententiæ tuæ ad theses redactæ, examine patebit. Tandem quid ista tua argumenta, magnopere adversarium tangunt? nondum enim constat; an dentur in sacris talia, an, quæ supra rationem, an, quæ ad veritates redigi non possint: si enim, quod tu Reformatis ex Scriptura argumentantibus regeris, velle proferre Scripturam, ubi de interprete Scripturæ quæstio agitatur, sit, si quicquam, præposterè agere; tu certè plus quam præposterè agis, qui non Scripturam solum, dum de Interprete disputas, sed vel explicatam eam citas, eaque in medium profers, quæ nisi jam de Interprete constet prius, ne quidem cogitari possunt. Reformati ea loca proferunt, quæ de Interpretationis modo & norma agunt, sed tuo judicio præposterè, de Interprete enim quæstio agitatur: tu autem non loca quædam de Interprete, sed veritates, Mysteria, aliaque magno numero, de quibus nisi post Interpretem descriptum, imo munere suo plane defunctum, nihil sciri potest, profers, & pro fundamento sternis. Quid si adversarius tibi tandem oggerat, se nondum novisse, istam, rerum in Scriptura contentarum, varietatem & differentiam, veritates & non veritates, mysteria & non mysteria, rationem superantia & non superantia? quid tandem habes quod regeras? En primariam libelli tui partem, quæque fere totum est quod adversarium propius tetigisse credi posset, subversam facili negotio. Et tute tibi tantum sumis animi, ut omnia Reformatorum argumenta rejicias, spernas, rideas? qui ne unicum quidem, cunctis viribus, quod soliditatem unius, quae magno numero habent Reformati, exaequet, excogitari potuisti? Omittendum etiam non est, quod nimia συνκαταβα-σις te huc abegerit. Notaveras p. 142. μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος ab adversario committi, eo quod ab in-terpretatione, ad rem quam debemus interpretari; (debueras dicere quam, interpretatione media, co-gnoscere & eruere debemus, res enim sub interpre-tationem proprie non cadunt, sed verba & phrases rem ipsam continentes, nobisque eam offerentes, eaedemum interpretandae veniunt, hac, de qua scribi-mus, interpretatione, quae realis dicitur, non quod res ipsas enodandas sumat aut explicandas, sed eas eruat erutasque ulteriori ruminationi tradat.) fit transitus, cumque hactenus quaesitum sit, an res aliqua sit dicta, jam quaeritur, an vera sit (possit esse diceret Paradoxus & nihil ultra) res illa, ut concludi possit an dicta sit. Bene hoc notasti, sed hic cursum sistere debueras, non ulterius de rebus rerumque diversita-te disputare. Hoc enim non rite observatum, & Paradoxum & te multosque alios seduxit, nimirum quod in negotio Interpretationis nihil ultra quae-ratur, quam, quid ex textus circumstantiis aut para-lellissimo, aut analogia fidei, hoc loco Deus dicere voluisse censendus est, nihil praeterea quodque id totum absolvit interpretis officium. Res autem, sic erutae, cujuscunque sint generis aut naturae, non ra-tionis arbitrio examinandae & decidendae, sed fide amplectendae veniunt, ac firmiter retinendae. Ut frustra sic rerum fingas figasque discrimina & ordi-nes, hoc loco nullius momenti, omnia enim, capti-vata ratione eaque normali usu orbata, fidei com-mittenda sunt, & admittenda, quae tali interpreta-tione media, eruta fuerunt & elicita. Et hinc ar-cessendum puto, quidquid à Socinianis aliisque, hac in re erratum est. Post erutam rem credendam, quo obloquentibus eatur obviam, illud quidem licet, ut quantum possumus, veritatem istam Scripturæ, nihil sanæ rationi adversum continere: sed interpretatione peracta, res contentas dispescere, de variis, varias rationis regulas, interpretaturo præfigere, non ex ipsa scriptura ortas, hoc est, quod displicet orthodoxis. Conciliatur ratio cum Scriptura, ut ratio dicit sententiam & dictatum rationis; non vero examinatur, vel componitur Scriptura ad rationem. Atque idcirco non sic debet intelligi, rationi consentanea esse omnia religionis capita, quasi ex ratione judicanda, vel ipsa cum ratione concilianda, ut cum ea in gratiam redeant: Scripturæ parum refert, an appareat rationis cum ea consonantia; plus rationis interest, hoc ut constet & sibi demonstretur.
units.tr: Yet Paradoxus also calls them truths, and rightly so, although they are not of the same nature as those we have called axiomatic. With equal success Wolzogen vigorously contends that there are many truths which reject the judgement of reason, and that there are some which cannot be discovered by reason. Our author urges this in the earlier book and again now at greater length, but without any need, since Paradoxus, or any Socinian, does not deny it. For although they would admit nothing except what is comprehended in the creed called the Apostles', they would at once admit more, and about these they would gladly confess what Wolzogen thinks must be wrung from them here with such labour: that many things in the Scriptures are such that they cannot be discovered by reason. The coming of Christ, his birth from a virgin, his works, and many things of that kind could be listed. Regarding these, Paradoxus or any of the Socinians will claim nothing more for their reason than what Wolzogen freely grants them, that these things reach so far as reason that it finds they are not contrary to reason. So the Socinians. We, however, frankly confess that there are very many things in the Christian religion which surpass reason, and yet must necessarily be believed by us, for this very reason: that, however much they surpass reason, they nevertheless stand set forth in the sacred letters and are most consonant with the reason they surpass. For something can surpass reason and yet applaud it. Such are nearly all the things contained in religion, especially the Christian. If you had known or considered this, Wolzogen, you could have spared yourself great labour. For what is the point of proving what our opponents embrace with both arms, indeed freely profess of their own accord? That something is above reason and something else is against reason, Smalcius too once knew, nor did they need a teacher in this matter, since they speak the same as you. These points concern the minor premise of the two rational propositions you have put forward, which the Socinians together with Paradoxus concede: namely that not all true senses are to be referred to axiomatic truths, and that among them there are some which cannot be discovered by reason. So on that minor premise you and they agree well, and all that you wrote over six or seven pages, proving things conceded on both sides, is useless or at least of no effect. Without any candour you had set yourself to attack these theses on p. 143: that everything that is delivered in the Scriptures can be referred to such truths, and that all the truths which Scripture delivers can be known by reason, that is, thought out. Yet in the sense in which you attack them, your Paradoxus will by no means accept them, but in quite a different sense, as we have already noted. Let us see what the major premise can say, not a contemptible opponent, Socinian or Paradoxus. This will be the major premise if those most solid propositions, elaborated with a great show of words, are reduced to form: whatever is not truth cannot be the philosophy or norm of reason. All of them will deny this major premise with one voice. For although the sense which the words contain, for example those that narrate the history of the Lord's passion, cannot be referred to those axiomatic truths whose subject and predicate, you would say, are joined by an eternal bond, yet it must be true, at least so as not to fall into them. So reason will always exercise its judgement here: whether that narrative, which otherwise might signify this or that, if it is put in that sense, contains nothing contrary to eternal truth, indeed nothing contrary to those truths which reason is judged already to have elicited from Scripture or from itself. The Socinians would reply to this, and you are so far from being able to answer anything that, once the battle is over, you dwell harmoniously in the same camp. For you concede to reason, regarding those things which you deny should be referred to truths, just as much as the Socinians ask, namely insofar as they ought to contain nothing that conflicts with a truth known to us, or that overthrows itself. Indeed you say you do not deny that some histories are narrated in Scripture which so depend on the truth of the facts that from them (NB.) they can receive all their light by interpretation. The same thing will plainly happen to the major premise of your second argument: they will deny that, once truth is placed above reason, it is by that very fact exempt from the judgement of reason. Indeed you do not even believe this to be true seriously and absolutely, as will be clear from an examination of your opinion reduced to theses in what follows. Finally, how do your arguments greatly touch the opponent? For it is not yet settled whether such things are in the sacred books, whether there are things above reason, whether there are things which cannot be reduced to truths. For if, as you retort to the Reformed who argue from Scripture, to wish to bring forward Scripture where the question concerns the interpreter of Scripture is, if anything, to act back to front, then you certainly act more than back to front, you who not only bring forward Scripture while disputing about the Interpreter, but cite it already explained, and produce things which, unless it is first settled who the Interpreter is, cannot even be thought of. The Reformed bring forward those passages which deal with the manner and norm of interpretation, but in your judgement they act back to front, since the question concerns the Interpreter. You, however, bring forward not certain passages about the Interpreter but truths, mysteries, and many other things, of which nothing can be known unless the Interpreter has first been described, indeed has fully discharged his office, and you lay them down as foundation. What if the adversary at last throws back at you that he does not yet know this variety and difference of things contained in Scripture: truths and non-truths, mysteries and non-mysteries, things surpassing reason and not surpassing it? What then have you to retort? Behold the principal part of your little book, which is almost the whole that could be thought to have touched the adversary more nearly, overturned with ease. And do you take so much courage as to reject, despise, and laugh at all the arguments of the Reformed? Could you, with all your powers, think up not even one that equals the solidity of any one of the many that the Reformed have? Nor must it be omitted that excessive συγκατάβασις has driven you here. You had noted on p. 142 that the adversary commits a shift into another genus [μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος], because it passes from interpretation to the thing which we ought to interpret. (You should have said the thing which we must know and bring out by means of interpretation, for things do not properly fall under interpretation; it is the words and phrases containing the thing and offering it to us that are to be interpreted, by that interpretation which is called real, not because it takes up the things themselves to unfold or explain them, but because it brings them out and hands them over, once brought out, to further rumination.) A transition is made, and since hitherto it has been asked whether some thing has been said, now it is asked whether that thing is true (Paradoxus could say it is possible, and nothing more) so that it may be concluded whether it has been said. You noted this well, but here you ought to have stopped, not gone on to dispute about things and the diversity of things. For this, not properly observed, has led Paradoxus, you, and many others astray: namely that in the business of interpretation nothing further is sought than what God is deemed to have wished to say in this place, from the circumstances of the text, or from the parallel passage, or from the analogy of faith, and nothing beyond; and that this completes the whole duty of the interpreter. But the things thus brought out, of whatever kind or nature, do not come up to be examined and decided by the judgement of reason, but to be embraced by faith and firmly held. So it is vain for you to feign and fix distinctions and orders of things, which are of no moment here. For all things, taken captive by reason and deprived of its normal use, must be committed to faith and admitted, whatever has been brought out and elicited by such interpretation. And from this, I think, is to be derived whatever the Socinians and others have got wrong in this matter. After the thing to be believed has been brought out, in order to meet objectors, it is indeed permitted, as far as we can, to hold that this truth of Scripture contains nothing contrary to sound reason. But once interpretation is complete, to distinguish the contents of things, and to set in advance for the interpreter various rules of reason for various things, not arising from Scripture itself, that is what displeases the orthodox. Reason is reconciled with Scripture in the sense that reason states its opinion and dictate; but Scripture is not examined, nor is it composed to suit reason. And for that reason it should not be understood thus, that all the heads of religion are consonant with reason, as if they were to be judged by reason, or to be reconciled with reason itself, so as to return into its favour. It matters little to Scripture whether there appears a consonance with reason; it matters more to reason that this be established and demonstrated to itself.

units.la: Atque id valet in omnibus, sive sint res facti, sive veritates, sive mysteria, sive non mysteria, cuncta enim hic, authoritate dicentis recipiuntur unicè. At de hisce paulo inferius. Sic vidimus argumenta Wolzogii debilia esse & ex turpi seductione ac errore orta, ut mihi quod ille in omnes Reformatos crimen conjicit, ipsi impingere liceat merito, confusissimâ enim obscuritate ista Wolzogiana involvuntur, argumenta autem maximè, quæ, quia ipsa non est satis explorate percepta quæstio, non possunt ex re ipsa esse petita, quæque ideo mihi improbandi necessitatem, vel laborem explicandi, necessariam alteram, alteram impossibilem imponunt. Statim ac, ante interpretationem, alicui normæ, præter ipsam Scripturam, locum dederat, non poterat non infelicissimo successu & in densa ignorantiæ caligine decertare. Quapropter frustra est, quod subinde de consensu, in rei summa, cum Reformatis, glorietur, ut cum ad finem libri prioris sic loquitur, Id jam conclusionis loco monuisse sufficiat, huc omnia tendere quæ sunt hactenus disputata, Scripturam per Spiritum efficacem esse interpretem Scripturæ. Sic sæpius idem inculcat, se reipsa cum Reformatis, quod ad rei summam convenire. At, Qui illa protestatio cum supra dictis conciliabitur? etenim singularem profitetur sententiam, loquendi modos & argumenta Reformatorum refutat, in terminis eorum sententiam rejicit & culpat. 2. Si vero res ipsa consideretur, invidiæ evitandæ causa, hæc subinda addita, perspicuum evadet, revera enim nihil minus quam Reformatorum tenet sententiam, dicit quidem, Scripturam se statuere per Spiritum efficacem Interpretem Scripturæ: verum ita ista verba explicat, ut nihil minus, quam Reformatorum sententiam complectantur, ubinam enim illi, quando Scripturam sui interpretem dicunt, per modum normæ infallibilis, ubinam inquam illi, eo, usum loquendi & rationem intelligunt? usum loquendi supponentes & rationi, omnem, in isto genere, usum denegantes apertissimè. Usus loquendi supponitur, absque eo enim Scriptura Scripturæ nomen non mereretur, præsertim divinæ; eoque posito, quæritur quidnam id sit, quod me, per modum objecti, doceat, convincat, persuadeat, verborum verum in ista congerie sensum, & dicunt solam Scripturam esse, hoc est, aut eundem illum locum, de quo quæritur, seu insita sua claritate, seu in circumstantiis, aut loca parallella &c. Neutiquam vero ratio hic usu venit, instrumenti vices fungitur in omnibus, & subjecti recipientis, normæ autem de qua hic disputatur, nullibi, nisi apud Socinianos & Paradoxum. Æque præposterum est, hic Spiritum ponere, is enim per modum objecti agens non consideratur unquam à Reformatis: Adeo ut Scripturæ Scripturam interpretem cum dicit & usum rationem ac Spiritum intelligit, toto cœlo aberrat, vel ab ipsa, ut ita loquar, substantia Doctrinæ Reformatorum; in eo Socinianis gratificans non parum, quod rationem ut normam, in Scripturæ Interpretatione admittat, quod totum illud est, de quo, Reformatis cum Socinianis, controversia intercedit. Sic solent consensum prætendere, qui vel maximè dissentiunt, donec ère sua esse iudicaverint dissensum palam profiteri; nihil æquè Remonstrantibus in ore erat, quam, se invariatam docere Reformatorum doctrinam, funditus eam interea in controversis quæstionibus subvertere omni conatu allaborantes. Hæc artificia hodie in memoriam revocanda & detegenda incumbunt iis, quibus veritas cordi est. Atque ista ad tractandi modum quem observat & animum quem erga Reformatorum sententiam gerit, dicta sufficient hactenus. Sciat autem lector nos non ulterius de utroque iudicium depromplisse, quam ex hoc tractatu de iis sententia ferri potest.
units.tr: This holds for all matters, whether they are matters of fact, truths, mysteries or non-mysteries, for here everything is received solely on the authority of the one speaking. But more on these things a little further on. Thus we have seen that Wolzogen's arguments are weak and arise from a shameful deception and error, so that I may fairly throw back at him the charge he brings against all the Reformed: for these Wolzogian positions are wrapped in the most confused obscurity, and his arguments especially, since the question has not been sufficiently clearly grasped in itself, cannot be drawn from the matter itself, and so impose on me either the necessity of refuting them or the labour of explaining them, the one necessary, the other impossible. As soon as, before interpretation, he gave some norm a place alongside Scripture itself, he could not help contending with most unhappy success and in the thick darkness of ignorance. So it is in vain that he so often boasts of agreement with the Reformed on the main point, as when at the end of the first book he speaks thus: It will suffice, by way of conclusion, to have pointed out that all that has been disputed so far tends to this: that Scripture is its own interpreter through the effective Spirit. Likewise he often insists that in reality he agrees with the Reformed on the substance of the matter. But how will that profession be reconciled with what was said above? For he professes a singular opinion, refutes the modes of speaking and the arguments of the Reformed, and rejects and blames their opinion in express terms. 2. But if the matter itself is considered, these statements, added here and there to avoid odium, will clearly show that he holds nothing less than the opinion of the Reformed. He does indeed say that he holds that Scripture is through the effective Spirit the interpreter of Scripture; but he so explains those words that they embrace nothing less than the opinion of the Reformed. For where do the Reformed, when they call Scripture its own interpreter, understand this by way of an infallible norm, and where, I ask, do they understand it of usage of language and of reason? They presuppose usage of language and most openly deny to reason any place of this kind. Usage of language is presupposed, for without it Scripture would not deserve the name of Scripture, especially of divine Scripture; and granting that, the question is what it is that teaches me, convinces me and persuades me, by way of object, of the true sense of the words in that mass. They say it is Scripture alone, that is, either that same passage about which the question is, by its inherent clarity or by its circumstances, or parallel passages, and so on. But reason by no means comes into play here; it serves as an instrument in everything, and as the receiving subject, whereas the norm under dispute here is found nowhere except among the Socinians and the Paradox. Equally absurd is it to posit the Spirit here, for the Reformed never consider the Spirit as acting by way of object. So when he says that Scripture is its own interpreter, and understands by this usage, reason and the Spirit, he is utterly wide of the mark, or of the very substance, so to speak, of the Reformed doctrine. In this he gratifies the Socinians not a little, in admitting reason as a norm in the interpretation of Scripture, and that is the whole point on which the controversy between the Reformed and the Socinians turns. Those who disagree most profoundly are wont to pretend agreement, until they judge the time right to profess their dissent openly; nothing was more often on the lips of the Remonstrants than that they taught the unchanged doctrine of the Reformed, while all the while they laboured by every effort to overturn it utterly on the disputed questions. It now falls to those to whom truth is dear to recall these tricks to mind and to expose them. Let these remarks suffice so far on the manner of treatment he follows and the attitude he bears towards the opinion of the Reformed. Let the reader know, however, that we have pronounced no judgement on either beyond what can be passed on them from this treatise.

units.la: Restat igitur ut aliquot thesibus ipsius sensa complectar, eaque paucis excutiam, agam autem candide & fideliter.
units.tr: It remains, therefore, that I take in hand his views under some theses, examine them briefly, and do so fairly and faithfully.

units.la: Prima thesis hæc erit, Controversiam de Interprete Scripturarum non ex Scriptura, sed ex ratione decidendam.Ubi de ipsa interpretatione quæstio est, nullo modo audiendam esse Scripturam puto.Sola ratio audiri hic debet, quæ, positis quibusdam principiis quæ- stionem omnem decidat oportet: Verum ubi de interprete Scripturæ quæstio agitatur, velle proferre Scripturam, id mihi videtur, si quicquam, præposterè fieri. De quibus ista dicenda habeo.
units.tr: The first thesis will be this: the controversy concerning the Interpreter of Scripture is to be decided not from Scripture but from reason. Where the question is about the interpretation itself, I think Scripture should in no way be heard. Only reason should be heard here, which, once certain principles have been laid down, ought to settle the whole question. But where the question concerns the interpreter of Scripture, to want to bring forward Scripture seems to me, if anything, to be done back to front. On these points I have the following to say.

units.la: Hanc thesin e diametro adversari communi ac universali Reformatorum sententiæ, qui ad unum omnes, de Scripturæ Interpretatione, ex ipsa Scriptura disputandum esse asserunt: ut vel ex illis, quæ Wolzogio hic in Paradoxo suo obversabantur, videre est. Scio aliud esse, hunc aut illum locum, posita nunc interpretandi certa regula & norma, ad istam regulam exigere, sicque verum ejus sensum ex eo elicere: aliud autem, normam illam & regulam quærere, quæ nobis, postea Scripturam interpretaturis amussis sit. Utrique illi determinando per se sufficere Scripturam Reformatorum statuunt Theologi & confessiones. Jam vero & posteriori id demonstrandum venit. Longa ratiocinatione hic non eget quæstionis indoles, quæ facti est, & ex ipso Paradoxo determinari omnis potest, qui eam, ut Reformatorum sensu sic determinatam tractat; non quod istius Ardelionis authoritatem vel tanti faciam, sed quod luculentissima ex Reformatorum Coryphæis desumta testimonia suppeditet, quæ id uberrimè doceant. Cap.xiii. Chamierum,Withake-rum,Polanum,Zanchium,Bezam, Altingium,Walæum ex Scriptura ea de re disputantes, imo totum negotium terminantes, infert. Cap. xii. Loca Scripturæ,ex Reformatorum sententia, totum quod in quæstione est, claré decidentia produxerat, additis absurdis & propriam hypothesin,ipsa praxi,subver-tentibus exceptionibus & cavillationibus. Illas probandi rationes, hoc loco, vindicare debuisset Wolzogius,ut vindicari facile possunt: at nihil minus agit, partes nostras deserit, omnesque istas, sub victrice manu,turpissimi & & absurdissimi adversa-rii, indefensas relinquit nostrorum selectas copias. Imo inimico tergum obvertens, aperte in nostros irruit, dicitque Scripturam, quam nostri audiunt, qua & felicissimè pugnant vincuntque hactenus hic tudiendam non esse, nec proferri debere, nec prola-tam refutari ab iis qui nondum de Interprete con-venerunt; jacto in omnium Reformatorum faciem hoc probro, Scripturam hic proferre velle, quam omnes proferunt, id sibi, præ cunctis altiora sapienti,videri, si quicquam, præposterè fieri. Si quisquam igitur præposterè Scriptura usus est, Reformati sunt ,eorumque Theologi ad unum omnes. O censuram ter quater absurdam,præposteram! & hic liber, pro Reformatorum causa scriptus audiet, qui eos deserit, culpat, imo proposteræ,præ omnibus, citationis Scripturæ,reos omnes agit publicè.
units.tr: I say that this thesis is diametrically opposed to the common and universal opinion of the Reformed, who all without exception assert that the interpretation of Scripture must be discussed from Scripture itself, as may be seen even from those things which were before Wolzogen in his Paradox. I know that it is one thing, once a certain rule and norm of interpreting has been posited, to bring this or that passage under that rule and so draw out its true sense; but it is another thing to seek that norm and rule which will be the standard for us afterwards when we interpret Scripture. The Reformed theologians and confessions hold that Scripture by itself suffices to determine both of these. Now the latter point has to be demonstrated. The nature of the question, which is one of fact, does not need a long argument, and it can be wholly determined from the Paradox itself, which handles it as already determined in the sense of the Reformed. Not that I think the authority of that busybody worth so much, but because it supplies the most splendid testimonies taken from the leaders of the Reformed, which teach this most abundantly. In chapter 13 he brings in Chamier, Whitaker, Polanus, Zanchius, Beza, Alting and Walaeus, disputing from Scripture on this very matter and even bringing the whole business to an end. In chapter 12 he had produced passages of Scripture which, according to the Reformed opinion, clearly settle the whole matter in question, adding absurd exceptions and cavils which subvert the very practice. Wolzogen ought at this point to have defended those grounds of proof, as they can easily be defended; but he does nothing of the kind. He deserts our side and leaves all those selected forces of ours undefended under the victorious hand of the most base and absurd adversary. Indeed, turning his back on the enemy, he rushes openly against our side and says that Scripture, which ours hear, and by which they have so far fought and conquered most happily here, is not to be heard, nor to be brought forward, nor, when brought forward, refuted by those who have not yet agreed on the Interpreter. Hurling in the face of all the Reformed this reproach, that to want to bring Scripture forward here, which all of them bring forward, seems to him, if anything, to be done back to front, he presents himself as wiser than all the rest. If anyone, then, has made back-to-front use of Scripture, it is the Reformed and all their theologians without exception. O censure thrice and four times absurd, back-to-front! And this book, written for the cause of the Reformed, will hear it: a man who deserts them, blames them, and indeed publicly makes all of them guilty of back-to-front citation of Scripture.

units.la: 2. Ut sententiæ Reformatorum, sic & veritati adversa isthæc thesis est. Totum autem negotium tanto lumine circumfusum judico, ut sese ipsum sua insita claritate expediat. Non minus quam si quis disputaret,an ab hominibus & ipsa ratione, an vero à bestiis, à bobus aut asinis, legitimus rationis usus perdiperdiscendus sit. Ex alia in aliam sphæram activitatis, ut sic loquar, ex alio in aliud genus sic transitur. Brevibus; in toto hoc negotio disputas, aut cum homine qui Scripturam, aut Verbum Dei, hominibus, ad salutarem cognitionem instruendis, datum agnoscit, aut cum eo, qui rejicit. Si cum hoc, non prius ille de ejus interpretatione sollicitus erit, aut cum fructu instruetur, quam de ejus divinitate fuerit convictus, quapropter hic duo erunt agenda; primum, proponenda insita divinitatis signa, quibus Scriptura abundat; atque illud erit medium morale, cui addendum secundum, oratio nimirum, ad interpretandam isti homini mentem illuminatam ac oculos apertos, quò divinam istam lucem, sese in istis signis prodentem{1}, recipere aptus evadat. Interea illi sufficiet talis interpretatio, qualem admittunt omnia hominum scripta mere humana. Cum illo autem, qui Scripturam, illo, quo dictum est modo admittit, aliter agier oportet, hoc enim in casu, res sese ipsa illustrat luculentissimè. Ponamus illud scriptum divinum esse, hominibus scriptum, ut inde ad salutem evadant sapientes, hoc enim admittunt, quotquot Scripturæ divinitatem amplectuntur: inde jam necessario sequitur, scriptum illud, intelligibiliter scriptum esse, hoc est, ut ejus sensus sit investigabilis ac inveniri queat; nam nisi & illud concedatur, prius concessum tollitur necessario, quod scripturam ponit divinam, hominesque ad salutem instruendi gratia scriptam esse. Qui finis, absque intelligibilitate, acquiri non potest. Ut, qui fide Scripturam recipiat, simul ejus credat intelligibilitatem. At ambigat jam de Interpretatione & quomodo perficienda sit, etenim ita in partes divisos & contraria sentientes, illos, qui Scripturam normam agnoscunt fidei, videns, necesse est, ut pravæ & perversæ interpretationis malo ista adscribat, quare de ea sollicitus, quid agendum dubitet, quæratque quidnam pro norma pro regula interpretationis sit sumendum, cujus ope adjutus, veram Dei menmentem expiscari valeat, atque hic rationem id determinare ac docere posse & debere putat Wolzogius : ego cum cunctis Reformatis Scripturam illud per se facere existimo.Rationem quod attiner, quid illa,praeter ea,quae jam novit is, qui Scripturae divinitatem agnoscit, docere hac in re potest ? per sermones & verba mentem explicari, & sapienti qui id secerit, usum loquendi,ut artium, Grammatices , Rhetorices &c. fundamenta, non subvertenda,sed sequenda incumbere: Barbarum fore aliàs , Deum autem sapientissimum, ut ne in intelligibile & Barbarum verbum suum evaderet, id satis superque scivisse & observasse: aliàs verbum ad salutarem cognitionem perducere potens esse negaretur. Haec fere omnia sunt, quae à ratione hic disserendo dici forsan possent, & à te tanto apparatu dicta sunt& explicata supra necessitatis modum.At omne illud jam novit is,quem nunc ponimus,de quo nunc disputamus ,admittit enim Verbum Dei in hominum gratiam , &,quo ii ad salutarem cognitionem pertingerent , scriptum esse , ac proinde intelligibiliter ; ut nihil ulterius evincas , quam, quod jam in hypothesi utrimque concessum est; quare jam positam & suppositam cognitionem, à ratione postliminio accersendam, præposteré cogitas. Scripturae unice se dedat oportet, qui eam tale Dei Verbum esse jam fide tenet , & patebit sua luce perspicuam , cœlestes veritates ilico menti objicere credendas. Fides illa,quæ supponitur hoc requirit, non minus , quam instinctus naturalis recenter natos ad ubera trahit , inde alendos & sustentandos. Sic anima jam fidelis, verbo illi inhærere, sese illi tradere , supernatulis vitæ instinctu , ultro docetur ibique lucem, lucernam ducemque inveniens, qui pote,ut, præter eam,quicquam normæ aut regulæ desideret, summæ jam & infallibili dedita ? Deprehendet statim , sentietque , hoc scriptum oculos illuminare, veritatem docere, animum suavissimo supernæ sapientiæ gustu afficere, ac deinceps ceps totum perfundere. Difficultates occurrentes solutas sparsim reperiet, sicque cum gaudio prose-ctum suum sentiet, lætusque eadem incedet via & salutaris sapientiæ plenam mensuram versus graf-sabitur. Interim, & illa experientia, & sacræ Scri-pturæ exertissima verba, hanc summam veritatis & infallibilem normam, suaque interpretationis unicam regulam esse, ultro menti oggerent & per-suadebunt. Sint viri sapientes qui loqui velint, lo-quantur sibi invicem intelligibiliter, hoc est, ad-hibitis signis mentem exprimere valentibus & so-litis, quis eò deinceps veniet stultitiæ, ut multo molimine indagandam putet istorum sermonum interpretandi regulam ac normam. Dum unus loquitur alter attendet & sic se mutuo intelligent. Loquitur Deus in verbo suo nobiscum, & intelli-gibiliter cum loqui necesse est, quid hic ultra re-quiritur, quam, supposita ex usu & legibus dicendi, verborum phrasiumque in se consideratarum in-telligibilitate, attendere ad ea quæ loquitur, ea ru-minando, conferendo &c. Implorata interim, pro subjecti per Spiritum Sanctum acquirenda aptitu-dine, gratia illuminante ac obsignante. Res ita cla-ra videtur, ut verbis magis perspicue exprimi non possit, quam ipsa se sponte intellectui conspicien-dam præbet. Miror itaque, tam longa rationum verborumque, eaque satis perplexa, serie, in negotio ita perspicuo, sese ipsum, ac lectorem suum, desati-gare voluisse Wolzogium. Certe difficiles nodos in scirpo fingere, artis non est, neque alios quam nugatores docet. Quid hic ratio investiget, de-terminet, judicet? quando omne id, cujus aliquod indicium à ratione expectari posset, in Scriptura ponitur, simul ac ea pro verbo Dei, eum in finem prolato, accipitur, impositerum suæ interpretatio-nis, ut & omnis veritatis supernaturalis, futura u-nica & sufficiens norma. Adversariorum impor-tunæ cavillationes, tam multa, super hac quæstione, scribendi necessitatem, nostris Theologis fecerunt unice, quandoquidem res ipsa tam apertæ veritatis sit, ut, vel ex ipsis terminis, totius controversiæ decisio sponte fluat. Concedatur, Scripturam verbum Dei esse, idque prolatum, quo homines sapientes reddantur ad salutem, & simul concedetur necesse esse, ut per se intelligi possit, id est, quantum in isto genere requiri potest, ad ingenerandam salutarem sufficere sapientiam, quæ veritas jam dicta, experientia, locisque sparsim occurrentibus, quæ eandem identidem inculcent, ultro pijs confirmatur. Admissa Scriptura ex hypothesibus convinci facili negotio possunt dissentientes, ex superabundanti autem tam multa argumenta Doctissimi Viri addiderunt, solidissima ad unum omnia, ut superius audivimus. Unicum Wolzogio in memoriam revocandum est: hac quæstione, religionem omnem in discrimen venire, omnemque in se continere religionem istam controversiam; nunc vero in ejus pertractatione, nullo modo, Scripturam audiendam docet; sola ratio, ait, hic judex sedet, & decidere debet: unde totam Wolzogii religionem à rationis arbitrio pendere, non absque ratione quispiam cogitaret. Quoniam vero plura notanda supersunt, & ab aliis summa & apex hujus controversiæ optimè sit pertractatus, hac vice ulteriori disquisitioni supersedebo.
units.tr: 2. This thesis is as contrary to the truth as it is to the opinion of the Reformed. I judge, however, that the whole matter is so bathed in light that it clears itself by its own inborn clarity. It is no different from asking whether the legitimate use of reason must be learned from men and from reason itself, or rather from beasts, oxen or asses. One passes from one sphere of activity to another, so to speak, from one kind to another. In short, in this whole matter you are disputing either with a man who acknowledges Scripture as the Word of God given to men to instruct them in saving knowledge, or with one who rejects it. If it is the latter, he will not be concerned about its interpretation first, nor will he be instructed with any profit, until he has been convinced of its divinity. Therefore two things must be done here. First, the inborn signs of divinity, with which Scripture abounds, must be set forth; and this will be the moral means. To it must be added a second, namely prayer, that the mind of that man may be enlightened and his eyes opened, so that he becomes fit to receive that divine light revealing itself in these signs.{1} Meanwhile, such an interpretation suffices for him as is allowed for all purely human writings. But with the one who admits Scripture in the way just described, one must proceed otherwise, for in this case the matter illustrates itself most brightly. Let us suppose that this writing is divine, written for men so that they may become wise unto salvation, for all who embrace the divinity of Scripture admit this. From this it necessarily follows that the writing is written intelligibly, that is, that its sense can be investigated and found. For unless this too is granted, the earlier concession is necessarily undone, namely that Scripture is divine and written to instruct men to salvation. That end cannot be attained without intelligibility. Thus whoever receives Scripture by faith at the same time believes in its intelligibility. But now he doubts about the interpretation and how it is to be carried out. For seeing that those who acknowledge Scripture as the rule of faith are divided into parties and hold contrary opinions, he must necessarily ascribe this to the evil of a depraved and perverse interpretation. Anxious about it, he wonders what is to be done and asks what is to be taken as the norm and rule of interpretation, with whose help he may be able to search out the true mind of God. Wolzogen thinks that reason can determine and teach this. I, with all the Reformed, think that Scripture does this of itself. As for reason, what can it teach in this matter beyond what he already knows who acknowledges the divinity of Scripture? That the mind is explained through speech and words, and that a wise man who does this should apply the usage of speaking, and the foundations of the arts (grammar, rhetoric, etc.), not to subvert them but to follow them: otherwise the speech would be barbarous. God, most wise, knew and observed this well enough, and more than enough, so that His Word would not turn into an unintelligible and barbarous word; otherwise it would be denied that He is able to bring His word to saving knowledge. These are nearly all the things that reasoning might perhaps say here, and you have said and explained them with great display, beyond what the necessity requires. But the man we now posit, about whom we now dispute, already knows all of this. For he admits that the Word of God was written for the benefit of men, so that they might attain saving knowledge, and therefore intelligibly. So you prove nothing further than what is already conceded on both sides in the hypothesis. Wherefore you think to bring in, by a backward and absurd route, from reason, a knowledge already posited and presupposed. Whoever already holds by faith that Scripture is such a Word of God must devote himself solely to Scripture, and it will be plain by its own light that heavenly truths are to be believed at once. The faith that is presupposed requires this, no less than natural instinct draws newborns to the breast to be nourished and sustained there. So the soul, already faithful, is taught of itself, by the supernatural instinct of life, to cleave to that Word and surrender itself to it. Finding there light, lamp and guide, what could it need beyond it, being already devoted to the highest and infallible norm, of any further norm or rule? It will at once perceive and feel that this writing enlightens the eyes, teaches truth, affects the mind with the sweetest taste of heavenly wisdom, and then pervades the whole person. The difficulties that arise it will find solved here and there, and so it will feel its progress with joy; glad, it will advance along the same way and grow toward the full measure of saving wisdom. Meanwhile, both that experience and the most express words of Holy Scripture will of themselves offer and persuade the mind that this is the highest and infallible norm and the sole rule of its interpretation. Let wise men who wish to speak, speak to one another intelligibly, that is, using the usual signs able to express the mind. Who then would come to such folly as to think that a rule and norm for interpreting these speeches must be sought with great labour? While one speaks, the other attends, and so they understand each other. God speaks with us in His Word, and since He must speak intelligibly, what more is required here than, given the intelligibility of words and phrases considered in themselves, from the usage and laws of speaking, to attend to what He says, ruminating on it, comparing it, and so on? Meanwhile, the subject should implore, for the aptitude to be acquired through the Holy Spirit, the illuminating and sealing grace. The matter seems so clear that it cannot be expressed in words more perspicuously than it presents itself of its own accord to the intellect to be seen. I wonder, therefore, that Wolzogen wished to weary himself and his reader with so long a series of reasonings and words, and those quite perplexing, in a matter so plain. Certainly, to fashion difficult knots out of a bulrush is not the art of the craftsman, and it teaches none but trifling men. What does reason here investigate, determine or judge, when everything from which some indication might be expected from reason is placed in Scripture, as soon as it is received as the Word of God, put forth to that end, and so is the future sole and sufficient norm both of its own interpretation and of all supernatural truth? The importunate cavils of the adversaries have made it necessary for our Theologians to write so much on this question. Yet the matter is of so manifest a truth that the decision of the whole controversy flows of its own accord from the very terms. Grant that Scripture is the Word of God, and that it was put forth so that men might be made wise unto salvation; at the same time it must be granted that it is intelligible in itself, that is, as far as can be required in this kind, sufficient to engender saving wisdom. This truth, already stated, is confirmed of its own accord in the pious by experience and by the passages that occur here and there, which repeatedly impress the same thing. Granted Scripture, dissenters can easily be convinced from their own hypotheses; and out of superabundance the most learned men have added many arguments, all most solid, as we heard above. One thing must be recalled to Wolzogen: in this question all religion is at stake, and this controversy contains all religion within itself. Yet in its treatment he teaches that Scripture is by no means to be heard; reason alone, he says, sits here as judge and must decide. Whence someone might reasonably think that all Wolzogen's religion depends on the judgment of reason. But since many things remain to be noted, and the sum and summit of this controversy has already been treated well by others, I will for this time forgo further inquiry.

units.la: 3. Hanc thesin nulla probabili ratione sufful-tam deprehendo. Debebat non nisi demonstrativa, ut vocant, argumenta dare, qui omnes Theologos, non solidæ argumentationis, accusare ausus est. Argumentorum autem loco, hasce duas cavillationes fabricavit, præposterè hic Scripturam proferri dixerat, cujus probatio prior sic sonat. Nec e-nim intelligi sine interprete Scriptura potest, & cum sit interpres materia disputationis, parata semper exceptio est; non recte intelligi Scripturam. Sic & p. 247. Sunt enim verba sine sensu, quia qui sensum debet e-ruere nondum certus Interpres. Interpres hic interpre-tandi regulam seu normam necessario notat, nam de ho-mine Interprete se non loqui, antea significa-vit author, & res ipsa alium sensum non patitur nisi unumquemque ad Script. intelligendam ho-mine alio egere quispiam somniet. At rem aliquam requiri ab ipsa Scriptura diversam, sine cu-jus ope ea intelligi non possit, ejusque verba sine sensu sint, ut prophanum nego, ac pernego, æque ac solis lucem aliam requirere lucem, qua istam videam, aut recte me videre evadam certior.
