Posito Scripturam Dei verbum esse, quo homines ad salu-tem instruantur, sponte patet, & verba sine sensu absque blasphemia dici non posse, & quænam sit interpretandi norma, nimirum, præter ipsam Scri-pturam, nulla, ut modo diximus. Ut absurdè veritatis hostes tam laboriosæ disputationis materiam hic dederint, Theologis Orthodoxis, quod etiam in pluribus experimur controversiis, in re, per se clara & perspicua, tam multum negotii facessentes.
units.tr: 3. I find that this thesis is supported by no probable reasoning. He ought to have offered demonstrative arguments, as they are called, since he dared to accuse all theologians of lacking sound argument. Instead of arguments, he has devised two quibbles. First, he says that Scripture is cited out of order here, and his first proof runs like this: Scripture cannot be understood without an interpreter, and since the interpreter is the subject of the dispute, the ready objection is always that Scripture is not rightly understood. So too on p. 247: The words are without sense, because the interpreter who must draw out the sense is not yet certain. Here "interpreter" necessarily denotes the rule or norm of interpretation, for the author has already made clear that he is not speaking of a human interpreter, and the matter itself allows no other sense unless someone dreams that each person needs another man to understand Scripture. But I deny, and utterly deny, as profane, that Scripture requires some thing other than itself, without whose aid it cannot be understood, and that its words are without sense; this is no more than to say that the light of the sun requires another light by which I may see it, or that I may become more certain that I see rightly. Granted that Scripture is the Word of God, by which men are instructed to salvation, it is plainly evident that its words cannot be said to be without sense without blasphemy; and, as we have just said, the only norm of interpretation is Scripture itself, and no other. How absurdly the enemies of the truth have supplied the matter for so laborious a dispute here, when we Orthodox theologians have found in many controversies that they make much trouble over a matter which is clear and perspicuous in itself.

units.la: Paratæ sint exceptiones, non recte intelligi Scripturam, neque enim istis exceptionibus unquam Wolzogius suo Interprete viam præcludet: Ille etiam, qui se ex ipsa Scriptura, verorum sensuum convinci quotidie, persentiscit, non magis ipsis exceptioni-bus dimovebitur; quam si quis, ex cæcorum nu-mero, me lucis aut visionis meæ incertum suis cavillationibus reddere tentaret. An Cartesiani propterea claræ & distinctæ perceptioni minus fi-dunt, eamve veritatis regulam esse minori certi-tudine sibi persuadent, quoniam multi sunt qui eos toto cœlo errare contendunt ? Et merito dubios se reddi non paterentur, si certis innixa & indubi-tatis fundamentis hæc regula foret, aliis licet con-tra mussitantibus.
units.tr: Let the objection be ready: Scripture is not rightly understood. For by such objections Wolzogius will never close off the way to his own interpreter. Nor will the man who perceives every day, from Scripture itself, that the true senses are being proved to him be moved by these objections any more than if someone from the number of the blind tried to make me doubt my light or my sight by his quibbles. Do the Cartesians therefore trust less in clear and distinct perception, or persuade themselves that this rule of truth has less certainty, because many contend that they are wholly in error? And they would rightly refuse to be made doubtful, if this rule rested on sure and indubitable foundations, even though others mutter against it.

units.la: Quid ni id omnibus, quibus per Dei gratiam, Scripturæ lucem, & interpre-tandi, interpretationemque sibi persuadendi, facul-tatem, & potentiam nosse datur, itidem liceat, ut exceptionibus, quantum possunt, obviam eun-tes, videre tamen se, quod resera vident, absque ulla hæsitatione certi permancant. Neque media de-sunt, sunt,quibus id quod ipsi certò vident, aliis etiam, licet adversariis, quantum ad objectivam convi-ctionem sufficit, demonstretur. Ex hypothesi utrin-que concessa, quantumvis obluctetur,aut aliam in-terpretationis normam obtrudere velit, ad scriptu-ram vel invitus pertrahi poterit. Concedit Scri-pturam tale Dei verbum esse, necesse ergo est, ut patulas auresilli praebeat,& mentem attentam: ego ex illa Scriptura, quam utrinque pro tali princi-pio agnoscimus, ac proinde intelligibiliter scri-ptam esse fatemur, ipsi dogmata credenda & mo-rum regulas depromam, quas si rejiciat, probabo adductis Scripturae Textibus,quos si me bene inter-pretari neget, ego ex circumstantiis aliisque ipsum convincam; si instet, se voces istas non intelligere, regeram Scripturam ex usu & regulis linguae scri-ptam esse, idque supponi, sin minus, ad versionem, & verbalem quam vocamus interpretationem hoc pertinere, non realem, de qua impraesentiarum quaestio agitatur, aliàs intelligibilem non fore, ac proinde tale verbum, quod in suo genere sapien-tem ad salutem reddere possit, non esse, quod con-tradicit hypothesi. Si autem diversam, ab ipsa Scriptura, interpretandi normam, adhibendam moneat, praeterquam, quod ea,quaecunque tandem sit, rationibus dispelli facile possit, iterum urgebo hypothesin, quae aperte convellitur, nisi sufficiens in suo genere, quo ad salutarem cognitionem per-tingam, agnoscatur, qualis non foret si alia praeter se ipsam norma, magis quam vel hominum dicta quibus alios docere volunt & instruere, indigeat. Quare & omnes, quod αὐτοκαταχρισίας[?], vel stupi-dae ignorantiae documentum est irrefragabile, quotquot se isti veritati & Scripturae perfectioni opponunt, sponte eo re ipsa duce deferuntur, ut Scripturam interpretari satagentes, ex Scriptura suae interpretationis firmamenta accersant, quod inPapistis non solum, sed etiam in Socinianis & i-pso Paradoxo deprehendimus. Ipse Wolzogius, qui hoc in Paradoxo recte notat, eodem argumento confutari potest solidissimè. Ponunt quidem Socinani, firmantque suas, ex ratione quasi desumtas, regulas; somniat & tales Wolzogius, quibus contradicere Scripturam credendum non sit: ad certamen vero quando deventum est, ex textu, ex Paralellis certant, si non unicè, saltem præcipue, ut vel ex ipso Socino in Joh. 1. ex Crellio, Schlightingio, aliisque videre est. Quorum ultimus ultro largitur, quoties de Scripturæ sensu aliunde constiterit, quicquid contradicat ratio falli eam necesse esse. Et sane, res aliter se habere non potest, nisi ex Scriptura ipsa, de alia, seu rationis, seu Patrum aut Conciliorum, seu Enthusiasticorum dictaminum norma, convincar. Pono enim, quod sæpius jam dictum est, Scripturam istam tale verbum, & quia Dei, intelligibile, sapientiæ salutaris esse principium. Ego, fidei Articulos ex isto verbo investigaturus, me in ejus scrutamine, unicè illi verbo trado, dedoque, neque aliam interpretationis normam necesse esse, quotidiano profectu experior, & claris Scripturæ verbis convincor. Tu quidem concedis, illud verbum, ad salutarem sapientiam nobis ingenerandam, datum principium esse; sed ultro dogmata rationis audienda, de ratione interpretationis modum normamque repetendam esse, tu oggeres id experientiam te & rationem docere: ego rationi non fido, eique, in isto negotio, arbitrium nego, tu certe me ad istam sententiam adigere nunquam poteris, nisi ex ipsa Scriptura, quam unicè admisimus utrimque; ex Scriptura autem me convicturus, omne illud verum esse quod ex Deo ducit originem, lumen esse quicquid à Patre luminum nobis impertitur, ac proinde rationem audiendam esse, non spernendam, non repudiandam: at rogo, undenam tibi constet, istorum locorum talem sensum esse, ut ex iis de admittendo rationis, saltem non plane declinando, arbitrio, convinci me oportere putes; si dicas ex aliis rationibus, extra Scripturam positis, petis principium, nam ego eas, in isthoc negotio, sic non admitto; si autem dicas ex ipsa Scriptura, quae si intelligibiliter scripta esse utrimque concedatur, non potest non censeri, illum rationis usum praecepisse, jam concedis omne quod volo, nimirum scripturam per se sufficere, quo de fidei veritatibus instruamur, convincamur. Unde concludo tam longè abesse, ut, quod Wolzogius Reformatis exprobrat, praepostere in hoc negotio Scriptura producatur, ut ea, solum nominata & posita, omnes sua luce ab eo dispellat tenebras, atque sic praepostere hic adhiberi non possit. Sequitur altera Wolzogii ratio, quae talis est. Ubi de ipsa in-terpretatione quaestio est, NULLO MODO audienda Scriptura est, quia de ipsa disputatur. Eandem rationem olim noverat Jesuita Tirinus, sic ille, Scripturae supremum Interpretem (ut plerique hereti-ci contendunt) non esse ipsammet Scripturam patet, quia de illamet hic est quaestio. Quam rationem sic refutat Maresius: Hoc soli Deo competit, ut Judex sedeat in sua causa. Æque ac Soli competit, non aliter, quam suo videri lumine. Quid si de ratione disputetur, an non ex ratione decidenda erit controversia? Quid si quis vel de principio cognoscendi, vel de regula exactae cognitionis dubium moveat, an ideo rationi valedicendum erit, quia de ratione ambigitur? Atque ista Wolzogio omnes Reformati Theologi convicti & expugnati ratiocinatione videntur.
units.tr: Why should it not likewise be allowed to all those to whom, by the grace of God, the light of Scripture and the faculty and power of interpreting and of persuading themselves of its interpretation are given, that, while they meet objections as far as they can, they nevertheless see what they really see and remain certain without any hesitation? Nor are there lacking means by which what they clearly see may be shown even to others, though adversaries, so far as objective conviction is concerned. Given the hypothesis granted on both sides, however much he struggles, or however much he wishes to thrust upon us some other norm of interpretation, he will be drawn to Scripture even against his will. He concedes that Scripture is such a Word of God, so he must needs lend it open ears and an attentive mind. I, from that Scripture which we on both sides acknowledge as such a principle, and therefore confess to have been written intelligibly, will draw for him the doctrines to be believed and the rules of conduct; if he rejects them, I will prove them by the adduced texts of Scripture; if he denies that I interpret them rightly, I will convict him from the circumstances and from other things; if he insists that he does not understand these words, I will retort that Scripture is written according to the usage and rules of language, and that this is presupposed; otherwise this would pertain to translation and what we call verbal interpretation, not to real interpretation, which is the question now under discussion; otherwise it would not be intelligible, and so such a word, which could render a man wise unto salvation in its own kind, would not exist, which contradicts the hypothesis. But if he advises that a norm of interpretation different from Scripture itself must be employed, then, besides the fact that such a norm, whatever it may be, can easily be dispelled by reasoning, I will again press the hypothesis, which is plainly overthrown unless Scripture is acknowledged to be sufficient in its own kind for attaining saving knowledge; it would not be so if it needed some norm other than itself, rather than the words of men by which they wish to teach and instruct others. Therefore all who set themselves against this truth and the perfection of Scripture are, by the very fact, led by the Scripture itself into self-condemnation [αὐτοκαταχρισίας], which is an irrefutable proof of stupid ignorance. Striving to interpret Scripture, they fetch the supports of their interpretation from Scripture; we see this not only among the Papists, but also among the Socinians and in the Paradoxa itself. Wolzogius himself, who rightly notes this in the Paradoxa, can be most solidly refuted by the same argument. The Socinians indeed lay down, and strengthen, rules which they seem to derive from reason; Wolzogius too dreams of such rules, by which Scripture is not to be believed when it contradicts them. But when they come to the contest, they fight from the text and from parallel passages, if not solely, at least chiefly, as may be seen from Socinus himself on John 1, and from Crellius, Schlichting and others. The last of these freely concedes that whenever the sense of Scripture has been established from elsewhere, whatever reason contradicts must necessarily be false. And indeed things cannot be otherwise, unless I am convicted from Scripture itself, by some other norm, whether of reason, or of the Fathers, or of the Councils, or of enthusiastic dictates. For I maintain, as has been said often already, that this Scripture is such a Word, and because it is of God, intelligible, the principle of saving wisdom. I, who am about to investigate the articles of faith from this Word, in my search surrender myself wholly to that Word, and I find by daily progress, and am convinced by the clear words of Scripture, that no other norm of interpretation is necessary. You indeed concede that this Word is the principle given for engendering in us saving wisdom; but you add of your own accord that the doctrines of reason must be heard, and that the manner and norm of interpretation must be sought from reason, and you assert that experience and reason teach you this. I do not trust reason, and in this matter I deny that it has any authority; you will certainly never be able to force me to this opinion unless from Scripture itself, which we both alone admitted. But if you intend to convict me from Scripture, that everything true which derives its origin from God is a light, and that whatever is imparted to us as light by the Father of lights, and therefore that reason is to be heard and not despised or rejected, then I ask: whence does it appear to you that these passages have such a sense that you think I must be convinced by them to admit the authority of reason, or at least not wholly to decline it? If you say from other reasons, placed outside Scripture, you beg the question, for in this matter I do not admit those reasons; but if you say from Scripture itself, which, if it is conceded on both sides to be written intelligibly, cannot but be judged to have prescribed that use of reason, you already concede everything I want, namely that Scripture by itself is sufficient for our being instructed and convinced concerning the truths of faith. Hence I conclude that it is so far from being the case that, as Wolzogius reproaches the Reformed, Scripture is produced out of order in this matter, that merely by being named and set forth it dispels all darkness from him by its light, and so cannot be employed here out of order. Follows Wolzogius's second reasoning, which is as follows. Where the question concerns interpretation itself, Scripture must by NO MEANS be heard, because it is itself under dispute. Long ago the Jesuit Tirinus knew this same reasoning, and he says: That Scripture itself is not the supreme interpreter of Scripture (as most heretics contend) is clear, because the question here is about that very Scripture. Maresius refutes this reasoning thus: This belongs to God alone, that he should sit as judge in his own cause. Just as it belongs to the Sun alone to be seen by no other light than its own. What if the dispute concerns reason: will the controversy not have to be decided by reason? What if someone raises a doubt about the principle of knowing, or about the rule of exact knowledge: will reason have to be bidden farewell because it is in doubt? And yet all the Reformed theologians seem to have been convicted and overcome by Wolzogius's reasoning in this way.

units.la: 2. Huic primae affinis est thesis altera, quae sta-tuit, quaestionem, qua quaeritur, quamobrem sta-tuamus hunc & non alium Scripturarum sensum, alterius naturae esse, quam illa, quae in auctoritatem loquentis Dei resolvitur, & res humanas concernere. Ergo auctoritate loquentis Dei non nititur, quan-do hunc locum, istum vel illum sensum habere pro-nunciat. Solius id fidei non est, neque Dei testimonio unice nititur. Hic videtur aliquid fidei, ac proinde authoritati Dei tribuere: non omne tamen. Alibi enim, Reformatis urgentibus, quod omnis Inter-pretatio fit controversia fidei, cum suo Paradoxo consentiens, haec verba adfert pro responsione ad Reformatorum argumentum: non facit ad fidem interpretatio quicquam nisi remotè, remotè facit tantum ad fidem. Non igitur fide credit, huic loco hunc subesse sensum: non enim in authoritatem Dei resolvitur ista quæstio. O miram Wolzogii religionem & fidem! Libro priore in ipso crudum effatum perstrinximus, quo in iis, quæ præter fundamentalia, eaque paucissima, reliqua sunt, nullum infallibilem interpretem agnoscit, quod non de homine interpretante, sed norma interpretandi intelligatur necesse est, nisi in fundamentalibus ho-minem aliquem pro infallibili colat interprete. En igitur omnem, de Scripturarum sensu, certitudinem sublatam, præterquam in fundamentalibus, quæque pauciora sint, quam vulgo credi solet, ac quidem Reformatis; Sociniani enim & Remonstrantes, aut Pontificii, explicitè credendorum justo au-ctiorem numerum non obtrudunt, unice Reformati supersunt, qui vulgo credunt plura esse, quam quidem Wolzogius censet, fundamentalia. Pauco-rum igitur, se ex sacris, infallibilem certitudinem hausisse, profitetur Wolzogius, quod sane non dif-ficulter credo: hoc autem non fero, quod plu-rium certitudinem acquiri posse, audacter neget. Quin justam suspicionem lectori injicit, an ullam ullius sensus scripturæ aut dogmatis credendi ab-solutam certitudinem sibi non solum acquisiverit, sed vel ab aliis acquiri posse hactenus credat. Præterquam in fundamentalibus nullum infallibilem interpretem agnoscit, sicque præter fundamentalia nihil absolute certum, ista certitudo enim, ab inter-pretationis pendet certitudine, sic antea, nunc vero & illa certitudo vacillat, imo tantum non omnis subvertitur. Quod sic probo. Fundamenta-les illi, atque unicè certi & indubitati articuli, non nisi adhibita interpretatione, hoc est, eruto verbo-rum rum eos exprimentium sensu, innotescunt: quod non negabit Wolzogius, qui recte omnia vel clarissima talem interpretationem exigere statuit, quippe qua unicè sensus verborum dicentis, ad mentem legentis, vel audientis, pertingat. Jam subsumo. At interpretatio, quodque hunc statuamus non alium Scripturarum sensum, in authoritatem loquentis Dei, ex ipsius sensu, non resolvitur, ac tandem, testimonio Dei non unicè nititur, atque, solius fidei non est, saltem ad fidem non facit quicquam nisi remotè. Quid hinc manifestiori sequela elicitur, quam, non infallibili, non unicè divino nixum testimonio, adeoque non absolutè fide divina, vel i-psos fundamentales, unicè aliàs ipsi certos, articulos recipi à Wolzogio: id est, nihil ab ipso certâ credi, & infallibili certitudine? Necesse autem non est, ut multis istam conclusionem Wolzogio extorqueam quam ultro largitur, Scriptura enim ipsi à Deo esse dicitur, sed interpretatio, ab hominibus. Judicium sit penes pium lectorem. Missa hac, ex Wolzogianis genuino nexu, certoque propulsante sequela, ad ipsam thesin revertor, de qua sic statuunt Orthodoxi, se in pronunciando, de hoc aut illo Scripturæ sensu, unicè divina inniti authoritate, adeo ut illum sensum hisce verbis subesse, detecto agnitoque ex divinis signis sensu divino ac infallibili, fide divina certi credant & intrepidi, & interpretatio, Scripturæ animam nobis & nucleum tradens, non ab hominibus sed à Deo sit, quā de re in primi, Reformatorum, atque inter eos, Clariss. Chamieri, argumenti vindiciis adversus Wolzogium & Paradoxum egi. Præter ea autem, quæ inibi objecta refutavi, nihil quidem difficultatis solvendum restat: in speciem tamen diversa quædam occurrunt, quæ hoc loco, ut ipsi abunde satisfiat, excutienda sunt. Primum est, quod ubi de interpretatione quæstio instituitur, de rebus humanis agatur, hæc enim res humanas concernit, ac proin-de longè alterius naturæ, ab illa, quæ in authoritatem loquentis Dei resolvitur. Idem inculcat paulo post, his verbis. Quia enim circa res versatur humanas; verba, voces, orationem, humanis quoque mediis expedienda est. Imprimis notari velim, quam exaête cum Paradoxo suo hicce loci conveniat Wolzogius. Distinguit homo prophanus inter Scripturam materialiter sumtam aut formaliter, illam vocat literas, syllabas, voces, & ex his conflatas orationes, hanc vero, rem, istis vocibus contentam, quarum posteriorem, hominis arbitrio eximit, priorem vero subjicit. Eodem plane modo Wolzogius, res humanas concernit, verba, voces, phrases, orationem. Non sibi magis quam Paradoxo similis: Sed absurda est utriusque cavillatio. Et materialiter & formaliter, hoc est tota & unicè divina sacra Scriptura est. Sint voces humanae, hoc est, ab hominibus, Deo sic dirigente & providentia sua id efficiente, excogitatae, jam postquam Deus iis utitur divinae fiunt, si usus humanus ejus humanas efficiat, quid ni & divinus usus faciat divinas. Communi utatur iis Deus significatione, adeo ut Dei usus, cum eo, qui hominum est, unus sit quoad voces sigillatim sumtas. Jam tamen ejus usus divinus est, significatio divina, & in constructione, in tantum singularis, nec ulla, usus mutatione, varianda aut mutanda: hoc est, ex mente Dei, talem, non alium sensum, sic prolata, efferunt: Quae veritatis vis, vel reluctanti haec verba extorsit. Usus enim vel consideratur in ipsa loquentium consuetudine, & sic mere humanus est: sed sic non facit interpretem Scripturae: vel spectatur ut adhibitus a Deo, qui vulgarem usum adhibendo suum facit, & ita quidem desumtus ab hominibus est, sed a Deo approbatus & usurpatus, jam Dei usus incipit esse. Igitur in Deum refunditur Interpretationis dignitas. At bone vir: annon sic tua destruis? sit quaestio, quare hoc, non alio, ista verba, istam orationem sensu sumas? quid te movebit, nonne authoritas Dei, quem certò vides ista verba, pro singulari suo divino usu, isto usurpasse, non alio significatu, quod te circumstantiæ, paral-lellismus, aliaque Scripturæ insita argumenta docent? necesse enim est ex admisso isto, singulari-ter divino,usu,id itidem admittas. An igitur interpretatio fidei non est, nisi remotè? An authoritate Dei: An testimonio Dei non nititur? Quorsum igitur istis obluctaris? quorsum negas? quorsum pueriliter ea refutare conatus es? quæ, præ nimia claritate, semper & ubique tegere ipse, aut celare, non potuisti. Alterum quod obtendi posset, ex-stat fere ad finem totius tractatus, conquirendæ e-nim sunt istæ margaritæ & colligendæ, non sine tædio: Scriptura, sic sonant verba, ejusque inter-pretatio magno à se intervallo distant. Nam Scriptura, ut est à Deo, nulli rei subjacere potest; interpretatio, quæ ab hominibus est, nil se indignum pateretur, si vel maximè à qua alia causa penderet. Oracula, sed ambigua, fundit noster. In tantum irretitum adversarium, ex Hoornbeekii manibus liberat, ut, licet interpretatio Scripturæ, ab alia, viliori qua, causa dependeat, id tamen, in Scripturæ majestatem, quo argumento Socinianos profligaverat vir incomparabilis, incurrere putandum non sit; errat enim in eo Hoornbeekius, quod Scripturam cum interpretatione sua, ut dignitate pari, conjunxerat: quæ tamen magno intervallo distant; non satis erat perspicuè dictum à Paradoxo, Scripturam, for-maliter licet, quod ad res contentas, eam alteri sub-jicere, improbum futurum fuisset, materialiter tamen, quod ad verba voces &c. ab alio pendere non esse ejus dignitati adversum. Aliis verbis & clarioribus idem responsum Hoornbeekio oggerendum erat. Distinguendam esse Scripturam, ab ejus interpretatione, hoc est, juxta Paradoxum, ejus materiale à formali: tam parum distat Wolzogius à Paradoxo; falsus uterque. Ego putem, Scripturam non magis differre ab ejus interpretatione quam solem in se ab eodem, ut sese luce sua nobis objicientem. Scripturam cum dico, verba non seorsim, vocesque ut sic intelligo: sed verborum vocumque ordinatam congeriem, per se id signatè significantem, quot alias Scripturæ rem contentam & significatam dicimus universam. Non aliter, quam, si quis patris sui ultimam voluntatem scripto consignatam, diceret testamentum: non voces,phrases,verba unquam designaret, quando de testamento loqueretur, sed verba Phrasesque ultimam voluntatem designantia, id est,verba cum isto significatu. Qui hominem dicit, animam dicit & corpus. Qui legem scriptam, verba, istum legislatoris jussum exprimentia. Ut ista tam longè à se invicem separando, ignorantiam suam prodiderit noster, & cum Paradoxo συμβίβασιν [?], longe, quam par est, majorem. At quid tum porro? multum ista distent: Scriptura, ut est à Deo, nulli subjacere potest, idem volebat Hoornbeekius, idem omnes Reformati: interpretatio autem, quae ab hominibus est,nil se indignum pateretur, si vel maximè à qua alia causa penderet. Quid hisce verbis velis, ego sanè non percipio: Scriptura tua, an non etiam sensum complectitur sibi insitum? vel an mutarum syllabarum tibi congeriem denotat, illud vocabulum? sensus vero, an non Dei sensus est, quem, ut expressit, sic intelligi à nobis voluntate signi voluit? Et quid tandem per interpretationem designas? an actum interpretantis, an normam interpretandi, an vero illud, quod in Scriptura est, quo perspecto homini verus verborum sensus pandatur & appareat? si primum, jam aberras à scopo in immensum: & quis unquam tam stupidus evasit, ut ista non distingueret, aut istum interpretantis actum, ab alia causa, præter ipsam Scripturam, dependere negaret? à Deo, ut causa prima; ab homine,ut secunda & proxima; ab aliis subinde hominibus,ut causis moraliter cooperantibus; à verborum artiumque cognitione, ut ministerialiter adjuvantibus, Scriptura licet sit, maneatque,unica regula & norma. Si secundum, an sic ab hominibus interpretandi norma repetenda tandem veniet? ab hominum voluntate & usu, fateor, verbis sua significatio est, sed ea solummodo explicationem verbalem, aut potius versionem, efficit, & in Scriptura, utpote intelligibiliter scripta, præsupponitur, uti jam sæpius notatum est; at si vel proinde interpretationem ab homine esse contenderes, inficias irem, quoniam, cum à Deo approbatus & usur-patus iste usus, jam Dei usus esse incipit, in Deum refundi debebit, non in homines, interpretatio. Si tertium, illud nimirum, quo tandem perspecto, deprehendere ac videre est, hunc sensum, his verbis inesse, jam falso id ab hominibus esse asseveras, hoc enim ipsa Scriptura in se habet, &, vel primo intuitu, vel accuratæ collationis medio, conspiciendum, ipsa præbet, & totum illud est, de quo disputamus; quapropter causam dedis, eaque dedita, turpiter petis principium, cum dicis interpretationem esse ab hominibus. Atque aliter accidere non poterat, postquam Paradoxo, dolosum in modum, tantum virum, Clariss. Hoornbeekium, quin totam Reformatorum causam, aggredienti, suppetias ferre, Wolzogio decretum erat.
units.tr: 2. Closely related to this first thesis is a second, which holds that the question on which we ask why we hold this and not another sense of Scripture is of a different nature from that which is resolved into the authority of God speaking, and that it concerns human affairs. So, he says, the authority of God speaking does not rest on this when he pronounces that this passage has this or that sense. It is not a matter of faith alone, nor does it rest solely on the testimony of God. Here he seems to grant something to faith, and therefore to the authority of God, but not everything. Elsewhere, when the Reformed press him, he takes the view that every interpretation is a matter of faith, and to support his Paradox he offers this reply to the Reformed argument: interpretation contributes nothing to faith except remotely. So it contributes to faith only remotely. Therefore he does not believe by faith that this passage has this sense, for this question is not resolved into the authority of God. O the strange religion and faith of Wolzogius! In the earlier book I already criticised his crude saying that, outside the fundamentals (and these are very few), he recognises no infallible interpreter. This must be understood not of the interpreting man but of the norm of interpreting, unless in the fundamentals he honours some man as an infallible interpreter. Behold, then, all certainty about the sense of Scripture is removed, except in the fundamentals, which are fewer than is commonly believed, and indeed fewer than the Reformed believe. For the Socinians and the Remonstrants, or the Papists, do not impose an explicit number of things to be believed that is larger than is just; only the Reformed remain, who commonly believe that there are more fundamentals than Wolzogius thinks. Wolzogius professes that he has drawn infallible certainty from Scripture only on a few points, which I readily believe; but I cannot bear that he boldly denies that the certainty of many points can be acquired. Indeed he gives the reader just cause for suspicion whether he has not only acquired for himself absolute certainty about any sense of Scripture or any doctrine to be believed, but even believes that others can acquire it so far. Apart from the fundamentals he recognises no infallible interpreter, and so apart from the fundamentals nothing is absolutely certain. For that certainty depends on the certainty of interpretation; thus before, and now even more, that certainty wavers, and indeed is almost wholly overthrown. I prove it thus. The fundamental articles, the only ones he holds certain and indubitable, become known only through interpretation, that is, by drawing out the sense of the words that express them. Wolzogius will not deny this, since he rightly holds that all things, even the clearest, require such interpretation, because only in this way does the sense of the words of the speaker reach the mind of the reader or hearer. Now I add the minor premise. But interpretation does not resolve our holding that this and not another sense of Scripture is the sense into the authority of the speaking God, nor, finally, does it rest solely on the testimony of God, and it is not a matter of faith alone; at least it contributes nothing to faith except remotely. What follows more clearly from this than that Wolzogius receives the fundamental articles themselves, which alone he holds as certain otherwise, as resting on no infallible testimony, and not wholly on the testimony of God, and so not absolutely by divine faith? That is, that he believes nothing with certain and infallible certainty. I need not force this conclusion from Wolzogius against his will, since he freely grants it. He says that Scripture is from God itself, but interpretation is from men. Let the devout reader judge. Setting aside this sequence, which is the genuine and certain consequence of Wolzogius's own premises, I return to the thesis itself. On this the Orthodox hold that when they pronounce on this or that sense of Scripture they rest solely on divine authority, so that they believe with divine faith, and fearlessly, that this sense lies in these words, the divine and infallible sense having been detected and recognised from divine signs; and that interpretation, which hands us the soul and kernel of Scripture, is not from men but from God. On this matter I argued, in the defence of the first book, against Wolzogius and the Paradox, for the Reformed, and among them the most distinguished Chamier. Apart from what I refuted there, nothing of real difficulty remains to be resolved; yet some things that look different come up here, and these must be examined so that he may be fully satisfied. The first is that when the question of interpretation is raised, the matter concerns human affairs, for this concerns human things, and therefore is of a nature far different from that which is resolved into the authority of the speaking God. He presses the same point a little later in these words: Since it is concerned with human things, words, voices and speech must also be dealt with by human means. I would have it especially noted how exactly Wolzogius agrees here with his own Paradox. The profane man distinguishes Scripture taken materially from Scripture taken formally: the first he calls letters, syllables, voices, and the speeches compounded from them; the second is the thing contained in these voices, and he removes the latter from the will of man but subjects the former to it. In exactly the same way Wolzogius says: it concerns human things, words, voices, phrases, speech. He is no more like himself than like the Paradox. But the quibble of both is absurd. Scripture, both materially and formally, that is wholly and solely divine Scripture. Let the voices be human, that is, devised by men, with God directing them and bringing this about by his providence; once God uses them they become divine. If human use makes them human, why should not divine use make them divine? God uses them in their common meaning, so that his use and that of men are one as regards the individual words taken separately. Yet his use is divine, his meaning is divine, and in the construction it is so singular that nothing in it may be varied or changed by any alteration of usage: that is, by God's mind they express this sense and no other. The force of truth has wrung these words even from one who resists: Usage is either considered in the very custom of the speakers, and so is purely human; but such usage does not make an interpreter of Scripture. Or it is regarded as taken up by God, who by adopting common usage makes it his own; and so indeed it is taken from men, but approved and used by God, and once it is God's use it begins to be God's. Therefore the dignity of interpretation is referred back to God. But, good sir, do you not destroy your own position by this? Suppose the question is why you take these words and this speech in this sense and not another. What will move you? Will it not be the authority of God, whom you clearly see to have used these words in this singular divine use and not in another meaning, as the context, parallelism and other features inherent in Scripture teach you? For if you admit that singular divine use, you must necessarily admit this as well. Is interpretation, then, a matter of faith only remotely? Does it rest on the authority of God, or not on the testimony of God? Why, then, do you struggle against these things? Why do you deny them? Why have you tried so childishly to refute them, things which, because of their great clarity, you could never hide or conceal anywhere or at any time? A second objection that might be made appears almost at the end of the whole treatise; for these pearls must be sought out and gathered, though not without weariness: Scripture, so the words sound, and its interpretation are far apart. For Scripture, as it is from God, can be subject to nothing; interpretation, which is from men, would suffer nothing unworthy even if it depended on some other cause. Our author pours out oracles, but ambiguous ones. He frees his entangled opponent from the hands of Hoornbeeck, so that although the interpretation of Scripture depends on another, baser cause, this is not thought to fall upon the majesty of Scripture. By this argument the incomparable man had overthrown the Socinians, but Hoornbeeck erred in this, that he joined Scripture with its interpretation as if they were of equal dignity, though they are far apart. It was not clearly enough stated by the Paradox that Scripture, formally, as to the things contained in it, would be wrong to subject to another, but materially, as to words, voices, etc., it is not contrary to its dignity to depend on another. The same answer had to be given to Hoornbeeck in other, clearer words: that Scripture must be distinguished from its interpretation, that is, according to the Paradox, its material from its formal aspect. Wolzogius differs as little from the Paradox, and both are false. I would say that Scripture differs from its interpretation no more than the sun differs from itself when it presents itself to us in its own light. When I say Scripture, I do not understand words separately, nor voices as such, but the orderly collection of words and voices which signifies something by itself, which we call the whole content and meaning of Scripture. It is no different from saying that if someone wrote his father's last will and called it a testament, he would never mean words, phrases or voices when speaking of the testament, but the words and phrases expressing the last will, that is, the words with that meaning. He who says man says soul and body. He who says written law means the words expressing the lawgiver's command. By separating these so far apart, our author has revealed his own ignorance, and his reconciling [συμβίβασιν] with the Paradox is much greater than is right. But what follows? Let them differ much: Scripture, as it is from God, can be subject to nothing. Hoornbeeck wanted this, and all the Reformed too. But interpretation, which is from men, would suffer nothing unworthy even if it depended on some other cause. What you mean by these words I certainly do not grasp. Does your Scripture include the sense that is inherent in it, or does that word denote for you a mere collection of dumb syllables? And the sense: is it not God's sense, which he intended to be understood by us by the meaning of his sign, just as he expressed it? And what, finally, do you mean by interpretation? The act of the interpreter, the norm of interpreting, or that which is in Scripture, by perceiving which the true sense of the words is opened and appears to a man? If the first, you go astray immeasurably from the point; and who has ever been so stupid as not to distinguish these, or to deny that this act of interpreting depends on some cause other than Scripture itself: on God as first cause, on man as secondary and proximate cause, on other men at times as morally cooperating causes, and on knowledge of words and arts as ministerially helping, although Scripture is and remains the one rule and norm. If the second, will the norm of interpreting then at last be drawn from men? I grant that the meaning of words comes from the will and usage of men, but this produces only a verbal explanation, or rather a translation, and it is presupposed in Scripture as intelligibly written, as has often been noted already. But if you were to contend that interpretation is from man on this ground, I would deny it, since once this usage has been approved and used by God it begins to be God's use, and interpretation must be referred back to God, not to men. If the third, namely that by perceiving which we grasp and see that this sense lies in these words, then you falsely assert that this comes from men. For Scripture itself contains this, and it is offered by Scripture, to be seen either at first glance or by the means of careful comparison; and this is the whole matter we are disputing. Therefore you concede the cause, and having conceded it you shamefully beg the question when you say that interpretation is from men. Nor could it have turned out otherwise, once Wolzogius had decided to attack, in a deceitful manner, so great a man as the most distinguished Hoornbeeck, and indeed the whole cause of the Reformed, and to bring aid to the Paradox.

units.la: 3. Ad hominis autem tribunal provocaturus, rationem humanam in solio collocare, ac tantum non in cœlum efferre debuit. Ac proinde, quæ tertia Wolzogii thesis erit, rationi tam tuto fidi posse statuit, quam Deo ipsi, verboque divino. Imo, ac si multum, de eo, quo ratio abundet, Deo gratificaretur, à comparatione, cum rationis certitudine, verbi divini probat certitudinem. Ita ut, sic disserit, ne ratione quidem certius innitamur divinis dictis. Qui hæc dicit non magis falli aut fallere potest quam ipsa ratio. Si autem & hic in transitu Medicum audire lubet, sic ille, lumine naturali nihil certius datur. Wolzogio multum redhostimenti debet divina veritas, pari quippe certitudinis, cum Diva Philosophia, seu ratione humana, laude abipso cohonestata ac redimita. Fateor equidem, verum non esse vero contrarium, aut unum altero magis verum; æque enim verum est, quod naturali-ter est verum, quam quod supernaturaliter (subtili-tates Metaphysicorum, qui ut ens, sic & entis asse-ctiones, analogicè de Deo & creaturis, non univocè prædicant, hac vice non respicio) Dei tamen veraci-tatem, & tutam ejus verbis adhibitam fidem, à ra-tionis certitudine arguere, næ id præposterum est, si quicquam. Uno verbo. Ratio denotat, vel fa-cultatem ratiocinantem, vel veritates seu primas seu inde ortas, illa harum subjectum, hæ, in ordi-nem digestæ, Philosophiam constituentes, objecti vices obeunt, in ista consideratione. Verum enim vero certissimum est, pro facultatis nostræ consti-tutione, eam ad veritates cognoscendas, aliasque, ex cognitis, eliciendas, magis vel minus aptam es-se: & quoniam, quod à nemine, præter fastuosam Pelagii progeniem, non creditur, per peccatum nos admodum corrupti sumus, ita, ut spiritualiter mortui, vel in ipsis naturalibus, & circa ea, debili-tati simus valde, nec viribus reliquis, quantulæcun-que sint, bene utendis apti, sequitur non nimis multa de ratione nostra in isthoc statu, nisi nos i-psos vana spe lactare lubeat, expectanda esse. Probant id omnis ævi sapientum quærelæ, docent innumeræ Philosophorum sectæ, Scepticorum at-que Academicorum dubitationes, portentosissimi denique, omnis generis, errores, & horrenda, etiam de divinis, dogmata. Ut vel ipsa Scriptura, & Eu-angelica revelatione externa adjuti, Christum rite cognoscere non valuerint, sed pro stultitia, quæ-cunque de ipso dicerentur, habuerint; homines a-liàs, scientiâ, ut sibi imaginabantur, onusti. Non nego quædam & certo cognosci, sed numero pau-ca putem, & certitudine sæpius vacillante: non tanta saltem certitudine, ut, absque cœlestis verita-tis vituperio, tam diversa æquiparanda, invicemque, eo modo, comparanda fuerint, ac si Verbi Dei fir-mata & infallibilis veritas, à comparatione, cum rationis certitudine, probari posset satis decenter. Ratio, non in idea, sed prout in subjecto, consideranda est, quæ fallere potest, fallitque sæpissime: nunquam Dei verbum, aut veritas divina. Quæ ut in se certa est, & objectum fallere nescium menti offert, sic promissiones continet, qua fulti subjecti, facultatis corruptæ, ineptæque restitutionem, &, ad majora percipienda, coaptationem sperare datur: quod in philosophia, & homine naturali non obtinet: Videmus de primis veritatis regulis, quibus ea, absque fallendi periculo, dignosci queat, hactenus disputari inter Philosophos, & quas hodie tantopere à multis, inter quos cum Paradoxo, etiam numerandus venit Wolzogius, laudari & commendari videmus, magnam partem fallaces esse nullus dubito: specimina quædam, hoc ipso tractatu exhibuimus. Quoniam vero, immodicus laudis Philosophiæ ebuccinator Paradoxus, suis Antagonistis propterea vapulat, nihil addam ulterius; sufficit lectorem, imprudentiæ Wolzogianæ, etiam in hoc negotio, vidisse argumentum. Ad aliam thesin propero.
units.tr: 3. Wishing to appeal to the tribunal of man, he ought to have set human reason on a throne and all but raised it to heaven. So, in what will be Wolzogius's third thesis, he holds that reason may be trusted as safely as God himself and the divine Word. Indeed, as if he were doing God a great favour by granting that reason abounds in certainty, he proves the certainty of the divine Word by comparison with the certainty of reason. So that, as he argues, we do not rely on divine sayings even with greater certainty than on reason. One who says this can be no more deceived, or deceive, than reason itself. If we may hear the physician again in passing, he says: nothing is given more certain than the natural light. Divine truth owes Wolzogius great thanks, since by him it is given the same certainty as the goddess Philosophy, or human reason, and is adorned and crowned with its praise. I admit indeed that truth is not contrary to truth, nor one truth more true than another; for what is naturally true is just as true as what is supernaturally true. (I am not here taking account of the subtleties of the Metaphysicians, who predicate being and its affections analogically, not univocally, of God and creatures.) Still, to argue God's truthfulness, and the trustworthy faith we place in his words, from the certainty of reason is, if anything, backwards. In a word: "reason" denotes either the faculty of reasoning, or truths, whether first truths or those derived from them. The faculty is the subject, while the truths, arranged in order and constituting philosophy, play the part of the object in this consideration. It is quite certain that, according to the constitution of our faculty, it is more or less fit for knowing truths and drawing others from what is known. And since (as no one believes except the arrogant progeny of Pelagius) we have been greatly corrupted through sin, so that we are spiritually dead, or at least weakened in natural things and in our dealings with them, and not fit to use even the remaining powers well, however small they are, it follows that not much is to be expected from our reason in this state, unless we care to flatter ourselves with vain hope. The complaints of the wise of every age prove this; the countless sects of philosophers teach it, and so do the doubts of the Sceptics and Academics; finally, the most monstrous errors of every kind, and horrible doctrines even about divine things. Even when aided by Scripture itself and the external revelation of the gospel, they have not been able to know Christ rightly, but have regarded whatever was said about him as folly, though they were men laden with learning, as they imagined. I do not deny that some things are known with certainty, but I think these are few in number, and their certainty often wavers: not so great a certainty, at least, that, without disparaging heavenly truth, such diverse things can be equated and compared with one another in the way that the firm and infallible truth of the Word of God could be fairly proved by comparison with the certainty of reason. Reason must be considered not in its idea but as it is in the subject, which can deceive and very often does; never the Word of God or divine truth. As the latter is certain in itself and offers the mind an object that cannot deceive, so it contains promises by which a subject so supported may hope for the restoration of its corrupt and unfit faculty, and for its adaptation to perceive greater things. This does not hold in philosophy or in the natural man. We see that the first rules of truth, by which it can be discerned without danger of error, have hitherto been disputed among philosophers, and that many today, among whom Wolzogius must be numbered along with Paradoxus, praise and commend them. I have no doubt that for the most part they are fallacious; we have shown some specimens in this very treatise. But since Paradoxus, the immoderate trumpeter of praise for philosophy, is for that reason beaten by his antagonists, I will add nothing further. It is enough that the reader has seen the instance of Wolzogius's imprudence, even in this business. I hasten to another thesis.

units.la: 4. Præterquam in fundamentalibus nullum agnosco infallibilem interpretem. i. e. interpretandi normam, sic enim verba sumi debere priori libro probavimus; Quem errorem, antea satis superque refutatum, hic solummodo repetere ob materiæ indolem debui.
units.tr: 4. Apart from fundamental matters, I acknowledge no infallible interpreter. That is, a norm of interpretation; for so the words must be understood, as we proved in the first book. Because of the nature of the subject, I had to repeat here this error, which was already refuted sufficiently and more than enough earlier.

units.la: §. Sequitur ergo thesis quinta, qua ad Enthusiastas relegat, quotquot ex eo, quod quisque sit suorum verborum interpres optimus, Deum Scripturæ Interpretem esse contendunt. Negatque, imo nullis argumentis adduci se patitur, ut credat, Scripturam esse interpretem Scripturæ. Adeo ut satis confectum esse putet, non fuisse huc illud addu-cendum, quisque suorum verborum optimus Interpres. Pagina præcedente serió cavet, ne eo adigatur: nec quia facimus Interpretationis judicem usum, ideo Deum facimus interpretem. Et ubi de Interprete Scripturæ ptura agitatur , velle proferre Scripturam , id mihi videtur , si quicquam, præpostere fieri.Negamus Deum dici posse proprie Scripturarum Interpretem. Et Spi-ritus quidem Sanctus creditus fuit nonnullis (Cha-mierum citaverat & Scarpium, quos, pro sua stu-piditate, diversum quid à reliquis Reformatorum Theologis sentire somniaverat Paradoxus) aperi-re sensum Scripturarum, illaque fidelibus interpreta-ri. NB. Quam sententiam explodit jure merito Ex-ercitator, & merum Enthusiasmum continere statuo. Proponenda hæc solummodo hic erant,fusè discus-fa suis quæque locis; nisi ex suo ore confutatum velit Wolzogium lector, sic αὐτοκατάκριτον [?] alibi veritate victum. Quando Scripturæ sui ipsius tri-buitur Interpretatio, non excluduntur interpretandi regulæ, quia sanè censentur in ea lingua includi qua-sunt conscriptæ Scripturæ: sed intelligitur secundum illas regulas, ex ipso verborum contextu fieri debere Interpretationem. Idque de universa Scriptura intelli-gendum. Singula autem loca per alia loca, instituta collatione, debent explicari. Quo sensu cum sciat Reformatos loqui, modo id verum, quod dicunt, credat,quid obluctatur,quid reprehendit, quid cul-pat,mirus disputator.
units.tr: §. Next comes the fifth thesis, by which he relegates to the Enthusiasts all who contend that God is the interpreter of Scripture because each person is the best interpreter of his own words. He denies, indeed he cannot be brought by any arguments to believe, that Scripture is the interpreter of Scripture. So much so that he thinks it is sufficiently settled that this should not have been adduced, that each is the best interpreter of his own words. On the preceding page he seriously takes care not to be driven to it: nor, because we make use of a judge of interpretation, do we therefore make God the interpreter. And where the interpreter of Scripture is under discussion, to wish to bring forward Scripture seems to me, if anything, backwards. We deny that God can properly be called the interpreter of the Scriptures. And the Holy Spirit indeed was believed by some (Chamier had cited, and Scarpius, whom Paradoxus, in his stupidity, had dreamed held a different view from the other Reformed theologians) to open the sense of the Scriptures and to interpret them to the faithful. NB. This opinion is rightly exploded by the Exercitator, and I judge it to contain pure Enthusiasm. These points were only to be set out here; each was discussed at length in its own place. Unless the reader wishes Wolzogius refuted from his own mouth, thus self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτον], overcome elsewhere by the truth. When interpretation is attributed to Scripture itself, the rules of interpretation are not excluded, because they are of course held to be included in the language in which Scripture was written; but it is understood that, according to those rules, interpretation must be made from the context of the words themselves. And this is to be understood of the whole of Scripture. Individual passages, however, must be explained by other passages, by making comparison. Since he knows the Reformed speak in this sense, provided he believes that what they say is true, what, then, does this marvellous disputant struggle against, what does he rebuke, what does he blame?

units.la: 6. Sexto, sic de ratione Philosophatur, ut plus quam instrumentalem usum in Scripturæ Inter-pretatione ei tribuat. Nolumus, inquit, hic usum rationis instrumentalem, quem vocant, asserere, quem præsupponimus. Ipsa enim Interpretatio, quæ sensum orationis cum verbis conjungit, quia judicio debet & intelligentia fieri, non potest sine ratione fieri. Bene se habent ista,nec est quod ista probet, at recte mo-net, principem difficultatem in eo minime versari: instrumentalem enim usum non negant Theologi Orthodoxi,de solo formali quæstio est. Petunt a-licubi Walemburgii Fratres, ut doceamus, Refor-matos non uti propositionibus à ratione, nisi uttanquam sola instrumenta ostendant veritatemconnexionum. Dixeram, inquit Coccejus,cum Au-gustino, gustino veritatem connexionum non institutam, sed animadversam esse ab hominibus & notatam, ut eam possint vel discere vel docere. Sed, inquit, ostendendum erat, Reformatos ratione uti ut instru-mento mero. Nonne claris verbis dixeram, fidem requirere σύνεσιν[?], ut instrumentum; & eam animad-vertere rerum rationem ? Dum hoc dixi, nonne satis ostendi, NB. omnem rerum rationem observatam non nisi ut instrumentum accedere ad fidem; non ut propter rationes notas credamus, sed &c. Concedunt ipsi, licere uti praepositionibus à ratione, Exam.Colon. editi 1664.pag. 62. lin. 12. si id licet, utique licet vel ad fundandam fidem, vel NB. tantum, ut sit instrumentum ad cognoscendum id, quod Deus per ver-bum suum testatur ad fidem. Utrique primum nega-mus: restat secundum. Hinc & alibi de Interpre-tatione sic instituit. Qui loquitur, ut Prophetans, sive narrator eorum, quæ Deus locutus est, ne egre-diator cancellos sermonis Dei, ut principii sive testi-monii. Nam etiamsi de eo, quod de Deo notum est, possumus loqui etiam cum gentibus, tamen de eis, quæ Deus revelavit, nihil nisi ex ore h.e. sermone Dei lo-qui possumus. Fides credit Deo & testimonio ipsius, & id non egreditur. Quare merito, & hisce con-sentiens, Hoornbeekius: An ratio judicet norma-liter; hoc quæritur; quorum verborum author tan-to majoris in toto hoc negotio faciendus est, quan-to majorem accuratioremque curam, atque indu-striam, in controversiis Socinianis discutiendis, de-monstravit, ipsiusque opera, majori cum applausu, ab omnibus Reformatæ doctrinæ amatoribus, ap-probata est. Wolzogius præterea regulam, quod idem est,ac si normam diceret, ducemque rationem dicere non veretur, imo regulam suppeditare ad quam res omnes etiam quæ sola revelatione inno-tescunt, sint exigendæ. Notandum vero in ante-cessum, quando rationi instrumentalis usus tribui-tur,eam tunc sumi pro subjecto recipiente, pro ea mentis facultate, quam aliàs intellectum vocamus: axiomata autem & veritates denotat, quando nor-ma dicitur aut regula. Adeo ut, accuratioris di-ctionis ergo, posteriore significatu, Philosophiam dicere liceat, quatenus eo denotat ordinatam veri-tatum naturâ cognoscibilium, atque artificiosam congeriem : quapropter Wolzògius, quod hic ra-tioni, alibi Philosophiæ adscribit. Ratio, inquit, ea disceptat, quæ Philosophiæ sunt. In refutatione eti-am adversarii, jam rationem, jam Philosopiam, pro-miscuè nominat. Vocem autem istam in hac dis-sertatione studio omisit, ne nimis manifestus com-periretur cum Paradoxo consensus. Nobis igitur vi-tio verti non poterit, si voces Synonimas, in hoc negotio, promiscuè sumserimus. Quod igitur ra-tioni ultra usum instrumentalem, quem præstat in omni, sive ea simplex sit, sive discursiva aut judi-cativa, perceptione, datur, id philosophiæ, quatenus ea denotat axiomata naturalia, tam prima, quam ex iis, ratiocinationis ope, educta, datum esse censeri debet. Hunc in modum, de rationis, seu Philoso-phiæ usu noster disserit. A Scriptura quidem una, à ratione vero, seu Philosophia, altera interpretan-dæ Scripturæ regula petenda est. Ad quam regulam, res omnes, facili negotio, exigantur. Alio loco, postquam usum rationis instrumentalem præsupponi dixerat, sic de normali loquitur, ducem quærimus, ministræ rationi, hoc est, rationi ut instrumento, normam quærimus & regulam, at dux est, & ministra sæpe ratio, hoc est, norma est & instrumentum sæpe ratio. Ut ratio sumta pro intellectu, sæpius in Scripturæ interpretatione, rationem, sumtam pro Philosophia, ducis normæque loco habeat : ut omnia, NB. nihil enim prorsus excipio, ut omnia, cujuscunque generis sint, revocet ad examen, videatque, an quicquam, eorum quæ putamus inesse Scripturis, sit manifestæ rationi contrarium. Idque non, post erutum Scripturæ sensum, absque ejus ullo præjudicio, aut arrogato, in ipsam Scripturæ Interpretationem, arbitrio, ut eo melius adversariis, contradictiones forsan veritati Scripturariæ affingentibus, eatur obviam: sed ante sensum elicitum & quidem sic, ut, in eliciendo sensu, ista ratio, seu Philosophia, pro arbitrio, regulâ, normáque sit & supicienda ac adhibenda. Quod, tam ex hac thesi, & sequentibus, Wolzogianis simul & Socinianis, universæ Scripturæ interpretandæ, Canonibus: quam ex aliis hujus libelli locis patet: sic res rationi disceptandas esse asserit, non ut instrumento solum- modo, ait pagina sequente, de instrumentali usu enim princeps difficultas non est, ducem quærimus instrumento, ac ministro: & deinde ut verba usus, sic ratio res ipsas disceptat, quæ certè norma- lem,& regulantem,ac antecedaneum, ut ita loquar, rationis seu Philosophiæ fundant usum: Hinc uti usus loquendi orationem, qui procul dubio id facit ut norma & regula prior ac superior, sic res quæ illa oratione traduntur ratio dijudicat. Adeo ut, quod hic ratio præstat, seu Philosophia, rationis vocet alicubi jurisdictionem, imo imperium. Ac tandem, nisi de normali usu loqueretur, aliis locis, quidnam rationi committendum, quid non, disquirere non posset, quoniam rationi, instrumenti instar consideratæ, quicquam subtrahi absurdissimum est. Verum ut sciamus, quousque hoc rationis sese extendat arbitrium, universaliter loquitur, cum dicit, omnia, cujuscunque generis sint, ad examen rationis esse revocanda. Hæc genuina Wolzogii sententia est, Reformatorum doctrinæ è diametro adversa, & Socinianæ exactissimè similis. Ratio interpretandæ Scripturæ regulam suppeditat, ad quam res omnes, omnes veritates, quas inesse Scripturæ putamus, ante erutum sensum, tanquam normam exigendæ sunt, ut, ne perversus, Scripturæ verbis, sensus inferatur. Sic Wolzogius. Contra-rium vero Reformati, quod vel ex uno Heidano abundè videre est. Quicunque, ait ille, in religionis negotio non hunc scopum sibi proponit, ut NB. tantum iis quæ Deus ad salutem in verbo suo revelavit, arctè inhærere inhærere decreverit, iisque suam credulitatem inædi-ficare: sed rationis propriæ modulo & ductu omnia metiri & dijudicare præsumit: hunc necesse est, cum à se omnem religionis normam mutuetur, vel perpetuo & in omnibus à Deo dissidere, & suis cogitationibus cogitationes Dei elidere: vel si in aliquibus, quod in valde paucis, iisque tantum NB. in quibus ratio con-sonat revelationi, (at exerte in reliquis alium Scripturæ & commodiorem sensum excogitandum dictat noster.) contingere necesse est. Deo dignas cogi-tationes & voluntati ejus conformes fovere depre-henditur, eum casu potius, quam certa & non fallaci via huc devenisse. Hoc vero non est rationem suam subjicere verbo, sed verbum rationi. Et cum verba sint signa conceptuum, quibus mentem nostram, aliis communicamus, quicunque verbis vim facit, rem ipsam, quantum in se est, tollit, & luci tenebras offundit. Et cum solus Christus in Ecclesia audiendus sit, qui quæ in sinu Dei apud Patrem vidit & audivit, enunciare & enarrare solus poterit, non est homini commit-tendum, ut rationem suam sibi in consilium (arbitrium dicit Wolzogen, regulam, ducem pro ju-risdictione agentem) adhibeat ut secundum ejus dictamen statuat, an ita se res habeat vel non: sed ut contrario processu, ex revelatione de re credenda sta-tuat. Secus si sit, ἀιχμαλωτίζεταί[?] πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τῆς χριστοῦ[?]. Nec unius Christi magisterium agnoscitur: sed fit quisque sibi fidei magister, & ratio evehitur in solium Dei. Quod qui tentat, ex fumo suo lucem dari cogitat. Idem ejus quondam Collega Hoornbeekius. Rationem, sic ille, hic adhiberi, ut instrumentum extra controversiam est, ut bene notat Wolzogius; sed rationem ideo audire, ut argumen-tum, vel normam secundum quam decisio fiat de mente S. Scripturæ, hæc est prodigiosissima μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος, atque tam indignum Scripturæ, quam in se improbum, quod ratio sibi ausit istud arrogare. Nec abnuit Spanhemius. Aliud, sic inquit, ratio-cinatione uti, ut instrumento ad deprehendendam veri-
units.tr: Sixthly, he philosophises about reason in such a way as to grant it more than an instrumental use in the interpretation of Scripture. "We do not want to assert," he says, "the instrumental use of reason, as they call it, which we presuppose. For interpretation itself, which joins the sense of a discourse to its words, must be done by judgment and understanding, and so cannot be done without reason." These statements are sound, and there is no reason to dispute them, but he rightly warns that "the principal difficulty does not lie in this at all." For the orthodox theologians do not deny the instrumental use; the question concerns only the formal use. Elsewhere the Walemburg brothers ask us "to teach" that the Reformed do not use propositions from reason except as mere instruments that show the truth of connections. "I had said," says Coccejus, "with Augustine," that the truth of connections is not instituted but observed and noted by men, so that they may either learn or teach it. But, he says, "it was necessary to show that the Reformed use reason as a mere instrument. Had I not said in plain words" that faith requires understanding [σύνεσιν] as an instrument, and that it notices the reasoning of things? "Since I have said this, have I not sufficiently shown, NB, that all observed reasoning of things comes to faith only as an instrument; not that we believe because of reasons known to us, but &c. They concede themselves that it is lawful to use propositions from reason (Examen Colon. edited 1664, p. 62, line 12). If that is allowed, then surely it is allowed either to found faith, or NB only that it be an instrument for knowing what God testifies through his word for faith. We deny the first; the second remains." Hence, and elsewhere, he sets out the matter of interpretation thus: "He who speaks as a prophet, or narrates the things God has spoken, must not go beyond the bounds of God's word as his principle or testimony. For even if we can speak with the Gentiles about what is known of God, yet about the things God has revealed we can speak only out of the mouth, that is, the word, of God." Faith believes God and his testimony, and does not go beyond it. Therefore, rightly and agreeing with these things, Hoornbeek: "Whether reason judges normally is what is asked. The author of these words is to be held in so much greater esteem in this whole business, as he has shown greater and more accurate care and diligence in refuting the Socinian controversies, and his work has been approved with great applause by all lovers of Reformed doctrine." Moreover, Wolzogen does not hesitate to call reason "a rule, which is the same as if he called it a norm and a guiding principle," and indeed to supply "a rule to which all things, even those made known by revelation alone, must be brought." It must be noted beforehand, however, that when an instrumental use is assigned to reason, it is then taken for the receiving subject, for that faculty of the mind which we otherwise call the intellect; but when it is called a norm or rule, it denotes axioms and truths. So for the sake of more exact speech, it is permissible in the latter sense to call it philosophy, insofar as the word denotes the ordered and skilfully assembled body of truths knowable by nature. That is why Wolzogen ascribes to philosophy what here he ascribes to reason. "Reason," he says, "judges those things which belong to philosophy." Even in refuting his opponent he names now reason, now philosophy, indiscriminately. In this dissertation, however, he deliberately omitted the word, lest the agreement with the Paradox be found too plain. So we cannot be blamed if in this business we use synonymous words indiscriminately. Therefore whatever is given to reason beyond the instrumental use which it exercises in every perception, whether simple, discursive, or judgmental, must be considered as given to philosophy, insofar as that denotes natural axioms, both first principles and those drawn from them by the aid of reasoning. In this way our author discourses about the use of reason, or philosophy. "The one rule of interpreting Scripture is to be sought from Scripture, but the other from reason, or philosophy. All things are to be brought to this rule with easy effort." In another place, after saying that the instrumental use of reason is presupposed, he speaks thus of the normative use: "We seek a guide, a minister to reason, that is, a norm and rule for reason as an instrument; but reason is often the guide and minister, that is, reason is often the norm and the instrument." So reason, taken for the intellect, often has in the interpretation of Scripture the place of guide and norm, which reason taken for philosophy holds: "that all things, NB, for I except nothing at all, that all things, of whatever kind, be referred to examination, and that one see whether anything we think to be in the Scriptures is contrary to manifest reason." And this is not done after the sense of Scripture has been drawn out, without any prejudice to it or any arrogated arbitrariness in the very interpretation of Scripture, so that contradictions, perhaps imputed by the adversaries to the truth of Scripture, may be the better met; but before the sense is elicited, and indeed in such a way that in eliciting the sense this reason, or philosophy, is to be used as the arbiter, rule, and norm, and be presupposed and applied. This is plain both from this thesis and the following ones, and from other places in this little book: Wolzogen asserts that "things are to be disputed by reason," not as a mere instrument, as he says on the following page. For it is not about the instrumental use that the chief difficulty lies: "we seek a guide, a minister as instrument." And then, as "usage disputes the words," so "reason disputes the things themselves," which certainly establishes a normative and governing, and, as I may say, antecedent use of reason or philosophy. Hence, as "usage of speech" (which without doubt does this as the prior and superior norm and rule), so "reason judges the things which are conveyed by that speech." So that what reason, or philosophy, does here, he elsewhere calls "jurisdiction," and even "empire." Finally, unless he were speaking of the normative use, he could not in other places inquire what must be committed to reason and what not, since it is most absurd to take anything away from reason when it is considered as an instrument. But that we may know how far this authority of reason extends, he speaks universally when he says that "all things, of whatever kind, are to be referred to the examination of reason." This is the genuine opinion of Wolzogen, utterly opposed to the doctrine of the Reformed, and most exactly like the Socinian one. Reason supplies a rule for interpreting Scripture, to which all things, all truths which we think to be in Scripture, are to be demanded as a norm before the sense is drawn out, so that a perverse sense may not be inferred from the words of Scripture. So Wolzogen. The Reformed, on the contrary, as one may see abundantly from Heidanus alone: "Whoever, he says, in the business of religion does not propose to himself this aim, namely NB only to cling closely to those things which God has revealed in his word for salvation, and to build up his belief in them, but presumes to measure and judge all things by the measure and guidance of his own reason, he must necessarily, since he borrows every norm of religion from himself, either dissent from God perpetually and in all things, and cancel God's thoughts by his own; or, if in some things, which only in very few, and NB only those in which reason agrees with revelation (but he dictates that in the rest another and more convenient sense of Scripture must be devised), it happens that he cherishes thoughts worthy of God and conformed to his will, he is found to have arrived there by chance rather than by a certain and infallible way. But this is not to subject one's reason to the word, but the word to reason. And since words are signs of concepts, by which we communicate our mind to others, whoever does violence to words removes the thing itself, as far as it is in him, and pours darkness over the light. And since only Christ is to be heard in the Church, who alone could declare and relate what he saw and heard in the bosom of God with the Father, it is not to be committed to man that he should take his reason as counsel (Wolzogen says arbitrium, a rule acting as a guide for jurisdiction) in order to decide by its dictate whether things are so or not; but by the contrary process he should decide from revelation about the thing to be believed. If it were otherwise, "every thought is brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ [αἰχμαλωτίζεται πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ]." Nor is the teaching of Christ alone acknowledged, but each one becomes a teacher of faith to himself, and reason is raised to the throne of God. Whoever attempts this thinks that light is given out of his own smoke." The same, his former colleague Hoornbeek: "That reason be employed here as an instrument is beyond dispute, as Wolzogen rightly notes; but to hear reason for this reason, as an argument or a norm by which the decision about the mind of Holy Scripture is made, this is a most monstrous transition to another kind [μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος], and as unworthy of Scripture as it is in itself wicked, that reason should dare to arrogate this to itself." Nor does Spanheim deny it: "It is one thing to use reasoning as an instrument for detecting the truth of connections, and another to use it as the measure of doctrines. The former must be done, the latter not. So that all reasonings must hold Scripture as their mistress and measure. Our weapons are the holy Scriptures. Only their selection and application..."

units.la: Spanh. Disp. de Conseq. Disput. Lxvii.§. 12. tatem connexionum, aliud eâ uti, ut mensura dogma-tum. Prius fieri debet, posterius non item. Ut omnia ratiocinia Scripturam habere debeant pro Domina & mensura. Arma nostra sunt Scripturæ sacræ. Delectus tantum & applicatio istorum armorum instituitur per ratiocinationes. Et merito à Deo destruuntur ratiocinationes, quæ se non submittunt revelationi, & instrumenta tantum sunt ejus melius & percipiendæ & explicandæ ac applicandæ. Periculosum enim nimis est, ait Cartwrigthus, in rebus fidei, rationi nostræ inniti, ℨ[?] illam veluti regulam & judicem rerum sacrarum constituere. Non aliud, sic Dallæus, (etiam ubi rationis usum, adversus Neomethodistas Pontificios, defendit) rationi nostræ jus vindicamus: quam ut ei liceat oculos aperire, verbumque divinum intueri, & quid in eo Deus offerat, ac proponat, & religiose & diligenter inspicere. Nempe, in illis quæ Theologicæ revelationis sunt, judicatur contradictio admitti, siquidem statuatur aliquid quod contra illam S. revelationem est; non, an dissonet à ratione: uti disserit Hoornbeek l. cit. p. 106. Tam longe ab isto normali arbitrio abest Vir Doctiss.
units.tr: Spanh. Disp. de Conseq. Disput. Lxvii. §. 12. It is one thing to use reasoning as an instrument for discerning the truth of connections, and another to use it as the measure of doctrines. The former ought to be done, the latter not. Thus all reasonings ought to have Scripture as their mistress and measure. Our weapons are the holy Scriptures. Only the selection and application of these weapons is carried out through reasonings. Reasonings that do not submit themselves to revelation are rightly destroyed by God, and are merely instruments of it, to be better perceived, explained and applied. For it is too dangerous, says Cartwright, in matters of faith to lean on our reason, and to set it up as it were as the rule and judge of sacred things. Dallaeus says much the same (even where he defends the use of reason against the Neomethodist Papists): we claim a right for our reason, that it may be allowed to open its eyes, to behold the divine word, and to examine religiously and diligently what God offers and sets forth in it. Certainly, in those things which belong to theological revelation, contradiction is judged to be admitted if it is laid down that something is against that holy revelation; not whether it dissonates from reason. So Hoornbeek argues in the work cited, p. 106. The learned man is as far from that normal judgment as can be.

units.la: Notatu digna sunt, quæ alicubi ex Chrysostomo referuntur. in 1. ad The. Hom.7. Divinis nisi[?] Scripturis, navis instar, vela fidei in sublime extendamus. Si in istis navigaverimus, aderit etiam nobis gubernator filius Dei. Si vero cogitationibus humanis innatabimus, non item. Quare non Scripturam ad rationem, sed omnem humanam sapientiam ad Scripturam examinari atque exigi oportere, Censet Confessio Gallicana. Quemadmodum Philosophiam seu rationem humanam è navicula projiciendam dicit Baco Verulamius, quando Scripturæ & Theologiæ sacrarium versus iter meditatur quispiam, ubi fides facit, ut, hoc sensu, non sit opus ratione, quæ verba sua fecit Heidanus. Neque, quæ idem ex Augustino refert, enim est, de illa majestate divinæ sapientiæ, humanæ vanitatis arbitrio disputandum. Nihil certe magis inauditum in Scholis Reformatorum est, quam in eruendo Scripturæ sensu, dictamina ratio-nis in antecessum consulere & ex ejus arbitrio pen-dere. Imo nec deinceps nimis multum, in conci-liandis, cum rationis dictamine, mysteriis, operæ locandum censent nostri, non enim religionis capita ad rationem trahenda sunt, tam ut cum ratione concilientur; quam quidem, ut ratio se submittat, & componat ad Scripturam: quoties enim conciliare ista non possumus, culpamus potius ingenium nostrum, ejusque stupiditatem, vel errorem, quam veritatem, Hoornb. p. 123. L. cit. Accusaverat Author istius Brevis disquisitionis Reformatos Atheismi, hanc au-tem thesin Atheismo propiorem opponit Hoornbeeckius, qua Socinani dicunt. Ratio nostra judex & norma est illorum, quæ etiam in Scriptura nobis credenda proponuntur. A qua thesi quam longe ab-fit Wolzogius, qui omnia rationi examinanda tradit, ejusque arbitrium & regulam, in interpretatione Scripturæ, agnoscit, ipse videat: ego saltem, multum diversitatis à Socinianorum sententia in isto libello hactenus deprehendere ne quidem omni studio potui, neque id poterit, qui à præjudiciis immunem adfert animum. Audivimus Wolzogiana, in alia euntes vidimus Reformatos, jam Sociniani ipsi audiendi restant: quo facto in proclivi erit ju-dicare, utri parti, propius accedat hic scriptor. Sic nostram sententiam, quam sibi oppugnandam præ-figunt, concipiunt: Deinde, sunt verba Brevis disquisitionis, quibus nostram recenset sententiam, in eo etiam non leviter peccant, quod ita Jolas sacras literas pro norma fidei ponant; ut principia veritatis, sive natura nota, sive è rerum consideratione deducta, Philosophica vocant, inde excludant. Solent enim alios vehementer eo nomine reprehendere, quod NB. Theologica ad Principia Philosophica exigant. Quod aperte faciendum dictat Wolzogius, qui omnia prius ad rationis examen, quo Scriptura rite ex-plicetur, revocanda docet. Eodem modo dictus Socinianus. Caterum, inquit, ad sacrarum literavum[?] genuinam mentem dignoscendam principia etiam illa, quae Philosophica appellant, advocanda sunt: Quae verba, ut Socinianum sensum pandentia, ci-tantur Hoornbeckio. Neque sese expediet noster, si dicat, se Scripturam examine majorem, ab omni superiori arbitrio immunem, quoties de ejus sensu constiterit, statuere, sed jam de interpretatione agi, quae rationis operam, imo arbitrium, quin jurisdi-ctionem non patitur solum, sed requirit. Eodem modo Schlichtingius apud eundem Hoornbee-kium. Non in id adhibenda ratio est, quasi Scripturae aliquid affirmanti vel neganti aliquid opponi possit: sed tantum ad declarandum, an quidpiam Scripturae contineat: si continere constet, quidquid tandem ratio contradicat, falli eam necesse est. Neque enim nos ad rationem recurrimus, quoties Scriptura contrarium aperte testatur, sed quoties de Scripturae mente dubitatur. In eo ista Wolzogianis meliora, quod in quibusdam tantam ponant perspicuitatem, ut ad rationis incudem ea revocare non sit necesse aut decorum, cum Wolzogius OMNIA, nihilo excepto, examinanda rationi tradat. Cum dubitatur, inquit porro homo Socinianus, an rem eo pacto se habere Scriptura definierit nec ne; rationem velle rejicere, quid aliud est; quam in tenebris lucem extinguere? &c. Et alibi nunquam ad rationis judicium confugimus quoties de Scripturae mente constat, sed cum vel de sensu Scripturae, vel de veritate dogmatis alicujus dubitatur. Atque hoc sensu, ad insipientes merito referendi sunt; qui dogmata fidei ad rationis examen admitti nolunt, dicit idem Hæreti- cus. A quibus, quantum distet Wolzogii sententia, scire velim, ego certe, si exactiorem comparationem instituere necesse sit, ostendere, facili negotio potero, Schlightingium non absurdiora, in isto negotio, docuisse, quam Ludovicum Wolzogium scripsisse vidimus. Sed tandem praetereundum non est, vel se ipso judice, idem revera Wolzogium sentire, cum suo Paradoxo, cujus sententiae summam sic proponit, antequam, quid scriptura velit innuere, percipiat, penes se putat, & rationem suam normam esse earum veritatum ad quas exigi sacra oratio debeat. Atque jam dudum probatum dedimus, Wolzogium ante erutum sensum, & quò bene sua cedat interpretatio, itidem, omnia, omnia nihilo excepto, cujuscunque tandem generis sint, ad rationis examen esse revocanda docere; quod procul omni dubio, unum idemque est, cum eo, quod hic ut summam sententiae Paradoxae rejicit. Ut jam argumentis Wolzogius refutandus vix videatur, qui ipse destruxit in calce, ea quae falso posuerat in initio. Neque id insolens est, tectis veritatis hostibus, ut in conflictu evadant se ipsis orthodoxoteroi, & ne palam cum adversariis idem sentire comperiantur, saepe sua ipsorum destruant themata. Res tota sua se luce ulterius conspiciendam offeret, si hujus Sociniano-Wolzogianae theseos sequentia, ejusdem commatis, considerentur quasi consectaria, & canones ex thesi supradicta sua sponte, & ex Wolzogii dictamine, propullulantes,
units.tr: Worth noting are the things cited somewhere from Chrysostom, in the first homily on 1 Thessalonians, hom. 7: Unless we spread the sails of faith on high, like a ship, in the divine Scriptures, we shall not be able to sail. If we sail in them, the Son of God will be our helmsman as well. But if we swim out into human thoughts, he will not be. Hence the Gallican Confession holds that not Scripture is to be examined and brought to the standard of reason, but every human wisdom must be examined and held to Scripture. As Bacon of Verulam says that philosophy, or human reason, must be thrown out of the little boat when someone sets out on the journey towards the sanctuary of Scripture and theology, where faith does the work, so that in this sense there is no need of reason; Heidanus made these words his own. Nor (what he likewise cites from Augustine) is there to be disputed, by the judgment of human vanity, concerning that majesty of divine wisdom. Certainly nothing is more unheard of in the schools of the Reformed than to consult the dictates of reason beforehand in drawing out the sense of Scripture, and to depend on its judgment. Indeed our people also think that not much labour should be spent, in reconciling the mysteries with the dictate of reason.
