For the chief points of religion are not to be dragged to reason, so that they may be reconciled with reason; rather, reason is to submit and conform itself to Scripture. For whenever we cannot reconcile these things, we blame our own intellect and its dullness or error, rather than the truth, Hoornbeek, p. 123, in the work cited. The author of this Brief Inquiry had accused the Reformed of atheism, but Hoornbeek opposes to it a thesis closer to atheism, which the Socinians hold: our reason is the judge and norm of those things which are also proposed to us in Scripture to be believed. How far Wolzogius is from this thesis, he himself may see. I, at least, have not been able, even with all my zeal, to find in this little book so far any great difference from the opinion of the Socinians, nor will anyone be able to do so who brings to it a mind free from prejudice. We have heard Wolzogius; we have seen the Reformed going the other way; the Socinians themselves remain to be heard. Once this is done, it will be easy to judge which side this writer comes closer to. They frame our opinion, which they set themselves to attack, thus. Next, these are the words of the Brief Inquiry in which they recount our opinion, they also sin not lightly in this, that they so make the holy letters the norm of faith as to exclude from them the principles of truth, whether known by nature or deduced from the consideration of things, which they call philosophical. For they are accustomed to rebuke others vehemently on this ground, that NB. they bring theological matters to philosophical principles. This is what Wolzogius openly dictates should be done, he who teaches that everything must first be referred to the examination of reason, by which Scripture is duly explained. The Socinian in the same way says: Moreover, for discerning the genuine mind of the sacred letters, those principles also which they call philosophical must be called upon. These words, as revealing the Socinian sense, are cited from Hoornbeek. Nor will our author extricate himself if he says that he decides about Scripture, which is greater than any examination and free from every higher judgment, whenever its sense has been established; but now the question is about interpretation, which not only admits, but requires, the labour of reason, indeed its judgment and even its jurisdiction. In the same way Schlichting, in the same Hoornbeek: Reason is not to be applied in such a way as if something could be set against Scripture when it affirms or denies something; it is only to be used for declaring whether something is contained in Scripture. If it is established that it is contained, then whatever reason may contradict, it must necessarily be mistaken. For we do not have recourse to reason whenever Scripture openly testifies to the contrary, but whenever doubt is cast on the mind of Scripture. In this respect these Socinian statements are better than Wolzogius's, in that they assert such clarity in some matters that it is neither necessary nor fitting to bring them to the anvil of reason; whereas Wolzogius hands over ALL things, nothing excepted, to be examined by reason. When it is doubted, the Socinian man goes on, whether Scripture has defined that the thing is so or not, what else is it to wish to reject reason than to extinguish the light in darkness? etc. And elsewhere: We never flee to the judgment of reason whenever the mind of Scripture is established, but only when doubt arises either about the sense of Scripture or about the truth of some doctrine. And in this sense, those who are unwilling to admit the doctrines of faith to the examination of reason are rightly to be counted among the foolish, says the same heretic. How far Wolzogius's opinion differs from these, I should like to know; I for my part, if a more exact comparison has to be made, shall be able to show with ease that Schlichting taught nothing more absurd on this matter than what we have seen Ludwig Wolzogius write. But in the end it must not be passed over that, even by his own judgment, Wolzogius really holds the same view as in his paradox, the sum of which he puts thus: before he perceives what Scripture wishes to imply, he thinks that the rule of the truths to which the sacred discourse ought to be brought lies with himself, namely his own reason. And we have already shown long ago that Wolzogius teaches that, before the sense is drawn out and in order that his interpretation may turn out well, all things, all things, nothing excepted, of whatever kind they may be, must be referred to the examination of reason. Without doubt this is one and the same thing as what he here rejects as the sum of the paradoxical opinion. So Wolzogius hardly seems to need refuting by argument, since at the end he himself destroys what he had falsely laid down at the beginning. Nor is it unusual, when the enemies of truth are hidden, that in the conflict they escape by making themselves appear more orthodox than others, and, so as not to be found openly agreeing with their adversaries, they often destroy their own theses. The whole matter will appear more clearly in its own light if the consequences of this Socinian-Wolzogian thesis are considered, as corollaries of the same kind, and canons which spring up from the thesis above of their own accord and from the dictate of Wolzogius.

units.la: 1. Primus eorum sic sonat, Ratio, seu Philosophia, definire saepe potest, an aliquis sensus conveniat verbis, nec ne conveniat. Idque, quia prae reliquis scriptis omnibus, ea est singularis scriptorum divinorum constitutio, ut meram contineant veritatem, de qua judicare quoque potest ratio. Reformati è contra Socinianum & falsum dicunt, ullibi rationem judicare & determinare, secundum se, & suam normam, de sensu sacrae Scripturae. Etenim hoc jam non est rationem adferre ut instrumentum solum, quo sensum percipias, & vel manum, qua apprehendas; sed imo ut argumentum, juxta quod de sensu Scripturae judices: aliud enim est dicere de doctrina aliqua, ejusque veritate, quae per rationem probari quoque potest, ut inquiratur vel ut sequamur id, quod convenientissimum etiam rationi visum sit; at ubi NB. de sensu verborum quaeritur, ut sic, ibi non videndum quid primo conveniat rationi; sed unicè quid menti & intentioni di[?]centis; nisi velis sensa dictorum ad examen rationis vocare & æstimare; quam esse Socinianorum & Remonstrantium sententiam vel hinc evincimus &c.
units.tr: 1. The first of these runs thus: Reason, or philosophy, can often define whether some sense agrees with the words or not. And this is so because, beyond all other writings, the divine writers have this unique constitution, that they contain pure truth, about which reason too can judge. The Reformed, on the contrary, say that the Socinian view is false: that reason nowhere judges and determines, of itself and by its own norm, the sense of holy Scripture. For this is no longer to bring in reason merely as an instrument by which you perceive the sense, and as a hand by which you grasp it; but rather as an argument by which you judge the sense of Scripture. For it is one thing to speak of some doctrine and its truth, which can also be proved by reason, so that it may be inquired into, or so that we may follow what has seemed most agreeable even to reason; but when the question is about the sense of the words as such, then one must not consider what first agrees with reason, but solely what agrees with the mind and intention of the speaker; unless you wish to call the meanings of statements to the examination and assessment of reason, which we prove is the opinion of the Socinians and Remonstrants even from this, etc.

units.la: Non enim, ut ex Heidano audivimus, est homini committendum, ut rationem suam sibi in consilium adhibeat, ut secundum ejus dictamen statuat, an ita se res habeat vel non: sed ut contrario processu ex revelatione de re credenda statuat. Et, si Scripturæ constitutionem respiciat noster, ea talis est, ut habeat authorem Deum, cujus verba, non decet, ut, à rationis humanæ dictamine normali, sensum accersant; quippe tali modo, tali constitutione scripta, ac ornata, ut, sibi mutuo facem accendentia, ipsa suum pandant sensum, mentemque detegant; adeo, ut rationis normali dictamine nunquam indigeant, ad salutem sapientes reddere apta. Sed sui immemor hic est Wolzogius, dum meram veritatem continere Scripturam dicit de qua judicare quoque possit ratio, Alibi enim negat 1. meram veritatem Scripturâ contineri, & 2. si vel meram contineret veritatem, eam tamen omnem ad rationis tribunal revocari posse. Nescio qui fieri potuerit, ut, in rebus, quæ totam involvunt controversiæ summam, tam turpem & manifestam commiserit contradictionem; Verba ex utroque loco, sibi invicem jungam, & mirari satis non poteris, hominis socordiam dicam, an ignorantiam. Præ reliquis scriptis omnibus, ea est singularis scriptorum divinorum constitutio, ut meram contineant veritatem, de qua judicare quoque posset ratio. Sic uno loco, altero autem plane contrarium. Omnia quæ Scripturæ habent ad veritates referri oportere, falsum esse, modo evicimus; verum id jam quæri potest, an omnes veritates Scripturæ ad rationis tribunal revocari possint. Id vero pernegamus. Non sufficit hæc contradictio, aliud adhuc mysterium hic latet, nimirum, vel ex ipsius Wolzogii judicio, totam causam Paradoxo tradendam esse, quod, non levi cavillatiuncula, sed firmissima ratione, demonstrabo. In hunc modum disserit pagina 192. se nihil habitu-rum quo sententiam Paradoxi labefactare posset NB si meras veritates, inquit, viderem contineri Scripturis. Hic autem diserissimis verbis sic loquitur, præ reliquis scriptis omnibus, ea est singularis seriptorum divinorum constitutio, ut meram contineant veritatem. Si argumentum velit, hoc habeat. Si meras veritates Scriptura continet, vicit, Wolzogio judice, Paradoxus. At meras veritates Scriptura continet, Ergo vicit, judice Wolzogio, Paradoxus. Illud habet p. 192. hoc vero p. 70. O miseram veritatis sortem! Siccine causa agetur, omnem quæ in se religionem continet? Tandem & hoc, ex isto Canone, sequitur, Rationi competere usum normalem antecedentem; hoc est, ante certo determinatum sensum, veritates rationis arbitrio disceptandas, ac tum demum de verborum sensu certo determinandum esse. Definire enim potest ratio an sensus aliquis conveniat nec ne conveniat. Sunt tua verba Wolzogi. At ante certo determinatum sensum, quo bene is eruatur, hoc fieri debere, res ipsa postulat; nisi post Scripturæ certum sensum inventum, ad rationis examen, eum deinceps adhuc revocandum arbitreris, quod certe omnem Socinianorum, hac in causa, superaret blasphemiam. Si vero ante certo determinatum sensum, quippe meram veritatem continens Scriptura, judicium rationis subire possit; Jam ultro largiris, hoc loco, quod unice in Paradoxo culpandum, vel saltem præcipue, dixisti alibi. Ille enim, sic Paradoxi sententiam proponis, aliquem primo sensum ex Scriptura eruit, necdum autem determinat, tum erutum, ad judicium rationis examinat, ut sciat an veritatem contineat, quam si deprehendat, tum ex veritate colligit verum sensum. Quod fieri, ex tua sententia potest, quando meram veritatem in Scriptura esse contendis. Imo licere, ultro hoc canone largiris, cum juxta illum, ratio definire sæpe possit an sensus aliquis conveniat nec ne. Quod revera nihil aliud est, quam victas dare manus, aliter pugnasses pro causa Dei & verbi divini, si Theologos legere cum Scriptura non dedignatus fuisses: nunquam bene cessit in religionis causa, novitatis & singularitatis studium. Odit superbos Deus. Hisce autem sic à Wolzogio positis, mirum non est, quod
units.tr: For it is not, as we have heard from Heidanus, to be entrusted to a man that he should take his own reason as counsellor, so that by its dictate he decides whether a matter is so or not; rather, by the opposite process, he should decide from revelation about the thing to be believed. And if our author considers the constitution of Scripture, it is such that its author is God, whose words we must not seek to draw out of the normal dictate of human reason. Indeed, it is written in such a manner and so arranged that its parts kindle a torch for one another, and so they disclose their own sense and reveal their meaning. Thus they never need the normal dictate of reason to make wise unto salvation those things that are suited to it. But Wolzogius forgets himself here, when he says that Scripture contains pure truth, about which reason too can judge. For elsewhere he denies both 1. that pure truth is contained in Scripture, and 2. that even if it contained pure truth, all of it could still be brought before the tribunal of reason. I do not know how it could have happened that, in matters which contain the whole sum of the controversy, he committed so shameful and so obvious a contradiction. I shall put the words from the two passages side by side, and you will not be able to wonder enough at the man's carelessness, or should I say his ignorance. Beyond all other writings, this is the unique constitution of the divine writings, that they contain pure truth, about which reason too could judge. So in one place; but in another he says plainly the opposite: That all the things that Scripture has must be referred to truths is false, as we have just proved; but it can now be asked whether all the truths of Scripture can be brought before the tribunal of reason. This we flatly deny. This contradiction is not enough; another mystery lies hidden here, namely that, by Wolzogius's own judgement, the whole cause must be handed over to the Paradox. I shall demonstrate this not by a slight quibble but by a most firm argument. He argues in this way on page 192, that he would have nothing with which he could shake the view of the Paradox, if I saw that pure truths are contained in the Scriptures. But here he speaks in the most explicit words: beyond all other writings, this is the unique constitution of the divine writings, that they contain pure truth. If he wishes to make an argument, let him have it thus: If Scripture contains pure truths, then, by Wolzogius's judgement, the Paradox has won. But Scripture contains pure truths. Therefore, by Wolzogius's judgement, the Paradox has won. He has the first on page 192 and the second on page 70. O wretched lot of truth! Is the cause to be pleaded thus, one that contains all religion within itself? Finally, from this canon it also follows that reason has a prior normal use, that is, before a sense has been fixed with certainty, the truths are to be disputed at the discretion of reason, and only then is the sense of the words to be determined with certainty. For reason can define whether a given sense agrees or does not agree. These are your own words, Wolzogius. But the thing itself demands that this be done before a sense has been fixed with certainty, by which it may be rightly drawn out; unless you think that after the certain sense of Scripture has been found, it must still be referred to the examination of reason, which surely would surpass all the blasphemy of the Socinians in this cause. But if Scripture, containing pure truth, can undergo the judgement of reason before a sense has been fixed with certainty, then you now freely concede, at this point, what you said elsewhere is to be blamed chiefly in the Paradox: For he, as you put the view of the Paradox, first draws out some sense from Scripture, but does not yet determine it; then, having drawn it out, he examines it by the judgement of reason, to know whether it contains the truth; and if he finds that it does, then from the truth he infers the true sense. This can happen, by your view, since you contend that pure truth is in Scripture. Indeed, you freely grant by this canon that it is lawful, since according to it reason can often define whether a given sense agrees or does not agree. This is really nothing other than giving up the struggle; you would have fought otherwise for the cause of God and the divine word, if you had not disdained to read the theologians along with Scripture. The zeal for novelty and singularity has never turned out well in a matter of religion: God hates the proud. Since these things have been laid down by Wolzogius in this way, it is no wonder that

units.la: 2. Secundo loco, Canonis instar, in Interpreta-tione observandi, & istum ponat, orthodoxis auri-bus non minus horridum ac absonum: Rationi deberi, omnia, quæ per consequentiam ex Scriptu-ris eliciuntur. Si enim ratio, seu Philosophia, nor-mæ vices in interpretationem obeat, necesse est, ut multarum veritatum analysis in rationem fiat, quod diserte inculcat Wolzogius. Ratio has, scili-cet veritatis emanationes, consequentias, præter ca-pita, doctrinæque fundamenta, quæ intra angustos li-mites circumscribuntur, ac pauciora sunt, quam vulgo credi solet, ex Scriptura profluentes docet, quemadmodum, non igitur instrumentaliter, sed per modum principii, quemadmodum illa pauca capita fundamentalia, in solam transscribuntur Scriptu-ram. Adeo ut, nisi credat paucissima, major pars eorum quæ credit, rationis, seu Philosophiæ authoritate, aut dictamine, credat: egregiam vero fidem! Quem errorem, superiori libro refutavi-mus, hic autem, quoniam in eo sumus, ut, quantum noster rationi seu Philosophiæ tribuat, quam de solio deturbasse videri vult, demonstremus, repe-tendus erat. Monuisse sufficiat, hanc thesin ab Orthodoxis totam rejici, quod antea satis superque probavimus, Dogmata fidei ex ratione non extruun-tur, nec in eam resolvuntur, dicit Altingius: quod vel ex Præceptoris sui Systemate discere potuerat, sic ibi Clarissimus Maresius. cum autem NB. orga-nice tantum & instrumentaliter concurrat ratio ad tales consecutiones ex Scriptura eliciendas & cognoscendas, sicut oculus & manus concurrunt in rebus ponderandis & mensurandis, sive exigendis ad amus-sim publicam, illarum consequentiarum certitudo NB
units.tr: 2. Secondly, a canon to be observed in interpretation, and one that he sets down, no less harsh and discordant to orthodox ears: that everything which is deduced from the Scriptures by consequence is owed to reason. For if reason, or philosophy, takes the place of a rule in interpretation, it is necessary that the analysis of many truths be made by reason, as Wolzogius expressly insists. Reason, he teaches, shows that these emanations of truth, the consequences, which flow from Scripture, are beyond the chief heads and foundations of doctrine, which are confined within narrow limits and are fewer than is commonly believed; and, as the few fundamental heads are transcribed into Scripture alone, so the rest are not derived instrumentally, but by way of a principle. So that, unless he believes the very few things, the greater part of what he believes is believed on the authority or dictate of reason or philosophy: a fine faith indeed! I refuted this error in the previous book; but since we are engaged here in showing how much he attributes to our reason, or philosophy, which he wishes to have been hurled from its throne, it had to be taken up again. It is enough to remind you that this thesis is wholly rejected by the orthodox, since we have already proved this sufficiently and more than sufficiently. The dogmas of faith are not built up from reason, nor are they resolved into it, says Altingius; he could have learned this from the System of his own teacher, where the most distinguished Maresius says thus: but since reason concurs only organically and instrumentally, NB, in deriving and knowing such consequences from Scripture, just as the eye and the hand concur in weighing and measuring things, or in bringing them to the public standard, the certainty of those consequences NB

units.la: Canon 2. non in humanam rationem, sed in revelationem divinam refunditur. Quam thesin si quis cum ista Wolzogiana, se conciliare posse putet, eum praestitisse credam, quod olim jactabat Weigelius, qui contradictoria, in schola gratiae, concilianda esse delirabat.
units.tr: Canon 2 is not referred to human reason, but to divine revelation. If anyone thinks he can reconcile this thesis with Wolzogius's, I should believe he has done what Weigel once boasted of, when he raved that contradictories were to be reconciled in the school of grace.

units.la: 3. Tertius autem Canon, uti priores absurditate superat, sic Wolzogii cum Paradoxo, saltem Socinianis, συμβίβασιν luculenter demonstrabit. Sic de eâ disserit, quem & universalem interpretandi regulam esse statuit. A Ratione quae petitur regula, ejusmodi est, ut, quod rationi manifesta contradictione repugnet, nil prorsus censeri debeat doceri Scriptura. Hactenus bene, congrua modo ac necessaria limitatio Orthodoxorum ne negligatur, quam hisce complectitur Hoornbeekius. Quae rationi re-pugnant, ea certo certius falsa esse nemo dubitare debet. Sic quidem si de articulo rationis & naturalis veritatis quaestio sit; at, si de veritate supernaturali, & hic veritas veritati nunquam quidem contraria, neque id quod Scriptura dicit rationi; tamen non hinc illorum veritas aestimanda & judicanda, si cum ratione conveniant, maxime, dum nostra hodie adeo est corrupta; quod tamen vult axioma hoc Socinianum; sed veritate ex sacra revelatione certa, extra dubium relinquitur, nec amplius contendendum, quicquid demum ex ratione ogganniatur[?]. Atque sic demum, omnium nostratium Theologorum haec constans est sententia, quicquid erroris convinci potest, illud à Scriptura esse alienissimum. Ita enim statuunt veritatem ve-ritati non posse esse contrariam, nec posse cum veritate consistere mendacium: ut recte mones. Hacte-nus tamen falsum est, Scripturam ulterius scrutaturo, atque interpretaturo, praefigendam in hunc modum rationem esse, ut, si bene fundatae firmataeque quid afferatur ex Scriptura quod videatur esse contrarium, commode sit explicanda Scriptura, & omnino secundum istam rationem. Neque etiam eo sensu statuunt nostri Theologi, quod iis tribuis pagina 150. modo citata. Hoc volunt, absolute verum esse, lumen rationis & fidei sibi mutuo non contradicere, in se consideratum utrumque atque in Idea, ut vocant; non autem, rationis axiomata praefigenda nobis esse, juxta quae interpretanda Scriptura sit: Licet enim quam cautissime & solemnissime, ut ita loquar, stipuleris, etiam atque etiam provi-dendum esse, ne, quod non assequitur ratio, id statim rationi repugnare credatur. Et si vel maxime contradictio nobis appareat alicubi, nil hic temere pronunciandum esse, donec luce meridiana clarius enitescat non posse sensum cum veritate consistere. Atque his legibus Paradoxi Interpretem, non aliis, admittas, Nondum satis periculis cautum erit & prospectum, quod vel ex eo apparet; quoniam omnes Sociniani, quin vel ipse Paradoxus, lubentissime spondebunt, se istis conditionibus, non aliter, rationem seu Philosophiam admitti, ad Scripturam interpretandam, velle, quod nisi sponte sua pateret, ex Socinianis & Paradoxo probatum darem, adeo ut & hic sibi de victoria gratulari merito possit, insulsus nugator, ea enim conditione à Wolzogio ipsius Interpres admittitur, quam ultro offert, spondetque se accuratissime observaturum; non enim temere quicquam pronunciari velle, Cartesianus credendus est, qui, non nisi post claram distinctamque perceptionem, de quoquam judicium depromendum, aut ferendum, iterum iterumque inculcat. Sic volunt nostri; solam Scripturam suae interpretationis normam esse & amussim; verum, explicata jam, & inventa, ex sola Scriptura, divina veritate, concedunt, licere, imo conducere, ut inventa jam, & fide credita veritas, adversus omnis generis insultationes defendatur, atque sic in eum finem, (quoniam religionis & mysteriorum fidei hostes, ex ratione naturali, contradictiones fingere ac absurditates praetexere satagunt) rationes illae, ex natura petitae, examinentur, dissolvantur, aut explicentur, quo sic, quantum pote, veritatis hostibus demonstretur,frustra se & incassum, toto illo Philosophiae apparatu, divinam fidem impetivisse: non vero, ante veritatem repertam, idque in Scripturae interpretatione, Philosophiae normam praefigendam esse, ea lege, ut si forsan hic aut ille sensus in rationem seu Philosophiam incurrat, alius sit excogitandus, aut, ut Wolzogius amat loqui, commode Scripturam explicandam esse atque omnino secundum istam rationem. Toto coelo ista differunt. Philosophiae dictamina interpretaturo normam regulamque praefigere, ea lege, ut, quid in eam incurrat, commode id explicandum atque alio sumendum sensu veniat, quod facit Wolzogius, longe aliud est, quam inventa & eruta veritate, absque ullo ejus praejudicio, Philosophium ad partes vocare, ut, quantum potest, ostendatur, sanam rationem Theologiae non adversari, idque ea lege, ut si vel clarissimè Philosophiae axiomata aliud poscere videantur, ratio tamen se submittere debeat & componere ad Scripturam, ostendaturque inter veram rationem & S. Scripturam repugnantiam esse non posse, quoniam verum sibi contrarium esse nequit, nec lumen lumini, vel id quod Deus dixit in Scriptura, ei quod idem dixit in natura; ideoque vel conciliationem utriusque proferimus, vel si id non possimus, culpamus potius ingenium nostrum, ejusque stupiditatem, vel errorem, quam veritatem. Conciliatur ratio cum Scriptura, ut ratio dicit sententiam & dictatum rationis: non vero examinatur, vel componitur Scriptura ad rationem. Atque idcirco non sic debet intelligi, rationi consentanea esse omnia religionis capita, quasi ex ratione judicanda forent, vel ipsa cum ratione concilianda, ut cum ea in gratiam & consensum redeant: Scriptura parum refert, an appareat rationis cum ea consonantia; plus rationis interest, hoc ut constet, ac sibi demonstretur: sic Hoornbeekius, sic Reformati. Nec mirum est, quoniam scriptura lumen est superius & majus, cui non magis conveniat, ad lumen rationis excuti, quam Solis ad candelae radios dios examinari. Et deinde infallibilem non solum, verum & tutam hic normam habemus, in Philosophia vero non item, prout ea jam subjectivè considerātur. Qua de re, egregie disserit, Clarissimus Maresius,ostendens, & certitudine & numero perceptiones Philosophicas fidei cedere persuasionibus. Tantum abest,ut haereticis largiantur nostri, quod statuit Wolzogius, axiomata Philosophiae, seu rationis, praefigenda, divinam veritatem scrutaturo, non lege, ut si quid iis videatur esse contra-rium commode & in alium sensum, sit explicanda Scriptura atque omnino secundum istam rationem; ut Heidano judice is sit domesticus Socini & Socinianorum sensus, imo fundamentum. Ipse suis verbis loquatur Veteranus Theologus. Licet enim, loquitur de Socinianis, quandoque videri nolint rationi humanae nimium tribuere, quod verae voces quandoque ab invitis pectoribus erumpant: tamen cum rem ipsam sine ambagibus eloquuntur, & domesticum sensum produnt, ita instituunt. Id nullo modo verum esse posse, cuiratio prorsus, communisque sensus repugnet: Idque eo usque extendit Socinus Lib. de Servatore parte iii. Cap. 6. ut hisce verbis loqui non erubescat. Cum ea quae fieri non posse aperte con-stat, divinis etiam oraculis ea fuisse, in speciem,di-serte attestantibus, nequaquam admittantur, & idcirco sacra verba NB. in alium sensum quam ipsa sonant quandoque explicantur. Commode atque omnino secundum istam rationem, ait Wolzogius, in alium sensum, quam sonant, ait Socinus, citante Heidano,atque domesticum hoc dicto sensum ille, hoc judice, prodidit. Quam longe igitur Wolzogius à domestico, juxta Heidanum, Socini sensu, abiit, videat lector, ego nullam inter eos diversitatem deprehendo. Alterum hujus consensus testem produco Smalcium, cujus verba idem refert in hunc modum. Quia ergo, ut in praecedentibus vidimus, rationi tantum non palmam deferendam esse pronunciant: non potuit aliter evenire, quin NB. in intelligendis[?] gendis & explicandis Scripturis eidem tantundem tri- buerent. Adeo ut, si rationi absurdum & contra- rium videatur,quod Scriptura disertissimè affirmat, praestat NB. modum aliquem dicendi comminisci, quo ista de Deo dici possint, quam ista simpliciter,& ut verba sonant, intelligere. Qui sunt impii Smal- cii flosculi ex Homilia viii. in 1. Joh. At idem, non solum reipsa, sed verbis fere, dicit Wolzogius. Quod certo, sic ratiocinatur adversus istam regu- lam Heidanus, nihil aliud est, quam rationem Scri- ptura praeferre, & sensum revelationi praepone- re & opponere, & verbo Dei vim facere, & sensum ejus, qui per verba ad animos nostros venit, vero suo intellectu spoliare, ut quod dicitur, quasi non dictum habeatur, & quod non dicitur, illi affingatur. Quid hoc aliud est, quam in hisce tenebris spiritualibus sibi de suo accendere lumen & se malleolis proprii ignis circumcingere: ut postea in focum ignis, quem de se succenderunt, eant, & propriis scintillis pereant. Uti de istis rationalibus loquitur Proph. Esa. C. II. illa e- nim est justa hujus peccati ἀντιμισθία, ut, contem- tum Prophetiae sequatur nudatio Prov. xxix. 18. & qui ad legem & testimonium non properat, neque facit secundum verbum illud, non oriatur ei lux matutina. Esa. viii.20. Etenim praerogativa Dei, to- tum hominem complectitur, non minus rationem, quam voluntatem ejus circumscribit: ut homo in uni- versum se abneget & accedat Deo. Quare sicut legi divinae obedire tenemur licet reluctetur voluntas, ita & verbo Dei fidem habere, licet repugnet ratio. Cum, si ea duntaxat credimus, quae sunt rationi nostrae con- sentanea, (qualia vel intima religionis mysteria censet Wolzogius) rebus assentiamur non auctori. Quod etiam suspectae fidei testibus praestare solemus. unde quanto mysterium aliquod divinum magis fue- rit absonum & incredibile, tanto plus in credendo ex- hibetur honoris Deo; & fit victoria fidei nobilior. Et certe, nisi in rebus fidei, rationem praecedat authori- tas, abrogatur Deo magisterium, & homo constituitur Judex Dei, cujus verba suo sensu in ordinem cogit. Cedro dignissima verba, quibus ita afficior, ut lubeat, adhuc quaedam exscribere. Necesse est, sic paulo post, pro summa regula homo habeat; ea NB. sola, quae nobis à Deo revelata sunt, ut extra omnem dubitationis aleam posita, esse amplectenda & credenda. NB. quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maximè clarum & evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videatur, non, ut Wolzogius putat, commode & quidem juxta istam rationem Scriptura explicanda est, sed soli tamen authoritati divinae potius, quam proprio nostro judicio esse fidendum & standum. Quid enim aliud est rationis naturalis nisus, in religionis negotio, quam religiosa quaedam insania, imo vero irreligiosa stultitia & rationale delirium? De Methodo autem, juxta hunc Wolzogii Canonem, sic loquitur. Perversa plane & sophistica methodus, dum sensum, quem ex Scripturis ipsis mutuari, atque ex illis exsculpere debuerant, illis impingunt, atque proprios & à se excogitatos sensus Spiritui sancto commodant, quasi ab illo hausti. Cum contra Scripturae sensus ex ipsis penetralibus Scripturae educendus fuit. Hactenus Heidanus cum quo eadem docet Altingius, qui de divinitate Christi, objectiones Socinianorum discussurus, ista praemittit.
units.tr: 3. The third canon, as it surpasses the earlier ones in absurdity, so it will clearly demonstrate Wolzogen's reconciliation [συμβίβασιν] with the Paradox, at least for the Socinians. He discusses it in this way, and he lays it down as the universal rule of interpretation: The rule sought from reason is of such a kind that nothing whatever should be taught in Scripture that is manifestly contradicted by reason. So far so good: the necessary and proper limitation of the Orthodox, which Hoornbeek includes here, should not be neglected. Whatever is opposed to reason, no one ought to doubt is most certainly false. This holds if the question concerns an article of reason and natural truth. But if it concerns supernatural truth, where truth is never indeed contrary to truth, nor is what Scripture says contrary to reason, nevertheless their truth is not to be assessed and judged by this, namely whether they agree with reason, especially since our reason today is so corrupted. This, however, is what this Socinian axiom wants. But once truth is certain from sacred revelation, it is left beyond doubt, and there is no further dispute about whatever at last may be devised from reason. And so at last: the constant view of all our theologians is this, that whatever error can be proved is most alien to Scripture. For they hold that truth cannot be contrary to truth, nor can a lie consist with truth, as you rightly warn. Yet it is false that, for one who is going to examine and interpret Scripture further, reason should be set in front as a standard in such a way that, if something drawn from Scripture that seems contrary to a well-founded and established point is brought forward, Scripture must be conveniently explained, and altogether according to that reason. Nor do our theologians lay this down in the sense you attribute to them on the page cited above (p. 150). They mean this: it is absolutely true that the light of reason and of faith do not contradict each other, each considered in itself and in its idea, as they say; but they do not mean that the axioms of reason must be set before us as the standard by which Scripture is to be interpreted. For although you stipulate most carefully and solemnly, so to speak, that we must take heed again and again, lest what reason does not reach be straightway believed to be opposed to reason. And even if a contradiction appears to us somewhere, nothing rash must be pronounced here, until it shines out more clearly than the midday sun that the sense cannot agree with truth. And only on these laws should you admit an interpreter of the Paradox, and on no others. Caution and foresight against dangers are still not sufficient, as is evident from this: all the Socinians, and the Paradox itself, will most willingly promise that they wish reason or philosophy to be admitted for interpreting Scripture only on these conditions and in no other way. I would have proved this from the Socinians and the Paradox if it were not plain of its own accord; so that this trifling babbler may rightly congratulate himself on victory here too, for on that condition his own interpreter is admitted by Wolzogen, which he offers of his own accord, promising that he will observe it most scrupulously. For a Cartesian must be believed not to wish to pronounce anything rashly, since he repeatedly and again insists that no judgment about anything is to be drawn or given except after a clear and distinct perception. So our men hold: Scripture alone is the rule and standard of its interpretation. But once the truth has been explained and found from Scripture alone, the divine truth, they concede that it is lawful, indeed advantageous, that the truth now found and believed by faith be defended against every kind of insult; and so, to this end (since the enemies of religion and the mysteries of faith strive to fabricate contradictions and pretend absurdities from natural reason), those arguments drawn from nature are examined, dissolved, or explained, so that, as far as possible, it may be shown to the enemies of truth that they have attacked divine faith in vain and to no purpose with all that philosophical apparatus. But it is not that, before the truth has been found, and in the interpretation of Scripture, the norms of philosophy are to be set in front, on this condition, that if perhaps this or that sense runs into reason or philosophy, another must be devised, or, as Wolzogen likes to say, Scripture must be conveniently explained and altogether according to that reason. These differ by the whole heaven. To set the dictates of philosophy as a norm and rule before one who is going to interpret, on the condition that whatever runs into them is conveniently explained and taken in another sense, which is what Wolzogen does, is far different from calling philosophy to the side of truth once it has been found and drawn out, without any prejudice to it, so that it may be shown, as far as possible, that sound reason is not opposed to theology; and this on the condition that, even if the axioms of philosophy most clearly seem to demand otherwise, reason must nevertheless submit and conform itself to Scripture, and it must be shown that there cannot be a contradiction between true reason and holy Scripture, since the true cannot be contrary to itself, nor can light be opposed to light, or what God has said in Scripture to what the same God has said in nature. Therefore either we bring forward a reconciliation of the two, or, if we cannot, we blame our own intellect and its dullness or error rather than the truth. Reason is reconciled with Scripture in that reason states the opinion and dictate of reason; but Scripture is not examined by reason, nor is it adjusted to reason. Hence it must not be understood that all the heads of religion are agreeable to reason, as if they were to be judged by reason, or as if they were themselves to be reconciled with reason so that they might return into favour and agreement with it. It matters little to Scripture whether its agreement with reason appears; it matters more to reason that this be established and demonstrated to it. So Hoornbeek, so the Reformed. Nor is this surprising, since Scripture is a higher and greater light, and it is no more fitting that it be shaken out by the light of reason than that the rays of the sun be examined by the flame of a candle. And further, we have here an infallible and safe norm, which we do not have in philosophy, insofar as philosophy is considered subjectively. On this matter the most distinguished Maresius disputes well, showing that philosophical perceptions yield to the persuasions of faith in both certainty and number. So far are our men from granting to the heretics what Wolzogen lays down, that the axioms of philosophy or of reason must be set before one who is going to examine divine truth, not on the condition that if anything seems contrary to them, Scripture must be conveniently explained in another sense and altogether according to that reason. According to Heidanus's judgment, this is the homegrown sense and foundation of Socinus and the Socinians. Let the old theologian speak in his own words. For although, he speaks of the Socinians, they sometimes wish not to seem to grant too much to human reason, since true words sometimes break out from unwilling breasts; yet when they speak the matter itself without circumlocution and reveal their homegrown sense, they lay it down thus: that cannot be true in any way which is wholly opposed to reason and common sense. Socinus extends this so far in his book On the Saviour, part iii, chapter 6, that he is not ashamed to speak in these words: since those things which it is clearly established cannot happen are by no means to be admitted, even though divine oracles seem to attest them expressly, therefore the sacred words NB. are sometimes explained in another sense than they sound. Conveniently and altogether according to that reason, says Wolzogen, in another sense than they sound, says Socinus, as Heidanus cites him; and by this saying, in his judgment, he revealed the homegrown sense. Let the reader see how far Wolzogen has departed from the homegrown sense of Socinus, according to Heidanus; I find no difference between them. I bring forward Smalcius as a second witness to this agreement, whose words the same author reports in this way: Because, as we have seen in what precedes, they declare that reason must be given the palm, not only in the first place, it could not happen otherwise than that NB. in understanding and explaining the Scriptures they would assign it the same authority. So that, if what Scripture most plainly affirms seems absurd and contrary to reason, it is better NB. to devise some manner of speaking by which such things may be said of God, than to understand these things simply and as the words sound. These are the impious little flowers of Smalcius from his eighth homily on 1 John. Yet Wolzogen says the same thing, not only in fact but nearly in words. What is certainly, so Heidanus reasons against this rule, nothing other than to prefer reason to Scripture, to set and oppose the sense to revelation, to do violence to the word of God, and to strip of its true meaning the sense that comes to our minds through the words, so that what is said is held as if it were not said, and what is not said is attributed to it. What else is this than to kindle a light for oneself out of one's own stock in these spiritual darkness, and to surround oneself with the torches of one's own fire, so that afterwards they go into the fire which they have kindled from themselves and perish by their own sparks? Concerning such rationalists the prophet Isaiah speaks in chapter 2 [Esa. C. II.]: for that is the just recompense [ἀντιμισθία] of this sin, that contempt of prophecy is followed by nakedness (Prov. 29:18), and he who does not hasten to the law and the testimony, nor act according to that word, the morning light does not rise for him (Isa. 8:20). For the authority of God embraces the whole man; it circumscribes his reason no less than his will, so that a man denies himself entirely and draws near to God. Therefore, just as we are bound to obey the divine law even though the will resists, so too we must have faith in the word of God even though reason opposes it. For if we believe only those things which agree with our reason (as Wolzogen judges even the innermost mysteries of religion to be), we assent to things, not to their author. This we are also accustomed to do with witnesses of doubtful faith. Hence the more a divine mystery is absurd and incredible, the more honour is shown to God in believing it, and the victory of faith is nobler. And certainly, unless in matters of faith authority goes before reason, the teaching office is taken from God, and man is made the judge of God, forcing his words into order according to his own sense. I am most affected by the very worthy words of Heidanus, so that I should like to copy out a few more of them. It is necessary, he says a little later, that man should hold as the supreme rule: NB. those things alone which have been revealed to us by God, placed beyond every chance of doubt, are to be embraced and believed. NB. Although perhaps the light of reason, most clear and evident, seems to suggest something else to us, it is not, as Wolzogen thinks, that Scripture must be conveniently explained, and indeed according to that reason, but rather that we must trust and abide by divine authority alone, not by our own judgment. For what else is the striving of natural reason in the matter of religion than a certain religious madness, or rather an irreligious folly and rational delirium? He speaks in this way about the method according to this canon of Wolzogen: a plainly perverse and sophistical method, when they impose on Scripture the sense which they ought to borrow from Scripture itself and draw out of it, and attribute to the Holy Spirit their own senses devised by themselves, as if drawn from him. Whereas the sense of Scripture ought to be educed from the innermost recesses of Scripture itself. So far Heidanus, with whom Altingius teaches the same thing, who, when about to discuss the objections of the Socinians concerning the divinity of Christ, sets out these things first.

units.la: Ratio nihil videt, aut valet, in hoc capite doctrinae, quod Apostolus magnum pietatis Mysterium nuncupat, 1.Tim. iii. 16. Et NB. falsum est principium Socinianorum, nihil credendum quod rationi repugnat.
units.tr: Reason sees nothing in this article of doctrine, which the Apostle calls the great mystery of godliness (1 Tim. 3:16), and has no power over it. And the principle of the Socinians, that nothing is to be believed which conflicts with reason, is false.

units.la: Et revera, rationem, prout est in subjecto, fidei mysteriis multoties contradicere, probat idem Clariss. Theologus. Ubi vocat falsam hypothesin: quod ratio sit norma contradictionis in Theologicis, & judicium de ea rationi conveniat. Nempe, in illis quae Theologicae revelationis sunt, judicatur contradictio admitti, siquidem statuatur aliquid quod contra illam S. revelationem est; licet non dissonet à ratione, ait Hoornbeekius, Et mirum certe, si ista Wolzogiana regula suspecta non foret, nihil enim, ea concessa, ulterius, vel ipsi Sociniani requirunt. Sic Brenius, inter istas, quas, in interpretando, ob-servari vult, generales regulas, hanc primo loco ponit. Nullam interpretationem S. Scripturæ admittendam esse, quæ cum sana ratione repugnat. In hæc verba, ex Resp. ad Ep. Waddingi, Episcopii sententiam refert, scriptor Lutheranus, in Tractatu quem de Scepticismo, præcipuè Remonstrantium, inscripsit, necessarium est, antequam sensus ullus S. Scripturæ probetur, ut à recta ratione eum non dissentire intelligatur. Contra quæ mala atrocia (Reformatis, pro suo candore alibi, bene multa Episcopius impegerat, placidum sc: caput) nullum certius præsentiusque remedium est, quam si de istis mysteriis nihil adseratur aut adseri jubeatur præter Scripturam; hactenus rectè, aut NB. nihil ex Scriptura quod ratio recta statim deprehendit falsum atque absurdum esse. Hæc Panacæa curari possent mala omnia & pax esset. Neque e-nim mens eorum est, de Sociniano-Remonstrantium sensu loquitur jam nominatus Episcopius, postula-re, ut recta ratio primum dictet, idcirco sensum istum sic interpretandum esse quia ratio humana dictat rem ita necessario fieri debuisse. Sed mens eorum est, po-stulare, ut, cum de sensu aliquo dubio quæritur, nihil admittatur ad eruendum sensum illum, quod contra rectam rationem, id est, quod absurdum est. Nemo certè Socinianorum, ne vel ipse Paradoxus, eo dementiæ venisse putandus est, ut velit, Scripturæ rationem opponi, quando jam de mente Sp: Sancti constat, sed, in ipso interpretationis opere, rationis regulam adhibendam censent, ne quicquam, rationi contrarium, Scripturæ verbis significari credatur: Ut superius, ex Schlightingio, aliisque, vidimus. Totum autem illud concedit, imo postulat Wolzogius. Et in eo certe maxima versatur difficultas. Optimè Vir Doctissimus G. J. Vossius. De ratione rectæ iidem judicant, minime ea nos fidei mysteria metiri oportere. Thomas Libr. IV. contra Gentes Cap. 1. Probanda est haec Theologia authoritate Sacrae Scripturae, non ratione naturali: sed tamen ostendendum est, quod rationi naturali non sit opposita, ut ab impugnatione infidelium defendatur. Sed tamen cum & majus Scripturae, & minus rectae rationis lumen pugnare inter se non possint: ratio quidem NB. praecedere fidem non debet, sed utiliter tamen subservit. Quemadmodum nimirum vinitores, prius terram effodiunt, quam vitem plantent: postmodo vero in locum suum terram recondunt: ita NB. ratio explodi debet, usque dum fides cordibus inseratur; sed ea ubi plantata erit, ratio recte admoveatur, ut fidem illustret. Nihil enim intolerabilius, ait Tilenus, quam quod in divinis judiciis nihil rectum putent nisi quod ad obliquissimam ingenii humani normam quadrat. Et certe si hac via Wolzogiana incedendum, & Scriptura, ubi rationi videtur contradicere, commode atque in alium sensum explicanda sit, actum erit de omnibus religionis Christianae mysteriis, ut bene notat Vir summus Guilielmus Tuissius, in negotio de praedestinatione, quippe ejusmodi est nostrorum Theologorum sententia, ut in eam, nisi ex sacris literis huc adacti, nunquam concederemus, tam sunt omnia judicio humano & affectibus carnalibus repugnantia.
units.tr: Indeed, the same distinguished theologian proves that reason, as it exists in the human subject, often contradicts the mysteries of faith. There he calls it a false hypothesis that reason is the rule of contradiction in theological matters, and that judgment about such matters belongs to reason. Certainly, in those matters which belong to theological revelation, a contradiction is judged to be admitted if something is asserted that is contrary to that sacred revelation, even though it does not dissent from reason, as Hoornbeeck says. And it would certainly be surprising if this rule of Wolzogius were not suspect, for once it is granted, the Socinians themselves require nothing further. So Brenius, among the general rules which he wants observed in interpreting, places this first: no interpretation of Holy Scripture is to be admitted which conflicts with sound reason. The Lutheran writer, in his treatise on Scepticism, which he wrote chiefly against the Remonstrants, cites Episcopius's view in these words, taken from his reply to the letter of Waddington: Before any sense of Holy Scripture is approved, it is necessary that it be understood not to dissent from right reason. Against these dreadful evils (with which Episcopius, elsewhere, in his candour, had rightly charged the Reformed, namely the placid head) there is no surer or more ready remedy than if nothing is asserted about these mysteries, or ordered to be asserted, except Scripture; so far rightly, or NB. nothing from Scripture which right reason at once perceives to be false and absurd. All evils could be cured by this panacea, and there would be peace. For the intention of Episcopius, who was named above, is not to demand, in the sense of the Socinian-Remonstrants, that right reason first dictate that a given sense must be interpreted thus because human reason dictates that the thing had to happen in this way. Rather, their intention is to demand that, when we inquire about some doubtful sense, nothing be admitted for bringing out that sense which is contrary to right reason, that is, which is absurd. Certainly no Socinian, not even Paradoxus himself, should be thought to have fallen into such madness as to want reason opposed to Scripture when the mind of the Holy Spirit is already clear; rather, they hold that in the very work of interpretation the rule of reason must be applied, lest anything contrary to reason be believed to be signified by the words of Scripture, as we saw above from Schlichting and others. Wolzogius, however, concedes all this, indeed demands it. And in this lies the greatest difficulty. The most learned man G. J. Vossius rightly says: The same men judge that we ought by no means to measure the mysteries of faith by right reason. Thomas, Book 4, Against the Gentiles, chapter 1. This theology must be proved by the authority of Holy Scripture, not by natural reason; yet it must be shown that it is not opposed to natural reason, so that it may be defended against the attacks of unbelievers. But since the greater light of Scripture and the lesser light of right reason cannot fight against each other, reason indeed NB. ought not to precede faith, but yet serves it usefully. Just as vinedressers first dig the earth before they plant the vine, and afterwards bury the earth again in its place, so NB. reason must be cast out until faith is implanted in the hearts; but when faith has been planted, reason is rightly applied to illuminate faith. For nothing is more intolerable, says Tilenus, than that in divine judgments people think nothing right except what fits the most crooked standard of the human mind. And certainly, if we must proceed by this Wolzogian way, and if Scripture, where it seems to contradict reason, must be conveniently explained into another sense, it will be all over with all the mysteries of the Christian religion, as the great Guilielmus Tuissius rightly observes in the matter of predestination. For the opinion of our theologians is of such a kind that we would never have agreed to it, unless we had been driven to it by the sacred letters, since all things are so repugnant to human judgment and carnal affections.

units.la: Quapropter pii simul, doctique inter Reformatos Theologi, non rationis axiomata excolenda, non Philosophica dogmata, quae regulae instar Scripturam interpretaturo praefigantur, addiscenda, docent, quò, quicquid iis adversari videatur, juxta Wolzogii mentem, commode explicari possit & quidem juxta istam rationem. Philosophiam amant laudantque, seu intra suos eam compescunt limites. Hominis mentem acuat, eique poliendae inserviat, instrumentalem denique praebeat usum, per ipsos licet: ab interpretationis norma, & arbitrio tamen, longe abesse jubent. Possem id sexcentis testimoniis docere, si necessitas exigeret, hac vice sufficient ea, quae incomparabilis Theologus, logus, simul & summus Philosophus, hac de re nobis tradidit verè aurea. Accurate delineavit quæ interpretaturo, aut necessaria sint, aut usui esse queant. In quibus, nullibi vel extremo digito attingit, id quod Wolzogius præcipue observandum jubet, rationis nimirum dictamina respicere, ne in ea incurrat ullibi Scripturæ interpretatio, idque ne quidem in negotio Sacramentario, ubi fidei analogia & Textuum paralellissimo, sensum verum demonstrat unicè: quamvis enim non negemus, ex superabundanti subinde, post peractam, & ex ipsa Scriptura stabilitam interpretationem, rationes naturales ad partes vocari posse: non tamen, dum de ipsa interpretatione agitur, atque ei eruendæ quispiam intentus est, quicquam, normæ loco, à cujus arbitrio pendeat ullo modo scrutator Scripturarum, admittendum præter ipsam Scripturam: hic rationem, seu Philosophiam, audire, ejusque jurisdictionem, arbitrium, decisionem admittere cum Wolzogio, id certe præposterum est, ac, ut ex Heidano audimus, Socinianorum sensus verè domesticus. Hinc ex cæcitatis naturalis consideratione (qua nostrapte natura, ad ea quæ Dei sunt intelligenda, ineptissimi sumus. 1. Cor. 11.14. Non minus quam Solem splendidissimè lucentem, si cæci simus, intueri illius lucem quiremus) Istam deducit interpretandi regulam, precibus Spiritum illuminationis petendum esse. Etenim, qui sine Sp. humano est, non potest quæ homo loquitur, percipere, ut Bos &c. Sic qui sine Spiritu Dei &c. Secunda causa, quæ intelligere Scripturas prohibet ac impedit, ipsi hæc est; nostræ carnis prudentia ac sapientia, quam dum adferimus ad lectionem & studium Scripturarum, minus simus idonei ad veram illarum intelligentiam assequendam, & eo magis absconditur à nobis cognitio sapientiæ Dei, quo plus adhibemus nostræ sapientiæ & prudentiæ. Hanc tradit Christus Matth. xi. Et Apostolus confirmat addita etiam ratione, 1. Cor. iii. Sapientia hujus mundi, “stultitia est apud Deum. & Rom. viii. Prudentia “carnis, inimicitia est adversus Deum. Hæc impedi-mento ipsis maximè Philosophis: dum enim ea quæ Deus tradidit Spiritu suo divino, voluerunt ipsi sua humana sapientia metiri & intelligere: in maxi-mos lapsi sunt errores, ut non immerito dixerit Ter-tullianus; Philosophos Patres esse hæreticorum. Ergo ad veram Scripturæ intelligentiam consequendam, se-cunda hæc esto regula, ut scilicet, dum ad illas accedi-mus, omni nostræ humanæ prudentiæ & ratiocinatio-nibus renunciemus, & seu infantes simpliciter subji-ciamus nos Deo in Scripturis nos docenti, captivantes omnem cogitationem nostram in obsequium Christi. Sic nostri rationi ac Philosophiæ valedicunt, cui omnia examinanda, & ad cujus dictamen, Scriptu-ram sæpe explicandam docet noster. Et certe, si animum ab omni præjudicio, ab omni præcon-cepta, ex quocunque tandem sit principio, de re-bus naturalibus, opinione, liberum, recte Philoso-phaturo necessarium esse dicant Cartefiani, quo claris & distinctis, rationis naturalis ope acquisitis, perceptionibus, unice intentus, feliciter ad veritatis cognitionem perducatur. Quid ni &, bene Scripturam interpretaturo, omni, ex alio principio, acquisita scientia, ultra ejus instrumentalem usum, valere jussa, unicè à Scripturæ dictamine pendere suadeatur? Deus certe, non minus, Scripturæ luce in Theologia, quam in Philosophia, eo, quod naturæ, dicitur, præsto erit sedulo scrutatori. Neque majori seductionis periculo sese exponit, qui in Philosophia Præceptorum dictis, aliisve præconceptis opinionibus indulget; quam si Scripturam religionisque mysteria scrutaturus, rationis dictamini eousque sese addicit, ut juxta rationem, si contrarium dicere videatur, commode Scripturam explicandam putet. Est enim certè humani ingenii brevior & angustior mensura, quam ut ad divinorum operum mensuratio nem adhiberi debeat: & iniquum est Deum nostro pede metiri. Et quoniam rationi humanæ,ex lapsu, magna caligo offusa est, & doctrina Euangelica pro-fundior & reconditior est, quam quo aut hominum aut vero etiam angelorum ratio penetrare potuit: id-circo operæprætium est, ut in mysteriis cœlestibus, ra-tioni præeat Verbi & Spiritus lumen. Quod si ratio aliud dictet, quam quod verbo consentaneum est, tum sicut ad rationis imperium cupiditates; sic ad Verbi divini magisterium ratio revocanda est, non Scriptu-ra juxta rationem explicanda commode. Propter-ea Tertulliano materia sapientiæ secularis, temera-ria audit interpres divinæ naturæ & dispositionis. A-lius est Piscatorum, alius Philosophorum Stylus. Qui & alibi Patriarchas Hæreticorum vocat Philosophos, & Philosophiam veritatis concussionem. Et certe, qui ad Theologiam ejus dictamina, tanquam in-terpretandæ Scripturæ normam, aliquatenus transferunt, ii recte per Philosophatas doctrinas hominum aquas vino miscentes dicuntur eidem Tertulliano. Ut Beatus Rhenanus non absque ra-tione dixerit. Vide quantum Christianismo semper nocuerit Philosophia. Quæ verba inquisitio Hispa-nica notavit, & deleri jussit, in Indice expurgato-rio edito Madriti Anno M D LXXXIV. Sub-mittamus, inquit Augustinus, nostras ratiunculas divinis effatibus. Quin & ipse Durandus de se suo-que scribendi modo: Modus autem loquendi ac scri-bendi, in cæteris, quæ fidem non tangunt, est, ut ma-gis innitamur rationi. Inquando fidem tangunt, plus acquiescere debemus auctoritati sacræ Scri-pturæ, quam cuicunque rationi humanæ: quia divina notitia, quam exprimit sacra Scriptura, plus excedit humanam notitiam, quam humana notitia bestiales &c.
units.tr: Therefore the pious and learned theologians among the Reformed teach that the axioms of reason are not to be cultivated, nor philosophical dogmas to be learned, which are set before the interpreter of Scripture as a rule, so that whatever seems to oppose them may, according to Wolzogius's mind, be conveniently explained, and indeed according to that reasoning. They love and praise philosophy, or else they confine it within its own limits. Let it sharpen the mind of man and serve to polish it; in short, let it offer an instrumental use, through its own means, if you like; but they bid it keep far from being the norm of interpretation and from its judgment. I could teach this with six hundred testimonies if necessity required, but for this occasion those things suffice which the incomparable theologian, and at the same time the highest philosopher, has handed down to us on this matter, truly golden words. He has accurately described what is necessary for the interpreter, or what can be useful to him. In these words he nowhere touches, even with a finger, that which Wolzogius especially orders to be observed, namely that one should look to the dictates of reason, so that interpretation of Scripture may not run into them anywhere, not even in the sacramentarian controversy, where the analogy of faith and the closest parallel of texts alone demonstrate the true sense. For although we do not deny that, after the interpretation has been completed and established from Scripture itself, natural reasons may sometimes be called in as a superfluous addition, yet while the interpretation itself is under discussion, and someone is intent on drawing it out, nothing may be admitted as a norm, on whose judgment the searcher of the Scriptures depends in any way, except Scripture itself. To hear reason, or philosophy, here, and to admit with Wolzogius its jurisdiction, judgment, decision, is certainly preposterous, and, as we hear from Heidanus, a sense truly native to the Socinians. From the consideration of natural blindness (by which, in our nature, we are most unfit to understand the things of God. 1 Cor. 11:14. Just as, if we were blind, we could not look at the light of the sun shining most brightly), he deduces this rule of interpretation: the Spirit of illumination must be sought by prayers. For he who is without the Spirit cannot perceive the things that a man speaks, as an ox does, etc. So he who is without the Spirit of God etc. The second cause, which prevents and hinders us from understanding the Scriptures, is this: the prudence and wisdom of our flesh, which, when we bring it to the reading and study of the Scriptures, makes us less fit to attain a true understanding of them; and the knowledge of the wisdom of God is hidden from us the more we apply our own wisdom and prudence. Christ teaches this in Matt. 11, and the Apostle confirms it, adding also the reason, in 1 Cor. 3: "The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." And Rom. 8: "The prudence of the flesh is enmity against God." This is most of all an obstacle for the philosophers: for while they wanted to measure and understand with their human wisdom what God has handed down by his divine Spirit, they fell into the greatest errors; so Tertullian rightly said that the philosophers are the patriarchs of the heretics. Therefore, to attain a true understanding of Scripture, let this second rule be: that when we approach it, we renounce all our human prudence and reasonings, and simply submit ourselves like infants to God, who teaches us in the Scriptures, bringing every thought captive to the obedience of Christ. Thus our men bid farewell to reason and philosophy, to which everything must be examined, and according to whose dictate our author often teaches that Scripture must be explained. And certainly, if they say that a mind free from every prejudice and every preconception, from whatever principle they may come, concerning natural things, is necessary for one who philosophizes rightly, as the Cartesians say, so that, intent only on clear and distinct perceptions acquired by the power of natural reason, he may be happily led to the knowledge of truth, why should it not be urged that one who wants to interpret Scripture well should, having bidden farewell to all knowledge acquired from any other principle beyond its instrumental use, depend solely on the dictate of Scripture? God, certainly, will be no less at hand to the diligent searcher in theology, with the light of Scripture, than in philosophy, with what is called the light of nature. Nor does anyone expose himself to a greater danger of deception who indulges in the sayings of his teachers or other preconceived opinions in philosophy, than one who, about to search the Scriptures and the mysteries of religion, so submits himself to the dictate of reason that he thinks Scripture may conveniently be explained according to reason, if it seems to say the contrary. For the measure of the human mind is certainly too short and too narrow to be applied to the measuring of the works of God, and it is unfair to measure God by our foot. And since a great darkness has been spread over human reason through the Fall, and the Gospel doctrine is deeper and more hidden than the reason of men or even of angels has been able to penetrate, it is therefore worth while that, in heavenly mysteries, the light of the Word and the Spirit go before reason. But if reason dictates anything other than what agrees with the Word, then, just as the passions are called back to the command of reason, so reason must be called back to the teaching of the divine Word, and Scripture must not be explained conveniently according to reason. Therefore to Tertullian the material of secular wisdom is the rash interpreter of the divine nature and arrangement. The style of fishermen is one thing, that of philosophers another. He also elsewhere calls the philosophers the patriarchs of the heretics, and philosophy the shaking of truth. And certainly those who transfer its dictates to theology, to some extent, as a norm for interpreting Scripture, are rightly said by the same Tertullian to be mixing water with wine through philosophizing human doctrines. As Beatus Rhenanus not without reason said: See how much philosophy has always harmed Christianity. The Spanish Inquisition noted these words and ordered them deleted, in the expurgatory Index published at Madrid in the year 1584. Let us submit our little reasonings, says Augustine, to the divine sayings. Indeed Durandus himself, about himself and his manner of writing, says: The manner of speaking and writing, in other matters which do not touch faith, is that we rely more on reason. But when they touch faith, we ought to acquiesce more in the authority of Holy Scripture than in any human reason, because the divine knowledge which Holy Scripture expresses far surpasses human knowledge, as human knowledge surpasses that of the beasts, etc.

units.la: Hactenus Wolzogii sententiam & quam bene eum Sociniana conveniat, atque illa,quam refutas-se videri vult, ob oculos posuimus, addita simul, in infinitum ab ea discrepante, unanimi Reformato-rum de isthac veritate professione. Poscerct jam ordinis ratio , ut argumentorum aciem struere-mus, Wolzogianis placitis evertendis aptam ac va-lentem. Neque hic quicquam ultra necesse foret, praeterquam exscribendi labor. Decem argumen-tis, veritatem probavit, adversus Socinianos, Cla-rissimus Hoornbeekius: quae omnia excepto tan-tum ultimo,non minus Wolzogianam subvertunt, quam Socinianam sententiam. Praeterquam enim, quod in summa rei haec cum illa conveniat; cer-tum est, omnia ista argumenta , omnem tollere ra-tionis, tam rerum credendarum, quam Scripturae interpretandae respectu , normalem usum, atque antecedaneum , quam licet in quibusdam non ad-mittere,juxta cum Orthodoxis videri velit Wolzo-gius , in aliis tamen , non admittit solum, sed re-quirit, poscitque, &, si bene omnia considerentur, saepius in omnibus ejus arbitrium audiendum & sequendum docet : omnia, nihil enim prorsus excipio, sic loquitur, omnia cujuscunque generis sint, revocet ad examen, videatque an quicquam eorum quae putamus inesse Scripturis, sit manifesta rationi contrarium. Cujusmodi si quid deprehendamus, affirmatè licet pronunciare, Scripturarum hanc mentem non esse. Adeo ut, si quid afferatur ex Scriptura, quod videatur esse contrarium, commodè erit explicanda Scriptura, & NB. omnino secundum istam rationem. Et quoniam verum vero contrarium esse non potest, duplex hinc explicandae Scripturae regula efflorescit, una à ratione petita &c. ut, quod rationi manifesta contradictione repugnet, nil prorsus censeri debeat docere Scriptura: & vel pietatis esse credo, sic explicare loquentem Deum in Scripturis, ut non sibi sit in natura contrarius.
units.tr: Hitherto we have set before our eyes Wolzogius's opinion, how well it agrees with the Socinian view, and the view he seems to want to have refuted, together with the unanimous profession of the Reformed on this truth, which differs from his view infinitely. The order of the argument now requires us to marshal a line of arguments, apt and strong for overturning Wolzogius's positions. Nothing more would be needed here, except the labour of transcription. The most distinguished Hoornbeek proved this truth with ten arguments against the Socinians. All of them, except only the last, overturn Wolzogius no less than the Socinian view. For apart from the fact that in substance his view agrees with theirs, it is certain that all these arguments remove the normal and prior use of reason, both with respect to the things to be believed and with respect to the interpretation of Scripture. Although Wolzogius, as he would like to appear in agreement with the Orthodox, does not admit this in some matters, in others he not only admits it but requires it and demands it. And if everything is carefully considered, he teaches that his judgement must more often be heard and followed in all things. He speaks thus of everything, and nothing at all do I except: whatever kind things are, he refers them to examination, and sees whether anything of what we think is contained in the Scriptures is manifestly contrary to reason. If we find anything of this sort, we may affirm outright that this is not the mind of the Scriptures. So much so that, if anything is brought from Scripture which seems to be contrary, the Scripture must conveniently be explained, and NB. altogether according to that principle. And since the true cannot be contrary to the true, a double rule for explaining Scripture springs from this: one drawn from reason, etc., namely that whatever is plainly contradicted by reason, Scripture ought to be judged not to teach at all; and I believe it is a matter of piety to explain God speaking in the Scriptures so that he is not contrary to himself in nature.

units.la: Non quidem aut Hoornbeekius, aut Reformato-rum quisquam, inter veram rationem, & Scriptu-ras, ullam pugnam revera esse contendit, cum id ne cogitari quidem possit: sed ob rationis corrup-tionem, fallibilitatemque, & Scripturae sacrae per-sectionem,infallibilitatem,atque eminentiam, hoc volunt,illam per se suae explicationi atque interpre-rationi tationi sufficere, ut, quamvis post interpretandi laborem jam pera-ctam, post sensus veri jam pera-ctam eductionem, absque ejus præjudicio inde o-riundo, conciliationem eorum quæ sana ratio in in contrarium dictare videri posset, quærere ex ipsorum sententia, quantum potè, liceat, hac ta-men conditione,ut,ea non inventa, Scripturæ ta-men sua constet in dicto sensu authoritas, ratio ogganiat quicquid velit: non liceat tamen in an-tecessum[?] rationis seu Philosophiæ arbitrium in interpretando admittere, &, juxta illius dictamina, Scripturam commode explicare. Atque id est, quod statuit Wolzogius, & solidissime refutat Hoornbeekius. At rationibus & argumentis ad-versus Wolzogium agere necesse non videtur: af-firmanti enim probatio incumbit, ille ponit, quod nos, cum omnibus orthodoxis, negamus, igitur non tam à nobis, quam ex Wolzogio expeti ar-gumenta debent & rationes probantes. Scriptu-ram scientiæ salutaris principium agnoscimus u-trimque, eamque intelligibilem esse supponimus, ego per se ipsam, suaque luce, satis superque talem esse contendo, quod tu in quibusdam concedis, Phi-losophiæ autem ac rationis opem in aliis requiri statuis, ego nego. Quo jam, sodes, argumento, aut ratione, tu me in tuam pertrahes sententiam, qua rationis & Philosophiæ normalis usus omnis à me eliminatus, restituatur, non me convinces argumentis aut rationibus ex ipsa Philosophia pe-titis,quam in hac controversia non audiendam con-tendo; non ex natura earum rerum quas Scriptu-ra continet, quia neque de ea ante interpretatio-nem quicquam constat, neque, tam rei cujusdam natura, quam quidem ejus existentia ut plurimum spectari solet in sacris, ubi, ut in historia, valet au-thoritas dicentis. Restat igitur, ut tu ex concessis illud probes, quod in quæstione est, hoc est, ex ipsa Scriptura, talem rationis usum normalem. Illud autem nec tentasti, nec, si vel omni vi contendif-ses, ses , probare potuisses. Hinc Scripturam hic audiendam non esse, verum ex ratione hanc quaestionem decidendam doces. Cumque in Theologicis valeat argumentum negativum, ut, quod Scripturae authoritate destituitur, cujus Scripturae non meminit, rejicere ac negare id omnino liceat, nihil praeterea ad refutandam Wolzogianam thesin requiritur quam quod authoritate Scripturae destituatur. Interea ne sibi satisfactum non esse conqueratur, Hoornbeekii lectionem commendo, qui decem argumenta adversus Socinianos, hac in parte vix quicquam a nostro dissentientes, profert solidissima. Decimum autem, ex Adversariorum concessis quod desumsit, Wolzogium non urget, fateor, at plurima suppetunt, quibus ejus defectus suppleri queat abunde, quaeque praecipue adversus Wolzogium producere consultum duxi, quo sic ipse sua destruxisse appareat; egregiae sane, atque omnes Theologos Reformatos superantis, non jactatae perspicuitatis, aut soliditatis, sed confusionis, ac ignorantiae in re Theologica, documentum illustre certumque. Tantam autem horum argumentorum hic libellus segetem protulit, ut spicilegium aliquod relinquendum jubeat brevitatis studium. Sequentia hac vice habeat lector.
units.tr: Neither Hoornbeek nor any of the Reformed contends that there is any real conflict between true reason and the Scriptures, since this cannot even be conceived. But on account of the corruption and fallibility of reason, and the perfection, infallibility and eminence of Holy Scripture, they hold that Scripture is sufficient in itself for its own explication and interpretation. So, although after the labour of interpreting has been completed, and the true sense has been drawn out, one may, without prejudice arising from it, seek, as far as possible by their own opinion, a reconciliation of those things which sound reason seems to dictate to the contrary. Yet on this condition: that if no reconciliation is found, the authority of Scripture in the sense so given nevertheless stands, and reason may say whatever it likes. But it is not permitted to admit the judgement of reason or philosophy as antecedent in interpreting, and to explain Scripture conveniently according to its dictates. This is what Wolzogius lays down, and what Hoornbeek most solidly refutes. But it does not seem necessary to act against Wolzogius with reasons and arguments. For the burden of proof lies on the one who affirms; he posits what we, with all the Orthodox, deny. Therefore arguments and reasons proving the point should be sought not so much from us as from Wolzogius. We both acknowledge Scripture as the principle of saving knowledge, and we suppose it to be intelligible. I contend that it is, through itself and by its own light, sufficiently and more than sufficiently such; what you concede in some matters, while you lay down that the help of philosophy and reason is required in others, I deny. By what argument or reason, then, pray, will you draw me into your opinion, by which the whole normal use of reason and philosophy, eliminated by me, is restored? You will not convince me by arguments or reasons drawn from philosophy itself, which I contend is not to be heard in this controversy; nor from the nature of the things Scripture contains, since nothing is established about that before interpretation, and in sacred matters, as in history, the authority of the speaker is generally what counts, rather than the nature of some thing, which is usually considered only regarding its existence. What remains, then, is for you to prove from concessions what is in question, namely, from Scripture itself, such a normal use of reason. You have neither attempted this, nor, even if you had contended with all your might, could you have proved it. Hence you teach that Scripture is not to be heard here, but that this question is to be decided from reason. And since in theological matters the negative argument holds, that what lacks the authority of Scripture, and what Scripture does not mention, may altogether be rejected and denied, nothing further is required to refute the Wolzogian thesis than that it lacks the authority of Scripture. Meanwhile, lest he complain that he has not been satisfied, I commend the reading of Hoornbeek, who in this part, scarcely differing from our view, brings forward ten most solid arguments against the Socinians. I admit that Wolzogius is not pressed by the tenth, which he draws from the concessions of the adversaries; but there are plenty of others by which his deficiency can be abundantly supplied, and which I thought it advisable to bring forward especially against Wolzogius, so that he may appear to have destroyed his own position by them: a clear and certain proof, indeed remarkable, and surpassing all the Reformed theologians, not of boasted perspicuity or solidity, but of confusion and ignorance in theological matters. But this little book has produced so great a harvest of these arguments that the love of brevity bids me leave some gleanings. The reader may have the following on this occasion.

units.la: Dictat Wolzogius, Scripturae plurimas partes dari, quae habeant aliquam historiam. Imo omnes, nulla excepta, pro historicis esse habendas. Atque hoc non solum de Scriptura, abstracto quodam, aut praeci-so sensu, sed de rebus asserit, quae nobis oratione sacra explicantur. Idque recte, quatenus omnia quae Scripturis continentur, fide dicentis unice recipienda sunt. Interpretatio autem in rebus historicis non habet rationis evidentiam: non potest; res non patitur. Habet tamen indubitatum assensum, quem damus legibus interpretandi. Philosophiae igitur & normalis ac praecedens rationis usus hic nullus obtinet. Deinde Historiam contradistinguit veritati, seu axiomati, ut videre est, quando probaturus non omnia ad veritates referri posse, longa sa-tis serie historiam, & quæ ad eam referuntur, nar-rat: & constare asserit, veritatum numero haberi non posse quidquid historicum est. At ubi non sunt veritates ibi NB. nullus rationis usus esse potest. Unde sic argumentor. Quicquid ad veritates non pertinet, in eo nullus rationis usus esse potest.ex p.193. Scriptura vero ad veritates referri non potest; tota enim est historica ex p. 27. veritatum autem numero haberi non potest quicquid historicum est, ex p.149. Ergo in Scriptura, nullus, modo dictus, rationis, seu Philosophiæ, usus locum habere potest. Iterum, Historiæ sunt considerandæ ut res facti, in quibus toti pendemus ab authoritate dicentis, ut Dei nobis dicentis authoritas pro omni ratione habeatur. Sicque fit, ut res quæ natura sua nil habent facti aut historiæ, induant tamen rerum historicarum naturam, quia ab authoritate dicentis suspenduntur. pag. 30. Rerum autem quæ facti sunt quæstio qua quid contigerit disceptatur p.134. ejus naturæ est, ut à variis circumstantiis pendeat ejus solutio, juxta p. 137. Cum autem circa verba, & voces, omnemque & materiam & speciem orationis versetur, aliæ circumstantiæ examinari non possunt, quam quæ sunt orationi affines. Omnes autem quæ orationem aliqua propinquitate attingunt, ad usum referuntur consuetudinemque loquendi. Hinc sic arguo, quorum determinatio unice ab usu loquendi petenda, in iis nullus rationis (hac notione) aut Philosophiæ usus; at omnium eorum, quæ Scriptura continet, determinatio, ab usu loquendi repetenda est. Ergo nullus rationis usus in &c. Majorem probo 1. Ex eo, quod Wolzogius ipse eâ ipsâ majore mea tanquam argumento utatur, ad Philosophiam seu rationem removendam.
units.tr: Wolzogius dictates: Very many parts of Scripture are given which have some history. Indeed all, none excepted, must be held to be historical. And he asserts this not only of Scripture, in some abstract or precise sense, but of the things which are explained to us in sacred speech. And he is right in this, insofar as everything contained in the Scriptures is to be received solely on the faith of the speaker. But interpretation in historical matters does not have the evidence of reason: it cannot; the thing does not allow it. Yet it has indubitable assent, which we give to the laws of interpretation. Therefore no use of philosophy, or of reason in its normal and prior role, holds here. Next he distinguishes history from truth, or from axiom, as one may see when, about to prove that not everything can be referred to truths, he narrates at considerable length a series of history and the things referred to it; and he asserts that it is established that what is historical cannot be counted among truths. But where there are no truths, there, NB., no use of reason can be. Hence I argue thus: In whatever does not pertain to truths, no use of reason can be. (from p. 193). But Scripture cannot be referred to truths; for it is wholly historical (from p. 27). But what is historical cannot be counted among truths (from p. 149).
