Therefore in Scripture no use of reason, or of philosophy, as just described, can have a place. Again, histories are to be considered as matters of fact, in which we wholly depend on the authority of the speaker, so that the authority of God speaking to us is held in place of all reason. And so it comes about that things which by their nature have nothing of fact or history nevertheless take on the nature of historical things, because they are suspended from the authority of the speaker (p. 30). But of matters of fact, the question in which what has happened is disputed (p. 134); it is of such a nature that its solution depends on various circumstances, according to (p. 137). But since it concerns words and voices, and the whole matter and form of speech, no circumstances can be examined other than those akin to speech. All those which touch speech by some closeness refer to usage and the custom of speaking. Hence I argue thus: where the determination is to be sought solely from the usage of speaking, there is no use of reason (in this sense) or of philosophy; but the determination of all the things Scripture contains is to be drawn from the usage of speaking. Therefore there is no use of reason in etc. I prove the major premiss, first, from the fact that Wolzogius himself uses this very major premiss of mine as an argument for removing philosophy or reason.

units.la: 2. Quod hæc duo, jam ab initio, ut destincta, ac diversa proposuit, rationem & usum loquendi.
units.tr: 2. That he set out these two things, reason and the usage of language, from the very beginning as distinct and different.

units.la: 3. Hoc ipso in loco p. 137. distinguit ut ex diversis petitam, quam ex usu, & eam, quam ex ratione haurimus, cognitionem. Neque etiam dubito, quin ultro majorem sit concessurus. Minorem autem sic demonstro. Cujus natura ea est, ut a variis circumstantiis ejus pendeat solutio, illius determi-natio ab usu loquendi &c. At totius Scripturæ ea est natura. E. Major exstat p.137. verbis jam citatis. Minorem probo in hunc modum. Omnis quæstio facti, quaque quæritur, quid contingerit nec ne, ejus naturæ est, ut a variis circumstantiis ejus pendeat solutio. At tota Scriptura est talis. Ergo &c. Major habetur p. 134. cum 137. Minorem suppeditat author verbis ex p. 30. citatis. Ex concessis igitur concludo, nullum rationis, seu Philosophiæ, in Scriptura interpretanda, istiusmodi usum esse. Ubique hic obtinet quod habet p. 132. Est quæstio facti, non juris; quæ pendet ab orationis circumstantiis, non ab evidentia demonstrationum; in qua quid Deus dixerit, quæritur, non, verumne sit, nec ne verum, quod dixit. Confer. p. 135. & 136. ubi fuse hæc omnia ad quæstionem facti, & eam, quæ de rei existentia est, referenda probat. Non enim aliud quæritur, quam an hæc aut illa veritas, seu hic aut ille sensus, hoc loco tradatur, ac proinde patet ejus naturæ esse, ut a variis circumstantiis ejus pendeat solutio, ais ipse p. 137. quare non aliter rationi hic nitimur, quam quod ratione prædita mens nostra colligit ea argumenta (qui usus tantum instrumentalis est) quibus persuadeatur. NB. Nulla autem adhibet principia, aut notiones communes, aliasve notionis faces, ut rem sibi probet. sic p.136. Unde sic adversus Wolzogium infero verbis Hoornbeekii. Non quæritur, inquit ille, in isthoc dubio, quid verum sit, vel debeat esse in re; sed quis sit sensus verborum; at de hoc ut aliunde judicetur, quam ex Sacra Scriptura, nunquid vides contra illud esse, solam Scripturam sacram esse normam fidei & vitæ perfectissimam? Ubi jam, prævium rationis examen & arbitrium? quorsum ista, a Wolzogio ficta, rationis regula? longius eam ipse removet p. 227, 228, 229, 233. in conflictu enim ad verita-tem tem propius accedere compellitur. Sic locis cita-tis, faciunt rationes praecipuè tres, ut credam per se-ipsum, de quovis authore loquitur absque discri-mine, explicari eum posse ac deberi. De scriptura deinceps sigillatim haec scribit, de eodem auctore disputamus qui sit per seipsum explicandus, neque sic ab inferiore judice provocatur ad superiorem: sed sententiam suam idem judex explicat, aut suum fa-ctum confitetur, de quo fit inquisitio, quisquis ille sit. Sic erumpit sparsim veritatis vis invicta. Haec verba, primo elidunt omnem rationis seu Philoso-phiae normalem & antecedaneum usum, quem su-periùs thesi VI, & Canonibus praescriptis, posue-rat Wolzogius, adeoque ulterioris refutationis onere nos levat vir bonus, tollitque ipse quod po-suerat[?]. Deinde hic manifestam deprehendimus contradictionem, cum iis, quae in superioribus, duobus in locis; notavimus, sic in metho-di, & erga Reformatos Wolzogiani animi exa-mine, thesi quinta dixerat. Deum esse Interpre-tem suae Scripturae non video. Negamus Deum dici posse proprie Scripturae Interpretem. Hic vero sen-tentiam suam idem judex explicare dicitur, Scri-ptura quando per Scripturam, idem · author, quando per seipsum explicatur. At quis ille in Scri-ptura Judex, Wolzogi, quae sententia, quam i-dem Judex explicet? Judex nonne Deus est, cu-jus Scriptura sententia, nonne Deus igitur Scri-pturam explicat seu Interpretatur? Qui igitur ne-gasti Deum esse Interpretem suae Scripturae? Deum Scripturae interpretem dici posse cur insi-ciatus es? Nihil ultra volunt Reformati, quam eundem judicem suam sententiam exponere, hoc est, Deum Scripturae Interpretem esse. Quorsum igitur singularem sententiam profiteris? quorsum à te, confusa saltem obscuritate, diversum esse Reformatorum sensum dicis? argumenta, quae id probant, quod hic ipse ponis in terminis, rejicis, explodis? Non equidem hunc capio disputandi modum, futilem sane & sibi saepius adversum. & hic lubricum video nostrum, dum plura, sua liberalitate, Paradoxo largitur, quam rei, qua disputatur, indoles ferre potest, aut ratio, pugnat: Verum enim vero, haec verba respicio, si-ve idem habeatur auctor Scripturæ, sive diversi, eo-dem modo eam per se ipsam explicabimus, ut alios authores vel per se ipsos vel per alios. Dixeram rei naturam de qua disputatio est, haec ferre non posse, quod certissimum est, nam, ut recte notat alibi, tenendum semper, Amanuenses quidem diver-sos esse, sed eundem auctorem omnia dictasse Deum. Quod nisi divinitus constet, & pro indubitato habeatur, ruit certe omnis, ex collatione variorum Scripturæ librorum, facta interpretatio, ruit sal-tem illius interpretationis infallibilitas ac certitudo divina. Quamvis enim authores diversi se mutuo explicent, non tamen id faciunt infalli-biliter certóque: scripserint puriori, vel Augu-stæo seculo, diversi Scriptores, non tamen ultra probabilitatem ascendit, omne, quod ex plurium collatione, de hujus aut illius sensu, protuleris argumentum; quod vel ex eo constat, quod quis-que suum quendam habeat peculiarem usum loquendi scribendique, certo verborum genere, certis formu-lis, certa ratione constructionis ambituque orationis utitur, quae liceat ejus appellare characterem autho-ris, quo Salustii dictio discernitur à dictione Caesaris, & à Virgilio distinguitur Ovidius. Qui sane charec-ter æque debet esse perspectus Interpreti, atque u-sus loquendi vulgaris, quia quidam est veluti usus sin-gularis ejus Auctoris quem explicamus: ut recte notasti antea. Neque etiam loquendi usus, quando interpretem Scripturæ eum efficis, prout à diversis usurpatur, sed quemadmodum à Deo approbatus est, & usurpatus, spectandus est, te judice p. 262. & 263. atque adeo, ut unius ejusdemque authoris. Qui pote igitur, ut hic, sive idem habeatur Author Scripturæ, sive diversi, eodem tamen modo eam per se ipsam explicatam iri asseras. Quoniam, si autho-res essent diversi... deri, nisi dubia & inania verba solo pondere ratio-nium explicuerit Philosophia! Hoc innuit, Deum sic intelligibiliter loquentem fidem mereri, ejusque sensum, quem verba, quem scopus, antecedentia quoque & consequentia docent & produnt, denique qui undique contractis locis parallellis apparet, pro vero sumendum, non perito, aut expectato, Philosophiæ, seu rationis, de re ipsa, dictamine. At tolluntur sic omnia, quæ de præuio, rerum omnium, per Philosophiam examine, p. 67. aliisque, à ratione petitis regulis, quas interpretaturo in antecessum consulendas statuit, antea dictaverat. Præsertim, si fieri nequeat, quod fieri non posse certum est, ut loco ipso, locique circumstantiis, ac parallellis, analogia item fidei, rité consideratis, alius, quam menti divinæ congruus, id est, verus; inibique intentus sensus eruatur. Non enim est is Deus, qui aut nesciat loqui, quod intelligatur, aut nolit, ait p.73. Unde & recte Interpretem dicit, qui mente jungat sensum cum verbis, illumque his inesse ex ipsa verborum textura cognoscit. Et verus demum sensus est, qui omnia complectitur quæ ex analogia loci inclusa textui sunt, quæque posthabitis cæteris omnibus ex ipsa orationis textura efflorescit. At quis sic tandem, rationis examini, seu arbitrio, locus superest, dum omne textus ipse, ejusque analogia ac paralellismus expediat: dum, hisce rite consideratis, falsum esse non possit quod ex textu elicitur, atque id est, quod volunt Reformati, quodque præcedentia, quæ de ratione nugatus est Wolzogius, inutilia reddit ac refutat, ut vel in transcursu inspicienti patet. Poscit id, & quæstionis omnis, quæ hic agitanda venit, natura, quam facti esse dixit noster. Adeo ut absurdè tantum operæ collocaverit, in probanda distinctione, eorum, quæ veritates continent, ab iis quæ non continent veritates, non enim hic quæritur proprie, quid verum sit, nec ne, scriptura enim præsupponitur non posse falsum docere rite expensa, sed an illa, vel ista veritas, aut, quid, hoc loco, tradatur; quæstio enim omnis hic facti & historiæ naturam induit. Imo credimus etiam ante- quam sciamus ait p. 29. Res enim Scripturæ, non quædam, non quatenus ratione non innotescunt, sed quatenus in Scriptura continentur, eæque uni-versæ, fatente Wolzogio, fidei subjectæ sunt, in sese quantamvis patiantur differentiam. Licet enim quædam subinde occurrant, quæ & sciri possint, & credi, hic tamen, non ideo credimus quia ratio di-ctat, sed quia Deus dicit, ait p. 52. adeo ut fides, quæ à sola pendet authoritate dicentis, (sicut scientia à lumine veritatis ipsius, quæque res ratione probatas vult) tota regnet Scriptura teste Wolzogio p. 30. Spectantur enim hic mera testimonia quibus probetur, ait p. 230. Omnia igitur quæ Scripturis traduntur, ut talia, ex ore, ex verbis Dei, hoc est, dicentis authoritate, unicè recipienda sunt, quod fieri sane non potest, si Philosophiæ aut rationis suffragium petendum sit prius. Fidei enim est, sunt verba Heidani sæpius citata, rationi præscribere, & id facere ut ne sit opus ratione. Quæ omnia, ratione silere tantisper jussa, ex Scriptura Scripturæ sensum petendum unicè esse, satis superque demonstrant.
units.tr: 3. In this same passage, p. 137, he distinguishes the knowledge we draw from usage, as coming from a different source, from the knowledge we draw from reason. Nor do I doubt that he will readily grant the major premise. I demonstrate the minor premise thus: whose nature is such that its solution depends on various circumstances of it, its determination is to be taken from the usage of language, etc. But the whole of Scripture is of this nature. Therefore, etc. The major premise stands at p. 137 in the words already cited. I prove the minor in this way: every question of fact, in which it is asked what has happened or not, is of such a nature that its solution depends on various circumstances. But the whole of Scripture is such. Therefore, etc. The major premise is found at p. 134 together with p. 137. The author supplies the minor in the words cited from p. 30. From these admissions I therefore conclude that there is no use of reason, or of philosophy, of this kind in interpreting Scripture. Everywhere what he says on p. 132 holds: It is a question of fact, not of right; it depends on the circumstances of the utterance, not on the evidence of demonstrations; in it what God has said is asked, not whether what he said is true or not. Compare pp. 135 and 136, where he proves at length that all these matters must be referred to a question of fact and to the question of the existence of a thing. For nothing else is asked than whether this or that truth, or this or that sense, is delivered in this place; and so it is plain that its nature is such that its solution depends on various circumstances, as you yourself say on p. 137. Therefore we do not rely on reason here in any other way than that our mind, endowed with reason (which use is merely instrumental), gathers those arguments by which it is persuaded. N.B. He brings in no principles or common notions, or other torches of notions, to prove his point, as on p. 136. Hence I infer against Wolzogius, in the words of Hoornbeek: He asks, in this doubt, not what is true, or ought to be true, in the matter, but what is the sense of the words; but that this be judged from elsewhere than Holy Scripture, do you not see that it is contrary to the teaching that Holy Scripture alone is the most perfect rule of faith and life? Where, then, is the prior examination and judgment of reason? What is this rule of reason, invented by Wolzogius? He removes it further still, at pp. 227, 228, 229 and 233; for in the conflict he is compelled to come closer to the truth. Thus, in the passages cited, the reasons chiefly are three, so that I believe through himself, he speaks of any author without distinction, that he can and ought to be explained. Afterwards he writes about Scripture piece by piece: We dispute about the same author, who is to be explained through himself, and in this way one does not appeal from a lower judge to a higher; but the same judge explains his own sentence, or confesses his own deed, about which the inquiry is made, whoever he may be. Thus the invincible force of truth breaks out here and there. These words, first, cancel every normal and antecedent use of reason or philosophy, which Wolzogius had laid down in thesis VI and in the canons prescribed above; and so the good man relieves us of the burden of further refutation, and he himself removes what he had laid down. Next, we find a manifest contradiction here with what he had said in thesis V, in the two passages noted above, in his method and in his examination of the mind of Wolzogius toward the Reformed: I do not see that God is the Interpreter of his own Scripture. We deny that God can properly be called the Interpreter of Scripture. But here the same judge is said to explain his own sentence: Scripture, when it is explained through Scripture; the same author, when he is explained through himself. But who, Wolzogius, is that judge in Scripture, and what is the sentence which the same judge explains? Is not the judge God, whose sentence Scripture is? Does not God therefore explain, that is, interpret, Scripture? Why, then, did you deny that God is the Interpreter of his own Scripture? Why did you deny that God can be called the Interpreter of Scripture? The Reformed want nothing more than that the same judge expound his own sentence, that is, that God is the Interpreter of Scripture. Why, then, do you profess a singular opinion? Why do you say that the sense of the Reformed differs from yours, if only by a confused obscurity? Do you reject, explode, the arguments which prove what you yourself here lay down in plain terms? I do not indeed approve this manner of disputing, certainly futile and often self-contradictory; and I see our man slipping here, while in his generosity he grants to the paradox more than the nature of the matter under dispute can bear, or reason: Truly, in truth, I regard these words: whether the author of Scripture is the same or different, we shall in the same way explain it through itself, as we explain other authors either through themselves or through others. I have said that the nature of the matter under discussion cannot bear this, which is most certain; for, as he rightly notes elsewhere, it must always be held that the amanuenses are indeed different, but God dictated everything to one and the same author. Unless this is established divinely and held as indubitable, certainly the whole interpretation made from the comparison of various books of Scripture falls; at least the infallibility and divine certainty of that interpretation falls. For although different authors explain one another, they do not do so infallibly and certainly: different writers may have written in the purer or in the Augustan age, yet whatever argument you bring forward from the comparison of several about the sense of this or that does not rise above probability. This is clear from the fact that each person has a peculiar usage of speaking and writing of his own, uses a certain kind of words, certain formulas, a certain order of construction and compass of expression, which may be called the character of the author, by which the diction of Sallust is distinguished from that of Caesar, and Ovid from Virgil. This character ought surely to be as well known to the interpreter as the common usage of language, since it is, as it were, a singular usage of that author whom we explain, as you rightly noted before. Nor again is the usage of language, when you make it the interpreter of Scripture, to be considered as it is used by different people, but as it has been approved and used by God, according to your judgment on pp. 262 and 263; and so as the usage of one and the same author. How, then, can you assert that, whether the author of Scripture is the same or different, it will be explained through itself in the same way? Since, if the authors were different... unless philosophy, by the weight of reasons alone, has explained words that are doubtful and empty! He hints that God, speaking so intelligibly, deserves faith, and that his sense, which the words, the scope, the things preceding and following teach and reveal, and finally which appears from parallel passages gathered from every side, is to be taken as true, not by the judgment of a philosophy, or of reason, that is skilled or expected, concerning the matter itself. But thus all those things are removed which he had earlier laid down: that the rules to be consulted in advance by the interpreter, drawn from reason, must undergo a prior examination of all things through philosophy (p. 67 and elsewhere). Especially if it cannot be done, which it is certain cannot be done, that from the place itself, and its circumstances and parallels, and likewise the analogy of faith, duly considered, another sense, agreeing with the divine mind, that is true, and intended therein, is brought out. For God is not one who either does not know how to speak so as to be understood, or is unwilling, he says on p. 73. Hence he rightly calls the interpreter one who in mind joins the sense with the words, and knows from the very texture of the words that the sense is contained in them. And finally the true sense is that which embraces all that is included in the text by the analogy of the place, and which, all others set aside, flourishes from the very texture of the expression. But who, then, in this way has any room left for the examination or judgment of reason, when the text itself, with its analogy and parallelism, settles everything; when, these things being duly considered, what is drawn from the text cannot be false? And this is what the Reformed want; and it renders useless and refutes what Wolzogius had babbled about reason before, as anyone who glances over it can see. The nature of the whole question that is to be discussed here demands this, the nature which our author said is one of fact. So absurdly has he spent his effort in proving the distinction between those things which contain truths and those which do not contain truths; for the question here is not properly what is true or not, since it is presupposed that Scripture, rightly weighed, cannot teach falsehood; but whether this or that truth, or what, is delivered in this place; for every question here takes on the nature of fact and history. Indeed we believe even before we know, he says on p. 29. For the things of Scripture, not some of them, not insofar as they are not known by reason, but insofar as they are contained in Scripture, and these all, as Wolzogius admits, are subject to faith, however much they differ among themselves. For although some things occasionally occur which can both be known and believed, here, we do not therefore believe because reason dictates, but because God says, he says on p. 52, so that faith, which depends solely on the authority of the one speaking (just as knowledge depends on the light of truth itself, and wants things proved by reason), reigns over all of Scripture, as Wolzogius testifies on p. 30. For here mere testimonies are considered, by which something is proved, he says on p. 230. Therefore all things that are delivered in the Scriptures, as such, from the mouth, from the words of God, that is, by the authority of the one speaking, are to be received solely; which certainly cannot happen if the vote of philosophy or reason must first be sought. For it belongs to faith, to use the words of Heidanus, often cited, to prescribe to reason, and to do so that there is no need of reason. All these things, which bid reason to be silent for the time being, sufficiently and more than sufficiently demonstrate that the sense of Scripture is to be sought from Scripture alone.

units.la: Addenda sunt, quæ reperiuntur p. 193. ubi Philosophiam, seu rationem, probat inutilem esse, in explicatione plerorumque locorum: hoc modo. Ubi illa scilicet ratio seu Philosophia veritates non invenit, aut si inveniat, ubi non sunt veritates naturales, ibi nullus ejus usus esse potest. Notandum quod infinitas hæc thesis & inextricabiles disputationes pariat, semper enim in antecessum disputari debe-bit, an veritas sit quod textus continet, si veritas, an naturalis nec ne, quod sciri in antecessum non potest, quoniam ante peractam interpretationem, quid textus contineat nec ne, inter ignota censendum est, procul omni dubio; ac proinde, an veritatem contineat nec ne, & si veritatem, an naturalem an supernaturalem; etiam an Philosophia ju-vante, vante, loci explicatio peragenda sit, an secus & sine illa, semper disquiri poterit. Quod nihil aliud est, quam totam Scripturam nasi cerei, ut dicunt, instar concipere, atque exponere ludibrio; sed de hisce postea. Nunc Wolzogium refutaturus, contendo, hac ratione evinci, non solum in multis, quod non tantum Paradoxi, sed, quod & Paradoxi & Wolzogii sententiam funditus evertit, in omnibus, Philosophiam inutilem esse. Ubi veritates non sunt, ibi, nullus rationis usus, at hic in tota Scriptura, licet veritates contineat bene multas, quaedam diverso etiam lumine cognoscibiles, & rationis, & revelationis, non tamen ut veritates, sed ut historiae, ut res facti, ut rei denique existentia, quaeque, non rei ipsius claritate, sed dicentis unicè ac referentis authoritate, sive veritates sint, sive non sint, recipienda veniunt omnia, vel ipso teste Wolzogio, res enim etiam illae, quae natura sua nil habent facti vel historiae, induunt tamen rerum historicarum naturam. Iterum, si quicquam, si bene multum, si omne, quod veritatem, eamque naturalem non continet, absque rationis seu Philosophiae arbitrio atque dictamine, explicari in Scriptura dicas Wolzogi, ego id de omnibus dixero, & summa cum ratione, tu enim, qui quaedam sal-tem (omnia aliquando dixeras) ex rationis arbitrio interpretanda censes, diversitatis rationem dare teneris, quam dare non poteris, utcunque te torqueas: audio quidem vanas, veritates inter, factaque distinctiones, quaedam naturalem, alia supernaturalem veritatem continere te dictantem audio: sed nonne vides bone vir haec frustra à te dici? qui enim, vel tu ista scire, aut ego ista pro veris recipere queam? dum nihil hactenus, utrique nostrum se ad Scripturam, postea intelligendam, jam interpretandam adhuc accingenti, de iis, quae deinceps demum innotescent, constare queat; tu, qui analogiam fidei, qui ipsam Scripturam, in universae de interprete quaestionis decisione, ea ratione, quia de utraque ante omnem interpretationem nihil constat, audiendam esse negas, hasce tuas di-stinctiones, quas eadem dispellit ratio, nobis ob-trudes? cum fungis te rem habiturum & bene credulis lucis filiis, perperam, crede mihi, somnia-sti, mi Wolzogi. Viden', sic, quo tu à multis, eo ego ab omnibus Philosophiam seu rationem ar-cendam esse, argumento demonstravi.
units.tr: It should be added what is found on p. 193, where he proves that philosophy, or reason, is useless in the explanation of most passages, in this way: Where that reason or philosophy does not find truths, or where, if it does find them, there are no natural truths, there can be no use of it at all. It should be noted that this thesis gives rise to endless and inextricable disputes. For it will always have to be argued beforehand whether what the text contains is a truth, and if a truth, whether it is natural or not. That cannot be known in advance, since before the interpretation is finished, what the text contains, or whether it contains anything, must without doubt be counted among the unknowns. Consequently it can always be asked whether it contains a truth or not, and if a truth, whether natural or supernatural, and also whether the explanation of the passage is to be carried out with the help of philosophy or without it. This is nothing else than to take the whole of Scripture, as they say, for a nose of wax and to expose it to ridicule; but of these matters later. Now, intending to refute Wolzogius, I contend that by this reasoning it is shown that philosophy is useless, not only in many cases, as the Paradoxist claims, but in all cases, which overturns both the Paradoxist's view and that of Wolzogius from the foundations. Where there are no truths, there is no use of reason. Yet in the whole of Scripture, although it contains many truths, some of them knowable by a different light, both of reason and of revelation, nevertheless they are not there as truths but as history, as matters of fact, and finally as the existence of a thing. All of these must be received, not by the clarity of the thing itself but on the sole authority of the one who speaks and reports, whether they are truths or not. Wolzogius himself bears witness to this: for even those things which by their nature have nothing of fact or history nonetheless take on the nature of historical things. Again, if you say, Wolzogius, that anything at all, or very much, or everything which does not contain a truth, and a natural truth at that, is to be explained in Scripture without the judgement and dictate of reason or philosophy, I will say the same of all things, and with the greatest reason. For you, who think that at least some things (at one time you said all things) are to be explained by the judgement of reason, are bound to give a reason for this difference, and you will not be able to give one however much you twist yourself. I hear you making vain distinctions between truths and facts, saying that some things contain a natural truth and others a supernatural truth. But do you not see, good man, that these things are said by you in vain? For how could you know these things, or how could I accept them as true, when nothing at all has yet been established for either of us, who are only now preparing ourselves to understand and then to interpret Scripture, about those things which will only become known afterwards? You, who deny that the analogy of faith and Scripture itself are to be heard in deciding the whole question about the interpreter, because nothing is established about either of them before all interpretation, are you pushing these distinctions of yours on us, which the same reasoning dispels? When you pretend that you are going to deal with those who are well believing sons of the light, you have, believe me, dreamed wrongly, my dear Wolzogius. Do you see how, by this argument, I have shown that philosophy or reason must be kept away not only from many, as you do, but from all?

units.la: Suum etiam illi exemplum objicimus, quando cri-minatur, obscurè, non satis dilucidè egisse Theolo-gos, qui Scripturam ex Scriptura interpretandam censent. Idem enim, quod ipse Paradoxo objicit, sibi à me objiciendum sciat Wolzogius: expli-cuerat Paradoxus, referente Wolzogio, locum, 1.Cor.II.14. at quomodo? Verba examinat, usum eorum vulgarem, antecedentia, consequentia, scopum adducit, loca similia, &c. Hunc agendi modum probat, quid aliud, inquit, hic faceremus aut ego, aut quivis alius qui ab usu loquentium, (qui ab ipsa Scriptura, quam cum dicimus, loquendi usum, à parte Scripturæ, præsupponimus) pendemus in NB. omni interpretatione. Imo non probat solum, sed Philosophiæ, sed rationis normalem in interpretando usum refutari, hac ipsa praxi, ab Exercitatore, putat: Ego autem & Wolzogianas hypotheses, eadem ista ratione, convello, hunc in modum. Qui à verborum examine, ab usu, ab antecedentibus, à consequentibus, à scopo, à parallelis &c. in interpretatione omni pendendum docet, is omne rejicit antecedens rationis arbitrium, idque non in quibusdam sed in omnibus, dicit enim NB. in omni interpretatione. At à verborum examine &c. Ergo. Major est Wolzogii, quâ ipse adversus Paradoxum utitur, estque universalis, concludens de omni interpretatione. Minor itidem est Wolzogii, uti jam vidimus. Conclusio autem est contra eundem, ut Canone tertio, ex ejus pag. 20. 21. 23. 67. eruto, patet. Huic affine est, quod alibi, objectis ab adversario locis, quorum expliexplicationem, Philosophiæ, seu rationis, normalem usum, requirere volebat Paradoxus, ita respondeat, ut propriam thesin destruat aperte; Sacramenta-les & Anthropologicos loquendi modos, retule-rat Paradoxus, ex Scriptura, eorum sensum eruen-dum, recte respondet Wolzogius, additque leges interpretandi, (non quæ Philosophiam seu ratio-nem includant, sed ei opponantur) ad usum linguæ exactas id totum definire) Scripturam hoc definire ipsam diceret Reformatus, supposito loquendi u-su, verborumque significatione. At si totum id ex Scriptura, hæc enim loquendi usum in se com-plectitur, eumque supponit, definiatur, ubi ratio-nis, quod posuit, arbitrium, ubi jurisdictio? ni-hil requiritur, præter totius negotii decisionem, quam, si ex Scriptura haberi posse, idque in istis materiis, statuat, quorsum igitur tam seria pro ra-tionis arbitrio, & cunctorum, nihilo excepto, exa-mine, disceptatio? videtur autem sentire infli-ctum sibi à se vulnus, & rationem de ponte deje-ctam videre omnem: hinc limitationem addit, sed præposteram: quanquam, inquit, neque velim ex-clusam rationem. Nec enim ii sumus qui nullas partes velimus rationis esse in interpretatione. Non pro instrumentali, quem dicimus, rationis usu e-rat disputatio, sed normali; clarius igitur Philoso-phiam dixisset, ut antea vidimus: at sero sapit, & suæ rationis memor evasit, noster disputator.
units.tr: We also object to him his own example, when he accuses the theologians, who hold that Scripture is to be interpreted from Scripture, of having explained things obscurely and not clearly enough. For Wolzogius should know that what he objects to the Paradoxist, the same I can object to him. The Paradoxist, as Wolzogius reports, had explained the passage 1 Cor. 2:14. But how? He examines the words, adduces their common usage, the preceding and following context, the aim, similar passages, etc. He approves this method of proceeding: what else, he says, would we do here, I or anyone else who, from the usage of speakers (which we presuppose, when we speak of Scripture, from the side of Scripture) depends in NB. every interpretation. Indeed, he not only approves this but thinks that the normal use of philosophy or reason in interpreting is refuted by this very practice of the Examiner. I, however, overturn Wolzogius's hypotheses by the same reasoning, in this way. Whoever teaches that every interpretation depends on the examination of words, on usage, on what goes before, what follows, the aim, parallel passages, etc., rejects every judgement of reason that precedes it, and this not in some cases but in all, for he says NB. in every interpretation. But the examination of words, etc., is the Examiner's method. Therefore... The major premise is Wolzogius's own, which he uses against the Paradoxist, and it is universal, concluding about every interpretation. The minor is also Wolzogius's, as we have now seen. The conclusion is against him, as is clear from the third canon, drawn from his pp. 20, 21, 23, 67. Akin to this is what he says elsewhere: when the Paradoxist had brought forward passages whose explanation, he wanted, required the normal use of philosophy or reason, Wolzogius answers in such a way as openly to destroy his own thesis. The Paradoxist had said that sacramental and anthropological modes of speaking must have their meaning drawn from Scripture. Wolzogius rightly replies, and adds that the laws of interpretation (not those which include philosophy or reason, but those which are opposed to it) define all this exactly according to the usage of the language. A Reformed writer would say that Scripture itself defines this, given the usage of speech and the meaning of the words. But if all this is defined from Scripture (for Scripture embraces the usage of speech in itself and presupposes it), where then is the judgement of reason which he posited, where its jurisdiction? Nothing is required except the decision of the whole matter, which he states can be had from Scripture, and in these subjects. Why then such serious disputation about the judgement of reason and the examination of all things, nothing excepted? He seems, however, to feel the wound he has inflicted on himself, and he sees that reason has been thrown from the bridge altogether. Hence he adds a limitation, but a senseless one: although, he says, I would not want reason to be excluded. For we are not of those who would want reason to have no part in interpretation. The dispute was not about the instrumental use of reason, as we call it, but about the normal use. He would therefore have spoken more clearly of philosophy, as we saw before. But our disputant has become wise too late, and mindful of his own reason.

units.la: Disputatur, an omnem, an aliquam saltem, nor-malem in interpretando usum præstet ratio seu Philosophia, probatum id voluit Paradoxus, re-futasse videri vult noster, dicitque totum negotium ex interpretandi legibus decidendum, quas rationi seu Philosophiæ opponit disparatè; nunc autem, post derogatam omnem rationi arbitrandi, decidendique facultatem, eamque alteri cuidam in universum injunctam, subdit, se nolle omnem rationem, seu Philosophiam exclusam, sed unde? an ex interpretatione? sic est, nam de ea dis-
units.tr: It is disputed whether reason or philosophy provides every normal use in interpreting, or at least some. The Paradoxist wanted to prove the affirmative. Our author wants to seem to have refuted it, and says that the whole business is to be decided by the laws of interpretation, which he sets against reason or philosophy as something separate. But now, after taking away from reason all power of judging and deciding, and assigning that power in general to some other thing, he adds that he does not wish to exclude all reason or philosophy. But from where? From interpretation? So it is, for the dispute is about that,

units.la: disquiritur, ea tota, aliunde perficienda dicitur, adeo ut sero nimis, rationis postliminio hic causam atque sic sui ipsius, agat. Sufficiat, valeat, vigeat ratio, Philosophia prolixe laudetur, totum modo interpretationis negotium expediat ipsa Scriptura, saltem, à rationis norma, nullatenus dependeat, hoc volunt Reformati, & contra Anonymum, imo vero contra se ipse hic concludit Wolzogius.
units.tr: and the whole of that is said to be carried out from elsewhere, so that, too late, reason, by a right of return, here pleads its own cause and so acts for itself. Let reason be sufficient, let it be strong and flourish, let philosophy be lavishly praised; let Scripture alone complete the whole business of interpretation, and let it depend in no way on the norm of reason. This is what the Reformed want, and against the Anonymous; indeed, against himself, Wolzogius here concludes.

units.la: Sic hactenus ex Wolzogio Wolzogium refutavimus, alia argumenta si velit lector, adeat Hoornbeckium loco superius citato, non enim consultum judicavi, huc ea transcribere. Unicum ex ipsa Gallicanæ Ecclesiæ Confessione publica repetendum restat; & absurda quædam, ex Wolzogianis sequentia, recensenda superstunt.
units.tr: Thus far I have refuted Wolzogius out of Wolzogius. If the reader wishes other arguments, let him consult Hoornbeek in the place cited above, for I have not judged it expedient to transcribe them here. One thing remains to be repeated from the public Confession of the Gallican Church itself; and some absurdities that follow from Wolzogius's views still remain to be listed.

units.la: Omnem humanam sapientiam, id est rationem, seu Philosophiam, ad Scripturæ divinæ regulam & præscriptum examinari oportere & exigi, docet di-cta Confessio, Articulo quinto. Hinc sic arguo, quod ad Scripturam omne exigendum, id Scripturæ, adhuc interpretandæ, regula, aut norma esse non potest, ei in omnibus arbitrium, jurisdictio, in antecessum, nulla competit. At sic res sese cum ratione, cum Philosophia, habet. Ergo &c. Eo ipso, quod dicatur omnis ad Scripturam exigenda, necesse est, ut Scriptura, aliàs enim amussis normæque vices obire non potest, per se, aut aliunde saltem, quam ex Philosophia, in antecessum intelligibilis atque interpretabilis, liceat verba fingere, statuatur. Atque hoc est, quod adversatur Wolzogio, qui ejus arbitrium, jurisdictionem, & regulam, interpretaturo præfigenda superius jussit.
units.tr: The said Confession, in Article 5, teaches that all human wisdom, that is reason or philosophy, ought to be examined and brought to the rule and prescription of divine Scripture. From this I argue thus: what is to be brought to Scripture cannot be the rule or norm of Scripture while it is still to be interpreted, since it has no judgement or jurisdiction over Scripture beforehand in any respect. But so it is with reason and with philosophy. Therefore etc. From the very fact that everything is said to be brought to Scripture, it is necessary that Scripture be established as intelligible and interpretable beforehand, otherwise it cannot serve as a rule and norm; it must not be allowed to invent words, either by itself or from elsewhere than from philosophy. And this is what opposes Wolzogius, who laid down beforehand that reason should have the judgement, jurisdiction and rule over what is to be interpreted.

units.la: Absurdorum ex Wolzogianis sequentium, magna licet copia enumerari posset, hac vice sex tantum proponam.
units.tr: Of the absurdities that follow from the Wolzogian position, a great many could be listed, but on this occasion I will set out only six.

units.la: 1. Primum est, Lutheranis ansam dari, majori cum veritatis specie, Socinianismum, hac in parte, Orthodoxis impingendi. Scimus quam sedulò cautéque semper nostri cavere studuerint, ne Socinianorum Philosophandi cacoethes ipsis merito exprobaretur, nec tamen istorum hominum du-ram crisin evitare potuerunt viri prudentissimi, si-mul atque ab isto crimine purissimi. Dixerit licet, defectum charitatis esse, quod Ekhardus, Stegmannus, Meisnerus, aliique nostros in eo cum Socinianis componant, Voetius. Et Elenchum ignorari Arnoldus. Dicteriis nihilominus infestant innoxiam & inculpabilem Ecclesiae doctrinam; quid autem nunc expectandum erit, postquam in terminis doceri viderint, quod antea, sine mendacio, Reformatis tribui nullo modo poterat. Sic, pro minus felici sua veracitate, olim nostra sensa referebat Ekhardus, placita rationis nobis quod sit quaedam quasi statera & mensura, cui res omnes, etiam Theologicas, commensurari, & si quod non exactè quadret, saltem in peregrinum sensum transformari oporteat. Crocius forsan hisce, idem quod Hunnio, respondisset. An nostri tantum Philosophiae tribuant, ut omnia, nihilo excepto, ejus examini ac arbitrio tradenda doceant, testantur commentarii. Ego non contendam cum hominis impudentia. Commentarii quae sunt in omnium manu confutant mendacium. Nunc autem idem à Pastore, & qui Reformatus, imo, vel in hoc scripto, orthodoxus audire gestit, docetur, urgetur, inculcatur: ut ex pagina 67. in fine pag. 20, 21 & 23. jam saepius ostendimus. Ecce communem Ecclesiae causam certissimo calumniarum æstui, ab infelici propugnatore, palam objectam & expositam; Sed adversarii omnem verè Reformatorum Theologorum multitudinem, imo confessiones, scriptaque publica, huic homini altùm contradicere saepius, noverint.
units.tr: 1. The first is that it gives the Lutherans an opportunity, with a greater appearance of truth, to charge the Orthodox on this point with Socinianism. We know how carefully and constantly our people have taken pains not to be deservedly reproached for the Socinians' itch to philosophize, and yet even the most prudent men have not been able to escape the harsh judgment of these people, even when they were most pure of that crime. One may say, it is a lack of charity that Ekhardus, Stegmannus, Meisnerus and others compare our people with the Socinians, as Voetius does. And Arnoldus says that the Elenchus is ignored. Nevertheless they attack the harmless and blameless doctrine of the Church with taunts. What, then, is to be expected now, after they have seen it taught in express terms what before, without falsehood, could in no way be attributed to the Reformed? Thus Ekhardus, with less felicitous truthfulness, once reported our views: the principles of reason are, as it were, a kind of balance and measure, to which all things, even theological ones, must be weighed, and if something does not square exactly, it must at least be transformed into a foreign sense. Perhaps Crocius would have answered these things as he answered Hunnius: our commentaries testify whether our people attribute so much to philosophy that they teach that all things, without exception, are to be handed over to its examination and judgment. I shall not contend with this man's impudence. The commentaries that are in everyone's hands refute the lie. But now the same thing is taught, urged and pressed by a pastor who is Reformed, indeed orthodox, in this very writing, and who eagerly wishes to be heard. As we have already shown several times, this is so from page 67 at the end, and from pages 20, 21 and 23. Behold the common cause of the Church, openly charged and exposed to the most certain storm of calumny by an unhappy champion. But our adversaries should know that the whole multitude of truly Reformed theologians, indeed the public confessions and writings, have often contradicted this man most strongly.

units.la: 2. Secundò hinc sequeretur, maximos Philosophos, felicissimos fore S. Scripturæ Interpretes, contra 1. Corinth. I. 18, 19, 20, 26, 27, 28. II. 6, 7. Actor. XVII. 18. &c. Quo argumento Socinianos premit Venerandus & Doctissimus D. P. De Witte, Ecclesiæ Leidensis insignis Pa-stor. Antehac etiam vidimus, quantopere ab isto consequente abhorrent Theologi pii atque orthodoxi.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, it would follow from this that the greatest philosophers would be the most felicitous interpreters of Holy Scripture, contrary to 1. Corinth. I. 18, 19, 20, 26, 27, 28. II. 6, 7. Actor. XVII. 18, etc. With this argument the venerable and most learned Dr. P. De Witte, the distinguished pastor of the Church of Leiden, presses the Socinians. We have also seen before how greatly pious and orthodox theologians shrink from that consequence.

units.la: 3. Revocabitur tandem Theologia Philosophi-ca, ac Scholastica, quamquam non ad Aristotelis, sed ad Cartesii amussim efformata. Scimus, quanto cum labore, turpem & adulterinam istam, Philosophiæ cum Theologia, commixtionem, impedire, prohibere, ac corrigere studuerint viri summi, Ecclesiarum Reformatores. Nunc vero postliminio, sed alia methodo, idem flagitium impune committetur. Si enim rationi, seu Philosophiæ, omnia examinanda, ad amussim suam exigenda, denique Scripturam, quotiescunque claræ rationi adversari videatur, omnino juxta rationis seu Philosophiæ dictamen & arbitrium explican-dam censeas, nullo modo evitari poterit, quin postliminio Scholasticorum tricæ ultro revocandæ erunt, idque ab iis, qui omnem Philosophiam ac Theologiam Scholasticorum spernunt ac re-jiciunt, eamque vel ipsos tyrones ridere omnem atque odisse cane pejus & angue docent, urgent-que; quo sic suas cariores reddant merces, easque felicius majorique pretio divendant. Scholastico-rum primi aliquot, & præcipui, certè non ita omni laude indigni videntur, neque tanto cum fastu, nisi ab ignorantibus, rejiciuntur, alii vero, inde, quod maxime laborant, suaque scripta magis noxia quam utilia evaserunt, vitium contraxerunt, quod veritatem supernaturalem omnem, rationi suæ, ac ingenio Philosophico, excutiendam dederint; hinc tortuosæ istæ, spinosæ, quodlibeticæ, infinito numero, omni fruge fructuque vacuæ, quæstiones propullularunt, & adhuc propullulant uberrim. Ast idem brevi videbimus necessario, si obtineat, quod vult Wolzogius, omnia, nihilo excepto, cujuscunque generis sint, rationis ad examen exigen-da, Scripturamque omnino juxta istam rationem explicandam esse. Neque, si id jam ageretur, deesset, nova, novarum quaestionum, ex Philosophia in Theologiam turpissima μεταβάσεις[?] quotidie transfilientium seges notanda ac refutanda. Doctrinam de gratia ac Praedestinatione, NOVA Methodo propositam, seu potius Pelagianismum, non tam incrustatum, quam palam expositum & aliquantulum interpolatum vidit hoc seculum, perperit, alia methodo, adultera Philosophia. Jam mundi actualem infinitatem non repugnare, homines in Luna, aliisque stellis non esse, non constare audies. Infinitatem Dei negatam, saltem labefactatam videbis. Immensitas nunc actus voluntatis erit in Deo, qui nullam aliam ob rationem immensus aut omnipraesens dicetur, quam quia cuncta gubernat ac sustentat. At aliud nunc ago, sufficient ista specimina, pauca quidem, sed ponderosa satis. Sic ab una parte qui expulsus hostis est, ab alia ultro admittetur.
units.tr: 3. Scholastic and philosophical theology will at last be recalled, though shaped not by the rule of Aristotle but by that of Descartes. We know with how much labour the greatest Reformers of the Churches strove to prevent, forbid and correct that shameful and adulterine mixture of philosophy with theology. Now, however, by a back door, though by another method, the same disgrace will be committed with impunity. For if everything is to be examined by reason or philosophy and brought to its rule, and if Scripture, whenever it seems to conflict with clear reason, must altogether be explained according to the dictate and judgment of reason or philosophy, it cannot in any way be avoided that the trifles of the Scholastics will be recalled by the back door. This will be done by those who scorn and reject all Scholastic philosophy and theology, and who teach and urge that even novices should laugh at and hate it more than a dog or a snake, so that they may make their wares dearer and sell them more profitably at a higher price. Some of the earliest and principal Scholastics do not seem so wholly unworthy of praise, nor are they rejected with such disdain, except by the ignorant. Others, however, because they laboured excessively and their writings turned out more harmful than useful, contracted a fault: they gave over all supernatural truth to be sifted by their own reason and philosophical wit. Hence those twisted, thorny, quodlibetical questions sprouted in infinite number, empty of all fruit and profit, and they still sprout abundantly. But we shall soon see the same thing happen necessarily if what Wolzogius wants prevails: that all things, of whatever kind, without exception, are to be brought to the examination of reason, and Scripture is to be explained altogether according to that reason. Nor, if this were already being done, would there be any lack of a new crop of new questions, shamefully leaping daily from philosophy into theology, to be noted and refuted. This century has seen the doctrine of grace and predestination, set forth by a NEW method, or rather Pelagianism, not so much encrusted as openly exposed and somewhat interpolated, brought forth by another method, by adulterated philosophy. Now you will hear that the actual infinity of the world is not repugnant, and that men are not in the Moon or other stars, which is not established. You will see the infinity of God denied, or at least weakened. Now the immensity of God will be an act of the will, and he will be called immense or omnipresent for no other reason than that he governs and sustains all things. But I am now doing something else; these specimens, few but weighty enough, will suffice. Thus the enemy expelled on one side is readmitted of his own accord from the other.

units.la: 4. Porro, si ad Philosophiae lancem, ac ratio-nis, expendenda cuncta erunt, variam habebimus aut eandem, certam aut incertam Scripturae explicationem, ac Theologiam, prout varia vel eadem, certa vel incerta Philosophia erit. Quod certe, nihil aliud est, quam lubricam vagamque fidem fingere, imo, quam fidem destruere & tollere funditus. Priori libro, fundamenta Cartesianae Philosophiae inepta vidimus, quibus veritatis certa cognitio inaedificari possit. Quam dum sectatur Wolzogius, imo in Theologiae sacrarium intrudit, denique Scripturam interpretaturo normam ac ducem praefigit, certitudine & infirmitate quanta ipsius Theologemata nitantur, conjectu haud difficile reliquit lectori. Nolim fidem a rationis ac Philosophiae dictamine pendentem facere, malim cum Apostolo ἀιχμαλωτίζειν πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τῆς χριστῷ[?] & verbi divini.
units.tr: 4. Furthermore, if everything is to be weighed in the scales of philosophy and reason, we shall have an explanation of Scripture and of theology that is varied or the same, certain or uncertain, according as the philosophy is varied or the same, certain or uncertain. This is certainly nothing other than to feign a slippery and wandering faith, indeed to destroy and utterly remove faith. In the earlier book we saw that the foundations of Cartesian philosophy are unfit for building on them any certain knowledge of truth. While Wolzogius follows that philosophy, indeed intrudes it into the sanctuary of theology, and finally prescribes it as the norm and guide for the one who is to interpret Scripture, it is not difficult for the reader to conjecture how great the certainty and how great the weakness on which his theological propositions rest. I would not wish to make faith depend on the dictate of reason and philosophy; I would rather, with the Apostle, bring every thought captive to the obedience of Christ [ἀιχμαλωτίζειν πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ] and of the divine Word.

units.la: 5. Miseranda foret gregis Christi conditio, ma-xima quippe ejus pars, Philosophiae cognitione, non multum imbuta, penetralia verbi perscruta-ri minimè posset; quod tamen ipsâ experientiâ a-liter sæpissimè accidere videmus, solitum enim divinæ gratiæ est, plurimos scientiæ atque experien-tiæ spiritualis thesauros, infantibus retegere, & à sapientibus ac intelligentibus occultare. Non enim inter vocatos multi sunt sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles. Verum quæ stulta sunt mundo, elegit Deus ut pudefaciat sapientes. Imo qui Christi oves ad virilem in Christo statum, ut non semper, quoad scientiam, maneant infantes, perducere conaretur pastor, Philosophiam rationisque dictamina, docere, imo inculcare deberet, quo sic, ad exigenda, ad examinanda Scripturæ, juxta rationem, loca, aptæ evaderent piæ mentes. Doctrinæ paucissima fundamenta, exili satis numero sufficere Wolzogio visa, quamvis cognoscerent, non tamen, juxta Petri monitum, crescere daretur in notitia Domini nostri & Servatoris Iesu Christi. Neque sermo Christi copiosè in ipsis habitare cum omni sapientia posset, ut docen-do atque admonendo se mutuo sufficerent, Philoso-phiæ nisi & rationis abdita perreptent prius. O negligentiam Pauli, Petri, imo omnium simul A-postolorum incomparabilem! quod unico illi, scrutamini Scripturas, ita fuerint intenti, ut Philoso-phiæ omnis obliti, Scripturam unice commendaverint, eamque ad salutem sapientes reddere posse tam sedulo inculcaverint.
units.tr: 5. The condition of Christ's flock would be pitiable indeed. Its greatest part, not much imbued with knowledge of philosophy, could scarcely search the innermost things of the Word. Yet experience itself very often shows the contrary, for it is the custom of divine grace to reveal the treasures of spiritual knowledge and experience to infants, and to hide them from the wise and intelligent. For not many wise according to the flesh are called, not many mighty, not many noble. But God has chosen the foolish things of the world to shame the wise. Indeed, if a pastor were trying to lead Christ's sheep to the manly state in Christ, so that they do not always remain infants as regards knowledge, he ought to teach, indeed to inculcate, philosophy and the dictates of reason, so that pious minds would thus become fit to examine the passages of Scripture by reason. Wolzogius thought that very few and rather small fundamentals of doctrine were enough, although, according to Peter's exhortation, one ought to grow in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Nor could the word of Christ dwell richly among them with all wisdom, so that by teaching and admonishing one another they might suffice, unless they first crept into the hidden things of philosophy and reason. O incomparable negligence of Paul, Peter, and indeed all the Apostles together! That they were so intent on the single injunction, search the Scriptures, that, forgetting all philosophy, they commended Scripture alone, and so earnestly insisted that it could make men wise unto salvation.

units.la: 6. Imo tota Christi Ecclesia infelix hactenus profecto nimis fuisse dicenda foret; Philosophiæ quippe seu rationis ope, tam necessariâ, ut ejus arbitrium, jurisdictio, ductusque scripturæ interpretaturo præsto esse debeat, hactenus eget. Quod negare non possunt, qui veram Philosophandi rationem, nunc demum, Cartesio exorto sydere, humanæ genti innotuisse, jactitant novelli homines. Quapropter veritatem divinam, ex Scripturæ in-tellectione unice addiscendam, ad nostra usque tempora in puteo latitasse simul docent : ante-quam enim Philosophandi vera,certa, tutaque ratio inventa fuit, fieri non potuit, ut non deesset ejus opera tam necessaria, adminiculum, quo sine, plurima quæ Scripturæ interpretationem spectant, perfici rite non queant. Imo toto cœlo omnes aberrasse non poterit inficiari Wolzogius, nisi inter veteres, Cartesianæ Methodi, ac Philosophiæ Cartesianæ sectatores, vixisse demonstraverit, tanta enim ejus veritas & certitudo est, ut sponte sua omnis veritatis curiosus indagator, per quascunque tandem ambages, fuisset tandem ad Cartesianam Philosophiam revolutus. Ut omnes, quotquot ante hoc seculum Philosophati, &, quod verae Philosophiae ope tantopere indiget, Scripturam interpretati sunt, aut Cartesiani fuerint, aut, tanto adminiculo non instructi, verae & solidae interpretationis, profluentisque, ex ea, Theologiae, semitam omnem, prætervecti. Error certe gravissimus, in eo tamen Socinianis peregrinus, quod horum sententia hodie nulla existat, illorum autem, ante hoc seculum, nulla fuerit, saltem vix esse potuerit vera Christi Ecclesia, in qua veritas, verae interpretationis ope unice eruenda, resonaret.
units.tr: 6. Indeed the whole Church of Christ would have to be called truly unhappy until now, for until now it has lacked the aid of philosophy or reason, which is so necessary that its judgment, jurisdiction and guidance must be at hand for the one who is to interpret Scripture. The new men who boast that, with Descartes arisen as a star, they have at last made known to the human race the true method of philosophizing cannot deny this. Therefore they teach at the same time that divine truth, to be learned solely from understanding Scripture, has lain hidden in a well until our own times. For before the true, certain and safe method of philosophizing was discovered, it could not be that this so necessary help was not lacking, the aid without which many things that concern the interpretation of Scripture cannot be rightly accomplished. Indeed Wolzogius cannot deny that all went astray by a whole heaven, unless he shows that they lived among the ancients as followers of the Cartesian method and philosophy. For so great is its truth and certainty that every curious seeker of truth, of his own accord, by whatever circuitous routes, would at last have been led back to Cartesian philosophy. So all who, before this century, philosophized and, which true philosophy so greatly needs, interpreted Scripture, were either Cartesians or, not being furnished with so great an aid, passed by every path of true and solid interpretation, and of the theology flowing from it. This is certainly a most grave error, yet in this respect foreign to the Socinians: their opinion does not exist today, while that of the others before this century did not exist. At least, the true Church of Christ, in which truth, to be dug out solely by the aid of true interpretation, resounded, could hardly have existed.

units.la: Frustra & incassum laborabit Wolzogius, si, quod veritatis adversariis solenne est (qui argu-mentorum robore ad incitas redacti ad exceptiones refugiunt, palliare studentes aut aliquantulum corrigere, quæ veritati adversa docuerunt prius) exceptionibus, evadendi rimam aperiendam credat.
units.tr: Wolzogius will labour in vain, if he believes that by means of exceptions he can open a crack for escape. This is the habit of the adversaries of truth, who, when pressed by the force of arguments, take refuge in exceptions, trying to disguise or somewhat correct what they had earlier taught contrary to the truth.

units.la: I. Primo enim si forsan dicat, se multa rationis jurisdictioni subducere, ut I. res facti, II. quicquid rationem superat p. 221. III. Res pure Theologicas p. 221. 216. imo IV. quicquid non est veritas p. 192. & breviter, mysteria, quæ supra rationem esse demonstravi, sic loquitur p. 273. ea quæ à mera Dei voluntate pendent, cum ratione nil habent commune: Historia &c. Atque satis longe à Socinianis, ut & à pugna cum Reformatis abesse. Non quidem, sic respondeo,specie ista carent,praesertim cum author tam prolixè de iis egerit, difficultatem tamen non tollunt,imo non minuunt. 1. Etenim rationi quaedam cum eximit, vel rationis respicit instrumentalem usum,vel normalem: si priorem, nihil; si posteriorem, cuncta illi subtrahenda statuunt Orthodoxi. Rationem, ut subjectum recipiens, & instrumenti loco, Theologo, aut Scripturas interpretanti, subserviens, in omnibus admittunt Orthodoxi, ne quidem iis, quae facti sunt, aut Mysteria continent, exceptis. Ut normam vero, nunquam in interpretatione agnoscunt: rationem ut normam audire, secundum quam decisio fiat de mente S. Scriptura, haec est prodigiosissima μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος[?]. atque tam indignum Scriptura, quam in se improbum, quod ratio sibi ausit istud arrogare, ait Hoornbeek. Exceptio autem, cum firmet regulam, in casibus non exceptis, uti loquuntur Juris Consulti, palam facit Wolzogius,se in multis, rationem normam reci-pere & regulam: non enim cogitandum est, eo jam venisse, ut in quibusdam, nequidem instrumentalem concederet rationi usum, quod absurdum est, & alibi ab ipso refutatur, ubi non de instrumentali, sed alio rationis usu,disputari, recte notat,p.67.
units.tr: I. First, if he perhaps says that he withdraws many things from the jurisdiction of reason, namely I. matters of fact, II. whatever surpasses reason (p. 221), III. purely theological matters (p. 221, 216), indeed IV. whatever is not truth (p. 192), and briefly mysteries, which I have shown to be above reason, he speaks thus at p. 273: those things which depend on the mere will of God have nothing in common with reason: History etc. And so he stands far enough from the Socinians, as also from conflict with the Reformed. Not so, I answer; these distinctions do not lack a show of plausibility, especially since the author has treated them at such length. Yet they do not remove the difficulty; indeed they do not even lessen it. 1. For when they withdraw certain things from reason, they have in view either its instrumental use or its normative use. If the former, then nothing is withdrawn; if the latter, the Orthodox hold that all such things must be withdrawn. The Orthodox admit reason in all things as the recipient of the subject-matter and as an instrument serving the theologian or the interpreter of Scripture, not excepting even matters of fact or those that contain mysteries. But as a norm they never acknowledge it in interpretation: to hear reason as a norm, by which a decision is made about the mind of Holy Scripture, this is a most monstrous transition into another genus [μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος], says Hoornbeek; and it is as unworthy of Scripture as it is wrong in itself that reason should presume to arrogate this to itself. But an exception, while it confirms the rule in cases not excepted, as the jurists say, plainly shows that Wolzogius, in many things, admits reason as norm and rule. For we must not think he has come to the point of granting reason not even an instrumental use in certain matters; that would be absurd, and he himself refutes it elsewhere, where he rightly notes (p. 67) that the dispute is not about the instrumental but about another use of reason.

units.la: Neque amplius quicquam hactenus evincit, quam non omnia rationis arbitrio & jurisdictioni cum Socinianis committenda, aut cum Reformatis eximenda, adeoque se neutri parti in universum addictum esse. 2. Quis dicet, quis probabit res quasdam facti esse & supra rationem? ante omnem enim interpretationem, de eorum, quae mediante interpretatione demum innotescunt, natura aut indole, similitudine aut diversitate determinatè statui quicquam non potest. Mysteria si referas, regerent tibi tuam Sociniani regulam, qua Scripturam, rationi quotiescunque adversari videretur, commode explicandam dictavisti, semperque commodam, & mysterio carentem, Scripturae dari posse interpretationem: si instes verba forsan, ac contextum, necessario mysterium inferre, commode aliàs quod explicari nequeant. Respondebit Socinianus com-modum dari posse ex ratione sensum, tuam vero superstitionem in causa esse, quod nolis, aut ignorantiam, quod nequeas commodiorem excogitare, ex Scriptura ipsos refutare non poteris, admissâ enim semel istâ explicandi regulâ, mysteriorum probatio saepissimè deficiet, in omnes enim se formas nexusque, commodioris interpretationis gratia, flectet humana ratio; periculo sane immenso & insuperabili, quicquid etiam ex Scriptura produces in medium, de eo semper eadem methodo, ex ipsa ratione disputandum erit in antecessum. 3. Historias excipiendo, & res facti totam tuam disputationem subvertis; Scriptura enim tota cum sit historica, atque facti instar habenda, ac, ut historica consideranda, juxta pag. 27. 30. universa necesse erit, ut rationi subducatur, quod nos contendimus, negatque Wolzogius. 4. Neque etiam seriò, aut in solidum, ista rationis arbitrio subducis, nisi manifestè tibi contradicas: sic enim p. 67. in fine, ubi omnia nihilo excepto, omnia, cujuscunque generis sint; rationis ad examen revocanda doces.
units.tr: Nor does he hitherto prove anything more than that not all things are to be committed to the judgement and jurisdiction of reason with the Socinians, nor withdrawn from it with the Reformed; and so that he is committed to neither party in general. 2. Who will say, or who will prove, that certain matters are facts and above reason? For before any interpretation, nothing can be determined with certainty about the nature or character, the likeness or the difference, of those things which become known only through interpretation. If you refer to mysteries, your own Socinian rule would answer you, the rule by which you laid down that Scripture, whenever it seemed to conflict with reason, must be conveniently explained, and that a convenient interpretation, free of mystery, can always be given to Scripture. If you press that the words and context perhaps necessarily imply a mystery, the Socinian will reply that a convenient sense can be drawn from reason, and that it is your superstition that is to blame, because you are unwilling, or your ignorance, because you cannot devise a more convenient one. You will not be able to refute them from Scripture. For once this rule of explanation is admitted, the proof of mysteries will very often fail, since human reason will bend itself into every form and connection for the sake of a more convenient interpretation. This is an immense and insurmountable danger: whatever you bring forward from Scripture, it will always have to be disputed beforehand, by the same method, from reason itself. 3. By excepting histories and matters of fact, you subvert your whole argument. For since all Scripture is historical, and must be regarded as a matter of fact, and, as historical, must be considered (according to pp. 27, 30), it will be necessary for the whole of it to be subjected to reason. This is what we contend, and what Wolzogius denies. 4. Nor do you withdraw these things from the judgement of reason seriously, or in full, unless you clearly contradict yourself. For thus at p. 67, near the end, you teach that all things, with nothing excepted, all things of whatever kind they are, must be brought to the examination of reason.

units.la: Porro p. 69. etiam circa ea quae vel longissime rationi subducenda videntur; quae nullam habent in re necessitatem, sed vel à Dei pendent mera voluntate, vel factum continent eorum, qui possent alio atque alio modo agere, saltem hoc rationi concedis, ut etiam atque etiam caveat NB. & cavere potest, ne quid putet tanquam verum narrari, quod aperto mendacio, repugnet rationi. Non igitur plenariè excipis aut subducis rationi, ea, quae vel maximè subduxisse vis videri. 5. Imo mysteria quam plurima, quamvis subduxisse videri velis, non tantum non subduxisse, sed ultra rationi tradidisse te, sic probo: 1. Concedis in omnibus rationi arbitrium, falsos sensus removendi, p.158.161. 2. Sic alibi disseris, in quantum veritates continet Scriptura, non habes quo labe-factes authoris Paradoxi eam sententiam, quae totius sui opusculi fundamentum non spernendum conti-net, quà statuit, à clarâ distinctaque perceptione omnem derivandam veritatem esse. Scriptura autem mysteria tradens, saepissime veritates continet, sic veritas est & aeterna & immutabilis, Deus est triunus, Christus debuit esse θεάνθρωπος [?] &c. in hisce igitur non habes quo labefactes Paradoxi sententiam: dices autem illas veritates supernaturales esse ac proinde p. 193. exceptas, quin p. 152, omnes Scripturae veritates ad rationis tribunal revocari posse pernegas: hinc p. 216. haec verba, id quaeritur an Theologicae veritatis judex sedere Philosophia possit, illud autem negant nobiscum omnes Theologi: sed statim regeret Paradoxus, te fassum esse, si meras veritates contineret, absque addita, naturalium à supernaturalibus, distinctione, nihil esse quo labefactari queat, sententia Paradoxi, illa saltem parte, qua reliquum omne quod statuit stabilitur, ac proinde, circa veritates omnes, rationis admittendum arbitrium: deinde te dixisse p. 67. omnia nihilo excepto rationis ad examen pertinere, sicque istam limitationem praeposteram esse & reliquis contradicentem: praeterquam quod hactenus nescias, an aliquid sit factum, an veritas, si veritas, an naturalis an supernaturalis: neque etiam id scire possis, nisi post peractam Scripturae interpretationem, quae autem si peragi possit ac debeat, antequam rationis arbitrium usu venire queat, rationi hinc normalem usum nullum, in Scripturae explicatione, competere, contra te concludo, quod erat concludendum. At dubium omne tollit, & dicis gratia quaedam excipi, non serio, egregie probant verba quae exstant pag.70. Quia prae caeteris scriptis omnibus ea est singularis Scriptorum Divinorum constitutio, ut meram contineant veritatem, NB. de qua judicare quoque potest ratio, & ita NB. definire saepe an aliquis sensus conveniat verbis nec ne conveniat. Viden' talem schesin cuncta induunt, qua rationis subire judicium juxta te queant, quorsum igitur istae evasoriae imo contradictoriae exceptiones ac limitationes? Tandem Theologicæ veritatis judex sedere ratio non potest, ais, juxta p.216. at, cum, ante interpretationem peractam, nescis an Theologicam contineat, hic locus, an aliam communem veritatem, unde hoc decidetur, ut sciam an hic admittendum sit, an non admittendum rationis judicium? Sequitur igitur necessario interpretationem Scripturæ, omne rationis normale judicium antecedere; ex Scripturæ enim interpretatione, quid ad rationem exigendum, quid non, demum innotescet, at Scripturæ, injurium foret, non fidere, nisi veritas, inde elicita, postliminio ad rationis trutinam exigatur, adeo ut antecedaneum rationis de rebus arbitrium, impossibile sit, & subsequens, Deo injurium. Taceo jam, quod omnis veritatis cujuscunque tandem naturæ, in se considerata, esse queat, ratio, hic sit Theologica; consideratur enim hic, non in se, sed à Deo dictata, hoc est Theologica. Theologicæ autem veritatis ratio judex sedere non potest pag. 216. Ergo nullius veritatis Scripturariæ judex sedere ratio potest. Quod erat demonstrandum. Atque hic author demum enucleatè tandem, de interprete scripsit, ac perspicuè.
units.tr: Further, at p. 69, even concerning those things which seem to be withdrawn from reason most of all, which have no necessity in the matter, but depend on the mere will of God, or contain the fact of those who could act in one way or another, you at least concede to reason this, that it take care, and take care again and again, NB. and can take care, that it does not think something is related as true which, by plain falsehood, contradicts reason. Therefore you do not wholly except or withdraw from reason those things which you most of all wish to appear withdrawn. 5. Indeed, many mysteries, although you wish them to appear withdrawn, you not only have not withdrawn, but have even handed over to reason beyond what is right. I prove it thus: 1. You concede to reason in all things the right to remove false senses (pp. 158, 161). 2. Elsewhere you argue that in so far as Scripture contains truths, you have no means of overthrowing the author's paradox, the view which contains the non-negligible foundation of his whole little work, by which he lays down that all truth must be derived from clear and distinct perception. But Scripture, when it hands down mysteries, very often contains truths: such as that truth is both eternal and immutable, that God is triune, that Christ had to be God-man [θεάνθρωπος], and so on. In these, therefore, you have no means of overthrowing the paradox's view. You will say, however, that those truths are supernatural and therefore excepted (p. 193); yet at p. 152 you deny that all the truths of Scripture can be called back to the tribunal of reason. Hence at p. 216 you write these words: the question is whether philosophy can sit as judge of theological truth, and all theologians deny this with us. But the paradox would immediately reply that you have confessed that, if Scripture contained mere truths, without the added distinction between natural and supernatural truths, there would be nothing by which the paradox's view could be overthrown, at least in that part on which everything else he lays down is founded; and therefore, concerning all truths, reason must be admitted to judge. Then you have said at p. 67 that all things, with nothing excepted, belong to the examination of reason; and so this limitation is preposterous and contradicts the rest. Besides, up to now you do not know whether something is a fact or a truth; if a truth, whether natural or supernatural; nor can you know this unless after the interpretation of Scripture has been completed. But if that interpretation can and must be completed before reason can come into use, then I conclude against you, as was to be concluded, that reason has no normative use in the explanation of Scripture. Yet you remove every doubt when you say that certain things are excepted by favour; the words which stand at p. 70 clearly prove that this is not serious: because, beyond all other writings, this is the singular constitution of the Divine Scriptures, that they contain pure truth, NB. about which reason can also judge, and so NB. often define whether a sense agrees with the words or not. Do you see what sort of schema they all put on, by which, according to you, they can come under the judgement of reason? Why then these evasive, indeed self-contradictory, exceptions and limitations? Finally, you say, according to p. 216, that reason cannot sit as judge of theological truth. But since, before the interpretation is completed, you do not know whether this passage contains a theological truth or some other common truth, by what means will it be decided for me whether reason's judgement is to be admitted here or not? It follows necessarily that the interpretation of Scripture must precede all normal judgement of reason. For it is from the interpretation of Scripture that it will at last become known what must be demanded of reason and what not. Yet it would be wrong to Scripture not to trust it, unless the truth drawn from it were afterwards brought back to the scales of reason. So the prior judgement of reason about things is impossible, and the subsequent one is an injury to God. I pass over now the point that whatever the nature of a truth may be, considered in itself, reason is here theological, for it is not considered here in itself but as dictated by God, that is, it is theological. But reason cannot sit as judge of theological truth (p. 216). Therefore reason cannot sit as judge of any truth of Scripture. Which was to be demonstrated. And here at last this author has written clearly and plainly about the interpreter.

units.la: 2. Dicet autem fortassis, quicquid sit, rationem intelligo illuminatam, at Resp. 1. Rationem contradistingui Spiritui & ut tertium, à Spiritu, ac loquendi usu, diversum quid, eam consideras, ut istam illuminatam rationem ego sic concipere non possim.
units.tr: 2. Perhaps he will say, whatever the case, that I mean reason as illuminated. But I reply, first: you set reason over against the Spirit and treat it as a third thing, distinct from the Spirit and from the usage of speech. You consider it in such a way that I cannot conceive of reason in that illuminated sense.

units.la: 2. Ratio illa, quam dicis, vel judicat juxta rationis dictamina, vel juxta ea quæ, supervenientis ope luminis, innotuerunt: si posterius, illa innotuerunt, vel immediato instinctu, (non quatenus immediatum dicitur, quod in ipsam mentem vi quadam penetrat hyperphysica, sed quod excludit & removet omne medium morale, neque ad aliud quid exigendum est) vel eò, qui, medio morali adhibito, menti superveniat; si illo, jam enthusiasmos doces, si hoc, jam ex Scriptura ipsa judicium recipis quod nos volumus: Verum si juxta rationis, quæ ex insitis principiis profluunt, axiomata judices, ratio illa, licet illuminata sit in se & subjectivè, non nisi ex naturali principio tamen judicare censenda est, quapropter illuminatio ista, aut non illuminatio, hic nihil ad rem ipsam facit, de qua disputamus. 3. Idem plane Sociniani excipiunt, neque tamen satisfacere eo censentur. Etiam Smalcius, ait Hoornbeeckius, in Præfat. c. Frantzium, non vult rationi judicium de sacris concedi, nisi illustratæ. Plura ex Brenio, Schlightingio, Crellio, aliisque videre poterit lector in præcedentibus. 4. Rogo quid intelligas per illuminatam rationem, an illam, quæ lumine infuso gaudeat? at sic in Scripturæ intellectione nos illuminari negasti antea. An illam, cui veritas objectivè clare præposita est? at sic ludis, ait Hoornbeeckius, & illuminationem Sp. Sancti quam videris ponere, non credis; aliud enim est, objectiva illa credendorum propositio, atque oblatio; aliud, subjectiva.
units.tr: 2. That reason, as you call it, either judges according to the dictates of reason or according to what has become known through the help of a supervening light. If the latter, then those things became known either by an immediate instinct (I do not mean "immediate" in the sense of something that penetrates the mind by some hyperphysical force, but in the sense of something that excludes and removes every moral means and needs no other thing to be brought to it), or through a moral means applied to the mind from outside. If the former, you are teaching enthusiasms. If the latter, you are already accepting from Scripture itself the judgment that we want. But if you judge by the axioms of reason, which flow from innate principles, then that reason, although it is illuminated in itself and subjectively, must be considered to judge only from a natural principle. Therefore that illumination, or the absence of it, has nothing to do with the matter itself that we are disputing. 3. The Socinians themselves take exactly this position, and yet they are not thought to satisfy the point. Even Smalcius, says Hoornbeeck, in his preface against Frantz, does not want judgment about sacred things to be granted to reason unless it is illuminated. The reader can see more from Brenius, Schlichting, Crell and others in the earlier parts. 4. I ask what you mean by illuminated reason. Is it the reason that rejoices in an infused light? But you denied earlier that we are illuminated in understanding Scripture. Is it reason to which truth is clearly set forth objectively? But this is play-acting, says Hoornbeeck, and you do not believe in the illumination of the Holy Spirit, which you seem to posit. For the objective proposal and offering of the things to be believed is one thing; the subjective is another.

units.la: 3. Tertio, sigillatim ad locum, quem ex pag. 23. citavi, saniorem in sensum interpretandum, excipiet forte noster, se quidem dicere, Scripturam rationi quotiescunque repugnare videtur, commode, in alium sensum, & quidem omnino juxta illam rationem explicandam esse: sed rationem se intelligere, quæ fidei analogiæ innixa sit, adeoque pro Philosophia non multum facere aut rationis authoritate. Respondeo 1. Idem dici de ratione absolutè, sine omne limitatione P. 20.
