A ratione, inquit, quæ petitur regula, ejusmodi est, ut, quod rationi manifesta contradictione repugnat, nil prorsus censeri debeat docere Scriptura; quare hic locus p. 23. istam limitationem quamvis admitteret, non tamen alius est authoris sensus, quam ille quem superius refutavimus. 2. rogo, an non eandem regulam sibi præfigat, etiam antequam ista fidei eruta analogia est, & in ea eruenda idem valeat, Scripturam commode explicandam, quando &c. 3. rationi contrarium &c. sic loqueris, per rationem autem hic p. 23, intelligis axioma procul omni dubio aliquod, de hoc autem quæro, an sit ex insitis principiis elicitum, an vero ex ipsa profluens Scriptura, si posterius, jam palpabilissimam committis verborum abusionem, non enim id rationi, sed Scripturæ, aut fidei analogiæ repugnare dici debet; si prius, (ut probabile reddit, quod dixeras antea, te regulam ex ipsa ratione efflorescentem proponere, deinde quod rationem Scripturæ soleas contradistinguere & fidei) jam deprehensus in errore es, quem frustra, vel mil-lenis exceptionibus, amoliri conaberis.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, our author will perhaps object to the passage I cited from page 23, which must be interpreted in a more sound sense. He says that he does indeed maintain that Scripture, whenever it seems to contradict reason, is to be explained conveniently in another sense, and indeed altogether according to that reason; but he says he understands the reason that rests on the analogy of faith, and so has little to do with philosophy or the authority of reason. I reply, first: the same thing is said absolutely of reason, without any limitation, on page 20. The rule that is sought from reason, he says, is such that nothing whatever should be thought to be taught by Scripture that is manifestly contradictory to reason. So even if this passage on page 23 admitted that limitation, the author's meaning is not different from the one I refuted above. 2. I ask whether he does not set himself the same rule even before this analogy of faith has been drawn out, and whether the same applies in drawing it out: that Scripture is to be explained conveniently when, etc. 3. You speak like this: contrary to reason, etc. By reason here, on page 23, you undoubtedly mean some axiom. But I ask whether it is drawn from innate principles, or whether it flows from Scripture itself. If the latter, you are already committing a most obvious abuse of words, for it should not be said to be contrary to reason but to Scripture or to the analogy of faith. If the former (as what you said before makes probable, namely that you propose as a rule something springing from reason itself, and then that you are accustomed to set reason over against Scripture and faith), then you are already caught in an error, which you will try in vain to remove even by a thousand exceptions.

units.la: 4. Quartò, maxima cum plausibilitate nobis ob- jiciet, & dicta, & praxin Reformatorum, in negotio Sacramentario, de quo sic scribit p. 209. Nam quæ de formula institutionis Eucharisticæ profert, de Paradoxo loquitur, illa putant Orthodoxi pæne omnes aliquod pati judicium rationis. In iis aliquod arbitrium rationis est. Respondeo 1. Vel putas, dum rationis judicium dicis, usum hic rationis admitti instrumentalem vel normalem: si illum, jam non erat dicendum pæne omnes, sed, omni absque limitatione, omnes, non putant, sed statuunt Orthodoxi; neque id hujus negotio Eucharistico sigillatim, aut præ aliis convenit, quod in omnibus, & circa omnia, ultrò concedunt, imo requirunt Orthodoxi. Deinde, vel intelligis judicium rationis, interpretationem præcedens, vel eam consequens; seu tale, quod se habeat, ut norma interpretandi, vel ut argumentum, ex superabundanti, factam interpretationem confirmans; si prius jam nullus, si posterius, jam absque omni limitatione dicere debuisses omnis statuit Orthodoxus. 2. Hæc saltem non est veritas naturalis, præter quam, nihil non rationi subducendum statuit pag. 216. ubi exertè Philosophia Theologicæ veritatis judex sedere non posse statuitur, & pag. 193, ubi veritates, easque naturales, unicè Philosophiæ rationisque docet admittere arbitrium, non alias, hæc autem, si veritas sit, saltem naturalis non est, adeoque vel ex judicio Wolzogii, hæc materia rationis antecedens & normale non patitur judicium. 3. Imo non est[?] veritas, sed res quædam, à libera Dei voluntate pendens, tales autem, Wolzogius, expressis verbis rationis arbitrium non ferre scripsit antea. 4. Fatetur leges interpretandi, ad usum linguæ exactas, ia[?] totum, quod de Eucharisticæ institutionis formula objicitur, definire. Usum vero loquendi rationi contradistinguit, quapropter necessario hic nulla habenda rationis ratio est, cum totum verborum usus expediat, vel ipso Wolzogio teste. 5. Toto cœlo aberrat in recensenda Reformatorum sententia, nihil minus illi, quam arbitrium rationis, aut judicium antecedaneum, hic admittunt, interpretaturo, ut juxta eam interpretationem dirigat, præfigendum. Quin & in ipsa illa materia, præter usum instrumentalem, rationi à Reformatis nihil tribui, fusè probat alicubi Coccejus, quid cogit, inquit, ut plus quam instrumentum sit ratio? quod multum abest ab arbitrio, à judicio antecedaneo, & normali. Nos non exigimus, ait Crocius, mysterium NB. ad rationis sensum; sed figmentum humanum tum Scripturæ auctoritate, tum argumentis à natura petitis, Scripturæ duce expugnamus. Non indulgere debemus rationi in re fidei, nec ejus decempeda metiri, sed captivum ducere omnem intellectum ad obediendum Christo 1.Cor. x. 5. Hunnius rectè monet, mysterium regni cœlestis accommodare nos non debere humanæ Philosophiæ regulis, aut ex captu nostro metiri. Sed NB vehementer fallit, falliturque, dum id facere Sacramentarios clamat, sic homo maledicus orthodoxos nominat. Ubi enim illi metiuntur captu suo mysteria? Hinc igitur cum argumentamur, non à ratione, sed à mysterio argumentum, ducimus. Post argumenta à natura veri corporis petita, cur non æque valeant adversus commentum ubiquitatis, quam adversus phantasma Marcionis? Viden' decisio ex rebus fidei, superaddita interea ex ratione desumta probatione. Multum ista à Wolzogiano arbitrio differunt, concessoque, in interpretatione Scripturæ, antecedaneo ac normali judicio. Hinc Zanchius, hac in re, Pontificiis & Lutheranis fidei analogiam & Scripturæ collationem neglectam exprobat; nulla rationis facta mentione, idque eo in loco, quo vel maxime ejus meminisse debuerat. Quin Hoornbeekius, ut Socinianismi insigne specimen,ex Theophilo Nicol. profert locum, quo rationis judicium antecedens admittit in explicatione institutionis Eucharisticæ.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, he will object to us, with great plausibility, both the sayings and the practice of the Reformed in the sacramentarian matter, about which he writes on page 209: For what they bring forward about the form of the Eucharistic institution, he says, speaks of a paradox. Almost all the Orthodox think that this suffers some judgment of reason. In these there is some decision of reason. I reply, first: either by saying "judgment of reason" you mean that the use of reason is admitted here as instrumental or as a norm. If the former, then you should not have said almost all, but, without any limitation, all the Orthodox do not think but establish. And this does not especially apply to this Eucharistic matter, or more than to others, for the Orthodox readily concede and indeed require it in all things and in every case. Next, do you mean a judgment of reason that goes before interpretation or one that follows it, that is, one that serves as a norm of interpreting, or as an argument, added over and above, confirming the interpretation made? If the former, then there is none at all; if the latter, then you should have said without any limitation that all the Orthodox establish it. 2. This, at least, is not natural truth, apart from which he establishes that nothing should be withdrawn from reason, on page 216, where it is expressly stated that philosophy cannot sit as judge of theological truth, and on page 193, where he teaches that only the truths that are natural, and only those of philosophy and reason, admit the decision of reason and no others. But this matter, if it is a truth, is not at least a natural truth. So, according to Wolzogen's own judgment, this matter does not admit the antecedent and normative judgment of reason. 3. Indeed it is not a truth but a certain thing dependent on the free will of God; and Wolzogen wrote earlier, in express words, that such things do not bear the decision of reason. 4. He admits that the rules of interpretation, exact with respect to the usage of the language, define everything that is objected concerning the formula of the Eucharistic institution. But he distinguishes usage of speech from reason. Therefore reason has necessarily no account to be taken of it here, since the whole usage of words settles the matter, even by Wolzogen's own witness. 5. He is entirely wrong in describing the view of the Reformed. They admit nothing less than a decision of reason or a preliminary judgment, to be set before the interpreter so that he may direct the interpretation by it. Indeed, Cocceius argues at length somewhere, in that very matter, that the Reformed attribute nothing to reason beyond an instrumental use: what compels, he says, that reason should be more than an instrument? This is far from a decision, from a preliminary and normative judgment. Croce says: we do not demand a mystery (NB) to be measured by the sense of reason; but we overthrow a human invention, both by the authority of Scripture and by arguments drawn from nature, with Scripture as our guide. We ought not to indulge reason in matters of faith, nor measure them with its rod, but to lead every understanding captive to obey Christ (1 Cor. 10:5). Hunnius rightly warns that we ought not to accommodate the mystery of the heavenly kingdom to the rules of human philosophy, nor measure it by our own capacity. But he is greatly mistaken, and he errs, when he cries that the Sacramentarians do this; so the slanderous man names the orthodox. For where do they measure mysteries by their own capacity? Hence when we argue, we draw the argument not from reason but from the mystery. After the arguments drawn from the nature of a true body, why should they not be equally valid against the fiction of ubiquity as against the phantasm of Marcion? Do you see the decision made from the matters of faith, with a proof drawn from reason added besides? These things differ greatly from Wolzogen's judgment, which concedes a preliminary and normative judgment in the interpretation of Scripture. Hence Zanchius, in this matter, reproaches the Papists and Lutherans for neglecting the analogy of faith and the comparison of Scripture; he makes no mention of reason, and that in the very place where he most ought to have remembered it. Indeed Hoornbeeck, as a notable specimen of Socinianism, quotes from Theophilus Nicolai a passage in which he admits a preceding judgment of reason in the explanation of the Eucharistic institution.

units.la: Ego igitur sic statuo, nunquam Scripturæ dicta ad rationis normam exigenda, eo quo dictum est sensu, verum è contra, humanam sapientiam omnem ad Sacræ Scripturæ regulam & præscriptum exigendam esse atque examinandam; ut recte docet Confessio Gallicana Artic. V. Regula autem illius esse non potest, ad quam, tanquam regulam, exigi ipsa debet. Neque jurisdictionem aut imperium (quibus terminis id quod rationi adscribit exprimit P. 69.) exercere, in eam, cui subjicienda est.
units.tr: Therefore I hold as follows: the sayings of Scripture are never to be brought to the standard of reason in the sense described, but on the contrary, all human wisdom is to be brought to, and examined by, the rule and prescription of Holy Scripture, as the Gallican Confession rightly teaches in Article V. Yet reason cannot be the rule to which Scripture itself must be brought as to a rule. Nor can it exercise jurisdiction or dominion (the terms by which the author expresses what he ascribes to reason, p. 69) over that to which it must be made subject.

units.la: Videri nunc possem officio meo functus, & præstitisse quod promisseram. Wolzogii quippe dissensum à Reformatis palam feci, & detectum refutavi. Reformatorum sententiam probavi & vindicavi. Verum Epilogi loco brevem sensus Wolzogiani ideam lectori conspiciendam dare consultum duxi, quo sic, collectis iis, quæ hinc inde dispersa apparent, unico obtutu, quid de ejus sententia statuendum sit, lectori pateat. Postquam transfigere cum Philosophia, seu ratione, sibi proposuerat, omnem illi, & in omnia, quæ Scripturæ interpretationem spectant, jurisdictionem & imperium derogare absurdum judicanti, limites ponere atque terminos, hujus jurisdictionis, necesse fuit. Præter instrumentalem usum, ad quem unice & libentissime in Scripturarum interpretatione rationem admittunt nostri, alium normalem agnoverat Wolzogen, quo dux sit, non solum ministra, ratio, quo imperium, jurisdictio, decisio sæpe illi conveniat, ut Scriptura, ex ejus dictamine, subinde interpretanda veniat, & omnino secundum illam. Res au-tem erant non exiguo numero, quas ferre istud im-perium vix posse sero deprehendebat, hinc, maxi-ma cum sedulitate, eas dispescuit, divisit, & ra-tioni suas partes injunxit, quas ultra non progre-deretur. Voluit autem dividere quod Deus con-junxerat, & partim rationi dare quod in univer-sum arbitrio Dei, in verbo suo, verbum luculen-tissime explicanti, relinquendum fuit. Videbimus igitur quid rationis arbitrio concedat & jurisdictio-ni, quidque ei subducat, cui ut instrumento nihil, ut normae, aut juxta effata sua, pro jurisdictione ju-dicanti, ducenti, arbitranti judici, omnia subtra-henda erant & subducenda. Sic autem partitus est operas ut admissae rationis jurisdictioni limites fi-geret.
units.tr: I might now seem to have discharged my duty and done what I promised. I have openly exposed Wolzogen's dissent from the Reformed, refuted it where I found it, and defended and established the Reformed view. But by way of an epilogue I thought it useful to set before the reader a brief outline of Wolzogen's position, so that, once the points scattered here and there are gathered together, the reader can see at a single glance what ought to be concluded about his view. Having resolved to reconcile philosophy, or reason, with theology, and judging it absurd to deny reason any jurisdiction and authority over everything that concerns the interpretation of Scripture, he was bound to set limits and boundaries to this jurisdiction. Besides the instrumental use to which our people admit reason in interpreting Scripture, and to which alone they admit it most willingly, Wolzogen recognised another, normative use, by which reason is not only a servant but a guide, and by which it often takes on the role of authority, jurisdiction, decision, so that Scripture is from time to time to be interpreted by its dictate and wholly in accordance with it. But there were a considerable number of matters which he later perceived could hardly bear such authority, so with the greatest care he sorted and divided them, and assigned to reason its own parts, beyond which it was not to advance. He wished, however, to divide what God had joined together, and partly to give to reason what in general ought to be left to the judgment of God in his Word, which explains the Word most clearly. We shall therefore see what he concedes to the judgment of reason and its jurisdiction, and what he withdraws from it. From reason, as from an instrument, nothing was to be withdrawn, but as from a norm, or by its own pronouncements, when it judges, leads, arbitrates as a judge, everything was to be withdrawn and taken away from it. Thus he arranged his work so as to fix limits to the admitted jurisdiction of reason.

units.la: 1. Eximit rationis imperio haec sequentia, brevi-ter ea solummodo enarrabimus ut faciliori via to-tum negotium percipiatur.
units.tr: 1. He removes the following matters from the authority of reason. I shall give only a brief account of them, so that the whole business may be grasped by an easier route.

units.la: 1. Quicquid non est veritas, axioma quoddam in-telligit, sic p. 143. & 144. Infinita sunt in Scriptura quae ad quaestionem facti sunt referenda, quorum cum nulla sint proprie dictae veritates, nec erit ulla secun-dum nostrum Exercitatorem Interpretatio: quae nulla veritate comprehenduntur, in istis a ratione sua desti-tuitur. Quae si enumerata velis, huc Omnia quae a mera Dei voluntate pendent, & non fundata in ejus natura sunt, sic p. 144. Quae sunt arbitrii divini, ibidem. Historiae. Prophetiae. Praecepta positiva. Caeremo-niae. Opus creationis. Promissa. Quam bene aut male haec non veritates dici debeant, nunc non dis-puto, ostendo quid rationis jurisdictioni eximat, ac imperio.
units.tr: 1. He understands whatever is not a truth to be a kind of axiom; so on pages 143 and 144: In Scripture there are infinite things which must be referred to questions of fact; since these have no truths properly so called, there will be, according to our Examiner, no interpretation of them; whatever is comprehended by no truth is deprived of its reason in these matters. If you wish these to be listed, here are: all things which depend on the mere will of God and are not grounded in his nature, so on page 144: things which belong to the divine will, ibid. History; prophecies; positive precepts; ceremonies; the work of creation; promises. I am not now disputing how well or badly these ought to be called non-truths; I am showing what he withdraws from the jurisdiction and authority of reason.

units.la: 2. Imo & aliquas veritates, omnes veritates Scrip-turae ad rationis tribunal revocari posse, id vero perne-gamus. Excipit autem veritates, quae sint Theolo-gicae, id quaeritur, inquit, an Theologicae veritatis judex sedere Philosophia seu ratio possit? illud autem negant nobiscum omnes Theologi. Confer 221. Sic satis tuto rationem admitti, ad judicium proferen-dum, putat, ista modo excipiantur. Non advertens, semper disputari posse, nunquam vero definiri, nisi jam facta interpretatione, quid veritas sit, quidque veritas Theologica. Sic in tricas sese & infinitum rixandi gurgitem immittit, imprudentissimus causæ publicæ defensor. Tu dices factum esse, alter veritatem; tu veritatem Theologicam, ille Philosophicam, finis autem hujus litis nullus erit, donec peracta fuerit interpretatio, qua mediante demum, cujus naturæ res hoc aut illo loco tradatur, sciri potest: at sciri hoc in antecessum debet, ut, an rationis in interpretatione hujus loci arbitrium admittendum sit, nec ne, certus evadam, verum sciri in antecessum non potest, en tricas, en nodos inextricabiles!
units.tr: 2. Indeed, he also withdraws some truths: we deny that all the truths of Scripture can be recalled to the tribunal of reason. He excepts, however, those truths which are theological: the question is, he says, whether philosophy or reason can sit as judge of theological truth? But all theologians deny this with us. Compare page 221. Thus he thinks reason may be admitted quite safely to pronounce judgment, provided only these matters are excepted. He does not notice that one can always dispute, but never settle anything, unless the interpretation has already been made, namely what truth is and what theological truth is. So this most imprudent defender of a public cause plunges himself into trifles and into an endless whirlpool of wrangling. You will say that it is a fact, the other that it is a truth; you that it is theological truth, he that it is philosophical truth; and there will be no end to this quarrel until the interpretation has been completed, through which alone one can know what kind of thing is being related in this or that place. But one must know this beforehand, so that I may be certain whether reason's judgment should be admitted in interpreting this passage or not; yet it cannot be known beforehand. See the trifles, see the inextricable knots!

units.la: 2. Videndum nunc, quid rationi subjiciat, ejusque jurisdictionis, judicii, ductus, arbitriique obnoxium faciat, & quousque. Miram hic offendet lector, & intricatissimam, imo sibi adversam sæpe perplexitatem. Jam largitur, jam negat, confusa rerum verborumque serie sua complexus.
units.tr: 2. We must now see what he subjects to reason, and to what extent, and so makes it liable to its jurisdiction, judgment, guidance and arbitration. Here the reader will meet with a remarkable and most intricate perplexity, often even contrary to itself. Now he grants, now he denies, embracing everything in a confused sequence of things and words.

units.la: 1. Concedit rationi seu Philosophiæ, ut omnia ad amussim suam exigat & expendat, antequam hoc aut illud Scripturæ inesse, pro certo afferatur. Sic pag. 67. Dux est sæpe ratio: primo ut omnia, nihil enim prorsus excipio, ut omnia, cujuscunque generis sint, revocet ad examen, idque ante factam Scripturæ interpretationem, & ut ea felicius succedat, quem in finem, omnino juxta istam rationem, explicanda Scriptura est, quando nimirum, hæc illi contradicere videtur, videatque, sic sonant sequentia, an quicquam eorum quæ putamus inesse Scripturis sit manifestæ rationi contrarium. Cujusmodi si quid deprehendatur, affirmate licet pronunciare, Scripturarum hanc mentem non esse, quin commode erit explicanda Scriptura, & omnino secundum istam rationem. Idem revera quod volunt Sociniani, neque enim quicquam ultra poscent, ut antehac vidimus, idem quod, ut sententiæ Paradoxæ summam, præcipuè carpendum judicavit p. 151. 152. 162. At sic actum de plerisque Christianæ fidei mysteriis erit, quæ, cum magnam partem rationi adversa appareant, non facile putabuntur inesse Scripturis, sed omnem, quo ea rejiciat, evadendi ansam, commodiores explicationes affatim obtrudendo, captabit & excogitabit temeraria ratio. Videatur certum, ut revera est, Deum genuisse ab æterno filium, dari tres personas divinas & unam tantum essentiam, Christum Deum esse & hominem, finitum & infinitum, moriendo vicisse mortem &c. ratio interim huic contradicat quantum possit, utri cedes potius rationi an Scripturæ? rationem claram & manifestam clamet hæreticus, commodam dari, saltem commodiorem, explicationem, & rationi magis congruam; quid regeres, quomodo te expedies Wolzogi? dices mysterium esse, rationi hic judicium non deferendum: at nondum id constare dicet hæreticus, commodam dari explicationem prætendet: parallelos locos si adferas, iterum tibi rationem objiciet, commodamque juxta eam, interpretationem. Et profecto, si ratio, ut norma, prius consulenda veniat, nunquam animos adiges ut credant, quæ rationem nisi captives, credi non possunt. Nam plerique homines indulgemus nostris cogitationibus & quæri-mus concinnas opiniones, ait Johannes à Lasco, Id commune malum est universæ humanæ naturæ. Sed repugnare discamus. Frustra saltem antea rationis limites posuisti, quam nunc in omnibus admittendam censes.
units.tr: 1. He concedes to reason, or philosophy, that it may test and weigh everything by its own standard before it is asserted with certainty that this or that is in Scripture. So on page 67: Reason is often the guide: first that everything, for I except nothing at all, that everything of whatever kind it may be, be referred to examination, and this before the interpretation of Scripture is made; and so that it may succeed more happily, to this end Scripture must be explained wholly according to that reason, namely when it seems to contradict reason; and let it see, as the following words run, whether any of those things which we think are in Scripture is contrary to clear reason. If anything of this kind is detected, one may confidently declare that this is not the mind of Scripture, so that Scripture may be conveniently explained, and wholly according to that reason. This is in truth what the Socinians want, for, as we have seen before, they ask for nothing more; the very thing which he judged should be especially attacked on pages 151, 152 and 162, as the sum of paradoxical opinions. But in this way most of the mysteries of the Christian faith will be undone, for since they appear in large part contrary to reason, they will not readily be thought to be in Scripture; rash reason will seize upon and devise every opportunity of escape by which to reject them, pressing forward more convenient explanations in abundance. Suppose it is certain, as in truth it is, that God begot the Son from eternity, that there are three divine persons and only one essence, that Christ is God and man, finite and infinite, that by dying he overcame death, and so on; meanwhile reason contradicts this as much as it can. Which will you yield to, Wolzogen: reason or Scripture? The heretic will cry out that reason is clear and manifest, that a convenient, or at least a more convenient, explanation, and one more in agreement with reason, is available. What will you reply, how will you extricate yourself? You will say it is a mystery and that judgment should not be surrendered to reason here. But the heretic will say that this is not yet established; he will claim that a convenient explanation is available. If you bring parallel passages, he will again object reason to you, and a convenient interpretation in accordance with it. And indeed, if reason is to be consulted first, as a norm, you will never bring minds to believe what cannot be believed unless reason is taken captive. For most men indulge our own thoughts and seek fine-spun opinions, says John à Lasco. This is a common evil of all human nature. But let us learn to resist it. You have in vain set limits to reason beforehand, which you now judge should be admitted in all things.

units.la: 2. Ad removendos falsos sensus rationem seu Philosophiam semper adhibendam, ejusque determinationi standum omnino esse. Rationem depellere erro-rem & falsum sensum removere statuit Paradoxus, Probè, subdit noster, hæc omnia. De hoc primo mu-nere Interpretis, quod in detegendo errore versatur, ipse satis vidit Exercitator, non magnam sibi litem motum iri. Rursus omne largitur Socinianis quod volunt: sufficit ipsis, modo sensus ad amussim rationis exigere & falsos rejicere ipsis detur. Hoc magis premunt Sociniani, ait Hoornbeekius, prae illo, quod ad eruendum verum sensum necesse est; maxime hoc urgere dicit, ut ad removendum falsum sensum admittatur ratio, in eo autem sibi ultro adstipulan-tem invenient Wolzogium: nec mirum est, quoniam in negativis, hoc est, in removendis iis, quae nos vera esse contendinus, tantum non unicè ver-santur. Nobis adversus Socinianos semper fere pro-bantis incumbunt partes, illis igitur, falsos sen-sus removisse, quicquid nos ex Scriptura probare volumus, satis erit. Hoc autem rationi commit-tendum docet Wolzogius. Sic patet quam serio rationem in multis non admittendam esse statuat, dum in omnibus ei suffragium, uti loquuntur, seu votum deferat negativum.
units.tr: 2. He holds that reason or philosophy should always be employed to remove false senses, and that its determination must be wholly abided by. The Paradoxical author decided that reason repels error and removes a false sense. Rightly, adds our author, all these things. Concerning this first office of the interpreter, which consists in detecting error, the Examiner himself saw well enough that no great dispute would arise for him. Again he concedes to the Socinians everything they want: it is enough for them if the senses are measured by the standard of reason and false ones are granted to be rejected. The Socinians press this more, says Hoornbeeck, than that which is necessary for drawing out the true sense; they especially urge this, that reason be admitted to remove a false sense; and in this they will find Wolzogen as a ready supporter. Nor is this surprising, since they are concerned almost exclusively with negatives, that is, with removing those things which we maintain to be true. Against the Socinians we are almost always the ones who bear the burden of proving; it will therefore be enough for them to have removed false senses from whatever we wish to prove from Scripture. Wolzogen teaches that this must be entrusted to reason. Thus it is plain how seriously he states that reason is not to be admitted in many matters, while in all matters he grants it a negative vote, as they say.

units.la: 3. Videtur omnes veritates rationis judicio sub-inde subjicere, hinc p. 192. exerte asserit, si meram veritatem contineret Scriptura, se non multum ad-versario reluctaturum.
units.tr: 3. He seems at times to subject all truths to the judgment of reason. Hence on p. 192 he plainly asserts that if Scripture contained only pure truth, he would not greatly resist his opponent.

units.la: 4. Imo palam, totum quod in Scriptura est, expressis verbis, rationis subjicit arbitrio, etenim p. 70. meram veritatem Scripturam continere docet, de qua, sic pergit, judicare quoque potest ratio. Tota igitur Scriptura rationi ejusque arbitrio subjacet, ut definire saepe ratio possit an aliquis sensus verbis conveniat nec ne conveniat. Atque sic tandem placi-dissime vivent, qui pugnare videbantur, & idem revera sentiunt, quantumvis in speciem differant, Wolzogius & Paradoxus. Nacta tandem defenso-rem est, de quo gloriari liceat, Ecclesia Reformata. Ego coronidis loco hoc aussim dicere. 1. Wolzo-gium longa & perplexa, de tribus istis, ad interpre-tationem Scripturae pertinentibus, Spiritu, ratione, ac verborum usu, dissertatione, ne semel quidem quaestionis scopum, aut Reformatorum sententiam attigisse, multo minus explicasse, prout debuerat, ac defendisse. 2. Multis referta erroribus esse, ea quae scripsit de singulis. Posterius passim priori, prius posterioribus libris probatum dedimus. Sententia Reformatorum est, non rationis dictamina seu Philosophiam, non hominum placita aut decisiones, non usum loquendi, aut Spiritum Sanctum, sed Scripturam suæ interpretationis unicam normam esse & amussim. Non tamen aut usum loquendi, aut rationem, aut Spiritum, in interpretando, spernunt, sed admittunt, sed requirunt; at longe à Wolzogio diverso sensu, non normæ instar aut regulæ, quæ unice quærenda Paradoxo erat, Wolzogio, & mihi, in hac disceptatione, sed usum verborum, ut à parte objecti, in ipsa Scriptura, ut sic loquar, præsuppositum, idque tam necessario, ut Scriptura Scriptura esse nequeat, nisi ex usu loquendi scripta comperiatur, quo mediante ultra verbalem tamen interpretationem seu versionem vix pertingat lector, hic autem realem quærimus: Spiritum Sanctum quod attinet, cum ad aptitudinem, aut potius aptificationem subjecti, sit venia verbo, requirunt Reformati, quando autem norma quæritur interpretandi, non nisi ab Enthusiastis, aut ignorantibus, ille obtrudi poterit, uti ratio, ultra instrumentalem usum, non admittitur, nisi à Socinianis. Usus præsupponitur, Spiritus subjectum format, & aptum reddit, dum ratio instrumenti vices obit, Scripturà interim ipså manente suæ interpretationis norma, & Spiritu sancto, in ea loquente, controversiarum judice supremo, & infallibili, sic intelligibiliter sententiam pronunciante, ut à quibusvis, in id incumbentibus, pro modulo perceptivitatis, naturaliter à naturalibus, spiritualiter à spiritualibus percipi queat, atque intelligi.
units.tr: 4. Indeed, he openly subjects everything that is in Scripture, in so many words, to the decision of reason. For on p. 70 he teaches that Scripture contains pure truth, of which, he goes on, reason can also judge. Therefore all of Scripture is subject to reason and its judgment, so that reason can often determine whether a given sense fits the words or does not fit them. And so at last those who seemed to be at odds live very peaceably together, and in fact think the same thing, however much they differ in appearance: Wolzogius and Paradoxus. The Reformed Church has at last found a defender of whom it may boast. By way of a crown, I venture to say this. (1) Wolzogius, in his long and perplexed dissertation on the three things that pertain to the interpretation of Scripture (the Spirit, reason, and the use of words), has not once touched on the aim of the question or the opinion of the Reformed, much less explained it as he ought and defended it. (2) What he wrote about each of these points is full of many errors. We have shown in many places that the latter is proved by the former, and the former by the latter, in my earlier books. The opinion of the Reformed is that Scripture alone, not the dictates of reason or philosophy, not human opinions or decisions, not the usage of speech, nor the Holy Spirit, is the sole norm and rule of its own interpretation. Yet they do not scorn, in interpreting, the usage of speech, reason, or the Spirit; they admit them and require them, but in a sense far different from Wolzogius's. In this dispute, Wolzogius and I are not seeking a norm or rule, which is what Paradoxus was seeking. Rather, the usage of words is presupposed, as it were on the side of the object, in Scripture itself, and so necessarily that Scripture cannot be Scripture unless it is found to be written according to the usage of speech. By means of that usage, however, the reader scarcely reaches beyond a verbal interpretation or version, whereas we seek the real meaning. As for the Holy Spirit, the Reformed require him for the fitness, or rather the making fit, of the subject (if I may use the word). But when a norm of interpretation is sought, he can be imposed only by Enthusiasts or the ignorant. Reason, beyond an instrumental use, is admitted only by the Socinians. The usage (of language) is presupposed; the Spirit forms the subject and makes it apt, while reason takes the place of an instrument. Meanwhile Scripture itself remains the norm of its own interpretation, and the Holy Spirit, speaking in it, is the supreme and infallible judge of controversies. Thus he pronounces the sense so intelligibly that it can be naturally perceived and understood by the natural, and spiritually by the spiritual, by whomever applies himself to it, according to the measure of his capacity to perceive.

units.la: Errata aliquot Typogr. graviora sic corrigat Lector, eaque ut & plura alia Authoris à prælo absentiæ imputet.
units.tr: Some of the more serious typographical errors the reader should correct as follows, and he should attribute these, along with several other faults, to the author's absence from the press.
